venues.name: 100 Sails Restaurant & Bar
venues.description: 100 Sails is the main restaurant of the Prince Waikīkī hotel, looking out over the Ala Wai small-boat harbour at the western edge of Waikīkī. Its stated position is that mocktails belong on the same level as the cocktails, and the kitchen backs that with method rather than assertion: the zero-proof drinks are built on house-made syrups and local ingredients, running to ginger lemongrass, hibiscus and ube. Ube — the purple yam that anchors a great deal of Filipino cooking in Hawaiʻi — is an unusual thing to put in a drink and gives it colour and a mild nutty sweetness. Mocktails are included in the daily happy hour rather than excluded from it.
signatureDrinks: Ginger lemongrass (local ginger simmered and infused for two days, house-made lemongrass syrup, fresh lemon juice, club soda)
Hibiscus (house-made hibiscus syrup, lemon, local yuzu)
Ube (Hamakua Coast ube, lime, ginger beer)
venues.longDescription:
100 Sails Restaurant & Bar occupies the ground floor of the Prince Waikīkī at 100 Holomoana Street, on the harbour side of Waikīkī where the district meets the Ala Wai boat basin. It is best known locally as a buffet room, with breakfast, lunch and dinner services and a Sunday brunch, and the view over the masts is the reason most people book it. The trading pattern is unusually wide — breakfast from 6.30am, lunch through the middle of the day, dinner to 9pm or 9.30pm — which makes it one of the few venues in this guide usable at almost any hour.

The non-alcoholic program is built on the same principle as the food: make the components rather than buy them. The mocktails use house-made syrups and local ingredients, and the three flavours the bar leads with — ginger lemongrass, hibiscus, and ube — are chosen for what they can do without a spirit. Ginger and lemongrass bring heat and aromatic length; hibiscus brings acidity and tannin, which is the closest a non-alcoholic drink gets to the structure of wine; and ube, the purple yam that runs through Filipino cooking across Hawaiʻi, brings body and a mild nutty sweetness plus a colour no other ingredient produces. Using local produce this way is not incidental in a hotel restaurant — it is the difference between a drink that belongs to this place and a generic sweetened juice. The detail that says most about the venue's intent is a small one: mocktails are included in the daily happy hour alongside the cocktails, rather than excluded from it. Happy-hour exclusion is the standard, quiet way a bar signals that the zero-proof list is a courtesy rather than a product, and charging full price for a drink with no spirit in it is the most common complaint non-drinkers have about hotel bars. Including them is the cheapest possible way to signal the opposite, and very few rooms do it.
venues.pressQuote: It is a standard for food to be farm-to-table, and we would like to do the same with beverages being farm-to-glass.

venues.name: 16-Bit Bar+Arcade
venues.description: 16-Bit is a 21-and-over retro arcade bar on East New York Street downtown, where the cabinet games are free to play and the money is made at the bar. That model happens to make it one of the easier nights out in Indianapolis for someone who is not drinking, because the reason to be there is the arcade rather than the round. The non-alcoholic list is longer than most bars manage and every drink is named in the same register as the cocktails: Kissed By A Rose is built on Seedlip Garden 108 with hibiscus, lemon, rose and mint, Gym Class Zero runs desert pear with lime and tonic, and Pinky and the Brain, Optimus Prime and Lisa Simpson fill out the simpler end.

venues.longDescription:
16-Bit began in Columbus, Ohio and brought its format to 110 East New York Street in downtown Indianapolis: a wall of free-to-play arcade cabinets and pinball machines, a 21-and-over door policy, and a bar that funds the games. The nostalgia is thorough — the drinks are named for cartoon and video-game characters, the machines are period-correct, and nothing costs a quarter. It is a loud, crowded, very specific kind of night out, and it is worth saying plainly that this format solves a problem non-drinkers have in ordinary bars, which is that the drink is the entire activity. Here it is not.

The zero-proof list is also better than it needs to be. Kissed By A Rose is the serious one: Seedlip Garden 108 — the pea-and-garden-herb expression of the London non-alcoholic distillate — with hibiscus, lemon, rose and mint, which drinks dry and floral rather than sweet. Gym Class Zero, the one INDYtoday singles out, is desert pear with lime and tonic. Below those sit a run of deliberately simple, deliberately nostalgic drinks: Pinky and the Brain is fruit punch and lemonade, Optimus Prime is lemonade with cranberry and Sprite, and Lisa Simpson is the house Shirley Temple. Visit Indy lists the bar in its Buzz-Free Drinks guide on that basis.

Hours are the other reason it earns a place here. 16-Bit runs to 2:30am on Friday and Saturday and opens at noon at weekends, which makes it one of very few places downtown where someone not drinking can stay out as late as everyone else and still have something to do. It sits two blocks from Monument Circle and a short walk from Cannon Ball Lounge at Hotel Indy, so the two combine into a straightforward downtown evening without alcohol.
venues.pressQuote: 16-Bit offers a menu with two zero-proof mocktails and two low-proof cocktails — the Gym Class Zero, made with desert pear, lime juice, and tonic, is particularly popular.

venues.name: 1833 Craft
venues.description: Closed for renovations since summer 2026; the bar says it will reopen in the fall, so check before you go. Salt Lake City's dedicated non-alcoholic speakeasy, opened in December 2024 inside a restored century-old Sugar House home known as The Eclipse House and run by sibling team Matthew and Kelly LaPlante. The entire menu is zero-proof — "0% Alcohol, 100% Heart" — built by co-owner and lead bartender Matthew, a former Salt Lake Tribune reporter who quit drinking but never left bar culture, with his sister Kelly, a designer, styling the room as a forest-green, 1920s-inspired lounge. The duo have developed 50-plus craft NA cocktails on premium spirits like Lyre's, Dhōs, Trejo's and Kentucky 74, finished with herbs from their own basement hydroponic garden. The name nods to 1833, the year of the Latter-day Saint "Word of Wisdom," and because nothing on the menu contains alcohol, no ID is required — a genuine cocktail experience for people in recovery, designated drivers, never-drinkers, and the sober-curious.
venues.address: 1398 S 1100 E, Salt Lake City, UT 84105
venues.hours: Temporarily closed for summer renovations; the bar says it reopens in the fall (checked 5 October 2026). Normal hours Thu-Fri 5pm-10pm; other times by special request
signatureDrinks: Libre Libre (herbal cola, dark cane, lime, hydroponic mint)
The Bartender's Affections (give three words, get a custom drink)
venues.longDescription:
Matthew LaPlante started 1833 Craft out of frustration with the alcohol-free options he encountered elsewhere. The bar's philosophy, as his sister Kelly puts it, is to not make non-alcoholic spirits behave like alcoholic ones, but to enjoy and appreciate them for what they are.

The crowd, the owners say, is a mix of people who have never drunk alcohol, those taking a break, those who don't want a weeknight hangover, and those in recovery. The signature "Bartender's Affections" pour invites guests to share three words and receive a custom drink built on the spot, and the seasonal menu rotates regularly. Hours are intentionally limited — Thursday and Friday, 5 to 10 p.m. — with other times by special request.
venues.pressQuote: We'd go out and the non-alcoholic cocktails on the menu, the mocktails on the menu, were just terrible. They just were not very exciting. They always left me disappointed.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Matthew LaPlante, co-owner and lead bartender

venues.name: 1923 Prohibition Bar
venues.description: 1923 Prohibition Bar is a hidden, 1920s-style speakeasy tucked inside The Shoppes at Mandalay Place at Mandalay Bay on the Las Vegas Strip, reached through a concealed door and known for its bourbon-and-burlesque atmosphere with live music, piano players, and weekend entertainment. While the menu is whisky- and cocktail-forward, the bar keeps a dedicated "Zero Proof" section for non-drinkers, anchored by Lyre's non-alcoholic spirits. The signature zero-proof builds are the Zer-Old Fashioned (made with Lyre's American Malt), Summer on the Wagon (Lyre's Pink Gin), and the Kats Meow. For non-alcoholic beer drinkers, the bar pours Lagunitas IPNA NA on draft. The speakeasy is open daily and offers a genuine cocktail-lounge experience without requiring guests to drink alcohol. A second 1923 location operates at The Venetian's Grand Canal Shoppes, but the Mandalay Bay original is the flagship.

venues.longDescription:
1923 Prohibition Bar is a hidden speakeasy inside The Shoppes at Mandalay Place, Suite 200B, on the indoor walkway that connects Mandalay Bay to the Luxor, next door to the Minus5 Ice Bar. The entrance is a bookcase, and finding it is the whole point, though no password is required once you have. Inside is a Roaring Twenties room — dim, plush lounge seating, low light, closer in feel to a New Orleans speakeasy than a Strip cocktail lounge. Live entertainment runs Friday and Saturday from around 9:30pm to midnight with no cover, billed as N.O.L.A. Nights and mixing musical performances with burlesque, and a separate magic show plays Friday through Sunday in a hidden chamber off the main room with a limited ticket count. A second 1923 has since opened at the Venetian's Grand Canal Shoppes, but the Mandalay Bay room is the original and remains the flagship.

The list is whisky- and bourbon-forward, which is what a Prohibition-themed bar is supposed to be, and the useful thing for a non-drinker is that it does not stop there. The bar keeps a dedicated Zero Proof section anchored on Lyre's non-alcoholic spirits, with three named builds: the Zer-Old Fashioned made with Lyre's American Malt, Summer on the Wagon made with Lyre's Pink Gin, and the Kats Meow. For anyone who would rather have a beer, Lagunitas IPNA non-alcoholic IPA pours on draft rather than arriving in a bottle from the back. The practical result is that a guest who does not drink can sit through a burlesque set in a dark speakeasy with a proper Old Fashioned glass in hand, which is a specific and surprisingly rare thing to be able to do on the Las Vegas Strip. The bar opens daily at 11am, running to midnight Sunday through Thursday and to 2am on Friday and Saturday.

venues.name: 1Watson
venues.description: 1Watson is the rooftop bar at the AC Hotel San Antonio Riverwalk on Soledad Street, and its named non-alcoholic drinks are the Pina Breezy and the Spicy Pal No Ma — the latter a zero-proof play on a Paloma, which is the right instinct in Texas, where grapefruit and salt are already the local drinking grammar. It runs late for a hotel rooftop, to midnight midweek and 1am at weekends, and adds a third downtown rooftop option for anyone not drinking, in a district where visitors substantially outnumber locals. Weekend brunch service from 10:30am extends the window further, and it is a few blocks from both other rooftops in this guide.

venues.longDescription:
1Watson is the rooftop at the AC Hotel San Antonio Riverwalk on Soledad Street, a few blocks from the river in the heart of the downtown hotel district. Visit San Antonio names two of its non-alcoholic drinks: the Pina Breezy and the Spicy Pal No Ma.

The second one is worth unpacking, because the joke in the name conceals a good decision. A Paloma is grapefruit, lime, salt and soda with tequila — and of the classic tequila drinks it is by far the most forgiving to build without alcohol, because its character lives in the grapefruit and the salt rather than in the spirit. Add chilli heat, as the "spicy" suggests, and you have a drink with bite, acidity and a savoury edge, which is precisely the combination that stops a zero-proof drink reading as a soft one. In Texas, where the Paloma is closer to a default than a cocktail, it is also the most culturally natural thing a non-drinker could be handed.

The hours are better than most hotel rooftops manage: 4pm to midnight through the week, to 1am on Friday and Saturday, with weekend brunch service from 10:30am. That gives it a longer useful window than High Praise, which is closed midweek entirely.

What San Antonio has downtown, taken together, is unusual: three rooftop bars — this, High Praise and The Moon's Daughters — all with named alcohol-free drinks, all within walking distance. For a visitor who is not drinking, that is a materially different experience from having to hope the one rooftop in town can improvise something.
venues.pressQuote: 1Watson: Pina Breezy and Spicy Pal No Ma.

venues.name: 20 Stories
venues.description: 20 Stories is a glamorous rooftop restaurant and cocktail bar nineteen floors above No.1 Spinningfields, wrapping an elegant dining room, a statement illuminated bar and an expansive terrace planted with silver birch trees around a firepit, with 360-degree views over the Manchester skyline. It is the flagship of The Evolv Collection — sister to 14 Stories in London and 24 Stories in Birmingham — was named Best Restaurant in Manchester at the British Restaurant Awards, and its menus are led by executive head chef Daniel Scott on regional Northwest produce. The non-alcoholic side is genuine: a varied alcohol-free spirits list built on brands like Caleño and Everleaf, plus a dedicated zero-proof section of the cocktail menu using the same house syrups, with a Mediterranean and tropical bent. It is a rare high-end Manchester rooftop where a non-drinker gets a proper printed list rather than a token mocktail.
venues.address: No.1 Spinningfields, 1 Hardman Square, Spinningfields, Manchester M3 3EB
venues.longDescription:
20 Stories sits 19 floors above Spinningfields, wrapping an elegant restaurant, a statement illuminated bar and an expansive rooftop terrace with silver birch trees, a firepit and 360-degree views over the Manchester skyline. It is the flagship venue of The Evolv Collection (sister to 14 Stories in London and 24 Stories in Birmingham) and was named Best Restaurant in Manchester at the British Restaurant Awards, with menus led by Executive Head Chef Daniel Scott that lean on regional Northwest produce.

The non-alcoholic program is a real one, not an afterthought. The bar carries a varied alcohol-free spirits list featuring UK zero-proof makers such as Caleño and Everleaf, and a matching section of the cocktail menu builds those spirits into house-syrup drinks with a Mediterranean and tropical bent, so a non-drinker gets the same considered cocktail treatment as anyone else. As Manchester's Finest puts it, this gives guests “more than enough reason to linger longer on that sun-trap of a roof terrace.”

Alongside the AF cocktails sits a substantial drinks program of over 600 wines and a contemporary cocktail list, with resident DJs on the terrace through the weekend. The combination of a marquee rooftop setting, an award-winning kitchen and a genuinely stocked zero-proof list makes it a strong pick for a special-occasion alcohol-free night out in the city centre.
venues.pressQuote: 20 Stories has a varied alcohol-free spirits list, featuring brands like Caleño and Everleaf, and a vibrant mixed drink menu to match, with a handful of tempting Mediterranean-inspired concoctions.
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: Manchester's Finest, The Best Places in Manchester for Alcohol-Free Drinking

venues.name: 2nd Shift Brewing
venues.description: 2nd Shift Brewing became the first brewery on The Hill, St. Louis' storied Italian neighborhood, when founders Steve and Libby Crider moved their 2009-vintage operation from New Haven, Missouri into an 18,000-square-foot warehouse in December 2016. Alongside the craft beer, the taproom pours Busy Bees N/A, a house line of non-alcoholic drinks crafted and packaged at the brewery: hop water, root beer, grape soda made with real cane sugar, and tangerine or unflavored sparkling water. With Central State Sandwiches in-house, dogs welcome inside and on the patio, and kids allowed with adult supervision, it's a laid-back neighborhood hangout where, as the brewery puts it, there's 'an option for everyone.'
venues.longDescription:
2nd Shift Brewing started as literally that: after Steve Crider got a homebrew kit for Christmas, brewing became the 'second shift' he worked around his day job as a welder. He and his wife Libby — a trained sommelier who manages the taproom and business side — founded the brewery in 2009 in New Haven, Missouri, then hunted for years for a St. Louis home before landing an 18,000-square-foot warehouse on The Hill. When the tasting room opened in December 2016, St. Louis Magazine noted it had 'the distinction of being the storied neighborhood's first brewery' — the first in the city's famous Italian enclave.

For non-drinkers, the draw is Busy Bees N/A, a house line of alcohol-free drinks crafted and packaged at the brewery — 'we believe in having an option for everyone,' as 2nd Shift puts it. The current lineup runs from hop water and root beer to a grape soda made with real cane sugar, plus tangerine-flavored and unflavored sparkling waters, available at the taproom and through the brewery's online store. Owner and head brewmaster Steve Crider highlighted the line in Feast Magazine's 2025 look at St. Louis' changing drinking scene: 'We have our own line of NA products named Busy Bees.' There's no non-alcoholic beer here — Busy Bees is sodas, hop water and sparkling water — but everything is genuinely house-made rather than bought in, a rarity even among NA-friendly breweries.

The taproom at 1601 Sublette Avenue is an easygoing neighborhood spot: Central State Sandwiches runs the in-house kitchen, dogs are welcome inside and on the patio, and kids are fine with adult supervision. The brewery's annual Cask Festival — its 10th edition is set for November 7, 2026 — draws guest breweries from as far away as Chicago's Revolution Brewing, a measure of the respect 2nd Shift commands among fellow brewers. Hours are limited to Wednesday through Sunday, with the week's longest pours on Friday and Saturday, so check before you go; groups of 15 or more are asked to give 24 hours' notice.
venues.pressQuote: We have our own line of NA products named Busy Bees.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Steve Crider, owner and founder, quoted in Feast Magazine

venues.name: 330 Main
venues.description: 330 Main is a non-alcoholic bar and coffee house on East Main Street in Chattanooga's Southside, owned and run by a husband-and-wife team, and it introduced the city to kava cocktails. The drinks list is built on kava extract in place of alcohol — cocktails and shots rather than the ceremonial shell-and-bowl service most kava bars offer — alongside yaupon tea carbonated and poured on draft, plus rotating house creations. The female owner's Filipino heritage shapes the food and drink; her partner came up through craft coffee, craft beer, cannabis and hospitality across the Southeast, and created Kavanooga, a kava tincture developed locally. Guests may bring in food from neighbouring businesses.
venues.longDescription:
Kava bars usually look one of two ways: a ceremonial room where the root is served traditionally from a bowl, or a wellness café where it sits on a menu next to matcha. 330 Main is neither. It is built as a bar — cocktails and shots, made with kava extract where the spirit would be — on East Main Street in Chattanooga's Southside, and it is fully non-alcoholic.

The couple who own it bring two different specialisms to the room. Her Filipino heritage runs through the food and beverage programme. He came up through craft coffee, craft beer, cannabis and hospitality across the Southeast, and is the creator of Kavanooga, a kava tincture developed locally — so the extract the bar builds on is a house product rather than a bought ingredient. That is the same vertical-integration signal that separates a serious alcohol-free programme from a token one anywhere else in this directory.

Alongside the kava drinks the bar pours yaupon on draft. Yaupon holly is the only caffeinated plant native to North America, and serving it carbonated on tap is a genuinely regional choice for a Southern bar — the sort of thing a good cocktail room does with an obscure amaro, applied to a category that usually settles for cola.

It also functions as a coffee house, which is what makes the hours work: doors at 9am seven days a week when open, running to 6pm midweek and 11pm on Friday and Saturday. That Friday and Saturday late service is the important part, because it is the window in which a non-drinker most often has nowhere to go.

One characteristic detail: guests are welcome to bring in food and drinks from other local businesses, which is a deliberately un-bar-like policy and tells you what the room is for.

A plain note, as always: kava is mildly psychoactive. This is a night out without alcohol rather than a substance-free room. Closed Monday and Tuesday.

Worth knowing for planning: 330 Main sits on the Southside within a few minutes' walk of Oddstory's taproom, with its five-category alcohol-free fridge, and of The Boneyard on Station Street, which stays open to 2am at weekends. That cluster is the reason this neighbourhood rather than downtown is where a non-drinker should start an evening in Chattanooga — it is the only part of the metro where you can move between three rooms across a night instead of settling into one and hoping.

venues.name: 36 Below
venues.description: A hidden underground speakeasy beneath Sip Coffee & Beer Garage in the Arcadia Lite neighborhood of Phoenix, 36 Below pairs a transportive, candlelit room with a dedicated 'Zero Proof' section of non-alcoholic glasses built with the same care as the cocktails. The menu rotates around immersive themes; on the current Midnight in Paris list every zero-proof drink is a $14 alcohol-free twin of a signature cocktail — Kiwi's Nest, Château de Chambord, Epernay, Monet's Garden, and Palais Garnier — built on N/A spirits, house cordials and foams. Earlier spirit-free builds such as the Artemis, Earth, and Foam on the Rim retired with the previous theme. DiningOut Phoenix listed it among the metro bars worth visiting specifically for a mocktail in May 2026. Entry is via the coffee shop above; reservations are advisable at weekends.

venues.longDescription:
You reach 36 Below through Sip Coffee & Beer Garage on Indian School Road — a daytime coffee shop and beer garden with a staircase at the back leading down to a candlelit room that shares neither its hours nor its mood. The speakeasy conceit is well worn in American bars by now, but the execution here is unusually complete: low light, close seating, a menu of drinks presented as compositions, and small plates built to be eaten in the dark. It sits a few doors from the Century Grand complex, making this short stretch of Arcadia Lite the densest concentration of serious cocktail work in Phoenix.

The non-alcoholic drinks get a named section rather than a footnote, and they are constructed rather than mixed. The menu rotates through immersive themes, and on the current Midnight in Paris list each of the five zero-proof drinks — all $14 — is an alcohol-free twin of one of the signature cocktails. The Kiwi's Nest Zero Proof works an NA kiwi cordial against taro-coconut milk and lime; the Château de Chambord swaps in an N/A spirit with tropical green tea, raspberry, lime, lemon perfume and rose water; the Epernay builds N/A gin with vanilla cordial, blueberry, lemon, N/A cardamom bitters and lemon-lime soda; Monet's Garden runs cantaloupe, honey, lemon and Free Brothers orange under a Jamaican lemon soda; and the Palais Garnier finishes basil, sage, honey and apple cordial with salt, cinnamon and a caramelized carrot foam. Earlier zero-proof compositions — the dessert-like Artemis, the oolong-and-peach Earth, Two of Cups, Enlightened, and Foam on the Rim — retired with the previous theme (a drink called Foam on the Rim survives on the current list only as a full-proof tequila cocktail). Mocktails also count toward the bar's multi-course Cocktail Experience packages, and the presentation remains the point as much as the flavour: these are drinks designed to look like the cocktails, which in a candlelit room where everyone is holding something ornate is more than an aesthetic consideration.

DiningOut Phoenix included the bar in its May 2026 guide to the best mocktails in the metro. Practicalities: it opens Tuesday to Sunday, from 4pm on weekdays and 3pm at weekends, closing at 1am on Friday and Saturday and earlier the rest of the week. The room is small, so weekend reservations are advisable, and the entrance through the coffee shop upstairs is easy to walk past entirely. It is a full cocktail bar, and the zero-proof menu is a genuine section of it rather than its identity.
venues.pressQuote: each elaborate beverage offers plenty of flavor

venues.name: 3rd Space Kava
venues.description: 3rd Space Kava on South University Drive is a fully alcohol-free bar open from noon until 2am, and to 3am on Friday and Saturday, built around pool, board games, gaming stations and a dense events calendar — karaoke nights, Guitar Hero tournaments and Magic: The Gathering play on the first and third Wednesday of the month. Dogs are welcome. Traditional kava comes as noble-root shells at three strengths: the lighter White Sand for sipping, the nuttier King's Kava, and the Ceremonial shell, the strongest of the three, plus a house watermelon Kokkaido shell made fresh daily and a concentrated kavalactone shot called The Roman. IMPORTANT: a large part of this menu is kratom, not kava — six kratom cocktails plus kratom shots, sodas and seltzers, all restricted to 21 and over. Kratom acts on opioid receptors and carries dependence risk that kava does not; order deliberately.
signatureDrinks: White Sand Shell (noble kava, lighter for sipping)
King's Kava Shell (robust, nutty, strong finish)
Kokkaido Shell (house watermelon kava, made fresh daily)
The Roman (kavalactone shot, equivalent to 3-4 shells)
venues.longDescription:
3rd Space Kava takes its name from the sociological idea of the third place — the room that is neither home nor work — and it is built accordingly. It runs from noon to 2am seven days a week, stretching to 3am on Friday and Saturday, and fills the space with things to do rather than just things to drink: pool, board games, gaming stations, karaoke nights, Guitar Hero tournaments, and Magic: The Gathering play on the first and third Wednesday of each month with open, tournament-style and draft formats. Happy hour runs buy-one-get-one on kava, and dogs are welcome. In Davie — a Broward County town whose evening options otherwise run to chain restaurants and sports bars — a room like this doing genuine late-night hours with no alcohol at all is a real piece of infrastructure for anyone not drinking.

The kava side is properly done. Traditional shells are poured from noble root at three graded strengths: the White Sand shell, a lighter drink for sipping; the King's Kava shell, robust and nutty with a strong finish; and the Ceremonial shell, the strongest of the three and traditionally the ceremonial preparation. A house Kokkaido shell built on watermelon kava is made fresh daily, and The Roman is a concentrated kavalactone shot the bar rates as equivalent to three or four regular shells. Prices for traditional shells start under $5.

One thing has to be flagged clearly rather than buried, because this directory is read by people in recovery. A substantial share of this menu is kratom, not kava. There is a dedicated kratom cocktail list running six drinks, a kratom drinks section with gold shots, sodas and seltzers, and kratom extract appears in several of the staff-pick builds too. The bar restricts all kratom to 21 and over, which is the responsible line, but the distinction still matters: kava is a South Pacific root with no alcohol and no known physical dependence, while kratom is a Southeast Asian leaf whose alkaloids act on opioid receptors, carries real dependence and withdrawal risk, is banned in several states, and whose concentrated 7-OH derivatives are under active federal scheduling. Plenty of people choose kava precisely because it is not that. Here, you need to read the menu section headers before you order.
venues.pressQuote: 3rd Space is more than just a kava bar – it's your escape into a safe space where our community grows and new connections spark

venues.name: 4 Hands Brewing Co.
venues.description: 4 Hands Brewing Co. has anchored St. Louis' LaSalle Park neighborhood since 2011, and its lineup now includes three house-brewed non-alcoholic beers: NA City Wide Hoppy Pale, NA Full Life Lager and NA Incarnation, a Mosaic-hopped IPA — all under 0.5% ABV. The tasting room at 1220 S. 8th Street backs them up with a mocktail list built on zero-proof spirits, Athletic Brewing Lite and local Excel sodas, plus food from Hi-Pointe Drive-In's kitchen and an upstairs arcade with Skee-Ball. City Wide, the brewery's civic flagship, donates $1 from every case sold to local nonprofit partners — a program that has generated close to half a million dollars.
venues.longDescription:
Kevin Lemp opened 4 Hands Brewing Co. in 2011 in LaSalle Park, the small historic neighborhood wedged between downtown St. Louis and Soulard. Fifteen years on it is one of the city's defining craft breweries, home to the 1220 Spirits distillery and Withered Oak whiskey line, with satellite taprooms in Chesterfield, Kirkwood and Lambert Airport. Its flagship City Wide pale ale doubles as a civic project: Sauce Magazine reported in 2026 that it has grown into the top-selling craft beer in St. Louis and the No. 1 pale ale in Missouri, with $1 from every case sold donated to local nonprofit partners — close to half a million dollars over the past decade.

The non-alcoholic program is unusually deep for a regional brewery. The current beer list includes three house NA beers, all under 0.5% ABV: NA City Wide Hoppy Pale, a showcase of Centennial, Citra and Simcoe hops with citrus, melon and tropical fruit notes and a dry, crisp finish; NA Full Life Lager, cheekily described as a 'beer flavored beer'; and NA Incarnation, a Mosaic-hopped IPA pouring amber with pineapple, passion fruit and candied citrus. At the LaSalle Park tasting room, Incarnation NA and Athletic Brewing Lite share the menu with a dedicated mocktail list — Hibiscus Bliss, Lavender Haze, Pioneer Punch and a Whiskey-less Sour, all mixed with zero-proof spirits — plus Excel sodas, so non-drinkers get real choices rather than a single token can.

4 Hands has become a fixture of St. Louis' sober-curious coverage: Feast Magazine's 2025 feature 'Brewing change' put the brewery at the center of the city's NA shift, with Lemp telling the magazine, 'Experimentation and innovation are important to us … and when we opened the brewery almost 14 years ago, we never thought we'd be producing NA beers or CBD seltzers.' The tasting room itself is a destination — Hi-Pointe Drive-In's kitchen on the main floor, a family-friendly upstairs arcade with Skee-Ball and classic games, and long hours seven days a week, opening at 11am daily. Smaller groups are seated first-come, first-served, while groups of 30 or more can book private space through the brewery's events form.
venues.pressQuote: What began as a single American Pale Ale has expanded into a robust portfolio that now includes City Wide Light Lager, City Wide Stout and a non alcoholic City Wide Hoppy Pale.

venues.name: 4 Noses Brewing Company
venues.description: 4 Noses Brewing Company runs a Denver taproom on Dahlia Street in Northeast Park Hill alongside its original Broomfield brewery, and in 2025 it launched Camp Zero, its first non-alcoholic beer. The brewery describes Camp Zero as "our easy-drinking adventure into alcohol-free beer", crafted with full flavour and made for trail breaks and mellow nights; the second batch is a tangerine guava blonde that Westword characterised as brewed with real fruit, lightly tart and plenty refreshing. Camp Zero is poured at the taproom and stocked by other Denver bars — Briar Common in Jefferson Park keeps it on its guest non-alcoholic can list. The Dahlia Street room opens from noon or early afternoon daily and closes by 9pm, and is family-friendly.
signatureDrinks: Camp Zero non-alcoholic tangerine guava blonde ale

naMenuItems.name: Camp Zero
naMenuItems.description: non alcoholic beer camp zero is our easy-drinking adventure into alcohol-free beer. crafted with full flavor and a spirit for the outdoors this brew is made for trail breaks and mellow nights and everything in between. for our second batch we went with tangerine guava. it is bright and refreshing. it is clean and easy and it's there for any adventure you want to throw at it. it's beer, just without the booze.

venues.longDescription:
4 Noses Brewing Company has been one of Colorado's better-known craft breweries since it opened in Broomfield in 2014, and its Denver taproom at 4040 Dahlia Street puts it inside the city in the Northeast Park Hill neighbourhood, as defined by Denver's own statistical boundaries. The reason it belongs in a non-alcoholic guide is Camp Zero, the brewery's first alcohol-free beer, launched in 2025 — a rare instance of an established Colorado craft brewery committing production capacity to the category rather than simply stocking someone else's cans.

The brewery's own description sets the tone: "Camp Zero is our easy-drinking adventure into alcohol-free beer. Crafted with full flavor and a spirit for the outdoors, this brew is made for trail breaks and mellow nights and everything in between." The second batch moved to a tangerine guava blonde, which 4 Noses characterises as "bright and refreshing... clean and easy", and which Westword's January 2026 round-up of Denver's non-alcoholic options described as "brewed with real fruit, this tangerine-guava blonde ale is lightly tart and plenty refreshing". That fruited-blonde format is a sensible choice for a non-alcoholic beer, since the fruit acidity covers for the body that dealcoholisation removes. Camp Zero is not confined to the brewery's own rooms: Briar Common in Jefferson Park lists 4 Noses Camp Zero Tangerine Guava Blonde on its guest non-alcoholic can shelf alongside Best Day Brewing, which means a drinker can find it around the city rather than only at source. The Dahlia Street taproom itself is a straightforward Colorado brewery room — opening at 2pm on weeknights, 1pm on Fridays and noon at weekends, closing by 9pm most nights and 8pm on Sundays. The non-alcoholic offer here is a single well-made beer rather than a built cocktail programme, which is why it is graded modestly, but it is a genuine one and it is brewed locally.
venues.pressQuote: Camp Zero. Brewed with real fruit, this tangerine-guava blonde ale is lightly tart and plenty refreshing.

venues.name: 8th Day Distillery
venues.description: 8th Day is a small-batch distillery, bottle shop and cocktail bar in the Circle City Industrial Complex on the Near Eastside, run by Matt and Jaime Lamping. They signed the lease in 2015 and began filling bourbon barrels, launched gin and rum into Indianapolis bars and shops, and opened the bottle shop and cocktail bar to the public in 2018. The room is deliberately living-room-ish, with a new local artist's work shown every quarter and regular pop-ups with other Indianapolis businesses. Mocktails sit on the rotating seasonal menu alongside the cocktails as a matter of course — the Overalls. is lemon with a lavender-thyme simple syrup and soda water.
venues.address: 1125 E Brookside Ave Suite D06, Indianapolis, IN 46202
venues.hours: Mon 4pm-9pm; Tue-Wed closed; Thu 4pm-9pm; Fri 4pm-11pm; Sat 2pm-11pm; Sun 3pm-8pm
signatureDrinks: Overalls. (lemon, lavender-thyme simple syrup, soda water)
venues.longDescription:
Matt and Jaime Lamping started 8th Day out of a recurring conversation about living without regrets — the name comes from asking what you would do with an eighth day in the week. Their answer was to make spirits. In 2015 they signed a lease on the Near Eastside, bought equipment and began filling bourbon barrels, then took gin and rum to market the hard way, walking them into Indianapolis bars, restaurants and liquor stores themselves. The public-facing bottle shop and cocktail bar followed in 2018, in Suite D06 of the Circle City Industrial Complex — a converted factory on Brookside Avenue that now holds studios, makers and small manufacturers, and which is one of the more interesting buildings in the city to spend an evening in.

The bar itself is unpretentious and domestic by design: the Lampings describe it as a hip living room, they rotate a new local artist's work into the space every quarter, and they run regular pop-ups in partnership with other Indianapolis businesses. The drinks menu rotates with the season and, unusually for a distillery bar, lists mocktails on it as standard rather than as a substitution — a distillery has every commercial reason to push its own spirits, so printing a zero-proof build is a deliberate choice. The Overalls. is the one local guides point to: lemon against a house lavender-and-thyme simple syrup, lengthened with soda water, which is a herbal, dry drink rather than a sweet one. Because the menu turns over seasonally, the specific non-alcoholic builds change; the practice of having them does not.

Opening hours are limited and worth checking before you set out — Thursday to Monday only, closed Tuesday and Wednesday, with the latest closes at 11pm on Friday and Saturday. Kan-Kan Cinema & Brasserie is about half a mile east in Windsor Park if you want to build an evening on this side of town.
venues.pressQuote: Overalls. — Lemon, Lavender/Thyme Simple, Soda Water.

venues.name: 967 Coffee Co.
venues.description: 967 Coffee Co. is a Yemeni coffeehouse on Alpharetta Highway in Roswell, named for Yemen's international dialling code. It opened during Ramadan in early 2025 and is fully alcohol-free. The trading hours make it one of the latest-running rooms of any kind in north Fulton County: 7am to midnight Sunday through Thursday, and 7am to 2am on Friday and Saturday. The drinks list runs Yemeni preparations and espresso side by side — Iced Adeni Chai and the Iced Yemeni Latte are the house pours, with qishr, Biscoff and pistachio lattes and a set of dragon fruit and strawberry refreshers filling out the board. Desserts sit alongside the coffee, and the seating is arranged for groups staying several hours rather than for takeaway trade.
venues.longDescription:
967 is the country calling code for Yemen, and the name is the whole thesis: the shop exists to serve Yemeni coffee to a suburb that had never had a place selling it. It opened in a suite at 11235 Alpharetta Highway in Roswell in the run-up to Ramadan in early 2025, and 285 South noted the arrival in its March 2025 survey of the Yemeni cafes then appearing across metro Atlanta — a cluster that also included Shibam in Alpharetta, Mokhaport in Tucker and, later, Haraz in Midtown. The Roswell site sits in a strip centre on the main north-south artery, which is unglamorous but well positioned for a room that does most of its business after dark.

The hours are the strongest argument for the place. 967 trades from 7am until midnight Sunday through Thursday and until 2am on Friday and Saturday, and it holds a full house late into the evening without pouring a drop of alcohol. That combination is close to unavailable elsewhere in north Fulton, where the late-night alternatives are bars or nothing. The drinks board keeps Yemeni tradition and modern cafe work in the same frame: Iced Adeni Chai and the Iced Yemeni Latte are the two house signatures, qishr — steeped from coffee cherry husks rather than the bean — represents the older end of the tradition, and pistachio and Biscoff lattes cover the sweeter, contemporary side. Dragon fruit and strawberry refreshers are the non-coffee option. Desserts and pastries are sold from the counter, and the seating plan favours long stays: booths and tables sized for groups rather than a queue of takeaway cups. Nothing on the premises is alcoholic, which puts 967 squarely in the same category as the kava lounges and dedicated alcohol-free bars closer to the city centre, just with a very different drinks list.
venues.pressQuote: In Roswell, Yemeni shop 967 Coffee opened its doors for Ramadan a few short weeks ago.

venues.name: A La Mousse
venues.description: A La Mousse is a Chinatown dessert cafe and tea house that opens at noon and runs to eleven at night, midnight on Friday and Saturday, with no alcohol on the premises at any point. The drinks are the reason to go rather than an afterthought to the cakes: fruit teas including a mango lychee and a passion fruit peach, a pomegranate strawberry lemonade, a lemonade mint tea, and milk-foam teas built on rose and on oolong. The matcha list runs to a cherry blossom matcha latte alongside peach, coconut and almond milk versions. For a city where almost every late option has a liquor licence, a Chinatown room serving properly built tea drinks until midnight is a genuinely useful address.
venues.longDescription:
A La Mousse trades on North 11th Street in Chinatown, and its shape is one Philadelphia has surprisingly few of: a dessert cafe that opens at midday, runs until eleven at night and midnight at weekends, and holds no liquor licence at all. It is the kind of room where a group can sit down at half past nine on a Saturday without anybody's evening being organised around a bar.

The drinks divide into three families. The fruit teas are the house's signature — a mango lychee, a passion fruit peach — brewed as tea and built with real fruit rather than syrup alone, which gives them the tannic backbone that stops a fruit drink from reading as squash. The lemonades run alongside them, a pomegranate strawberry and a lemonade mint tea, both sharp rather than sweet. Then there are the milk-foam teas, a Taiwanese format in which a salted, lightly whipped dairy cap sits on top of cold tea: the rose and the oolong versions are the ones to order, and the technique matters because the salt in the foam cuts the sugar underneath and gives the drink two distinct halves as you go down the glass.

The matcha list is longer than most dedicated coffee shops manage — a cherry blossom matcha latte, plus peach, coconut and almond milk builds — and there is a buttercream Oreo milkshake for anyone who has given up pretending.

The cakes are the other half of the business and are what the name refers to. That is worth saying plainly for a non-drinking audience: the hardest part of an evening without alcohol is often the last hour, when a drinking group orders another round and there is nothing to order alongside them. A dessert menu at eleven at night solves that better than any mocktail does.

On alcohol, the position is evidence-based — the menu carries no alcoholic item and the venue holds no licence — rather than a claim the business makes in those words. Nothing psychoactive beyond tea and coffee is served.

venues.name: Abigail Hall
venues.description: Abigail Hall is a 40-seat cocktail bar on the ground floor of the Woodlark Hotel downtown, set in the 1907 Cornelius Hotel's former Ladies Reception Hall and named for suffragist Abigail Scott Duniway. Its menu carries a standalone "No-Proof Cocktails" section plus further spirit-free drinks built on zero-proof spirits such as Pathfinder, Wilderton Citrus, and Sanbitter.
signatureDrinks: Sanbitter Spritz (Sanbitter n/a aperitif, grapefruit, ginger beer)
Rossellini Soda (pomegranate honey or roasted peach syrup, soda, vanilla cold foam)

naMenuItems.name: Sanbitter Spritz
naMenuItems.description: sanbitter n/a aperitif, grapefruit, ginger beer

venues.longDescription:
Abigail Hall is a 40-seat cocktail bar and gathering place on the ground floor of the Woodlark Hotel in downtown Portland. The room occupies what was originally the Ladies Reception Hall of the former Cornelius Hotel (built circa 1907–1908), and the bar is named after Abigail Scott Duniway, the Oregon women's-rights advocate and suffragist. Its design leans into that history, with a fireplace, a reproduction of the building's early-1910s penny-tile floors and green wainscot walls, leather banquettes, and hand-painted murals by local artist Michael Paulus. It opened in late 2018 as part of the Woodlark and also offers a weekend high-tea service.

The non-alcoholic program is a genuine focus rather than an afterthought, and Abigail Hall keeps a rotating slate of intricate, well-garnished zero-proof drinks alongside its cocktail list. Veteran mixologist Jared Wegner builds the spirit-free menu around NA spirits and the deep flavors of coffee and tea. Recent and signature no-proof drinks include the Oolong Goodbye (Pathfinder NA spirit, oolong syrup, lemon), the Sanbitter Spritz (Sanbitter NA aperitif, grapefruit, ginger beer), the Rossellini Soda (pomegranate-honey or roasted-peach syrup, soda, vanilla cold foam), and the Spiritless Veil (Wilderton citrus, hibiscus, lime).
venues.pressQuote: Veteran mixologist Jared Wegner not only incorporates zero-proof spirits into Abigail's menu, but also utilizes the complex flavors of coffee and tea to elevate beverages.

venues.name: Absinthe Brasserie & Bar
venues.description: Absinthe Brasserie & Bar has been the pre-theatre anchor of Hayes Valley for decades, a French-Californian brasserie on the corner of Hayes and Gough with a long marble bar and a classics-heavy cocktail list. Its alcohol-free drinks are printed under their own heading, n/a cocktails, and are all $12 against $16 to $18 for the full-proof list. Four are named: Coda Leger, built on pomegranate with lemon, lime, vanilla and seltzer; Mister Rogers, a lighter build of lime, mint and ginger beer; Absinthe Lemonade, made with lemon, cranberry and ginger; and Bright Red Shirts, which uses a house non-alcoholic Campari-style syrup with orange, lemon and seltzer to reproduce a bitter aperitivo. The kitchen serves lunch and dinner Wednesday through Sunday.
signatureDrinks: Coda Leger (pomegranate, lemon, lime, vanilla, seltzer)
Bright Red Shirts (house n/a Campari syrup, orange, lemon, seltzer)
venues.longDescription:
Absinthe Brasserie & Bar occupies the corner of Hayes and Gough, a block from the Opera House and Davies Symphony Hall, and has been the default pre-performance room in Hayes Valley for long enough that its bar is part of the neighbourhood's furniture. The format is a French-Californian brasserie: a raw bar, steak frites and a long menu of pre-Prohibition and mid-century cocktails, served under pressed tin from a marble counter. It trades Wednesday through Sunday, from 11:30am to 10pm on weekdays and from 11am at weekends, which covers both the matinee and the evening curtain.

The non-alcoholic drinks are given a dedicated section of the cocktail list, headed n/a cocktails, with every drink at $12 against $16 to $18 for the alcoholic ones. There are four. Coda Leger is the longest and most aromatic, built on pomegranate with lemon, lime, vanilla and seltzer. Mister Rogers is a stripped-back mule of lime, mint and ginger beer, and is the natural order for anyone who wants something dry and cold rather than sweet. Absinthe Lemonade is the house lemonade cut with cranberry and ginger. Bright Red Shirts is the most technically interesting of the group: the bar makes a non-alcoholic Campari-style syrup in house and lengthens it with orange, lemon and seltzer, producing the bitter red aperitivo that an alcohol-free drinker in a room full of spritzes usually has to go without. The names echo the full-proof list, which is built on similarly playful titles — a Ginger Rogers, a Bee's Knees, a Berry Collins — so the alcohol-free drinks read as part of the same menu rather than as a concession printed at the bottom of the page. The restaurant is closed Monday and Tuesday, which is worth checking before a pre-theatre booking, and the bar serves the full menu throughout. Given how many people pass through this corner on their way to an 8pm curtain, a four-drink zero-proof list at a third below cocktail prices is one of the more practically useful alcohol-free offerings in the city centre.
venues.pressQuote: Absinthe is huge with multiple rooms, including one that you can rent out for private parties

venues.name: ABV
venues.description: ABV is a Mission District cocktail bar that opened in summer 2014, founded by Erik Reichborn-Kjennerud, Ryan Fitzgerald, and Todd Smith (a founding Bourbon & Branch bartender). It was named Imbibe Magazine's 2015 Bar of the Year and ranked #39 in the inaugural North America's 50 Best Bars (2022), the only San Francisco bar on that list. The menu is organized by base spirit, with dedicated "LOW ABV" and "0% ABV" sections that make the no/low offering a standing, structured part of the program rather than an afterthought. The non-alcoholic cocktails ($14) center on a house "n/a aperitif" and bright, fresh builds — the N/A Negroni (n/a aperitif, charred grapefruit tonic), Flightless Bird, Green Dream (tarragon, lemon, ginger, tonic), and Jumpstart (carrot, ginger, turmeric, lemon, soda) — alongside Lagunitas Hop Water and IPNA. ABV makes drinks to order and runs a late kitchen until midnight.

venues.longDescription:
ABV opened in the summer of 2014 at 3174 16th Street in the Mission, founded by Ryan Fitzgerald, Todd Smith and Erik Reichborn-Kjennerud, three long-serving Bay Area bartenders. Fitzgerald and Smith had worked together since 2006 at Bourbon & Branch, where Smith was a founding bartender; Reichborn-Kjennerud ran Dalva and its back room, the Hideout, where the three of them settled on the idea. Imbibe Magazine named ABV its 2015 Bar of the Year, writing that it "may have first opened its doors last summer, but the seed of the bar were sown several years ago." In 2022 ABV placed No. 39 on the inaugural North America's 50 Best Bars list, the only San Francisco bar to appear on it. The bar is open 4pm to 2am daily and runs its kitchen until midnight, which makes it one of the more reliable late options in the neighbourhood.

The menu's structure is what makes ABV dependable for someone who is not drinking. Rather than a single catch-all list, it is broken into sections by strength, with standing "LOW ABV" and "0% ABV" runs that function as permanent architecture rather than seasonal goodwill — the zero-proof section has been on the menu for years and survives each redesign. The 0% ABV cocktails are $14 and currently comprise the N/A Negroni (house non-alcoholic aperitif and charred grapefruit tonic), the Flightless Bird (n/a aperitif, orange juice, lemon juice and salt), the Green Dream (tarragon, lemon, ginger and tonic), Jumpstart (carrot, ginger, turmeric, lemon and soda) and the Passionfruit Fix (lime, passionfruit and a salted rim). The house-made non-alcoholic aperitif anchoring two of them is the reason the N/A Negroni reads as a negroni rather than as a bitter soda, and it is the piece of the programme that would be hardest for another bar to copy. Lagunitas Hop Water at $5 and Lagunitas IPNA at $7 cover the beer slot, and Leitz dealcoholized sparkling rosé is poured at $15. Everything is made to order.
venues.pressQuote: Our 2015 Imbibe 75 Bar of the Year—ABV in San Francisco—may have first opened its doors last summer, but the seed of the bar were sown several years ago.

venues.name: Accent Wine Parlor
venues.description: Accent Wine Parlor is a wine shop and tasting room in the historic Citizens Building on North High Street downtown, opened in August 2021 by sommelier Gregory Stokes with chef Joshua Dalton of Veritas. It works as both retail and a room to sit and drink in, running daily tastings, weekly classes and local delivery across the Columbus metro alongside bottles from $10 to collector prices. For non-drinkers the relevant part is a maintained non-alcoholic collection rather than a token bottle or two — alcohol-removed still and sparkling wines from producers including Leitz, and Copenhagen Sparkling Tea, the Danish tea-based alternative that behaves like wine at the table rather than like a soft drink. The shop also makes its own syrups. Open Tuesday to Saturday afternoons and evenings.
signatureDrinks: Leitz "Eins Zwei Zero" Non-Alcoholic Brut Rosé Sparkling

naMenuItems.name: Leitz "Eins Zwei Zero" Non-Alcoholic Brut Rosé Sparkling

venues.longDescription:
Accent Wine Parlor opened in August 2021 at 49 North High Street, in the historic Citizens Building on the downtown stretch of High below the Short North. It is led by sommelier Gregory Stokes together with chef Joshua Dalton, whose Veritas sits a few blocks north on Gay Street, and it was conceived as a corrective: Stokes told Columbus Navigator at the opening that they built it "because we saw that no one was doing wine retail the way that we thought it should be done." In practice that means a shop that is also a parlour — a room designed to be sat in and drunk in, with bottles from around $10 through to collector wines, rather than a rack-lined retail unit with a tasting counter bolted on.

The reason it belongs in a non-alcoholic guide is that the alcohol-free selection is a maintained collection rather than a shelf of leftovers. The shop stocks alcohol-removed still and sparkling wines from serious producers — Leitz, the German house whose de-alcoholised Rieslings are among the few that survive the process with acidity intact, is the anchor — alongside Copenhagen Sparkling Tea, the Danish blend of brewed teas that is built to occupy the same place at a table as a wine: tannic, aromatic, structured enough to sit through a course. That distinction matters for anyone who has tried to make a dinner work on sparkling water. Accent also produces its own syrups, runs daily tastings and weekly classes, and delivers across the Columbus metro as well as shipping nationally, so a bottle can be tried in the room before a case goes home. Hours are Tuesday to Saturday, 1pm to 9pm, with Mondays by appointment only. One practical note: because Accent is a shop as much as a bar, the alcohol-free bottles can be bought to take away as well as drunk in, which is unusual in Columbus — most venues with a good zero-proof list will pour one but not sell one. For anyone hosting, that makes it the most reliable place downtown to pick up an alcohol-removed sparkling wine that will hold up on a dinner table.
venues.pressQuote: We created Accent because we saw that no one was doing wine retail the way that we thought it should be done.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Gregory Stokes, Accent Wine Parlor sommelier and co-founder

venues.name: Adam Reid at The French
venues.description: Adam Reid at The French is one of Manchester city centre's most decorated tasting-menu restaurants, set in the Edwardian dining room of the Midland Hotel on Peter Street. Chef-patron Adam Reid, a BBC Great British Menu winner, took over the room in 2016 following Simon Rogan's departure and has built a reputation for bold, playful modern-British cooking rooted in Northern ingredients; the restaurant holds four AA Rosettes and a listing in the Michelin Guide, and its courses are finished and explained tableside by the kitchen team. It earns a place in a non-alcoholic directory for its drinks programme: alongside the traditional wine flight, it offers a full non-alcoholic flight designed to pair with each course, positioned as a direct alternative rather than a token substitute, and the sommelier team will build bespoke soft or zero-proof pairings on request. It is one of the few tasting-menu destinations in the city where the alcohol-free option is a designed part of the experience.
venues.address: The Midland Hotel, 16 Peter Street, Manchester M60 2DS
venues.hours: Mon-Tue closed; Wed-Thu 6pm-8:30pm; Fri 5pm-8:30pm; Sat 4pm-8:30pm; Sun closed
venues.longDescription:
Set in the Edwardian dining room of the Midland Hotel on Peter Street, Adam Reid at The French is one of Manchester city centre's most decorated tasting-menu restaurants. Chef-patron Adam Reid, a BBC Great British Menu winner, took over the room in 2016 following Simon Rogan's departure and has built a reputation for bold, playful modern-British cooking rooted in Northern ingredients. The restaurant holds four AA Rosettes and a listing in the Michelin Guide, and its multi-course menus are finished and explained tableside by the kitchen team.

The reason it earns a place in a non-alcoholic directory is its drinks programme. Alongside the traditional wine flight, the restaurant offers a full non-alcoholic flight designed to pair with each course of the tasting menu, positioned as a direct alternative to the wine pairing rather than a token substitute. The Good Food Guide notes plainly that "there are two wine flights (alcoholic and non-alcoholic)," and the knowledgeable sommelier team will also swap in soft drinks or non-alcoholic cocktails to match individual dishes.

The format has evolved over the years between the longer Signature Menu and a shorter six-course Initials Menu introduced for lighter summer dining, but the two-flight structure has remained a consistent feature. For a sober or sober-curious diner wanting a genuine special-occasion meal in Manchester, this is a rare case where the alcohol-free path is thought through course by course.

The room itself is formal and ornate, service runs Wednesday to Saturday for dinner only, and the setting inside a landmark hotel makes it a true occasion venue. Booking well ahead is advised, and the non-alcoholic flight should be requested with the reservation.
venues.pressQuote: There are two wine flights (alcoholic and non-alcoholic), otherwise consult the knowledgeable and helpful sommelier.

venues.name: ADRIFT Mare
venues.description: ADRIFT Mare is a Mediterranean restaurant and cocktail bar from Michelin-starred chef David Myers, perched on the 25th floor of Hotel AKA Brickell with terrace views over Biscayne Bay. The kitchen draws on the French Riviera, the Balearic islands, Italian produce, Levantine hospitality, and the Greek isles, serving breakfast, lunch, and dinner daily. The cocktail program was built by acclaimed bartenders Moe Aljaff and Juliette Larrouy, whose résumés include Himkok and Two Schmucks. Its zero-proof side is small but real: alcohol-free cocktails such as Chai Life and Palm Paradise lean on spice, citrus, and freshness, alongside Lyre's-based non-alcoholic aperitivo classics that mirror the bar's spritz-forward sensibility. Resident magazine featured the mocktails in its 2025 Dry January roundup. It's a polished hotel-rooftop option for a sit-down dinner with credible non-alcoholic choices rather than a dedicated NA bar.
venues.longDescription:
ADRIFT Mare sits on the 25th floor of Hotel AKA Brickell, a Mediterranean restaurant and cocktail bar from Michelin-starred chef David Myers with terrace views over Biscayne Bay. The kitchen pulls from the French Riviera, the Balearics, Italian produce, Levantine hospitality and the Greek isles, and serves breakfast, lunch and dinner daily rather than only in the evening.

The bar programme is the reason it earns its place. It was built by Moe Aljaff and Juliette Larrouy, bartenders whose backgrounds include Himkok in Oslo and Two Schmucks in Barcelona — both rooms that have appeared on the World's 50 Best Bars list. Bartenders from that tier treat a zero-proof drink as a construction problem rather than an inconvenience, and it shows in the approach: the alcohol-free cocktails lean on spice, citrus and freshness rather than sugar, with Chai Life and Palm Paradise the named builds, alongside Lyre's-based non-alcoholic aperitivo classics that mirror the bar's spritz-forward sensibility.

Spritz-forward matters more than it sounds on a Miami rooftop. The spritz is the one cocktail category that translates almost perfectly without alcohol — it is built on bitterness, dilution and bubbles rather than on spirit weight — so a bar whose house style is already spritzes has a structural advantage in making a good zero-proof list.

Resident Magazine featured the mocktails in its Dry January round-up, noting that the restaurant approaches zero-proof drinking with Mediterranean clarity.

It is a polished hotel rooftop for a sit-down meal with credible non-alcoholic choices, not a dedicated NA bar — but the all-day service makes it usable at breakfast and lunch as well as for an evening. Ask what the bar team can build off-menu; with backgrounds like theirs, the printed zero-proof list understates what is possible.
venues.pressQuote: Each mocktail complements the menu's coastal sensibility, making Dry January feel considered rather than corrective.

venues.name: Adrift Tiki Bar
venues.description: Adrift Tiki Bar is an immersive Polynesian and Caribbean-inspired tiki bar on South Broadway in Denver, established in 2011 and bought in 2016 by current owner Loren Martinez, who also runs Little Man Ice Cream. The room is a full tropical build: a totem-pole-flanked bar, pufferfish lights, and an outdoor patio with a firepit, with a kitchen turning out spice-route Polynesian and Caribbean plates to match the rum-forward list. The menu carries a dedicated "On Dry Land (No ABV)" section — Anchored Tides (ginger, lime, demerara, Leopold Bros non-alcoholic aperitif), the N/A Mai Tai and N/A Painkiller (both built on Ritual N/A Rum), and the P.O.G. of passion fruit, orange and guava — plus a Mash Gang non-alcoholic IPA. A separate "In Shallow Water" section lists low-ABV cocktails for guests moderating rather than abstaining. Vince Polizzi is bar manager.

venues.longDescription:
Adrift Tiki Bar has been at 218 South Broadway since 2011 and has been owned since 2016 by Loren Martinez, who also runs Little Man Ice Cream. The build is committed rather than decorative: a bar flanked by totem poles, pufferfish lights overhead, a patio with a firepit, and a kitchen sending out Polynesian and Caribbean plates along the spice route the rum list implies. Tiki is a format that depends on layered juice, syrup and spice work as much as on spirit, which is why it converts to zero-proof better than most cocktail styles, and Adrift has leaned into that. In January 2025 the bar formalised what had been ad-hoc requests into a printed low- and no-ABV programme, framed by then-bar manager Jacoby Morciglio as multi-touch cocktails rather than fruit juice on the rocks; Vince Polizzi now runs the bar and Rob Duran is general manager.

The current cocktail menu carries two relevant sections. On Dry Land (No ABV) holds four drinks. Anchored Tides ($13) is the bitter one, ginger, lime and demerara against Leopold Bros non-alcoholic aperitif, and the menu describes it as bold, bitter and balanced. The N/A Mai Tai ($13) rebuilds the classic on Ritual N/A Rum with lime, orange and almond. The N/A Painkiller ($13) uses the same rum with pineapple, coconut, orange and nutmeg. The P.O.G. ($10) is the simplest and cheapest, passion fruit, orange and guava. A Mash Gang non-alcoholic IPA is stocked at $5. Alongside them, In Shallow Water lists genuinely low-ABV cocktails for guests who want to moderate rather than abstain, which is a distinction most bars do not bother to draw. Visit Denver's December 20, 2025 spirit-free guide went as far as to say the best non-alcoholic drinks in Denver may be here, and Westword's January 2026 round-up named the zero-proof Painkiller and Mai Tai specifically. The bar is closed Sundays and Mondays, runs to 10pm midweek and to midnight on Friday and Saturday, and keeps soft drinks at $5, so the zero-proof cocktails sit in a clear middle tier between a soda and a $16 rum drink. The patio and its firepit are the seats to ask for.
venues.pressQuote: It's possible that the best non-alcoholic drinks in all of Denver are at Adrift Tiki Bar. Sure, they have that whole tropical vibe advantage — we can't think of any other spot in town with pufferfish lights — but the spirit-free program is strong here, where the non-alcoholic painkillers and mai tais are every bit as complex and carefully crafted as their boozy counterparts.

venues.name: Aera
venues.description: Aera is a steakhouse and sushi restaurant from Toronto's Oliver & Bonacini Hospitality group, perched on the 38th floor of The Well in King West with sweeping city views. The bar runs a dedicated "Spirit-Free" section on its printed drinks menu, with four named, ingredient-listed alcohol-free cocktails served alongside the full bar list. Executive Chef Binit Pandey has described the kitchen's unhurried, technique-forward approach as built for the room's views.

venues.longDescription:
Aera is a steakhouse and sushi restaurant from Toronto's Oliver & Bonacini Hospitality group, occupying the 38th floor of The Well — the mixed-use tower at 8 Spadina Avenue that anchors the King West district. The restaurant opened in 2026 and pairs a dining room and bar with Open Aera, a rooftop patio 38 floors above the city; daily happy hour runs 4-6pm, and Friday and Saturday nights bring bottle service with DJs from 9pm. Open Aera and the bar are 19+ on Thursday through Saturday from 5pm and on Sundays of long weekends, while the main dining room remains open to all ages.

The bar treats non-alcoholic drinking as a proper, named section of the menu rather than an afterthought: a dedicated "Spirit-Free" list runs alongside the Signature, Classic and seasonal Feature cocktails, each drink built with a full ingredient line rather than a generic "mocktail" label. The Cipriani Bellini ($12) pairs Oddbird non-alcoholic blanc de blancs with peach nectar; the Petit Hugo ($12) is elderflower cordial, fresh mint and soda water over a 0% blanc de blanc sparkling wine; and the Blackberry Mojito ($12) combines a non-alcoholic rum with blackberry, fresh mint and soda water. A rotating feature, The Reset ($12), adds ginger, lemon, pomegranate, ginger beer, soda and a ginger candy garnish.

The program has drawn outside notice: Oliver & Bonacini's own "Booze-Free Cocktails" editorial singles out the Cipriani Bellini by name among its alcohol-free pours, and Executive Chef Binit Pandey has spoken to blogTO about the kitchen's unhurried pace suiting a room built around its views — "We take time to prepare food and the guest has the time to wait for it, to enjoy the view."
venues.pressQuote: The menu fits the place. We take time to prepare food and the guest has the time to wait for it, to enjoy the view.

venues.name: Affäre
venues.description: Affäre is a modern German restaurant at 1911 Main Street in the Crossroads Arts District, opened in May 2012 by chef Martin Heuser and his wife Katrin Heuser, who moved to Kansas City from Germany in 2007. Martin learned to cook at his family's restaurant Im Steinhaus in Bonn — a 15th-century stone building his family has owned for nearly two hundred years — earned a Master Chef Diploma and worked in two Michelin-starred kitchens; Katrin completed her sommelier diploma through the International Sommelier Guild in Calgary. The Pitch, reviewing it two months after opening, described a menu of small and exquisitely presented plates which arrive at the table arranged like tiny sculptures. The dining room occupies the cavernous former Bar Natasha space. Dinner runs Tuesday to Sunday, 4.45pm to 9pm, closed Mondays, with a children's menu and high chairs available. Affäre keeps non-alcoholic house drinks and a non-alcoholic beer alongside its wine list, but does not publish its drinks menu online, so ask what is being poured.
venues.longDescription:
Affäre opened in May 2012 at 1911 Main Street, in a Crossroads space so large The Pitch compared it to a roller rink, previously home to the cabaret-restaurant Bar Natasha. It is the work of chef Martin Heuser and his wife Katrin, who moved from Germany to Kansas City in 2007 with their four children and spent five years here before opening. Martin's training is unusually deep-rooted: he learned to cook at his family's restaurant, Im Steinhaus in Bonn, which occupies a stone building dating to the early fifteenth century and has been in the family for nearly two hundred years. He holds a Master Chef Diploma and worked in two Michelin-starred kitchens before emigrating. Katrin completed her sommelier diploma through the International Sommelier Guild in Calgary and runs the beverage side. The cooking is contemporary German rather than the heavy stereotype — The Pitch, reviewing the two-month-old restaurant in 2012, described a menu of small and exquisitely presented plates which arrive at the table arranged like tiny sculptures, and that format has held.

For a non-drinker, this is a room where the beverage thinking is genuinely serious — a working sommelier runs it, and the kitchen's small-plate format suits a long meal built around something other than wine. Affäre keeps house-made non-alcoholic drinks and a non-alcoholic dark beer alongside the list. The honest caveat is that the restaurant publishes no drinks menu online: the everyday food and beverage menus load through a widget that does not render, and the only downloadable documents on the site are seasonal specials and a parking diagram. That means any named zero-proof drink circulating online, including on this page previously, cannot be checked against the restaurant itself, and the list is best confirmed when you book or on the night. Two practical notes that are firmly established: dinner runs Tuesday to Sunday with a last seating at 9pm and the restaurant is closed Mondays, and it genuinely welcomes children, keeping a kids' menu, booster seats and high chairs — unusual at this level of cooking.
venues.pressQuote: Non-alcoholic cocktails are so pleasing to people because they are about inclusion.

venues.name: Agency
venues.description: Agency is the nation's first fully hybrid cocktail lounge, set inside the restored Dubbel Dutch Hotel in Milwaukee's Yankee Hill / Cathedral Square area. Every drink on the menu can be ordered full-proof or completely spirit-free — guests flip a two-sided coaster (gold side up for non-alcoholic, black for alcoholic) to signal their choice, so ordering a zero-proof round never requires a conversation. Founded by Ryan Castelaz of Discourse Coffee, the bar was a 2025 James Beard Award finalist for Best New Bar — one of only five nationwide. Because the spirit-free and spirited builds are made with equal craft, it is one of the strongest zero-proof-friendly rooms in the country.
signatureDrinks: Dealer's Choice (bespoke 'dream drink' improvised to your taste, full-proof or zero-proof; single) $25
venues.longDescription:
Opened inside the historic Dubbel Dutch Hotel in late August 2024, Agency bills itself as the nation's first fully hybrid cocktail bar: an entire menu in which every drink is engineered to taste equally complete with or without alcohol. It began as a hybrid pop-up tied to founder Ryan Castelaz's Discourse Coffee before moving into the hotel, and it reflects Castelaz's conviction that a non-alcoholic-only room can feel exclusionary — so rather than making guests choose between a "wet" bar and a "dry" one, Agency lets each person decide round by round. As Castelaz frames the mission, it is about giving people "true agency over their drinking experience."

Guests communicate their preference through a simple, discreet ritual — a two-sided coaster flipped gold-side up for a spirit-free drink or black-side up for a spirited one — so no one has to call attention to themselves. The list rotates as a themed series, and earlier theatrical signatures like the clarified milk-punch Interstellar have rotated off with it. The current menu, "The Unindexed Series Vol. 3," is a journey into Greek mythology: five experiential builds named for Apollo, Poseidon, Dionysus, Persephone, and Zeus, each paired with a small plate curated by chef Zach Panoske of Sinta, alongside a craft list that runs from a French Spritz to a Tomato Martini 2.0. The room's most popular order remains the Dealer's Choice, on which guests pick a flavor profile and let the bar improvise a "dream drink" — orderable, like the rest of the list, in either a full-proof or zero-proof version; the printed menu marks only a rare exception (a Chartreuse tasting flight) as not available non-alcoholic.

The approach has drawn national attention: Agency was named a finalist for Best New Bar at the 2025 James Beard Awards, one of only five nationwide. For non-alcoholic drinkers, the significance is that the spirit-free menu is not an afterthought but the equal half of the program — a fully realized, award-caliber cocktail experience whether or not there is alcohol in the glass. Agency is open Wednesday through Saturday evenings, and reservations, especially for its multi-course thematic tasting experiences, are strongly recommended.
venues.pressQuote: Every drink on the menu can be made alcoholic or completely booze-free, with the promise that the N/A version isn't a pale substitute.

venues.name: Aguasal by José Andrés
venues.description: Aguasal by José Andrés opened in June 2025 inside the Andaz Miami Beach in Mid-Beach, the first of the José Andrés Group's planned dining takeover of the oceanfront resort. Named for agua salada (Spanish for saltwater), the all-day coastal-Mediterranean restaurant draws on Mallorca and Mykonos, with dishes like Kumamoto oysters, mussels saganaki, and whole snapper served indoors or on the terrace. The bar program carries a small but intentional zero-proof selection: two named spirit-free cocktails — the Cardamom & Ginger (cardamom, citrus, sakura, ginger beer) and the Mediterranean Milk Punch (lavender-cardamom tea, pomegranate, fenugreek, mint, dairy-clarified) — alongside Athletic Brewing's Free Wave non-alcoholic Hazy IPA, fresh juices, Per'la coffee, and Art of Tea infusions. A separate upstairs bar, Bar Centro, extends the group's spirit-free options. Aguasal sits steps from the sand on Collins Avenue.
