venues.longDescription:
When The Ball & Biscuit opened at 331 Massachusetts Avenue in June 2010, Indianapolis did not really have a craft cocktail bar, and the city has spent the fifteen years since treating it as the one that started things. It was a side project for Trevor Belden, a local attorney, built with bartender Zach Wilks — who went on to found the Wilks & Wilson syrup and bitters company, a line you still find behind bars across the Midwest. The name comes from the 1930s ribbon microphone that everyone called the ball and biscuit, and original mics and studio gear hang through a narrow, dark room that runs to brown spirits, pre-Prohibition classics, old-school DJ nights and serious charcuterie.

The zero-proof program is the part that matters here, and it is not decorative. Seven named non-alcoholic drinks sit on the same menu as the cocktails, priced and built with the same components. The Spritz AF layers Lyre's Italian Orange and Lyre's Aperitif Rosso over lemon and orange juice and lengthens it with Fre non-alcoholic sparkling brut; the New Fashioned is a straight-faced alcohol-free reading of an old fashioned; The Whole Garden is the floral one, built on zero-proof brut; and the Twist of Fate runs ginger syrup and basil concentrate against lemon and club soda. The bar will also add CBD or delta-8 to a drink for a small upcharge, which is worth knowing in advance if you are avoiding psychoactives as well as alcohol — it is an opt-in, not a default. Hours run late for the neighbourhood, to midnight Sunday through Thursday and 2am on Friday and Saturday, and Mass Ave puts three other venues on this list within a five-minute walk. The wider point is that Ball & Biscuit is the closest thing Indianapolis currently has to a bar that would satisfy someone used to a dedicated alcohol-free room. Since Memento Zero Proof shut in Fishers in 2024, the city has had no fully alcohol-free cocktail bar at all, and the zero-proof depth has migrated into ordinary bars — which means the question is no longer where the sober bar is, but which bars have actually done the work. Seven named builds, a Lyre's and Fre backbone, and fifteen years of bartending culture behind them is as close as the city gets. Expect a loud, dark, shoulder-to-shoulder room at weekends; a Tuesday visit is a different bar entirely.
venues.pressQuote: This Mass Ave hotspot offers seven uniquely crafted non-alcoholic beverages, from the "New Fashioned," a buzz-free take on the old fashioned, to the floral "The Whole Garden," featuring zero-proof brut.

venues.name: Bangkok Supper Club
venues.description: A lively West Village Thai restaurant inspired by Bangkok's late-night dining scene, with an award-winning cocktail program that includes a Seedlip-based non-alcoholic option.
venues.longDescription: Bangkok Supper Club is an inventive Thai restaurant at 641 Hudson Street in the West Village, channeling the energy of Bangkok's late-night food scene with deep U-shaped booths and a buzzy, social atmosphere. Its cocktail program is led by Suwincha "Chacha" Singsuwan, named the Michelin Guide New York 2024 Exceptional Cocktails Award winner. For non-drinkers, Time Out highlighted the bar's spirit-free "Beets 'N' Cream," which (in its zero-proof form) infuses Seedlip with beets and is shaken with mango, honey and lemon, then topped with a cream cheese float. Non-alcoholic options are not broken out into a dedicated section of the printed menu, so sober-curious guests should ask the bar for the spirit-free version, but the kitchen's Michelin-recognized mixology makes it a worthwhile stop for a thoughtfully made alcohol-free drink in a high-energy setting.
venues.pressQuote: Infusing Seedlip with beets, this cocktail keeps it interesting with a shake of mango, honey and lemon, topped with a cream cheese float.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Morgan Carter, Time Out New York

venues.name: Bantha Tea Bar
venues.description: Bantha Tea Bar, on Penn Ave between Garfield and Bloomfield, is a solar-powered tea house built largely from recycled materials and an explicitly alcohol-free space to hang out without drinking. The menu runs deep on loose-leaf black, green and herbal teas, joined by Sweet Unity Farms coffee, matcha, ceremonial cacao, MUD\WTR and house lemonades — no alcohol is served at all. It has also been the closest thing Pittsburgh has to a kava bar: Keystone Newsroom's February 2026 survey of the city's kava scene found that Pittsburgh has no dedicated kava bar and named Bantha the only cafe in the city with kava on its menu, mixed with almond milk, coconut milk, ginger beer or lemonade, or taken as a shot of house concentrated extract. Bantha's own published menu does not currently list kava, so call ahead if that is why you are going. The room runs poetry readings and regular community events.
venues.longDescription:
Bantha Tea Bar sits on Penn Avenue between the Garfield and Bloomfield neighborhoods, in a solar-powered building assembled largely from recycled materials in partnership with the Fourth River Workers Guild, and it describes itself as a permaculture tea bar and a socially and environmentally engaged member of the Bloomfield-Garfield community. It has spent years as one of Pittsburgh's few genuinely alcohol-free places to spend an evening rather than a morning — nothing alcoholic is served at any hour. The core of the menu is loose-leaf tea served hot by the cup: Earl Grey, Scottish Breakfast, pinewood-smoked Lapsang Souchong, a classic chai blended with cardamom, cinnamon, cloves and orange peel, and an Ancient Phoenix Puer from two-hundred-year-old trees. Around it sit Sweet Unity Farms coffee, matcha, ceremonial cacao, MUD\WTR and house-made lemonades, plus small eats and sweets. What keeps the room full is the programming — poetry readings, an eclectic assortment of art, and a steady calendar of community events that give the space what local coverage describes as a bar-like vibe rather than a cafe one.

It has also been the closest thing this city has to a kava bar, and that deserves stating carefully. Keystone Newsroom's February 2026 survey of where to drink kava in Pittsburgh found that the city has no dedicated kava bar at all, and identified Bantha as the only cafe in it serving kava — mixed with almond milk, coconut milk, ginger beer or lemonade, taken straight as a shot of Bantha's own concentrated extract, or in the form of Leilo, a ready-to-drink canned kava that could be spiked with that extract. Bantha's own current published menu does not list kava, so treat the offering as worth phoning ahead about rather than as a certainty. Kava itself is a psychoactive drink made from the ground root of a South Pacific shrub and drunk socially in place of alcohol: it contains no alcohol whatsoever, but it is mildly sedative and mildly intoxicating on its own terms, a distinction that matters if your recovery rules out intoxicants generally rather than alcohol specifically.
venues.pressQuote: The local space already attracts an alternative crowd with its poetry readings, eclectic assortment of art, and bar-like vibe, so offering kava alongside organic teas isn’t surprising.

venues.name: Bar 473
venues.description: Bar 473 sits on Admiral Boulevard in Tulsa's Kendall-Whittier neighbourhood, open from 3pm and running to midnight midweek and 2am on Friday and Saturday. Its alcohol-free drink is the Horchata Colada — pineapple, coconut, lime and cinnamon — which builds a piña colada on a horchata base rather than a rum one, using cinnamon and the creaminess of the coconut to supply the weight the spirit would otherwise carry. It is a dessert-leaning drink and honestly so, and a good answer for anyone who wants something substantial rather than another citrus highball. Kendall-Whittier puts it a short drive east of downtown rather than within walking distance of the other rooms here.
signatureDrinks: Horchata Colada — pineapple, coconut, lime, cinnamon
venues.longDescription:
Bar 473 is a neighbourhood bar on Admiral Boulevard in Kendall-Whittier, east of downtown Tulsa, and it keeps genuinely late hours — 3pm to midnight from Tuesday to Thursday and on Sunday, and 3pm to 2am on Friday and Saturday.

The alcohol-free drink is the Horchata Colada, and the idea behind it is better than most. A piña colada without rum is normally a thin, over-sweet disappointment, because the rum is carrying more structural weight than people realise. Rebuilding it on a horchata base — the rice-and-cinnamon drink — replaces that weight with body from the grain and warmth from the cinnamon, while pineapple and coconut keep the colada character and lime cuts the richness.

That is worth flagging as a general point for readers who find most mocktails unsatisfying: the drinks that work best without alcohol are usually the ones that replace what alcohol was doing rather than simply omitting it. Alcohol contributes weight, warmth and a slight burn; fat, spice, tannin and heat are the tools that stand in. This drink uses two of them.

It is also, honestly, a sweet drink and closer to a dessert than to an aperitif. That is a feature rather than a flaw — a substantial, sweet, cold drink is exactly what many people want at eleven at night, and the alternative on offer in most bars at that hour is a soda.

Tulsa Remote ranked it among the city's must-try mocktails in January 2025.

Graded three: one documented build, no printed zero-proof section, no non-alcoholic spirits programme verified. Closed Monday.
venues.pressQuote: Horchata Colada: pineapple, coconut, lime, and cinnamon

venues.name: Bar Banane
venues.description: Bar Banane is a lively cocktail bar on the Ossington Strip in Toronto, pairing an elevated, French-inflected small-plates menu — lobster croustade, smoked sturgeon rillettes, steak tartare — with an ambitious twelve-drink signature cocktail list. Its non-alcoholic beverages get a standalone "Non-Alcoholic Beverages" section on the menu, priced at the same $14 as the house cocktails rather than tacked on as an afterthought: Optional Side Quest (elderflower, clarified grapefruit, genmaicha tea, tonic), Pear-odactyl (mango aloe, pear juice, lemon) and Extremely Safe for Work (passion fruit, clarified lemon, orange, chili). Destination Toronto, the city's official tourism organization, singled the bar out for showing "just how far and creative you can go when building a non-alcoholic beverage."

venues.longDescription:
Bar Banane sits on the Ossington Strip, one of Toronto's busiest restaurant-and-bar corridors, at 227A Ossington Ave. It's open Wednesday and Thursday from 6pm to midnight and Friday and Saturday from 6pm to 2am, closed Sunday through Tuesday. Reservations run through OpenTable, though the bar holds space for walk-ins, and groups of six or more are asked to contact the bar directly rather than book online.

The menu leans French and internationally minded, running from canapés like nova scotia lobster croustade and smoked sturgeon rillettes through snacks such as savoury churros and steak tartare to large plates including a lobster roll "américaine" and steak "frites" with sauce béarnaise. The cocktail list runs to twelve elaborate signature drinks priced $21–29, built on ingredients like mezcal, roku gin, toki japanese whisky, bumbu rum, aquavit and pandan vodka — among them the forbidden negroni (toasted coconut gin, white fig vermouth, campari) and midnight ceremony (toki whisky, barley shochu, banana, matcha, hojicha). The wine list runs deep across red, white, sparkling and rosé, and the beer and cider selection includes a house collaboration, the Rainhard x La Banane Lager, brewed with Toronto's Rainhard Brewing.

Non-alcoholic drinks get their own standalone section on the menu — "Non-Alcoholic Beverages" — rather than being folded in with soft drinks, and all three are priced at $14, matching the bar's house cocktails rather than being discounted as an afterthought. The options are Optional Side Quest (elderflower, clarified grapefruit, genmaicha tea, tonic), Pear-odactyl (mango aloe, pear juice, lemon) and Extremely Safe for Work (passion fruit, clarified lemon, orange, chili).

The program has drawn outside notice, too: Destination Toronto, the city's official tourism organization, featured Bar Banane in a roundup of the city's non-alcoholic drinks, writing that the bar "showcases just how far and creative you can go when building a non-alcoholic beverage" and singling out the Mango Aloe and Genmaicha Tea combination as proof the drinks are "sure to wow and impress any date."
venues.pressQuote: The team behind Bar Banane on the Ossington Street strip showcases just how far and creative you can go when building a non-alcoholic beverage. From Mango Aloe, Genmaicha Tea, and so much more, expect the unexpected. The drinks and atmosphere at this buzzy bar are sure to wow and impress any date.

venues.name: Bar Benjamin
venues.description: Bar Benjamin is a second-floor craft cocktail bar that opened in May 2025 above The Benjamin Hollywood on Melrose Avenue, from The Hundreds co-founder Ben Shenassafar with partners Jared Meisler and Kate Burr. The cocktail program — developed by Jason Lee (n/soto, Baroo) and beverage director Chad Austin — is known for elaborate, food-driven drinks, and the non-alcoholic list is a genuine priority rather than an afterthought: Austin, who is five years sober, builds the zero-proof cocktails with the same rigor as the full menu. Named NA drinks on the current menu include the Smiley Face (a mango-margarita riff with yellow bell pepper syrup, fermented mango, acid-adjusted pineapple, Wilderton Citrus Bitter, and Optimist Smoky), plus Aura Farm, Bangkok Dangerous, and Tepache Bird. The room is intimate and reservation-friendly, with walk-in bar seating.

venues.longDescription:
Bar Benjamin opened in May 2025 on the second floor above The Benjamin Hollywood at 7174 Melrose Avenue, taking over the space that briefly held the Moon Room and, before that, Bathtub Gin. It comes from Ben Shenassafar, co-founder of the streetwear label The Hundreds, with partners Jared Meisler — known for The Roger Room and Bar Lubitsch — and culinary consultant Kate Burr. Time Out described an Art Deco-inspired room of low wood-panelled ceilings, mohair booths and custom carpeting, with a balcony bar looking out at the Hollywood Hills, entered under a glowing red neon BAR sign and rising into something more old-school elegance than influencer bait. The cocktail list was created by Jason Lee, of n/soto and Baroo, with beverage director Chad Austin, formerly of Bootlegger Tiki, and the kitchen runs bar food at a high specification: triple-fried Kennebec chips, deviled eggs with crispy capers, tuna toast with Castelvetrano olives, a wagyu pastrami sandwich on a house-baked rye bun, steak tartare with Calabrian chile, and chips with golden osetra caviar.

The zero-proof section exists because Austin needed it to. I'm five years sober, so I always pay close attention to NA menus when I'm out, he told Resy in January 2026 — and, he added, he often does not order, because the drinks feel like an afterthought. The four drinks on his own list are correspondingly dense. Bangkok Dangerous is the most ambitious: a smoky non-alcoholic spirit and Dr. Zero Amaro with peanut butter, red miso, gochujang, ginger lemongrass tea, honey, lime and fish sauce. Smiley Face works an agave non-alcoholic distillate with Wilderton Citrus Bitter, fermented mango, yellow bell pepper and acid-adjusted pineapple — savoury, smoky and bright, in Austin's description, familiar but totally new. Aura Farm combines a tequila alternative with St. Agrestis Phony Negroni, Bordelet pear cider, strawberry, gochujang and lemon, and Tepache Bird is Aplos Ease with Wilderton Red Bitter, tepache and lime. A taro milk punch built with hemp spirit, genmaicha, lemongrass and cinnamon has also appeared on the list. The bar does not print prices on its published menus. It opens at 6pm Tuesday to Saturday, to midnight midweek and 1am from Thursday, with reservations through Resy.
venues.pressQuote: I'm five years sober, so I always pay close attention to NA menus when I'm out. Unfortunately, I often don't order because the drinks feel like an afterthought.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Chad Austin, Bar Benjamin beverage director

venues.name: Bar Bianco
venues.description: Tucked into a historic 1890s brick bungalow beside Pizzeria Bianco on downtown's Heritage Square, Bar Bianco is chef Chris Bianco's wine-and-cocktail bar — and, in practice, the room where you wait for a table at one of the most famous pizzerias in the United States. Most of its non-alcoholic drinks pair Seedlip spirits with house-made syrups, producing layered, low-sweetness builds like the citrusy Vinifera Spice and the herbal Mariposa Milk. Phoenix New Times has singled out that Seedlip-and-housemade-syrup pairing as exactly what separates the list here from the sweetened juice most restaurants hand to non-drinkers while they wait for a table.
venues.longDescription:
Bar Bianco sits in an 1890s brick bungalow on Heritage Square, the small cluster of surviving Victorian buildings marooned in downtown Phoenix among the towers and the convention centre. It belongs to Chris Bianco, whose Pizzeria Bianco next door has been called the best pizza in America often enough that the wait for a table became a structural feature of the operation — and Bar Bianco is where that wait is spent. The room is low-ceilinged and dark in a way that reads as old rather than styled, with a garden outside that is the better seat for most of the Phoenix year.

A wait bar is exactly the situation where non-drinkers usually get handled worst: everyone else is given a glass of wine and a reason to be patient, and you are given a soda. Bar Bianco does not do that. Its zero-proof drinks are built on Seedlip non-alcoholic spirits and finished with the same house-made syrups used across the cocktail list, which keeps them dry and layered rather than sugary. The Vinifera Spice runs citrus-forward; the Mariposa Milk is the herbal one. Phoenix New Times has picked out that pairing — a named NA spirit plus a house syrup — as the thing that distinguishes the list.

The bar keeps daytime-into-evening hours, 11am to 9pm Monday through Saturday, and closes Sundays. Two practical notes. It is a wine bar attached to a restaurant, so the alcohol-free options are a section of a list whose centre is Italian wine. And because the room exists partly to absorb the pizzeria queue, it is busiest exactly when the restaurant is — arrive early or late if you want a seat rather than a standing spot. Heritage Square itself is worth the detour in daylight — the bungalows are among the last pre-1900 buildings left in central Phoenix.
venues.pressQuote: the chef has expanded his empire to include multiple locations of Pizzeria Bianco, as well as other spots like Tratto, Bar Bianco, Pane Bianco

Signature mocktails include the Cut Above Mezcal Sour (Cut Above NA mezcal, coconut water, lapsang, jalapeno, lemon, vegan foamer), a Seedlip Highball and a Seedlip Espresso Martini, plus Red Ribbon seltzer and house-made lemonade and citrus soda. It is frequently cited among the city's best mocktail bars.

venues.longDescription:
Bar Botanico is a plant-filled cocktail bar on Butler Street in Lawrenceville, and it runs one of the strongest zero-proof lineups in Pittsburgh — a city where, as local reporting has noted, the alcohol-free options are thinner than its bar scene would suggest. The room is dense with greenery, which suits the drinks: the spirit-free list is built on real non-alcoholic distillates rather than assembled from juice, and it covers registers most bars skip entirely.

The signature is the Cut Above Mezcal Sour, made with Cut Above's non-alcoholic mezcal alongside coconut water, lapsang souchong, jalapeno, lemon and a vegan foamer. That build is worth unpacking, because it demonstrates exactly what separates a considered zero-proof drink from a poor one. Lapsang souchong is a pine-smoked tea, and it supplies the smoke that mezcal would otherwise bring; the jalapeno provides heat; the lemon gives acid; and the vegan foamer supplies the texture and head that alcohol and egg white normally create. Four different ingredients each doing a job that alcohol would have done — that is the actual craft of spirit-free bartending. Alongside it the bar pours a Seedlip Highball and a Seedlip Espresso Martini, the latter being one of the harder drinks to render convincingly without vodka, plus Red Ribbon seltzer and house-made lemonade and citrus soda for anyone wanting something simpler.

It is frequently cited among the city's best places to drink without alcohol, and its Lawrenceville location puts it on the same stretch as most of Pittsburgh's better bars, so a mixed group has no reason to go anywhere else. Open most nights from 5pm, with weekend afternoons from 2pm, closed Tuesdays. With Solace still to open in the same neighbourhood and Bantha Tea Bar a mile away in Garfield, Lawrenceville is quietly becoming the part of Pittsburgh where drinking less is easiest — and Bar Botanico is currently the most accomplished room in it.

venues.name: Bar + Cart
venues.description: Bar + Cart Restaurant and Lounge opened in the former Khyber Pass Cafe space on Grand Avenue in St. Paul's Macalester-Groveland neighborhood, a partnership between longtime collaborators Ralena Young and Brian Riess. Young, an accomplished Twin Cities beverage director, anchors a serious drink program — and that extends to one of the metro's deepest zero-proof lists. The "Free Spirit" menu currently runs six house non-alcoholic cocktails spanning smoky to sweet — White Fox (coconut water, orange blossom, banana, egg white, cherry-bark vanilla), Up In Smoke (coconut water, grapefruit, jalapeño, basil, smoked salt), Hibiscus Punch, Fruit of the Desert, Devil in the Garden, and Lucky Me — alongside bottled St. Agrestis Phony Negronis in both the classic and mezcal styles. Axios Twin Cities named it the most expansive non-alcoholic list in its January 2026 Dry January roundup. The food leans elevated-comfort, from Coney Island dogs to fresh oysters.

venues.longDescription:
Bar + Cart opened in the former Khyber Pass Cafe space on Grand Avenue in St. Paul's Macalester-Groveland neighbourhood, a partnership between longtime collaborators Ralena Young and Brian Riess. Young is an accomplished Twin Cities beverage director, and her presence explains why the drinks here run deeper than the elevated-comfort food menu — Coney Island dogs at one end, fresh oysters at the other — would lead you to expect.

The zero-proof list is the reason it belongs high on any Twin Cities list. The Free Spirit menu currently runs six house non-alcoholic cocktails deliberately spread across the flavour spectrum rather than clustered at the sweet end, which is the single most common failing of a spirit-free list. White Fox is the technical showpiece, combining coconut water and orange blossom water with banana, egg white, lemon and cherry-bark vanilla — egg white doing the structural work that alcohol otherwise provides. Up In Smoke goes the opposite direction entirely: coconut water, grapefruit, jalapeño, basil, lime and smoked salt, a savoury and genuinely spicy drink. Between them sit Hibiscus Punch, built on hibiscus flowers with winter spices and citrus peel; Fruit of the Desert, which leans on grapefruit, lime, agave and Jarritos grapefruit soda; Devil in the Garden, using acid-adjusted Concord grape with lavender, lemon and pomegranate; and Lucky Me, a coconut, pandan and lime build. Bottled St. Agrestis Phony Negronis are stocked in both the classic and mezcal styles for anyone wanting the bitter register.

Axios Twin Cities named it the most expansive non-alcoholic list in the metro in its January 2026 Dry January round-up, describing "a cozy Grand Avenue bar/restaurant" with "the most expansive list of nonalcoholic options... ranging from smoky to sweet." Six house builds across smoke, spice, floral, sour and tropical is a complete bar programme by any measure. Open Monday through Saturday, to midnight at the weekend, closed Sundays.
venues.pressQuote: Bar + Cart, a cozy Grand Avenue bar/restaurant, had the most expansive list of nonalcoholic options, with nine distinctive mocktails ranging from smoky to sweet.

venues.name: Bar 'Cino
venues.description: Bar 'Cino is an Italian bar and restaurant on Newport's Washington Square, and it does something almost no other venue does: it prints the mocktails as the drinks, then offers to make them alcoholic for an upcharge. Four year-round non-alcoholic builds sit on the menu at $7 to $12, three of them made from shrubs and fresh juice and one built on the Spiritless range. Open daily from 11:30am.
signatureDrinks: The Bright Side ($7) — orange shrub, lime, cranberry, ginger
Spicy Pal-No-Ma ($7) — grapefruit, lime juice, spicy simple, jalapeño, sea salt
Rumor Has It... ($12) — Spiritless white cane, Spiritless coffee, vanilla, cream, fresh espresso
venues.longDescription:
Bar 'Cino occupies a corner of Washington Square in the middle of Newport, doing wood-fired Italian food and a proper bar programme, and it is worth the trip from Providence for one detail of menu design. On most drinks lists the cocktails are the drinks and the mocktails are an afterthought in a box at the bottom. Here the four non-alcoholic builds are simply listed as drinks, with the note 'make it a cocktail ($14.)' beside them. The alcoholic version is the modification. It is a small piece of typography that changes the experience of ordering entirely.

Three of the four are built from scratch ingredients rather than substitutes. Lambrufaux — the name a play on Lambrusco — runs a house blackberry shrub with lemon and soda, the vinegar giving it the tannic grip a red-wine spritz would have. The Bright Side is an orange shrub with lime, cranberry and ginger. The Spicy Pal-No-Ma is the paloma with the tequila simply removed and the gap filled with work: grapefruit, lime, a spicy simple syrup, fresh jalapeño and a sea-salt rim. All three are seven dollars, which is roughly half what a comparable drink costs in Providence.

The fourth, Rumor Has It, is the one built on finished non-alcoholic product — Spiritless white cane and Spiritless coffee with vanilla, cream and fresh espresso, an espresso-martini analogue at twelve dollars. Spiritless is one of the better American distilled-then-dealcoholised producers, so this drinks closer to the original than most.

Bar 'Cino sits inside the Providence-Warwick metro but has its own Newport character — Washington Square is the civic heart of the old colonial town, and the room fills with a mix of locals and visitors from late morning onward. A note on published lists: Rhode Island Monthly credited this bar with a Don't Call Me Shirley and a Pearly There. Neither is on the current menu; two of the four have rotated since. The four above are what was pouring when we checked.
venues.pressQuote: four original mocktails on the menu year-round

venues.name: Bar Contra
venues.description: Bar Contra is a technically ambitious cocktail bar on Orchard Street in the Lower East Side, from chefs Jeremiah Stone and Fabian von Hauske-Valtierra (of the former Michelin-starred Contra and Wildair) with mixologist Dave Arnold. It was named a winner of the inaugural NYC's Best Bars for NA Awards 2025 for its deeply experimental non-alcoholic menu, and its drink list carries a few low-ABV and no-ABV options alongside its $21 craft cocktails and creative small plates.

venues.longDescription: Bar Contra is the cocktail-driven evolution of Contra, the acclaimed Michelin-starred tasting-menu restaurant that chefs Jeremiah Stone and Fabian von Hauske-Valtierra ran at 138 Orchard Street for nearly a decade. For the bar, Stone and von Hauske teamed with mixologist Dave Arnold (of the bygone Booker & Dax and Existing Conditions), bringing high-precision technique to a more relaxed snacks-and-drinks format where bartenders chill glasses with liquid nitrogen and clarify drinks via centrifuge. The list is organized into shaken, stirred, carbonated and on-the-rocks cocktails, most priced at $21, and notably includes a few low-ABV and no-ABV (non-alcoholic) options built with the same from-scratch care. In January 2026, Bar Contra was named a winner of the inaugural NYC's Best Bars for NA Awards 2025 (presented by Bright Nights Social and Boisson), with Time Out reporting it "surprised judges with a deeply experimental NA menu built around seasonal produce, house ferments, clarified juices, toasted spices and the occasional curveball ingredient." Spirited signatures include the tequila-based Saltair (served with a Modelito sidecar), plus the Passion Fruit Lowball, Piscola, Firefly Mule and Candarin Orange. The food menu pairs high-end small plates with the drinks in a stylish, minimalist room.
venues.pressQuote: On the Lower East Side, Bar Contra surprised judges with a deeply experimental NA menu built around seasonal produce, house ferments, clarified juices, toasted spices and the occasional curveball ingredient.

venues.name: Bar Esmé
venues.description: Bar Esmé is the à la carte bar adjoining Esmé, the one-Michelin-star Lincoln Park restaurant opened in August 2021 by chef Jenner Tomaska and his partner Katrina Bravo. Where the flagship serves a tasting menu built around rotating collaborations with artists, the bar is a smaller, more casual route into the same kitchen without committing to the full format. Drinks are led by beverage director Stevan Miller, who also oversees Esmé and the group's French brasserie Petite Edith, and whose stated approach is the reverse of the usual order: non-alcoholic cocktails, he told Third Coast Review in 2026, are something he thinks of before every other part of the menu. A current zero-proof example is Apple Island — apple with habanero and agave, force-carbonated so it lands with the bite of a hard soda. Note that the bar does not publish a working drinks list online, so the rotating menu is best read on arrival, and any zero-proof drinks named in pre-2026 coverage predate the current beverage team. Service runs Wednesday to Sunday from 5pm.
venues.longDescription:
Bar Esmé is the à la carte bar attached to Esmé, the one-Michelin-star restaurant at 2200 N Clark Street in Lincoln Park opened in August 2021 by chef Jenner Tomaska and his partner Katrina Bravo. Where the main dining room serves a tasting menu built around rotating collaborations with artists, the bar is the way into the same kitchen without committing to the full format — a smaller room, a shorter menu, and a considerably lower barrier to entry for anyone who wants to taste this cooking on a weeknight. The restaurant serves Wednesday through Sunday from 5pm.

The drinks are run by beverage director Stevan Miller, who oversees the programmes at Esmé, Bar Esmé and the group's French brasserie Petite Edith, and who came to beverages sideways — he started as a barista in California before a colleague suggested he train as a sommelier. His stated approach to zero-proof drinks is the most useful thing to know about this bar: non-alcoholic cocktails, he told Third Coast Review in February 2026, are something he thinks of before every other part of the menu. That is the opposite of the usual sequence, where a zero-proof option is reverse-engineered from a finished cocktail list, and it shows in a drink like Apple Island — apple with habanero and agave, force-carbonated so it arrives with the bite of a hard soda rather than the flatness of a juice. Miller has named it as one of the drinks he is proudest of. Two practical notes. Bar Esmé does not publish its current drink list in a working form — the menu and about pages linked from Esmé's own navigation return errors — so the list rotates and is best read on arrival. And because the beverage team changed before 2026, any zero-proof drinks named in older coverage of this bar should be treated as historical rather than current.
venues.pressQuote: Non-alcoholic cocktails are something I think of before I do every other part of the menu.

venues.name: Bar Franca
venues.description: Bar Franca is a Euro-style cocktail and sound bar on South Main Street in the Historic Core of Downtown Los Angeles, open only Thursday to Saturday from 9pm to 2am. It is licensed, and its drink menu carries a titled Zero Proof and Low ABV section: Bonfire Water, made with fresh-pressed watermelon, hibiscus and Lyre's Italian Spritz; Espresso Esplatore, built on Pathfinder Hemp and Root with espresso, tonic and citrus; and Palomanada, with grapefruit, citrus, agave, soda and salt. Estrella Galicia Zero Proof is stocked in cans alongside two low-alcohol Stiegl radlers. The room has tall ceilings, floral wallpaper, a long bar and semi-separate lounge seating, and the music programming is the point as much as the drinks.
venues.address: 438 S Main St, Los Angeles, CA 90013

Espresso Esplatore - Pathfinder Hemp & Root, espresso, tonic, citrus
Palomanada - grapefruit, citrus, agave, soda, salt
venues.longDescription:
Bar Franca occupies a shopfront on South Main Street in the Old Bank District, the stretch of the Historic Core where Downtown's bar scene is densest, and it describes itself as a stylish little Euro-cocktail sound bar. The sound part is not decoration: the programming leans on guest selectors and the room is built around the system, which puts it closer to a listening bar than to a cocktail lounge. Tall ceilings, floral wallpaper, a long bar and semi-separate lounge seating; golden lighting throughout.

The drink menu carries a section headed Zero Proof and Low ABV, and there are three house builds in it. Bonfire Water is fresh-pressed watermelon and hibiscus lengthened with Lyre's Italian Spritz, the non-alcoholic Aperol analogue, which gives it the bitter-orange backbone the fruit would otherwise lack. Espresso Esplatore is the most substantial of the three - Pathfinder Hemp and Root with espresso, tonic and citrus - and reads as a bar drink rather than a coffee. Palomanada is the simplest, grapefruit and citrus with agave, soda and salt, and it is the one to order if you want length rather than intensity. Alongside them the fridge carries Estrella Galicia's Zero Proof lager in cans, and two Stiegl radlers at 0.5% and 0.9%, which are worth flagging as genuinely low-alcohol rather than alcohol-free for anyone avoiding it entirely.

The practical detail that matters most here is the schedule, because it is unusual and easy to get wrong. Bar Franca opens three nights a week and it opens late: Thursday, Friday and Saturday only, 9pm to 2am, closed Sunday through Wednesday. That makes it a genuinely late-night option in a city where most kitchens and many bars have wound down by midnight, and it makes a wasted trip very easy on any other night. It is a short walk from the Pershing Square Metro station and sits among enough other Main Street bars that it works as one stop rather than a destination on its own. Note also that the low-ABV items share the section heading with the zero-proof ones, so read the menu rather than ordering by the header.

venues.name: Bar Hygge
venues.description: Bar Hygge is a Fairmount brewpub open since 2016, run by owners Stew and Julie Keener, Tom Baker, and Peggy Zwerver. Named for the Danish concept of cozy contentment (pronounced "huu-guh"), it houses Brewery Techne, a 10-barrel brewhouse pouring rotating house draft and cask beers alongside contemporary American boards and comfort-food entrees. The venue is recognized for an inclusive, sober-friendly approach: alongside the bar's cocktails and draft wines, it stocks alcohol-removed wine, a zero-proof amaro, and signature non-alcoholic cocktails. Visit Philadelphia's zero-proof guide highlights two named mocktails — "Amateur Jazz," built on Ritual's gin alternative with cinchona bark, herbs, citrus, and soda, and "Spice Up Your Life," made with Seedlip Garden 108, caramelized pineapple, strawberry oleo saccharum, jalapeño, lemon, and soda — plus a lavender lemonade and a Ritual/Seedlip spritz. Located near Eastern State Penitentiary, it's a neighborhood favorite for drinkers and non-drinkers alike.
venues.longDescription:
Bar Hygge has traded in Fairmount since 2016, run by Stew and Julie Keener with Tom Baker and Peggy Zwerver. The name is the Danish word for cosy contentment — pronounced roughly huu-guh — and the room is built to it. Inside is Brewery Techne, a ten-barrel brewhouse pouring rotating house draft and cask beers alongside contemporary American boards and comfort food.

Cask beer is worth pausing on, because it is rare in American brewpubs and it tells you something about the house. Cask ale is unfiltered, unpasteurised and naturally carbonated in the vessel it is served from, poured at cellar temperature by hand pump rather than pushed with gas. It is more work, it spoils faster, and it is done by people who care about beer as a craft rather than as a product.

That same disposition shows in how the bar treats people who are not drinking. Visit Philadelphia's zero-proof guide describes it as a beloved neighbourhood bar known for creating an inclusive atmosphere for all guests, and the stock backs that up: alcohol-removed wine, a zero-proof amaro, and signature non-alcoholic cocktails alongside the beer. A zero-proof amaro is the notable item — amaro is the bitter Italian digestif category, and having a genuine bitter option means a non-drinker can end a meal the way everyone else does rather than switching to something sweet.

The named drinks are Amateur Jazz and Spice Up Your Life, plus a Lavender Lemonade and an NA Spritz. Four builds is a real list for a brewpub, where one non-alcoholic beer is more typically the whole answer.

A brewpub is also a forgiving format socially: people order at their own pace, the beer is the topic of conversation rather than the intoxication, and a cask-ale bar attracts people who want to taste rather than to drink volume. Open Tuesday to Friday from four, and from ten in the morning at weekends, closing at eleven.
venues.pressQuote: Bar Hygge is one of Fairmount's beloved neighborhood bars, known for creating an inclusive atmosphere for all guests — including those choosing to skip the alcohol.

venues.name: Bar Iris
venues.description: Bar Iris is a Japanese-influenced craft cocktail bar at 2310 Polk Street in Russian Hill / Polk Gulch, opened in early 2022 as the sibling to chef David Yoshimura's Michelin-starred restaurant Nisei next door. The program leans on Japanese spirits and long, seasonal ingredient lists, and its non-alcoholic offering is unusually deep: the bar keeps a standalone alcohol-free menu that currently runs nine N/A cocktails named for Japanese places, from the Kyoto — a non-alcoholic martini of Amass and Dhōs N/A spirits with Aplos Arise, narazuke brine and tsukemono — to the Yakushima (Okinawa purple yam, Wilderton Earthen, kalamansi, li hin mui), alongside a bottle list of dealcoholized sake, sparkling wine and riesling. Several cocktails on the main list are also marked as available non-alcoholic, and The San Francisco Standard has reported that more than half its cocktails can be made without alcohol.

venues.longDescription:
Bar Iris opened in early 2022 at 2310 Polk Street as the bar sibling to Nisei, chef David Yoshimura's Michelin-starred tasting-menu restaurant next door in Russian Hill / Polk Gulch. Where Nisei is formal and reservation-bound, Bar Iris takes walk-ins, and it inherited the restaurant's Japanese framing: a spirits list heavy on Japanese whisky and shochu, ice and glassware treated as part of the drink, and service explicitly modelled on omotenashi. Under bar manager Timofei Osipenko the cocktail list has run to ten-ingredient builds using yuzu kosho, hojicha, calamansi and Okinawan purple yam, and the bar earned Pearl Recommended Bar recognition in 2025. It is closed Monday and Tuesday and opens at 3pm on Friday and Saturday, later in the week.

The alcohol-free programme is not a footnote but a separately published menu, and the printed list is a starting point rather than a boundary — the bartenders will build to a guest's description. The current N/A list runs nine cocktails named for Japanese places, priced $20 to $21, essentially at parity with the $21–$23 full-proof list: among them the Aichi (Seward N/A gin, red shiso, N/A riesling, Muri Yamile, honey, Q soda), the Kyoto — an N/A martini of Amass and Dhōs N/A vodka with Aplos Arise, narazuke brine and tsukemono — the Tokyo (Amass N/A gin, N/A vermouth, Pathfinder N/A amaro, N/A sake, Aplos N/A bitters), and the Yakushima (Okinawa purple yam, Wilderton Earthen, kalamansi, li hin mui). Several cocktails on the main list carry an "also available as n/a" note, and a non-alcoholic bottle list backs it all: Suntory Free beer, Origami "zero" dealcoholized sake, Odd Bird blanc de blancs, Non 3 verjus bubbles, Dr. Lo dealcoholized Mosel riesling and a Saint Viviana sauvignon blanc, currently sold by the bottle only. Earlier lists carried the Heiwa, Osaka Bay, Ninjin Sour, the Okinawa and a Tsukemono Martini; those have rotated off, which is the point, because the alcohol-free list turns over on the same cycle as the alcoholic one instead of sitting static for years. Surveying the city's best non-alcoholic drinking in December 2023, The San Francisco Standard noted that "more than half the cocktails on this Polk Street Japanese-style bar's list can be made without alcohol."
venues.pressQuote: More than half the cocktails on this Polk Street Japanese-style bar's list can be made without alcohol.

venues.name: Bar Julian
venues.description: Bar Julian is the rooftop bar on top of Thompson Savannah in the Eastern Wharf development, the tallest roof in the city, looking straight down the Savannah River. Its cocktail list prints a section headed Booze-Free carrying four drinks between $12 and $14, all built on non-alcoholic spirits — a zero-proof agave, a zero-proof London dry, Lyre's cane spirit and a zero-proof aperitif — rather than assembled from juices. The kitchen is Mediterranean-leaning and shareable, and the bar keeps unusually long hours for Savannah, opening at 7am for coffee and running to 11pm, or midnight on Friday and Saturday.

venues.longDescription:
Thompson Savannah anchors the Eastern Wharf development downriver from the historic waterfront, and Bar Julian occupies its top floor — the highest rooftop bar in the city, with the river running directly below and the bridge to the north. The room went through a Mediterranean-forward refresh that reworked both the space and the food menu, and the bar programme was rebuilt with it.

The alcohol-free drinks sit under a heading that tells you how the bar thinks about them: Booze-Free, printed on the cocktail list rather than segregated onto a separate card. All four are spirit-led. Perfect Timing, at $12 the cheapest, runs a zero-proof agave spirit against acidified pineapple, agave and saline — a salted, sour drink rather than a sweet one. Turning a Page is the most involved: a zero-proof London dry with clarified chai concentrate, raspberry and lemon, a build that requires actual bar technique to clarify and hold. Caribbean Firewater takes a zero-proof aperitif with a fermented fruit blend, citrus and tonic, and lands closest to a bitter highball.

One drink on the section needs a plain flag. Sunrise Highway is built on Lyre's cane spirit with watermelon juice and a lime CBD seltzer — the CBD is in the mixer, not the spirit, and anyone avoiding cannabinoids should order around it. The rest of the list is free of them.

The hours are the other reason to know about this place. Bar Julian opens at 7am and stays open to 11pm on weekdays and midnight at weekends, so unlike most of Savannah's better zero-proof lists it is not a 4pm-onwards proposition. The food is shareable and Mediterranean — flatbreads, kebabs, wood-grilled oysters, lamb shoulder.
venues.pressQuote: Bar Julian is the jaw-dropping rooftop bar above Thompson Savannah, with impressive views of the historic downtown.
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: Visit Savannah, Where to Find Incredible Mocktails in Savannah

venues.name: Bar Kamon
venues.description: Bar Kamon is a Japanese cocktail bar hidden behind a door inside Asa Bakery in East Village, working with Japanese spirits, house-made ingredients, clarified cocktails and highballs. Its printed menu carries a line for dealer's choice mocktails: the bartenders will build to your preference using a range of non-alcoholic spirits, house syrups and sodas. There is no fixed zero-proof list, so nothing is named here — but the stock behind the bar is real, and one of the team describes themselves on the bar's own site as a sober bartender who makes their own amari. There is no fixed zero-proof list, so this is a policy rather than a menu, and it is the reason the bar is listed here: the non-alcoholic bottles are stocked and the house syrups that go into the full-strength drinks are available to you. Seatings run from half past five, closed Tuesdays, to ten most nights and eleven on Friday and Saturday.
venues.hours: Mon 5:30pm-10pm; Tue closed; Wed-Thu 5:30pm-10pm; Fri-Sat 5:30pm-11pm; Sun 5:30pm-10pm
venues.longDescription:
Bar Kamon is reached through a discreet door inside Asa Bakery on 14th Street in East Village, and it is a Japanese bar in the specific sense — seasonal menus organised around the spirits and regions of Japan, clarified cocktails, highballs built with care, house-made ingredients and a short list of small bites rather than a full kitchen. It seats a small number of people at a time and takes reservations.

The zero-proof offering here is a policy rather than a list. Printed on the drinks menu, under the cocktails, is a line for dealer's choice mocktails: the bartender will make what you want using a variety of non-alcoholic spirits, house-made syrups and sodas. That is a meaningful difference from a bar that will grudgingly assemble juice and soda — it means the non-alcoholic bottles are stocked and the syrups that go into the full-strength drinks are available to you.

We do not name any drinks for this bar, and that is deliberate. There is no printed zero-proof list, so any drink name we published would be a guess at what one bartender made on one night, and it would go stale immediately. Tell the bar what you like — smoky, bitter, citrus-forward, tea-based — and let them build it, the same way the dealer's choice works on the alcoholic side.

One detail on the team page is worth knowing, because it explains why the offer exists at all: a member of the bar staff describes themselves in their own words as a sober bartender who enjoys botany and herbalism and uses those hobbies to make their own amari. A bar with a sober bartender behind the stick tends to take the question seriously.

Hours are limited and worth checking: the bar is closed on Tuesdays and opens at half past five, running to ten most nights and eleven on Friday and Saturday, with the kitchen calling last orders an hour before close.

One practical note for anyone searching: the bar calls itself Bar Kamon on its own site and its own menu, but map apps list the same address as Kamon Craft Cocktail Bar, so a map search on the full name is the reliable route. The format is worth understanding before you go. This is a small room reached through a bakery, seating a few dozen people, and it runs on reservations and seatings rather than on walk-ins and a crowd; the bar also takes full buyouts for up to fifty guests and runs industry nights. The drinks are Japanese in method as well as in ingredient — clarified cocktails, highballs built with attention to the ice and the pour, house-made syrups and infusions — and the small bites, a Korean cucumber salad and a vegetarian umami croquette among them, are made to go with the drinking rather than to be dinner.
venues.pressQuote: Tucked behind a discreet door inside Asa Bakery in San Diego's East Village, Bar Kamon blends Japanese bartending traditions with modern cocktail techniques.

venues.name: Bar Kap
venues.description: Bar Kap is a cocktail bar that opened in August 2026 inside the House of Tan Yeok Nee, the 1880s Teochew mansion at 101 Penang Road that is a gazetted national monument. The menu, titled the Kapitan's Archives, is arranged in four eras of the house's history, and each era carries one drink printed at zero strength. Last Call is built on oolong, roasted barley, honey and chenpi; Sister Act on white tea, cucumber, coriander, rojak flower and quinine; TCM Drawer No.3 on soy milk, ginger, honeydew, chestnut honey and gula melaka; and Gong Fu Merchant on aged tea, black date and rock sugar. It is open every day from 5pm to midnight.

venues.longDescription:
The House of Tan Yeok Nee was built in the 1880s for a Teochew merchant who, in the bar's own telling, arrived from elsewhere and made his stature through will and enterprise, and it has been a gazetted national monument since 1974. In the years since, the railway took its front land for the station on Tank Road, it served as St Mary's Home and then as the Salvation Army's base, and it has been restored more than once. Bar Kap, opened in August 2026 by GAIA Group, a member of the Karim Group, uses that timeline as its menu. The Kapitan's Archives runs through four eras: Kapitan for Tan Yeok Nee's own time, Station Master for the railway years, Order for the charitable decades, and Dynasty for the present. Each cocktail is paired with an object from an imagined collection, an abacus, a whistle, a medicine drawer, drawn on the menu beside the drink. Honeycombers reviewed it in its August 2026 new-bars round-up and made the point that matters here: each part also includes a zero-proof drink.

Those zero-proof drinks are printed with an empty strength meter rather than sidelined on a separate card, and three of the four are unambiguous. Last Call (S$18), in the Station Master era, is oolong, lemon, roasted barley, honey, chenpi dried mandarin peel, saline and gold. Sister Act (S$18), in the Order era, is white tea, cucumber, coriander, rojak flower, sea salt and quinine. TCM Drawer No.3 (S$18), in the Dynasty era, is a soy milk drink with ginger, honeydew, chestnut honey and gula melaka, and Honeycombers notes it can be spiked with coconut rum on request, which is the version to decline. The fourth, Gong Fu Merchant (S$20) in the Kapitan era, is listed at zero strength with aged tea, fizz, vinegar, black date and rock sugar, but its ingredient line also says amaro; ask whether that is a non-alcoholic amaro before ordering, because the menu does not say. Prices carry service charge and GST on top. The bar opens every day from 5pm to midnight, sits a few minutes from Dhoby Ghaut MRT, and takes reservations online.
venues.pressQuote: Each part also includes a zero-proof drink, like the TCM Drawer No. 3 ($18).

venues.name: Kindred
venues.description: Kindred is a vegan cocktail bar and restaurant in South Park, open since 2015 and styled as "equal parts evil lair and Victorian cocktail salon," pairing plant-based fare with craft drinks and a death-metal soundtrack. Voted Best Vegan Bar in the U.S. by VegNews and a Tales of the Cocktail honoree, it keeps a dedicated "Zero-Proof" menu its team treats "just as intentional and special as any other part of the menu." Named alcohol-free options include the Kiss of Steel (cold-brew, oat milk, cinnamon, coconut, orange twist), the Zombie Prescription (pineapple-turmeric shrub, grapefruit, lemon, cinnamon, ginger, agave), the tropical-goth Miracle Cure (pineapple, lime, coconut, passionfruit, Thai basil, lemongrass, charcoal), and a Phony Negroni. It ranked among Yelp's Top 25 U.S. mocktail spots.
venues.longDescription:
Kindred has been on 30th Street in South Park since 2015, and it is the rare bar whose own description of itself is accurate: equal parts evil lair and Victorian cocktail salon. It is entirely vegan, the soundtrack is death metal, the ceiling is covered in ornate gothic detail, and VegNews voted it the best vegan bar in the United States. It is also a Tales of the Cocktail honoree, which is the part that matters for the drinks — this is a serious cocktail bar wearing an unserious costume. The same team went on to open Mothership, the sci-fi tiki bar a few blocks away, so the two together give South Park an unusual concentration of good zero-proof drinking.

The non-alcoholic list is a standing Zero-Proof menu that the team has said it treats "just as intentional and special as any other part of the menu," and the builds bear that out across a genuinely wide range of registers. The Kiss of Steel is essentially a dessert-adjacent coffee drink — cold brew, oat milk, cinnamon and coconut with an orange twist. The Zombie Prescription is built on a pineapple-turmeric shrub with grapefruit, lemon, cinnamon, ginger and agave, which puts real acid and heat into the glass rather than sugar. The Miracle Cure is the tropical-goth showpiece, combining pineapple, lime, coconut and passionfruit with Thai basil, lemongrass and charcoal, and there is a Phony Negroni for anyone who wants the bitter aperitif register covered. Yelp placed Kindred among its top twenty-five mocktail spots in the country. For a non-drinker who is also vegan, this is one of the very few bars anywhere where every single thing on both menus is available to you — which is a rarer experience than it should be.

venues.name: Bar Lina
venues.description: The basement aperitivo bar beneath Lina Stores' Brewer Street delicatessen, the Italian grocer that has anchored Soho since 1944. Upstairs is all fresh pasta and hanging salumi; downstairs the green-and-brass bar pours a negroni-led list with an unusually well-built page of virgin cocktails. Three zero-proof drinks are constructed with the same cordials-and-bitters seriousness as the boozy side: Essenza on Amaro 0% with lemon balm cordial and a strawberry and lavender soda, Euphoria on Amaro 0% with raspberry, mint and tonic, and Ananas & Menta on Gin 0% with pineapple cordial and a pepper bitter. Aperitivo snacks come from the deli, and the room works as well for an early evening as a nightcap.

venues.longDescription:
Lina Stores has been feeding Soho since 1944, and its pistachio-green Brewer Street shopfront is one of the neighbourhood's most recognisable survivors. Bar Lina is the cellar beneath it: a small, low-lit aperitivo bar that takes the delicatessen's Italian instincts and applies them to drinks. The list is negroni-led on the alcoholic side, but the reason it belongs in this directory is the Virgin Cocktails page, which is written with a care that most Soho bars still reserve for the hard stuff. All three builds start from zero-proof Italian bases rather than fruit juice, and all three read like drinks someone argued over: Essenza pairs Amaro 0% with lemon balm cordial, fresh lemon and a strawberry and lavender soda; Euphoria works Amaro 0% against raspberry, mint and tonic; Ananas & Menta sets a gin alternative against pineapple cordial, mint and a pepper bitter that gives the finish actual grip.

The room itself is the other half of the appeal. It is genuinely small, which keeps the volume conversational, and the aperitivo format means the kitchen requirement is handled by the deli upstairs: plates of salumi, cheese and filled focaccia arrive at the bar rather than a full menu, so the drinks stay the point. An alcohol-free order here does not feel like a workaround, because the Italian aperitivo tradition the bar draws on was always about bitterness, ritual and something salty alongside, none of which requires alcohol. Hours run to 11.30pm through the week, late enough for a post-dinner stop, and the Sunday afternoon opening makes it one of the more civilised places in central London to end a weekend without a drink. For anyone working through Soho's cocktail row on a dry month, this cellar is the stop that asks the least explaining: order the Essenza, take the stool by the bar, and the evening runs itself.
venues.pressQuote: This cosy, speakeasy-esque bar under Soho's iconic Italian delicatessen Lina Stores offers up a trio of non-alcoholic cocktails

venues.name: Bar Lina
venues.description: Bar Lina is the low-lit aperitivo-bar sibling of Lina Stores' Manchester restaurant, tucked behind the Quay Street dining room opposite the Opera House. Styled after late-1960s and 70s Italian design — dark-red monochrome, velvet banquettes, chrome and mirrored walls, with Italo disco DJs at weekends — it pairs Italian spirits and cocktails with a genuine alcohol-free offering. The zero-proof list is a concise but well-considered range of alcohol-free cocktails, all built around a 0% amaro spirit, backed by a rotating line-up of craft 0% beers on tap and in cans.

venues.longDescription:
Bar Lina opened in 2025 as the sultrier sibling to Lina Stores, the London-born Italian deli-and-restaurant group whose Quay Street site is its first opening outside the capital. It sits behind the ground-floor restaurant in the Spinningfields corner of Manchester city centre, directly opposite the Opera House, and leans hard into Italian aperitivo culture — post-work drinks that carry on into laid-back cocktails late into the night.

The room contrasts an industrial architectural shell with Italian design from the late 1960s and 70s: a monochrome dark-red colour scheme, plush velvet banquettes, chrome accents and mirrored walls that lend it a low-lit, speakeasy feel. An 80s Italo disco soundtrack runs throughout, with DJ nights spinning Italo disco, funk and electronic music on Fridays and Saturdays until late. The bar keeps late hours — Wednesday through Saturday, running to 1.30am — and welcomes walk-ins.

The drinks list celebrates Italian spirits and ingredients, from the signature Bloody Martini (tomato, Mancino Secco vermouth and vodka) to a wine list drawn from across Italy, but the alcohol-free side is a deliberate part of the offering rather than an afterthought. Manchester's Finest describes it as "a concise but well-considered range of alcohol-free cocktails, all based around a 0% amaro spirit," letting the bar rebuild spritz-style Italian aperitivi without the alcohol. Alongside the zero-proof cocktails there is a solid selection of modern, crafty 0% beers on tap and in cans from breweries including Hawkshead, Jever and Schneider Weisse — enough to see out a full alcohol-free evening, from aperitivo through to a late nightcap.
venues.pressQuote: The aperitivo bar offers a concise but well-considered range of alcohol-free cocktails, all based around a 0% amaro spirit.

venues.name: Bar Margaret
venues.description: Bar Margaret is a craft cocktail bar in the Village of West Greenville, the arts district a mile west of downtown, and its alcohol-free drinks sit under a heading that tells you the whole attitude: Don't Call Them Mocktails. The builds use non-alcoholic gin and bourbon rather than juice, worked against house components including a zingy lime syrup, citrus zest and ginger beer, and the bar is explicit that its staff play with flavour the same way with or without the alcohol. Open from noon Tuesday through Saturday — an unusually early start for a cocktail room — to 11pm midweek and midnight at weekends, closed Sunday and Monday.
venues.longDescription:
The Village of West Greenville is the old textile district turned arts quarter, about a mile west of downtown, and Bar Margaret is its cocktail bar. The name of its alcohol-free section — Don't Call Them Mocktails — is a small piece of menu writing that carries a lot of information.

The word mocktail has a problem, and bars that take this seriously keep trying to escape it. It frames the drink as an imitation of something else, and it carries the association of sweet, childish, unserious. Naming the section against that is a statement that the drinks are their own thing, and Bar Margaret backs it with construction: non-alcoholic gin and bourbon as bases rather than fruit juice, cut with a sharp house lime syrup, citrus zest and ginger beer.

That choice of two spirits rather than one matters more than it looks. A bar stocking only a zero-proof gin can build the sour and the highball; adding a bourbon alternative opens the whole dark-spirit side — the old fashioneds, the sours with weight, the drinks people order in winter. Very few bars in this directory stock both.

The bar's own framing is that its staff love playing with flavour with or without the alcohol, and the useful implication for a customer is that describing what you like will get you somewhere here rather than getting you a cranberry and soda.

The hours are worth knowing. Bar Margaret opens at noon Tuesday through Saturday — genuinely early for a cocktail bar and a real advantage if you want a drink in the afternoon rather than the evening — and closes at 11pm midweek, midnight on Friday and Saturday. Closed Sunday and Monday, so plan the weekend around it.
venues.pressQuote: Bar Margaret staff loves to play around with flavors, with or without the alcohol.
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: TOWN Carolina, Mocktails for Dry July

venues.name: Bar Margot
venues.description: Bar Margot is the cocktail lounge on the mezzanine of the Four Seasons Hotel Atlanta in Midtown, a low-lit room that trades from mid-afternoon to late and has become a standing recommendation for spirit-free drinking in the district. Its zero-proof cocktails are built as direct translations of the spirits list rather than as a separate afterthought menu, each one mirroring a specific alcoholic drink on the same card. Named alcohol-free pours include the Lil' Coltraine, made with smoked guava and rosemary, and the Garden Party, a cucumber and hibiscus drink. The kitchen serves American and globally-inspired plates with a Southern accent, and the neighbouring Brasserie Margot handles full dining. Service is hotel-standard, which in practice means the non-alcoholic order arrives without comment.

venues.longDescription:
Bar Margot occupies the mezzanine level of the Four Seasons Hotel Atlanta at 75 14th Street NE, a half-flight above the lobby in the heart of Midtown. The room is deliberately dim and unhurried — banquettes, low tables, a long bar — and DiningOut's 2026 zero-proof survey described it as moody, relaxed, and exactly the kind of room that makes you want to stay for another round. It opens at three in the afternoon every day and runs to eleven, or midnight on Friday and Saturday, sitting in the gap between an afternoon meeting spot and a proper late bar. The food menu injects American and globally inspired cooking with a Southern accent; the adjacent Brasserie Margot handles full French dining for anyone who wants a table rather than a stool.

The non-alcoholic side is programmed rather than improvised. The zero-proof drinks are not a separate afterthought menu but direct translations of the spirits list: DiningOut Atlanta describes each one as reading like a direct translation of something on the cocktail menu, with the Lil’ Coltraine pulling smoked guava and rosemary from its alcoholic counterpart and the Garden Party reaching a cucumber-and-hibiscus profile without leaning on St-Germain to get there. Two named drinks anchor the list. The Lil' Coltraine is built on smoked guava with rosemary, using smoke and herb to supply the weight that alcohol normally provides. The Garden Party is the lighter of the pair, a cucumber and hibiscus drink that reads floral and dry rather than sweet. Both are made behind the same bar, with the same ice, glassware and garnish discipline, as the signature alcoholic pours like the Lazy Suze-n and the Gin Margot. Because Bar Margot is a fully licensed hotel lounge with a deep spirits list, it sits at a four on our scale: the spirit-free programme is real, named and continuously maintained, but the room is not alcohol-free.
venues.pressQuote: The mezzanine perch inside the Four Seasons Midtown is moody, relaxed, and exactly the kind of room that makes you want to stay for another round.

venues.longDescription:
Bar Moga is a 1920s-era Japanese cocktail bar on West Houston Street, built around the Taishō-period idea of yōshoku — Western dishes absorbed and remade inside Japanese cooking — with jazz, shochu and Japanese whisky at its centre. The name refers to the moga, the modern girls of 1920s Japan who cut their hair and went out drinking, which tells you the register: not a reverent temple to Japanese bartending but a room about a moment when Japan and the West were busy borrowing from each other. It opens from 5pm, to 12.30am on Friday and Saturday, with weekend brunch from noon.

It was one of seven winners at NYC's Best Bars for NA 2025. Worth being precise here, because the awards are often described wrongly: they run a single flat, unranked winners tier rather than named categories, so Bar Moga is a winner, not a category winner. The judges described a non-alcoholic menu that follows a journey from morning to night, starting with a coffee-based drink, culminating in an amber sky and finally a white night — praising the creativity and the fact that the drinks deliver what they promise. That structure is real and it is the reason to come: the ZERO-PROOF section runs five drinks, all $14, arranged as a day. Morning In Ethiopia opens with coconut water, Seedlip Garden, caramel, espresso, Kentucky 74, cardamom and nutmeg. Daydreaming is the bright midpoint — lemon, yuzu, agave, shiso and Topo Chico. Amber Sky is dusk, on Lyre's Italian Spritz with orange, grapefruit, lemon, rose and honey, and it is the one the trade rates: Sam Bail, who founded the awards, called it a perfectly balanced and delicate sour, noting approvingly that it uses aquafaba rather than egg white for texture. Twilight follows on Lyre's dark cane spirit with shiso, yuzu, lavender, oat, wasanbon and matcha. Byakuya — white night — closes on Hakkaisan amazake with sakura, orange and pomegranate.
venues.pressQuote: The Amber Sky is a perfectly balanced and delicate cocktail that's basically a sour, served up, made with a non-alcoholic bitter aperitif, grapefruit, lemon and beautiful notes of rose. I also appreciate that it uses aquafaba instead of egg whites.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Sam Bail, quoted by Morgan Carter

venues.longDescription:
Moon — publicly branded Bar Moon — is a jewel-box cocktail lounge perched above Post Oak Boulevard in Houston's Uptown/Galleria district, inside the BLVD Place complex, sitting directly above the Italian restaurant Tavola. The venue opened in November 2025 as a joint venture between The Bastion Collection — the hospitality group behind Michelin-starred Le Jardinier — and Café Natalie, Houston's longtime leader in luxury events; the collaboration operates under the banner Bastion Events, led by Bastion Collection COO Deleon Pinto and Café Natalie owner/partner Chris Nguyen.

The kitchen and bar are overseen by a Michelin-pedigreed team: Culinary Director Alain Verzeroli, a protégé of Joël Robuchon whose career spans roughly ten Michelin stars, sets the culinary direction alongside Executive Chef Marco Incerti (who also runs Tavola's kitchen) and Executive Pastry Chef Salvatore Martone. Head Bartender Joao Diniz leads the drinks program, spirited and zero-proof alike. The room leans into its lunar theming with emerald-green velvet walls, tigerwood paneling, and faux emeralds suspended from the ceiling, paired with live jazz nights and DJ sets; walk-ins are welcome, though table service after 8:30pm requires a reservation via Resy or OpenTable.

Diniz's bar extends the same ingredient-driven precision to guests skipping alcohol. Moon's $10 zero-proof list is built from scratch rather than off-the-shelf NA spirits: Verjuice (red verjus, Three Cent grapefruit soda), Rice & Shine (toasted rice, pineapple, lapsang tea, warming spices), Laguna (garam masala, coconut water, cacao nibs), and Familiar Tides, a salted-pineapple-and-lime margarita riff finished with cilantro salt foam. Houston Press singled out the program in its 2026 Dry January mocktail guide, writing that 'the jewel-box cocktail bar perched above Post Oak Boulevard brings the same precision to its zero-proof offerings as its spirited menu.'
venues.pressQuote: The jewel-box cocktail bar perched above Post Oak Boulevard brings the same precision to its zero-proof offerings as its spirited menu.

venues.longDescription:
Bar Mordecai is a cocktail bar and restaurant on Dundas Street West in Toronto's Little Portugal / Dundas West neighborhood, styled after the hotel lobby bars of decades past and inspired by the aesthetics of Wes Anderson's films. Downstairs from the main room sits the Green Room Bar alongside four private karaoke rooms, each themed around a different era of musical history. The kitchen runs a shared-plates menu built to work as snacks or a full meal, and the bar pours local and international beer and wine alongside its cocktail list. Bar Mordecai is open Wednesday through Sunday evenings — from 6pm, and from 8pm on Sunday — and closed Monday and Tuesday.

The venue's printed menu carries a dedicated "NON-ALC OFFERINGS" section rather than treating alcohol-free drinks as an afterthought. Two named zero-proof cocktails anchor it: the Gems by the Pond ($11), made with JNPR ginger non-alcoholic gin, guava, coconut, lemon, cucumber and soda, and the Pink Lloyd ($11), built from Martini Floreale aperitivo, Bark & Bitter Novara, Noa sweet vermouth, Lucano Amaro Zero and an orange slice. The same section lists a Godspeed Brewery Jasmine and Peach Iced Tea ($6), non-alcoholic beer including Guinness 0.0, Corona Cero and Bellwoods' "Stay Classy" IPA, and non-alcoholic wine — Mionetto De-Alc Prosecco and Prima Pavé Bianca D'Or.

NOW Toronto included Bar Mordecai in its January 2026 roundup of Toronto bars taking mocktails seriously, writing that "whether you like it tropical and fresh or dark and bitter, there's a mocktail for you at Mordecai," and singling out its "zero proof Guiness."
venues.pressQuote: "Whether you like it tropical and fresh or dark and bitter, there's a mocktail for you at Mordecai. They even have zero proof Guiness!"

venues.name: Bar None
venues.description: Bar None is a zero-proof evening bar in Chicago's West Loop, running Friday to Sunday from 5pm to 11pm inside Froth, the coffee cafe in the lobby of The Duncan at 1515 W Monroe St. It launched on 28 February 2026 from Heritage Hospitality Group, the team behind Froth, with beverage director Luke Nevin-Gattle (previously Bunker and Larry's). Every cocktail is genuinely alcohol-free, built on real NA spirits at $13 — a St. Agrestis Phony Negroni, an espresso martini with Ritual rum alternative and Pathfinder, Good Vibrations with Ritual gin alternative and Giffard elderflower, a spicy margarita with Ritual agave and Lyre's Italian orange, and a Gold Rush — alongside nine non-alcoholic beers and ciders at $6 and Leitz Eins Zwei Zero wines at $9. IMPORTANT: the venue brands itself a THC-integrated sober lounge. Any cocktail can be upgraded with a 2.5mg THC microdose for $4, and it sells 5mg THC seltzers at $9. The alcohol-free drinks stand on their own, but anyone avoiding all intoxicants should order without the upgrade and skip the seltzers.
