venues.longDescription:
Brick & Mortar occupies an upstairs room at 567 Massachusetts Avenue in Central Square, reached through an unmarked door next to Central Kitchen, and has been one of the anchors of Cambridge's cocktail scene for years. Alongside service it runs a programme of craft cocktail classes for groups, which is unusual for a bar of its size and has become part of its identity. Boston Magazine, in the guide to the city's best mocktails it updated in January 2026, wrote that this hip Cambridge bar, known especially for its adventurous cocktail menu and craft cocktail classes for groups, does not neglect its alcohol-free patrons — and noted that the zero-proof menu is stacked with a classic negroni and a jumbo strawberry-infused spritz. The bar prints the alcohol-free drinks as a named section of the standing menu, which is the practical difference between a real programme and a bartender's improvisation.

The three drinks on that section are all $15, the same order of price as the alcoholic cocktails, and each is described on the menu with the same detail. Less Than Zero is presented as a zero-alcohol spritz, combining Stappi Italian Red with Spirit of Milano non-alcoholic amaro, strawberry, fresh lime and grapefruit, served over ice. The Count Camillo is a zero-proof negroni named for Camillo Negroni himself, stirred from Landry London Dry non-alcoholic gin, Lyre's Italian Orange non-alcoholic aperitivo and non-alcoholic Lucano amaro and served over a large rock. Hong Kong Garden is the outlier, flagged on the menu as low-ABV rather than fully zero, and is shaken from a non-alcoholic ginger spirit with pineapple, lime and Peychaud's bitters over a large rock; Boston Magazine measured it at 0.2% ABV, lower than a typical kombucha, which is worth knowing for anyone avoiding alcohol strictly. The bar opens at 3pm Monday through Friday and 5pm on Saturday, running to midnight early in the week and 1am from Thursday, and is closed on Sundays.
venues.pressQuote: This hip Cambridge bar, known especially for its adventurous cocktail menu and craft cocktail classes for groups, does not neglect its alcohol-free patrons.
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: Boston Magazine, "Here's Where to Drink Creative Mocktails around Boston", updated January 2026

venues.name: Bridge Road Brewers Brunswick
venues.description: Bridge Road Brewers' 350-seat Melbourne brewery and dining hall is one of the rare beer venues where the alcohol-free option is brewed in-house rather than bought in. The Beechworth brewery, founded by Ben and Maria Kraus in 2005, brews its own sub-0.5% ABV 'Free Time' range - a hazy pale hopped with Citra, Simcoe and Enigma, plus a Hazy IPA and an Alc-Free Stout - and pours it on tap alongside its full-strength lineup across 30 tap lines. For a working craft brewery, having a genuine house AF beer line on the pour list makes the zero-proof choice a real one, not an afterthought.
signatureDrinks: Free Time Alc-Free Hazy Pale - sub-0.5% ABV hazy pale ale hopped with Citra, Simcoe and Enigma; juicy hop aroma, low bitterness, clean finish (28 IBU)
Free Time Alc-Free Hazy IPA - sub-0.5% ABV alcohol-free hazy IPA from the house Free Time range
Free Time Alc-Free Stout - sub-0.5% ABV alcohol-free stout brewed in-house
venues.longDescription:
Bridge Road Brewers opened its first Melbourne venue in Brunswick East as the younger sibling of the award-winning Beechworth brewery that Ben Kraus and his wife Maria established in 2005. The split-level, U-shaped brewery and dining hall seats around 350 across a public bar with high-tops and booths, a small wine-focused cellar bar, and dog-friendly beer gardens spilling onto Nicholson Street and Bluestone Way. Studio Y designed the interiors, where - in Broadsheet's description - orange and blue dominate the space, with terracotta upholstery and a royal blue bar.

The draw for non-drinkers is that Bridge Road brews its own alcohol-free beer rather than stocking someone else's. The house 'Free Time' range is a full sub-0.5% ABV line: the flagship Free Time Alc-Free Hazy Pale is hopped with Citra, Simcoe and Enigma for a juicy hop aroma, low bitterness and a clean finish at 28 IBU, and is joined by a Free Time Hazy IPA and a Free Time Alc-Free Stout. The beer is made from just water, malt, hops and yeast, with the low alcohol a result of the brewing and fermentation process.

The venue runs 30 unique taps across two bars, with continually rotating selections from both the Beechworth and Brunswick brewhouses, so the Free Time pours sit within an actual working brewery's lineup. Head chef Jabili Mchawala runs an ingredient-led modern Australian kitchen - grilled eggplant with Asian seasonings, brisket with chilli-beer sauce and Afghan mustard pickles, jerk chicken with cornbread - open daily from noon to 9pm.

Open seven days from midday until late, it's a large, casual, family- and dog-friendly room where ordering alcohol-free doesn't mean stepping outside the craft-beer experience - the AF beer came out of the same brewhouse as everything else on tap.
venues.pressQuote: Orange and blue, perfect opposites on the colour wheel, dominate the space.

venues.name: Bright Nights Social
venues.description: Bright Nights Social is an alcohol-free pop-up bar and events platform founded by Sam Bail, running sober dance parties, mixology classes and social gatherings at rotating venues across New York — there is no permanent location, and its own line is that all of NYC is its venue. It has been going since 2022 and has hosted more than 100 events. It was called Third Place Bar until January 2026, when Bail renamed it, writing that three years and nearly a hundred events in, Third Place Bar had grown into many things, just not an actual bricks-and-mortar bar. Her framing of the mission is precise: it is not about sobriety as an identity, but about creating a space where alcohol isn't the default. Events have included tea bars, bagel-making classes and full dance parties with DJs and a complete non-alcoholic bar. Bright Nights Social also presents the NYC's Best Bars for NA awards, which judge the city's non-alcoholic drinks programmes. Confirmed active: it is co-hosting a zero-proof mixer in Manhattan in late August 2026.
venues.longDescription:
Bright Nights Social is Sam Bail's alcohol-free events platform, running sober dance parties, mixology classes and social gatherings at rotating venues across New York. There is no permanent room and there never has been — its own summary is that it has been going since 2022, has hosted more than a hundred events, is pop-up based with no permanent location, and that all of New York City is its venue. It ran as Third Place Bar until January 2026, when Bail renamed it. Her explanation of why is worth having in full, because it is unusually honest about what these projects actually become: when she first launched Third Place Bar she was not even one month sober, she wanted somewhere to go and there was nowhere, so she set out to create one starting with pop-up events — and three years, nearly a hundred events and thousands of guests later, it had grown into many things, just not an actual bricks-and-mortar bar. So she changed the name.

The positioning matters as much as the events. Bail's own line is that Bright Nights Social is not about sobriety as an identity, but about creating a space where alcohol is not the default — which is a meaningfully different proposition from a recovery space, and the reason its rooms fill with people who are cutting down, driving, pregnant, on medication, or simply not drinking tonight. The programming is deliberately varied rather than bar-shaped: a tea bar, a bagel-making and bagel-eating class, and a full dance party with DJs and a complete non-alcoholic bar to close out Dry January are all recent examples. Bail also presents the NYC's Best Bars for NA awards, which judge the city's non-alcoholic drinks programmes and which several venues in this guide have won or been shortlisted for — an unusual position, since it makes her both an organiser of alcohol-free nightlife and its most active critic. On current activity: it is confirmed on the calendar as co-hosting a zero-proof mixer in Manhattan in late August 2026, so this is a live operation rather than an archive. Follow the site for the schedule; there is no address to turn up at.
venues.pressQuote: I don't drink, but I still wanted nightlife — dancing, music, meeting new people, getting out of the house on a Friday or Saturday night.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Sam Bail, founder of Bright Nights Social

venues.name: Broken Shaker
venues.description: Broken Shaker is the rooftop bar on top of the Freehand Hotel in the Historic Core of Downtown Los Angeles, a James Beard Award finalist and winner of Tales of the Cocktail's Best American Hotel Bar. It is licensed, and its LA drink menu carries a dedicated Beer, Wine and Spirit Free tab plus a titled Mocktails section priced at $14: the Verbena Spritz with tangerine, lemongrass, lime leaf and lemon; Violet Thems, marked non-alcoholic and built on Ritual tequila alternative with lavender butterfly-pea orgeat, vanilla and spritz; and Call Me Mother, on Ritual gin alternative with guava, rose water, house-made lemonade and quinine. The rooftop has a pool, palms and sunset views over Downtown, with DJ sets on Friday and Saturday nights.
signatureDrinks: Verbena Spritz - tangerine, lemongrass, lime leaf, lemon $14
Violet Thems (non alcoholic) - Ritual tequila alternative, lavender butterfly pea orgeat, vanilla, spritz $14
Call Me Mother - Ritual gin alternative, guava, rose water, house made lemonade, quinine $14
venues.longDescription:
Broken Shaker began in Miami Beach, where it won a following and a James Beard nomination for a bar built on homemade elixirs and fresh, slightly unhinged ingredient combinations, and the Los Angeles outpost sits on the roof of the Freehand Hotel at Eighth and Olive in the Historic Core. Time Out describes it as a James Beard nominated rooftop bar concept where trendy clientele and youngish Angelenos from all over flock to a quirky, colorful and palm-laden rooftop, with eclectic, moderately priced cocktails, equally colorful garnishes, great finger food and excellent sunset views of Downtown. There is a pool on the deck, DJ sets on Friday and Saturday nights, and the whole thing sits eleven floors above one of the densest bar districts in the city.

Alcohol is very much the main event, and the house cocktails run $17 to $18. What earns the listing is that the LA menu treats the alcohol-free drinks as a named part of the programme rather than a courtesy. There is a whole menu tab headed Beer, Wine and Spirit Free, and within it a Mocktails section at $14 - a real price for a real drink, notably not the two-dollar soda pricing that signals a bar is not trying. Three sit on the current list. The Verbena Spritz is the fruit-and-herb one: tangerine, lemongrass, lime leaf and lemon, long and sharp. Violet Thems, flagged on the menu as non alcoholic, is built on Ritual's tequila alternative with a lavender butterfly-pea orgeat, vanilla and a spritz, and it is the most visually theatrical thing on the list. Call Me Mother uses Ritual's gin alternative with guava, rose water, house-made lemonade and quinine, which gives it the tonic bitterness that makes a long drink read as a bar drink rather than a squash.

Two practical notes worth having before you go. First, the rooftop is inside a hotel, so access is via the Freehand lobby and the lift, and it can be busy with hotel guests as well as walk-ins on weekend evenings. Second, the venue's own menu page currently lists narrower hours than some other listings, with an evening-only schedule Thursday to Sunday; the pool deck and the bar keep different clocks, so check on the day if you are making a special trip rather than passing through Downtown.
venues.pressQuote: trendy clientele and youngish Angelenos from all over flock to this quirky, colorful and palm-laden rooftop bar

venues.name: Brooklyn Kava
venues.description: Brooklyn Kava was the borough's first kava bar and remains its defining one — a full-service cafe on Suydam Street in Bushwick, a short walk from the Myrtle-Wyckoff subway hub, open late and serving no alcohol. It opened around 2015; Brooklyn's other early kava bar closed in 2018. The menu runs traditional kava alongside fresh coffee, teas and other non-alcoholic drinks. TWO THINGS TO KNOW BEFORE VISITING. First, its website (brooklynkava.com) is dead — the domain returns a Squarespace "account has expired" error — so Instagram is the only channel it maintains, and current hours and prices are best confirmed there or in person. Its Instagram remains substantial and active, and third-party listings were still being updated in mid-2026, so this is a lapsed website rather than a closed business. Second, it is alcohol-free but not necessarily substance-free: an older directory listing describes kratom being served in hot and iced teas and in mocktails, by red, green, white and yellow vein. We could not confirm that against any current source, and no dosage guidance or age policy is published anywhere we could find. Ask at the counter.
venues.longDescription:
Brooklyn Kava opened on Suydam Street in Bushwick around 2015 as one of the borough's first two kava bars — the other closed in 2018, leaving this one as the original and, by most accounts, still the defining one. It is a full-service cafe rather than a bar-shaped room, a short walk from the Myrtle-Wyckoff subway hub, serving traditional kava alongside proper coffee and a range of teas, and it stays open late. One of its longtime kavatenders once summed up the early years neatly: for the longest time, he thought, people had no idea what they were doing there. That has changed — Bushwick now has a small cluster of kava bars, and this is the one they all followed.

Two practical things need saying, and neither is a reason not to go. The first is that its website is dead: brooklynkava.com returns a Squarespace notice saying the account has expired, which we verified directly rather than taking on trust. That is not evidence of closure — a lapsed hosting bill looks identical to a closed business from outside, and we have been burned both ways. Here the other signals point the right way: the Instagram account is substantial and maintained, and third-party listings were still being updated in the middle of 2026. Treat it as trading, but confirm hours on Instagram rather than from a search result. The second is the botanical question that applies to every kava bar. Kava itself is psychoactive — that is the point of it, and the reason the room works as an evening out without alcohol. But an older directory listing also describes Brooklyn Kava serving kratom, in hot and iced teas and in mocktails, offered by red, green, white and yellow vein. We could not confirm that against the venue's own current menu, because there is no current published menu to check, and no dosage guidance or age policy appears anywhere we could find. If you are avoiding kratom specifically, ask at the counter before ordering — the staff here have a long reputation for explaining exactly what they serve.

venues.name: Brooklyn Tea
venues.description: Brooklyn Tea is a loose-leaf tearoom in Castleberry Hill, the second location of a specialty tea company founded in Bedford-Stuyvesant in 2017 by tea sommelier Alfonso Wright and his wife Jamila, an Atlanta native. The Atlanta shop opened in February 2022 and is run by Kerri-Ann Thomas, a Spelman graduate and long-time friend of the founders. It carries more than fifty loose-leaf teas served hot or iced, alongside coffee, vegan and non-vegan food, and the company's Notorious B.I.G. cookies. Masala chai lattes, the Cucumber Melon iced tea and the Cold Killer detox blend are the regular orders. No alcohol is served. The company's stated mission is to open tea shops in predominantly Black neighbourhoods where loose leaf has not been readily available. (The Atlanta tearoom appeared to be temporarily closed from early September 2026, with no announcement from the company. Check before you go.)
venues.longDescription:
Brooklyn Tea was founded in 2017 by Alfonso Wright, a certified tea sommelier, and his wife Jamila Wright, who grew up in Atlanta. The company's stated purpose is to put serious loose-leaf tea into predominantly Black neighbourhoods where it has not historically been sold, starting in Bedford-Stuyvesant. The Atlanta tearoom at 329 Nelson Street SW in Castleberry Hill was the second location, opening in February 2022, and Secret Atlanta covered it that April. Day-to-day it is run by Kerri-Ann Thomas, who was born and raised in Brooklyn and graduated from Spelman College, and whose friendship with the founders is how the Atlanta shop came about. The room is deliberately modern rather than chintzy — clean lines, generous indoor seating, free wifi — with artwork by Adeana Berry and India Linsey honouring Notorious B.I.G., Jay-Z and other New York figures on the walls.

The tea list is the substance: more than fifty loose-leaf blends, sold by the cup hot or iced and by the tin to take home, with sachets and house blends stocked alongside. Masala chai lattes are the volume order; the Cucumber Melon iced tea and the Cold Killer detox blend are the two named house pours that regulars ask for. Coffee is available for anyone who wants it, and the kitchen runs an all-day menu with a strong vegan section — vegan waffles, plant-based English muffin sandwiches — plus the Notorious B.I.G. cookies the company is known for. Afternoon and high tea service can be booked, and from April through October the shop hosts a Saturday block party outside with food and a live DJ. No alcohol is served or licensed. Brooklyn Tea sits at a four rather than a five on our scale because it trades Tuesday to Saturday, 10am to 5pm: a genuinely serious alcohol-free room, but a daytime one, and it closes before the evening begins.

One caution: the Atlanta tearoom appeared to be temporarily closed from early September 2026, with no announcement from the company, whose site still lists it. Check before you travel.

venues.name: Brunswick Aces
venues.description: Brunswick Aces is billed as Australia's first permanent non-alcoholic bar and bottle shop, an attached distillery in Brunswick East that produces its own zero-proof botanical spirit, Sapiir. Founded by CEO Stephen Lawrence and co-founder Cameron Hunt, the bar pours a 0% cocktail list built on the house Hearts Sapiir - a juniper-forward, wattleseed-scented gin alternative - alongside NA beer from Heaps Normal, and zero-proof wine and spirits from Ovant, NON and Sweden's Gnista. The room has since reopened to serve a small full-strength selection, but the menu and identity remain firmly non-alcoholic-first. It is Australia's first non-alcoholic bar, and it inverts the usual ratio: the menu carries exactly one alcoholic drink, a single gin and tonic, and everything else is alcohol-free.
signatureDrinks: King Louis - coconut water, cucumber-mint cordial and house-distilled Hearts Sapiir (0%)
venues.longDescription:
Opened as Australia's first permanent non-alcoholic bar and bottle shop, Brunswick Aces sits behind a working botanical distillery at 124 Weston Street in Brunswick East. Co-founders Stephen Lawrence and Cameron Hunt built custom stills to produce Sapiir, a gin-like zero-alcohol spirit; the distillery turns out roughly 3,000 litres of juniper-forward non-alcoholic infusions a week, with the Hearts Sapiir variety carrying notes of sweet citrus and native Australian wattleseed.

The bar's drinks list is anchored on that house spirit. The signature King Louis stirs Hearts Sapiir with coconut water and a cucumber-mint cordial, and the kitchen backs the cocktails with cheese and charcuterie boards. Beyond the house pours, the fridges and shelves stock non-alcoholic beer from Heaps Normal, plus zero-proof wine and spirits from Ovant (Margaret River), NON (Melbourne) and Gnista (Sweden), all available by the glass or bottle.

Attached to the bar is an in-house non-alcoholic bottle shop for taking product home, and the distillery door runs tours and cocktail masterclasses through the week. The bar itself trades Thursday to Saturday evenings from 5pm as walk-ins only, while the distillery door keeps daytime and later hours.

The venue has since reopened its doors to all drinkers, adding a small full-strength offering, but its whole reason for being - and the overwhelming majority of the menu - is the zero-proof program, making it the flagship alcohol-free destination in Melbourne.

The inversion is the entire point, and Time Out captures it neatly: at most bars a non-drinker is the minority, and at Brunswick Aces you are the majority. The bar stocks exactly one alcoholic drink — a single gin and tonic, kept as a wry nod to ordinary bars carrying one lemon, lime and bitters — and every other thing on the list is alcohol-free.

That makes the range far wider than a zero-proof section can ever be. Time Out lists non-alcoholic beer, wine and spirits from Heaps Normal XPA, Songbird, Ovant, GNISTA, NON and Vandestreek Playground IPA, with the wines available by the glass as well as the bottle — a detail that matters, because being unable to order one glass is what quietly pushes non-drinkers onto soft drinks everywhere else. The house also distils its own alcohol-free spirits, which are mixed with juices, extractions and syrups across the cocktail list. For anyone who has spent an evening reading a card looking for the one drink they can have, the experience of reading this one is the reason to make the trip to Brunswick.
venues.pressQuote: Moderate and sober drinkers from Perth to Sydney and even the US and UK have contacted us not only keen to visit, but also asking us to open venues in their home cities.

venues.name: Buena Vida Tea Bar & Garden
venues.description: Buena Vida Tea Bar and Garden is a fully alcohol-free loose-leaf tea bar on Montana Avenue in Santa Monica, founded by Mayra Vazquez, who styles herself and her staff Tearistas. It serves organic loose-leaf teas brewed to order, including on a teapresso machine, alongside sweet and savoury treats, and it has an outdoor tea garden terrace. Named pours include Dragonwell Longjing, China's best-known green; Jasmine Silver Needle, aromatic with floral and citrus notes; Persian Delight, a blend of premium black tea and rose petals; and Rosa de Jamaica, a hibiscus iced tea. The shop also sells teaware, runs a tea club and makes TEArrariums and plant arrangements. Reservations are recommended, and it is closed Mondays. No alcohol is served.
signatureDrinks: Dragonwell Longjing - China's favourite green tea
Jasmine Silver Needle - aromatic, floral and citrus notes
Persian Delight - premium black tea with rose petals
Rosa de Jamaica - refreshing hibiscus iced tea
venues.longDescription:
Buena Vida sits on Montana Avenue in Santa Monica, a few blocks up from the ocean on a street better known for boutiques than for anywhere to sit, and it is a tea bar in the way a wine bar is a wine bar - the leaf is the product, not the accompaniment. Founder Mayra Vazquez describes the venture as a mutual exploration of exceptional loose-leaf teas and the best ways to enjoy them, and her framing of the drink itself is the shop's whole thesis: tea is a sensation, an experience, a journey to wellness, comfort, tranquility and the good life. She and her staff go by Tearistas, and the stated aim is to find teas worth the attention and then steep each one properly enough to get the full flavour out of it, which in practice means brewing to order, sometimes on a teapresso machine, rather than dunking a bag.

The pours are organic loose leaf and the named ones cover a useful spread. Dragonwell Longjing is the pan-fired green from Zhejiang that is China's best-known tea, nutty and sweet rather than grassy. Jasmine Silver Needle is the aromatic one, scented with jasmine over a white-tea base, with floral and citrus notes. Persian Delight is a blend of premium black tea and rose petals, which is the closest thing on the list to a dessert. Rosa de Jamaica is hibiscus, served iced, and is the one to order in summer - sharp, deep red and caffeine-free. Alongside the tea there are sweet and savoury treats, teaware for sale, and TEArrariums and plant arrangements, which is a fair signal of how much the room leans into being a garden as well as a bar. There is an outdoor tea garden terrace, and a tea club subscription designed to run from novice to enthusiast.

Nothing served here contains alcohol, which makes it straightforwardly usable for anyone who is not drinking - a different proposition from a bar with a good non-alcoholic list. The trade-off is the clock: this is a daytime venue and a fairly short one, open 11am to 3pm Tuesday through Friday and 11am to 4pm at weekends, closed Mondays. Reservations are highly recommended and can be made by phone or email, and the room is small enough that walking in at a weekend without one is a gamble. Montana Avenue has metered street parking; the Santa Monica end of the Metro E Line is about a mile and a half away.
venues.pressQuote: Tea is a sensation, an experience, a journey to wellness, comfort, tranquility and the good life
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Mayra Vazquez, Buena Vida Tea founder

venues.name: Buffalo Traders Lounge
venues.description: Buffalo Traders Lounge is a cocktail bar at 950 East Fulton Street in East Hills, describing its remit as bringing the art of cocktail culture to the local community of Grand Rapids. It is routinely named among the better cocktail bars in West Michigan, and it takes zero-proof drinking seriously enough to stock for it specifically, keeping Little Saints and Tor's Tonics behind the bar for non-alcoholic builds. Named options include the Mock Mule, made with lime, simple syrup and ginger beer, and the Better Spritz, built on a non-alcoholic aperitif and soda. The bar will also make a Zero Proof Dealer's Choice, handing the decision to the bartender in the same way its full-proof list does.
venues.address: 950 Fulton St E, Grand Rapids, MI 49503
signatureDrinks: Mock Mule (lime, simple syrup, ginger beer)
Zero Proof Dealer's Choice (bartender's custom zero-proof build)
venues.longDescription:
Buffalo Traders Lounge sits at 950 East Fulton Street, on the East Hills stretch of Fulton, and states its purpose plainly: to bring the art of cocktail culture to the local community of Grand Rapids. It has held a place near the top of West Michigan cocktail lists for years, and it is a bartender's bar in the sense that the room is built around the drinks rather than around food or a beer wall. Hours run Tuesday through Thursday 4pm to 10pm, Friday and Saturday 4pm to midnight, and Sunday 2pm to 10pm.

The non-alcoholic program is worth distinguishing from the ordinary case, because the ordinary case is a bar that says its bartenders will happily make you something. Buffalo Traders buys inventory for the purpose. It stocks Little Saints, a CBD-based non-alcoholic spirit, and Tor's Tonics, a Michigan-made botanical tonic line, and builds with them rather than reaching for juice and soda — neither of which maps to a brand slug in this registry, which is why none is listed against the venue. The standing named drinks are the Mock Mule, a straightforward lime, simple syrup and ginger beer build, and the Better Spritz, which puts a non-alcoholic aperitif with soda in the Italian idiom. The more interesting option is the Zero Proof Dealer's Choice: guests can hand the decision to the bartender exactly as they would from the full-proof menu, which is the clearest signal a cocktail bar can send that its zero-proof drinks are made by the same people to the same standard. For a guest who wants to sit at a serious cocktail bar and drink something built rather than poured, this is the most direct option in East Hills, and it is a short walk from both Kava Kasa and Sacred Springs.

venues.name: Builders Arms Hotel
venues.description: This landmark Gertrude Street gastropub, run by chef Andrew McConnell's Trader House group, backs its wine and cocktail program with a genuinely built-out non-alcoholic list. The zero-proof offering spans AF beer, alcohol-free cocktails, AF red, white and sparkling wine, AF spritzes and mocktails, letting a non-drinker order across the full menu rather than settling for soda. It's one of the reasons the pub earns a place on Australian no/low guides Pub With No Booze and NoLo Life, the latter awarding it a full five-star rating for its range of AF and LA drinks. The Gertrude Street pub keeps a well-considered non-alcoholic list of beer and cocktails, under the same Andrew McConnell and Anthony Hammond stewardship the kitchen has had for over a decade.
venues.longDescription:
The Builders Arms Hotel is an iconic corner pub on Gertrude Street in Fitzroy that has been at the forefront of Melbourne food and drink for over a decade under Andrew McConnell and Anthony Hammond of the Trader House group. Over the years the site has cycled through fine-dining rooms Moon Under Water and the Chinese restaurant Ricky & Pinky before returning to its current form as a bistro, but the classic front bar with its counter service and lively neighbourhood crowd has stayed constant throughout.

What sets it apart for non-drinkers is a deliberately considered non-alcoholic list rather than a token afterthought. Pub With No Booze features the hotel specifically for its "well thought out non alcoholic list," noting you can settle in for people-watching on Gertrude Street over an alcohol-free beer or cocktail. Australian no/low guide NoLo Life goes further, rating the venue five stars for an "excellent range of AF and LA drinks" that covers AF beer, AF cocktails, AF red, white and sparkling wine, AF spritzes and RTDs, and mocktails.

The room itself pairs classic pub architecture with McConnell-standard dining: a restrained cream, blue and grey bistro with attentive table service, a lively front bar, and a compact, lived-in courtyard for warmer days. The kitchen is known for seasonal menus and signature plates like its fish pie, steaks, oysters and whipped cod roe, so the zero-proof drinks sit alongside a genuine dinner destination rather than a drinks-only bar.

The hotel is open seven days from midday until late at 211 Gertrude Street, Fitzroy, a short walk from the Smith Street and Brunswick Street precincts.

A pub is a harder test than a cocktail bar, and this one has been passing it for a while. Pub With No Booze calls the Builders Arms an iconic Gertrude Street hotel that has sat at the forefront of food and wine under Andrew McConnell and Anthony Hammond for more than a decade, and says there is no better spot to watch Melbourne go by — now with a beer or cocktail from a well-thought-out non-alcoholic list.

That combination is the useful part. Pubs are where most social drinking actually happens, and they are also where a non-drinker is most likely to be handed a lemonade. A front bar on Gertrude Street with both alcohol-free beer and alcohol-free cocktails means the person not drinking can stand in the same room, order in the same round and hold the same shape of glass, which is most of what anyone wants from a pub. The dining room behind it operates at a considerably higher standard than the phrase "pub food" suggests, so it also works as somewhere to eat properly.
venues.pressQuote: We don’t know a better spot to experience what Melbourne has to offer than sitting on Gertrude St and watching the parade go by. Now you can do that with a beer or cocktail from their well thought out non alcoholic list.

venues.name: Bula Kafe
venues.description: Bula Kafe is St. Petersburg's original kava bar and coffee house, open in Historic Kenwood since 2009 and tracing its roots to Nakava — North America's first kava bar. The founder, from Vanuatu, built it around noble kava from Vanuatu and the Solomon Islands, served alongside locally roasted coffee, matcha, and ethnobotanical teas in a fully alcohol-free nakamal. A repeat "Best of the Bay" kava winner, it anchors St. Pete's claim as the country's unofficial kava capital — a title earned by dozens of kava bars across Pinellas County. Open 7am to 2am most nights and to 3am at weekends, it is one of the few rooms in the region genuinely available across the whole day without alcohol. Kava is alcohol-free but psychoactive and mildly sedating; alcohol-free is not substance-free.
venues.longDescription:
Bula Kafe has been open in Historic Kenwood since 2009, which makes it St. Petersburg's original kava bar and one of the oldest in the United States. Its lineage runs back further still: it traces to Nakava, North America's first kava bar, and its founder is from Vanuatu — the archipelago where kava drinking is a civic institution rather than an import. That provenance shows in what is served. The kava is noble varietal from Vanuatu and the Solomon Islands, prepared and poured in a nakamal, the Ni-Vanuatu term for the space where kava is drunk communally.

The context matters as much as the room. St. Petersburg is often called the unofficial kava capital of the United States, with dozens of kava bars across Pinellas County, and Bula Kafe is the venue that started it — the reason a mid-sized Florida city has more kava bars than most countries outside the Pacific. It has taken Best of the Bay honours repeatedly. Alongside the kava it serves locally roasted coffee, matcha and ethnobotanical teas, and it runs from 7am to 2am most nights and to 3am at weekends, which makes it one of the few places in the region genuinely open across the whole day and night without alcohol.

The honest caveat belongs here as at every kava venue, and this one is well placed to make it: kava is alcohol-free but not inert. It is mildly sedating, psychoactive, and has documented case reports of liver injury; many Florida kava bars also pour kratom, which acts on opioid receptors with real dependence and withdrawal risk. Nothing served here contains alcohol, and that is a different claim from nothing served here having an effect. For someone avoiding alcohol socially, this is among the best rooms in the country to do it. For someone in recovery from a substance-use disorder, the distinction is worth weighing before walking in — and the staff here, who have been serving kava longer than almost anyone in the country, are the right people to ask about what is in a shell before ordering one.
venues.pressQuote: Best Kava Bar: Bula Kafe
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Creative Loafing Tampa Bay, Best of the Bay 2021 readers' pick
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: Creative Loafing Tampa Bay, Best of the Bay 2021

venues.name: Bula Kava House
venues.description: Bula Kava House opened on 22 March 2011 at 3115 SE Division Street and is one of the oldest kava bars in the United States, marking fifteen years in 2026. Owner Judd Rench's reasoning still heads the site: kava makes a safe alternative to alcohol and other intoxicants, and he figured a Pacific Northwest kava bar would be a great place to socialise or to use something that has been used medicinally for pain, insomnia and anxiety for thousands of years. Kava varieties change daily and are listed on a blackboard rather than published online, so prices for the traditional shells have to be seen in person. What is published: kava shots at $3.50 for 2oz, or a flight of four for $12 — The Glow Up, Dragonfuel, Coconut Kiss and Guava Kava — plus smoothies at $8.25–$9, cold-pressed juices at $6–$9, açaí and yogurt bowls at $10–$16, and $3 wellness shots. NOTE: we found no kratom, kanna, blue lotus or THC anywhere; CBD is sold only as a $2 tincture add-on. But no dosage guidance, age policy or health warning is published anywhere current. Open to midnight, 1am Friday and Saturday.
signatureDrinks: Traditional kava shells (blackboard, price not published)
venues.longDescription:
Bula Kava House opened on 22 March 2011 on SE Division Street and passed fifteen years in 2026, which makes it one of the oldest kava bars in the United States and older than most of the American kava scene. Owner Judd Rench's account of why is still at the top of the site and has not needed updating: kava makes a safe alternative to alcohol and other intoxicants, and he figured a Pacific Northwest kava bar would be a good place to come and socialise, or to use something that has been used medicinally to treat pain, insomnia and anxiety for thousands of years. Willamette Week's verdict from the early days remains the most honest introduction anyone has written: kava tastes like dirt, that is not figurative language, and it is not a reason to pass on Bula — because kava promotes socialisation and relaxation, and those traits are reflected in the room's warm feel. It opens at noon and runs to midnight, 1am at weekends.

The practical thing to know is that the core product is not published online. Kava varieties change daily and are written on a blackboard, so if you want a traditional shell you will have to see what is on and ask the price in person. What is printed covers everything around it, and it is a genuinely broad daytime menu: kava shots at $3.50 for two ounces, or a flight of four for $12 — The Glow Up, Dragonfuel, Coconut Kiss and Guava Kava — which is the sensible way in for a first visit. Then smoothies from $8.25 to $9, built on oat milk or coconut water with things like bee pollen, cacao nibs, almond butter and dates; cold-pressed juices from $6 to $9; açaí and yogurt bowls from $10 to $16; and four $3 wellness shots. On the botanical audit: we checked the printed menu, the full online catalogue and every page we could reach, and found no kratom under any name, no kanna, no blue lotus and no THC. CBD appears only as a $2 tincture you can add to a smoothie or juice. That is a cleaner shelf than most American kava bars. What is missing is any published safety information — no dosage guidance, no age policy, no pregnancy or driving warning appears anywhere current. Kava is psychoactive; ask the staff, who have been doing this for fifteen years.
venues.pressQuote: Kava tastes like dirt. That's not figurative language, nor is it a reason to pass on Bula Kava House… Kava promotes socialization and relaxation, traits reflected in Bula's warm vibe.

venues.name: Bula Kavananda
venues.description: Bula Kavananda is a fully alcohol-free kava bar and coffee house in Seminole Heights — the Tampa-side outpost of St. Pete's Bula tribe. It pours kava sourced from Vanuatu alongside ZEAL coffee, botanical and hemp teas, kombucha on tap, yerba mate, and cacao shots, in a community-minded room built for winding down without alcohol. First-timers get a shell of kava on the house.  Open daily 7am to 2am — a nineteen-hour day, and very little else in Tampa is available at either end of it without alcohol as the organising principle. Kava is alcohol-free but psychoactive; alcohol-free is not substance-free.
signatureDrinks: Stay Cool Kava (strawberry, mango passion, pineapple)
venues.longDescription:
Bula Kavananda is the Tampa-side room of the Bula group whose original, Bula Kafe, opened in St. Petersburg in 2009 and is generally credited as the venue that started Pinellas County's kava culture. This outpost sits in Seminole Heights and runs daily from 7am to 2am — a nineteen-hour day, which is the single most useful fact about it. Very little else in Tampa is open at either end of that range without alcohol being the organising principle.

The kava is sourced from Vanuatu, the archipelago where the drink is a civic institution rather than a wellness import, and it is served alongside ZEAL coffee, botanical and hemp teas, kombucha on tap, yerba mate and cacao shots. First-time visitors are given a shell of kava on the house, which is a small gesture that does real work: kava is genuinely unfamiliar to most people, it tastes like nothing else, and being handed one without having to commit money to the experiment is how a curious non-drinker becomes a regular.

The room is built for staying rather than passing through, in the manner of a nakamal — the Ni-Vanuatu term for the space where kava is drunk communally — and it draws a neighbourhood crowd rather than a destination one.

The caveat belongs here as at every kava venue and should not be softened by the coffee-house framing. Kava is alcohol-free but psychoactive and mildly sedating, with documented case reports of liver injury; many Florida kava bars also pour kratom, which acts on opioid receptors and carries dependence and withdrawal risk. Nothing served here contains alcohol. That is a narrower claim than nothing served here having an effect, and for anyone in recovery the difference is the whole question.  For everyone else it is simply one of the easiest rooms in Tampa to spend an evening in without a drink.
venues.pressQuote: Best Kava Bar 2022 | Bula Kavananda Kava Bar & Coffee House
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Creative Loafing Tampa Bay, Best of the Bay 2022 readers' pick
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: Creative Loafing Tampa Bay, Best of the Bay 2022

venues.name: Bundobust Brewery
venues.description: Bundobust Brewery is the working brewery and 150-seat taproom of the celebrated vegetarian Indian street-food group, set in a converted car park beneath the glass atrium of Oxford Street's grand St James Building. It brews its own beer on site, including KOPRA, a 0.5% alcohol-free double-dry-hopped pale made in collaboration with Manchester's Cloudwater, which pours on the taplist beside a proper Desi non-alcoholic range of iced masala chai, Alphonso mango lassi and Indian sodas. All the food is Gujarati-inspired and fully vegetarian and vegan, so the no-and-low drinker is genuinely catered for rather than an afterthought.
venues.address: St James Building, 61-69 Oxford Street, Manchester M1 6EQ
signatureDrinks: Iced masala chai shaken with Oatly oat milk
venues.longDescription:
Bundobust was started in Leeds in 2014 by Mayur Patel and Marko Husak, who met over a Bradford street-food collaboration in 2013. Patel's family run Prashad, one of the UK's most highly regarded Gujarati restaurants, while Husak came from the craft-beer world of The Sparrow Bier Cafe; together they built a group that pairs modern, all-vegetarian Indian street food with serious beer. Bundobust Brewery opened on Manchester's Oxford Street in 2021 as the group's own working brewery, carved out of a former multistorey car park inside the grand Edwardian St James Building on the Oxford Road corridor.

The room is a casual, open-plan taproom and restaurant seating around 150, with communal beer-hall benches, huge chrome fermentation tanks visible throughout the space and the building's enormous skylights letting daylight pour down through the atrium above. Sixteen keg lines and two cask lines pour Bundobust's own beers alongside collaborations and guest pours, and the kitchen sends out sharing-plate Gujarati street food that is entirely vegetarian and vegan.

The non-alcoholic offer is a real part of the taplist rather than a token gesture. The headline pour is KOPRA, a 0.5% ABV alcohol-free double-dry-hopped pale brewed as a collaboration with Manchester's Cloudwater, where Sabro hops give a creamy coconut character over bright lemon-lime citrus and a finish of blood orange. Beyond the AF beer there is a proper Desi soft-drinks programme: an in-house iced masala chai shaken with Oatly Barista oat milk and topped with whipped oat, a house mango lassi made with sweet, creamy Alphonso mangoes, and a rotating run of Desi soft drinks and Indian sodas. The kitchen-led bar can also build mocktail versions of its cocktails, making this one of the stronger low-and-no options in central Manchester.

venues.name: Bungalow by Middle Brow
venues.description: Bungalow by Middle Brow is the Logan Square brewery, bakery and pizzeria that Middle Brow Beer Co. opened after eight years of contract brewing, and it runs a properly built non-alcoholic cocktail list under an N-A heading on its drinks menu. Three house zero-proof drinks anchor it: a Middle Brow Paloma with Lyre's N/A tequila, sudachi and sparkling grapefruit; an Amaro Negroni with Seedlip 94, non-alcoholic Amaro Lucano and Lyre's Red Aperitivo; and a Dark and Stormy with Lyre's N/A dark rum, Pathfinder hemp root amaro, lime and ginger beer. A house shrub and soda, an Anti-Zero N/A IPA from Chicago's Revolution Brewing and a Domaine Montrose N/A sparkling rose sit beside them. The room opens at 8am for coffee and toast and runs through naturally leavened pizza in the evening.

venues.longDescription:
Middle Brow Beer Co. spent eight years brewing on other people's equipment before it built the Bungalow on Armitage Avenue in Logan Square. The room it produced is part brewery, part bakery and part pizzeria: rustic brick, a trio of foeders - the tall wooden barrels used for long aging - looming over the dining area, a long bar, and a patio that takes the overflow in warm weather. Mornings run on coffee and toast with cream cheese, fruit and honey; evenings run on naturally leavened, thin-crust pizza. The brewery donates fifty percent of its profits to local social-justice organizations, a policy it states publicly and Time Out has repeated in its review.

The drinks menu is largely made in-house, and unusually for a brewery the non-alcoholic section is a built-cocktail list rather than a shelf of imports. Under an N-A heading sit three house drinks: the Middle Brow Paloma at $14, made with Lyre's N/A tequila, sudachi and sparkling grapefruit; the Middle Brow Amaro Negroni at $13, combining Seedlip 94 with a non-alcoholic Amaro Lucano and Lyre's Red Aperitivo; and the Middle Brow Dark and Stormy at $15, built on Lyre's N/A dark rum, Pathfinder hemp root amaro, lime and ginger beer. A fourth house build, a blueberry, fig leaf and spice shrub lengthened with soda, joins them at $7. Packaged options include Anti-Zero, the non-alcoholic counterpart to Anti-Hero IPA from Revolution Brewing a few miles north in Chicago, at $8, and a Domaine Montrose N/A sparkling rose from France by the glass at $14. Because the bar opens at 8am and closes at 10pm, it works as a non-drinker's venue across the whole day - a coffee stop, a pizza dinner and a zero-proof nightcap in the same room, with the same list. The morning trade matters here as much as the evening one: toast with cream cheese, fruit and honey is the main attraction before noon, served alongside coffee and beer, which means the same N-A list is on the table for someone walking in at 9am. Ninety-five percent of the beverages served are made in-house, and the bar also keeps a natural wine list for the drinkers at the table.
venues.pressQuote: After eight years of contract brewing, Middle Brow Beer Co. finally opened a home of its own on a bustling stretch of Armitage Avenue in Logan Square.

venues.name: Burden of Proof
venues.description: Burden of Proof is a fully alcohol-free bottle shop and market on Mission Street in South Pasadena, and by its own count it holds the largest non-alcoholic selection in Los Angeles - more than 450 beers, wines, spirits and ready-to-drink cocktails, alongside specialty groceries. It opened in late 2024, the San Gabriel Valley's first shop of its kind, run by co-owners Obreanna McReynolds and Dean Peterson. The stock spans dealcoholized wine and beer, botanical spirits such as Pathfinder's whiskey alternative, and functional drinks built on adaptogens and nootropics. A free tasting runs every Saturday from 1pm to 4pm, which is the practical answer to a category where a $30 bottle can be a $30 mistake. Nothing sold here contains alcohol.
signatureDrinks: Non-alcoholic beer - over 450 NA products in total
venues.longDescription:
Burden of Proof opened in South Pasadena in December 2024, and it filled a specific hole rather than a general one. Los Angeles already had non-alcoholic retail, but almost all of it sat on the westside; the San Gabriel Valley had none. Co-owners Obreanna McReynolds and Dean Peterson opened this as the SGV's first, and McReynolds told LAist plainly that they had always wished LA had something like it, especially on the east side. The shop's own framing of why it exists is worth quoting because it avoids the moralising the category often falls into: not drinking, for a night or a lifetime, should be just as fun and delicious as the alternative.

The range is the largest in the region - more than 450 non-alcoholic beers, wines, spirits and canned cocktails by the shop's own count, plus specialty goods and groceries. It covers the three quite different things people mean by non-alcoholic. There is dealcoholized wine and beer, made as wine or beer and then stripped. There are botanical spirits built from scratch to be their own thing, Pathfinder's hemp-and-root whiskey alternative among them. And there is the functional end - drinks formulated around adaptogens and nootropics, which do something rather than simply taste of something. Those categories behave very differently in a glass, and knowing which one you are buying is most of the skill.

Which is what the shop is really selling. McReynolds is candid that walking in and seeing all the products is intimidating, and the answer is the free tasting every Saturday from 1pm to 4pm - the single most useful thing any shop in this category can offer, because a bottle you dislike at $30 is what stops most people trying a second one. She has also described the part she finds most rewarding as watching customers in the shop start comparing notes with each other. Practical notes: the shop is closed Mondays, runs noon to 8pm Tuesday to Saturday and noon to 6pm on Sunday, and sits on Mission Street a few minutes' walk from the South Pasadena Metro A Line station, which makes it reachable without a car from much of the eastside.
venues.pressQuote: We had always wished that LA had something like this, especially on the east side.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Obreanna McReynolds, Burden of Proof co-owner

venues.name: Burdock Brewery
venues.description: Burdock Brewery is a craft brewery and restaurant on Bloor Street West in Bloordale Village, one of three Toronto locations for a brewing company that has been making beer in the city since 2015. Rather than stocking an outside brand, Burdock brews its own non-alcoholic beer line in-house: DuckZ, a 0.5% ABV IPA; Deluxe Zero .5, a 0.5% ABV lager; and Salt Lick, a 0.5% ABV lime sour beer, all sold in 355mL cans. ELLE Gourmet named Burdock's non-alcoholic beer among the city's best. The Bloor St. location pairs its beer shop with a full kitchen serving seasonal, locally sourced food.
signatureDrinks: DuckZ (Non-Alc IPA, 0.5% ABV, 355mL can) — "Our tiny 0.5% IPA with all the hop flavour and foam of a Burdock IPA — and none of the buzz!" Tasting notes: grapefruit, lime zest, melon, papaya. Contains barley.

Deluxe Zero .5 (Non-Alc Lager, 0.5% ABV, 355mL can) — "the same smooth-honey-biscuit foam-lovin' greatness as it's full strength daddy, but with zero point five % alcohol." Tasting notes: "Smooth, malty, refreshing, ahhhhh." Contains barley, wheat.
Salt Lick (Non-Alc Lime Sour Beer, 0.5% ABV, 355mL can) — refreshing lime sour with a hint of salt. Tasting notes: "Key lime, not too sour, not too salty."
venues.longDescription:
Burdock Brewery has been making beer in Toronto since 2015. It now operates three locations: a production brewery and tavern in Kensington Market at 184 Augusta Ave., with a mezzanine viewing area over the brewhouse; a bar at 6 Denison Square; and this restaurant and retail beer shop at 1184 Bloor St. West in Bloordale Village. The Bloor St. location is the only one built around a full kitchen, serving food made with seasonal, local ingredients alongside beer from the shop, and — like the Kensington site — it hosts live music through Burdock's Music Hall programming.

Where most breweries' non-alcoholic options come from an outside supplier, Burdock brews its own zero-proof beer in-house. DuckZ is a 0.5% ABV non-alcoholic IPA — described as "our tiny 0.5% IPA with all the hop flavour and foam of a Burdock IPA — and none of the buzz," with tasting notes of grapefruit, lime zest, melon and papaya (it contains barley). Deluxe Zero .5 is a 0.5% ABV non-alcoholic lager, pitched as carrying "the same smooth-honey-biscuit foam-lovin' greatness as it's full strength daddy, but with zero point five % alcohol," tasting "smooth, malty, refreshing, ahhhhh" (it contains barley and wheat). Salt Lick rounds out the line as a 0.5% ABV non-alcoholic lime sour beer with a hint of salt — "key lime, not too sour, not too salty." All three are sold in 355mL cans through Burdock's shop and online store.

Burdock's non-alcoholic beer has drawn outside recognition: in a roundup of the best non-alcoholic beers for St. Patrick's Day, ELLE Gourmet's Bobbe Hayes wrote that "Toronto's Burdock Brewery has an incredible non-alcoholic stout," citing it as a standout among the city's zero-proof options.
venues.pressQuote: Toronto's Burdock Brewery has an incredible non-alcoholic stout.
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: ELLE Gourmet, "Best non-alcoholic beers for St. Patrick's Day"

venues.name: Burial Beer Co.
venues.description: Burial Beer Co. was born in the summer of 2013 out of a renovated transmission shop at 40 Collier Avenue — as the brewery puts it, before it was the South Slope. Three founders moved from Seattle and opened nine months later on a 30-gallon brewhouse producing 150 barrels a year, with no employees, doing everything themselves including tending the bar. It now anchors Asheville's densest brewing district and has opened outposts elsewhere; the original taproom is the one it calls the crypt from which its story was born. For non-drinkers it keeps a Burial-branded non-alcoholic beer on the board — Chaosmachine, a non-alcoholic IPA under 0.5% ABV made with barley and oats and hopped with Citra and Mosaic — often alongside a second rotating NA option. One of the city's most sought-after beer names therefore has a spot for the non-drinker too. Note that Burial's NA cans are contract-packaged rather than confirmed brewed on site.
venues.longDescription:
Burial Beer Co. was born in the summer of 2013 out of a renovated transmission shop at 40 Collier Avenue in the South Slope — as the brewery puts it, before it was the South Slope. Three founders moved from Seattle and opened nine months later on a 30-gallon brewhouse producing 150 barrels a year, with no employees, doing everything themselves including tending the bar. Co-owner Jess Reiser has described the journey since as quite a whirlwind, which is fair for a brewery that now anchors Asheville's densest brewing district and has opened outposts elsewhere. The original taproom is the one the brewery calls the crypt from which its story was born, and describes as relaxed and rough around the edges — two bars, indoor and outdoor seating, a full kitchen serving until 9pm, wine and slushies. It opens at noon daily and runs to midnight on Friday and Saturday. The adjoining music venue, Eulogy, is ticketed and 18 and over, with no pets.

For a non-drinker the picture is genuinely promising but needs one caveat. Burial brews Chaosmachine, a non-alcoholic India pale ale under 0.5% ABV, made with barley and oats, whirlpooled with Citra, Mosaic and Cryo hops and dry-hopped with Citra again — a hop-forward beer built by a brewery known for hop-forward beer, rather than a token low-alcohol product bought in from elsewhere. It sells in six-packs of 12oz cans at $15. The caveat is that Chaosmachine does not appear on the taproom's own current beer list, which runs to eighteen beers, all of them alcoholic. It is sold as a packaged year-round product through Burial's shop, and with two bars and a bottle selection on site the odds of finding it here are reasonable — but it is not confirmed as pouring, so this is a venue worth asking about on arrival rather than travelling to on the assumption of a non-alcoholic pint.
venues.pressQuote: Chaosmachine Non-Alcoholic India Pale Ale ... Made with barley and oats. Whirlpooled with Citra, Mosaic and Cryo. Dry-hopped with Citra.

venues.name: Burial Beer Co. House of Relics
venues.description: Burial Beer Co.'s Charlotte outpost, House of Relics, occupies a storied Plaza Midwood building and features 36 draft lines across two bars, a rooftop deck, and a downstairs bottle shop. The taproom carries Burial's own Chaosmachine Non-Alcoholic IPA (under 0.5% ABV) alongside third-party NA options from Untitled Art, giving sober-curious visitors real craft options. Opened in summer 2022, it remains one of Charlotte's most design-forward brewery taprooms.
venues.longDescription:
Burial Beer Co.'s House of Relics opened on 11 June 2022 at 1214 Thomas Avenue in Plaza Midwood, the Charlotte outpost of the Asheville brewery founded in 2013. The building has history it makes use of: the taproom draws its look from the vintage clothing store that occupied the space before it, and the result has been described as moody diner's club meeting a seventies pool bar. It runs two bars carrying 36 Burial draft lines between them, plus cocktails and wine, with a rooftop bar above. There is no kitchen of its own. Burial chose Plaza Midwood deliberately — its Charlotte general manager called the neighbourhood probably the most Asheville neighbourhood in Charlotte, which is a fair description of a district built on record shops, tattoo studios and independent bars. It opens at 1pm on weekdays and noon at weekends, running to midnight on Friday and Saturday.

For a non-drinker the position here is honest but qualified. Burial produces Chaosmachine, a non-alcoholic India pale ale under 0.5% ABV, brewed with barley and oats, whirlpooled with Citra, Mosaic and Cryo hops and dry-hopped with Citra — a genuinely hop-forward beer rather than a token low-alcohol one, sold in six-packs of 12oz cans at $15. What cannot be confirmed from Burial's own published information is whether Chaosmachine is actually pouring or stocked at this taproom on any given day: the brewery's Charlotte beer list runs to eighteen current beers and does not include it, and the product page does not say which locations carry it. With 36 rotating draft lines and a bottle shop, the odds are reasonable, but this is a venue worth phoning ahead about rather than travelling to on the assumption. If Chaosmachine is on, it is one of the better non-alcoholic IPAs made by a craft brewery rather than an NA specialist; if it is not, the room has cocktails and wine but no confirmed zero-proof beer.
venues.pressQuote: We couldn't be more excited to share a new Burial realm here in the Queen City. It was surreal to get the doors open and hear everyone's shared excitement.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Matt Moore, taproom manager, Burial Beer Co.

venues.name: Butcher & Bee
venues.description: Butcher & Bee is a vegetable-forward, Middle Eastern–leaning restaurant in East Nashville's Historic Edgefield, on Main Street. It opened in 2015 as the second location of the Charleston original, founded in 2011 by restaurateur Michael Shemtov; both are now run by Nashville's Honest to Goodness Hospitality group (also behind Redheaded Stranger and Fancypants). The kitchen is known for mezze and shareable plates — whipped feta with fermented honey, hummus bowls, shakshuka, and avocado crispy rice. Every menu carries a dedicated non-alcoholic section. Current zero-proof offerings are a rotating Seasonal Gazoz (a macerated-fruit shrub topped with sparkling water — apricot, rosemary and cardamom at the time of writing) at $10, the Tin Lizzies (Lucano NA Amaro, Crema espresso, Giffard Aperitif Syrup, orange oil) at $12, and Untitled Art's 'American Gold' non-alcoholic lager at $6, plus Boylan's sodas; a Papaw's Punch on earlier menus has been dropped.
signatureDrinks: Seasonal Gazoz (macerated fruit shrub and sparkling water; apricot-rosemary-cardamom at the time of writing) $10
Tin Lizzies (Lucano NA Amaro, Crema espresso, Giffard Aperitif Syrup, orange oil) $12
venues.longDescription:
Butcher & Bee occupies 902 Main Street in Historic Edgefield, East Nashville, the second outpost of a restaurant that began in Charleston. The cooking is vegetable-forward with a Middle Eastern lean, built around mezze and shared plates rather than individual mains — whipped feta with fermented honey, avocado and crispy rice with winter greens, serrano dressing and spicy peanuts, seared wild mushroom, and a turnip cacio e pepe that turns a pasta idea into a vegetable one. Weekend brunch is a substantial part of what the kitchen does, running from 10am on Saturdays and Sundays with a stewed-tomato shakshuka served with two soft-baked eggs, labneh and olive tapenade, and Bubbie's short stack of pancakes under chocolate tahini maple syrup. Dinner service starts at 5pm Monday through Thursday. The kitchen asks guests with coeliac disease or allergies to speak to a server directly, since cross-contamination is possible.

What earns the restaurant a place here is a small design decision repeated on every menu: the non-alcoholic drinks are printed in the same place and the same type as everything else — on earlier menus under a heading that read "Buzz Free" — so a non-drinker reads the menu the same way everyone else does rather than asking what there is. The list is short and specific. The Tin Lizzies ($12) is the one that shows real thought — Lucano non-alcoholic amaro with espresso from local roaster Crema, Giffard aperitif syrup and orange oil, effectively a zero-proof espresso-and-amaro drink rather than a sweet substitute. The Seasonal Gazoz ($10) is a macerated fruit shrub lengthened with sparkling water, rotating through combinations — apricot, rosemary and cardamom on the current card, pineapple-coconut-lime and strawberry-sumac-rose before it — which makes it the drink to ask about since it changes. Below those sits Untitled Art's 'American Gold' non-alcoholic lager at $6, with Boylan's sodas alongside; the Papaw's Punch of Giffard aperitif syrup, lemon and soda that earlier menus carried has been dropped. It is not a long list, and it does not pretend to be; what it is instead is a properly composed one, priced in line with the bar rather than at soft-drink markup, on a menu where nobody has to ask a special question to find it.
venues.pressQuote: The restaurant has thrived as maybe the most vegetable-forward non-vegetarian dining destination in town.

venues.name: Butter Bar & Kitchen
venues.description: Butter Bar & Kitchen is a neighbourhood gastropub in Burlington's New North End, well away from the downtown bar strip, serving burgers, fried chicken, salads and a full weekend brunch with espresso drinks and baked goods. Its ordering menu lists Mocktails as a category in its own right, printed alongside Specialty Cocktails rather than folded into the soft drinks — a small formatting decision that reliably signals a kitchen has actually built the drinks. It is one of very few options for a considered alcohol-free drink outside the city centre. Open Wednesday to Sunday evenings from 4:30pm, with brunch from 9am on Saturday and Sunday.
venues.hours: Wed-Thu 4:30pm-8:30pm; Fri 4:30pm-9pm; Sat 9am-2pm & 4:30pm-9pm; Sun 9am-2pm & 4:30pm-8pm; Mon-Tue closed
venues.longDescription:
Almost everything in this city guide is downtown or in the South End. Butter Bar & Kitchen is neither: it sits in a shopping plaza on North Avenue in the New North End, the residential half of Burlington above the hill, and it serves the neighbourhood rather than the visitor. That is exactly why it is worth recording — a non-drinker who lives up here should not have to drive into town for a decent drink.

The restaurant is a gastropub in the straightforward sense: burgers, fried chicken, salads, a kids' menu, cocktails made with Vermont distillers' spirits and a local beer list. Weekend brunch runs from 9am with breakfast classics, espresso drinks and baked goods, which makes it one of the few daytime rooms in this guide.

The alcohol-free evidence is a formatting detail that turns out to be a reliable signal. Butter's own ordering menu lists Mocktails as a category, printed alongside Specialty Cocktails and Beverages rather than dropped in among the sodas. Kitchens that do not actually make alcohol-free drinks do not create a menu category for them; the ones that do almost always have a bartender who cares. The specific drinks are not published in a form that could be read for this listing, so none are recorded here and the entry is graded three rather than four.

The hours need watching. Butter is closed Monday and Tuesday entirely, opens at 4:30pm Wednesday through Sunday, and closes early by bar standards — 8:30pm midweek, 9pm on Friday and Saturday, 8pm on Sunday. Brunch service runs 9am to 2pm on Saturday and Sunday. Plan around it rather than turning up late.

venues.name: Butterjoint
venues.description: Butterjoint is a bar and restaurant at 208 North Craig Street in North Oakland, serving Pittsburgh comfort food and French bistro classics. It opened next door to Legume in late 2012 under Trevett and Sarah Hooper, and absorbed that restaurant's space when Legume closed for good in February 2020; the Hoopers sold the business in November 2023 to George Austin, who had been their executive chef since 2021 and still runs it. Its non-alcoholic drinks sit under a menu heading called "Hold the Booze" and run across all three lists. There is one house zero-proof cocktail at a time, currently the Concrete Jungle bird ($12) built on house-made non-alcoholic rum and non-alcoholic Campari with pineapple, lime, cinnamon and jalapeño; Leitz sparkling Riesling is poured as the non-alcoholic wine ($10); and the beer list carries Guinness Zero, Bitburger Premium Pils and an Aslin blackberry-and-blueberry sour at $6 a can. The cocktail slot rotates several times a year, so the name changes even though the section does not.
venues.longDescription:
Butterjoint is the surviving half of one of the most consequential restaurant projects Pittsburgh has had. Trevett and Sarah Hooper opened Legume on South Braddock Avenue in Regent Square in June 2007, moved it to North Craig Street in 2011, and opened Butterjoint as the more casual bar next door in late 2012. Legume closed permanently at the end of February 2020 and the two rooms became one under the Butterjoint name. The Post-Gazette's assessment when the Hoopers stepped away was that their seventeen-year run as restaurant owners changed the course of dining in Pittsburgh. In November 2023 they sold the business to George Austin, who had been their executive chef since 2021 and who put it plainly: he is carrying on, as much as he can, what Trevett and Sarah started here. The awards belong to that earlier era and are worth stating precisely — Legume was a 2018 James Beard semifinalist for Outstanding Restaurant, and Trevett Hooper a 2013 semifinalist for Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic. Semifinalist in both cases, not finalist, and not for Butterjoint itself.

The food is Pittsburgh comfort cooking crossed with French bistro: pierogi with caramelised onions and sour cream at $17, a burger at $21, moules frites at $30, steak frites with ramp chimichurri at $52, and milk-bread rolls with local Hatch chile butter at $8. The non-alcoholic drinks have their own heading, and it is a good one — "Hold the Booze" — which reads like the bar talking rather than a marketing department. What sits under it is a single rotating house cocktail plus a properly stocked shelf. The current cocktail is the Concrete Jungle bird at $12, built on house-made non-alcoholic rum and non-alcoholic Campari with pineapple, lime, cinnamon and jalapeño — house-made, which is the detail that matters, because most bars buy those bottles in. Leitz sparkling Riesling is the non-alcoholic wine at $10, and cans run $6: Guinness Zero, Bitburger Premium Pils, and an Aslin blackberry-and-blueberry sour. Be aware the cocktail slot genuinely rotates — it has held at least three different drinks in three years — so ask what is on rather than arriving for a name.
venues.pressQuote: Trevett and Sarah Hooper's 17-year run as restaurant owners changed the course of dining in Pittsburgh.

venues.name: The Butterscotch Den
venues.description: The Butterscotch Den on Broadway is the third of the Irish Hospitality Group's Sacramento bars, stocking the same St. Agrestis Phony Negroni and Guinness 0 as the others and staying open to 2am on Friday and Saturday. Its value is location: Broadway and Oak Park sit south of the downtown and Midtown cluster where nearly every other venue in this guide is concentrated, so this covers a part of the city that would otherwise require a drive to drink anything decent without alcohol. It opens at 4pm every day and is the southernmost venue in this guide. Broadway itself has gained restaurants and bars over the past decade, so a night out here no longer means heading into Midtown.
venues.longDescription:
The Butterscotch Den sits on Broadway in the Oak Park area, south of downtown Sacramento, and completes the Irish Hospitality Group's trio alongside The Snug and Ro Sham Beaux. It stocks the same alcohol-free products: the bottled St. Agrestis Phony Negroni and Guinness 0.

Geography is the argument for listing all three separately rather than treating them as one entry. Look at where Sacramento's alcohol-free options actually are: Juju and Dive Bar downtown, Kupros and Ro Sham Beaux in Midtown, Revival at Downtown Commons, Teetotalist in Midtown. That is one relatively small area, and it serves the people who live and work in it. Broadway and Oak Park are a different part of the city with their own population, and a bar there stocking reliable zero-proof products means somebody local does not have to drive into the centre to have a decent drink without alcohol.

The same reliability argument applies as at its sibling venues. A bottled Phony Negroni is not a craft cocktail, but it is bitter, herbal, properly made and identical every time — which for a neighbourhood bar is exactly the right level of ambition. Nobody expects a Broadway local to run a zero-proof programme; stocking two good products consistently is a better and more sustainable commitment.

Hours run to midnight through the week and 2am on Friday and Saturday, seven days. Between this, The Snug and Ro Sham Beaux, the group gives Sacramento three geographically spread late-night options with the same dependable stock — which is a quietly significant contribution to the city's scene.

Oak Park itself is worth a word. It has changed considerably over the past decade, with Broadway gaining restaurants and bars that draw people from across the city, and it now supports a night out on its own terms rather than as a detour from Midtown. A bar there carrying the same alcohol-free stock as its central siblings means that growth includes people who do not drink — which is not automatic, and does not happen unless an operator decides it should.
venues.pressQuote: Irish Hospitality Group (The Snug, Ro Sham Beaux, The Butterscotch Den): Phony Negroni by St. Agrestis, Guinness 0, and various NA cocktails.

venues.name: Cabin Boys Brewery
venues.description: Cabin Boys is a Tulsa brewery in Kendall-Whittier that keeps Big Drop Brewing Co.'s Pine Trail Pale Ale on for anyone not drinking — a genuine non-alcoholic pale ale at 0.5% from one of the best-regarded alcohol-free brewers in the world, rather than a token domestic lager. In a brewery taproom the specific choice of NA beer matters more than the fact of having one: Big Drop brews to be alcohol-free from the start rather than removing alcohol afterwards, which is why its beers taste like beer. Open from 4pm midweek and noon at weekends, closing at 9pm early in the week and 11pm from Thursday.
signatureDrinks: Big Drop Brewing Co. Pine Trail Pale Ale — non-alcoholic, 0.5%
venues.longDescription:
Most brewery taprooms that stock a non-alcoholic beer stock whatever the distributor pushed, which is usually a mass-market lager and usually disappointing. Cabin Boys, in Tulsa's Kendall-Whittier neighbourhood, keeps Big Drop's Pine Trail Pale Ale — and that specific choice is the reason the taproom is in this guide.

Big Drop is a British brewer that makes only alcohol-free beer, and it does it by brewing to 0.5% from the start rather than making a full-strength beer and stripping the alcohol out afterwards. The difference is audible in the glass: de-alcoholised beers tend to lose their body and their hop aromatics along with the ethanol, and the good ones spend a lot of effort putting those back. A beer designed never to have alcohol in it does not have to. Pine Trail is Big Drop's pale ale and it is one of the more convincing alcohol-free beers made anywhere.

Stocking it is a considered decision by a brewery that could easily have stocked nothing, and Tulsa Remote picked it out in its January 2025 ranking of the city's alcohol-free drinking.

This entry is graded three, which is the correct level for a taproom whose alcohol-free offer is one imported beer rather than a programme of its own — Nothing's Left, a few blocks away, actually brews its non-alcoholic line, and Bend and Burlington in this directory have breweries doing the same. What Cabin Boys offers is the simplest and often most wanted thing: a good beer, in a brewery, that happens to have no alcohol in it.

Open 4pm to 9pm Monday through Wednesday, to 11pm on Thursday, noon to 11pm on Friday and Saturday, and noon to 7pm on Sunday.
venues.pressQuote: Big Drop Brewing Co. Pine Trail Pale: non-alcoholic pale ale

venues.name: Café Beermoth
venues.description: Café Beermoth is an award-winning independent craft-beer café-bar in Manchester city centre, tucked off Spring Gardens with its public entrance on Brown Street. Run by the team behind the long-running Beermoth beer shop, it was named Central Manchester CAMRA's Pub of the Year 2026 and pours rotating cask and keg alongside a 450-strong bottle-and-can list. Crucially for non-drinkers, its fridges hold a genuinely deep alcohol-free bank led by around eight fresh options from dedicated no-alcohol brewery BRÜLO. A coffee bar by day and a beer café by night, it is an easy alcohol-free choice at any hour.
signatureDrinks: BRÜLO Lust For Life DDH IPA (AF)
BRÜLO King For A Day pale (AF)
venues.longDescription:
Café Beermoth is the bar-and-café arm of Beermoth, the specialist beer business founded by Jeremy Stull and Scott Davies, who opened their first shop on Tib Street in the Northern Quarter in early 2013. Inspired by the beer cafés of the Low Countries, the venue has a modern, unfussy feel reminiscent of Belgium, built around the drink rather than a theme. Its official address is on Spring Gardens, though the public entrance is around the corner on Brown Street — and in January 2026 the original Beermoth bottle shop relocated here after almost 13 years on Tib Street. That June the café was crowned Central Manchester CAMRA's Pub of the Year 2026.

The beer line-up is serious: a house beer (Stone's Throw, brewed with Runaway) plus six rotating British cask ales on handpull and eleven keg lines running key-keg conditioned beers from breweries across the UK, including a dedicated Augustiner Helles tap that Beermoth was the first place in the UK to pour. Behind the bar sits a bottle-and-can list of more than 450 beers weighted towards Belgium, Germany and wild-fermented American brews, alongside cheese and charcuterie plates. It trades as a coffee bar by day and a beer café into the evening, and takes card only.

For alcohol-free drinkers the fridges are the real draw. Manchester Confidential singled the café out for stocking 'a whopping eight fresh options from dedicated non-alc brewery BRÜLO' — the Glasgow zero-alcohol specialist whose range here runs from the Lust For Life DDH IPA and King For A Day pale to a Cascadian Tides stout, a 5 Fruit Gose and a 7 Grain 7 Hop. That is a curated, rotating alcohol-free bank rather than a token can or two, and it sits alongside low-ABV imports such as Rothaus and Früh. Combined with the all-day coffee, it makes Beermoth one of the easiest places in central Manchester to spend an evening without alcohol.
venues.pressQuote: Beermoth has a whopping eight fresh options from dedicated non-alc brewery BRULO.

venues.name: Café Hollander Hilldale
venues.description: Café Hollander sits in the Hilldale shopping district on Madison's west side and works the Belgian café format — a long beer list, mussels and frites, a big terrace. Its relevance here is narrow but real: the kitchen pours non-alcoholic sparkling wine and will build it into a mimosa with orange juice, which sounds slight until you have tried to order brunch without alcohol in a room where everyone else is having one. Madison Eats Food Tours names it in the metro's must-try non-alcoholic round-up on that basis. It is the west side's most convenient sit-down option and one of the few with genuine weekend brunch service.
