venues.longDescription:
Catalina Kitchen + Bar opened on 12 September 2023 at 1942 E 7th Street in the Elizabeth on Seventh development, and its lineage is unexpected for Charlotte: it is the first North Carolina restaurant from the Ditka Restaurant Group, the Chicago company that opened its original Ditka's in 1997 and named itself for its partner Mike Ditka, the Hall of Fame player and Bears head coach. The Charlotte room runs to 5,800 square feet with booths, high-tops, bar seating and a patio, next door to Rosemont and across from Puerta, with free parking in the Elizabeth on 7th garage — genuinely useful in that part of town. The cooking is coastal comfort food at upper-casual prices: a half-pound Ditka Burger with aged cheddar at $18, seafood tagliatelle with bay scallops, lump crab and shrimp at $26, a Sonoma chicken salad at $21 for dinner and $15 at lunch, and a 40-day wet-aged ribeye. Happy hour runs weekdays from 3pm to 6pm with fresh-shucked oysters at $2.50 each.

The zero-proof drinks have their own printed heading and are priced flat at $11, and two of the four are built on Lyre's rather than juice. Almost Rita uses Lyre's non-alcoholic blanco with cold-pressed lime and agave — a straight margarita build with the tequila swapped rather than a sweetened substitute. No-Jito pairs Lyre's non-alcoholic white cane with mint and cold-pressed lime. The other two are made from scratch ingredients: a Hibiscus Rose Fizz of hibiscus-infused water, rose and ginger beer, and a Lavender Lemonade combining lemonade with a lavender-infused syrup, cold-pressed lemon and fizzy water. Both of those carry a printed option to add rum or vodka for $4, which is a small but genuinely thoughtful piece of menu design: it means a mixed table can order the same drink and only some of them take the spirit. Best Day Brewing's non-alcoholic Kölsch is $6. There is no non-alcoholic wine on the list.
venues.pressQuote: Catalina Kitchen + Bar features an extensive cocktail and mocktail menu, with signature zero-proof options including the Queen City Spritz and Lavender Lemonada demonstrated on air by Kitchen & Bar Manager Hector Lopez.

venues.name: Catbird
venues.description: Catbird is the rooftop bar at the Thompson Dallas, occupying the upper floors of the old National tower on Elm Street, and its current menu carries a printed Non-Alcoholic Cocktails section. Barbie Girl builds Lyre's London Dry against rhubarb syrup under a matcha concentrate float; Canned Responses runs lychee, coconut and almond into something closer to a tiki drink; and Shoots & Ladders is made with a house-fermented pineapple bamboo tepache. Heineken 0.0 is on the beer list. The section is offered the other way round too — any of the three can be made spirited for a small supplement, which is a rare and genuinely useful courtesy for a mixed table where one person is drinking and another is not.

venues.longDescription:
Catbird occupies the upper floors of the Thompson Dallas, in the old National tower on Elm Street, and trades on the view as much as the drinks. Its non-alcoholic offering is printed as its own section — Non-Alcoholic Cocktails — on a menu refreshed in July 2026, which is worth noting in a city where zero-proof lists have a habit of appearing each January and quietly vanishing by March. A rooftop bar is also one of the harder rooms to enjoy without alcohol, because the whole format is built around lingering over a drink, so a real list here does more work than the same list would in a restaurant.

The three builds are genuinely constructed drinks. Barbie Girl uses Lyre's London Dry with rhubarb syrup and floats matcha concentrate on top, giving it both bitterness and a visual identity — it does not arrive looking like a soft drink. Canned Responses works lychee, coconut and almond into something closer to a tiki drink. Shoots & Ladders is the most interesting technically, built on a house-fermented pineapple bamboo tepache, a Mexican fermented-fruit drink whose funk and acidity does the work alcohol usually does; it is the one to order if you miss complexity rather than sweetness. Heineken 0.0 backs them up on the beer list.

The detail that lifts this entry is reciprocity: the section runs in both directions, and any of the three can be made spirited for a small supplement. That means a table does not have to split its order between a cocktail menu and a mocktail menu — everyone orders the same drink and specifies. A note for anyone arriving from press coverage: articles have credited Catbird with drinks called Bullet Train, Beach Ritual and Faded Ember, built on Pathfinder, Seedlip and Leitz. Those came from a Death & Co. residency rather than the house menu and are not currently served. The three above are what the bar actually pours. One practical note on timing. A rooftop is a view bar first, so the value of the room changes with the light — arrive before sunset and the drink is incidental to what you came for; arrive late and it is the drink doing the work, which is when a real non-alcoholic list earns its place.

venues.name: Catch Dallas
venues.description: Catch Dallas keeps a dedicated "Zero Proof" section on its cocktail list with four crafted spirit-free builds rather than a token Shirley Temple. The non-alcoholic espresso martini is built on Lyre's Coffee Originale with salted vanilla and coconut water, while the Watermelon Mojito uses Seedlip Grove 42 with fresh watermelon, mint and lime. Athletic Brewing's Upside Dawn non-alcoholic beer is also poured. The zero-proof list runs alongside the same premium seafood, sushi and steak dining room the national Catch brand is known for.

venues.longDescription:
Catch Dallas is the upscale seafood, sushi and steak restaurant from the national Catch brand, which opened in the historic Maple Terrace building at 3005 Maple Avenue in Uptown Dallas in 2025 — the chain's eighth location, joining New York, Los Angeles, Las Vegas and Miami. The dining room is known for whole branzino, Allen Brothers prime steaks, tableside wagyu fried rice and nigiri and sashimi with fish sourced from Japan's Toyosu Market, set around a glass-walled cellar of more than 500 wine selections overseen by Pappas Bros alum Ben Reynolds.

The bar runs a named "Zero Proof" section on its cocktail menu. Named builds include an Espresso Martini (Lyre's Coffee Originale, salted vanilla, coconut water), a Lychee Martini (lychee, pressed coconut water, lemon, orange blossom), a Watermelon Mojito (watermelon, Seedlip Grove 42, mint, lime) and a Makrut Lime Spritz (makrut lime leaf, grapefruit, lemon, Topo Chico). Athletic Brewing's Upside Dawn is available as a non-alcoholic beer pour.

The zero-proof program was highlighted in DiningOut's Dry January guide to Dallas's best zero-proof cocktails, which singled out the vanilla-forward espresso martini. Weekend brunch service (Saturday and Sunday) also offers zero-proof options alongside its specialty cocktails.
venues.pressQuote: A non-alcoholic espresso martini crafted with vanilla-forward Lyre's Coffee Originale, a nonalcoholic coffee liqueur, salted vanilla, and coconut water.

venues.name: Cavaña
venues.description: Cavaña is a Latin American rooftop bar on the seventeenth floor of the LUMA Hotel in Mission Bay, with a dance floor, a DJ and skyline views over the ballpark. It trades to midnight on weeknights and 1am on Friday and Saturday. The alcohol-free drinks are printed under a spirit-free heading on the main cocktail menu and run to six: Maracuyá, built on Almave agave spirit and Wilderton Citrus with aperitivo, passionfruit agave and lime; Phoney Mezcal Negroni, with a Peruvian agave distillate, Pathfinder amaro and Abstinence blood orange aperitif; Guava Fresca; Michelada-Nada, made with non-alcoholic cerveza and the house michelada mix; Chicha Morada, the Peruvian purple corn punch; and Bananito, spiced banana oat milk with a cold brew float.

venues.longDescription:
Cavaña sits on the seventeenth floor of the LUMA Hotel at 100 Channel Street, overlooking Mission Bay, the creek and Oracle Park. The Infatuation describes it as a Latin American bar that manages to make Mission Bay feel as though it has been given the Miami treatment, complete with a dance floor and a DJ playing reggaeton, and notes that the crowd is a mix of dressed-up visitors and locals stopping for a drink and a bowl of ceviche before a Giants game. The bar runs to midnight from Sunday through Thursday and to 1am on Friday and Saturday, opening early on Saturday afternoons.

The non-alcoholic drinks are printed on the main cocktail card under a spirit-free heading, immediately after the full-proof list, and there are six of them — more than most licensed bars in the city carry, and covering a wider range of styles. Maracuyá is built on Almave, the de-alcoholised blue agave spirit, with Wilderton Citrus, an aperitivo, passionfruit agave and lime. The Phoney Mezcal Negroni combines a Peruvian agave distillate with Pathfinder amaro and Abstinence blood orange aperitif, giving the bitter-and-smoky profile that is hardest to reproduce without alcohol. Guava Fresca is lighter, made with a blood orange aperitivo, fresh lime, guava and soda water. Michelada-Nada uses a non-alcoholic cerveza with the bar's own michelada mix, which is a genuinely rare listing. Chicha Morada is the traditional Peruvian purple-corn punch cooked with pineapple, apple and cinnamon, and Bananito is a dessert-leaning build of spiced banana oat milk with a cold brew float. Fieldwork's non-alcoholic grapefruit blonde ale is stocked in cans alongside them, and a set of aguas and Mexican sodas — agua de piedra sparkling water, Coca-Cola Mexicana, Fever-Tree ginger beer and pineapple Jarritos — rounds out the alcohol-free half of the menu. Because the bar is on a hotel roof with a dance floor and live music, the practical value of six spirit-free builds is that a guest can spend a whole night out here on the same terms as everyone else at the table.
venues.pressQuote: Cavaña is a Latin American bar that somehow manages to make Mission Bay feel like it’s gotten the Miami treatment, complete with a dance floor and DJ spinning reggaeton.
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: The Infatuation, Best Restaurants In Mission Bay

venues.name: Cave Valley Kava
venues.description: Cave Valley Kava is Louisville's first kava lounge, opened in 2022 by a founder who goes by Stevie, in a small stone house on Crums Lane in the city's South End. Nothing served here contains alcohol. It doubles as an all-ages live music venue — shows run any night of the week — and the room holds a zine library, a rack of cassettes for sale and a standing commitment to local artists, which makes it function as a genuine third place rather than a shop with chairs. Alongside kava it pours teas, coffee and ginger kombucha, and blends smoothies with kratom, kava and CBD. Be clear on what that means: kava and kratom are alcohol-free but psychoactive, so this is a night out without alcohol rather than a guaranteed sober space.
venues.longDescription:
Louisville has tied more of its identity to alcohol than almost any American city — bourbon is the tourism product, the export and the civic story — and Cave Valley Kava exists as a deliberate answer to that. It opened in 2022 in a small stone house on Crums Lane in the South End, marked by a tiny light-up OPEN sign, and it is the first kava lounge the city has had. Louisville Public Media covered it in 2023 as a South End business built on live music and easy sipping; the founder, Stevie, framed the point as sharing the contentment found in kava in a town whose social life runs on whiskey.

The room is not a bar imitation. It is an all-ages live music venue that books shows any night of the week and is listed as such by touring booking directories, and it keeps a zine library, sells cassettes and shows work by local artists. The drinks are kava by the shell, brewed teas, coffee, ginger kombucha, and smoothies blended with kava, kratom and CBD. For a non-drinker in Louisville this is the closest thing to a dedicated alcohol-free bar the city has: since no fully alcohol-free cocktail bar has ever opened here, the alternatives are ordinary bars with good zero-proof menus, which is a different proposition on a difficult night.

Two honest cautions, because our readers include people in recovery. First, kava contains no alcohol but is psychoactive and mildly sedating, and Cave Valley also serves kratom, which is a stronger and more contested substance with real dependence potential. Neither is the same as an alcohol-free café, and anyone whose sobriety is abstinence-based should know that before walking in. Second, the South End location puts it well outside the walkable Butchertown-NuLu-Highlands triangle where most of this guide sits — it is a twenty-minute drive from downtown, not a stop on a night out. Check the venue's Instagram for hours and show listings, which change with the gig calendar rather than following a fixed schedule. What Cave Valley demonstrates, and what makes it worth the drive, is that the alternative to a bourbon bar does not have to be a coffee shop. The room has the things that make a bar work — a late licence-free evening, live music, people who recognise you, something in your hand that took effort to prepare — assembled without alcohol and without pretending to be a cocktail lounge. In a city that has produced a nationally distributed non-alcoholic bourbon but not one alcohol-free bar, that gap is conspicuous, and this small stone house on Crums Lane is currently the only thing filling it.
venues.pressQuote: Kava is a plant-derived drink used in some South Pacific cultural ceremonies and is commonly drunk by people looking for an alternative to alcohol.

venues.name: CBD Provisions
venues.description: CBD Provisions is the Texas brasserie on the Main Street frontage of The Joule hotel downtown, and its drink menu carries a printed Mocktails section built on serious non-alcoholic spirits rather than juice and soda. The Agave Maria and Green Jardin both use Almave, the non-alcoholic blue agave distillate, the first with lime and passion fruit and the second with cucumber, jalapeño and agave. The Café de Olla Frío works Lyre's non-alcoholic espresso-malt spirit against espresso, charred orange and piloncillo — a genuine after-dinner drink rather than a soft option. Because the room serves breakfast through dinner seven days a week, the list works at a business breakfast, a weekend brunch and a late dinner alike.

venues.longDescription:
CBD Provisions occupies the Main Street frontage of The Joule and has been one of downtown Dallas's more reliable restaurants for a decade, a Texas brasserie in a hotel that takes its art collection as seriously as its cooking. Its non-alcoholic drinks arrive under a printed Mocktails heading, and the choice of base spirits tells you the bar has thought about the category properly rather than reaching for the fruit juice.

Two of the three are built on Almave, the non-alcoholic blue agave distillate developed with Lewis Hamilton — a product designed to behave like blanco tequila rather than to taste of nothing, and one still uncommon on Dallas back bars. The Agave Maria pairs its reposado expression with lime and passion fruit; the Green Jardin takes the blanco into cucumber, jalapeño and agave, which is the closest a zero-proof drink gets to a spicy margarita in this city, and the one to order if what you miss is heat rather than sweetness. The third, Café de Olla Frío, uses Lyre's espresso-malt spirit with espresso, charred orange and piloncillo, echoing the Mexican spiced coffee it is named for; it is a genuine after-dinner drink, which is the slot zero-proof lists most often leave empty.

What makes the list useful in practice is where it sits. This is a full-service restaurant serving breakfast through dinner seven days, in a hotel, on a downtown block where much of the competition closes between services. That means the mocktails work at a business breakfast, a weekend brunch and a late dinner alike — three occasions where ordering a soft drink usually marks you out, and where being handed something built on a real distillate does not. The room never signals that a guest who is not drinking has ordered the lesser thing, which in a hotel brasserie of this class is the whole point. Almave is worth knowing by name if you are ordering zero-proof around Dallas, because it is the variable that separates a spicy-margarita substitute that works from one that tastes of cordial. Very few bars in this guide stock it, and the two drinks built on it here are the strongest agave-led non-alcoholic pours we have recorded in the city.

venues.name: Cease and Desist Book Club
venues.description: Cease and Desist Book Club is a downtown Spokane speakeasy hidden behind a bookcase on North Washington Street, with a literary conceit that runs through the drinks — a vanilla saffron old fashioned, a Bananas Foster, a Spring Cleaning. It keeps a mocktail list built to the same theme, so a non-drinker gets a drink that belongs to the concept rather than one that sits outside it. The room is small, dim and shelved wall to wall, and it keeps the longest hours of any cocktail bar in this guide: 4pm to 2am Tuesday through Saturday, with earlier closes on Sunday and Monday.
venues.address: 108 N Washington St Suite 100, Spokane, WA 99201
venues.longDescription:
The entrance is a bookcase. Cease and Desist Book Club opened downtown on North Washington Street as a speakeasy for people who like books as much as bars, and the fit-out follows through — shelves to the ceiling, low light, a small room that seats fewer people than want to be in it on a Friday.

The drinks carry the conceit. A vanilla saffron old fashioned is the most-praised thing on the list; a Bananas Foster and a Spring Cleaning show the range. Crucially for this guide, the bar keeps non-alcoholic drinks built to the same theme rather than a generic pair of mocktails bolted on, so someone not drinking is handed something that belongs to the room. That is a small distinction with a large effect: the experience of a themed bar is the theme, and being excluded from it is what makes a soda water feel like a consolation.

This listing is graded three and records no signature drinks. The bar's non-alcoholic list is not published online in a form that could be read for this guide, and one aggregator's description of it could not be independently corroborated — a caution earned the hard way elsewhere in this city, where a directory credited another Spokane restaurant with "sophisticated zero-proof pairings" that turned out to be soda and lime-ade. What is well attested is that the mocktails exist and are made to the theme; ask at the bar.

The hours are the strongest practical argument for it. Wednesday through Saturday the room runs 4pm to 2am, Tuesday to midnight, and Sunday and Monday from 5pm to 11pm — seven days a week, and later than anywhere else in this guide. For anyone who does not drink but does want to be out at midnight in downtown Spokane, the options are this and very little else.

venues.name: Cedar Tea House
venues.description: Cedar Tea House on Rainier Avenue South in Columbia City calls itself Seattle's premier sobriety-friendly tea house and kava bar, and it is built explicitly as a late-night sanctuary rather than a daytime cafe: doors Wednesday to Saturday from 5pm to 2am, with last call for kava at 1:30am. It is run by three people with distinct roles — Hector Ayala as kava master, Daneca (Thalay) Trần as artist and mindfulness practitioner, and Alexia Parmer as musician and community builder — and the programme reflects that mix, pairing healing teas and kava ceremonies with music and community events. The drinks list runs past twenty selections and is genuinely composed rather than assembled: the Mojo Jojo combines sage tea with fresh lime, mint, agave and chia seeds; the Plum Fairy layers house plum syrup with rose, butterfly pea flower, lemon and lavender; the Triple OG uses house-made grape purée with ginger and rose tea.

venues.longDescription:
Cedar Tea House sits on Rainier Avenue South in Columbia City and describes itself as Seattle's premier sobriety-friendly tea house and kava bar. The phrasing is deliberate — sobriety-friendly rather than merely alcohol-free — and the operating hours back it up: Wednesday through Saturday, 5pm to 2am, with last call for kava at 1:30am. That is a bar's schedule in a city where the alcohol-free alternative usually closes at 6pm, and the whole proposition rests on it. The house calls itself a late-night sanctuary, and the three people running it have divided the work along unusually clear lines: Hector Ayala is the kava master, Daneca (Thalay) Trần is an artist and mindfulness practitioner, and Alexia Parmer is a musician and community builder. Between them they run kava ceremonies, a healing tea programme and a music and events calendar, which is a more ambitious remit than most rooms of this size attempt.

The drinks are the part that separates it from a straightforward kava bar. The full list runs past twenty selections, and the signature builds are composed with the care of a cocktail menu rather than a tea counter: the Mojo Jojo combines sage tea with fresh lime, mint, agave and chia seeds; the Plum Fairy layers a house plum syrup with rose, butterfly pea flower, lemon and lavender, taking its colour shift from the butterfly pea; and the Triple OG works house-made grape purée against ginger and rose tea. Those are drinks somebody would order because they want them, which is the whole test of a spirit-free menu. Kava sits alongside as the anchor and deserves the plain description this audience is owed: it is the ground root of a South Pacific shrub steeped in water, containing no alcohol at all, drunk socially across the Pacific for roughly three thousand years, and genuinely relaxing and mildly intoxicating in its own right. Between Cedar and Swamp Cow, Seattle finally has two late-night rooms where not drinking is the default rather than the exception.

venues.name: Centraal Grand Café & Tappery
venues.description: Centraal Grand Café & Tappery is a Belgian- and Amsterdam-inspired grand café and taproom from Milwaukee's Lowlands Group, anchoring the Kinnickinnic Avenue bar district in Bay View. Alongside one of the city's largest tap programs, it keeps a standing "Free Spirited" menu of zero-proof cocktails, NA beers and booze-free bubbles that runs year-round rather than only during Dry January. Spirit-free builds include the Faux-Fashioned and the Lekker Tropikaal Mule. Open daily from 8 a.m., it works as both a morning café and an evening drinking hall.

venues.longDescription:
Centraal Grand Café & Tappery sits on the corner of Kinnickinnic and Lincoln avenues in Bay View, part of Milwaukee's Lowlands Hospitality Group, whose European-style grand cafés are built around world-class beer lists. Inspired by Amsterdam's Centraal Station and the grand cafés that surround it, the room pours from more than 75 taps spanning bier, wine, coffee, craft soda, cocktails and cider, with Dutch touches and homages to the country's cycling culture woven through the artwork and beer list.

The draw for non-drinkers is the venue's standing "Free Spirited" menu of NA cocktails, NA beers and soft drinks — a permanent fixture rather than a seasonal gimmick, which is why it appears on Visit Milwaukee's mocktail trail. Named zero-proof cocktails include the Faux-Fashioned (Kentucky 74, Fee Brothers aromatic bitters, simple, orange and cherry), the Lekker Tropikaal Mule (Undone Not Rum, pomegranate-passionfruit purée, lime and ginger beer), the Spritz in the Sun and a Caramelized Pineapple Margarita, alongside spirit-free sparkling options such as an NA Mimosa and a White Peach Bellini.

On the taproom side, the alcohol-free pours include Athletic Brewing's Cerveza Atlética Copper next to NA Chouffe, Stella Artois Liberté and rotating NA craft options. Because Centraal also serves a full bar, it is a hybrid rather than a fully alcohol-free venue, but the breadth of its standing zero-proof list makes it a dependable stop for sober guests. Located at 2306 S. Kinnickinnic Ave., it is open daily from 8 a.m., closing at 10 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and 11 p.m. on Friday and Saturday.
venues.pressQuote: Located amid the bustling bar district of Kinnickinnic Ave. in Bay View, the taproom and restaurant is the perfect place to meet up for a bite and a drink off their "Free Spirited" menu of NA cocktails, beers and soft drinks.

venues.name: Central Standard Crafthouse & Kitchen
venues.description: Central Standard Crafthouse & Kitchen is the downtown restaurant and bar attached to Central Standard's craft distillery, occupying a renovated five-story building in East Town with a scratch kitchen, a cocktail bar, and a rooftop terrace. The same distilling craft behind its spirits goes into a standing lineup of zero-proof drinks, including the Hornchata (rice milk, cinnamon, vanilla), a matcha tonic, a ginger tonic, and a spirit-free Old Fashioned, alongside Athletic Brewing's Run Wild non-alcoholic beer. Multiple Milwaukee publications single it out as one of the city's leading spots for non-alcoholic cocktails.

venues.longDescription:
Central Standard Crafthouse & Kitchen is the food-and-drink flagship of Central Standard Craft Distillery, set inside a renovated multi-story building at 320 E. Clybourn St. in Milwaukee's East Town. The property pairs a main-floor restaurant and bar with a scratch kitchen and a rooftop terrace, and the distillery's award-winning spirits anchor the cocktail list. It operates seven days a week, with dinner nightly, weekday happy hour, and weekend brunch.

The venue treats its zero-proof drinks with the same distilling craft it applies to its spirits. Milwaukee Magazine's mocktail roundup highlights the Hornchata, made with rice milk, cinnamon, vanilla, and simple syrup, while OnMilwaukee's guide to the city's best zero-proof cocktails notes house builds such as a matcha tonic, a ginger tonic, and a zero-proof Old Fashioned, plus Athletic Brewing's Run Wild non-alcoholic beer on the menu. The kitchen and bar will also craft mocktails to stand in for alcohol pairings, so non-drinking guests get a full spirit-free experience rather than an afterthought.

Because it is a working distillery and full-service bar, Central Standard still pours alcohol throughout the menu, but its non-alcoholic program is substantial and repeatedly recognized. Visit Milwaukee's non-alcoholic drinks directory lists it among the city's notable zero-proof destinations, crediting the team's distilling know-how for the balance of the drinks.
venues.pressQuote: Central Standard Crafthouse & Kitchen uses its distilling know-how to craft balanced zero-proof options.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Visit Milwaukee, N/A Cocktail & Mocktail Makers directory

venues.name: Century Grand
venues.description: One of Arizona's most ambitious cocktail destinations, Century Grand houses three distinct concepts under one roof — the train-car experience Platform 18, the apothecary-styled Grey Hen Rx, and the below-deck tiki bar UnderTow — and is now operated by the Barter & Shake hospitality group. A repeat national-awards finalist, the bar team distils its own alcohol-free spirits in house and uses them across all three rooms, so the zero-proof builds are made from the same base as everything else rather than assembled from juice. Named non-alcoholic drinks run across the concepts: the Constable's Companion at Platform 18 (gin alternative, mint, poblano, lime), Chart the Course and Mark My Words at Grey Hen Rx, and the Shipless Sailor below deck at UnderTow.
venues.address: 3626 E Indian School Rd, Phoenix, AZ 85018
venues.longDescription:
Century Grand is less a bar than a building full of them. Behind an unremarkable Indian School Road frontage in Arcadia sit three separate concepts, each with its own room, menu and conceit: Platform 18, built as a 1920s railway carriage complete with scenery moving past the windows; Grey Hen Rx, an apothecary-styled room of tinctures and bitters; and UnderTow, the below-deck tiki bar that had a cult following before the rest existed. The group is now operated by Barter & Shake, and it has been a repeat finalist in national bar awards.

The reason it belongs on a non-alcoholic directory is unusual, and it is not the mocktail list. The bar team distils its own alcohol-free spirits in house and uses them across all three concepts — which means a zero-proof order is not a bartender improvising with fruit juice but the same programme running on a different base. The results carry names of their own rather than being described as versions of something else. Platform 18 pours the Constable's Companion, a gin alternative with mint, poblano and lime. Grey Hen Rx has Chart the Course (bourbon-inspired, with peach, pineapple and lemon), Mark My Words (rum and plum tea) and the yuzu-led Prayer at Mid-day, plus non-alcoholic bubbles. UnderTow builds the Shipless Sailor from a rum substitute with cinnamon, clove, orgeat, hibiscus, lime and pineapple.

Phoenix New Times, surveying metro bars where alcohol-free drinks are actually on the menu, noted in January 2024 that the three-bars-under-one-roof concept "doesn't exclude designated drivers". Two practical points: each concept has its own door policy and UnderTow in particular needs a reservation, and the venue is a full-strength cocktail destination — the alcohol-free work is a genuine parallel programme, not the character of the place.
venues.pressQuote: The three-cocktail-bars-under-a-single-roof concept ... doesn't exclude designated drivers

venues.name: Ceremony
venues.description: Ceremony is Hampton Roads' dedicated dry bottle shop and the anchor of the region's alcohol-free scene — a curated wall of non-alcoholic beer, wine and spirits alongside mixers, bitters and sustainable bar tools, run on a zero-waste model. It was founded in Virginia Beach in 2022 and has since grown to multiple locations across Virginia and into North Carolina, which makes it one of the few alcohol-free retailers anywhere to have proven the format can scale. The Norfolk shop on Baldwin Avenue is the flagship, and the company has extended beyond retail into a non-alcohol pop-up bar inside a local coffee shop.
venues.longDescription:
Ceremony began in Virginia Beach in 2022 as Hampton Roads' first dry bottle shop, and the Norfolk store on Baldwin Avenue in Chelsea is now its flagship. The proposition is simple and unusually complete: non-alcoholic beer, wine and spirits, plus the mixers, bitters and bar tools needed to actually build a drink at home, curated rather than piled up, and run on a zero-waste model.

What makes it significant beyond Norfolk is that it worked. Dedicated alcohol-free retail is a hard business — thin margins, a young category, a customer base still forming — and the sector's casualty rate is high. Richmond, two hours west, has just lost both a dry bottle shop and its only alcohol-free bar. Ceremony has gone the other way, expanding to several Virginia locations and across the state line into North Carolina, with more announced. Very few alcohol-free retailers anywhere have demonstrated the model scales, and that makes this one worth paying attention to.

The range is the reason to visit rather than order online. Non-alcoholic spirits in particular are difficult to buy blind: the category is full of products that taste like nothing or like perfume, prices run high, and a bad bottle sours people on the whole idea. A curated shelf with someone behind the counter who has tasted everything solves that in a way no website can. The bitters and mixers matter just as much, because most of what makes a drink feel like a drink lives in those bottles rather than in the base spirit.

Ceremony has also pushed past retail into service, running a non-alcohol pop-up bar inside a Norfolk coffee shop — the same shared-premises model that keeps alcohol-free bars viable elsewhere. Practical notes: closed Mondays, 11am to 7pm Tuesday to Saturday, and noon to 5pm on Sunday. There is a second Hampton Roads outlet operating as a booth inside Painted Tree Boutiques on Laskin Road in Virginia Beach. That second site is a booth within a larger boutique rather than a standalone shop, so treat the Norfolk store as the real destination if you want the full range and someone to talk to about it. The company has also announced further Virginia openings, which suggests the expansion has not finished.

venues.name: Châm Pang Lanes
venues.description: Châm Pang Lanes is a bowling alley, bar and Vietnamese-leaning kitchen on Harney Street in downtown Omaha, and it is listed in the city's own curated drinks guide for its spirit-free offerings. The format is the argument for it: bowling gives an evening a structure that is not the round, which is consistently the single most useful thing for someone who does not drink, and the room is busy and social without the pace being set by anyone's glass. Open from 4pm, to midnight midweek and 2am on Friday and Saturday, with a noon start at weekends. Lanes book up at weekends, so reserve ahead if bowling is the plan.
venues.longDescription:
Châm Pang Lanes combines three things that do not usually appear together: a bowling alley, a bar with a champagne-forward list, and a kitchen doing Vietnamese-influenced food. It is on Harney Street in downtown Omaha and it is one of the busier rooms in the city.

It appears in this guide for a reason that has more to do with format than with any drink. The hardest part of an evening out without alcohol is rarely the first hour; it is the third, when the room's entire tempo is set by other people's rounds and there is nothing to do but drink and wait. An activity venue removes that completely. Bowling sets the pace instead, everyone has something to do with their hands, and nobody is counting whose glass is where.

That is why this directory lists activity venues alongside cocktail bars, and it is why Shuffles in Tulsa, The Archives in Burlington and this room all earn places. For readers in early sobriety in particular, a night with a structure is a substantially easier proposition than a night in a bar.

The alcohol-free offer here is documented by Omaha's curated local drinks guide as part of the city's spirit-free options, and this entry is graded three accordingly: the offer is real and third-party attested, but there is no published list, no named build that could be verified, and so nothing further is claimed. Ask at the bar.

Hours are 4pm to midnight Monday through Thursday, 4pm to 2am on Friday, noon to 2am on Saturday and noon to 10pm on Sunday. Lanes get booked at weekends, so reserve if bowling is the plan rather than the excuse.

venues.name: Char & Stave
venues.description: Char & Stave is an all-day cafe and cocktail bar in Ardmore, opened March 21, 2022 by Jared Adkins, owner and master distiller of Phoenixville's Bluebird Distilling, with head distiller Scott Gilbert. The concept — "coffee made by whiskey people" — uses Bluebird's spent bourbon barrels to age coffee beans, drawing vanilla, caramel, and spice notes into the roast. The 42-seat space pours espresso, nitro cold brew, barrel-aged espresso, and signature lattes by day, then shifts to cocktails in the evening. For zero-proof drinkers, the menu carries a dedicated, clearly labeled section, "Handcrafted Non-Alcoholic Options, for here or to-go," that mirrors the cocktail list. Named alcohol-free builds include a Barrel-Aged "Old Fashioned," a Matcha "Mojito," an Espresso Tonic, a Chai Blossom, Espresso Y Amaro, and Flora & Fauna. A second location operates in Chestnut Hill.

venues.longDescription:
Char & Stave opened on 21 March 2022 in Ardmore — on the Main Line, west of the city — founded by Jared Adkins, owner and master distiller of Phoenixville's Bluebird Distilling, with head distiller Scott Gilbert. The concept is summarised in their own phrase: coffee made by whiskey people. Bluebird's spent bourbon barrels are used to age green coffee beans before roasting, drawing vanilla, caramel and spice out of the wood and into the coffee.

That process is worth understanding, because it explains why the place matters to a non-drinker. A barrel that has held bourbon for years is saturated with the compounds the spirit left behind — vanillin from the charred oak, caramelised wood sugars, coconut-scented lactones. Resting coffee in that barrel transfers those aromatics without transferring meaningful alcohol. The result tastes like the flavours people associate with whiskey, delivered in a cup with no spirit in it, which is about as direct an answer as exists to what someone misses about a dram.

The forty-two-seat room works as an all-day venue: espresso, nitro cold brew, barrel-aged espresso and signature lattes by day, shifting to cocktails in the evening. For zero-proof drinkers it keeps a dedicated and clearly labelled section, "Handcrafted Non-Alcoholic Options", available for here or to go — and the labelling is the part that counts, since a clearly headed section means ordering without a conversation.

The hours are the strongest argument. Seven in the morning until eleven at night from Monday to Thursday, and until midnight on Friday and Saturday. Very few cafés anywhere run to midnight, and a room that serves both a morning espresso and a late-evening barrel-aged coffee covers the entire day for someone who wants a venue rather than a bar. It is on the Main Line rather than in the city, so plan the journey — the Paoli/Thorndale regional rail line runs to Ardmore.
venues.pressQuote: Phoenixville's Bluebird Distilling is set to expand with an all-day coffee and cocktail bar called Char & Stave Coffee in Ardmore on Monday, March 21

venues.name: Charlie was a sinner.
venues.description: Charlie was a sinner. is an all-vegan cocktail bar and small-plates restaurant in Philadelphia's Midtown Village, opened in 2014 by Nicole Marquis, the restaurateur behind the HipCityVeg and Bar Bombón plant-based ventures. The dimly lit, candle-lit room — brass bar top, button-tufted banquettes, antique fixtures — is fully plant-based across food and drink. Its craft cocktail program runs deep, and alongside the spirited list it keeps a standing "Zero Proof" section of roughly four non-alcoholic cocktails around $11, built on house-made syrups, cordials, and even a house-made zero-proof gin rather than off-the-shelf substitutes. Current zero-proof pours include No Regrets (house zero-proof gin, lemon, sparkling water), Spicy Pineapple (pineapple, agave, lime, house spice blend), a Basil Fennel Lemon Soda, and a Blackberry Ginger Soda. Visit Philly highlights it as "an upscale respite" on alcohol-heavy 13th Street that "always has several zero-proof options."

venues.longDescription:
Charlie was a sinner. opened in 2014 in Midtown Village and is entirely plant-based across both food and drink — one of the earlier ventures from Nicole Marquis, the restaurateur behind HipCityVeg and Bar Bombón. The room is deliberately dark and atmospheric: brass bar top, button-tufted banquettes, antique fixtures, candlelight. Visit Philly's assessment captures its position well — amid the alcohol-heavy nightlife of 13th Street, it is an upscale respite that always keeps several zero-proof options going.

That standing "Zero Proof" section runs to roughly four non-alcoholic cocktails at around eleven dollars, and the construction is what distinguishes it. The drinks are built on house-made syrups and cordials, and the bar makes its own zero-proof gin rather than buying a commercial substitute. That is a meaningful difference. A bought bottle is a fixed flavour the bar has to work around; a house infusion means choosing the botanicals — juniper, citrus peel, spice — to suit the specific drinks being poured, which is the same freedom a bar has with its syrups and almost never exercises with spirits.

The named drinks span the range. No Regrets and the Spicy Pineapple sit at the cocktail end, while the Basil Fennel Lemon Soda and Blackberry Ginger Soda are house sodas — and the fennel is the interesting choice there, an anise-scented vegetal note that is savoury rather than sweet, doing the job a botanical spirit would.

The vegan constraint helps here in the same way it does elsewhere. A bar that cannot use egg white has to solve foam and texture another way, usually with aquafaba, and a kitchen practised at building richness without dairy is already fluent in the thinking a good alcohol-free drink requires.

The hours make it a genuine night out: four in the afternoon until eleven most nights, and until two in the morning on Friday and Saturday.
venues.pressQuote: Amidst the alcohol-heavy nightlife on 13th Street, Charlie was a sinner. is an upscale respite that always has several zero-proof options on its menu priced around $11.

venues.name: Charlotte's Wine Bar & Tapas
venues.description: A Mount Pleasant wine bar on Coleman Boulevard, opened in September 2025, pairing a rotating global wine list with shareable tapas, flatbreads and boards. Alongside the wine program it keeps a standing alcohol-free selection: non-alcoholic wines in sparkling, rose and pinot noir, plus NA beer, a zero-proof Paloma, sparkling waters and Italian sodas. The room also hosts live music, tastings and themed events.
venues.address: 320 W Coleman Blvd, Mount Pleasant, SC 29464
venues.longDescription:
Charlotte's Wine Bar & Tapas opened on West Coleman Boulevard in Mount Pleasant in September 2025, owned by Lynn Fleer. The concept centers on a rotating selection of U.S. and international wines by the glass and bottle, served with chef-crafted small plates, oven-fired tapas, artisan flatbreads and charcuterie boards meant for lingering and sharing.

For non-drinkers, the bar carries a dedicated alcohol-free lineup: NA wines in sparkling, rose and pinot noir styles, a non-alcoholic beer, a zero-proof Paloma, plus sparkling waters and Italian sodas. The space rounds out its programming with live music, wine tastings and themed nights.
venues.pressQuote: Charlotte's Wine Bar offers a selection of alcohol-free wines—Sparkling, Rose, and Pinot Noir. Additionally, they have a non-alcoholic beer and Paloma cocktail, sparkling waters, and Italian soda.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Charming Inns of Charleston, "Cocktails & Mocktails in Charleston" guide

venues.name: Chartreuse Kitchen & Cocktails
venues.description: Midtown Detroit farm-to-table restaurant from James Beard 2026-27 "Ones to Watch" chef Doug Hewitt, with a dedicated non-alcoholic drinks menu.
venues.address: 15 E Kirby St, Suite D, Detroit, MI 48202
venues.hours: Mon closed; Tue-Thu 5pm-9pm; Fri 11:30am-2pm & 5pm-9:30pm; Sat 5pm-9:30pm; Sun 4pm-8pm
venues.longDescription:
Chartreuse Kitchen & Cocktails opened in 2015 in the Park Shelton building on Kirby Street in Midtown Detroit, directly across from the Detroit Institute of Arts. Chef Doug Hewitt and owner Sandy Levine built it around a seasonal, farm-to-table menu and a deep collection of the French herbal liqueur the restaurant is named for; the Detroit Free Press named it its Restaurant of the Year in 2016. In June 2026, Hewitt was named to the James Beard Foundation's 2026-27 TasteTwenty class — chefs recognized as "Ones to Watch" for cooking and for work beyond the kitchen — with a Taste America stop planned in Detroit that September.

The drink list carries a standalone non-alcoholic section rather than a couple of afterthought mocktails. Named drinks include Seedlip & Cola, built on the Seedlip non-alcoholic spirit; Spiced Brazilian Limeade; Pickle Mule; and Coffee Lime & Tonic, alongside housemade sodas and teas that rotate with the kitchen's seasonal menu.

The space is known for its bright green walls, living wall of succulents, and dried-flower arrangements — a deliberate contrast to Detroit's long winters — with a front cocktail bar where guests can order just snacks and drinks without committing to a full seasonal tasting menu. It sits in the Cultural Center pocket of Midtown, alongside the DIA, the Detroit Public Library, and Wayne State.
venues.pressQuote: The menu may change with the seasons, but at Chartreuse Kitchen & Cocktails in Midtown Detroit, spring is always in the air.

venues.name: Chartreuse Sisters
venues.description: Chartreuse Sisters is a French-American fusion patisserie and dry bar at 800 Wealthy Street SE, owned and run by sisters Alyson and Mallory Caillaud-Jones. Alyson heads the beverage program and Mallory is head pastry chef, and the shop's own tagline lists what it sells in order: pastries, NA cocktails, espresso. No alcohol is served. The pastry side is French-American — eclairs, large macarons, savoury galettes — on a menu that rotates monthly around local seasonal fruit and vegetables, made in house and sourced locally where possible. The non-alcoholic cocktail list rotates alongside it. The pair started out baking in their parents' home kitchen before opening the storefront, which occupies a preserved historic building on Wealthy Street.
venues.address: 800 Wealthy St SE, Grand Rapids, MI 49506
signatureDrinks: The Owls Are Not What They Seem (orange sec, ginger beer, cranberry juice, maple syrup, cranberries & crystallized ginger)
venues.longDescription:
Chartreuse Sisters is run by Alyson and Mallory Caillaud-Jones, who began by baking out of their parents' home kitchen and opened their storefront at 800 Wealthy Street SE as, in their own words, a dream come true. The division of labour is clear: Mallory is head pastry chef and Alyson heads beverage, and the shop presents itself as a patisserie and a dry bar in equal measure rather than a cafe with a sideline. Its own tagline reads "Pastries • NA Cocktails • Espresso". The building is a preserved piece of Grand Rapids history and the sisters make a point of hosting guests inside it; products are made in house and sourced locally where they can be, and the business states a commitment to buying from small businesses working on similar principles.

The menu rotates monthly around whatever local fruit and vegetables are in season, which applies to the drinks as much as the pastry case — the non-alcoholic cocktail list turns over rather than sitting static, alongside a full espresso, latte and tea program. The pastries are French-American fusion: eclairs, outsized macarons, savoury galettes, and sweets the sisters trace to their French-American heritage and to food and drink they encountered travelling. The best-documented drink is The Owls Are Not What They Seem, built from orange sec, ginger beer, cranberry juice and maple syrup and garnished with cranberries and crystallized ginger. Opening hours are short and weekend-weighted — Thursday through Sunday, 9am to 3pm — so this is a daytime venue rather than an evening one. A note on location: press coverage of the opening placed the shop in East Hills, which is how the Uptown business district describes the stretch, but the City of Grand Rapids neighbourhood boundary runs along Wealthy Street and puts this building on the Baxter side.
venues.pressQuote: Chartreuse Sisters offers a rotating selection of mocktails in addition to coffees, espressos, lattes, teas and more.

venues.name: Chattanooga Culture
venues.description: Chattanooga Culture is a fermentation lab on Vance Avenue with a kombucha and kava lounge attached, established in 2022 as a holistic wellness-led food and beverage company. It brews its own kombucha locally and works across cultured foods more broadly, serving that alongside kava and handcrafted mocktails in a small lounge space, and it sells at the Main Street Farmers Market as well. Nothing it pours contains alcohol. The lounge keeps limited but genuinely social hours — noon to 6pm on Thursday and noon to 10pm on Friday and Saturday — and programmes events including sound baths in the room.
venues.longDescription:
Chattanooga Culture began in 2022 as a fermentation business rather than a bar, and that origin is the reason the drinks are worth a trip. It is a working fermentation lab — kombucha brewed on site from local ingredients, with a broader interest in cultured foods generally — and the kombucha and kava lounge is the retail face of it, on Vance Avenue in Ridgedale, east of downtown.

What that means in practice is that the non-alcoholic drinks here are made by fermentation specialists rather than by a bartender working around an absent spirit. Kombucha done properly is a complex, sour, faintly funky drink with real structure, and it is one of the few things a non-drinker can order that has the same conversational weight as a glass of natural wine. Served alongside kava and handcrafted mocktails, it makes for a drinks list with no alcohol in it and no sense of substitution either.

The operation is not only a lounge. Chattanooga Culture sells at the Main Street Farmers Market and describes itself as a holistic, wellness-based food and beverage company, so the room doubles as a tasting space for the brewing side. It also programmes events — sound baths among them — which is a different kind of evening out from a bar, and a genuinely useful one for readers who are avoiding drinking environments rather than just avoiding drinks.

The hours are the significant constraint and should be planned around: Thursday noon to 6pm, Friday and Saturday noon to 10pm, and closed Sunday through Wednesday. The Friday and Saturday evening service is the one that matters for a night out.

One straightforward note: kava is served here and is mildly psychoactive, which readers in recovery may want to weigh. The kombucha side is a live ferment and contains only the trace alcohol any kombucha does.

venues.name: Cheeky & Dry
venues.description: Cheeky & Dry is Seattle's first and only fully alcohol-free bottle shop, a 750-square-foot family-owned store at 6120 Phinney Ave N opened in November 2023 by Kirstin and Yura Vracko. Kirstin started it after her husband went to rehab for alcohol use and she stopped drinking in solidarity with him, looking for products that would carry her through the ritual of a drink at night — she has said she built the shop she wished existed. Its own rule is absolute: every bottle is 0.5% ABV or less. The catalogue runs to roughly 250 products across non-alcoholic spirits (gin, whiskey, agave, aperitivo), wines still and sparkling, beers, ready-to-drink cocktails, mixers and bitters, with brands including Pathfinder, Three Spirit, Little Saints, Parch, Aplos, Free Spirits, Leilo and Opius. There is a counter for tasting samples before you buy. NOTE FOR ANYONE AVOIDING ALL INTOXICANTS: we checked the full catalogue and found no THC at all, but it does stock kava products, one kava-and-kratom elixir, and one CBD coffee at 25mg per serving.
venues.longDescription:
Cheeky & Dry is the shop Kirstin Vracko wished existed, and she has said so in exactly those words. She and her husband Yura opened it in November 2023 in a 750-square-foot storefront on Phinney Ave N, and the reason is not a marketing story: her husband went to rehab for alcohol use, she stopped drinking in solidarity with him, and — as she told KNKX — he went in, she stopped drinking, they both felt ten times better, and she was left looking for products that would get her through, wanting to go through the ritual of having a cocktail at night. What she found instead, in the shop's own phrase, was sad seltzers, overly sweet pretend drinks and a serious lack of options that felt grown-up. The store opened into immediate demand. The line stretched eighteen deep on one January day, and Vracko told the Seattle Times that since the moment they opened it had been busy every day, not just Dry January. The Seattle Times' description is the useful one for finding it: it looks like just another hipsterish natural wine shop unless you read the zero-proof fine print on the labels.

The rule here is refreshingly absolute — every bottle in the shop is 0.5% ABV or less — and the range is organised like a real drinks retailer rather than a novelty aisle: non-alcoholic gin and botanicals, whiskey, rum and bourbon alternatives, agave spirits, aperitivos and digestivos, still and sparkling wines, wine alternatives, beer, ready-to-drink cocktails, mixers and bitters. Roughly 250 products, with Pathfinder, Three Spirit, Little Saints, Parch, Aplos, Free Spirits, Leilo and the amaro-style Opius among them, and a counter where you can taste before committing — which matters more in this category than in any other, because a bad non-alcoholic bottle is expensive and undrinkable. One thing to know if you are avoiding all intoxicants rather than only alcohol. We read the entire catalogue and found no THC in it anywhere, which is unusual and to the shop's credit. It does stock kava — several products, including a concentrated kava spirit — one elixir that combines kava with kratom and is marked 18-and-over, and one coffee infused with 25mg of CBD per serving. Everything is labelled; just read past the ABV.
venues.pressQuote: Cheeky & Dry is Seattle's first and only dedicated non-alcoholic bottle shop, nestled in the lively Phinney Ridge neighborhood.

venues.name: Chelsea Corner
venues.description: Chelsea Corner is a long-running Knox-Henderson neighbourhood bar with a big patio, and it keeps a printed Zero Proof / Mocktail Menu that is deeper than most dedicated cocktail bars manage. Ritual Zero Proof does the heavy lifting: a zero-proof espresso martini, a Tommy's margarita and a cucumber mint spritz that adds Lyre's Classico. Beyond the cocktails there is Lyre's sparkling by the glass or as mimosas and bellinis, a michelada built on Heineken 0.0, and several Athletic Brewing varieties. It opens at ten on weekend mornings and runs to two on Friday and Saturday nights, so it works as an actual night out rather than a dinner reservation.
signatureDrinks: Espresso Martini Zero Proof (Ritual tequila alternative, cold brew)
Tommy's Margarita (Ritual tequila alternative, agave, lime)
Cucumber Mint Spritz (Ritual gin alternative, Lyre's Classico, cucumber, mint, lime)
venues.longDescription:
Chelsea Corner has been a Knox-Henderson fixture for years — a big patio, a neighbourhood crowd, the sort of bar people end up at rather than plan for. Its zero-proof offering is correspondingly unpretentious and, measured by breadth, one of the strongest in Dallas: a printed Zero Proof / Mocktail Menu that covers cocktails, sparkling wine, beer and a michelada. Breadth is the right measure for a bar like this, because the people who need it are not making a special trip; they are arriving with a group that chose the venue for other reasons.

Ritual Zero Proof anchors the cocktails. There is a zero-proof espresso martini built on the tequila alternative with cold brew, a Tommy's margarita with agave and lime, and a cucumber mint spritz that combines Ritual's gin alternative with Lyre's Classico sparkling. A watermelon fresca covers the fruit-forward end. What sets the list apart is what surrounds it: Lyre's Classical Sparkling available by the glass and as non-alcoholic mimosas and bellinis, which makes weekend brunch work properly for a non-drinker, a michelada built on Heineken 0.0, and several Athletic Brewing varieties. The michelada is the sleeper entry — a savoury, salted, chili-edged beer drink is one of the few things that genuinely does not need alcohol to work.

The practical value here is the hours and the format. This is a bar that opens at ten on weekend mornings and runs to two on Friday and Saturday nights, with a patio big enough to absorb a group — so it functions as an actual night out rather than a dinner reservation, which is the harder gap to fill without alcohol. A non-drinker can start at brunch with a Lyre's mimosa and still be holding something built rather than poured at midnight, in the same room, off the same printed menu.
venues.pressQuote: Cucumber Mint Spritz with Ritual gin, cucumber, mint, lime, and simple syrup

venues.name: Chez Maggy
venues.description: Chez Maggy is the ground-floor French restaurant of the Thompson Denver hotel on Market Street, and the first restaurant outside Los Angeles from Michelin-starred chef Ludo Lefebvre. It is named for Lefebvre's late mother-in-law Margaret, a Colorado native who was killed by a drunk driver in 2019 — context that gives the restaurant's zero-proof list more weight than a hotel bar's usual courtesy offering. Visit Denver describes a delectable selection of zero-proof cocktails, naming the Earl Grey Bliss, built on tea-infused Ritual zero-proof gin with lemon and honey, and a St. Agrestis Phony Negroni made with the brand's non-alcoholic mezcal. The kitchen applies the same approach to the food, cooking classic French dishes with Colorado ingredients. Bar M, in the hotel lobby, is the companion cocktail room.

venues.longDescription:
Chez Maggy occupies the ground floor of the Thompson Denver at 1616 Market Street, in the Union Station neighbourhood that most Denverites still call LoDo, and was the first restaurant that Michelin-starred, James Beard-nominated chef Ludo Lefebvre opened outside Los Angeles. The restaurant is named in honour of Lefebvre's late mother-in-law, Margaret — Maggy — a Colorado native who was struck and killed by a drunk driver in 2019. That fact sits behind the room rather than on the menu, but it explains why the zero-proof list here is built with the same attention as the wine list rather than being an afterthought at the bottom of the page.

The cooking is Lefebvre's take on classic French cuisine using ingredients native to Colorado: Belgian endive salad, a hearty bolognese, steak frites, all worked from local sourcing. The drinks follow the same logic of doing the familiar thing properly. Visit Denver's December 2025 guide to alcohol-free cocktails in the city describes the offering directly: "While you'll find plenty of French vino on the menu, there's also a delectable selection of zero-proof cocktails like the Earl Grey Bliss (tea-infused Ritual zero-proof gin, lemon and honey) and St. Agrestis Phony Mezcal Negroni." The Earl Grey Bliss is the house-built drink of the pair, infusing Ritual's zero-proof gin with Earl Grey before lengthening it with lemon and honey, which gives it tannin and bitterness rather than the flat sweetness that sinks most alcohol-free cocktails. The Phony Negroni uses St. Agrestis's non-alcoholic bottling, one of the few zero-proof products that reads convincingly as an aperitivo. The restaurant serves from 7am on weekdays and 8am at weekends through to 9pm or 10pm, so it covers breakfast, lunch and dinner; the connected Bar M, in the Thompson's lobby, runs a separate cocktail programme with the same kitchen behind it.
venues.pressQuote: While you'll find plenty of French vino on the menu, there's also a delectable selection of zero-proof cocktails like the Earl Grey Bliss (tea-infused Ritual zero-proof gin, lemon and honey) and St. Agrestis Phony Mezcal Negroni.

venues.name: Cholita Taqueria
venues.description: Cholita is a Los Angeles-style taqueria on Broad Ripple Avenue serving tacos and Mexican street food, with a bar that takes its non-alcoholic drinks seriously enough to build them from a proper base. The Fauxjito is the drink Indy Maven picked out: Seedlip Garden 108 — the herbal expression made from peas, rosemary, thyme and spearmint — worked into a mojito structure with lime and mint, so the herbal weight comes from the distillate rather than from sugar. In a neighbourhood whose bar scene runs heavily to margaritas and late-night drinking, a restaurant with a competent zero-proof build and a full dinner menu is a genuinely useful thing to know about.
venues.longDescription:
Cholita sits at 1001 Broad Ripple Avenue, on the block where the neighbourhood's restaurant row meets its bar strip, and serves Los Angeles-style tacos and street food — the griddle-and-salsa end of Mexican cooking rather than the combination-plate end. It runs a Tacokase counter service alongside the main dining room and a separate cantina space, and it keeps genuinely long weekend hours, opening at 11am on Saturday and Sunday and running to 11pm on Friday and Saturday nights.

The non-alcoholic entry is the Fauxjito, and it is worth explaining why it counts. Broad Ripple is not a difficult place to find a virgin margarita; it is a difficult place to find one that is not a glass of sweetened lime cordial. Cholita builds its mojito on Seedlip Garden 108, the pea-and-garden-herb distillate from the London producer that effectively created the non-alcoholic spirits category, and the rosemary, thyme and spearmint in that base carry the herbal register that rum and muddled mint would otherwise have to supply between them. Indy Maven named it in its round-up of the city's best mocktails on that basis. It is one of four venues in this guide pouring Seedlip, alongside Sundry & Vice, 16-Bit and Union Jack Pub two doors down.

For planning purposes, this is a restaurant first: the bar is part of a dinner rather than a destination in itself, and the zero-proof list is one strong build rather than a printed section of the sort you get at The Fountain Room or The Inferno Room. But it is an easy, unfussy place to eat well without drinking in a neighbourhood that does not otherwise make that easy, and the kitchen opens at 4pm on weekdays and 11am at weekends. Reservations are taken and are worth having on a Friday or Saturday.
venues.pressQuote: Fauxjito — made with Seedlip Garden 108, which is an herbal blend of peas and traditional garden herbs including rosemary, thyme, and spearmint.

venues.name: Chop Steakhouse & Bar
venues.description: Chop Steakhouse & Bar is a modern steakhouse on Grand Avenue in the centre of Coconut Grove, open from 11am every day and running to midnight from Wednesday through Saturday, which makes it one of the later kitchens in the Grove. Its alcohol-free list runs to three named builds rather than a single afterthought: a Sparkling Yuzu Limeade, a more herbaceous Green Tea Sour, and a Berry Shrub that brings mixed berries together with ginger beer, fresh citrus, cane sugar and a hint of balsamic — a genuine shrub build rather than a sweetened juice. Secret Miami documented all three in December 2025. The restaurant serves brunch, lunch, happy hour, dinner and a late-night menu.
signatureDrinks: Berry Shrub (mixed berries, ginger beer, fresh citrus, cane sugar, balsamic)
venues.longDescription:
Chop Steakhouse & Bar occupies Suite 101 at 3015 Grand Avenue, on the main commercial spine of Coconut Grove, and describes itself as an upscale-casual room serving brunch, lunch, happy hour, dinner and a late-night menu. The trading hours are the practical point of difference in a neighbourhood that closes early: doors at 11am seven days a week, with last service at 11pm on Monday, Tuesday and Sunday and midnight from Wednesday through Saturday. That gives the Grove a late seat at a bar for anyone who is not drinking.

The alcohol-free list carries three named builds, which is more than most steakhouses manage. The Sparkling Yuzu Limeade is the brightest of the three, built on yuzu and lime and served sparkling. The Green Tea Sour is the herbaceous one, using tea to give the drink tannin and grip in place of the bitterness a spirit would supply. The Berry Shrub is the most technically interesting: mixed berries with ginger beer, fresh citrus and cane sugar, finished with a subtle hint of balsamic, which is a proper shrub construction — vinegar used as an acid to give a non-alcoholic drink length and a dry finish. Secret Miami documented all three by name in its December 2025 survey of fifteen Miami venues, listing the restaurant under Coconut Grove and describing the trio as thoughtful zero-proof sips that pair with the steakhouse menu. Ingredient specifications for the Yuzu Limeade and Green Tea Sour are not published in detail, so only the Berry Shrub carries a full build in this entry. The restaurant posts as @chopsteakhouseusa. Coconut Grove is thin ground for documented alcohol-free drinking — Amal on Main Highway is the other entry in this catalogue nearby — so a steakhouse with three named builds and a midnight close fills a real gap in the map. Bookings run on (305) 692-0762.
venues.pressQuote: Pairing perfectly with its modern steakhouse menu, this hotspot brings a refreshing twist of thoughtful zero-proof sips like the Sparkling Yuzu Limeade and Green Tea Sour, which offers something more herbaceous.

venues.name: Chyna Club at Fontainebleau Las Vegas
venues.description: Chyna Club is an upscale Chinese restaurant and cocktail destination on level 1 of Fontainebleau Las Vegas, a concept from Wagamama and Hakkasan founder Alan Yau set adjacent to the casino floor and high-limit gaming area. Its beverage program, overseen by Director of Beverage Development Juyoung Kang, treats zero-proof drinks with the same culinary rigor as its full cocktails, using teas for tannin and umami, starches for mouthfeel, and oils that coat the palate. The signature non-alcoholic creation, "Heaven," is built from rice-water tea infusion, oleo-saccharum (citrus-infused sugared oil), fig jam and Supasawa, while "Made You Look" pairs jasmine pearl and green tea with cucumber and watermelon, taking its lilac hue from color-shifting butterfly pea tisane. Kang told Las Vegas Weekly that interest in mocktails has grown because "we raised the conversation and we raised their awareness, [so] people are more confident in ordering it." The restaurant is open evenings (typically Wednesday-Sunday, 5:30-9:30pm), with business-casual attire and reservations recommended.
venues.address: 2777 S Las Vegas Blvd, Level 1, Las Vegas, NV 89109
signatureDrinks: Heaven (rice-water tea infusion, oleo-saccharum, fig jam, Supasawa)
Made You Look (jasmine pearl and green tea, cucumber, watermelon, butterfly pea tisane)
venues.longDescription:
Chyna Club sits on level 1 of Fontainebleau Las Vegas, the $3.6 billion resort that opened at the north end of the Strip in December 2023, positioned next to the casino floor and the high-limit gaming area. The restaurant is a concept from Alan Yau, the restaurateur behind Wagamama and Hakkasan, with Richard Chen as executive chef cooking modern Cantonese; The World's 50 Best has singled out both the kitchen and the bar as among the best in the city. The room is designed for evening service and reads accordingly: business-casual attire, reservations recommended, dinner Wednesday through Sunday from 5:30pm.

The beverage program is overseen by Juyoung Kang, Fontainebleau's director of beverage development, who is responsible for the drinks across all thirty-six of the property's food and beverage outlets and has created roughly three hundred original cocktails for it. Kang arrived at bartending sideways — she was studying filmmaking and marketing at Temple University in Philadelphia, took a restaurant job, and got pushed behind the bar mid-shift at a busy wedding with the words "we need you behind the bar, you're smart, you can figure it out" — then taught herself spirits, sharpened the craft in Los Angeles, and moved to Las Vegas to help open The Cosmopolitan. What matters here is that she applies the same construction logic to zero-proof drinks that she applies to spirited ones, reaching for teas to supply tannin and umami, starches to supply the mouthfeel that alcohol otherwise provides, and oils that coat the palate. The signature non-alcoholic build, Heaven, is made from a rice-water tea infusion, oleo-saccharum, fig jam and Supasawa; Made You Look pairs jasmine pearl and green tea with cucumber and watermelon and takes its lilac colour from a colour-shifting butterfly pea tisane. Kang has framed the category's growth as a matter of confidence rather than demand, telling Las Vegas Weekly that "we raised the conversation and we raised their awareness, [so] people are more confident in ordering it."
venues.pressQuote: At Chyna Club, Kang brings the mocktail Heaven down to earth with an infusion of rice water tea, oleo-saccharum (a citrus-like sugared oil), fig jam and Supasawa cocktail mix.

venues.name: Cinderlands Beer Company
venues.description: Cinderlands Beer Company was founded in 2017 by two married couples — Jamie and Joanna Warden and Paul and Emily Schneider — and its Warehouse on Smallman Street in the Strip District is its largest site and main production centre: 17,500 square feet in an 1880 building, two 40-foot bars with sixteen draft lines, a built-in bocce court, dome hockey and shuffleboard, and a covered, heated second-floor patio. Its own non-alcoholic line is Hop Run, a 0.0% sparkling hop water brewed and canned in Pittsburgh that showcases Citra and Mosaic hops, sold as a 12oz can ($4) and used as the base of a small printed section called "Hop Run Mocktails": a Cranberry Lime Refresher and a Hop Run Mule, both $6. Food is smokehouse pub cooking — smoked wings ($12), pulled pork ($13), a jumbo pretzel ($15) — with a kids' menu. The taproom took a Great American Beer Festival gold medal in 2021.
venues.longDescription:
Cinderlands was founded in 2017 by two married couples, Jamie and Joanna Warden and Paul and Emily Schneider, and the Warehouse on Smallman Street is the big one — its largest location and its main production centre. The building dates from 1880 and runs to 17,500 square feet across two floors, with two forty-foot bars carrying sixteen draft lines, a built-in bocce court, dome hockey, shuffleboard and a covered, heated patio upstairs. Jamie Warden's line as it was about to open in 2019 was that the project had been over three years in the making, with thousands of hours of work, blood, sweat and tears in it. The food is smokehouse pub cooking with prices that have not run away: smoked wings and fried pickles at $12, pulled pork at $13, loaded nachos at $11, a jumbo pretzel at $15, and a genuine kids' menu with grilled cheese at $5. It opens at 11.30am most days and 10.30am on Sunday.

What brings a non-drinker here is Hop Run, and it is worth understanding what it actually is. Hop water is not non-alcoholic beer — there is no malt and no fermentation, so there is nothing to de-alcoholise. It is water, carbonation and hops, which means it delivers the aroma and the dry bitter finish that make an IPA satisfying without any of the sugar, calories or alcohol. Cinderlands brews and cans its own in Pittsburgh, showcasing Citra and Mosaic, and prints it unambiguously at 0.0% — a genuine zero rather than the 0.5% that most "non-alcoholic" beer carries, which matters to anyone who avoids even trace alcohol. A can is $4. Better still, the bar treats it as an ingredient rather than a consolation: there is a printed section headed Hop Run Mocktails holding a Cranberry Lime Refresher and a Hop Run Mule, both $6, both built on it. That is the difference between a brewery that stocks something for the designated driver and one that has thought about them.
venues.pressQuote: This is a project that's over three years in the making, so naturally we can barely contain our excitement as we rapidly approach our opening date. There are thousands of hours of work, blood, sweat and tears put into this.

venues.name: Citizen Cider
venues.description: Citizen Cider presses cider from Vermont and New York apples at its Flynn Avenue press house, where the Press House Pub serves cider-inspired pub food, the full cider range, a bar and non-alcoholic options. Its alcohol-free product is The Clean Mayor, a genuine 0.0% ABV cider — the flagship Mayor dealcoholised and then blended with real ginger and lemon juice, giving it a lemon nose and a crisp apple finish. Co-founder Kris Nelson also helped develop Zero Gravity's Rescue Club non-alcoholic beer, which makes this one address responsible for two of the three alcohol-free drinks Vermont producers are best known for. Open from noon daily, to 9pm midweek and 7pm on Monday and Tuesday.
signatureDrinks: The Clean Mayor — 0.0% ABV dealcoholised cider blended with ginger and lemon juice
venues.longDescription:
Citizen Cider started in 2010 with three founders, a borrowed press and a plan to make cider from Vermont apples rather than concentrate, and it has since become one of the defining drinks businesses of the state. The Flynn Avenue press house is where the fruit is actually pressed, and the Press House Pub attached to it is a relaxed room serving cider-inspired pub food alongside the full range, a proper bar and a set of non-alcoholic choices.

The alcohol-free one is The Clean Mayor. Citizen's Mayor line has been its best-known cider for years, and this is the logical extension: the cider dealcoholised to a true 0.0% and then blended with real ginger and lemon juice rather than left flat and stripped. The result carries a lemon aroma, a clear ginger note and a crisp apple finish, and it does the job a good NA drink has to do in a room full of drinkers — it looks and behaves like the thing everyone else is having.

There is a broader Vermont story sitting behind this address. Citizen co-founder Kris Nelson also worked with Zero Gravity to develop Rescue Club, the non-alcoholic beer line launched in January 2021 and brewed a mile north on Pine Street. Between Rescue Club, The Clean Mayor and Switchback N.A. next door, three of the alcohol-free drinks Vermont producers are best known for trace back to a few blocks of Burlington's South End, and two of them to the same person.

The pub is family-friendly, open from noon every day, closing at 9pm Wednesday through Saturday, 8pm on Sunday and 7pm on Monday and Tuesday. It is a five-minute walk from Switchback's tap room, which makes an afternoon of it entirely possible without a drop of alcohol.

venues.name: Citizen Public House
venues.description: A gastropub in the middle of Old Town Scottsdale that has been trading since 2011 and passed its fifteenth anniversary in February 2026, Citizen Public House is best known locally for the Original Chopped Salad — and, less obviously, for treating its non-alcoholic list as part of the bar program rather than an afterthought. The spirit-free builds run on real NA spirits: the Gemini pairs Seedlip Grove 42 with butterfly pea flower tea, ginger syrup and lemon, and the Nojito works pressed mint, elderflower tea syrup, lime and soda. Phoenix New Times included it in its round-up of metro bars where alcohol-free drinks are actually printed on the menu.

venues.longDescription:
Citizen Public House opened in Old Town Scottsdale in 2011 and marked fifteen years in business in February 2026 — an unusually long run for a Valley restaurant, and long enough that its Original Chopped Salad has become the dish people name before they name the address. The room is a gastropub in the proper sense rather than the marketing one: a full kitchen and a serious bar given equal weight, open daily from 4pm to 10pm, with happy hour running the first two hours every day of the week rather than being rationed to weeknights. Its position in the middle of Old Town puts it within walking distance of most of Scottsdale's bar district, which matters if the rest of your group is drinking and you are not — leaving is easy.

The non-alcoholic side is constructed the same way as the spirited one. Rather than sweetened juice, the bar works from real alcohol-free spirits. The Gemini is Seedlip Grove 42 — the citrus-forward expression — with butterfly pea flower tea, ginger syrup and lemon, a build that shifts colour as the acid hits the tea and reads as a drink rather than a novelty. The Nojito skips the rum in favour of pressed mint, elderflower tea syrup, lime and soda, keeping the herbal bite that usually gets lost when a mojito is made without alcohol and simply sweetened instead.

Phoenix New Times named the venue in its January 2024 survey of metro Phoenix bars where alcohol-free options appear on the printed menu rather than being improvised on request. That is the distinction that decides whether an evening works: a bartender who has to invent something is a bartender you are apologising to. Two things are worth knowing before you go. This is a full-service bar with a substantial alcohol list, not an alcohol-free room, so the zero-proof section is a part of the menu rather than the character of the venue. And the kitchen is the main event here — the format assumes you are eating, not perching at the bar for one drink.
venues.pressQuote: Non-alcoholic Seedlip Grove 42 is the centerpiece of Citizen Public House's Gemini, which features butterfly pea flower tea, ginger syrup and lemon.

venues.name: Citrus Club at The Dewberry
venues.description: A rooftop cocktail bar on the 8th-floor terrace of The Dewberry, a 1960s-modernist hotel facing Marion Square in downtown Charleston, billed as the highest rooftop in the city. The drink list is built around citrus-forward cocktails and "lite bites," and it carries a small standing spirit-free section rather than just off-menu substitutions. Zero-proof options include the house Dewberry Tea Spritz and a Seedlip-based mocktail, plus non-alcoholic beer and sparkling wine.

venues.longDescription:
Citrus Club sits on the 8th-floor terrace of The Dewberry, the restored mid-century-modern hotel on Meeting Street across from Marion Square, and is open daily from noon (to 8pm most days, 10pm Thursday through Saturday). It is primarily a citrus-themed cocktail bar, but its printed menu lists named non-alcoholic drinks alongside the cocktails.

The zero-proof offerings include the Dewberry Tea Spritz, built on the hotel's proprietary tea blend with lemon, agave, and sparkling mineral water, and a Seedlip Notas de Agave mocktail with bay leaf, peppercorn, and lime. The bar also stocks non-alcoholic beer (Untitled Art) and non-alcoholic sparkling wine (Oddbird Blanc de Blancs), and staff will prepare its inventive cocktails without spirits on request.
