venues.name: City Hall Bistro
venues.description: City Hall Bistro sits inside The Adolphus, the 1912 Beaux-Arts hotel downtown, and runs a Free Spirited section that appears on all four of its current menus — lunch, dinner and both in-room lists — rather than surfacing only for Dry January. The Blood Orange Mocktail is built on Ritual's tequila alternative with blood orange and ginger thyme; the Adolphus Spiced Tea combines Ritual's rum alternative with Seedlip Garden 108, orgeat and lemon into something warm-spiced and long. Clausthaler non-alcoholic beer rounds it out. One caution: the hotel publishes conflicting opening hours across two of its own official pages, so we have recorded none — call before planning breakfast or a late dinner.
signatureDrinks: Blood Orange Mocktail (Ritual tequila alternative, blood orange, ginger thyme)
Adolphus Spiced Tea (Ritual rum alternative, Seedlip Garden 108, orgeat, lemon)
venues.longDescription:
The Adolphus has been the grand hotel of downtown Dallas since 1912, and City Hall Bistro is its all-day dining room, facing the old municipal building that gives it its name. The detail that earns it a place here is not the size of its non-alcoholic list but its permanence: the Free Spirited section is printed on all four of the hotel's current menus — lunch, dinner and two in-room lists — which means it is a standing part of the operation rather than a January promotion that quietly disappears in February. Very few venues in this guide can demonstrate that, because very few publish enough menus to prove it either way.

Both builds use real non-alcoholic spirits. The Blood Orange Mocktail runs Ritual's tequila alternative into blood orange with ginger and thyme, which gives it a savoury edge rather than the flat sweetness a blood orange drink usually lands on. The Adolphus Spiced Tea is the more considered of the two, combining Ritual's rum alternative with Seedlip Garden 108, orgeat and lemon into something warm-spiced and long — a drink built for a hotel lobby in a way a fruit spritz would not be, and the better order if you are settling in rather than passing through. Clausthaler, the German non-alcoholic beer, sits alongside them.

The in-room listing is worth drawing out, because it solves a problem most of this guide cannot. A hotel guest who does not drink can order a properly built zero-proof cocktail to their room at the same time as everyone else at the bar downstairs — the minibar is usually where sober travel gets bleakest. A practical caution to close on: the hotel's own website publishes conflicting opening hours for the restaurant across two official pages, so we have recorded none rather than guess. Call the hotel rather than trusting a listing, particularly if you are planning breakfast or a late dinner. It is also, for what it is worth, one of the few entries in this guide where the non-alcoholic list has survived a change of season in print rather than in a press release — the strongest evidence available, short of calling, that what you read is what you will actually be poured.

venues.name: City Works Eatery & Pour House
venues.description: City Works at The Shops at Clearfork runs a printed "Zero-Proof (Spirit-Free)" section of roughly eleven items — unusually deep for a beer-forward restaurant. The strongest build is the Peace Punch, made with Seedlip Grove 42, orange and pineapple juice, cream of coconut, lime and grenadine. Others include a Garden Nojito (cucumber, mint, lime, lavender and raspberry syrups), a Mellow Mule with blueberry syrup and ginger beer, and a Strawberry Soothe. Some items in the section are house lemonades and dirty sodas rather than mixed drinks.

venues.longDescription:
City Works is best known for a tap wall of ninety-odd beers, which makes the size of its non-alcoholic list a genuine surprise. The Clearfork location's drink menu carries a section printed as "Zero-Proof (Spirit-Free)" running to around eleven items — deeper than most dedicated cocktail bars in the metroplex manage, and a useful answer to the problem of being the non-drinker at a table that came for the beer.

The headline build is the Peace Punch, which uses Seedlip Grove 42 — the citrus expression of the British non-alcoholic distillate — with orange and pineapple juice, cream of coconut, lime and grenadine. It is the one drink on the list constructed like a bar cocktail rather than a soft drink. Around it sit a Garden Nojito built on cucumber, mint and lime with lavender and raspberry syrups, a Mellow Mule that runs cucumber and honey syrup into blueberry and ginger beer, and a Strawberry Soothe.

An honest caveat for anyone choosing where to spend an evening: not every item under that heading is a mixed drink. Several are house lemonades and dirty sodas, which pad the count. The section is genuine and clearly labelled, and the Seedlip build in particular is a real zero-proof cocktail, but the depth is not quite what eleven items implies. It is a large, loud, family-friendly room in a shopping district rather than a destination bar — which is exactly what makes it useful on a night when the group wants beer and you do not.

venues.name: Civil Libation
venues.description: Civil Libation is a Virginia Beach bistro whose drinks menu is laid out as a flowchart, and it carries a full named section headed 'dry libations' rather than a couple of afterthoughts — Giggle Juice, I Don't Give a Fig and Purple Rain among them, built on seasonal ingredients. A dedicated section with its own heading and its own names is the practical difference between a venue where you order confidently and one where you ask what can be made without alcohol. It is also one of the few substantive alcohol-free offerings on the Virginia Beach side of Hampton Roads rather than in Norfolk.
venues.address: 2135 General Booth Blvd #132, Virginia Beach, VA 23454
venues.hours: Mon closed; Tue-Thu 4pm-9pm; Fri 4pm-10pm; Sat 10am-10pm; Sun 10am-9pm
venues.longDescription:
Civil Libation is a bistro on General Booth Boulevard, inland from the Virginia Beach oceanfront, and it does something with its drinks list that is worth more than any single recipe: it prints the alcohol-free options as their own named section, headed 'dry libations'.

That sounds like formatting. It is actually the whole problem solved. The hardest part of ordering without alcohol in an ordinary restaurant is not the absence of good options — plenty of bars can make something decent — it is the transaction: catching the server's attention, explaining, waiting while they check, then accepting whatever comes back. A named section removes all of it. You read, you choose, you order, exactly as everyone else at the table does, and nothing about the exchange marks you out.

The drinks themselves carry the same tone as the rest of the menu, which is presented as a flowchart — Giggle Juice, I Don't Give a Fig, Purple Rain — and Coastal Virginia Magazine notes they are built on seasonal ingredients rather than a fixed set of syrups. The naming matters more than it appears: calling them 'dry libations' rather than 'mocktails' frames them as drinks in their own right, and a good number of people who have stopped drinking will tell you the word mocktail is itself part of the problem.

It is also, straightforwardly, one of the few substantial alcohol-free offerings on the Virginia Beach side of Hampton Roads. The region's depth is concentrated in Norfolk — Ceremony, Only You, Gershwin's — so a venue holding up the beach end has extra value for anyone staying near the oceanfront. Hours run from 4pm Tuesday to Friday, with 10am openings at weekends for brunch; closed Mondays. Being inland on General Booth rather than on the oceanfront strip, it also draws locals rather than holiday crowds, which makes it a calmer room than anything on Atlantic Avenue.
venues.pressQuote: Civil Libation features a flowchart-inspired mocktail menu with sassy named selections under "dry libations" including "Giggle Juice," "I Don't Give a Fig" and "Purple Rain," all crafted with seasonal ingredients.

venues.name: Civil Provisions and Bar
venues.description: Civil Provisions and Bar is a neighbourhood diner and bar on Mississippi Avenue in Signal Mountain, the town on the ridge above Chattanooga, serving from 11am to 9pm seven days a week and from 10am on Sunday. Its alcohol-free entry is the Soli Swizzle, made with fresh lemon juice, pineapple and grapefruit juice, a seasonal shrub and bubbles — the seasonal shrub being the part that matters, since a house shrub rotates with what is available and gives the drink acidity and depth that straight juice cannot. It is the only venue in this guide outside the city proper, and the only all-day one.
venues.longDescription:
Signal Mountain is the town on the ridge north-west of Chattanooga, a thousand feet above the river and a fifteen-minute drive up from the city, and Civil Provisions is its restaurant and bar — an all-day neighbourhood room on Mississippi Avenue rather than a destination, which is precisely why it is in this guide.

Every other venue here is a downtown evening proposition. Civil Provisions opens at 11am and serves until 9pm seven days a week, with a 10am start on Sunday, which makes it the only place in this guide where someone can get a properly made alcohol-free drink at lunchtime on a Tuesday.

The drink is the Soli Swizzle: fresh lemon juice, pineapple and grapefruit juice, a seasonal shrub and bubbles. The seasonal shrub is the interesting component and the reason the drink grades where it does. A shrub is fruit and sugar preserved in vinegar, and it does two jobs an alcohol-free drink badly needs — it supplies acidity with more complexity than citrus alone, and it carries a savoury edge that stops the whole thing reading as a fruit punch. That the shrub is seasonal means the kitchen remakes it through the year rather than buying a bottle.

NOOGAtoday named the Soli Swizzle in its round-up of Chattanooga's non-alcoholic drinking, which is the corroboration for this listing.

The grading is three: one named build, no printed zero-proof section, no non-alcoholic spirits programme documented. What earns it a place is coverage — geographic and temporal. A metro guide that only lists downtown bars open after five is not much use to a family on the mountain on a Sunday morning, and this is the entry that fixes that.
venues.pressQuote: The Soli Swizzle mocktail is made with fresh lemon juice, pineapple + grapefruit juice, a seasonal shrub, and bubbles.
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: NOOGAtoday, Local mocktails + non-alcoholic drinks in Chattanooga

venues.name: Clavel Mezcaleria
venues.description: Founded in the summer of 2015 by Lane Harlan and Carlos Raba, Clavel is a family-run Sinaloan taqueria and mezcaleria in Remington that nixtamalizes its own corn in-house and was a 2024 James Beard finalist for Outstanding Bar, its third nomination in the category. The zero-proof drinks are a full named section of the menu, "Refrescos Sin Alcohol," priced at $11-12 alongside the mezcal cocktails rather than buried at the back. House-made ingredients carry the list: El Curandero blends the kitchen's tres chiles shrub with limon, Topo Chico and chile salt; Malabarista is built on house beet kvass with ginger, tamarindo, pina and a turmeric-marigold salt; and Horchata Real layers house black rice-coconut-pandan horchata with Cafe de Chiapas cold brew and raw wildflower honey. All four micheladas are also available sans alcohol.

venues.longDescription:
Clavel was founded in the summer of 2015 at 225 W 23rd Street in Remington by Lane Harlan and Carlos Raba, and Raba's summary of the reception is worth keeping: they were called fools for opening a taco place in Remington. Raba was born and raised in Culiacán, Sinaloa, taught to cook by his mother and five aunts, and holds a black belt in Brazilian jiu-jitsu; Harlan was born in Pampanga in the Philippines, raised around the United States and settled in Baltimore at seventeen. She co-owns the bar with her husband Matthew Pierce. The kitchen nixtamalises its own corn — the ancient alkaline process that turns dried maize into masa — from small farms in Oaxaca and Puebla, which is the difference between a good tortilla and a great one. Aguachile of raw butterflied shrimp cured in lime is the specialty at $18, with queso fundido at $16 and tacos at $5.50 each. In 2024 Clavel was a James Beard Award finalist for Outstanding Bar. It takes no reservations.

The non-alcoholic list here is one of the deepest in the country, let alone Baltimore: a full printed section headed "Refrescos Sin Alcohol" running eight drinks, nearly all built on house-made ferments and shrubs rather than bought-in substitutes. El Curandero ($11) uses a house tres chiles shrub with limón, Topo Chico and chile salt. Malabarista ($12) is the most unusual, built on house beet kvass — a lacto-fermented beet drink — with ginger, tamarindo, piña and a turmeric-marigold salt. Horchata Real ($12) layers a house black rice, coconut and pandan horchata over Chiapas cold brew and raw wildflower honey. Beyond those sit Sandia Madura with watermelon and serrano, Tormenta Tropical on an ají dulce-pandan-banana shrub, Reina Carmesí with a house red aperitivo and yuzu, El Chilango, and Rosa Morado with guayaba and timur peppercorn — all $12. Every michelada on the menu is also available without alcohol. One correction worth making plainly: a widely-read local round-up listed Clavel's Suero as alcohol-free, but the venue's own menu puts it under cocteles, built on mezcal.
venues.pressQuote: Clavel's delicious tacos with homemade tortillas and ceviche may steal the show, but its non-alcoholic cocktails rival it.

venues.name: Clemente Bar
venues.description: Clemente Bar opened in October 2024 on the second floor of chef Daniel Humm's three-Michelin-star Eleven Madison Park, in NoMad/Flatiron at the corner of Madison Avenue and East 24th Street. It is a collaboration with — and named for — Italian artist Francesco Clemente, whose original murals swirl through the room and around the back bar. The bar comprises a 38-seat Lounge serving à la carte food and drinks, plus a nine-seat Studio offering a five-course tasting with cocktail pairings. Like EMP, the food is fully plant-based. The beverage program, overseen by EMP's drinks team, includes a dedicated menu of "soft cocktails" and a fully non-alcoholic pairing option available with the Studio tasting menu. Named zero-proof drinks include the Proxy Fizz (Seedlip Garden, cucumber, green apple, amazake) and a non-alcoholic Kalimotxo. Clemente Bar entered North America's 50 Best Bars at No. 11 in 2025, winning the Best New Opening Award, and ranked No. 15 in 2026.

venues.longDescription:
Clemente Bar opened in October 2024 on the second floor of Eleven Madison Park, Daniel Humm's three-Michelin-star restaurant at Madison Avenue and East 24th Street, and it is the most decorated room in this guide. It entered North America's 50 Best Bars at number 11 in 2025, taking the Best New Opening Award, and ranked number 15 in 2026.

It is named for the Italian artist Francesco Clemente, who made the original murals that run through the room and around the back bar — a collaboration rather than a decorative commission. The space divides into a 38-seat Lounge serving à la carte food and drinks and a nine-seat Studio offering a five-course tasting with cocktail pairings. As at Eleven Madison Park, the food is entirely plant-based.

What earns it a place here is that the non-alcoholic drinking is treated as a first-class programme rather than an accommodation. The bar runs a dedicated menu of "soft cocktails", and — the detail that matters most — the Studio tasting menu can be taken with a fully non-alcoholic pairing. A pairing is a much harder thing to build than a good individual drink: it has to carry a five-course meal, change register between courses, and hold its own against a kitchen operating at three-star level. Very few restaurants anywhere attempt it seriously. Named zero-proof drinks include the Proxy Fizz, built on Seedlip Garden with cucumber, green apple and amazake, and a non-alcoholic Kalimotxo.

The honest caveat is straightforward: Clemente Bar serves alcohol, and it is an expensive, formal room that requires planning. It is not a casual alternative to a local bar and it is not an alcohol-free space.

What it is, instead, is proof of a specific point this directory keeps making. The most common assumption about not drinking is that it means accepting a lesser version of the evening. A bar ranked among the best on the continent, attached to one of the best restaurants in the world, which will construct a full non-alcoholic pairing for a tasting menu, is the clearest available evidence that this is a choice about what is in the glass rather than a downgrade of the occasion. For a special evening in New York where someone at the table is not drinking, there is nothing better in the city.
venues.pressQuote: The folks at Clemente Bar and Studio, perched above Eleven Madison Park (and from the same team), know how to take care of their guests. That extends from the service all the way to the fully non-alcoholic cocktail pairing that's available with their tasting menu.

venues.name: Clementine Cocktail Bar
venues.description: Clementine is a theatrical cocktail bar in the centre of Providence, near Trinity Rep, where the drinks arrive with smoke bubbles and perfumed vapour and the list runs to eight tightly-made cocktails. Its non-alcoholic side is properly built rather than tacked on, including an alcohol-free Negroni and two fresh-fruit builds. Open Wednesday to Sunday, until 1am at weekends.

venues.longDescription:
Clementine opened on Washington Street in the centre of Providence, a few doors from Trinity Repertory Company, and it approaches a cocktail list the way a museum approaches a collection — eight drinks, each one built to be looked at as well as drunk. One arrives as a flute of Italian aperitifs capped with a quivering smoke bubble that bursts at a touch and releases a cloud of perfumed vapour. It is a room that takes presentation seriously, and that instinct carries over to the drinks made without alcohol.

The non-alcoholic offering is genuinely constructed rather than improvised. It includes an alcohol-free Negroni — the hardest classic to render without spirit, because the drink is nothing but bitterness, sweetness and botanical weight, with no fruit to hide behind — alongside a honeydew-and-lime build and a third that runs floral, sweet and sour. Three distinct builds covering bitter, fresh and floral is a real spread; most bars in this metro manage one.

The room is small, lively and elegant in equal measure, with a good music programme and a food menu designed for sharing across a table rather than eating alone at the bar. It also does a brisk private-party trade, so the space can be booked out. Hours are worth checking before you go: it is closed Monday and Tuesday entirely, opens at four Wednesday through Saturday, and runs a shorter Sunday from three until nine.

We have not published the drink names and prices here. Clementine's own drinks page currently returns an error rather than a menu, so while its non-alcoholic builds are documented in current Providence coverage, we could not check them against the bar's live list. Given how fast lists rotate in this city, treat the shape of the programme as reliable and the specific names as worth confirming when you order.

venues.name: Cliff's Taphouse
venues.description: Cliff's Taphouse is a neighborhood bar and restaurant in Kansas City's Martini Corner, opened in 2021 by Larry Kime, a former manager of the South Plaza institution Nick & Jake's. It took over the former Ollie's Local space at 3044 Gillham Road, leaning on a dozen-plus local taps, scratch American food, and a deliberately inclusive, family-style atmosphere — the name honors a Chicago beat cop who "welcomed all into his world." Though best known for fully-leaded craft beer dinners, the bar keeps a standing, clearly-labeled non-alcoholic section: Athletic Brewing IPA and Hazy IPA, Boulevard Quirk Superfruit N/A, Guinness 0, Heineken 0.0, Paulaner Weizen Radler, and Border Baseline Pale Ale, mostly $6–$7. Several house cocktails — Eva's Bourbon Berry Smash, Bucky's Botanicals, and Chan's Brew — can be made as mocktails on request.

venues.longDescription:
Cliff's Taphouse opened on 16 April 2021 at 3044 Gillham Road in Martini Corner, in the space that had been Ollie's Local, from Larry Kime — formerly the manager of Nick & Jake's on the South Plaza, who brought staff and chef Laura Valdivia with him. The name is a tribute rather than a founder: Cliff was a Chicago police officer in the 1960s whose favourite spot was a dark corner bar with a big sign out front. In Kansas City Magazine described a polished, modern bistro with a covered patio bordering the parking lot and sitting slightly below street level. The kitchen is broader than the taphouse label suggests, running flatbreads including a wild mushroom and a pear and brie, three burgers, beef tenderloin, grilled Atlantic salmon and a chef's meatloaf, plus weekend brunch from 10am. Happy hour runs Tuesday to Friday, 3pm to 6pm, and the bar is closed Mondays.

A place with taphouse in the name takes its beer list seriously — around twenty taps, many from local breweries — and the reason it belongs here is that the non-alcoholic side was built to the same standard rather than treated as a single token can in a fridge. Seven non-alcoholic options are printed with prices on the drinks menu, which is more than many dedicated bars carry: Athletic Brewing's Hazy IPA at $6 and its standard IPA at $7, a Paulaner Weizen Radler at $7, Guinness 0 at $7, Heineken 0.0 at $7, a Quirk non-alcoholic superfruit seltzer at $7, and — the one worth singling out — Border Baseline Pale Ale at $7, brewed non-alcoholic a mile and a half away in the Crossroads. That gives a non-drinker a genuine spread of styles in one room: hoppy, hazy, stout, lager, wheat and seltzer. Beyond the packaged options, three cocktails on the menu carry an asterisk marking them as available as mocktails — Eva's Bourbon Berry Smash, Bucky's Botanicals and Chan's Brew — so the bar will build a zero-proof version to order rather than pointing you at the cans.
venues.pressQuote: The taphouse also sells a full lineup of non-alcoholic beers and seltzers, incredible considering they are known for their exclusive and delicious Beer Dinners, which are fully alcoholic.

venues.name: Clio
venues.description: Clio is an Old Market restaurant and bar on Howard Street in Omaha, open 11am to 10pm most days and to 11pm at weekends — the widest hours of any venue in this guide. Its alcohol-free offer covers all three of the things a non-drinker actually wants: a built cocktail in the Apricotta, a low-sugar long drink in its shrub and soda, and a proper beer in Athletic Brewing's Run Wild IPA. Most venues manage one of those three. A shrub — fruit preserved in vinegar — is the component that gives an alcohol-free drink acidity and savoury depth rather than sweetness, and having one on the menu is a reliable sign the bar makes its own.
venues.longDescription:
Clio sits on Howard Street in the Old Market, the restored warehouse district that is Omaha's main eating and drinking quarter, and it is open from 11am to 10pm Monday through Thursday, to 11pm on Friday and Saturday, and midday to 9pm on Sunday. Seven days, all day, no closed evening — which makes it the default answer in this guide when everything else is shut.

The alcohol-free offer is unusually complete in shape rather than in length. Three things sit on it, and they are the three different things people actually want. The Apricotta is a built, named cocktail for someone who wants an occasion drink. The shrub and soda is a long, low-sugar option for someone settling in for a meal. Athletic Brewing's Run Wild IPA covers the person who simply wants a beer and does not want a conversation about it.

Most venues in this directory manage one of those three and assume it covers everyone. It does not: the person celebrating something and the person having a Tuesday dinner want opposite drinks, and being handed the wrong one is how non-drinkers end up feeling catered for rather than served.

The shrub is the component worth noting for anyone reading menus elsewhere. A shrub is fruit preserved in vinegar and sugar, and it delivers sharp acidity plus a savoury edge that citrus alone cannot. Bars that list one are almost always making it in-house, because nobody stocks a bought shrub — so it functions as a shorthand for a kitchen that prepares its own drink components.

Omaha's local drinks writing documents all three by name.

Clio is a two-minute walk from The Berry & Rye and Laka Lono, in the middle of the Old Market.
venues.pressQuote: Located within the heart of the Old Market, this is a favorite for those who love authentic Mediterranean fare.
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: Hurrdat ONE, 10 Best Zero-Proof & Nonalcoholic Bars in Omaha, Nov 18, 2025

venues.name: Cloak & Dagger
venues.description: Cloak & Dagger occupies a corner site on West 11th Street in the heart of Tremont, a short walk from Lincoln Park, and reads as a warmly lit private study — leather-bound books, antiques and heavy furniture, low light, a room Cleveland Scene has described as combining ease with expectation. Its drinks and its entire kitchen are vegan and made from scratch. The bar changes its whole menu on a schedule and publishes each one as a numbered volume rather than a list, so regulars track it by book number rather than by season; the current edition is Book 22, "Whiskey Bent & Hellbound". Three or four drinks on each book are available spirit-free, priced and presented like the rest of the list and built with the same technique rather than served as juice.
venues.longDescription:
Cloak & Dagger occupies a corner site on West 11th Street in the heart of Tremont, a short walk from Lincoln Park, and reads as a warmly lit private study: leather-bound books, antiques and heavy furniture, low light, the kind of room Cleveland Scene has described as combining ease with expectation. The bar changes its entire menu on a schedule and publishes each one as a numbered volume — the current edition is Book 22, "Whiskey Bent & Hellbound" — so regulars track the room by book number rather than by season. Everything served, drinks and food alike, is vegan and made from scratch in house; it is one of the very few serious cocktail bars in the city where that is the default rather than an accommodation, which by itself makes it the easiest booking in Tremont for a mixed group with dietary constraints.

The non-alcoholic side is run as part of the same programme rather than bolted on. Three or four drinks on each book are available spirit-free, listed and priced alongside the rest rather than tucked into a footnote, and Cleveland Magazine's 2026 mocktail roundup singled the bar out for the care involved. The current benchmark is the Smaller Acts at $16 — coffee, hazelnut and a pinch of sea salt built into something closer to a dessert cocktail than a soft drink, where the texture and the salt do the work alcohol usually does in carrying bitterness and length. Because the list turns over with each book, the specific zero-proof builds change; what stays constant is that there are always several, and that they are made to the standard of the whiskey drinks the bar is known for.

The room opens at 4pm six nights a week and runs to midnight, or 1am on Fridays and Saturdays, with the kitchen closing at 10pm and happy hour from 4pm to 6pm early in the week.
venues.pressQuote: The Smaller Acts is a silky, nutty mocktail balancing coffee, hazelnut and a touch of sea salt for a smooth, luxurious finish.

venues.description: Clockwork Champagne & Cocktails is the lobby lounge of the Fairmont Royal York, an Art Deco champagne-and-cocktail bar in Toronto's Financial District named for the hotel's landmark clock. Alongside a list of more than 96 champagnes and shareable seafood towers, it runs a dedicated "Spirit Free" menu of three Seedlip-based cocktails, each built out with its own full ingredient list rather than a token mocktail. The program has drawn a dedicated feature from Canada's 100 Best. Weekend Afternoon Tea is also served by reservation.

venues.longDescription:
Clockwork Champagne & Cocktails occupies the lobby lounge of the Fairmont Royal York at 100 Front Street West, opposite Union Station in downtown Toronto. The room is built around the hotel's storied clock — the source of the bar's name — and leans into Art Deco elegance, with live piano and DJ sets, a list of more than 96 champagnes, and refined small plates and seafood towers meant for sharing. Weekend Afternoon Tea runs Saturday and Sunday, 11:00 AM to 4:00 PM, by reservation only.

The bar's "Spirit Free" menu treats non-alcoholic drinking with the same care as its champagne list, building three named cocktails on Seedlip's distilled non-alcoholic spirits. Smoke on the Water pairs Seedlip Grove with ancho chili, cranberry, apple, maple, verjus, allspice and ginger ale ($17); Green Heat combines Seedlip Garden with cucumber-and-cilantro oleo, lemon, chili and smoked sesame ($19); and Spice Road mixes Seedlip Spice with masala chai, coconut, lime, pineapple, cardamom, nutmeg and mint ($18).

The beverage program is overseen by Director of Beverage James Grant, a World Class Global Bartender of the Year (2021) and Canada's 100 Best Bartender (2022). Canada's 100 Best has singled out the spirit-free cocktails as "designed to deliver the same complexity, balance, and sense of occasion as the classics," crafted in partnership with Seedlip.
venues.pressQuote: Clockwork's spirit-free cocktails are designed to deliver the same complexity, balance, and sense of occasion as the classics. In partnership with Seedlip — the world's first non-alcoholic spirit — the menu features elevated, meticulously crafted drinks that feel thoughtful, celebratory, and undeniably refined.

venues.name: Close Company
venues.description: Close Company is the Atlanta bar from the team behind Death & Co, opened on 6 November 2025 on the plaza level of an office tower at 505 North Angier Avenue in the Old Fourth Ward. The group describes it as the unbuttoned, less formal sibling of the New York original — a bi-level room with a disco ball, weekend DJs and cocktails priced well below Death & Co's. The zero-proof list is treated as part of the menu rather than an appendix, and is priced in line with the rest of it. Named alcohol-free drinks include the Dangerous Rickey with non-alcoholic gin, celery cordial and garden herb tonic, the Chennai Cobbler built on N/A vermouth with mango and yogurt, the Parakeet, and a Phony Negroni.

venues.longDescription:
Close Company is the second concept from the hospitality group behind Death & Co, and Atlanta got one of the first. It opened on 6 November 2025 in Suite 320 on the plaza level of Tower 2 at 505 North Angier Avenue, beside the parking garage entrance of a black office building in the Old Fourth Ward — a location DiningOut described as looking like it has absolutely nothing going on inside. The company's own framing is that Close Company is "the unbuttoned, unpretentious younger sister of Death & Co: a little louder, a little looser, and unapologetically fun". In practice that means a bi-level room built around the bar, a spinning disco ball, DJs at the weekend, a 1970s palette, and food that runs to French onion pastry pockets and lemon pepper pockets rather than anything precious.

The pricing is the point of the concept, and it applies to the non-alcoholic drinks as much as the full-proof ones. The group has been explicit that efficiencies in service and technology let Close Company sell cocktails at a fraction of Death & Co's prices, with drinks starting around $9, and the zero-proof section sits inside the same list rather than being pushed to the back. Four alcohol-free drinks are named on the menu: the Dangerous Rickey, built on non-alcoholic gin with a celery cordial and a garden herb tonic; the Chennai Cobbler, which uses a non-alcoholic vermouth with mango and yogurt for weight; the Parakeet, an agave-leaning drink with a non-alcoholic aperitif and green apple; and a St. Agrestis Phony Negroni served straight. The construction logic is the same as the alcoholic list — cordials, acid balance, dilution measured rather than guessed — which is what separates a real zero-proof programme from a token juice list. The bar trades to midnight midweek and 2am on Friday and Saturday, and is closed on Sunday.
venues.pressQuote: NYC cocktail institution Death & Co opened its scrappier Atlanta sibling in Old Fourth Ward in late 2025, tucked inside a building that looks like it has absolutely nothing going on inside.

venues.name: Cloudstreet
venues.description: Cloudstreet is chef Rishi Naleendra's two-Michelin-starred restaurant on Amoy Street, where sommelier Vinodhan Veloo (formerly of Odette) runs a formal course-by-course non-alcoholic pairing at S$168++ alongside the wine flights. Built from clarified juices, teas, ferments and house infusions, it runs to drinks like the Jack & Jill (jackfruit, coconut water, curry leaves, de-alcoholised sherry) and a blue-pea compressed-apple juice matched to the opening Hokkaido scallop course. This is a genuine zero-proof tasting experience matched dish-for-dish, not an afterthought poured on request.

venues.longDescription:
Cloudstreet opened in 2019 as the flagship of Sri Lankan-born chef Rishi Naleendra, who previously earned Singapore's first Michelin star for an Australian restaurant at Cheek by Jowl. The Amoy Street dining room, all pale timber and soft light, holds two Michelin stars in the 2025 MICHELIN Guide Singapore and has featured on Asia's 50 Best Restaurants, where it placed No. 26 in 2023. The cooking is contemporary and personal, drawing on Naleendra's Sri Lankan roots and Australian training across a tasting-menu-only format.

Dining is by tasting menu: dinner (Tuesday to Saturday) is an eight-course menu at S$398++, while lunch (Friday and Saturday) offers a six-course at S$248++ or the eight-course. Beverage pairings are offered at three tiers - a standard wine pairing at S$268++, a Prestige pairing at S$568++, and a dedicated Non-Alcoholic pairing at S$168++.

The non-alcoholic pairing is the work of sommelier Vinodhan Veloo, who oversees a 400-plus-label cellar and treats the zero-proof flight with the same course-by-course intent as the wine. Rather than off-the-shelf mixers, the pairing is built from clarified juices, teas, ferments and house infusions distilled from fruits, herbs and spices - drinks Veloo positions as carrying a complexity comparable to wine. Named pours have included the Jack & Jill (jackfruit, coconut water, curry leaves and de-alcoholised sherry), a sparkling yoghurt whey with fermented jackfruit and cardamom water, and a blue-pea and compressed-apple juice served against the opening Hokkaido scallop course.

Because the pairing is offered as a formal menu option at a two-star restaurant and constructed dish-by-dish rather than assembled ad hoc, it stands as one of Singapore's more serious restaurant non-alcoholic programmes - the zero-proof answer to a fine-dining wine flight.
venues.pressQuote: Veloo offers both alcoholic and non-alcoholic pairings; our favourites have to be the blue pea and compressed apple juice with the first course of Hokkaido scallops

venues.name: Cloudwater Brew Co (Unit 9 Taproom)
venues.description: Cloudwater Brew Co is one of the UK's most acclaimed modern craft breweries, and its Unit 9 taproom sits right beside the brewhouse on the Piccadilly Trading Estate, a short walk behind Manchester Piccadilly station. The 20 keg and two cask lines pour fresh from a cold store beneath the room, and — crucially for non-drinkers — Cloudwater brews its own alcohol-free beer. The board and fridge routinely carry several of the brewery's own 0.5% beers, led by the Fresh AF Hazy IPA, so a zero-proof pint here is made to the same standard as everything else.
venues.address: Unit 9 Piccadilly Trading Estate, Gidding Rd, Manchester M1 2NP
venues.longDescription:
Cloudwater Brew Co was founded in 2014 by Paul Jones and James Campbell, with brewing beginning in February 2015, and it rose almost immediately to the front rank of British craft beer — within two years RateBeer had named it the fifth-best brewery in the world, the first UK brewery ever to make that top ten, and by 2017–18 it had climbed to second globally. The brewery built its reputation on a constantly evolving, seasonal range of hazy IPAs, pale ales and barrel-aged beers. In July 2018 it opened Unit 9, a dedicated taproom immediately next to the brewhouse on the Piccadilly Trading Estate, tucked just behind Manchester Piccadilly station.

The taproom is an industrial, warehouse-style room built entirely around freshness: it sits on a mezzanine above a 3°C cold store from which all 22 lines — 20 keg and two cask — are drawn, so every pour comes straight from tank at cellar temperature. There is a shop corner selling the latest cans, bottles and Cloudwater merch, street-food traders set up most weekends, and the space is dog-friendly, wheelchair accessible via a lift, and open to children with their parents until 8pm (card payment only). It opens Tuesday to Sunday, from mid-afternoon midweek and from noon at weekends.

What earns Cloudwater its place here is that it brews its own alcohol-free beer rather than buying it in. The flagship is Fresh, a 0.5% AF Hazy IPA the brewery calls "the ultimate thirst-quencher", brimming with zesty orange and succulent peach hop character at just 28 calories a 440ml can. The taproom's board and fridge regularly run a whole spread of the brewery's own 0.5% brews alongside it — AF IPAs such as Chubbles, the Kopra alcohol-free pale, a Margarita AF Gose and fruited AF sours like a Lychee & Watermelon Aviation Sour — and there is even a monthly alcohol-free beer subscription, The Lowdown, for drinking the same range at home. Cloudwater was an early pioneer of the category, having launched a range of hopped, low-calorie soft drinks (Cloudwater Soda, originally Good Call) back in 2019. For anyone skipping alcohol, that makes Unit 9 a rare thing: a genuinely world-class craft brewery whose zero-proof beers are made in the very same brewhouse, and served just as fresh, as the full-strength ones.

venues.name: Club Kava
venues.description: Club Kava sits just east of I-95 in Hollywood and is explicit about being a zero-proof room rather than a bar that happens to stock alternatives: traditional fresh-pressed kava shells, a house mocktail list it describes as bright and refreshing, and coffee, served from 10am to 2am every day of the week. Walk-ins are the norm. The venue's own account of its founding is modest and worth repeating, because it describes what a lot of people are actually looking for — it started with a simple wish for a place to land at the end of the day, with no agenda and no pressure. Notably for Broward County, where kava and kratom are poured side by side almost everywhere, Club Kava's published menu covers kava, mocktails and coffee with no kratom listed on it.

venues.longDescription:
Club Kava sits just east of I-95 in Hollywood, and its own account of why it exists is worth quoting because it describes what a great many people are actually looking for: it started with a simple wish — a place to land at the end of the day, with no agenda and no pressure. That is a more honest statement of purpose than most hospitality copy manages, and the room is built to deliver it. Walk-ins are the norm, there is no booking system to negotiate, and it trades from 10am to 2am every day of the week.

The menu is short and deliberate: traditional fresh-pressed kava shells, a list of house mocktails the bar describes as bright and refreshing, and coffee. Kava is the ground root of Piper methysticum, a shrub native to the South Pacific islands, prepared as a cold water infusion and drunk socially across Fiji, Vanuatu, Tonga and Samoa for roughly three thousand years. It contains no alcohol. It tastes earthy and bitter, numbs the lips and tongue on the first mouthful, and is mildly sedative — relaxing and sociable rather than intoxicating in the way alcohol is. Fresh-pressed preparation, which Club Kava specifies, means the root is worked in water at the bar rather than reconstituted from an extract, and it is generally the marker of a room that takes the drink seriously.

The most significant thing about this venue for the audience this directory serves is what is *not* on the menu. Across Florida, kava bars almost universally pour kratom alongside kava — under names like K-Tea, Kra-tea, Mitra tea, or simply by vein colour — and this directory has to flag that on venue after venue. Club Kava's published menu covers kava, mocktails and coffee, with no kratom listed on it. That distinction matters because kratom is the leaf of a Southeast Asian tree whose alkaloids act on the opioid receptors; it produces tolerance and a genuine withdrawal syndrome in regular users, several US states ban it outright, and concentrated 7-hydroxymitragynine products derived from it face active federal scheduling. Kava carries no comparable dependence profile.

For anyone whose recovery rules out intoxicants with dependence potential rather than alcohol specifically — which is a large and under-served share of the people searching for rooms like this — that makes Club Kava one of the more straightforward places in Broward County to walk into and order from without having to interrogate the menu first. As always, confirming at the bar costs nothing, and the staff here are described consistently as willing to explain what kava is to anyone encountering it for the first time.
venues.pressQuote: Club Kava started with a simple wish—a place to land at the end of the day, with no agenda and no pressure, just somewhere easy to settle in

venues.name: Coa Cantina
venues.description: Coa Cantina is a Mexican restaurant and bar on Merle Hay Road in north-west Des Moines, and it will build its margarita and its paloma spirit-free, with non-alcoholic beers stocked alongside. That combination is more useful than it sounds: the two drinks people most want at a Mexican table are both citrus-and-agave builds where the tequila is one component among several, and having NA beer as well means a non-drinker can choose rather than accept. Open from 3pm Wednesday through Sunday, to midnight midweek and 2am from Thursday, closed Monday and Tuesday.
venues.address: 1250 Merle Hay Rd, Des Moines, IA 50311
venues.longDescription:
Coa Cantina sits on Merle Hay Road in north-west Des Moines, away from the downtown and Ingersoll clusters where most of this guide is concentrated, and it earns its place by covering two needs at once.

The first is the drinks. A margarita is lime, agave and tequila; a paloma is grapefruit, lime, agave and tequila with soda. In both, the citrus and the agave are doing the majority of the flavour work, which makes them among the most convincing cocktails to build without alcohol — far more so than anything spirit-forward. Coa makes both spirit-free, which means a table sharing a plate of tacos can all order roughly the same thing.

The second is the beer. Stocking non-alcoholic beer alongside the mocktails is the part most venues skip, and it addresses a different customer entirely: the person who does not want an occasion drink, does not want to explain themselves, and just wants what everyone else is having. Between a built spirit-free margarita and a cold NA beer, this room can serve both moods, which very few in this guide can.

This entry is graded three. The drinks are documented as spirit-free versions of the house cocktails rather than as their own named builds, there is no printed zero-proof section verified, and the specific NA beer brands stocked could not be confirmed.

The hours run 3pm to midnight on Wednesday and Sunday and 3pm to 2am Thursday through Saturday, closed Monday and Tuesday. The 2am close is worth noting — along with The Bartender's Handshake and Bellhop it is one of only three rooms in this city guide licensed that late, which makes it one of the few genuine options for a Des Moines night that runs past one in the morning without alcohol.

venues.name: Cobalt Grille
venues.description: Cobalt Grille is a Laskin Road restaurant in Virginia Beach's Hilltop area whose non-alcoholic drinks are the work of a named mixologist, Windsor Swink, rather than an anonymous back-bar decision. That attribution is the signal worth acting on: when a venue credits a person with its zero-proof creations, the drinks tend to be developed rather than improvised, and they tend to stay on the menu. It shares an address block with Ceremony's Virginia Beach outlet inside Painted Tree Boutiques, which makes the two an easy pairing for anyone on the beach side of Hampton Roads. Note it opens at 3pm and closes entirely on Sundays, which catches people out.
venues.longDescription:
Cobalt Grille sits on Laskin Road in the Hilltop area of Virginia Beach, inland from the oceanfront and closer to where people actually live than to the boardwalk hotels. It is a neighbourhood restaurant with a bar that takes itself moderately seriously.

The detail Coastal Virginia Magazine records is that the non-alcoholic drinks are credited to a specific person: mixologist Windsor Swink. That attribution is worth more than it might appear. Most zero-proof drinks in restaurants are the product of nobody in particular — a manager's guess, a supplier's suggestion, a recipe copied from somewhere. When a venue names the person who built them, it usually means the drinks were developed with the same process as the alcoholic list, tasted properly, and given menu space on merit. It also means somebody is accountable for them, which tends to keep them from quietly disappearing.

The individual builds are not documented in the detail that would justify a higher grade, so a 3 is the honest call here. What is documented is that they exist, that they are described as creative rather than standard, and that they come from a person rather than a default.

The practical value is geographic. Hampton Roads' alcohol-free depth is heavily concentrated in Norfolk — Ceremony, Only You, Gershwin's and the rest are all across the water — which leaves anyone staying in Virginia Beach with a longer drive than they expected. Cobalt Grille is one of a small handful of options on the beach side, and it happens to share an address block with Ceremony's Virginia Beach outlet inside Painted Tree Boutiques. Note it is closed Sundays and opens at 3pm. Hilltop is a short drive from the oceanfront hotels, so it is a realistic dinner option for visitors willing to leave the boardwalk for an evening.
venues.pressQuote: Cobalt Grille serves creative non-alcoholic drinks created by mixologist Windsor Swink.

venues.name: Cobra
venues.description: Cobra is an Asian-American bar on South High Street in the Brewery District, opened in October 2023 by four owners — Alex Chen and Jack Bennett, who helped open Watershed Kitchen + Bar, and David Yee and Josh Spiers, both previously of Oddfellows. It bills itself as a "good night bar," pairing a cocktail programme built on Asian ingredients with handmade noodles served late. The non-alcoholic drinks are treated as an extension of that flavour perspective rather than a fallback: the Pool Float is a no-proof build that carries the serrano and cilantro notes of the bar's Above Ground Pool cocktail, and All Gas No Brakes is a no-proof boilermaker pairing Pathfinder's non-alcoholic amaro with a locally owned non-alcoholic IPA. Bar manager David Yee was one of the bartenders Forbes surveyed on 2025 drink trends.
signatureDrinks: All Gas No Brakes (no-proof boilermaker: Pathfinder NA amaro and NA IPA)
venues.longDescription:
Cobra opened in October 2023 at 684 South High Street, a few doors up from Law Bird in the Brewery District, under four owners: Alex Chen and Jack Bennett, who had helped open Watershed Kitchen + Bar, and David Yee and Josh Spiers, who came from Oddfellows. The concept is an Asian-American neighbourhood bar — the owners' shorthand is a "good night bar" — with a kitchen turning out handmade noodles and other late-night food long after most Columbus kitchens have closed, and a room that stays open until 2am six nights a week. National attention followed quickly, and the bar has since been named among the country's best new openings.

The non-alcoholic list is where the bar's stated philosophy is easiest to see. Bar manager David Yee was among the bartenders Forbes canvassed for its 2025 beverage trend predictions, and used the space to argue that low- and no-proof drinks were becoming central rather than supplementary. The two builds he pointed to are instructive. The Pool Float is a zero-proof drink engineered to carry the serrano-and-cilantro backbone of Above Ground Pool, one of the bar's full-proof cocktails, so that the non-drinking guest gets the same flavour idea rather than a sweeter substitute. All Gas No Brakes is a no-proof boilermaker: Pathfinder's non-alcoholic amaro poured alongside a non-alcoholic IPA from a locally owned brewer, which in Columbus means Good Liar, the city's own zero-proof beer brand. Both are built from the same Asian-American flavour vocabulary as the rest of the menu — the point Yee makes is that the NA drinks are a way of sharing that perspective with guests who are not drinking, not a way of parking them. The kitchen is a real part of the proposition rather than a bar-snack afterthought — handmade noodles and Asian-American cooking served until late, in a city where most kitchens close by ten — which makes Cobra one of the more practical late-night options for someone who is not drinking but wants to be out. The room stays open until 2am six nights a week and closes Tuesdays.
venues.pressQuote: A drink trend we're seeing is doubling down on the importance of low and no-proof options in the bar. At Cobra, we use our NA offerings as a way to share our Asian American flavor perspective with our guests who choose not to imbibe.

venues.name: Codependent Cocktails + Coffee
venues.description: Codependent Cocktails + Coffee is an all-day cocktail and coffee bar at the base of The Independent condo tower in downtown Austin, opened by Kevin Burns and Merrill Alley of design firm Urbanspace. The concept is Italian luxury meets Austin hospitality — mid-century modern interiors, floor-to-ceiling windows, aperitivo culture-inspired drinks, and an Instagram-friendly aesthetic that doubles as a coworking spot before 4pm (the cutoff after which laptops are no longer welcome). The cocktail program is well-regarded across Austin's bar scene, and Visit Austin's official tourism blog highlights Codependent's non-alcoholic offerings as one of the strongest in town, calling out the Well Manoered Monk (NA tequila, cucumber, pineapple) and Tell Me Something Good (prickly pear, coconut water). The menu also includes Athletic Brewing non-alcoholic beer alongside the broader coffee and cocktail program. A private speakeasy with homemade ingredients sits behind the main bar.

venues.longDescription:
Codependent Cocktails + Coffee occupies the base of The Independent tower downtown, opened by Kevin Burns and Merrill Alley of the design firm Urbanspace. The room is mid-century modern with floor-to-ceiling windows, and the concept is Italian aperitivo culture crossed with Austin hospitality. It runs as a coworking space in the mornings and afternoons — laptops are welcome until 4pm and pointedly not after.

That all-day structure is what makes it work for a non-drinker, because it means the venue has a purpose at every hour rather than only after dark. Aperitivo culture helps too: the Italian aperitivo is built on bitterness, dilution and low strength, which is the one drinking tradition that translates almost intact without alcohol. A bar whose house style is already spritzes and bitter aperitifs is starting from a much better position than one built on spirit-forward drinks.

Visit Austin describes the mocktails as leaning fresh and lightly textured, naming the Well Manoered Monk — a non-alcoholic tequila with cucumber and pineapple — and Tell Me Something Good, built on prickly pear and coconut water. Coconut water is an interesting choice: it carries a mineral salinity that gives a drink body without sugar, which is the recurring problem zero-proof drinks have to solve. Athletic Brewing non-alcoholic beer is available alongside the cocktail and coffee programmes, and a small private speakeasy with house-made ingredients sits behind the main bar.

The hours are the widest of any bar on this Austin list — from 8am on weekdays, 9am at weekends, running to 11pm early in the week and 1am on Friday and Saturday. Somewhere you can have a coffee at nine in the morning and a properly built zero-proof aperitivo at eleven at night, without changing venue or explaining yourself at either end, is a genuinely useful address downtown.
venues.pressQuote: This sleek downtown spot features mocktails that lean fresh and lightly textured. We suggest ordering the Well Manoered Monk (NA tequila, cucumber, and pineapple) or Tell Me Something Good (prickly pear and coconut water).

venues.name: The Coffee Bar at The Durham
venues.description: The ground-floor coffee bar at The Durham hotel on East Chapel Hill Street serves Counter Culture coffee from 7am and keeps an explicit "Spirit Free" section on its beverage menu — five named builds from $5 to $9, including a Lyre's Italian Orange Ruby Spritz with lime, soda and falernum, a Pear Shrub with honey and local sage, a carrot Vitamin Tea and a properly made Shirley Temple on the hotel's own grenadine. It also makes the Durham Coffee Soda, the house cold-brew soda on Markola coffee syrup, club soda and lemon that Town & Country credited barista Mark Daumen with putting on the map. Open until 9pm daily, it is the metro's most useful all-day non-alcoholic room — and, to be clear, the programme belongs to this coffee bar, not to The Roof upstairs. Alcohol and CBD drinks are also served.

venues.longDescription:
The Durham is a mid-century hotel on East Chapel Hill Street, and the room worth knowing about is not the rooftop bar but the coffee bar on the ground floor. It opens at seven in the morning, closes at nine at night, and carries a printed "Spirit Free" section on its beverage menu — which makes it the only venue in this guide you can use for a breakfast meeting and an evening drink without changing anything about your order.

The spirit-free list is five deep and covers a genuine range. The Ruby Spritz is the most cocktail-like, built on Lyre's Italian Orange with lime, soda and falernum for spice. The Pear Shrub uses a vinegar-based shrub with honey and local sage over soda, which gives it the acidity that keeps a long drink interesting. Vitamin Tea is a carrot tea with orange and honey. The Pom-Hib Spritzer is the simplest and cheapest at five dollars, and there is a properly made Shirley Temple built on the hotel's own grenadine with Mexican sprite and luxardo cherries — a drink usually served badly, made well here.

Separately, the coffee side produces the Durham Coffee Soda, which has become the thing this room is known for: Markola coffee syrup, club soda and lemon, served long over ice. There is also a Durham Coffee Milk and a shaken cold brew vanilla latte. The coffee itself is Counter Culture, roasted in Durham, which is the local detail that earns the hotel some credibility with the city.

One clarification, because published guides have it wrong: the non-alcoholic programme belongs to this coffee bar, not to The Roof, the hotel's rooftop cocktail bar upstairs. The Roof serves craft cocktails and small plates and does not run a comparable zero-proof list. If you have read about spirit-free drinks at The Durham, this is the room they were describing. Note the venue also serves alcohol and CBD drinks, so it is not an alcohol-free space.
venues.pressQuote: here you'll find the city's best barista, Mark Daumen, who put coffee sodas on the map with his cult-favorite Markola coffee syrup
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: Town & Country, North Carolina travel guide, October 2025

venues.name: Colita
venues.description: Colita is a Tex-Oaxacan restaurant from chef Daniel del Prado's DDP Restaurant Group (the Martina and Bar La Grassa team), open since October 2018 in a converted former gas station at 54th & Penn in southwest Minneapolis's Armatage neighborhood. Named after del Prado's first dog, it pairs Oaxacan-influenced barbecue, creative tacos, and mole-driven dishes with a well-regarded bar program in a fully gluten-free kitchen. The drinks menu carries a dedicated "Zero Proof" section of four house-made, $10 non-alcoholic cocktails built with the same care as its alcoholic list — fruit-, herb-, and tea-forward sodas finished with carbonation. Named pours include the rose-and-raspberry Rosas, the citrus-and-lychee Naranjitas, a cinnamon coconut-milk Horchata, and the honey-sarsaparilla 3leche Miele. The program is a real, named NA list but a focused one — a strong complement to the meal rather than a full standalone bar menu.
