venues.longDescription:
Dark Horse Bar & Eatery spent a decade serving Lowertown before closing in February 2025, and reopened that July under new ownership — a relaunch run by chef Shane Oporto in the kitchen and Sarah McDonough on the floor, backed by Eclective, the hospitality group behind Saint Paul Brewing and Can Can Wonderland. The reopened room pairs elevated bar food, including a signature burger and pizzas, with a cocktail list that was rebuilt from scratch.

What makes the relaunch notable here is that the non-alcoholic drinks were treated as part of that rebuild rather than as an afterthought bolted on later. The dedicated Zero Proof section runs at $9 a drink and everything in it is made in house: a Ginger Beer built on house ginger syrup with cayenne and soda, which gives it genuine heat rather than the flat sweetness of a commercial bottle; a Squirt using a house grapefruit cordial with soda; and a Tepache, the lightly fermented Mexican pineapple drink made with piloncillo and cinnamon. That last one is the tell. Tepache takes days to ferment, produces a faint natural effervescence and a complexity that no syrup can imitate, and no bar makes it unless somebody there actually cares about what non-drinkers are handed. Athletic Brewing's Free Wave and Upside Dawn are stocked alongside for anyone wanting a beer.

The Star Tribune's assessment of the reopened programme captures the standard being applied: "Non-alcoholic and low-proof beverages receive just as much care in building flavors as the standard classics such as the Old Fashioned or Vesper martini." For a neighbourhood bar in Lowertown — a district that empties out badly when there is nothing on at the ballpark — having a room that treats a $9 zero-proof drink as worth fermenting for is a real asset. Tuesday through Sunday, late on Friday and Saturday.
venues.pressQuote: Non-alcoholic and low-proof beverages receive just as much care in building flavors as the standard classics such as the Old Fashioned or Vesper martini.

venues.name: Darling Aviary
venues.description: Darling Aviary is a rooftop bar above K Street in downtown Sacramento, named by Visit Sacramento among the city's mocktail venues though without its drinks documented individually. Rooftops are usually the least accommodating format for a non-drinker, since the entire proposition is a cocktail at sunset with nothing else to do — so a rooftop that makes the city's official mocktail list is worth knowing. It runs late, to 1:30am on Friday and Saturday, and opens from 11am at weekends. Because the individual drinks are not documented, ask what is available on arrival; Dive Bar is a short walk away with three named options as a fallback.
venues.longDescription:
Darling Aviary is a rooftop bar on K Street in downtown Sacramento, a few doors from Dive Bar and within easy reach of most of the city centre. Visit Sacramento, the city's official destination organisation, names it among the venues serving mocktails, though it does not document the individual drinks — which is why the grade here is an honest 3 rather than higher.

The format is the reason it is worth including anyway. Rooftop bars are the least forgiving venue type for someone not drinking. There is no food to focus on, no game to play, no music loud enough to occupy attention; the whole experience is constructed around holding a cocktail while the light goes. Nowhere is the difference between your evening and everybody else's more visible, and nowhere is a glass of soda more conspicuous.

So a rooftop that turns up on a city's official mocktail list is doing something the format does not require of it. It suggests the bar has thought about the guest who is not drinking rather than assuming that guest simply will not come.

The hours are among the more useful in the guide: 4pm to 11pm early in the week, opening at 2pm on Friday and 11am at weekends, and running to 1:30am on Friday and Saturday. Late weekend service and a K Street location put it in the middle of downtown Sacramento's night, so it works as a late stop after dinner elsewhere.

Because the drinks are not publicly documented, it is worth asking what is available rather than arriving with expectations — and Dive Bar, with three named mocktails, is a short walk away as a fallback.

Worth adding that Sacramento summers reach well past a hundred degrees, which changes what a rooftop is for. Through July and August the appeal is the evening after the heat breaks, and cold non-alcoholic drinks are in genuinely high demand — alcohol dehydrates, and nobody sitting outside at ninety-five degrees is well served by a second negroni. Rooftop bars in hot cities tend to sell more zero-proof drinks than their menus suggest, and this is a good place to ask what the bartender can build.
venues.pressQuote: Darling Aviary is named among Sacramento venues serving mocktails.

venues.name: Daru
venues.description: Daru is an acclaimed Indian-ish restaurant just off the H Street Corridor at 1451 Maryland Avenue NE, opened in August 2021 by chef Suresh Sundas and beverage director Dante Datta in a former neighbourhood grocery. Sundas practises a border-defying Indian fusion that pulls off unusual pairings - reshmi chicken kebab with blue cheese, a creamy spinach lasagna made with paneer, smoky black dal with a dollop of burrata. Datta runs an inventive bar rooted in South Asian technique, and the non-alcoholic side is a properly headed section rather than an afterthought: a mango and peach lassi with dahi yoghurt, salt and sugar; masala chai; a Mango Daisy with lemon, sugar and salt; a fizzy tamarind soda of tamarind tea, lime and soda; plus Clausthaler N/A dry-hopped IPA, Thums Up and Limca. Roughly 40 seats indoors with a patio.
signatureDrinks: Fizzy tamarind soda (tamarind tea, lime, soda) $8
Mango & peach lassi (dahi yogurt, salt, sugar) $4
Clausthaler n/a dry hopped IPA, Germany $8
venues.longDescription:
Daru opened in August 2021 at 1451 Maryland Avenue NE, a block off the H Street Corridor, in a space that used to be a neighbourhood grocery. The name is the Hindi word for liquor, which is a pointed joke for a restaurant whose non-alcoholic list is this good. Chef Suresh Sundas cooks what the restaurant calls Indian-ish - a border-defying fusion that takes real risks and mostly lands them, with reshmi chicken kebab served with blue cheese, a creamy spinach lasagna built on paneer, and smoky black dal finished with a dollop of burrata. Beverage director Dante Datta runs the bar on the same principle, taking inspiration from everywhere while staying rooted in South Asian techniques and ingredients; Washingtonian, placing Daru at number 57 on its 100 Very Best Restaurants 2026, described his cocktails - a Bangalorean rum spiked with garam masala, amaro, tamarind and mole - as just as inventive as the food.

The alcohol-free drinks sit under their own heading on the menu, Beverages w/o Alcohol, and the range is wider than most restaurants manage. The Mango Daisy, at $8, is the most popular of them: mango with lemon, sugar and salt, which is the salted-fruit balance that makes Indian street drinks work rather than a sweet purée. The fizzy tamarind soda, also $8, is built from tamarind tea with lime and soda, and it is the sharper, more savoury option. On the simpler side there is a mango and peach lassi made with dahi yoghurt, salt and sugar at $4, and a masala chai at the same price. For anyone who wants a beer there is Clausthaler's non-alcoholic dry-hopped IPA from Germany at $8, and the fridge carries two Indian sodas, Thums Up cola and the lemon-lime Limca, at $4 each.

Practical notes. The room is intimate - roughly forty seats indoors, with additional patio seating - and it serves dinner only, 5pm to 10pm seven days a week, with a happy hour from 5pm to 6.30pm. Because the non-alcoholic drinks are priced between $4 and $8 rather than at cocktail prices, a table that is not drinking here spends noticeably less than at most restaurants of this standard.
venues.pressQuote: Dante Datta's cocktails—including a Bangalorean rum spiked with garam masala, amaro, tamarind, and mole—are just as inventive

venues.name: Davie Kava
venues.description: Davie Kava is an alcohol-free kava bar on West State Road 84, and its hours are the whole argument for it: doors at noon every day, closing at 1am at the start and end of the week and running to 5am from Wednesday through Saturday. Very little else in western Broward is open at that hour without a liquor licence. The menu is organised into four blocks — traditional kava shells, Happy Teas, cold brew and specialty drinks — with the shells as the anchor. IMPORTANT for readers in recovery: the tea side of a Florida kava bar menu is normally kratom rather than kava, and Davie Kava does not publish its ingredient list online, so ask at the bar before ordering anything from the tea board. Kratom acts on opioid receptors and carries dependence risk that kava does not.
venues.longDescription:
Davie Kava sits on West State Road 84, the service road running parallel to I-595 through western Broward, and the single most useful fact about it is the closing time. It opens at noon every day. It closes at 1am on Monday, Tuesday and Sunday — and at 5am from Wednesday through Saturday. There is very little else in this part of the county open at four in the morning that does not hold a liquor licence, and for anyone working night shifts, leaving a late job, or simply awake when the rest of the suburb is not, that window is the whole proposition.

The room is organised as a bar rather than a cafe, and the menu is published in four blocks: traditional kava shells, Happy Teas, cold brew, and specialty drinks. Kava shells are the anchor and the thing the venue leads with. Kava itself is the ground root of Piper methysticum, a shrub native to the South Pacific, prepared as a cold water infusion and drunk socially across Fiji, Vanuatu, Tonga and Samoa for roughly three thousand years. It contains no alcohol. It tastes earthy and bitter, numbs the lips and tongue on the first mouthful, and is mildly sedative rather than intoxicating in the way alcohol is — which is exactly why it functions as a social drink and not merely as a soft one. Kava also shows reverse tolerance, meaning regular drinkers usually need less rather than more to feel it, so a first visit rewards a slow pace across an hour or two rather than treating a shell like a shot.

Davie Kava joins Kavana Kava Bar, 3rd Space and Kamp Kava in giving this one Broward town four dedicated alcohol-free rooms — an unusual density for a place with no bar district and no walkable centre, and a reminder that the kava format has become the practical backbone of the alcohol-free scene across Florida in a way that dedicated zero-proof cocktail bars never managed.

One caution belongs here rather than in a footnote, because this directory is read by people in recovery. Davie Kava does not publish its ingredient lists online, and on a Florida kava menu the tea section is normally kratom rather than kava. The two are not equivalent. Kratom is the leaf of a Southeast Asian tree, Mitragyna speciosa, whose principal alkaloids act on the opioid receptors; regular use produces tolerance and a genuine withdrawal syndrome, several US states ban it outright, and its concentrated 7-hydroxymitragynine derivatives are the subject of active federal scheduling. Kava carries no comparable dependence profile. Ask at the bar what is in the cup before ordering anything from the tea board — staff will tell you.
venues.pressQuote: Davie Kava is South Florida's #1 kava bar, located in Davie, FL

venues.name: Daydreamer
venues.description: Daydreamer is a cocktail and Champagne bar on East 6th Street, next door to Suerte restaurant. The venue is a collaboration between veterans of Austin bars including Kitty Cohen's, Frazier's, and The White Horse, and the concept centers on caviar, champagne, and martinis — The Infatuation describes the theme bluntly as just that. The interior is intimately decorated with soft lighting, and the back patio features a swimming pool. A taco truck operates out back. The martini program is the standout, and reviewers note that the bartenders accommodate zero-proof mocktail requests, though specific NA drinks are not publicly named on the menu.
venues.longDescription:
Daydreamer is a cocktail and champagne bar on East 6th Street, next door to Suerte, and a collaboration between veterans of Kitty Cohen's, Frazier's and The White Horse. The concept is caviar, champagne and martinis, stated about that plainly. The interior is small and softly lit, the back patio has a swimming pool, and a taco truck runs out the back.

The martini programme is the reason people go, and it is also the reason a non-drinker should know what they are walking into. A martini bar is a difficult room in which not to drink: the whole format is built on one very cold, very strong, very simple drink, and there is no fruit or bubbles to hide behind in a zero-proof version of it. Bartenders here do accommodate zero-proof requests and reviewers say so consistently, but there is no published list of named non-alcoholic drinks — you are asking rather than ordering.

If you do ask, the useful move is to describe a texture rather than a drink. A martini's appeal is temperature, dilution and a clean saline finish rather than the gin itself, and a bar with this much attention to that particular drink can usually build something dry, cold and savoury if told that is what you want. Asking for a mocktail tends to produce something sweet; asking for something bracing and savoury tends not to.

The hours are unusually generous — 3pm to 2am Monday to Friday and from noon at weekends — and the pool patio and taco truck make it as viable in daylight as at midnight. That flexibility is worth something. An afternoon on a patio by a pool is a much easier proposition without a drink than a 1am room built around martinis, and this is the same venue either way.

venues.name: Dayglow
venues.description: Dayglow is a multi-roaster specialty coffee bar at 3206 West Sunset Boulevard in Silver Lake, opened in late 2017 by Tohm Ifergan, formerly of Portola Coffee Roasters. Time Out gave it five stars in 2025, describing it as part neighbourhood hangout and part subscription service, a haven for serious coffee drinkers and dabblers alike — and noting that the standout part of the menu is its house signature drinks, which take a craft-cocktail approach to dispensing caffeine. The multi-roaster claim is real and unusually deep: its retail shelf carries well over a hundred beans from roasters including Tim Wendelboe, Coffee Collective, La Cabra, Prolog, Friedhats, Dak, Nomad, Monogram and Morgon alongside its own house roasts. Its signature drinks include the Military Latte, the Warhol, the Totoro and a strawberry matcha. PLEASE NOTE: Dayglow publishes its bean shop online but not its café drinks menu, and the third-party listings that appear to carry it are stale or fabricated — so we cannot give current prices or ingredients for the signature drinks. Seating is limited and there are few outlets, so it is not a laptop café. Open daily 7am to 7pm. Ours is the Silver Lake location; there are five others.
venues.address: 3206 W Sunset Blvd, Los Angeles, CA 90026
venues.longDescription:
Dayglow opened on Sunset Boulevard in Silver Lake in late 2017, from Tohm Ifergan, who had come from Portola Coffee Roasters down in Costa Mesa, and the coffee trade press described it at the time as a neon-bright beacon not unlike the city itself. The premise was to give customers unusual coffees and a side of information with them, and nearly a decade on that is still the shape of it. Time Out gave the Los Angeles rooms five stars in 2025 and put the appeal plainly: part neighbourhood hangout and part subscription service, a haven for serious coffee drinkers and dabblers alike, where the standout part of the menu remains the slightly pricey house signature drinks, which take a craft-cocktail approach to dispensing caffeine. That last phrase is exactly why a non-drinker should care — these are constructed drinks with syrups, spices and textures rather than a latte with flavouring in it, and the signature list is where the interest lies: the Military Latte, the Warhol, the Totoro and a strawberry matcha are the ones people come back for.

The multi-roaster claim is the other reason to come, and it holds up under checking. Dayglow's retail shelf carries well over a hundred different beans, and the roasters on it are a serious international list — Tim Wendelboe and Nomad, Coffee Collective and Prolog out of Copenhagen, La Cabra, Friedhats, Dak, Morgon, Monogram, Rogue Wave — alongside its own house roasts, at anything from $20 to $84 a bag. Very few American cafés stock at that breadth, and for someone who has replaced an evening drink with an interest in coffee, this is close to the best shelf in the city. Two honest limitations. We cannot give you current prices or recipes for the signature drinks, because Dayglow publishes its online store but not its café menu, and the third-party listing sites that appear to carry it turned out to be stale or, in one case, padded with fabricated boilerplate — we would rather say so than repeat numbers we cannot stand behind. And practically, Time Out's caveat is worth passing on: seating is limited and outlets are scarce, so this is a place to drink coffee and talk rather than to work. There are five other Dayglow rooms including West Hollywood, Larchmont and Venice; this entry covers Silver Lake.
venues.pressQuote: Part neighborhood hangout, part subscription service, Dayglow's L.A. locations are havens for serious coffee drinkers and dabblers alike.

venues.name: DC Brau Brewing
venues.description: DC Brau Brewing is a craft brewery and taproom at 3178-B Bladensburg Road NE in Ivy City, co-founded by Brandon Skall and Jeff Hancock as one of the District's pioneering modern breweries. Its non-alcoholic beer, NA Brau, launched in late April 2024 and is billed as the first canned non-alcoholic beer brewed by a DC brewery. It is a 0.3% ABV pale ale modelled on DC Brau's flagship The Public, using the same Centennial and El Dorado hops with Caramel 40 and Munich malts for a pale golden colour. Rather than tunnel pasteurisation the brewery uses a hybrid Lallemand yeast strain plus Chinova Bioworks' Chiber mushroom-fibre extract as a natural antimicrobial, which preserves flavour and carbonation. It is sold in cans across the region and pours on the taproom list Thursday to Sunday.
venues.longDescription:
DC Brau was one of the breweries that restarted commercial brewing in the District, and it operates a taproom at 3178-B Bladensburg Road NE in Ivy City, the industrial pocket in Northeast that has become the city's brewing and distilling quarter. It was co-founded by Brandon Skall and Jeff Hancock. The reason it belongs in this directory is NA Brau, which launched in late April 2024 and is billed as the first canned non-alcoholic beer brewed by a DC brewery - a distinction Washingtonian and DC Beer both noted at the time.

The beer itself is a 0.3% ABV pale ale modelled directly on The Public, DC Brau's flagship pale ale, using the same Centennial and El Dorado hops along with Caramel 40 and Munich specialty malts, which is where the pale golden colour comes from. The production method is the interesting part and it is worth explaining, because it is why the beer does not taste stripped. Most non-alcoholic beer is either dealcoholised after fermentation or stabilised with tunnel pasteurisation, and both processes cost flavour and carbonation. DC Brau instead uses a hybrid Lallemand yeast strain that produces very little alcohol in the first place, then protects the finished beer with Chiber, a mushroom-fibre extract from Chinova Bioworks that works as a natural antimicrobial. The result keeps its carbonation and its hop character; Skall has said that in trials it is very hard for people to discern that it is NA. What lands in the glass is light, crisp and grassy.

Practical notes. The taproom is open Thursday through Sunday only - 3pm to 9pm on Thursday and Friday, 1pm to 9pm on Saturday and 1pm to 7pm on Sunday - and NA Brau is on the taproom list alongside the full alcoholic range. Cans are also sold widely at bars, restaurants and retailers across the region, so this is one of the few entries here you can drink without visiting. Ivy City is not walkable from a Metro station; it is a short drive or bus ride from NoMa-Gallaudet.
venues.pressQuote: DC Brau will be the first DC brewery to sell a canned non-alcoholic beer.

venues.name: De La Playa Records & Leisure
venues.description: De La Playa Records & Leisure is a fully alcohol-free hybrid record shop and community space in LA's Highland Park, opened in mid-2024 by three co-founders with roots in Long Beach and the Harbor area: John David Preap ("Bles"), Diego "Fuego" Guerrero, and Jon Paul Lourenço. The shop pairs thousands of vinyl records — hip hop, reggae, jazz, cumbia, salsa, funk, house — with a retail selection of 100-plus non-alcoholic beverages, including Greek- and Italian-style amaros, NA IPAs, de-alcoholized wines, and ready-to-drink cocktails. On weekends, the founders run "Bar Non," a made-to-order zero-proof cocktail stand on the patio (think an NA rum build with ube, cinnamon, maple, and black walnut, or a non-alcoholic Paloma with hopped grapefruit bitters), alongside guest DJ sets, listening parties, and vendor events. The founders deliberately chose to stay alcohol-free — one of LA's clearest dedicated-NA anchors.
signatureDrinks: NA rum (ube, cinnamon, maple, black walnut)
venues.longDescription:
De La Playa Records & Leisure is an alcohol-free record shop and community space at 110 South Avenue 56 in Highland Park, opened in June 2024 by three co-founders whose reasoning was refreshingly unsentimental. There are enough alcoholic bars in the neighbourhood, John David Preap told L.A. TACO at the opening; we just wanted to create an alternative space for people to listen to music and chill. Preap, who goes by Bles, is a first-generation Cambodian-American raised in the Harbor Area and came to the idea through his work as beverage director at Melody Lounge in Chinatown, where he also DJs. His partners are Diego Fuego Guerrero, a first-generation Mexican-American raised in Long Beach who is an associate civil engineer for Los Angeles County in his other job, and Jon Paul Lourenço, known as Soulchild Seb, also raised in Long Beach to parents from the Azores. Both are established DJs, and Guerrero and Lourenço designed most of the room themselves — an ode to the founders' roots in Long Beach and the Harbor area, worked through a tropical, jungle-minded interior heavy with plants. Notably, the alcohol-free identity was a deliberate choice rather than a licensing constraint, though Lourenço has said they briefly considered a beer and wine licence before deciding the process was too gnarly.

The shop pairs thousands of records — hip hop, reggae, jazz, cumbia, salsa, funk and house — with a retail range of more than a hundred non-alcoholic drinks, taking in Greek and Italian-style amari, non-alcoholic IPAs, de-alcoholised wines and ready-to-drink cocktails. Anything on the shelf can be bought and drunk in the space rather than taken away, which is what makes it function as a bar rather than a bottle shop. At weekends the founders run Bar Non, their own made-to-order zero-proof cocktail pop-up, on the patio alongside guest DJ sets, listening parties and visiting vendors; opening-weekend drinks included a build on non-alcoholic rum with ube, cinnamon, maple and black walnut, and a Paloma finished with hopped grapefruit bitters. The shop is open Wednesday to Sunday, 11am to 7pm, with the Bar Non patio running Saturdays and Sundays.
venues.pressQuote: There are enough alcoholic bars in the neighborhood; we just wanted to create an alternative space for people to listen to music and chill.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: John David Preap, De La Playa co-founder

venues.name: Dear Daphni
venues.description: Dear Daphni is a Greek restaurant on the ground floor of The Laurel in Rittenhouse, and its non-alcoholic drinks draw on the eastern Mediterranean pantry rather than on a generic syrup rail. The Honey Bee combines a non-alcoholic gin with sumac honey, lemon and Pinamor — sumac being the dark red, intensely tart berry that Levantine and Greek cooking uses where others would reach for lemon, and which gives the drink an acidity quite unlike citrus. A second build runs a non-alcoholic rum with pineapple, lime and Persian cucumber. Dinner runs from four in the afternoon to ten, and to eleven on Friday and Saturday.
signatureDrinks: Honey Bee — non-alcoholic gin, sumac honey, lemon, Pinamor
Non-alcoholic rum with pineapple, lime and Persian cucumber
venues.longDescription:
Dear Daphni occupies the ground floor of The Laurel on South 20th Street, a block off Rittenhouse Square, cooking a modern Greek menu — mezze, whole grilled fish, a wood fire. It opens at four in the afternoon and runs to ten most nights, eleven on Friday and Saturday.

The non-alcoholic drinks are worth attention because they are built from the restaurant's own pantry rather than from the generic sweet-and-sour rail that most kitchens use for this category. The Honey Bee pairs a non-alcoholic gin with sumac honey, lemon and Pinamor, and sumac is the ingredient doing the interesting work. It is the dried and ground berry of the sumac shrub, deep red, and it carries a sharp, almost fruity sourness that runs through Greek, Turkish and Levantine cooking wherever a cook wants acidity with body rather than the thin brightness of a lemon. Infused into honey and set against a juniper-led alcohol-free spirit, it produces something genuinely difficult to describe by reference to any standard cocktail — which is the highest compliment available to a zero-proof drink, since most of them are defined by what they are imitating.

The second build runs a non-alcoholic rum with pineapple, lime and Persian cucumber. Persian cucumbers are thin-skinned, seedless and markedly less watery than the standard variety, so they contribute flavour rather than dilution — the reason they turn up in Mediterranean salads and, here, in a glass.

The wider case for a Greek restaurant as a night out without alcohol is the way the food is served. A mezze table arrives in waves and is shared, which means the evening's rhythm is set by dishes landing rather than by rounds being bought, and the meal has natural pauses built into it. Add drinks constructed from the same spice shelf as the cooking, and ordering alcohol-free stops being a substitution and becomes part of the same meal.

venues.name: Dear Irene
venues.description: Dear Irene is an intimate downtown room doing small plates and cocktails, and it is the Bend bar most often recommended to people who want a proper night out without alcohol. Its Path Less Taken is built on Pathfinder with bitters and drinks like an old fashioned. Small plates run to Oregon crab arancini and king salmon tartare. Closed Sunday and Monday.
signatureDrinks: Path Less Taken — Pathfinder non-alcoholic spirit and bitters, in an old fashioned register
venues.longDescription:
Dear Irene is a small, low-lit room on Brooks Street in downtown Bend, a few steps off the main drag near Drake Park, serving small plates and a tightly-made cocktail list. It is the venue Visit Bend's own zero-proof guide singles out for the specific experience of not being the odd one out — the situation where one person at the table is drinking and the other is not, and the bar makes that feel unremarkable rather than awkward.

The Path Less Taken is the drink that earns it. It is built on Pathfinder — the hemp-derived, distilled non-alcoholic spirit made in Oregon, bitter and herbaceous in a way that behaves like an amaro — with bitters, landing squarely in old fashioned territory: spirit-forward, aromatic, meant to be sipped slowly. That is the hardest register for a zero-proof drink to hit, because there is no citrus or fizz to carry it, and it is the register most non-drinkers miss most. There is also a Monkey Business, named for the mischievous-monkey wallpaper in the bathroom, which tells you something about the room's sense of humour.

The food is not an afterthought — Oregon crab arancini, king salmon tartare, the kind of cooking that makes a drinks-led room work as a full evening. Because the space is small and it opens only Tuesday through Saturday from half past four, booking is sensible, particularly at weekends and through the summer season.

Alongside Bar RBC a few blocks away, this is the strongest evidence that Bend's zero-proof scene has moved past mocktails-as-consolation into something built with intent.
venues.pressQuote: where I'd send anyone looking for an intimate, elevated spot to enjoy zero-proof drinks and small plates without feeling like the odd one out

venues.name: Dearly Beloved
venues.description: Dearly Beloved is a self-described "cocktail restaurant" from Machine Hospitality Group, which opened in May 2024 in River North's former Kiki's Bistro space at 900 N Franklin St. The beverage program is led by mixologist and beverage director Aneka Saxon, who sourced ingredients on travels through six countries. Alongside its spirited menu, the venue maintains a permanent "Zero Proof Cocktails" section rather than a one-off list — a commitment Saxon highlights as core to the program. Named non-alcoholic builds include Clearly Cultured (with Seedlip Grove), Understory (Heywell lime adaptogen soda), Fresh Cut Grass (dandelion honey, grasshopper syrup, liquid chlorophyll, lime), and Soda Pop (orgeat, oat milk, coconut soda, orange flower and rose water). A Happy Hour zero-proof option, Zeal Without the Rest, uses the Crodino NA aperitif. In January 2025 the venue hosted Chicago's Spirit-Free Cocktail Fest, pouring eight zero-proof drinks.
signatureDrinks: Clearly Cultured (Seedlip Grove, probiotic yogurt clarification, lime, Mallorca melon, hibiscus, ginger, rose water) $15
Understory (Heywell lime adaptogen sparkling water, espresso, Giffard gingembre syrup, cream) $14
Fresh Cut Grass (dandelion honey, grasshopper syrup, liquid chlorophyll, lime, soda) $13
Soda Pop (dragonfruit, almond, coconut milk, coco-rico coconut soda, orange flower water, rose water, lime) $13
venues.longDescription:
Dearly Beloved opened in 2024 at 900 N Franklin Street in River North, in the space that was Kiki's Bistro for decades, and calls itself a cocktail restaurant rather than a bar or a restaurant — co-owner Chireal Jordan has explained the label plainly, saying the drinks are the star of the show. It comes from Machine Hospitality Group, with beverage director Aneka Saxon running the drinks and chef Kristofer Lohraff the food, which is vegetable-forward and carries vegan, vegetarian and gluten-free options through the menu rather than in a separate corner of it, including carrot mochi with coconut curry and an okonomiyaki. The room keeps genuinely late hours — 4pm to 1am midweek and to 2am on Friday and Saturday, closed Monday and Tuesday — with happy hour from 4pm to 6pm Wednesday through Sunday. Walk-ins are welcome and reservations preferred.

The zero-proof drinks are a permanent section of the standing menu headed "Zero Proof Cocktails", not a seasonal guest appearance, and they are among the most technically ambitious in the city. Clearly Cultured ($15) is the showpiece: Seedlip Grove clarified with probiotic yogurt, then built out with lime, Mallorca melon, hibiscus, ginger and rose water — milk-clarification technique applied to a non-alcoholic base, which is a genuinely difficult thing to get right. Understory ($14) is the one to order after dinner, combining espresso and cream with Giffard gingembre syrup over a Heywell lime adaptogen sparkling water. Fresh Cut Grass ($13) does what its name promises with dandelion honey, grasshopper syrup, liquid chlorophyll, lime and soda. Soda Pop ($13) is the softest, layering dragonfruit, almond and coconut milk with coconut soda, orange flower and rose water. During happy hour a fifth appears — Zeal Without the Rest at $10, built on Crodino, the Italian non-alcoholic aperitif, with adaptogen soda and sunflower honey. The bar also programmes around the category: in January 2026 it hosted a Spirit-Free Cocktail Fest featuring eight zero-proof drinks from visiting Chicago bartenders.
venues.pressQuote: Our menu always has a dedicated Zero-Proof section. We are just lucky enough to get to highlight it in January.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Aneka Saxon, Beverage Director, Machine Hospitality Group

venues.name: Death & Co
venues.description: Death & Co Denver is the second outpost of the New York cocktail bar, opened in 2018 inside The Ramble Hotel in Denver's River North Art District. Founders David Kaplan, Alex Day and Ravi DeRossi opened the original Death & Co in a windowless Manhattan room in 2007, where it helped lead the modern craft cocktail movement. The Denver location is a multi-bar complex within the boutique hotel: the marquee lobby bar with 1930s decor and plush velvet seating, the DC/AM coffee and brunch bar serving 7am to 3pm daily, the seasonal outdoor Garden, and Suite 6A, a mezzanine lounge overlooking the lobby bar. The bar keeps a standing Zero Proof section on its Denver menu, currently the Vibe Shift, Porch Swing, Business Casual and Cap Gun, alongside non-alcoholic wine and beer. Opening bar manager Alex Jump, since departed to open The Peach Crease Club, is widely credited as a founding figure of Denver's modern non-alcoholic bar scene.
signatureDrinks: Vibe Shift (NA: Seedlip Garden, Pathfinder, ginger, cinnamon, grapefruit, lime, NA Kolsch)
Porch Swing (NA: Lyre's Pink Gin, Three Spirit Livener, Seedlip Garden, watermelon, white balsamic, lemon)
Business Casual (NA: Giffard NA Aperitif, red verjus, black tea)
Cap Gun (NA: Almave Humo, Lyre's Coffee, Three Spirit Nightcap, lapsang souchong, orange)

naMenuItems.name: Vibe Shift

venues.longDescription:
Death & Co Denver opened in 2018 inside The Ramble Hotel at 1280 25th Street in the River North Art District, the first expansion of a bar that founders David Kaplan, Alex Day and Ravi DeRossi had opened in a windowless East Village room in 2007. The Denver site is not one bar but four rooms with different jobs. The lobby bar runs full table service under 1930s decor, velvet seating, crystal chandeliers and dried flower arrangements; DC/AM operates as a neighbourhood cafe from 7am to 3pm daily; The Garden is a seasonal outdoor space open Wednesday through Sunday afternoons and evenings; and Suite 6A is an intimate mezzanine lounge overlooking the lobby, available for private events. The bar that opened here was, by design, a test of whether the New York programme could be rebuilt at altitude rather than franchised, and the non-alcoholic list has been part of that from the first menu rather than bolted on later. The Ramble Hotel itself is a fifty-room boutique property, and the bar's position in its lobby means the room fills early and holds a mixed crowd of hotel guests and neighbourhood regulars; service runs to 11pm most nights and to 12:30am on Fridays and Saturdays.

The current menu carries a standing Zero Proof section of four drinks built the same way as the full-proof list. Vibe Shift combines Seedlip Garden and Pathfinder with ginger, cinnamon, grapefruit, lime and a non-alcoholic Kolsch. Porch Swing runs Lyre's Pink Gin, Three Spirit Livener and Seedlip Garden against watermelon, white balsamic and lemon. Business Casual is the bitter, low-sugar option, just Giffard non-alcoholic aperitif, red verjus and black tea. Cap Gun is the smoky one, using Almave Humo with Lyre's Coffee, Three Spirit Nightcap, lapsang souchong and orange. Non-alcoholic wine and beer are listed alongside. The programme's reputation was built by opening bar manager Alex Jump, who was hired to launch the Denver room and told 5280 that she had never worked at an establishment with non-alcoholic drinks on the menu before it; she has since left to open The Peach Crease Club in the same neighbourhood. Westword's January 2026 Dry January round-up described the bar as countering the cloying reputation of the category. Earlier menus have carried different builds under the same section heading, among them a Carda Ballista of red verjus, paprika, cardamom and Pathfinder, and an Autumnal Incense of maple, clove, orange and chocolate bitters, which is a fair guide to how often the list turns over.
venues.pressQuote: When Alex Jump started bartending 13 years ago, a customer asking for a nonalcoholic option usually sent her scrambling to dust off an expired bottle of O'Doul's. In fact, she didn't work for an establishment with NA drinks on the menu until she was hired to open the Denver location of illustrious NYC cocktail bar Death & Co in 2018.

venues.name: Death & Co Los Angeles
venues.description: Death & Co Los Angeles is the first West Coast location of the cocktail brand founded in New York's East Village on New Year's Eve 2006, and it opened in the Arts District of downtown Los Angeles at the end of 2019 from the Death & Co team of David Kaplan, Alex Day and Devon Tarby with Ravi DeRossi — the same group behind the Normandie Club, Bibo Ergo Sum and the Walker Inn. The main room runs a seasonal menu organised into six sections, from the lightest and most refreshing through the most spirituous, with zero-proof drinks treated as one of those sections rather than an appendix; a separate walk-up Standing Room bar operates Thursday to Saturday. The zero-proof list currently holds three built cocktails at $16–$18 on genuine non-alcoholic spirits including Seedlip, Ritual, Giffard and Wilderton, backed by non-alcoholic wine and beer from NON, Lyre's, Athletic and Suntory.
