venues.longDescription:
Death & Co Los Angeles is the first West Coast outpost of the cocktail bar that opened in Manhattan's East Village on New Year's Eve 2006 and became, in short order, one of the most influential rooms in American drinking. The Los Angeles location arrived at 818 East 3rd Street in the Arts District at the end of 2019, from David Kaplan, Alex Day and Devon Tarby alongside Ravi DeRossi — a team that had already opened the Normandie Club, Bibo Ergo Sum, the Walker Inn and Honeycut in the city. The main bar is a subterranean lounge running a seasonal menu of roughly twenty-five drinks; a separate walk-up Standing Room bar, with a much shorter list, operates Thursday to Saturday. The kitchen is more serious than bar snacks implies, running oysters with calamansi mignonette, yellowfin tuna crudo with mango shrub and coconut milk, wagyu steak tartare, buttermilk fried jidori chicken with hot honey and Thai basil, and a lamb burger with sumac pickles.

The reason this room matters to non-drinkers is structural. Death & Co explains that its menu is comprised of six sections, starting from the lightest and most refreshing cocktails, followed by more spirituous and zero-proof drinks — so "Zero Proof" is a named section of the main list, ordered alongside everything else, not a separate card produced on request. The current list runs three drinks. Cruise Control ($17) combines Seedlip Notas de Agave and Giffard non-alcoholic aperitif with strawberry shrub, grapefruit, honey, lime and fizz. Tenth Planet ($16) builds a Thai tea cordial with Ritual zero-proof rum, pineapple, cinnamon and yuzu. Living Dead ($18) is the most spirit-forward, using Ritual zero-proof gin and Wilderton Earthen with pistachio, lemon and New Orleans-style non-alcoholic bitters. Directly beneath them the printed menu carries a non-alcoholic wine and beer block that is deeper than most bars manage: NON's salted raspberry and chamomile and its cherry and coffee sparklings at $16, Lyre's Classico sparkling at $14, Athletic's Mexican-style Copper and Free Wave hazy IPA at $9, and Suntory All-Free at $7. The bar opens at 6pm nightly, to 2am on Friday and Saturday, with reservations through SevenRooms.
venues.pressQuote: This low-lit subterranean cocktail spot requires reservations on busy nights

venues.name: Deep Dive
venues.description: Deep Dive is Renée Erickson's jewel-box cocktail lounge beneath the Amazon Spheres at 620 Lenora Street in South Lake Union, opened in August 2018 as part of her Sea Creatures group, with the space curated by Curtis Steiner of the Ballard home store Steinerlf. It is deliberately theatrical — curios on shelves and under specially lit bell jars, metal grooves overhead that the Seattle Times' critic read as ribs, leaving her feeling she was in the bowels of a sea creature. That same review was not uncritical: it found the energy in the oddly shaped room never quite sparks, and that the glamour ends up stage-set-like. The food has included a much-discussed $18 hot dog. It keeps a dedicated non-alcoholic menu called "Above Water", documented as including the Sinless Sour (Pathfinder, orgeat, lemon) and A Bitter Whisper (Pathfinder with Wilderton Lustre and Wilderton Aperitivo). PLEASE NOTE: Deep Dive's website is behind a security check we cannot pass, and the menu file it previously published has been taken down, so we cannot confirm the current Above Water list or its prices — check on arrival. A clarification: Erickson won a James Beard Award in 2016, but for The Whale Wins, not for Deep Dive. Strictly 21+.
venues.longDescription:
Deep Dive sits beneath the Amazon Spheres in South Lake Union and opened in August 2018, one of two Renée Erickson rooms in that development. Seattle Met's line on opening was cheerfully unimpressed with its own hype — it's called Deep Dive, it's beautiful, and there's a Renée Erickson-style hot dog on the menu. The space was assembled by Curtis Steiner, owner of the Ballard home store that bears his name, and it is dense with curios on shelves and under specially lit bell jars. The Seattle Times' review is the most vivid account of what that actually feels like, and it is worth quoting in full rather than cherry-picking: the metal grooves overhead look like ribs, the critic wrote, she saw mangled fingers and mannequin hand displays, and she felt she was in the bowels of a sea creature. She was also blunt about the room's limits — that no matter how full it is, and it is almost always full, the energy never quite sparks; that it is meant to feel glamorous but ends up stage-set-like, all artifice and no heart. Readers can decide which of those appeals. The bar is strictly 21-and-over with physical ID required.

For a non-drinker the draw is a dedicated menu with a name that fits the conceit: Above Water. Two of its drinks are documented — the Sinless Sour, built on Pathfinder with orgeat and lemon, and A Bitter Whisper, which layers Pathfinder with both Wilderton Lustre and Wilderton Aperitivo, giving it two separate bitter registers rather than one. That is a serious build, and consistent with a bar of this budget. What we cannot do is confirm what is on the list today, and we would rather say so than guess. Deep Dive's website sits behind a security challenge we cannot get past, and the cocktail menu file it used to publish has since been taken offline, so the current Above Water drinks and their prices are unverifiable from outside. Treat the two named above as indicative of the style rather than as a promise. One clarification while we are here, because it travels with every Erickson venue: she won the James Beard Award for Best Chef: Northwest in 2016, and that award was for The Whale Wins, two years before Deep Dive existed.
venues.pressQuote: Deep Dive, located underneath the Amazon Spheres, features an "Above Water" menu with alcohol-free cocktails like "Sinless Sour" and "A Bitter Whisper."

venues.name: Deir Cafe Antioch
venues.description: Appeared to be temporarily closed as of mid-October 2026, after a fire was reported at its Haywood Lane address on 13 October 2026 - check the cafe's own channels before going. Deir Cafe Antioch is the second location of Yousef Gumiza's fully alcohol-free Palestinian coffeehouse, on Haywood Lane in the Antioch neighbourhood of Nashville, and it is the one that keeps the late hours: before the closure it opened seven days a week from 9am until 1am. It took over the former La Princesa Market space, first reported in January 2026. The menu follows the original in Wedgewood-Houston - Mediterranean-inflected signature lattes including the Baklawa latte and the Golden Lotus with biscoff and caramel, fruit refreshers named in Arabic such as Roman for pomegranate and Ward for rose, matcha, smoothies and pastries. No alcohol is served at any hour, which is the point: it was built as a night cafe for a community that does not drink.
signatureDrinks: Golden Lotus Latte - biscoff and caramel
venues.longDescription:
Appeared to be temporarily closed as of mid-October 2026: local reporting placed a fire at 105 Haywood Lane on 13 October 2026, and the cafe has shown as closed since. Check its own channels before making the drive; the rest of this page describes the cafe as it ran before the fire.

This is the second Deir Cafe, and it is the one that does what its owner said he wanted to do all along. Yousef Gumiza opened the original on Hagan Street in Wedgewood-Houston, named for Deir al-Balah in Gaza, where his family is from. He told WPLN in March 2025 that night cafes are what his family loves and that people hang out until 1am - a normal way to spend an evening across the Middle East, and one that does not require a bar. The Hagan Street room closes at 6pm and could not deliver that. The Antioch shop can: it runs 9am to 1am, seven days a week, and serves no alcohol at any point.

What Now Nashville first reported the expansion in January 2026, with permit filings showing Deir taking over the La Princesa Market space at 105 Haywood Lane. Antioch is inside Metro Nashville-Davidson County, about eight miles southeast of downtown, and it is one of the most linguistically diverse parts of the city - the location is a deliberate one rather than a suburban overflow.

The drinks carry over from the original. The signature lattes lean Mediterranean: a Baklawa latte, a Golden Lotus latte built with biscoff and caramel, a Strawberry Dubai Chocolate latte, a Banana Spice latte. The cold side is named in Arabic for the fruit in the glass - Roman for pomegranate, Ward for rose, Khokh for peach, Passion Habibi for passion fruit. Matcha, smoothies and pastries including croissants fill out the rest, and the kitchen leans Mediterranean. Two practical notes. First, this is a cafe rather than a bar: there is no cocktail-style zero-proof list, and what you are buying is a table, a pot and a room that stays open when everything else in the neighbourhood has shut. Second, the 1am close is the whole reason to know about it, and it is unusual enough in Nashville that it is worth confirming on the day before making the drive.
venues.pressQuote: We love night cafes. Like, that's our thing. People hang out till 1 a.m.

venues.name: Deir Cafe
venues.description: Deir Cafe is a fully alcohol-free Palestinian coffeehouse on Hagan Street in Wedgewood-Houston, open seven days a week from 7am to 6pm. Owner Yousef Gumiza named it after Deir al-Balah, his family's city in Gaza, and built it as a community room as much as a cafe: it keeps a dedicated prayer space alongside the counter. The drinks are Mediterranean-inflected rather than standard third-wave - a Baklawa latte, a Golden Lotus latte with biscoff and caramel, a Strawberry Dubai Chocolate latte, a Banana Spice latte - plus fruit refreshers named in Arabic: Roman for pomegranate, Ward for rose, Khokh for peach. Matcha, smoothies and pastries fill out the list. No alcohol is served. A second Deir Cafe on Haywood Lane in Antioch appeared to be temporarily closed as of mid-October 2026, after a fire was reported at that address.
signatureDrinks: Golden Lotus Latte - biscoff and caramel
venues.longDescription:
Deir Cafe takes its name from Deir al-Balah, the city in Gaza that owner Yousef Gumiza's family comes from, and which translates roughly as Monastery of the Date Palm. Gumiza has been explicit about why that matters to him: he wanted to invent something out of his own history rather than import a template, and the cafe is the result. The Nashville Banner profiled it in April 2026 as a cultural hub for the city's Muslim community, and WPLN, Nashville's public radio station, had featured it a year earlier in a story about Muslim-owned coffeehouses keeping late hours through Ramadan and beyond. There is a dedicated prayer space inside, which is unusual for a Nashville coffee bar and central to how the room is used.

The drinks are where the Mediterranean influence shows most plainly. The signature lattes are built on regional flavours - a Baklawa latte, a Golden Lotus latte with biscoff and caramel, a Strawberry Dubai Chocolate latte, a Banana Spice latte - and the cold refreshers are named in Arabic for what is in them: Roman for pomegranate, Ward for rose, Khokh for peach, and a passion fruit build the shop calls Passion Habibi. Matcha drinks, smoothies and pastries including croissants round it out, and nothing on the list contains alcohol. Gumiza's own line about the business is that they serve memories, traditions and a taste you will not find anywhere else.

One caveat worth stating plainly, because it decides whether this is an evening venue or not: the Hagan Street shop currently closes at 6pm, seven days a week. Gumiza's ambition is the late-night cafe - he told WPLN that night cafes are the thing his family loves and that people hang out until 1am - and that is exactly how the second Deir Cafe on Haywood Lane in Antioch ran until mid-October 2026, when it appeared to close temporarily after a fire was reported at the address. Check its channels before planning a night out there. For a quiet afternoon in Wedgewood-Houston, within walking distance of the gallery district, this is the one.
venues.pressQuote: We love night cafes. Like, that's our thing. People hang out till 1 a.m.

venues.name: Delafia
venues.description: Delafia is a small natural wine bar and retail shop on South Roxboro Street in Durham's Hayti neighbourhood, pouring low-intervention wine from small producers by the glass and selling it by the bottle, with a short food menu and coffee alongside and the feel of a speakeasy more than a shop. Its own invitation is to come in for a nibble and a pour from a rotating menu of low-intervention wines, beer and non-alcoholic bevs, which puts alcohol-free drinks on the same rotating list as everything else rather than in a fixed section; Discover Durham lists it among the shops curating non-alcoholic products locally and beyond, in the same group as LouElla and Beer Study. There is no published list and no named zero-proof cocktails, so call or ask what is open this week. Open from four, to ten early in the week and midnight Thursday through Saturday.
venues.longDescription:
Delafia is a small natural wine bar and bottle shop on South Roxboro Street in Hayti, the historically Black neighbourhood south of downtown Durham. It deals in low-intervention wine from small producers — a rapidly changing list, sold by the glass at the bar or by the bottle to take away — and it has the feel of a speakeasy more than a shop, with a short menu of things to eat and coffee served alongside.

The non-alcoholic element is real but modest, and worth describing precisely. The bar's own invitation is to come in for a nibble and a pour from its rotating menu of low-intervention wines, beer and non-alcoholic bevs, which puts alcohol-free drinks on the same rotating list as everything else rather than in a fixed section. Discover Durham includes it on the city's official non-alcoholic page among the shops curating non-alcoholic products locally and beyond, in the same group as LouElla and Beer Study.

What that means in practice is that there is always something alcohol-free worth drinking here, chosen by people who take drinks seriously, but there is no published list to check before you go and no named zero-proof cocktails. If you want to know what is open this week, call or ask. For a natural wine bar — a category that has been slower than most to take non-alcoholic drinking seriously — having it on the rotating menu at all is meaningful.

This is a venue that sells alcohol and is built around wine, so it is not a room for anyone who would rather not be around it. Hours run from four in the afternoon, to ten early in the week and midnight Thursday through Saturday.
venues.pressQuote: non-alcoholic products made locally and beyond

venues.name: Delah Coffee (Sansome Street)
venues.description: Delah Coffee's Financial District cafe sits at Sansome and Clay, on the edge of Chinatown, and pours the same alcohol-free Yemeni list that the group's original SoMa shop opened with in 2022. It runs 6am to 8pm on weekdays and 7am to 9pm at weekends, an earlier close than the SoMa flagship but still well past the point where most downtown coffee counters shut. The traditional preparations are the draw: Sana'ani, the house black coffee with cardamom; Jubani, a light roast cooked with cardamom, ginger and cinnamon; Arabian Qawah, light roast boiled with cardamom; and Adeni chai, Yemeni black tea simmered with cream and the house spice blend. Turkish delights, honeyed pastries and savoury turnovers are baked daily.
signatureDrinks: Jubani (light roast with cardamom, ginger and cinnamon)
Adeni Chai (Yemeni black tea with cream and Delah spices)
Arabian Qawah (light roast boiled with cardamom)
venues.longDescription:
Delah Coffee's second San Francisco location occupies a corner unit at 450 Sansome Street, where the Financial District runs into Chinatown, and serves the same menu as the Fourth Street original that Omar and Majed Jahamee opened in South of Market in July 2022. Delah was, by KQED's account, the first Yemeni coffee shop in the Bay Area; the category has since expanded to more than twenty cafes across the region, and Delah itself now has locations in Oakland, Berkeley, Dublin, San Diego and Naperville, Illinois. The brand takes its name from the Arabic word for the long-spouted pot used to serve Yemeni coffee, and the cafes are built to be sat in rather than passed through.

No alcohol is served anywhere on the premises. The Sansome Street shop opens at 6am on weekdays for the office trade and closes at 8pm, running later at weekends to 9pm — enough to make it an after-work or early-evening option in a part of the city where the alternatives are almost entirely bars. The core list is traditional rather than confected. Sana'ani is the house-style black coffee cooked with cardamom. Jubani is a light roast simmered with cardamom, ginger and cinnamon. Arabian Qawah is a light roast boiled with cardamom and served in small cups. Adeni chai, the most ordered drink in most Yemeni cafes, is black tea cooked down with cream and Delah's own spice mixture. Drip coffee brewed from the house beans and an iced Yemeni latte cover the more familiar orders. Everything sits between roughly four and seven dollars. The pastry case carries Turkish delight, honey-soaked sweets and savoury turnovers baked fresh each day, which in practice means the cafe works as a light dinner as much as a coffee stop. Because the group prints one menu across all its locations, the Sansome Street shop pours exactly what the Fourth Street original does; the difference between the two is trading hours and the character of the surrounding blocks, which here means an after-work crowd from the surrounding towers rather than the student and late-night trade that fills SoMa.

venues.name: Delah Coffee (SoMa)
venues.description: Delah Coffee is the original San Francisco Yemeni coffeehouse, opened in SoMa in July 2022 by Omar Jahamee, then eighteen, with his uncle Majed Jahamee. KQED credits it as the first Yemeni coffee shop to open in the Bay Area, ahead of the wave of more than twenty that followed. The Fourth Street cafe is entirely alcohol-free and trades from 6am to 11pm on weeknights and to midnight on Friday and Saturday, which makes it a genuine late option rather than a morning-only stop. The drinks are traditional: Sana'ani, the house black coffee with cardamom; Jubani, a light roast with cardamom, ginger and cinnamon; Arabian Qawah; and Adeni chai, Yemeni black tea cooked with cream and Delah's own spice blend. Turkish delights and turnovers baked daily fill the counter.
signatureDrinks: Jubani (light roast with cardamom, ginger and cinnamon)
Adeni Chai (Yemeni black tea with cream and Delah spices)
Arabian Qawah (light roast boiled with cardamom)
venues.longDescription:
Delah Coffee opened on Fourth Street in South of Market in July 2022, started by Omar Jahamee — eighteen years old at the time — together with his uncle Majed Jahamee. The Oaklandside reported the family's story in November 2023, and KQED's June 2026 account of the Bay Area's Yemeni coffee boom names Delah as the first Yemeni coffee shop to open in the region, the start of a wave that has since put more than twenty across the Bay. The name is the Arabic word for the traditional long-spouted coffee pot, and the logo is drawn from the same object; the group has since expanded to Oakland, Berkeley, Dublin, San Diego and Naperville, Illinois, but the SoMa room remains the original.

No alcohol is served, and the trading hours are what make the cafe useful to anyone going out without it: 6am to 11pm Monday through Thursday, 7am to midnight on Friday and Saturday, and 7am to 11pm on Sunday. The drinks list is short and traditional rather than sweetened into a milkshake menu. Sana'ani is the house-way black coffee with cardamom. Jubani is a light roast cooked with cardamom, ginger and cinnamon. Arabian Qawah is a light roast boiled with cardamom, and Adeni chai is Yemeni black tea simmered with cream and Delah's own spice mix. A drip coffee brewed from the house beans and an iced Yemeni latte round out the everyday orders, with prices in the four-to-seven dollar range that put a full evening's drinking well below the cost of one cocktail elsewhere in the neighbourhood. The counter carries Turkish delight, honey-soaked pastries and savoury turnovers baked fresh each day. The room fills late, particularly with students and with people who want somewhere to sit and talk that is neither a bar nor a chain coffee shop closing at seven.
venues.pressQuote: Delah Coffee in San Francisco was the first Yemeni coffee shop to open in the Bay Area in 2022.

venues.name: Delbar
venues.description: Delbar — Farsi for "heart, captured" — is a Persian and Middle Eastern restaurant opened in Inman Park in May 2020 by owner Fares Kargar. The flagship sits in the Inman Quarter development and has grown into a small Atlanta group with additional locations in Buckhead and Old Milton; the restaurant is recognized in the MICHELIN Guide. The food leans on shared mezze, kebabs, and family recipes rooted in Iranian cooking. For non-drinkers, Delbar maintains a real, named zero-proof section on its beverage menu rather than generic sodas. Signature options include the Sharbat e Zereshk, a barberry-and-lime sharbat described as tropical and refreshing, and an Iced Coconut Chai Tea built on Persian tea and ginger. The NA program is house-made and culturally grounded in Persian sharbat tradition — a smaller, curated list at a full-service restaurant.
venues.address: 870 Inman Village Pkwy NE, Suite 1, Atlanta, GA 30307
venues.longDescription:
Delbar — Farsi for heart, captured — opened in Inman Park in May 2020 at 870 Inman Village Parkway, from chef and owner Fares Kargar. Opening a restaurant in May 2020 was not a plan anyone would have chosen, and it has since become the anchor of a small Atlanta group: the Persian street-food stall Bibi at Ponce City Market, a second Delbar in Alpharetta, a Buckhead location in November 2024, and the French-Mediterranean Eden with its rooftop Garden of Eden at Star Metals in 2025. The Inman Park original is recognised in the MICHELIN Guide. The cooking is Persian and Middle Eastern, built on shared mezze, kebabs and family recipes.

Its non-alcoholic list is smaller than a dedicated cocktail bar's and more interesting than most, because it is not really a mocktail list at all. The Sharbat e Zereshk is a barberry and lime sharbat; the Iced Coconut Chai Tea is built on Persian tea with ginger and coconut.

Sharbat is worth understanding, because it reframes what is on offer. It is a Persian tradition of fruit, flower and herb syrups let down with water or ice, and it goes back centuries — a fully developed non-alcoholic drinks culture that existed long before the Western zero-proof category was invented, in a region where abstaining from alcohol was the norm rather than the exception. Barberry, the zereshk of the name, is intensely sour and slightly tannic, which is exactly the quality that makes a drink taste finished rather than sweet.

The practical consequence is that a non-drinker at Delbar is not being offered a substitute for something else. They are being offered the drink the food was built alongside. That is a rarer thing than a ten-item zero-proof menu, and for a long mezze dinner it works better than most of them.

venues.name: Delilah Miami
venues.description: Delilah Miami is a 1920s-themed waterfront supper club from the h.wood Group, the Los Angeles hospitality company co-founded by John Terzian and Brian Toll. It opened in December 2023 inside The Four Ambassadors on Brickell Key, with a terrace and yacht slips overlooking Biscayne Bay. The concept pairs elevated American cuisine with art-deco styling and nightly live entertainment that builds into a late-night lounge. The bar is cocktail-forward, and Delilah carries a short but genuine non-alcoholic section on its menu, building zero-proof serves with the same approach as its full cocktail list. The two named alcohol-free drinks are the Sun's Out (Lyre's N/A rum, elderflower, lime, mint, on the rocks) and the Peacemaker (Lyre's Italian Spritz, grapefruit, lime, topped with tonic), each $16. It is the Miami outpost of the wider Delilah restaurant group.
venues.hours: Mon closed; Tue-Thu 5pm-11pm; Fri-Sat 5pm-12am; Sun closed
venues.longDescription:
Delilah Miami is a 1920s-themed waterfront supper club from the h.wood Group, the Los Angeles hospitality company co-founded by John Terzian and Brian Toll, which opened in December 2023 inside The Four Ambassadors on Brickell Key. It has a terrace and yacht slips over Biscayne Bay, art-deco styling, elevated American food and nightly live entertainment that escalates into a late-night lounge as the evening goes on.

A supper club is a format organised around drinking from the first course to the last, and the later it gets the more true that becomes. Delilah carries a short but genuine non-alcoholic section built with the same approach as its full cocktail list rather than as a separate, simpler set. The Sun's Out uses Lyre's non-alcoholic rum with elderflower, lime and mint over ice. The Peacemaker is Lyre's Italian Spritz with grapefruit and lime, topped with tonic — a spritz shape, which is the right call for a room where most people are holding a coupe.

Both are $16, and the price is worth noting rather than glossing. Charging cocktail money for a zero-proof drink signals that it takes cocktail work, and it means the non-drinker is a full participant in the room's economics rather than a discounted guest. Resident Magazine described the drinks as built with the same attention as the cocktail programme.

It is the Miami outpost of the wider Delilah group. Expect a dress code, a door, and prices to match the setting — this is a night out rather than a dinner, and the two named alcohol-free drinks are what make that night out available to someone who is not drinking. Brickell Key is a short causeway from downtown and effectively an island, so plan the journey — this is not somewhere you pass on the way to something else.
venues.pressQuote: built with the same attention as its cocktail program

venues.name: Demi
venues.description: Demi is James Beard Award-winning chef Gavin Kaysen's intimate North Loop tasting-menu restaurant, opened in early 2019 next to his flagship Spoon and Stable and operated under Soigné Hospitality Group. With roughly 20 counter seats wrapping an open oval kitchen, it serves a seasonal, reservation-only multi-course menu and is a Relais & Châteaux member. Alongside the wine pairing, Demi runs a parallel non-alcoholic "Temperance Pairing" (around $85, about eight curated zero-proof drinks) built from teas, juices, shrubs, and fermented or infused preparations designed to match each course. Beverage director Jessi Pollak leads the program. Mpls.St.Paul Magazine called the non-alcoholic pairing "just as good and wildly original" as the wine, citing a hibiscus, beet, apple, black pepper, and black trumpet mushroom "red." Demi is regularly cited among the few U.S. tasting menus doing non-alcoholic pairings seriously.
venues.longDescription:
Demi is James Beard Award-winning chef Gavin Kaysen's intimate tasting-menu restaurant in the North Loop, opened in early 2019 next door to his flagship Spoon and Stable and run under Soigné Hospitality Group. There are roughly twenty counter seats wrapping an open oval kitchen, the seasonal multi-course menu is reservation-only, and the restaurant is a Relais & Châteaux member. It is, by most reckonings, the hardest table to get in Minneapolis.

It is also one of the most important restaurants in the United States for anyone who does not drink, because of what runs alongside the wine pairing. Demi offers a parallel non-alcoholic Temperance Pairing — around $85 for roughly eight curated zero-proof courses — built from teas, juices, shrubs and fermented or infused preparations, each matched to a specific plate. Beverage director Jessi Pollak leads the programme. Mpls.St.Paul Magazine judged the non-alcoholic pairing "just as good and wildly original" as the wine, singling out a "red" built from hibiscus, beet, apple, black pepper and black trumpet mushroom — which gives a fair sense of the technical ambition involved. Building savoury, tannic, earthy drinks that hold up against eight consecutive courses is a genuinely difficult problem, and very few kitchens anywhere attempt it.

What elevates it beyond technique is the stated intent. Pollak has described the goal in terms that have nothing to do with mixology: "I want people, when they experience the temperance menu at Demi or drink an NA cocktail at any of the Soigné restaurants, to feel normal and cared about. That's all that matters to me." That is the entire problem this directory exists to solve, articulated by someone at the top of the profession. At a counter where every other guest is being poured something considered, being handed sparkling water is a small, repeated exclusion across three hours. Demi removed it. Wednesday through Sunday, evenings only, booking essential.
venues.pressQuote: I want people, when they experience the temperance menu at Demi or drink an NA cocktail at any of the Soigné restaurants, to feel normal and cared about. That's all that matters to me.

venues.name: DENMARK on High
venues.description: DENMARK on High is a second-floor cocktail lounge in the restored Yankee Trader building — now Yankee on High — at the southern gateway to the Short North, overlooking the Columbus Convention Center. It opened in 2014 in what had been a furniture showroom, and is built around a no-television, no-distraction room and a from-scratch bar programme: house bitters, house infusions, house syrups and shrubs. The current menu carries a small non-alcoholic section rather than a token line, with two built drinks — Not A Dream, a tropical construction of non-alcoholic gin, fruit purée, coconut cream and lime, pineapple and orange juice, and the Cucumber No-Jito of lime juice, mint syrup and cucumber soda. The bar also runs small-group cocktail classes and opens Wednesday to Saturday evenings only.
venues.address: 463 N High St, 2nd Floor, Columbus, OH 43215
venues.hours: Mon-Tue closed; Wed-Thu 5pm-11pm; Fri-Sat 5pm-12am; Sun closed
signatureDrinks: Not A Dream (N/A gin, fruit purée, coconut cream, lime, pineapple and orange juice)
Cucumber No-Jito (lime juice, mint syrup, cucumber soda)
venues.longDescription:
DENMARK opened in 2014 on the second floor of 463 North High Street, in the Yankee Trader building that had just come out of a three-year restoration and now trades as Yankee on High. The building is the traditional gateway to the Short North from downtown, and the bar occupies what had been a furniture showroom, with windows looking across to the Columbus Convention Center. The room is deliberately undistracted — no televisions — and the house line is that everything is made from scratch: bitters, infusions, syrups and shrubs are produced in-house rather than bought, which is the reason the cocktail list carries as many unfamiliar ingredients as it does.

The non-alcoholic offering is modest in length but genuine in construction, and it sits on the same printed menu as the cocktails rather than being held back for anyone who asks. Not A Dream is the more ambitious of the two: a non-alcoholic gin base built out with fruit purée, coconut cream and a mix of lime, pineapple and orange juice into something closer to a tiki drink than a spritz. The Cucumber No-Jito is the lighter option, lime juice and mint syrup lengthened with cucumber soda, and reads as a proper long drink rather than a soft one. Both are priced well below the full-proof list, which runs from around $13 for the shaken and refreshing band up to $16 for the spirit-forward stirred drinks. Beyond the two builds, the bar keeps a short beer and wine list at $8 and $10 respectively. DENMARK also runs small-group cocktail classes, hands-on sessions in which guests make two drinks of their choosing and work through the fundamentals — a format that works as an evening out in its own right. Opening is Wednesday through Saturday from 5pm.
venues.pressQuote: A modern cocktail lounge serving world-class drinks in an intimate, elevated space, overlooking the Columbus Convention Center.

venues.name: Denver Café & Kava
venues.description: Denver Café & Kava opened on East Colfax in Park Hill in early 2026 as a deliberate zero-proof hangout — a room designed so that there is no pressure to drink, rather than a bar with a good alternatives list. It runs 7am to 2am every day of the week, which is the longest trading day of any alcohol-free venue in the city. The menu covers kava, mocktails, coffee and a range of Chinese and Vietnamese teas, plus small bites, and the calendar is community-led: open-mic nights, local vendor markets and themed parties. The founding team — Kevin Bloom, Elizabeth Leung, Cam Webbe, Jayden MacDonald and Jack Kestian — met as customers at Golden Kava Lounge, west of the city, and built this one together.
venues.longDescription:
Denver Café & Kava took over 5501 East Colfax Avenue in Park Hill in early 2026, and its origin story is unusually specific about why it exists. The founding team — Kevin Bloom, Elizabeth Leung, Cam Webbe, Jayden MacDonald and Jack Kestian — did not come from hospitality backgrounds looking for a concept. They met each other as customers at Golden Kava Lounge out in Golden, decided the city proper needed the same thing, and opened one. That is the clearest possible statement of what a kava bar is for: it is a room people go to often enough that they meet each other there.

The hours make the intent concrete. Doors at 7am, close at 2am, seven days a week. Nothing else in Denver's alcohol-free category trades that long a day; it means the same room works as a morning coffee stop, an afternoon workspace and a late-night alternative to the Colfax bar strip it sits in the middle of. East Colfax is a street with a long and specific reputation for drinking, and a venue on it that closes at last call without ever having served alcohol is doing something structurally useful rather than symbolic.

The drinks list is broader than most kava bars manage. Kava anchors it — a South Pacific root, ground and infused in water, alcohol-free, earthy and numbing on the lips, mildly sedative and drunk socially in place of alcohol across Fiji, Vanuatu, Tonga and Samoa. Around it sit a proper mocktail programme, coffee, and a notably good range of Chinese and Vietnamese teas, along with herbal botanical drinks and small bites. The tea selection in particular sets it apart from the kava-and-kratom template that most American kava bars follow.

The programming is where it earns the café half of its name. Open-mic nights, local vendor markets and themed parties run through the calendar, and the room is arranged for people to stay in rather than pass through. For anyone in Park Hill, City Park or the neighbourhoods along the eastern half of Colfax, this is now the default answer to wanting somewhere to be in the evening that is not a bar — and, unlike most of the Denver kava scene, it is inside the city rather than out in Lakewood, Golden or Westminster.

venues.name: Departure Restaurant + Lounge
venues.description: Departure is a pan-Asian rooftop restaurant and lounge on the 15th floor of The Nines hotel downtown, with two patios and city, river, and mountain views. Its beverage menu includes a dedicated "Zero Proof" section of named non-alcoholic cocktails — such as the Sunburst and Mood Ring — alongside non-alcoholic beers.

naMenuItems.name: More Passion
naMenuItems.description: passion fruit lemon pathfinder n/a hemp liqueur

naMenuItems.name: Fever Tree
naMenuItems.description: club soda tonic or ginger beer

venues.longDescription:
Departure Restaurant + Lounge is a modernist, pan-Asian restaurant and rooftop lounge on the 15th floor of The Nines hotel in downtown Portland, atop the historic 1908 Meier & Frank building. Opened in 2009 as the flagship of Sage Restaurant Group, it pairs a teak-clad indoor dining room beneath a long skylight with two open-air terraces overlooking Pioneer Courthouse Square, the Willamette River and the Cascades. Its menu spans Asian street-food starters, sushi, dim sum and kushiyaki skewers, and the kitchen was led for roughly a decade by Top Chef finalist and James Beard winner Gregory Gourdet before his departure.

Departure's bar, known for one of the largest sake and shochu lists in Portland, also maintains a dedicated "Zero Proof" section for non-alcoholic guests. House zero-proof cocktails include the Sunburst (calamansi, seven-spice, soda water) and the Mood Ring (jasmine green tea, butterfly pea flower, lemon, lime, soda water), and the lounge stocks non-alcoholic beers including Best Day "Electro Lime" cerveza.
venues.pressQuote: From its perch atop the historic Meier & Frank building (now home to the Nines Hotel), Departure has long reigned as king of the downtown rooftop patios.

venues.name: Deschutes Brewery Bend Public House
venues.description: Deschutes is the brewery that put Bend on the beer map in 1988, and its downtown public house pours Black Butte N/A — the non-alcoholic version of the porter that made the company's name, with the roasty, chocolatey depth of the original intact. Dark beer is the hardest style to render without alcohol, which makes this one of the more technically impressive NA pours in Oregon. Open daily from 11am.
signatureDrinks: Black Butte N/A — non-alcoholic version of the flagship porter, roasty and chocolatey
venues.longDescription:
Deschutes opened on Bond Street in downtown Bend in 1988 as a small brewpub and became one of the defining American craft breweries. The public house is still on the same site, and it remains the place most visitors start a Bend beer trail. For anyone not drinking, the reason to come is Black Butte N/A.

Black Butte Porter is the beer Deschutes built its reputation on, and rendering it without alcohol is a genuinely hard technical problem. Alcohol carries body, sweetness and aromatic weight, and dark beers depend on all three — strip it out carelessly and a porter collapses into thin, sour coffee water. The N/A version holds the roast and the chocolate character of the original, which is why it stands out in a category dominated by pale, hoppy styles that are far more forgiving to dealcoholise. If you have tried non-alcoholic beer before and concluded it only works as an IPA, this is the pour that argues otherwise.

The public house itself is a large, warm room with a long bar and a menu built around pub food done properly — the kind of place that fills with families early and stays busy late. It sits a block from Drake Park and the Deschutes River, so it works as an end point for a walk along the water.

Bend's non-alcoholic scene leans heavily on hop-forward beer, which is what a town of trail runners and climbers tends to want after a day out. Black Butte N/A is the counterweight: the one to order when the evening has cooled off and a bright IPA is the wrong shape of drink. Cases are generally available to go alongside the full-strength range.
venues.pressQuote: their black butte n/a keeps that roasty, chocolatey depth intact

venues.name: Desert Edge Brewery
venues.description: One of Salt Lake City's oldest brewpubs — opened in Trolley Square in 1972 (originally "The Pub") and brewing its own beer on-site since 1995. For non-drinkers, the menu carries a documented NA lineup: the house Pub's Hop Water Seltzer NA, Heineken 0.0, and Athletic Brewing's Run Wild non-alcoholic IPA. A full espresso bar — lattes, mochas, americanos and steamers — makes it an easy daytime or alcohol-free evening stop, alongside a from-scratch New American kitchen and award-winning beers.
venues.address: 273 Trolley Square, Salt Lake City, UT 84102
venues.longDescription:
Tucked into the historic Trolley Square shopping center near 600 East, Desert Edge keeps a casual, regulars-first feel alongside a small outdoor patio that's pleasant in the evening. Because the brewery sells its beer only at the pub, the NA-curious can sit at the same bar as the craft-beer crowd and still order a zero-proof pour or an espresso drink without feeling out of place.

The brewery opened in Trolley Square in 1972 and added its own on-premise brewing in 1995; its from-scratch kitchen and award-winning beers — including a Great American Beer Festival gold for its Happy Valley Hefeweizen — have made it a steady fixture of the central-city scene for over five decades.

venues.name: Deviant Kava
venues.description: Deviant Kava is an entirely booze-free, two-floor "third space" that opened in Parkville, Missouri in 2024, founded by three friends (including owner Wesley Straight) who wanted to bring the community feel of the kava scene to greater Kansas City. Set in a refurbished home about 15 minutes north of downtown KC near Park University, it pairs traditionally brewed kava and kratom tea with a full alcohol-free cocktail bar, specialty coffee (Café Corazón espresso), Hugo Tea, kombucha, yerba mate, and nootropic wellness drinks. The zero-proof menu includes named mocktails like the Captain's Daiquiri and Ashes to Ashes, plus made-to-order alcohol-free Negronis and margaritas. The space spans a bar and lobby, a fireplace room with plants and a library, and upstairs study nooks and a piano, with a deck overlooking the Park University campus. It is positioned as a sober-friendly community hub.
venues.longDescription:
Deviant Kava opened in Parkville, Missouri, at 405 Main Street, and describes itself in one sentence that explains the whole project: it is the result of three friends coming together to bring the sense of community in the kava scene to Kansas City. The room is a booze-free third space designed, in its own words, for people who want something beyond the typical coffee shop or bar — moody lighting, warm wood, and a deliberate mix of bar seating, comfortable chairs and big communal tables so it works for both a solo afternoon and a group. It runs across two floors, and The Pitch, visiting in December 2025, catalogued an upstairs level, a game room and a cosy nook with a fireplace, plus what it called the sweetest front porch and a back patio. The hours are the giveaway that this is built as an all-day room rather than a night-time one: 7am to 10pm Monday through Saturday, from 8am on Sundays.

The drinks split three ways. Traditional kava is the centre — brewed and bottled in house — alongside Leilo kava seltzers in flavours running from raspberry hibiscus and tangerine mango through to a lime margarita and a piña colada. The espresso programme is more serious than a kava bar usually bothers with, built on beans from local roaster Café Corazón: Florida Man layers espresso with orange essence, raw honey, whipped cream, nutmeg and fresh orange zest; Black Velvet works a black sesame simple syrup with vanilla and roasted sesame seeds; Samoan Hotspot pairs Ghirardelli chocolate with a serrano pepper syrup. Zero-proof cocktails round it out, including non-alcoholic negronis and margaritas. Two caveats worth knowing. The venue does not publish prices anywhere online, so the list is priced only in person. And alongside kava it sells kratom drinks — both are psychoactive, and kratom in particular is one that anyone in recovery will want to make a deliberate decision about rather than encounter by surprise.

venues.name: Devil Takes A Holiday
venues.description: Devil Takes a Holiday is a dark, demon-themed cocktail lounge on St Paul Street in downtown Burlington, run by Taylor Watts, who styles himself Head Devil. Its alcohol-free drinks are printed as atonements — a standing section of the rotating menu rather than an off-list favour — and they are built the way the alcoholic cocktails are, from bases, shrubs and syrups the bar makes itself. Watts has demonstrated the approach publicly on Vermont Public, showing a spiced cranberry shrub finished with non-alcoholic sparkling wine and a hot buttered drink built on a cocoa-and-brown-sugar scrub. Open from 5pm most nights, 4pm on Friday and Saturday, with a Sunday afternoon service.
venues.longDescription:
The name is a joke about a night off, and the room follows through — black walls, playful demonic artwork, low light and a music mix that keeps a small space lively. Devil Takes a Holiday opened on St Paul Street in downtown Burlington and quickly became the city's reference point for a certain kind of drink: made from scratch, a bit theatrical, and not remotely apologetic about it.

What earns it a place here is the atonements. That is the heading the bar prints over its alcohol-free drinks, and they are treated as a standing part of a rotating menu rather than as a request the bartender improvises against. Head Devil Taylor Watts and his staff build their own bases and flavours for them — the same house shrubs, syrups and infusions the alcoholic list draws on. His argument, made to Vermont Public, is that everything spirits can do you can do without them, which is a stronger claim than most bartenders will make out loud.

He has also shown the work. Demonstrating for the same broadcast, he built a cranberry shrub from equal parts cranberries, sugar and water with allspice and cinnamon, cut with an equal measure of apple cider vinegar, then finished it over ice with club soda or non-alcoholic sparkling wine, white cranberries, ginger and lime. The second was a hot buttered drink: dark brown sugar, butter, salt, cinnamon and cocoa powder worked to the consistency of a sugar scrub, then hot water and marshmallows. Neither is a menu item — the list rotates, which is why no signature drinks are recorded in this entry — but both show the technique the atonements come out of.

The food is a short list of bar snacks with deviled eggs as the house specialty. Doors at 5pm most nights, 4pm on Friday and Saturday, and an unusual 2pm start on Sunday.
venues.pressQuote: All these things that spirits can do, you can do with non-alcoholic drinks as well.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Taylor Watts, Head Devil, Devil Takes A Holiday

venues.name: Dew Drop Inn
venues.description: Dew Drop Inn is a women-owned gastropub at 17th and Downing in Denver's Uptown neighborhood, opened in 2021 by the team behind two of Denver's classic dive bars — the Horseshoe Lounge and the Embassy Tavern. Named Westword's Best New Bar in 2022, the venue blends a neighborhood-bar warmth (all-day $8 beer-and-shot specials, two daily happy hours running open–6pm and 10pm–close) with a serious gastropub program: Bangkok-style mussels, charcuterie, muffuletta, fried chicken, with 85% of the menu prepared gluten-free. The bar runs a named non-alcoholic program called 'clear-headed cocktails' — six rotating NA cocktails alongside two NA beers and a non-alcoholic prosecco, called out by 303 Magazine in their 2025 Sober Summer mocktail roundup. Named NA selections include the Be Nice (NA gin, lavender bitters) and the Cosmonaught (orange liqueur, cranberry, citrus). The space — tiger-print wallpaper, exposed brick, long wooden bar — is consciously designed to 'make regulars,' a philosophy the founding team has carried through 20 years of Denver hospitality.

venues.longDescription:
Tucked on a tree-lined block at 17th and Downing in Denver's Uptown neighborhood, Dew Drop Inn takes the sober-curious drinker seriously without making a production of it. The bar's dedicated 'clear-headed cocktails' section — six inventive zero-proof drinks, two NA beers, and an NA prosecco — sits alongside the regular cocktail list on equal footing. That parity is the point: this is a neighborhood bar first, and everyone at the table is supposed to have a good time.

The NA standouts documented by 303 Magazine's 2025 sober summer roundup are the Be Nice, built on NA gin with lavender bitters, and the Cosmonaught, a citrus-forward riff using NA orange liqueur, cranberry, and fresh citrus. The bar was opened in May 2021 by longtime Denver bar operators Leigh Jones, Margaret Moore, and Kiendl Smith — the same team behind the Horseshoe Lounge and Embassy Tavern — with food anchored by chef Fush, a 22-year Falling Rock Tap House veteran whose kitchen turns out spicy red curry mussels, Japanese-style fried chicken, and gluten-free-friendly small plates that hold their own against the drinks.

Dew Drop Inn earned Westword's Best New Bar 2022 honor and has since picked up a Best Mussels in Denver 2025 nod from the same publication, which called it a bar that 'continues to thrive as a neighborhood go-to.' The space is small and unhurried — exposed brick, warm wood bar, a sidewalk patio out front for warmer months. Reservations are not accepted, dress is casual, and the dual happy hours (open until 6pm and again from 10pm to close, Monday through Friday) make it as practical as it is charming. It's a solid choice for mixed-drinking groups, sober diners who want a full night out without a separate 'mocktail menu' experience, or anyone looking for a pre-show drink before the nearby Ogden Theatre.
venues.pressQuote: Be Nice (n/a gin, lavender bitters) and the Cosmonaught, a bright, citrusy blend of orange liqueur, cranberry and citrus were the best selections of the day. Big flavors, island energy, and a fun sober-friendly spot to hang, Dew Drop Inn welcomes you and your party with grace.

venues.name: Diego's East Side
venues.description: Diego's on Wayland Square is the East Side outpost of a Rhode Island Mexican group, and its bar builds non-alcoholic drinks with the same fresh-produce approach as its margaritas. Two standing builds are documented — one on apple cider reduction with cranberry, ginger and cinnamon, the other a cucumber, mango and lime build lengthened with ginger beer. A sibling room trades in Newport.
venues.longDescription:
Diego's began in Newport and its East Side room sits on Wayland Square, the small, walkable cluster of shops and restaurants on the far side of the Seekonk River from downtown Providence. The food is Mexican-influenced and produce-driven, and the bar has a reputation built on margaritas made from fresh juice rather than sour mix — which turns out to be exactly the foundation a good non-alcoholic list needs.

Two alcohol-free builds are documented in current Rhode Island coverage, and they are constructed rather than poured. The first runs an apple cider reduction against cranberry, ginger, lemon and cinnamon over soda — an autumnal, spiced drink with real body, the reduction doing the work of concentrating flavour that alcohol would otherwise carry. The second is brighter and built for the food: cucumber, mango and agave with lime, lengthened with ginger beer. Between them they cover a cold-weather sipper and something that stands up to chilli heat, which is a sensible pair for this kitchen.

Wayland Square is a pleasant place to be on foot, and the room is family-friendly earlier in the evening, so this works as a dinner destination rather than a late bar. Note that the group runs a Newport location as well; the drinks lists are broadly similar but not identical, and the address above is specifically the East Side room.

We have not published prices or a full current list, since Diego's does not publish its drinks menu online and the specific builds move seasonally. The two above were current in Rhode Island Monthly's zero-proof guide.
venues.pressQuote: Falling Down (apple cider reduction, cranberries, ginger, lemon, soda, cinnamon)

venues.name: Dishoom King's Cross
venues.description: Dishoom's King's Cross branch is the largest and most theatrical of the group, opened in 2014 inside a former Victorian railway transit shed — a godown, in Bombay parlance — on Stable Street behind Granary Square. Dishoom was founded by cousins Shamil and Kavi Thakrar, who opened their first site in Covent Garden in 2010 as a tribute to the old Irani cafés of Bombay, the all-day institutions built by Zoroastrian Persian immigrants; the main hall here recalls a 1920s Irani café, crowned by an art deco clock modelled on the one at Bombay's Victoria Terminus. It is regularly called the best mocktail bar in London, and the non-alcoholic list is a proper menu section rather than an afterthought: a Teetotal Espresso Martini, a Sober Negroni and a rotating range of 0% beers, served all day alongside the Bombay food.

venues.longDescription:
Dishoom is the homage-restaurant group founded by cousins Shamil and Kavi Thakrar, who opened their first site in Covent Garden in 2010 as a loving tribute to the old Irani cafés of Bombay — the all-day institutions built by Zoroastrian Persian immigrants. The King's Cross branch, which opened in 2014, is the largest and most theatrical Dishoom of all, set inside a former Victorian railway transit shed (a godown, in Bombay parlance) on Stable Street behind Granary Square. The main hall recalls a 1920s Irani café, crowned by an art deco clock modelled on the one at Bombay's Victoria Terminus and hung with Indian-Independence-era posters and portraits of Gandhi, Bhagat Singh and Sarojini Naidu; more than a hundred restored pieces of period Bombay furniture dress the room. Downstairs, in the building's former stables, sits the Permit Room bar, named for the licences once required to drink under the Bombay Prohibition Act of 1949.

Dishoom takes its non-alcoholic drinking as seriously as its cocktails: built by the group's Daru-walla, the list runs to a full run of alcohol-free "Teetotal Tipples" rather than a token mocktail or two. The Sober Summer Negroni layers green apple and apricot over no-alcohol gin, no-alcohol vermouth and a no-alcohol bitter syrup, finished with crisp desiccated apple; the Marine Drive Spritz lengthens Crossip non-alcoholic spirit with Cabernet Rosé grape juice and soda; and the Crystal All-Clear Mojito muddles a house cordial of mint, cardamom and lime with non-alcoholic aperitivo and soda. There is a Teetotal Espresso Martini of Baba's espresso, black cardamom, cinnamon syrup and ginger, alongside more experimental builds — Mr Xavier's Mule (a chai-charged cold brew lashed with ginger beer and orange cordial, plus lion's mane, zinc and turmeric), the Balaram Street Iced CB-Tea (Darjeeling, jasmine and a grapefruit-mango fizz laced with CBD) and the No-Hafta Colada, a frozen pineapple-and-coconut number with lime, pitaya and papaya.

Beyond the mock-cocktails, the Indian soft-drink canon is done properly. Thick, cold lassis run from Mango & Fennel and Rose & Cardamom to Salted, with wellness-leaning options such as the Raspberry Super-Lassi (kefir, tremella mushroom and aloe vera) and a protein-packed Beyond Breakfast lassi. House Chai is brewed the traditional way or with oat milk, and there are cooling sharbats — Watermelon, Passion Fruit and the tart-salty Kala Khatta — plus a fresh Nimbu Soda and nostalgic Indian bottled sodas including Thums Up, Limca and Pallonji's raspberry. Fresh juices, Ayurvedic-leaning wellness shots and Baba's own Chikmagalur coffee round out a genuinely deep teetotal menu, making King's Cross one of the most rewarding places in London to eat and drink well without alcohol.
venues.pressQuote: At Dishoom, as well as top Indian dishes, a selection of chai drinks, and several lassis to choose from, there are also alcohol-free takes on classic cocktails. From a sober negroni to a dry espresso martini, all of their teetotal drinks have all the drama of a cocktail, so there's zero risk of feeling left out.

venues.name: Dishoom Manchester
venues.description: Dishoom Manchester occupies a grand former Freemasons' Hall on Bridge Street, recreating the all-day romance of an old Bombay Irani café beneath enormous stained-glass windows. The group was founded by cousins Shamil and Kavi Thakrar as a tribute to the Irani cafés built by Zoroastrian Persian immigrants in Bombay; this branch opened in 2018 and leans into its building's past, with marble café tables, portraits on the walls and design nods to the Lodge Rising Star of Western India. Waiting guests are handed complimentary cups of chai, and a basement Permit Room bar sits below the main hall, named for the licences once required to drink under the Bombay Prohibition Act of 1949. Alcohol-free drinking is a proper menu section here — a full run of "Teetotal Tipples" served all day, including a Sober Summer Negroni, a Crossip-based Marine Drive Spritz and a Teetotal Espresso Martini, alongside lassis, chai, sharbats, 0% beers and alcohol-free sparkling wine.

venues.longDescription:
Dishoom is the homage-restaurant group founded by cousins Shamil and Kavi Thakrar, who opened their first site in Covent Garden in 2010 as a loving tribute to the old Irani cafés of Bombay — the all-day institutions built by Zoroastrian Persian immigrants. The Manchester restaurant, which opened in 2018, sits inside a grand former Freemasons' Hall on Bridge Street and leans into the building's past: the design nods to the Lodge Rising Star of Western India (founded in Bombay in 1843) and the story of Indian Freemasonry, with marble café tables, portraits on the walls and light pouring through enormous stained-glass windows. As at every Dishoom, waiting guests are handed complimentary cups of chai, and a basement Permit Room bar — named for the licences once required to drink under the Bombay Prohibition Act of 1949 — sits below the main hall.

Dishoom takes its non-alcoholic drinking as seriously as its cocktails, running a full section of alcohol-free 'Teetotal Tipples' rather than a token mocktail or two. The Sober Summer Negroni layers green apple and apricot over no-alcohol gin, no-alcohol vermouth and a no-alcohol bitter syrup, finished with desiccated apple; the Marine Drive Spritz lengthens Crossip non-alcoholic spirit with Cabernet rosé grape juice and soda; and the Crystal All-Clear Mojito muddles a house cordial of mint, cardamom and lime with soda and non-alcoholic aperitivo. There is a Teetotal Espresso Martini of Baba's espresso, black cardamom, cinnamon syrup and ginger, alongside more experimental builds — Mr Xavier's Mule (a chai-charged cold brew lashed with ginger beer and orange cordial, plus lion's mane and turmeric), the Balaram Street Iced CB-Tea (Darjeeling, jasmine and a grapefruit-mango fizz laced with CBD), the Expert Instructress's Matcha Sour (matcha, lime and moringa under a velvety kefir-yoghurt top) and the No-Hafta Colada, a frozen pineapple-and-coconut number with dragon fruit and papaya.

Beyond the mock-cocktails, the alcohol-free range is genuinely deep. Zero and low-alcohol beers include Kingfisher 0.0, an ON Beer IPA and a Collider Unwind session IPA brewed with lion's mane and ashwagandha, and there is an alcohol-free organic sparkling wine, Selbach-Oster 'Funkelwürtz Zero'. The Indian soft-drink canon is done properly too: thick, cold lassis run from Mango & Fennel and Rose & Cardamom to Salted, plus wellness-leaning options such as the Raspberry Super-Lassi (kefir and tremella mushroom) and a 20g-protein Beyond Breakfast lassi. House Chai is brewed the traditional way or with oat milk, and there are cooling sharbats — Watermelon, Passion Fruit and the tart-salty Kala Khatta — a fresh Nimbu Soda, nostalgic Indian bottled sodas including Thums Up, Limca and Pallonji's raspberry, fresh juices, Ayurvedic-leaning wellness shots and Baba's own Chikmagalur coffee, making Dishoom one of the most rewarding places in Manchester to eat and drink well without alcohol.
venues.pressQuote: With an extensive list of 'teetotal tipples', alcohol-free drinks at Dishoom are no afterthought.

venues.name: Dishoom Shoreditch
venues.description: The Shoreditch branch of London's Bombay-cafe group, and the most useful one for anyone not drinking: the drinks menu carries a named Teetotal Tipples section, eight alcohol-free builds priced and written like the rest of the cocktail list. A Sober Summer Negroni runs green apple and apricot through no-alcohol gin and bitter syrup, the Teetotal Espresso Martini works espresso against black cardamom and ginger, and the Crystal All-Clear Mojito clarifies the house cordial with a zero-proof aperitivo. Around them sit house chai, Bombay sodas and the full all-day kitchen, from bacon naan rolls at breakfast to black daal at midnight, in a room that takes bookings and holds space for walk-ins.

venues.longDescription:
Dishoom built its reputation on transplanting the Irani cafes of old Bombay to London, and the Boundary Street branch carries the formula deep into Shoreditch: veranda tiles, ceiling fans, all-day cooking and queues that start before the doors open. What earns it a listing in an alcohol-free directory is the drinks list's structure. Where most restaurant groups scatter a mocktail or two among the soft drinks, Dishoom writes a named Teetotal Tipples section, eight drinks introduced as absent of any alcohol, each with a full build and a price that signals the bar takes them as seriously as the paid-by-the-measure page. The standouts read like proper cocktails because they are: the Sober Summer Negroni sets green apple and apricot against no-alcohol gin, vermouth and bitter syrup; the Teetotal Espresso Martini pulls espresso through black cardamom, cinnamon and ginger; the Crystal All-Clear Mojito clarifies a house mojito cordial with mint, cardamom, lime and a zero-proof aperitivo.

The setting does the rest of the work. Because the room runs from breakfast chai through to a midnight close at the end of the week, an alcohol-free visit slots in at any hour without ceremony: a morning meeting over a bacon naan roll, an afternoon of house chai, or a full evening around the black daal with a teetotal round that costs and drinks like the real thing. The Permit Room bar downstairs pours the same zero-proof list, so waiting for a table is not a soda-water sentence either. Shoreditch has no shortage of bars with a token virgin option, but a kitchen-anchored room where eight alcohol-free drinks are named, built and priced with intent remains unusual, and for groups that mix drinkers with non-drinkers it removes the usual negotiation entirely. Booking ahead helps at peak times, though the walk-in queue moves faster than its reputation suggests.

venues.name: Dive Bar
venues.description: Dive Bar on K Street is best known for the mermaids swimming in the tank above the bar, and it keeps a proper mocktail menu underneath them — Cranberry Crab, Sailor's Delight and Pineapple Passenger among them. The spectacle is the reason to include it: a bar where the entertainment is overhead rather than in the glass gives a non-drinker something to actually be there for. It also runs 3pm to 2am every single day, which makes it the most consistently available option in this guide by a wide margin. No closed days at all, which no other Sacramento venue here can claim.
venues.longDescription:
Dive Bar on K Street is a downtown Sacramento institution for one reason: a large aquarium above the bar in which performers dressed as mermaids swim through the evening. It is genuinely strange and completely committed, and it has been drawing people in for years.

That matters here more than the drinks do. The recurring difficulty of a sober night out is not the absence of a good glass but the absence of anything else happening — in a conventional bar, drinking is the activity, and being the person not doing it leaves several hours to fill. Venues where something else is going on, whether that is pinball, mini golf, live music or a mermaid in a tank, solve the problem structurally rather than compensating for it. They are systematically underrated in alcohol-free guides.

The mocktails are real, named and on the printed menu: Cranberry Crab, Sailor's Delight and Pineapple Passenger, all fitting the nautical theme, plus further options. These are approachable drinks rather than technical ones, and the grade reflects a solid rather than an inventive programme.

The hours are the other significant point, and they are exceptional: 3pm to 2am, seven days a week, with no closed days. Look at the rest of this guide and the contrast is stark — Juju closes Sunday and Monday, Shangri-la opens four days, Bike Dog shuts Mondays, Teetotalist runs as an events programme. When a plan forms late or changes, Dive Bar is the Sacramento venue that will simply be open, and it will have something named on the menu for whoever is not drinking.

One thing to set expectations on: it is loud, it is busy at weekends, and it is unapologetically a spectacle bar rather than a quiet room. For someone newly sober who finds crowded drinking environments difficult, that may be the wrong choice, and Kupros or Wildwood would serve better. But for a group night out where one or two people are not drinking, the calculus flips — the mermaids give everybody the same thing to look at, and nobody is counting what is in anyone's glass.
venues.pressQuote: Dive Bar: Cranberry Crab, Sailor's Delight, Pineapple Passenger.

venues.name: Doberman Drawing Room
venues.description: Doberman Drawing Room is a cocktail-forward lounge and social club in Las Vegas' 18b Arts District, opened April 30, 2025 by Corner Bar Management in a 3,400-square-foot space styled after a moody 19th-century drawing room with private booths and an indoor atrium garden. The bar program is led by mixologist and partner Juyoung Kang (formerly of Fontainebleau's Collins bar), whose globally inspired, story-driven cocktails extend to a genuine spirit-free offering. The standing menu includes alcohol-free numbers such as the Coffee Cheesecake (a booze-free espresso martini with malt, coffee, honey, parmesan and nutmeg) and Good Vibrations (tomato, lychee, lemongrass, strawberry, white pepper and sumac). For Dry January 2026 the bar introduced "Zero-100," a two-menu tasting that pairs a sober-curious lineup with the regular drinking menu, featuring zero-proof cocktails like the Faux Fashioned (Lyre's Traditional Reserve with Lucano N/A Amaro), the Confetti (Lyre's Amaretto, zero-proof herbal liqueur, lemon and egg whites) and the Blush 75 (sparkling watermelon with Lyre's Pink Gin). Reservations (via SevenRooms) and walk-ins are both welcome; guests must be 21+ with a dressy-casual dress code.
signatureDrinks: Coffee Cheesecake (alcohol-free espresso martini with malt, coffee, honey, parmesan and nutmeg)
Good Vibrations (tomato, lychee, lemongrass, strawberry, white pepper, sumac)
Faux Fashioned (Lyre's Traditional Reserve + Lucano N/A Amaro)
Confetti (Lyre's Amaretto, zero-proof herbal liqueur, lemon, egg whites)
Blush 75 (sparkling watermelon with Lyre's Pink Gin)
venues.longDescription:
Tucked at 1025 S. 1st Street in the heart of the 18b Arts District, Doberman Drawing Room opened on April 30, 2025 as the latest concept from Corner Bar Management. The 3,400-square-foot room channels the moody elegance of a 19th-century drawing room, with heavy wood, private seating and booths, and an indoor atrium garden. It functions as both a public cocktail bar (reservations and walk-ins welcome) and a membership social club, with selection based, the team says, on "personality and passion rather than status."

The beverage program is overseen by mixologist and partner Juyoung Kang, previously of Fontainebleau Las Vegas, who describes her approach simply: "Every sip has a point of view. Every detail is intentional." That intentionality carries through to the non-alcoholic side of the menu. Alongside spirit-forward signatures, the bar keeps standing alcohol-free options such as the Coffee Cheesecake and the savory Good Vibrations, and for Dry January 2026 it launched "Zero-100," a two-menu tasting experience that lets a table mix sober-curious and traditional drinkers. The zero-proof lineup leans on Lyre's non-alcoholic spirits across drinks like the Faux Fashioned, Confetti and Blush 75, making Doberman a credible stop for anyone in the Arts District looking for a crafted, alcohol-free pour.
venues.pressQuote: Go booze-free and try a mocktail like the Coffee Cheesecake, an alcohol-free espresso martini with malt, coffee, honey, parmesan and nutmeg.

venues.name: Dobra Tea
venues.description: Dobrá Tea is a Bohemian-style tea house at 1937 Murray Avenue in Squirrel Hill, established in 2012 by the Society of Tea Devotees, the Czech tea collective, and owned by Nathaniel Pantalone. It serves over 100 loose-leaf teas from around the world alongside light vegetarian fare, and describes what it is aiming for as a space somewhere between a bar and a church — a place for relaxation and community. That is the practical appeal for a non-drinker: low light, cushions, low tables and no pressure to turn the table, in a room that stays open until 10pm on weeknights and 11pm on Friday and Saturday, which is exactly when other alcohol-free options in Pittsburgh run out. The list is organised by category the way a wine list is by region — white, green, oolong, black and pu'er teas, the house chai blends it calls Specialteas, tisanes and herbal infusions, and an iced range. Food is mezze-leaning: hummus and baba ganoush plates, several pita preparations, dolmades, miso soup, and a long list of sweet bites including halva and baklava. Prices are not published online.
signatureDrinks: Memories of Prague (black tea with chocolate)
venues.longDescription:
Dobrá Tea is a Bohemian-style tea house at 1937 Murray Avenue in Squirrel Hill, established in 2012 by the Society of Tea Devotees, the Czech tea collective whose rooms run across Central Europe and a handful of American cities. Its own description of what it is trying to be is the best line anyone has written about it: a space somewhere between a bar and a church, a place for relaxation and community. That is not a throwaway — it is the operating principle, and it explains why the room works for the purpose most alcohol-free venues struggle with. You can sit here for three hours. Nobody will hurry you, the lighting is low, there are cushions and low tables, and the whole design assumes you came to stay rather than to be turned over. Nathaniel Pantalone owns it. It opens late for a tea house — until 10pm on weeknights and 11pm on Friday and Saturday — which is precisely the window when a non-drinker in Pittsburgh runs out of options.

The list is not a mocktail menu and does not pretend to be. It is tea, over a hundred of them, ordered by category the way a wine list is ordered by region: green, black, oolong, white, yellow and pu'er, then the house blends it calls Specialteas, then tisanes, yerba maté and an iced range. The Specialteas are where its character sits, and they are named like postcards — Memories of Prague, a black tea with chocolate; Taste of Kashmir, an oolong with spices; Sweet Smell of Jerusalem, black tea with cinnamon; Touareg, the Moroccan mint; and four different chais including a minty Kerala and a chocolate Bombay. One item deserves singling out for anyone who misses the ritual more than the alcohol: Staroborshov, listed among the iced teas, is a chilled tea served as a "beer" — a genuine old Czech tea-house tradition rather than a novelty, and about as close as a soft drink gets to the shape of the thing it replaces. Food is mezze-leaning and mostly vegetarian. One limitation: no prices are published online.

venues.name: Dōgon by Kwame Onwuachi
venues.description: Dogon is James Beard Award-winning chef Kwame Onwuachi's Afro-Caribbean fine-dining restaurant inside The Potomac Hotel (the former Salamander Washington DC) at 1330 Maryland Avenue SW on the Southwest Waterfront, drawing on Nigerian, Jamaican, Trinidadian and Creole traditions. Its beverage programme was developed with Derek Brown, the nationally known bartender behind Positive Damage and a leading advocate for mindful drinking, and centres on a dedicated Low & No menu so that every dish can be paired with either a full cocktail or a spirit-free one. Named non-alcoholic drinks include Get Your Flowers, built on Fluere Spiced Cane with spiced pineapple syrup and grenadine, the botanical R_(n/a)_G&T on Fluere Botanical with Giffard Pamplemousse and elderflower, plus Astronomy Club and the Sigi Tolo Rickey. Dinner Tuesday to Saturday.
venues.longDescription:
Dogon by Kwame Onwuachi opened in September 2024 on the Southwest Waterfront, inside what was then the Salamander Washington DC - the former Mandarin Oriental, renamed The Potomac Hotel in August 2026 when it joined Marriott's Autograph Collection. Onwuachi is a James Beard Award winner and Top Chef alum, best known outside DC for Tatiana in New York, and the cooking here is Afro-Caribbean, pulling on Nigerian, Jamaican, Trinidadian and Creole traditions. The restaurant took its name and its framing seriously from the start, and the recognition came fast: since opening it has been named among the best restaurants on the continent by World's 50 Best, the New York Times and Bon Appetit. Time Out has called Onwuachi a master of Afro-Caribbean flavours deserving of the fine-dining treatment.

The drinks deserve their own attention, because the programme was built with Derek Brown - a nationally known bartender, founder of Positive Damage, and one of the most prominent advocates in American bartending for mindful drinking. What that produced is a dedicated Low & No menu structured so that each course can be paired either with a full cocktail or with a spirit-free one, which is a different and better proposition than a short list of alcohol-free options bolted onto the end of a wine pairing. The named zero-proof drinks show the same construction logic as the alcoholic ones. Get Your Flowers is built on Fluere Spiced Cane with lemon, lime, spiced pineapple syrup, grenadine and cherry. The R_(n/a)_G&T uses Fluere Botanical with Giffard Pamplemousse and elderflower, tonic and edible flowers. Astronomy Club and the Sigi Tolo Rickey round out the list, the latter a nod to a star in Dogon cosmology. The programme leans deliberately on Black-owned and non-alcoholic brands and on creative riffs on the classics rather than on an afterthought soda list.

Practical notes. Dinner runs Tuesday through Saturday from 5pm to 10pm, with the restaurant closed Sunday and Monday, and reservations go through Resy. Because it sits inside a hotel on the Southwest Waterfront rather than on a restaurant strip, it is worth planning the trip: the Waterfront Metro station is the closest, and the Wharf's bars are a short walk away if the evening continues.
venues.pressQuote: Onwuachi is a master of Afro-Caribbean flavors deserving of the fine-dining treatment.

venues.name: Dogwood at The Pine Shed
venues.description: Dogwood at The Pine Shed pairs a good music programme with mocktails that keep up with the rest of the night — the Bend room most often named by locals as the one that makes staying booze-free easy without dropping out of the evening. Open Tuesday to Sunday, to midnight Thursday through Saturday.
venues.longDescription:
Dogwood at The Pine Shed is on 2nd Street in midtown Bend, and Visit Bend's zero-proof guide describes it in the terms that matter most for a night out without alcohol: good music, and mocktails that keep up with the night. The writer, who spent a year booze-free, named it the place that kept the streak intact while staying social — which is a more useful recommendation than a list of ingredients.

That distinction is worth drawing out. A great deal of alcohol-free hospitality is designed around the assumption that not drinking means going home early, so the drinks are built for the first hour of an evening and nothing after it. What makes a venue like this work is that the mocktails are made to be ordered repeatedly across a long night — balanced rather than sugary, so the third one is as good as the first — in a room with enough going on that staying is the natural choice.

The hours support that: it opens late morning and runs to midnight Thursday, Friday and Saturday, eleven on Sunday, closed Mondays. That late window is genuinely scarce in Bend, a town that gets up early and where many of the best rooms are shut by nine.

We have not published named drinks or prices. Dogwood does not publish its cocktail list online and the mocktails rotate, so anything specific would be out of date quickly. The programme's existence and its quality are attested by the city's own tourism board as of June 2026.
venues.pressQuote: one of those places that just works: good music and mocktails that keep up with the night

venues.name: Doma Bar
venues.description: Doma Bar is a lesbian-owned and QPOC-operated cocktail bar on Pine Street in Burlington's South End Arts District, opened as a deliberate counterweight to venues that ask people to hustle, mask, perform and optimise. It keeps beer, wine and zero-proof drinks on hand at all times and runs a large non-alcoholic menu rather than a token pair of options — a policy choice that follows directly from the room's premise, since a bar built around belonging cannot make a third of its guests order soda. Open Tuesday to Saturday from 5pm, to midnight at weekends, closed Sunday and Monday.
signatureDrinks: Doma Spritz (NA: an earthy, herbaceous non-alcoholic liqueur with zero-proof sparkling white wine and a dash of hibiscus syrup)

naMenuItems.description: an earthy, herbaceous non-alcoholic liqueur with zero-proof sparkling white wine and a dash of hibiscus syrup

venues.longDescription:
Doma Bar describes itself as proudly lesbian-owned and QPOC-operated, and it is explicit about what it is for: a counterweight to every space that asks you to hustle, mask, perform or optimise, built instead around warmth, acceptance, joy, opulence, family and care. That is an unusually direct mission statement for a cocktail bar, and it has a practical consequence that lands squarely in this directory's territory.

A room whose entire proposition is belonging cannot afford to have a category of guest who is stuck with cranberry and soda. Doma keeps beer, wine and zero-proof drinks on hand at all times and runs what it calls a large non-alcoholic menu — not a pair of mocktails appended to the cocktail list, but a parallel section. For anyone who has spent an evening in a bar being handed a glass of Coke while everyone else reads a menu, the difference is the whole experience.

The bar sits at 388 Pine Street in the South End Arts District, a stretch that has become Burlington's most interesting drinking corridor — the Venetian Soda Lounge is a few blocks south, Zero Gravity's beer hall further down the same street. Doma is the newest and the smallest of them, and the one most likely to have something on that you did not expect.

This entry records no signature drinks, because the non-alcoholic list is not published online and this directory does not print a drink name it has not seen on a current menu. What is well evidenced is the standing commitment, stated by the bar itself.

Hours are Tuesday and Wednesday 5pm to 10pm, Thursday to 11pm, Friday and Saturday to midnight. Closed Sunday and Monday.
venues.pressQuote: Beer, wine, and zero-proof always on hand.
