venues.longDescription:
DOMU is the flagship of chef-owner Sean 'Sonny' Nguyen's Orlando restaurant group, opened in November 2016 inside Audubon Park's East End Market. Nguyen, the son of Vietnamese refugees who settled in Winter Haven, Florida, began his culinary career in 2007 at Bento Asian Kitchen in Gainesville and trained in traditional Japanese noodle-making under Chef Kotani at Korin in New York before opening DOMU; the restaurant has held Michelin Bib Gourmand recognition every year since 2022, and Nguyen was a 2025 James Beard Award semifinalist for Best Chef: South.

The drinks menu treats non-drinkers as a real category rather than an afterthought, listing five named mocktails: Nada Colada, Lemony Snicket, Mango Lychee Lemonade, Virgin Daiquiri, and Rosey Pom. The bar also pours non-alcoholic 0.0% Sapporo alongside its seasonal cocktail, sake, and Japanese whisky program.

'My number one memorable recognition is going to be the Michelin Guide Bib Gourmand award for Domu at East End,' Nguyen has said of the honor, calling it the highest recognition he never thought the restaurant would get. DOMU has since grown into a small restaurant group with additional locations in Orlando's Dr. Phillips neighborhood and Jacksonville's St. Johns Town Center, alongside sister concepts Tori Tori and Edoboy, and the original East End Market location was featured on Netflix's 'Somebody Feed Phil.'
venues.pressQuote: My number one memorable recognition is going to be the Michelin Guide Bib Gourmand award for Domu at East End.

venues.name: Don Artemio Mexican Heritage
venues.description: Don Artemio is a heritage Mexican restaurant on Fort Worth's West 7th corridor whose drink menu carries a dedicated Zero Proof Cocktails section — a real printed heading rather than a substitution offered on request. All four are house builds on fresh juice and sparkling mineral water rather than non-alcoholic spirits: Fresca works cucumber, orange, lime, agave and jalapeño; El Jarrito leans savoury with grapefruit, lime, tamarind chipotle and guajillo; La Chica Fresa pairs strawberry with jamaica; and La Cariñosa keeps it to lemon and honey. The restaurant serves a full bar alongside them, and opens from 11am most days and 10am on Sundays.
signatureDrinks: Fresca (cucumber, orange, lime, agave, jalapeño, sparkling mineral water)
El Jarrito (grapefruit, lime, tamarind chipotle, guajillo, sparkling mineral water)
La Chica Fresa (lime, strawberry, jamaica, sparkling mineral water)
La Cariñosa (lemon, honey, sparkling mineral water)
venues.longDescription:
Don Artemio takes its name and its cooking from Coahuila, and it has become one of the most decorated Mexican restaurants in Fort Worth since opening on the West 7th corridor. Its bar programme is built around agave spirits, but the printed drink menu also carries a section headed Zero Proof Cocktails — a real menu heading rather than a substitution offered on request, and one the restaurant keeps year-round rather than wheeling out each January.

The four zero-proof drinks are all house builds finished with sparkling mineral water, and they follow the same flavour logic as the kitchen. Fresca is the vegetal one, combining cucumber, orange, lime and agave with a jalapeño edge. El Jarrito is the most interesting to order if you usually drink mezcal: grapefruit and lime against tamarind chipotle and guajillo, which delivers the smoke and heat that a non-drinker normally has to give up entirely. La Chica Fresa pairs strawberry with jamaica — hibiscus, a staple of Mexican aguas frescas — and La Cariñosa is the simplest of the set, lemon and honey lengthened with mineral water.

Notably, none of these lean on non-alcoholic spirit substitutes. They are built from juice, syrup, chile and citrus, which is both cheaper to execute and, in this kitchen's hands, more authentically Mexican than a Seedlip pour would be. That is worth stating plainly because this guide often treats a real distillate as the mark of a serious list, and Don Artemio is the clearest case in the metroplex of a kitchen reaching the same standard by a different route — the aguas frescas tradition it draws on has never needed alcohol to be taken seriously. The room is a full-service restaurant with a complete bar, so a mixed table works comfortably: the zero-proof drinks arrive in the same glassware and at a similar pace as the cocktails, which is the detail that decides whether anyone feels singled out.
venues.pressQuote: Upscale authentic Mexican restaurant on West 7th Street has a menu of fine zero-proof cocktails available year-round.

venues.name: Doshi House
venues.description: Doshi House is a fully alcohol-free vegetarian cafe in Houston's Third Ward, so its coffee, tea, and tonic menu is non-alcoholic by default rather than a side program bolted onto a bar. The espresso bar runs on beans from Houston roaster Greenway Coffee, and the tea list spans a 36-hour brewed chai latte, Japanese matcha, and traditional karak cha masala chai. A separate 'Tonics & Infusions' section builds composed non-alcoholic drinks from real ingredients, like a tamarind-dates-jalapeño elixir and a hibiscus-lavender-rose blend, giving the drink list the same intentionality most bars reserve for cocktails.
signatureDrinks: Elixir Tonic (tamarind, dates, jalapeño, lemon, cane syrup)
venues.longDescription:
Deepak Doshi, who left a corporate job, opened Doshi House in the Historic Third Ward in April 2012, inside a corner building that had operated as an art gallery since November 2010. He kept the space's rotating local artwork rather than converting it into a conventional coffee shop, and it has become a gathering spot for students from nearby Texas Southern University and the University of Houston as well as neighborhood regulars, near Emancipation Park and the Project Row Houses public-art site.

Because Doshi House is a vegetarian cafe that has never served alcohol, every drink on its menu is non-alcoholic by design rather than by special accommodation. The coffee side runs on beans from local roaster Greenway Coffee via espresso and cortado, while the tea program includes a 36-hour brewed chai latte, Japanese matcha, and traditional karak cha masala chai. A dedicated 'Tonics & Infusions' menu adds house-made non-alcoholic builds such as a tamarind-dates-jalapeño elixir, a Korean ginseng and chrysanthemum tonic, and a hibiscus-lavender-rose blend.

Houston Press critic Katharine Shilcutt reviewed the cafe in 2012, writing that beans from Greenway Coffee were "put to excellent use in well-made cortados and frappes that contain Doshi's own homemade caramel or chocolate," and describing the space as "an art space, community meetingspot and vegetarian cafe in one." As of July 2026 the cafe remains open daily from 7:30am to 3:00pm at 3419 Emancipation Ave.
venues.pressQuote: Coffee comes from local roaster David Buehrer of Greenway Coffee, whose beans are put to excellent use in well-made cortados and frappes that contain Doshi's own homemade caramel or chocolate.

venues.name: Double Chicken Please
venues.description: An acclaimed Lower East Side cocktail bar split into two spaces: the walk-in Free Range front room serving kegged "taptails" and small plates, and The Coop, a reservation-driven back room famous for conceptual, food-inspired culinary cocktails. The Coop menu offers mocktail versions of several signature drinks, making it a solid stop for non-drinkers.
signatureDrinks: Grapefruit with a Grudge (mocktail version available)
venues.longDescription: Double Chicken Please was founded by Taiwanese bartenders GN Chan and Faye Chen, who ran cocktail pop-ups out of a vintage yellow VW minibus starting in 2017 before opening their permanent Lower East Side home at 115 Allen Street in autumn 2020. The bar is split into two rooms: Free Range, a walk-in front bar (renovated in late 2024) pouring kegged seasonal "taptails," and The Coop, a reservation-led back room built around culinary cocktails that mimic dishes such as Cold Pizza, Japanese Cold Noodle, Key Lime Pie and Thai Curry. It debuted at No. 6 on The World's 50 Best Bars in 2022, was named No. 1 on North America's 50 Best Bars in 2023, and ranked No. 41 on The World's 50 Best Bars in 2025. For non-drinkers, The Coop menu lists mocktail versions of several of its signature builds, including Key Lime Pie, Japanese Cold Noodle, Grapefruit with a Grudge and Gilded Orchard, plus a decaffeinated take on the Cuppa Sunshine.
venues.pressQuote: Double Chicken Please is a double act. Up front, Free Range is a straightforward LES bar.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Julien Levy, Time Out New York

venues.name: Double Knot
venues.description: Double Knot is the Miami location of Michael Schulson's modern izakaya, brought south from Philadelphia and set on NW 2nd Avenue in Wynwood, serving sushi, sashimi and robatayaki alongside an elevated chef's tasting menu. Its documented alcohol-free build is the Blood Knot, which blends pineapple with a blueberry simple syrup and citrus soda — expressive without being heavy, in RESIDENT's December 2025 description. Dinner is the only service, from 5pm nightly, running to midnight on Friday and Saturday, with a daily happy hour from 5pm to 7pm. For anyone eating their way through Wynwood without drinking, it sits within a few blocks of Uchi, R House and Rosemary's, all of which run their own zero-proof lists.
signatureDrinks: Blood Knot (pineapple, blueberry simple syrup, citrus soda)
venues.longDescription:
Double Knot occupies 2550 NW 2nd Avenue in Wynwood and is the Miami outpost of the restaurant Michael Schulson opened in Philadelphia, described by the group as a modern izakaya. The menu is split between sushi and sashimi, robatayaki, and what the restaurant calls an elevated chef's tasting menu. Service is dinner only, starting at 5pm every day and running to 10pm on Monday and Sunday, 11pm from Tuesday through Thursday, and midnight on Friday and Saturday, with a happy hour from 5pm to 7pm.

The alcohol-free build documented at the bar is the Blood Knot, which blends pineapple with a blueberry simple syrup and citrus soda. RESIDENT documented it in the December 2025 Miami round-up and wrote that the drink feels expressive without being heavy, and that it mirrors the restaurant's modern izakaya energy while offering a polished zero-proof alternative. It is a single named build rather than a full section, which is why the programme is graded as real but modest, and the restaurant's public site does not publish a wider non-alcoholic list. What makes the entry worth having is geography: Double Knot sits within a few blocks of Uchi on NW 25th Street, R House on NW 2nd Avenue and Rosemary's on NW 25th Street, all of which run documented alcohol-free lists of their own, so a guest planning a Wynwood evening without drinking now has a cluster of options within walking distance rather than a single destination. The restaurant posts as @doubleknot_mia and takes reservations on (305) 564-6899. One practical note: the restaurant does not open for lunch, so the earliest a guest can sit down is 5pm, and the happy hour in the first two hours is the cheapest window for anyone who wants the bar rather than the tasting menu. The restaurant's own site lists that schedule and the 5pm-to-7pm happy hour.
venues.pressQuote: It mirrors the restaurant’s modern izakaya energy while offering a polished zero-proof alternative.

venues.name: Double Standard
venues.description: Double Standard occupies the historic Rand Building downtown and pours some of the most carefully built zero-proof drinks in San Antonio. Smoke & Mirrors is made with Tenneyson Black Ginger, the non-alcoholic bitter aperitif, and Dreaming of You is a passionfruit build that runs sweeter for anyone who wants it. The name is a small joke that lands well here — a bar called Double Standard applying a single standard to both halves of its menu — and the late hours help, running to midnight midweek and 2am on Friday and Saturday in the middle of the downtown hotel district.
venues.address: 114 E Houston St, San Antonio, TX 78205
signatureDrinks: Smoke & Mirrors - non-alcoholic Tenneyson Black Ginger
venues.longDescription:
Double Standard sits in the Rand Building on East Houston Street, one of downtown San Antonio's handsome early-twentieth-century commercial blocks, and it has become a fixture of the city's cocktail scene. Both Visit San Antonio and CultureMap single out its zero-proof drinks, which is unusual — official tourism copy tends to mention that mocktails exist rather than name them.

Smoke & Mirrors is the one that shows the thinking. It is built on Tenneyson Black Ginger, a non-alcoholic aperitif designed around bitterness and ginger heat rather than sweetness, which gives the drink an actual finish. Bitterness is the hardest quality to achieve without alcohol, because most bitter compounds in a bar arrive dissolved in spirit; a bar that buys a dedicated NA aperitif to solve that has taken the problem seriously. Dreaming of You covers the other end of the range, a passionfruit build for anyone who wants something bright and fruit-forward.

The hours are a real advantage. Double Standard opens at 11:30am and runs to midnight through the week and 2am on Friday and Saturday. Sober nightlife thins out badly after eleven in most American cities, and San Antonio's better zero-proof options skew early — Hash closes at 7pm, Box St. at 4pm. A downtown bar with properly built alcohol-free drinks still serving at one in the morning fills a genuine gap.

Its location in the Rand Building puts it within a few minutes' walk of the River Walk, the Majestic Theatre and most of the downtown hotels, which makes it the easiest recommendation in this guide for a visitor who is not drinking and does not want to plan around a car. It is also open every single day, which sounds unremarkable until you notice how many of San Antonio's better alcohol-free options close two or three days a week. Between the 11:30am opening and the 2am close at weekends, it covers more of the clock than anything else in this guide, which makes it the safe default when a plan changes late. The Rand Building setting helps too — it is a handsome room rather than a hotel lobby, so an evening here feels like a destination rather than a fallback, which matters more than it should when you are the one not drinking.
venues.pressQuote: Double Standard: Smoke & Mirrors (with non-alcoholic Tenneyson Black Ginger) and Dreaming of You passionfruit mocktail.

venues.name: Double Zero
venues.description: Double Zero is a neighborhood Italian restaurant in Emory Village, owned by Fredrico Castellucci III with John Castellucci as culinary director (part of the Atlanta-based Castellucci hospitality group). The kitchen centers on traditional Neapolitan-style wood-fired pizza — built on a heirloom-yeast-starter dough and "double zero" (00) flour that gives the restaurant its name — alongside handmade pasta and shareable Southern Italian dishes. Beyond its Italian wine list and cocktails, Double Zero keeps a dedicated "zero proof cocktails" section on its beverage menu, with three named non-alcoholic drinks: the Bermuda Triangle (rosemary, orange, lime, brine, soda), So Fresh So Clean (turmeric, lime, pomegranate, soda), and Orange is the New Black (orange and lemon juice, fresh ginger, club soda). The space is casual and family-friendly, with bar games including shuffleboard and foosball.
venues.address: 1577 N Decatur Rd NE, Atlanta, GA 30307
venues.longDescription:
Double Zero is a neighbourhood Italian restaurant at 1577 North Decatur Road in Emory Village, owned by Fredrico Castellucci III with John Castellucci as culinary director, part of the Atlanta-based Castellucci hospitality group. The kitchen is built around Neapolitan-style wood-fired pizza made with an heirloom yeast starter and the double-zero flour that gives the restaurant its name, alongside handmade pasta and shareable southern Italian dishes. The room is casual and family-friendly, with shuffleboard and foosball.

The bar keeps a named zero proof cocktails section rather than leaving non-drinkers to the soft drinks, and the three drinks on it are more considered than the count suggests. The Bermuda Triangle combines rosemary, orange and lime with brine and soda. So Fresh So Clean runs turmeric against lime and pomegranate. Orange is the New Black is orange and lemon juice with fresh ginger and club soda. Resy noted in 2024 that the restaurant offers three non-alcoholic cocktails to accompany its southern Italian cooking.

The brine in the Bermuda Triangle is the detail worth pulling out. A few drops of salt solution in a drink suppresses bitterness and amplifies aroma, which is why it turns up in serious cocktail bars — and in a zero-proof drink it does more work still, because there is no alcohol to carry the aromatics or give the drink weight on the palate. A bar that reaches for saline rather than more sugar is one that has thought about why non-alcoholic drinks usually fall flat.

Rosemary, turmeric and fresh ginger across three drinks is a herb-and-spice list rather than a fruit-juice one, which is what makes them work next to a wood-fired pizza. The restaurant serves Monday to Thursday from 5pm to 9pm and until 10pm on Friday and Saturday, and is closed Sunday.
venues.pressQuote: Double Zero offers three nonalcoholic cocktails to accompany its fresh southern Italian cuisine. Enjoy your Neapolitan-style pizza with a Bermuda Triangle, a bright zero-proof cocktail made with rosemary, orange, lime, brine and soda.

venues.name: Down on Grayson
venues.description: Down on Grayson sits beside the Pearl, the former brewery complex that has become San Antonio's most-visited food district, and it carries the longest named zero-proof list in this guide — a spicy blackberry lemonade, a prickly pear "No"-jito, a Strawberry Basil Smash and a blood orange crème soda. Four distinct named drinks is a genuine menu section, and the range matters: there is something tart, something herbal, something spicy and something creamy, which means a non-drinker can order differently across an evening instead of repeating one sweet glass. It sits just outside the Pearl, open 11am to 10pm seven days a week, which is more consistent than most of the city.
venues.address: 303 E Grayson St, San Antonio, TX 78215

venues.longDescription:
Down on Grayson is on East Grayson Street next to the Pearl, the converted brewery complex that has become the centre of gravity for eating and drinking in San Antonio. That location matters: the Pearl draws enormous numbers of visitors, and almost everything in it is organised around a bar.

Its zero-proof list is the longest properly named one in this guide, and the composition is the interesting part. A spicy blackberry lemonade brings heat and tartness. The prickly pear "No"-jito uses a fruit that is genuinely of this landscape rather than imported for colour, and pairs it with mint. A Strawberry Basil Smash goes herbal. A blood orange crème soda goes rich and creamy, which almost no mocktail menu attempts.

That spread is worth more than any single drink. The failure mode of alcohol-free menus is monotony: two or three variations on sweet fruit, so a non-drinker who stays for three hours drinks the same thing three times and leaves cloyed. Four drinks across four different registers means the second one can be different from the first, which is exactly what everyone else at the table takes for granted.

The hours are good and unfussy — 11am to 10pm most days, to 11pm on Friday and Saturday, seven days a week, which is more consistent than most of San Antonio's alcohol-free options. Being a step outside the Pearl proper, it is also usually easier to get into than the venues inside the complex, and it sits within a short walk of Isidore and the Brooklyn Avenue cluster. That whole corner — Grayson, Brooklyn and the Pearl — is where a group with mixed drinking plans will have the easiest evening in San Antonio.
venues.pressQuote: Down on Grayson: Spicy blackberry lemonade, prickly pear "No"-jito, Strawberry Basil Smash, blood orange crème soda.

venues.description: Dragonfly Detroit — cocktail bar in New Center with a dedicated Alcohol-Free Cocktails menu section and NA beer on happy hour.

venues.longDescription:
Dragonfly opened in January 2022 as the casual, colorful counterpart to Freya, the tasting-menu restaurant next door — both part of Sandy Levine's Detroit restaurant group, with Freya's kitchen supplying the food menu. The bar sits at 2929 E. Grand Boulevard in New Center (enter on the Beaubien side), and its drink program has been shaped by bartender Tara Jagodzinski, whose resume includes the Library inside the Detroit Club and Peterboro.

The "Alcohol-Free Cocktails" section of the menu isn't a token gesture: BBB (blood orange, blackberry oleo), Purps (coconut cream, pineapple, cinnamon, ube), and Wonder When Winds of Winter (apple cider vinegar, palm sugar, pear) draw on the same house-made syrups, purees, and shrubs used across the bar's full cocktail list, rather than a bottled substitute poured as an afterthought.

Happy hour (Tuesday through Saturday, 5–7pm) extends the same treatment to beer: Ted Segers' "Unleaded" brew sits on the $5 happy-hour list right alongside the beer-and-a-shot special, priced and positioned as a normal choice rather than a special request.

Dragonfly and Freya share a building in New Center, with rotating artwork from Detroit artists on the walls and a small-plates food menu prepared by Freya's kitchen. The pairing gives Dragonfly access to a serious culinary kitchen while keeping its own identity as the neighborhood's happy-hour bar, where non-alcoholic drinks have had equal billing on the menu since opening.
venues.pressQuote: The whole idea behind (Dragonfly) was low-ABV (alcohol by volume), health-conscious cocktails.

venues.name: Dram & Draught
venues.description: The Durham branch of Dram & Draught sits on West Main Street near Brightleaf Square and runs the same standing "Spirit-Free" menu section as its Raleigh sibling, at slightly lower prices — an $8 Phony Negroni is worth knowing about in a metro where most zero-proof cocktails now land at twelve dollars. Three named builds cover a sparkling spritz on Töst's alcohol-free rosé with lemon, elderberry and ginger, St. Agrestis' bittersweet bottled negroni served straight, and the Honey Trap, built fresh from grapefruit, honey, ginger and lemon for anyone avoiding spirit analogues entirely. The Töst rosé is also sold by the bottle. This is a whisky-and-draught bar rather than a non-drinkers' destination, so it works best for a mixed group; doors are open to midnight during the week and two in the morning on Friday and Saturday.

venues.longDescription:
The Durham room of Dram & Draught is on West Main Street near Brightleaf Square, and it carries the same "Spirit-Free" section as the Raleigh original with a couple of dollars off each drink. For a metro where most non-alcoholic cocktails now land at twelve dollars, an eight-dollar Phony Negroni is worth knowing about.

The three builds are the same in composition. The Sunday Spritz uses Töst's alcohol-free sparkling rosé lengthened with lemon, sugar, elderberry and ginger — the closest thing on the list to a glass of something celebratory. The Phony Negroni is St. Agrestis' bottled non-alcoholic negroni poured straight; it is properly bitter, which is rare in this category and the reason it appears on so many bar lists nationally. The Honey Trap is built fresh from grapefruit, honey, ginger and lemon, and is the one to order if you would rather avoid non-alcoholic spirit analogues entirely.

The bar itself is a whisky-and-draught room, so this is a venue that works for a mixed group rather than a destination for non-drinkers specifically. Hours run to midnight during the week and two in the morning on Friday and Saturday.

One detail that trips up anyone trying to check first: both locations share a single phone number, so a search by phone will not tell you which room you have found — go by the postcode or the location-specific menu page. The generic menu URL on the group site returns a "location not found" error and must be approached through the Durham location page.

venues.name: Dram & Draught
venues.description: Dram & Draught's Raleigh room sits at the base of the One Glenwood building on the edge of Glenwood South and keeps a standing "Spirit-Free" section on its cocktail menu — three named builds plus Töst's alcohol-free sparkling rosé by the bottle at $36. The list runs on finished non-alcoholic product rather than juice: the Sunday Spritz on Töst with lemon, elderberry and ginger, St. Agrestis' bottled Phony Negroni served straight for $9, and the Honey Trap built fresh from grapefruit, honey, ginger and lemon. The bar is a whisky-and-draught room, so a mixed group is well served on both sides, and the doors stay open until two in the morning seven days a week — the latest non-alcoholic option in the city. The Durham sibling runs the same three drinks at slightly lower prices.

venues.longDescription:
Dram & Draught's Raleigh bar occupies a suite at the base of the One Glenwood building on the edge of Glenwood South, and it is the metro's most useful late-night non-alcoholic option: the doors stay open until two in the morning every day of the week, and the spirit-free list is available the whole time.

That list sits under its own "Spirit-Free" heading on the cocktail menu, which is the structural detail that separates a real programme from a bartender's improvisation. The Sunday Spritz is built on Töst's alcohol-free sparkling rosé with lemon, sugar, elderberry and ginger. The Honey Trap is the only one made purely from fresh ingredients — grapefruit, honey, ginger and lemon — and is the most cocktail-like of the three. The Phony Negroni is simply St. Agrestis' bottled non-alcoholic negroni served as it comes, which is an honest way to put a bittersweet, genuinely adult drink in front of someone without pretending to build it from scratch.

Beyond the cocktails, the Töst rosé is available by the bottle at thirty-six dollars, which makes this a workable venue for a group where only some people are drinking. The wider bar is built around whisky and draught beer — the name is not decorative — so there is a deep list on the other side for anyone in the party who wants it.

A practical note for anyone checking the menu in advance: the site's generic menu page returns a "location not found" error, and you have to go through the Raleigh location page to see this list. The Durham sibling runs the same three drinks at slightly lower prices. Published Triangle round-ups still credit the bar with four different drinks — Blue Rain, Exactly Where I'm At, Thyme and Space and a Lyre's-based spritz — but the menu has rotated since.

venues.name: Dray
venues.description: Dray's second location is a 100% non-alcoholic bottle shop at 5 Columbia Street in Central Square, Cambridge, inside the Market Central complex, opened in January 2025 roughly a year after founder Pat Dooling's original South End store. It is styled like a high-end wine and spirits merchant, with the same catalogue behind it: roughly 138 non-alcoholic beers, 83 non-alcoholic wines, 63 zero-proof spirits, 45 ready-to-drink cocktails and 19 mixers and accessories, covering Seedlip, Lyre's, Ghia, Three Spirit, Kin Euphorics, Dr. Zero Zero and Martini among others. Nothing on the shelves contains meaningful alcohol. Staff advise by flavour and occasion rather than by brand, and the shop trades Tuesday to Sunday from noon to 8pm, closed Mondays.
venues.longDescription:
Dray opened its Central Square shop in January 2025, less than two years after founder Pat Dooling launched the original South End store in late 2023. The Cambridge site sits at 5 Columbia Street inside the Market Central development, a short walk from the Central Square T stop, and extends the format across the river into a neighbourhood with a dense student and graduate population that has been one of the faster-moving markets for alcohol alternatives. WBZ NewsRadio 1030 covered the grand opening, quoting the intent behind the design directly: that it is meant to look exactly like a high-end liquor store or wine shop, with the one key difference that everything is non-alcoholic. That framing is the whole proposition. The fixtures, the shelf talkers and the merchandising are borrowed wholesale from conventional drinks retail.

The assortment is the same deep catalogue Dray runs in the South End and is organised by category rather than by wellness claim. Non-alcoholic beer is the largest section, spanning pilsners, hazy IPAs, stouts and sours; non-alcoholic wine covers still red and white, sparkling and rose; zero-proof spirits stand in for gin, whiskey, tequila, amaro and aperitivo; and there is a substantial ready-to-drink shelf of pre-mixed cocktails and functional seltzers, plus mixers, tonics, bitters and glassware. Stocked brands include Seedlip, Lyre's, Ghia, Three Spirit, Kin Euphorics, Dr. Zero Zero and Martini, and the range turns over as new producers reach the US market. Because the shop holds no alcohol at all, it serves a function a licensed store cannot: someone avoiding alcohol entirely can browse the full inventory without having to navigate around it. Staff make recommendations by flavour profile and occasion rather than steering to a house brand. The Cambridge shop keeps the same trading pattern as the South End original, opening Tuesday to Sunday from noon to 8pm and closing on Mondays.
venues.pressQuote: It's intended to look exactly like a high-end liquor store or wine shop, just one key difference — that everything's non-alcoholic.

venues.name: Dray
venues.description: Dray is a 100% non-alcoholic bottle shop at 18 Union Park Street in Boston's South End, opened in late 2023 by founder Pat Dooling and reported at the time as the city's first dedicated alcohol-free retail store. Nothing in the shop contains meaningful alcohol: the range is built to mirror a conventional wine and spirits merchant, and Dray's own catalogue currently lists roughly 138 non-alcoholic beers, 83 non-alcoholic wines, 63 zero-proof spirits, 45 ready-to-drink cocktails and a further 19 mixers and accessories. Staff work as advisers rather than clerks, steering customers between categories, and the shop runs tastings and community events. It trades Tuesday to Sunday from noon to 8pm and is closed Mondays. A second Dray opened in Central Square, Cambridge.
venues.longDescription:
Dray was opened in the South End in late 2023 by Pat Dooling, who had stopped drinking and found that the non-alcoholic products he wanted were scattered across the internet rather than sold anywhere he could browse them. The Boston Globe covered the opening on November 23, 2023 as a bottle shop for the sober-curious, Boston.com followed on December 4, 2023 calling it Boston's first non-alcoholic bottle shop, and Edible Boston profiled the business in its Edible Food Find column on November 15, 2024. Dooling has been direct about the intent behind it, telling Boston.com that it had become something of a mission for him to eat away at the societal norm of drinking. The Union Park Street shop is deliberately merchandised like a high-end liquor store rather than a health-food aisle, on the theory that the shopping experience matters as much as the liquid.

The range is the deepest in the city and is organised the way a drinks merchant would organise it. Non-alcoholic beer is the largest category by count, followed by non-alcoholic wine covering still, sparkling and rose, then zero-proof spirits standing in for gin, whiskey, tequila, amaro and aperitivo, then ready-to-drink cocktails and functional seltzers, and finally mixers, bitters, tonics, glassware and accessories. Brands stocked include Seedlip, Lyre's, Ghia, Three Spirit, Kin Euphorics, Dr. Zero Zero, Martini and De Soi, and the assortment turns over as new producers appear. Because there is no alcohol on the premises at all, Dray also functions as a place where people who do not drink can browse without negotiating a liquor store, which is a large part of why it reads as a destination rather than a shop. Staff make recommendations by flavour and occasion rather than by brand, and the business runs tastings and events alongside retail. Hours are Tuesday to Sunday, noon to 8pm; the shop is closed on Mondays.
venues.pressQuote: It's become a little bit of my mission to eat away at the societal norm of drinking.

venues.name: Drink Me! Tea Room
venues.description: A reservation-only afternoon tea room on Warner Road in south Tempe, open four days a week and closing at 5pm. The draw for non-drinkers is a tea service built around loose-leaf blends plus a small list of named mocktails — the Two Days Slow and the Jack of Hearts — which DiningOut Phoenix highlighted in its May 2026 round-up of metro bars worth visiting for a mocktail. Worth being clear about: despite the tea-room format it is not alcohol-free, and its own materials advertise "special-tea cocktails" alongside the tea. Reservations are required and the short opening hours make walk-ins impractical.
venues.longDescription:
Drink Me! Tea Room runs a traditional afternoon tea service from a small unit on Warner Road in south Tempe, open Thursday to Sunday from 11am to 5pm and closed the other three days. Reservations are required rather than merely encouraged: the room is small, and the format — full tea service with tiered stands, brought to the table in courses — does not lend itself to dropping in. There is a retail side as well, with loose-leaf teas and treats sold to take away, so a visit can be a purchase rather than a sitting.

For a non-drinker the appeal is structural rather than a matter of menu detail. This is an entire venue whose core offering is tea, operating in the middle of the day, at hours when almost every other social option in the metro is a bar. Nobody has to explain themselves, and nobody is holding a drink you are not. Alongside the loose-leaf service the kitchen makes a short list of named mocktails — the Two Days Slow and the Jack of Hearts among them — and DiningOut Phoenix picked the room out in its May 2026 guide to the best places in metro Phoenix for a mocktail.

One correction belongs here plainly, because the format invites exactly the wrong assumption. This is not an alcohol-free venue. The tea room's own materials advertise "special-tea cocktails" alongside the tea service, so alcohol is poured. It earns its listing on a genuine named non-alcoholic drinks list and a daytime format that suits people who are not drinking — not because the room is dry. The short week and the 5pm close are the other things to plan around: this is an afternoon, booked in advance, not a place to end up.
venues.pressQuote: the cocktail, mocktail, and tea options also impress

venues.name: Drip Drop Cocktail Room
venues.description: Drip Drop Cocktail Room is a craft cocktail bar at 445 Bridge Street NW, in the middle of the Bridge Street run on the West Side. It carries between twenty and twenty-five hand-crafted cocktails that rotate through the year, and its distinguishing practice is that every mixer is made fresh in house — syrups, cordials and all — from what the bar describes as responsibly sourced and thoughtful ingredients. That house-made base is what gives its non-alcoholic drinks something to be built from, and the bar keeps named zero-proof options rather than improvising: the Flint Tropics, the French Connection and the Blood Moon were all listed among downtown Grand Rapids' best non-alcoholic drinks in October 2025.

venues.longDescription:
Drip Drop Cocktail Room opened on Bridge Street NW and sits in the densest concentration of drinking venues on the West Side, a few doors from The Knickerbocker and around the corner from Gin Gin's. The bar runs a rotating list of twenty to twenty-five hand-crafted cocktails that changes across the year, and its central claim is about inputs rather than technique: all of its mixers are made fresh in house from responsibly sourced ingredients, including the syrups that would normally arrive in a bottle. For a cocktail bar, that is a meaningful investment; for its zero-proof drinks, it is close to decisive, because a non-alcoholic cocktail has nothing to hide behind. Strip out the spirit and what remains is the syrup, the citrus and the balance, so a bar making its own components can produce a drink with real structure while a bar working from commercial mixes cannot.

That shows in the named drinks. In October 2025 the Downtown Grand Rapids business alliance published a guide to the best non-alcoholic drinks in the centre of the city and listed three of Drip Drop's by name — the Flint Tropics, the French Connection and the Blood Moon — placing it alongside Max's South Seas Hideaway and Cafe Jazzy Rose rather than in a list of places that will accommodate a request. One caveat worth stating: the bar's own published cocktails menu does not carry a separate non-alcoholic section, so the zero-proof builds are documented through that local coverage rather than through the venue's own site, and the specific names may rotate with the seasonal list. Trading hours are Tuesday through Thursday 4pm to midnight, Friday 4pm to 2am, Saturday 2pm to 2am and Sunday noon to 8pm, closed Monday — which makes it, along with Kava Kasa, one of the few genuinely late options in the city for someone who is not drinking.
venues.pressQuote: Drip Drop Cocktail Room: Flint Tropics, French Connection, Blood Moon — among downtown Grand Rapids' best NA drinks.

venues.name: Dry Humor
venues.description: Dry Humor is the Pioneer Valley's first exclusively non-alcoholic bottle shop, and nothing on its shelves contains meaningful alcohol — zero-proof beer, wine and spirits, canned craft mocktails and functional drinks, all under 0.5% ABV. Elizabeth "CJ" Mutti started it in May 2023 as an online and pop-up operation delivering across Hampshire County and Holyoke, then opened the Union Street shop in January 2025. It is LGBTQ and women-owned, and free local delivery runs to Easthampton addresses. Afternoon and weekend hours only, so check before setting out.
venues.hours: Mon closed; Tue 10am-7pm; Wed-Fri 11am-7pm; Sat 10am-6pm; Sun 11am-6pm
venues.longDescription:
Dry Humor sells nothing but non-alcoholic drinks. That sounds like a small distinction until you have stood in an ordinary bottle shop trying to find the two shelves that apply to you, and it is the whole reason this business exists. The stock runs from canned craft mocktails through de-alcoholised wine and beer to zero-proof spirits and functional beverages, everything under 0.5% ABV, sourced through the same regional wholesalers that supply the valley's liquor stores.

Elizabeth Mutti, who goes by CJ, built it out of her own experience and her family's. She has spoken publicly about growing up with two alcoholic parents and losing her brother at 37 to alcoholism, and about deciding she wanted somewhere that celebrated drinking culture without the alcohol in it rather than somewhere that treated not drinking as an absence. Dry Humor started in May 2023 as an online shop and a pop-up, running deliveries around Hampshire County and Holyoke and setting up at events, and it took until January 2025 to become a room you could walk into at 79 Union Street.

What the shop is good for, practically. It is the only place in the Pioneer Valley where the whole selection is relevant, so it works for stocking up before hosting rather than for a single bottle on the way somewhere. Prices sit close to the alcoholic equivalents, which surprises people — the de-alcoholisation step (reverse osmosis, vacuum distillation or controlled fermentation, depending on the producer) is an added cost rather than a saving, and Mutti has been upfront about explaining that rather than pretending it away. Free local delivery covers Easthampton addresses.

The hours are the thing to plan around: afternoons Tuesday to Friday, late mornings at weekends, closed Mondays, with the occasional seasonal break posted to Instagram. It is a small independent shop rather than a chain, and it keeps small-shop hours. Worth checking the day before rather than driving over on spec.
venues.pressQuote: Why not have a space just for people like myself who just don't want to drink, but who still want to participate in that culture?
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Elizabeth "CJ" Mutti, Dry Humor founder, to the Daily Hampshire Gazette

venues.name: Dunedin MockFusion
venues.description: Dunedin MockFusion is a dedicated alcohol-free mocktail bar and herbal apothecary in downtown Dunedin, opened in May 2025 by a holistic practitioner. It blends a neighborhood-bar feel with craft mocktails, specialty coffee and tea, mushroom coffee, and custom in-house wellness blends made from organic and wildcrafted ingredients, and hosts community workshops — a genuinely sober "third place" rather than a bar with a token NA list.  Founded by England Davis with Sabryna Wright and Ashlynne Barnes, from an idea Davis had carried for a decade: the communal feel of a neighbourhood bar combined with a natural apothecary, minus the alcohol.
venues.longDescription:
MockFusion opened in downtown Dunedin on 18 May 2025, the result of an idea its founder England Davis had been carrying for a decade: combine the communal atmosphere of a neighbourhood bar with the properties of a natural apothecary, and leave out the alcohol. Davis runs it with Sabryna Wright and Ashlynne Barnes. The framing Davis gave the Tampa Bay Times is the clearest statement of intent any venue in this directory offers — it is like Cheers, everyone is glad they came, but it is a place where humans connect without alcohol.

The offering runs across three registers rather than one. Craft mocktails are the evening trade; specialty coffee and tea carry the day; and custom wellness blends and mushroom coffee sit alongside as the apothecary half of the concept. That breadth is deliberate. A venue serving only mocktails competes with every bar in town on the single axis where it has removed its own main product, whereas one that also does the morning coffee and the afternoon tea is simply the place people go.

Dunedin itself matters to how this works. It is a walkable, low-rise town north of Clearwater with a dense main street and a strong brewery culture — which is to say the local default is emphatically alcoholic, and a fully alcohol-free room in the middle of it fills a real absence rather than a theoretical one.

Everything served is free of alcohol. Practical notes: it is a small room in a small downtown, parking is street-based and gets tight at weekends, and the coffee and tea trade means it is genuinely usable in the daytime rather than only as an evening alternative.  Dunedin's brewery-dense main street makes the contrast sharper: this is the one room on it where nobody has to explain themselves.
venues.pressQuote: It's like Cheers. Everyone's glad they came, but this is a place where humans connect without alcohol.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: England Davis, MockFusion founder, to the Tampa Bay Times

venues.name: Dutch Courage
venues.description: Dutch Courage is Baltimore's first gin-centric cocktail bar, opened in December 2019 by Brendan Dorr and Eric Fooy in a 1,500-square-foot rowhouse at 2229 N Charles Street in Old Goucher. Dorr set out to make somewhere deliberately bright: so many cocktail bars are dark and moody, he said before opening, but they wanted a place where you can have a cocktail at night and actually read the menu. The Baltimore Banner has written that the bar is redefining the non-alcoholic scene with its creative mocktails. Its zero-proof drinks include the N.A. Groni (a botanical gin syrup with orange oil, orange bitters and jasmine Tortuga kombucha), the First Lady (Seedlip Grove 42, grapefruit, rose water, sparkling non-alcoholic chardonnay and rosebuds) and the Emerald Mage (lemon, rosemary, spiced grenadine). The list rotates and the bar publishes its menus as PDFs that cannot be read online, so confirm the current roster on arrival. Snacks run to pickled vegetables with a herbed buttermilk dip. Open from 4pm daily, with happy hour weekdays 4–6pm. The same owners run the rum bar Pink Flamingo in Remington.
signatureDrinks: N.A. Groni (botanical gin syrup, orange oil, orange bitters, jasmine Tortuga kombucha)
First Lady (Seedlip Grove 42, grapefruit, rose water, sparkling non-alcoholic chardonnay, rosebuds)
venues.longDescription:
Dutch Courage opened in December 2019 at 2229 N Charles Street in Old Goucher, Baltimore's first gin-centric cocktail bar, from industry veterans Brendan Dorr and Eric Fooy in a 1,500 square foot rowhouse. Dorr's design brief was a small rebellion against the prevailing style: so many cocktail bars are dark and moody, he said before opening, but they wanted somewhere you could have a cocktail at night and actually read the menu. The name is the English idiom for the courage found in a drink, which for a gin bar is about as apt as it gets. Snacks run to pickled vegetables with a herbed buttermilk dip. It serves from 4pm daily, to 1am on Friday and Saturday, with happy hour weekdays from 4pm to 6pm and reservations through OpenTable.

The non-alcoholic list is the reason The Baltimore Banner wrote that this gin haven is redefining the non-alcoholic scene with its creative mocktails — a strong claim about a bar whose entire identity is a spirit. The N.A. Groni is the signature: a botanical gin syrup with orange oil and orange bitters, lengthened with jasmine-flavoured Tortuga kombucha, which supplies the fermented acidity that makes a negroni work without either the gin or the Campari. The First Lady is built on Seedlip Grove 42 with grapefruit, rose water, a sparkling non-alcoholic chardonnay and rosebuds — a genuine three-component drink rather than a spirit-and-mixer. The Emerald Mage works lemon and rosemary against a spiced grenadine. The list rotates, and the bar publishes its menus as PDFs that cannot be read online, so prices and the current roster are best confirmed on arrival. Worth noting for anyone comparing: the same owners' rum bar Pink Flamingo, a mile away in Remington, was a 2026 James Beard semifinalist.
venues.pressQuote: Old Goucher's gin haven, Dutch Courage, is redefining the non-alcoholic scene with its creative mocktails.

venues.name: Eagle Park Brewing Company
venues.description: Eagle Park Brewing Company is a Milwaukee brewery and taproom on the Lower East Side whose Hamilton Street location is the home of Solid State, its dedicated non-alcoholic beer line launched in January 2026. Rather than dealcoholizing a finished product, Eagle Park brews Solid State with a specially engineered yeast so it ferments to under 0.5% ABV while still tasting like full-strength beer. The four-beer N/A lineup — a Hazy IPA, a Pale Ale, a Mexican Lager with Lime, and a Cran-Orange Sour — is sold by the can for drinking in the taproom and in six-packs to go. As a working brewery it also pours a full slate of alcoholic beer, so the zero-proof cans sit alongside the regular tap list rather than replacing it.
signatureDrinks: Solid State N/A Mexican Lager with Lime
venues.longDescription:
Eagle Park Brewing Company runs a taproom at 823 E. Hamilton St. on Milwaukee's Lower East Side, and in January 2026 it became one of the few Wisconsin breweries to build its own non-alcoholic line from the ground up. That line, Solid State, followed more than a year of research and development aimed at making beers that genuinely taste like beer without the flavor loss that can come from stripping alcohol out of a finished batch. Co-owner Jake Schinker framed the approach plainly to Urban Milwaukee: "All of these beers are brewed like beer, because they are beer."

Instead of dealcoholizing, Eagle Park ferments Solid State with a specially engineered yeast that keeps every beer under 0.5% ABV. The launch lineup runs four styles — a Hazy IPA hopped with Citra and Mosaic, a Pale Ale built on Citra and Simcoe, a Mexican Lager with Lime, and a Cran-Orange Sour — all packaged in 12-ounce cans. Reviewing the set for Milwaukee Magazine, Chris Drosner wrote that the pale ale "drinks like an exceptionally light pale ale – one that, if it were, say, 4% ABV, people would call a crusher." The cans are listed on the taproom's current menu at about $6 for on-site drinking and $9 for a to-go six-pack, and the line also distributes across southeastern Wisconsin through Beer Capitol Distributing.

The Hamilton Street taproom is a full working brewery, so Solid State shares the room with Eagle Park's alcoholic beer rather than replacing it — this is a strong zero-proof option within a bar, not an alcohol-free venue. It's open Sunday 11 a.m.–9 p.m., Monday through Friday 3–10 p.m., and Saturday 11 a.m.–10 p.m., with all four Solid State beers available by the can and in to-go six-packs.
venues.pressQuote: This beer is thin, yes, but it just drinks like an exceptionally light pale ale – one that, if it were, say, 4% ABV, people would call a crusher.

venues.name: Earl Giles Restaurant & Distillery
venues.description: Earl Giles Restaurant & Distillery is the flagship home of Earl Giles, a Minneapolis brand founded in 2015 by hospitality veterans Jesse Held and Jeff Erkkila that began as a non-alcoholic elixir and mixer company. Named for Erkkila's great-grandfather — a Prohibition-era pilot who flew "medicine" across the northern U.S. — the 18,000-square-foot Logan Park venue pairs a full distillery and canning line with a "Drinks Apothecary" flavor lab holding 600-plus globally sourced extracts and a wood-fired scratch kitchen. The drinks program is built almost entirely on house-made syrups, elixirs, and extracts, and the bar carries an extensive spirit-free menu alongside its cocktails. Named zero-proof pours include an NA Old Fashioned (Good Trip house NA spirit, black walnut molasses) and the Paez (yerba mate, jasmine, pineapple, coconut water). The space centers on a 60-foot bar carved from a single Monkey Pod tree.
venues.address: 1325 Quincy St NE, Suite 100, Minneapolis, MN 55413
venues.longDescription:
Earl Giles Restaurant & Distillery in Northeast Minneapolis has a backwards origin story that makes it unusually well suited to this directory: the brand started in 2015 as a non-alcoholic elixir and mixer company, founded by hospitality veterans Jesse Held and Jeff Erkkila, and only later added a distillery. Most bars arrive at good zero-proof drinks by working backwards from cocktails. Earl Giles arrived at cocktails by working forwards from syrups, which is why the spirit-free side of the menu here reads as the original business rather than an accommodation. The name comes from Erkkila's great-grandfather, a Prohibition-era pilot who flew "medicine" across the northern United States.

The Logan Park venue runs to 18,000 square feet and pairs a full distillery and canning line with a wood-fired scratch kitchen and a Drinks Apothecary — a flavour lab holding more than six hundred globally sourced extracts. The room is anchored by a sixty-foot bar carved from a single Monkey Pod tree. Nearly the whole drinks programme is built on house-made syrups, elixirs and extracts, and the bar carries an extensive spirit-free menu alongside the cocktails rather than beneath them. Named zero-proof pours include a non-alcoholic Old Fashioned built on the house Good Trip NA spirit with black walnut molasses — a genuinely convincing version of a drink that is very hard to do without alcohol, because the sweetness and the wood have to come from somewhere — and the Paez, which combines yerba mate and jasmine with pineapple and coconut water. Given the depth of the extract library, it is also one of the few bars in the Twin Cities where asking the bartender to build something spirit-free to your taste is likely to produce something considered rather than a glass of juice. Open daily, from late morning at weekends.
venues.pressQuote: Earl Giles, a Minneapolis company specializing in non-alcoholic elixirs, has unveiled plans to open a distillery.

venues.name: Earls Kitchen + Bar — Legacy West
venues.description: Earls in Legacy West prints two alcohol-free sections — Zero Proof for the mixed drinks and Non-Alcoholic for beer and soft options. The two strongest builds use Seedlip: a Picante Margarita on Seedlip Notas de Agave and Seedlip Spice with smoky pepper and lime, and a Coconut Mango Cooler on Seedlip Spice with basil and lime. Cheaper builds include an Italian Spritz, a Strawberry Hibiscus Mule and a rotating sparkling lemonade, with Guinness 0 and Athletic Brewing's Run Wild on the beer list.

venues.longDescription:
Earls is a Canadian group that has built a small Texas presence, and its Legacy West room is a large, late-opening restaurant-bar in Plano's most walkable shopping district — the sort of place a group ends up after work. Its drink menu splits alcohol-free options across two printed sections, Zero Proof for mixed drinks and Non-Alcoholic for beer and soft drinks, which between them make it one of the more dependable suburban options in this guide.

Two of the six zero-proof builds are made with Seedlip. The Picante Margarita is the most complete drink on the list, combining Seedlip Notas de Agave — the range's tequila-facing expression — with Seedlip Spice, smoky pepper and lime, and it is priced accordingly. The Coconut Mango Cooler runs Seedlip Spice into coconut, mango, basil and lime. The remaining four are simpler and cheaper: an Italian Spritz, a Strawberry Hibiscus Mule, a strawberry Arnold Palmer and a rotating sparkling lemonade, which gives a table a range of price points rather than one expensive option.

The non-alcoholic beer list is better than most suburban restaurants bother with, carrying Guinness 0 and Athletic Brewing's Run Wild IPA alongside Michelob Ultra Zero. With a kitchen open to midnight most nights and 1am at weekends, it covers the late slot that Plano otherwise leaves to full bars.

venues.name: East End Brewing Company
venues.description: East End Brewing Company was founded by Scott Smith in 2004 and has run its Larimer brewpub at 147 Julius Street since 2013, alongside a Mt Lebanon taproom and a seasonal pop-up garden in Chateau. It brews its own named non-alcoholic beer, Dry Hop, inspired by its flagship Big Hop American Ale, and the taproom also pours Barmy Soda — started by East End's own head brewer — plus hop water and non-alcoholic seltzers. Smith reads the shift as a pushback against the alcohol arms race, and describes what the brewpub has become rather than what he set out to build: he used to think they were a beer company, and while they are, they are a community gathering place that happens to make beer. Food is a rotating weekly Pizza of the Week with dips, salads, pretzels, breadsticks and soups; the menu is published only as an image. Its Big Hop Harvest Ale topped USA Today's 10Best readers' poll for best fall seasonal beer in both 2024 and 2025. Closed Mondays; the kitchen shuts an hour before the bar.
venues.hours: Mon closed; Tue-Thu 5pm-10pm; Fri 4pm-10pm; Sat 12pm-10pm; Sun 12pm-8pm
venues.longDescription:
East End Brewing has been going since 2004, which makes Scott Smith something close to the dean of Pittsburgh craft brewing, and the Larimer brewpub at 147 Julius Street has been its home since 2013. There are two other sites — a Mt Lebanon taproom and a seasonal pop-up garden in the Chateau neighbourhood — but Julius Street is the one with the pizza oven. The food is a rotating Pizza of the Week that changes every Wednesday, with dips, salads, pretzels, breadsticks and soups around it. Smith's own account of what the place turned into is the most honest thing any brewery owner has said about the last decade: he used to think they were a beer company, and while they are, they are a community gathering place that has beer that they make. His read on why people are drinking less is equally direct — habits have changed, and it is a pushback against the alcohol arms race that was going on at one time. People are not going out for beers; they are going out to do something and maybe having some beers.

The brewery makes its own non-alcoholic beer, Dry Hop, built after its flagship Big Hop — which, for accuracy, the brewery itself labels an American Ale rather than an IPA. Alongside it the taproom pours hop water, non-alcoholic seltzers, and Barmy Soda, a separate small company started by East End's own head brewer, which is the sort of thing that only happens in a brewery that takes its soft drinks seriously. Two honest caveats. Dry Hop does not appear on East End's published beer list and no ABV for it is printed anywhere we could find, so ask whether it is 0.0% or 0.5% if the distinction matters to you. And the food menu is published as a photograph rather than text, so it cannot be read in advance. One piece of context worth knowing about every Pennsylvania brewery on this site: state law bars any business holding a liquor licence from selling hemp products, so unlike breweries in many other states, you will not find THC seltzers sitting next to the non-alcoholic beer here.
venues.pressQuote: a pushback against the alcohol arms race that was going on at one time
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Scott Smith, founder of East End Brewing

venues.name: Eastern Market Brewing Co.
venues.description: Detroit brewery in Eastern Market brewing its own named non-alcoholic beer line — 313 N/A IPA, Dad Bod, and the Rotten Pretty sour series — as part of a 2026 push to become "Michigan's N/A beer."
venues.longDescription:
Eastern Market Brewing Co. opened in 2017 in Detroit's Eastern Market district, co-founded by Dayne Bartscht as a full production brewery and taproom rather than a bar reselling other companies' beer. The taproom sits at 2515 Riopelle St., in the same historic wholesale-produce district that gives the brewery its name.

Unlike venues that stock a token non-alcoholic import, Eastern Market Brewing ferments its own N/A beer in-house. The lineup is anchored by 313 N/A IPA, the brewery's best-selling non-alcoholic release, which has repeatedly sold out and returns in 2026 with a refreshed label and expanded production. It's joined by Dad Bod, a new hazy N/A IPA built to be juicy and approachable, and Rotten Pretty, a new series of N/A sour beers debuting in tangerine and grapefruit with more flavors planned through the year.

In January 2026, founder Dayne Bartscht announced the brewery's 2026 goal was "to be known as Michigan's N/A beer," pointing to shifting consumer behavior (Gallup data cited in coverage put 2025 U.S. drinking rates at a record-low 54%, down from 67% in 2022) as the reason to double down on the category. The push includes new retail partnerships with Busch's and Total Wine, including in-store tastings.

The taproom keeps the same community-brewery feel that built its regular crowd: live music, trivia nights, and a running club round out the space alongside the beer list, open Tuesday through Sunday.
venues.pressQuote: Our goal for 2026 is simple. We want Eastern Market Brewing Co. to be known as Michigan's N/A beer.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Dayne Bartscht, Founder, Eastern Market Brewing Co.

venues.name: Easy Bistro & Bar
venues.description: Easy Bistro & Bar is a MICHELIN-listed French-leaning restaurant in Chattanooga's West Village, one of the city's long-standing fine-dining rooms and part of the group that also runs Main Street Meats and Little Coyote. Its alcohol-free option is the Sober Sunset — orange, grenadine, lemon and tonic water — an unfussy, bitter-edged long drink that works across a meal rather than only before it, which is the harder thing for a restaurant to get right. Dinner runs from 4pm seven nights a week, to 9pm midweek and 10pm on Friday and Saturday.

venues.longDescription:
Easy Bistro has been one of Chattanooga's better restaurants for a long time — French-influenced cooking, an oyster programme, a MICHELIN Guide listing, and a move to the West Village on Chestnut Street that gave it a larger and better room. It sits in the same group as Main Street Meats and Little Coyote, which between them account for a substantial share of the serious cooking in the city.

The alcohol-free drink is called the Sober Sunset, which is a more honest name than most restaurants manage, and it is built on orange, grenadine, lemon and tonic water. That specification is worth reading carefully, because the tonic is doing the important work. Quinine gives the drink bitterness, and bitterness is what an alcohol-free drink usually lacks — it is the quality that makes a drink sippable across a two-hour dinner instead of cloying after half a glass. Grenadine and citrus supply sweetness and acid; the tonic keeps the whole thing dry enough to sit alongside food.

NOOGAtoday recorded the Sober Sunset in its guide to drinking without alcohol in Chattanooga, which is where this listing's evidence comes from.

This entry is graded three. There is one documented build, no printed zero-proof section on the published menu and no non-alcoholic spirits programme this directory could verify, so nothing further is claimed here. What a reader gets is a genuinely good restaurant where the drink they are handed has been thought about — which, at this level of dining, is not something to take for granted.

Service runs from 4pm every night, to 9pm Sunday through Thursday and 10pm on Friday and Saturday. Booking is advisable at weekends.
venues.pressQuote: The Sober Sunset is made with orange, grenadine, lemon + tonic water.
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: NOOGAtoday, Local mocktails + non-alcoholic drinks in Chattanooga

venues.name: Eatery A
venues.description: Eatery A is a Mediterranean wood-fired restaurant on Ingersoll Avenue, well regarded locally and open seven days a week from 11am — 9am at weekends, with a daily happy hour from 2pm to 6pm. Its documented alcohol-free drink is a Virgin Pimm's of pomegranate, mint, cucumber and lemon, which is a genuinely sensible piece of thinking: a Pimm's Cup is already a long, herbaceous, fruit-heavy drink where the spirit is the least assertive component, so removing it costs less than it would almost anywhere else on a cocktail list.
signatureDrinks: Virgin Pimm's — pomegranate, mint, cucumber, lemon
venues.longDescription:
Eatery A is a wood-fired Mediterranean restaurant on Ingersoll Avenue, one of the better-regarded rooms in Des Moines, and it keeps a single documented alcohol-free drink — but a well-chosen one.

The Virgin Pimm's is smarter than it looks. A Pimm's Cup is one of the few classics where the spirit is genuinely secondary: the drink is mostly lemonade, cucumber, mint and fruit, with Pimm's No. 1 contributing a gentle bitter-herbal note at around 25% ABV heavily diluted. Take the alcohol out of a martini and there is nothing left. Take it out of a Pimm's and you still have essentially the same long, herbaceous, refreshing drink. Eatery A's version uses pomegranate, mint, cucumber and lemon, which covers the fruit, the herb and the acid.

That is worth knowing as a general strategy rather than just as a menu item. If you are in a bar with no alcohol-free list and need to order something decent, the drinks to ask for are the ones where the spirit was doing the least work — a Pimm's, a spritz, a mojito, a tiki build — rather than the ones where it was doing all of it.

Des Moines' tourism board documented the drink in January 2026.

This entry is graded three: one named build, no printed zero-proof section verified, no non-alcoholic spirits programme confirmed. What Eatery A adds to the guide is coverage. It serves 11am to 10pm Monday through Thursday, 9am to midnight on Friday and Saturday and 9am to 9pm on Sunday — seven days, breakfast onwards at weekends, with a daily happy hour from 2pm to 6pm. On the Ingersoll stretch alongside Fresko and The Bartender's Handshake, it is part of the most dependable few blocks in the city.
venues.pressQuote: Virgin Pimm's (pomegranate, mint, cucumber, lemon)

venues.name: Ebreeq Coffee House
venues.description: Ebreeq Coffee House is a Yemeni coffeehouse on the Euclid Avenue side of the 200 Public Square tower in downtown Cleveland, opened in May 2025. It serves no alcohol. The 2,200-square-foot room was built around Yemeni coffee made the traditional way, with traditional Yemeni pastries alongside, and its co-owners include Ali Alwasim, Abdulhamed Alduais and Dia al-Baadani. The drinks the local press picked out are mufawar, Yemeni coffee with cream and cardamom; qishr, coffee husks brewed with ginger and cinnamon; and Adeni chai, a sweet spiced milk tea. Sabayah, a layered bread with butter and honey, is the food to order. It opens 7am to 8pm on weekdays and 8am to 9pm at weekends, so it is a daytime and early-evening room, not a late one.
venues.longDescription:
Ebreeq Coffee House opened in May 2025 on the ground floor of 200 Public Square, the 45-storey office tower on the square, with its entrance on the Euclid Avenue side. Cleveland Magazine introduced it that February under the headline Yemeni Coffee Comes to Cleveland, naming Abdulhamed Alduais and Ali Alwasim as co-owners and describing a 2,200-square-foot room with a culturally inspired interior and traditional Yemeni music; the design is by Pontia Architecture of New Albany, Ohio. Alwasim told the magazine the aim was the original way of coffee, rich and full of flavour. Signal Cleveland, which interviewed co-owner Dia al-Baadani after the opening, began its piece with the smell of cardamom at the door.

The drinks are the Yemeni standards. Signal Cleveland listed mufawar, Yemeni coffee with cream and cardamom, and qishr, which is brewed from coffee husks with ginger and cinnamon and drinks more like a spiced tea. Cleveland Magazine singled out the Adeni chai, a sweet tea of black tea leaves, milk, sugar and spices, and sabayah, a layered bread made with butter and honey and sprinkled with black cumin. Al-Baadani told Signal that the coffee comes from Haraz, the mountain region of Yemen where the cherries are picked by hand. The shop describes itself in one line as authentic Yemeni coffee and traditional sweets. We have taken the drink names from that reporting, published in 2025, and have not been able to read the cafe's current ordering menu, so ask at the counter for what is on now.

It serves no alcohol, and Signal Cleveland framed Yemeni coffeehouses in general as offering the social side of coffee house culture as an alternative to alcohol and nightlife. One caution on that point: the hours are shorter than they were. When it opened the cafe was reported as trading daily until 10pm; its own profile now gives 7am to 8pm from Monday to Friday and 8am to 9pm on Saturday and Sunday. That makes Ebreeq the place for an alcohol-free meeting downtown during the day or straight after work, and the North Olmsted coffeehouses the ones to choose for a late night. It sits on Public Square itself, in the middle of downtown.
venues.pressQuote: The smell of cardamom greets you at the door of Ebreeq Coffee House

venues.name: ECHO - Taste & Sound
venues.description: ECHO - Taste & Sound is an intimate vinyl hi-fi listening lounge and bar in the Las Vegas Arts District, opened in March 2025 by sober chef-owner Natalie Young (formerly of the long-running Fremont East brunch spot EAT) and entrepreneur Tom McAllister. Set in a mid-century-modern room of warm wood, acoustic panels, plants and vintage furnishings spun on a McIntosh sound system, it pairs elevated small plates with curated vinyl. As a sober owner, Young made an inclusive beverage program a priority from the start, with bar talent drawn from the storied (now-closed) Downtown Cocktail Room. The menu carries a dedicated "Non-Alcoholic Cocktails" section that mirrors classic spirited drinks using zero-proof substitutes -- including an N/A Old Fashioned (n/a bourbon, n/a amaro, simple syrup), Caught in the Rain (n/a rum, pineapple, mango, orange, coconut), Ring of Fire (n/a tequila, mango, orange, firewater bitters) and Take 5 (non-alcoholic amaro, cold brew, seasonal syrup) -- plus a separate "Mocktails" section of original non-spirited creations such as Cool Cat, Chef's Jam and Bright Size Life (ube syrup, lemon, soda).
venues.address: 1301 S Main St #160, Las Vegas, NV 89104

Take 5 (non-alcoholic amaro, cold brew, seasonal syrup)
Bright Size Life (ube syrup, lemon juice, soda)
