venues.longDescription:
Fig & Ash sits at 514 East Ohio Street in Deutschtown on the North Side, and it took chef Cory Hughes three years, seven months and twenty-four days to build — a figure he counted precisely, because the site was two derelict late-19th-century buildings when he started. It opened in October 2020, in the middle of the pandemic, and made Pittsburgh Magazine's 25 Best Restaurants list for 2026, which described it as serving comfort food with a thoughtful, elevated touch on a cosy stretch of East Ohio Street. Everything comes off a custom wood-fired grill built locally, and the room is a genuine one: a reviewer described it as comfortable, professionally done but not overly designed, with a plethora of houseplants throughout and every nook and cranny filled with quirky art. There are three ways to sit — the dining room, a four-season covered patio, or the chef's counter. Burrata salad is $18, scallop toast $21, meatloaf of short rib and pork belly $36, a double-cut pork chop $38, yellowfin tuna $38.

The non-alcoholic drinks are printed under a heading that simply says MOCKTAILS, and there are two of them, both $10. Match-A Made in Heaven is matcha with strawberry syrup, coconut milk and tonic — the tonic is what saves it, because matcha and coconut alone would be a milkshake, and the quinine gives it the dry finish a drink needs before food. Celer-ous-ly, Noah? is the more interesting of the pair and the more unusual thing to find on any menu: celery juice with juniper, caraway, fennel, soda and a mint sprig. Celery, juniper, caraway and fennel are four green, aromatic, faintly bitter things stacked on each other, and the result is closer to a dry vermouth than to a soft drink — exactly the register a wood-fired kitchen calls for. Two honest caveats. This is a short list, and it rotates: an earlier menu carried a fennel-and-orgeat drink called It's The Fennel Countdown that has since gone. And no non-alcoholic beer or wine brands are listed, so the two mocktails are effectively the whole offering.
venues.pressQuote: Located on a cozy stretch of restaurants along East Ohio Street, Fig & Ash serves comfort food with a thoughtful, elevated touch.

venues.name: FIG
venues.description: FIG (Food Is Good) is a James Beard Award-winning fine-dining restaurant on Meeting Street downtown, opened in 2003 by chef Mike Lata and partner Adam Nemirow. It won the 2018 James Beard Award for Outstanding Wine Program, and that bar rigor extends to a small seasonal zero-proof section that changes with the menu. The bar pours Seedlip-based non-alcoholic drinks and a turmeric tonic, and will build NA cocktails to order. General manager Lane Becker has spoken publicly about FIG applying the same competitive standards to non-alcoholic drinks as to the rest of the list.
venues.longDescription:
FIG has been a benchmark for ingredient-driven, regional cooking in Charleston since 2003 under chef/owner Mike Lata, earning a string of accolades including the 2018 James Beard Award for Outstanding Wine Program. The same beverage discipline shows up in a modest but genuine zero-proof offering: a seasonal menu that typically lists a couple of non-alcoholic drinks (including a turmeric tonic), with bar staff who work with the non-alcoholic spirit Seedlip and will make NA cocktails to order.

The non-alcoholic program is a thoughtful complement rather than a dedicated AF concept. General manager Lane Becker has described FIG's guests as people focused on the quality and provenance of what they eat and drink, noting that "the same competitive forces that drive decision making on the rest of the drink menu now apply to this category." Dinner is served Tuesday through Saturday from 5pm; reservations run through Resy, with walk-in seats at the bar.
venues.pressQuote: At places like FIG, our guests are interested in the quality and provenance of the things they're eating and drinking. For people who make a point to eat farm-fresh produce and drink low-intervention wine, it makes sense that they're thinking about the impact that drinking has on their health in general.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Lane Becker, general manager at FIG, quoted in Charleston City Paper

venues.name: Fiji Kava
venues.description: Fiji Kava is a small kava room in the Dillingham Trade Center in Kalihi, across from Honolulu Community College, run by Daya Nand for more than thirty years — the longest-running kava business on Oʻahu. It serves no alcohol and sells one thing: pure powdered kava root imported from Fiji, prepared and sold by the cup at around $5, by the bottle, or by the bag for customers who want to make it at home. Weekends run an all-you-can-drink arrangement at $40. Kava is psychoactive and mildly sedating, which anyone visiting for the first time should know. The room is plain and the trade is regular rather than touristic.
venues.hours: Mon-Tue 10am-5pm; Wed closed; Thu 10am-5pm; Fri-Sat 12pm-8pm; Sun closed
signatureDrinks: Fijian kava, prepared fresh and served by the cup
venues.longDescription:
Fiji Kava occupies Suite 107B of the Dillingham Trade Center at 1007 Dillingham Boulevard, in Kalihi, directly across from Honolulu Community College. Daya Nand has been running it and selling kava from the same tucked-away shop for over thirty years, which makes it comfortably the longest-established kava business on Oʻahu — it predates the current wave of kava lounges by decades and has outlasted most of them. Several of the island's better-known kava rooms have closed in recent years, including Hale Noa, Kava Kafé in Kapahulu, and Kava Roots and Uluwehi's on the North Shore, which makes a three-decade run worth noting on its own.

The offer is narrow and traditional. Nand imports pure powdered kava root from Fiji rather than blending or flavouring it, and sells it three ways: prepared by the cup at around $5, by the bottle to take away, or by the bag for customers preparing it themselves at home. At weekends there is an all-you-can-drink arrangement at $40, which is the format most regulars use and which reflects how kava is actually drunk in the Pacific — over hours, in company, in repeated small shells rather than as a single serving. Fijian kava is generally heavier and more sedating than the Hawaiian 'awa poured at 'Awa Hou down the road, so the two are not interchangeable experiences. As with every kava venue in this guide, the honest framing applies: there is no alcohol here and none is served, but kava is psychoactive, and for some people in recovery that distinction matters enough to avoid it. Opening hours are limited and worth checking before travelling — 10am to 5pm Monday, Tuesday and Thursday, noon to 8pm Friday and Saturday, closed Wednesday and Sunday.
venues.pressQuote: For 32 years, Daya Nand has been sharing kava from his tucked-away shop off Dillingham Boulevard.

venues.name: Fiorella (Clement Street)
venues.description: Fiorella's Clement Street restaurant is the original of the four-location San Francisco group founded in 2015 by Boris Nemchenok and Brandon Gillis, serving wood-fired pizza, house pasta and Italian antipasti in the Outer Richmond. Its non-alcoholic offering is modest but genuine and printed on the same card as the cocktails: Like a Virgin, a $14 zero-proof build of prickly pear essence, fresh lime juice, sparkling water and mint, sits directly beneath the house negroni and margarita at the same price. Best Day Brewing's non-alcoholic Hazy IPA is stocked at $6, the cheapest beer on a list that runs to $11, and the restaurant also pours Far West's dry cider. Dinner runs nightly, with no weekend lunch service at this location.
signatureDrinks: Like a Virgin (N/A) — prickly pear essence, fresh lime juice, sparkling water, mint
Best Day Brewing Non-Alcoholic Hazy IPA
venues.longDescription:
Fiorella opened on Clement Street in the Outer Richmond in 2015, the first restaurant from Boris Nemchenok and Brandon Gillis, and the group has since grown to four San Francisco locations in the Sunset, Noe Valley and on Polk Street. The Clement Street room established the format the others follow: a California-inflected Italian menu of wood-fired pizzas, house-made pasta, antipasti and seasonal plates, served in a neighbourhood dining room decorated with murals of local figures. It is a short walk from Ocean Beach Cafe at the western end of the Richmond, and it serves dinner seven nights a week, opening at 4:30pm on Saturday and Sunday and at 5pm the rest of the week.

The alcohol-free drinking here is smaller in scale than at the group's Sunset and Noe Valley restaurants, but it is real and it is on the printed beverage menu rather than available only on request. The cocktail card lists five drinks, and the last of them, Like a Virgin, is marked N/A: prickly pear essence, fresh lime juice, sparkling water and mint, at $14, the same price as the house negroni, the Passione Margarita and the Sanguine Spritz above it. The beer list carries Best Day Brewing's non-alcoholic Hazy IPA at $6 — Best Day is brewed across the bay in Sausalito — alongside Ghost Town's pilsner and IPA and Far West's Nu Dry cider, and at $6 the alcohol-free beer is the least expensive beer on the list rather than a premium-priced substitute. Non-alcoholic beverages otherwise run to sparkling water, Tejava iced tea, house lemonade and Linea coffee. For a neighbourhood Italian restaurant in a part of the city with very little zero-proof provision, that combination is a step above the usual soda gun. The group's Sunset restaurant runs a longer alcohol-free list, including a Noperol Spritz and an N/A Lucano Old Fashioned, so guests who want a deeper choice from the same kitchen have that option a few blocks south; the Clement Street room is the one to book for the original dining room and the neighbourhood it was built for.

venues.name: Fiorella (Noe Valley)
venues.description: Fiorella's Noe Valley restaurant sits on 24th Street and serves the group's California-Italian menu of wood-fired pizza, house pasta and seasonal plates. Its cocktail card carries six drinks, two of which are marked N/A and priced level with the alcoholic ones at $14: the Noperol Spritz, built from Giffard and Mionetto non-alcoholic aperitivos with non-alcoholic sparkling wine and seltzer, and Like a Virgin, made with prickly pear, fresh lime juice, seltzer and mint. The beer list stocks Rationale's non-alcoholic West Coast IPA at $8 next to Ghost Town and Humble Sea. Having a third of the cocktail list built without alcohol, at the same price, makes this one of the stronger neighbourhood restaurant programmes on the south side of the city.
signatureDrinks: Noperol Spritz (N/A) — Giffard and Mionetto NA aperitivos, NA sparkling wine, seltzer
Like a Virgin (N/A) — prickly pear, fresh lime juice, seltzer, mint
venues.longDescription:
Fiorella's Noe Valley dining room is on 24th Street, the neighbourhood's main commercial strip, and is the fourth of the San Francisco restaurants opened by Boris Nemchenok and Brandon Gillis since they started the group on Clement Street in 2015. The menu is the group's California-inflected Italian one — wood-fired pizza, house-made pasta, antipasti — and the room does a substantial family trade, with dinner service every night from 5pm and an earlier 4:30pm start at weekends. A happy hour runs Monday to Thursday from 5pm to 6:30pm.

The non-alcoholic drinks are the reason the Noe Valley branch is worth singling out from its siblings. The printed cocktail list holds six drinks, and two of them carry the N/A marker, both at $14 against $14 to $15 for the alcoholic ones. The Noperol Spritz is the more constructed of the two: Giffard's non-alcoholic aperitivo is combined with Mionetto's alcohol-free aperitivo, non-alcoholic sparkling wine and seltzer, producing a bitter-orange spritz rather than a sweetened orange soda, and it is served in the same glassware as the Hugo and the Noe Valley Spritz beside it. Like a Virgin is the lighter option, built from prickly pear with fresh lime juice, seltzer and mint. The beer list carries Rationale's non-alcoholic West Coast IPA at $8, listed among the draught and bottle options rather than in a separate box, and the soft drinks run to a house lemonade, house iced tea, Mighty Leaf teas and Linea drip coffee. Having a third of the cocktail list built without alcohol, at price parity, puts this restaurant well ahead of the neighbourhood norm. Noe Valley has very little in the way of a bar scene and almost nothing built for people who are not drinking, so a restaurant that will put a proper bitter spritz in front of a guest without a conversation about it is worth knowing about. The happy hour, which discounts drinks between 5pm and 6:30pm from Monday to Thursday, applies to the same list.

venues.name: Fiorella (Polk Street)
venues.description: Fiorella's Polk Street restaurant serves the group's California-Italian menu at the northern end of Polk Gulch, where the street runs up towards Russian Hill. Its beverage card lists Like a Virgin as an N/A cocktail at $14, built from prickly pear essence, fresh lime juice and sparkling water and served tall, at the same price as the house negroni, Passione Margarita and espresso martini printed above it. The same drink appears on the weekday happy hour at $8, alongside discounted wine by the glass. Rationale's non-alcoholic West Coast IPA is stocked at $6, the cheapest beer on the list. Dinner runs nightly, with no weekend lunch service at this location.
signatureDrinks: Like a Virgin (N/A) — prickly pear essence, fresh lime juice, sparkling water, served tall
venues.longDescription:
Fiorella's Polk Street restaurant occupies a corner at Polk and Green, at the point where Polk Gulch runs into Russian Hill, and is the second of the four San Francisco locations opened by Boris Nemchenok and Brandon Gillis after the original on Clement Street in 2015. The format is the group's California-inflected Italian one: wood-fired pizza, house-made pasta, antipasti and a short list of mains, served in a bright corner dining room with a bar along one side. Dinner runs seven nights, to 10pm on Friday and Saturday, and the kitchen opens at 5pm every day.

The alcohol-free provision is smaller here than at the group's Noe Valley and Sunset restaurants, but it is printed on the same beverage card as everything else and priced level with the cocktails. Like a Virgin is listed under the cocktail heading and marked N/A: prickly pear essence, fresh lime juice and sparkling water, served tall, at $14 — the same price as the house Negroni, the Passione Margarita and the espresso martini sitting above it on the page. The drink also appears on the Monday-to-Thursday happy hour menu at $8, next to the discounted spritz and margarita, which means the restaurant extends the same offer to guests who are not drinking as to those who are. On the beer list, Rationale's non-alcoholic West Coast IPA is stocked at $6, cheaper than every alcoholic beer and cider on the page. The rest of the non-alcoholic column runs to Ferrarelle sparkling water, Mexican-style sodas, a house lemonade, house iced tea, Mighty Leaf hot teas and Linea drip coffee with free refills. The offering is narrower than the group's Sunset and Noe Valley rooms, which each carry a second built N/A cocktail, so a guest who wants a bitter spritz rather than a long fruit drink is better served at those; what the Polk Street restaurant does have is a single properly made zero-proof cocktail available at every service, on the happy hour, and priced the same as everything else on the card.

venues.name: Fiorella (Inner Sunset)
venues.description: Fiorella is a California-inflected Italian restaurant founded in 2015 by Boris Nemchenok and Brandon Gillis, who opened the original on Clement Street in the Richmond District before expanding to four San Francisco locations. The Inner Sunset branch at 1240 9th Ave serves wood-fired pizzas, house pastas, and seasonal Italian plates, plus a heated rooftop. Beyond the food, the Sunset location runs a genuine named non-alcoholic cocktail program: its official cocktail menu lists zero-proof drinks alongside the full bar, built on NA aperitivos and amari rather than simple sodas. Options include the Noperol Spritz (Giffard and Martini & Rossi NA aperitivos with Good Twin NA sparkling wine), the Like a Virgin (prickly pear essence, lime, mint, sparkling water), the Harvest Moon (Pathfinder NA amaro, lemon, honey, soda), an N/A Lucano Old Fashioned, and a Blackberry Cooler.
venues.longDescription:
Fiorella is a California-inflected Italian restaurant group founded in 2015 by Boris Nemchenok and Brandon Gillis, who opened the original on Clement Street in the Richmond District and have since expanded to four San Francisco neighbourhoods. The Inner Sunset branch at 1240 9th Avenue sits a block from Golden Gate Park and serves wood-fired pizzas, house pastas and seasonal Italian plates, with a heated rooftop that makes it usable in Sunset weather. The dining rooms are known for wallpaper printed with local landmarks and neighbourhood figures, a detail carried across every location. Service runs lunch Wednesday through Sunday and dinner nightly, and the room takes walk-ins more readily than most restaurants of its standard in the city.

What earns the Sunset location a listing is that its official cocktail menu carries named zero-proof drinks built on non-alcoholic aperitivos and amari rather than the usual retreat to lemonade and soda. The list includes the Noperol Spritz, which uses Giffard and Martini & Rossi non-alcoholic aperitivos topped with Good Twin dealcoholized sparkling wine; the Like a Virgin (prickly pear essence, lime, mint and sparkling water); the Harvest Moon (Pathfinder non-alcoholic amaro, lemon, honey and soda); an N/A Lucano Old Fashioned; and a Blackberry Cooler. The Noperol Spritz is the significant one, because an Italian restaurant that can serve a credible bitter spritz to a non-drinker solves the single most common ordering problem of the category — the aperitivo hour is the moment a table splits, and here it does not have to. The alcohol-free drinks sit on the same printed cocktail menu as the full-proof list, so ordering one requires no special request. Note that the non-alcoholic programme documented here is specific to this Inner Sunset location; the other Fiorella branches publish their own separate beverage menus and should not be assumed to match it. The rooftop is heated and the restaurant keeps a full lunch service Wednesday through Sunday, so the zero-proof list is available in the afternoon as well as at dinner.

venues.name: Firangi Superstar
venues.description: Firangi Superstar is a modern Indian restaurant and bar on Craig Road, built as a sequence of four rooms dressed like film sets — the Officer's Club, the Old Railway Room, the Elephant Palace and the Jungle Lodge — each with a distinct look and mood. The cooking reinterprets Indian dishes through an East-meets-West lens, and the bar carries that playfulness into its non-alcoholic drinks rather than defaulting to a lime soda. Tatler Asia has documented named zero-proof builds including the Masalada Colada, a spiced take on the piña colada, and a strawberry-pistachio sour rounded out with guava and citrus. The vegetarian cooking is a genuine strength rather than a token section.
signatureDrinks: Masalada Colada - a spiced non-alcoholic take on the piña colada
Strawberry-pistachio sour with guava and citrus
venues.longDescription:
Firangi Superstar takes its name from the Hindi word for a foreigner, and the whole restaurant is a joke about that outsider's gaze — an affectionate send-up of the colonial-era clubs and railway hotels through which Western visitors historically encountered India. It is laid out as four connected rooms, each dressed as a different set: the Officer's Club, the Old Railway Room, the Elephant Palace and the Jungle Lodge. The effect is theatrical without tipping into kitsch, and it makes the room a genuine occasion venue on a Craig Road strip that is otherwise fairly restrained.

The cooking follows the same logic. Dishes are modern Indian reinterpreted with unexpected global influences rather than regional recreations, and the kitchen is confident enough to be funny about it — the vegetarian section, in particular, is a real strength rather than a couple of obligatory paneer dishes, with plates like the Wada You Want showing off what the kitchen can do without meat.

That willingness to play carries into the drinks, which is what earns the restaurant a place here. Rather than treating non-drinkers as a rounding error, the bar builds named zero-proof drinks with the same spice-forward palette as the food. Tatler Asia has documented the Masalada Colada, a spiced non-alcoholic reading of the piña colada in which the Indian masala vocabulary is used to add warmth and complexity to what is normally a very sweet template, and a strawberry-pistachio sour rounded out with guava and citrus — pistachio being a natural bridge between Indian dessert flavours and the creamy texture a sour needs. Both are constructed drinks that make sense specifically at this restaurant. It is worth confirming what is currently pouring when you arrive, since the drinks list moves with the menu.
venues.pressQuote: Masalada Colada, strawberry-pistachio sour with guava and citrus.

venues.name: Fitz on 4th
venues.description: Fitz on 4th is a fully vegan restaurant and bar on South 4th Street in Queen Village, and its zero-proof drinks are built with the same care as its food. The Super Fruit Martini uses a zero-proof gin with a super-fruit blend, a cranberry reduction and lemon, finished with a silky foam — and the foam matters, because a vegan kitchen cannot reach for egg white, so the texture has to come from aquafaba or a plant protein instead. Lia's Lavender Lemonade is the lighter option. A hundred-per-cent vegan room is a natural fit for this directory: the kitchen is already used to building flavour without a default ingredient, which is exactly the problem a good non-alcoholic drink has to solve.

venues.longDescription:
Fitz on 4th trades on South 4th Street in Queen Village, and it is entirely vegan — not a restaurant with a vegan section, but a kitchen and bar with no animal products anywhere on the premises. That constraint is the most interesting thing about its drinks.

The Super Fruit Martini is built on a zero-proof gin with a super-fruit blend, a cranberry reduction and lemon, and it is finished with what the menu calls a silky foam. In a conventional bar that foam would be egg white or, increasingly, a commercial foaming agent derived from it; a shaken sour gets its dense pale head that way, and the texture is half of why the drink works. A vegan bar cannot do that, so the foam has to come from aquafaba — the viscous liquid from cooked chickpeas, which whips almost identically — or from a plant protein. Either way it is a deliberate technical choice, and it is the sort of detail that separates a bar building drinks from one pouring them.

The cranberry reduction is the other tell. Reducing juice concentrates its acid and sugar together and thickens the body, which gives the drink weight in the mouth. Weight is the quality that non-alcoholic drinks most often lack, because ethanol itself contributes viscosity that water cannot replace.

Lia's Lavender Lemonade is the simpler counterpart, floral and sharp, and works as the long drink of the pair.

There is a broader point about why a vegan restaurant tends to be a good bet for a non-drinker. Both disciplines involve building a familiar experience while a default ingredient is off the table, and a kitchen that has spent years working out how to make food satisfying without butter, cream or stock has already internalised the habit of thinking in terms of fat, acid, salt and texture rather than reaching for the obvious. That habit transfers directly to the bar.

Closed Mondays; open from four in the afternoon midweek and from noon Friday through Sunday, closing at ten throughout.

venues.name: Fizzy's Fountain & Liquors
venues.description: Fizzy's is Omaha's grown-up soda fountain, opened in March 2020 in the Little Bohemia district on South 13th Street: a retro room with vintage rotary phones at the booths for ordering, house-made sodas, mocktails, boozy milkshakes and diner food like a fried bologna sandwich. The soda-fountain premise is the point for a non-drinker — the house sodas are made in-house and are the signature product rather than the consolation, so ordering alcohol-free here means ordering the thing the bar is actually known for. One caveat: it is strictly 21-and-over despite the format, so it is not a family stop.
signatureDrinks: House Sodas (NA: add 2 scoops of coneflower vanilla ice cream + $5)

naMenuItems.name: House Sodas
naMenuItems.description: add 2 scoops of coneflower vanilla ice cream + $5

venues.longDescription:
Fizzy's Fountain & Liquors opened in March 2020 — timing that would have finished most bars — and survived to become one of the more distinctive rooms in Omaha. It is in Little Bohemia, the South 13th Street district, and the concept is a classic American soda fountain rebuilt for adults: booths with vintage rotary phones you use to place your order, a retro fit-out, house-made sodas, mocktails, boozy milkshakes and diner food including a fried bologna sandwich and a short rib melt.

The reason it grades well for alcohol-free drinking is structural rather than a matter of any single drink. At a soda fountain, the soda is the product. The house sodas here are the thing the bar is known for and the thing it makes itself, which means a non-drinker ordering one is ordering the signature rather than the substitute — the exact inversion of the usual bar experience, where the alcohol-free option is whatever was left over. The mocktail list sits alongside them.

There is one caveat that has to be stated plainly, because the format invites the wrong assumption. Fizzy's is 21-and-over. A soda fountain with milkshakes on the menu sounds like somewhere to bring a family, and it is not — the door policy is adults only, which is a disappointment worth discovering here rather than on the pavement outside with children in tow.

The hours are the other constraint and they are tighter than most: closed Monday and Tuesday entirely, 5pm onwards Wednesday through Friday, with a split weekend service that adds 11am to 3pm on Saturday and Sunday.

This entry records no signature drinks. The house sodas rotate and the mocktail list is not published in a readable form, so what is documented here is the standing premise, which is well attested by Omaha's local press.
venues.pressQuote: By day, Fizzy's Fountain & Liquors serves up classic comfort food and retro sodas in Little Bohemia.
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: Hurrdat ONE, 10 Best Zero-Proof & Nonalcoholic Bars in Omaha, Nov 18, 2025

venues.name: Flamingo Kava & Acai Bar
venues.description: Flamingo is the east Orlando outpost of a concept that started in Rockledge on the Space Coast, and it runs a genuine dual menu: acai bowls, smoothies and plant-based builds for the daytime, and kava shells anchoring the room as it turns social after dark. It opens at 9:30am and closes at midnight, every day, with no alcohol served. The location on Corporate Boulevard puts it between the University of Central Florida campus and the Quadrangle office park, which gives it an unusually mixed crowd — students, east-side residents and people finishing work. The teas and smoothies are built around plant ingredients marketed for stress and anxiety rather than as indulgences.
venues.longDescription:
Flamingo is the east Orlando outpost of a concept that began in Rockledge, on the Space Coast, and it runs a genuinely dual menu rather than a token one. The daytime half is acai bowls, smoothies and plant-based builds; the evening half is kava, with shells anchoring the room as it turns social after dark. It opens at 9:30am and closes at midnight, every day, and serves no alcohol.

That dual structure is a sensible answer to a real problem in this category. A room that only sells kava has to persuade people to try an unfamiliar bitter root before it can sell them anything at all; a room that also sells acai bowls has a reason for people to walk in on a Tuesday lunchtime and discover the rest later. It also means the space carries a mixed crowd through the day rather than sitting empty until evening.

The location on Corporate Boulevard puts it between the University of Central Florida campus and the Quadrangle office park, which gives it an unusually varied mix — students, east-side residents, and people finishing work. The Muddy Root's Orlando room is a few hundred metres away, so this corner of east Orlando now has two alcohol-free rooms within walking distance, a density the city centre does not match.

Kava is the ground root of Piper methysticum, a shrub native to the South Pacific islands, prepared as a cold water infusion and drunk socially across Fiji, Vanuatu, Tonga and Samoa for roughly three thousand years. It contains no alcohol. It tastes earthy and bitter, numbs the lips and tongue on the first mouthful, and is mildly sedative rather than intoxicating in the sense alcohol is. Because kava exhibits reverse tolerance, regular drinkers typically need less rather than more to feel it, so a first visit is best paced slowly across an hour or two.

The teas and smoothies are built around plant ingredients the venue markets for stress and anxiety rather than as indulgences, which places Flamingo closer to the wellness end of the kava spectrum than to the late-night-bar end — the midnight close notwithstanding.

As with most Florida kava rooms, Flamingo does not publish a full ingredient breakdown online, and this directory will not assert whether kratom is served here without evidence either way. Given that the two are poured side by side across most of the state, and given that kratom acts on the opioid receptors and carries tolerance and withdrawal risk that kava does not, the sensible approach for anyone avoiding it is to ask at the counter what a given drink is made from before ordering.

venues.name: Fleur de Thé
venues.description: Fleur de Thé is a fully alcohol-free tea salon in Tower Grove South, opened in October 2024 by Johannesburg-born "teapreneur" Colleen Vucinovich. Reservation-only high tea services trace four traditions — Cape Town, Versailles, Windsor and Udaipur — paired with roughly 20 Palais des Thés loose-leaf teas from Paris. At the salon's tea bar, every pour stays at 0% alcohol: Copenhagen Sparkling Tea, tea elixirs, tea flights and botanical mocktails built on Abstinence zero-proof spirits, like the Tea Posy with Water Garden tea, Abstinence Cape Floral and grenadine. It's one of the rare St. Louis venues where the entire drink list is non-alcoholic by design, not as an afterthought.

naMenuItems.name: Sparkling Pairing
naMenuItems.description: sparkling tea is a crisp and refreshing start to your delectable tea service. it is also the perfect partner to celebrations.

naMenuItems.name: Signature Pairing
naMenuItems.description: a tea elixir crafted to heighten flavor, balance the palate, and offer a quietly indulgent, alcohol-free expression of the tea experience.

venues.longDescription:
Colleen Vucinovich, a native of Johannesburg, South Africa, emigrated first to England and then to St. Louis, where she and her husband Craig opened Fleur de Thé in October 2024 in Tower Grove South's former Crispy Edge space. The self-described "teapreneur" built the salon as a gathering place — an elegant 60-seat dining room dressed in chandeliers, floral wallpaper and rattan-back French chairs, with a sleek tea bar anchoring the back of the room. The menu is organized around four prix-fixe high tea services that trace her journey: Cape Town, Versailles, Windsor and Udaipur, each pairing tea sandwiches, scones and pâtisserie with a different national tradition.

Everything poured here is non-alcoholic — the salon's own site notes its sparkling tea and tea elixirs are 0% alcohol, and the bar program is built without a drop of booze. Roughly 20 Palais des Thés loose-leaf teas from Paris span white, green, oolong, black and fermented styles, served as personal pots, tasting flights or the base of house "tea-tails": mocktails mixing premium tea infusions, house-made syrups, fruit purées, Copenhagen Sparkling Tea imported from Denmark, and zero-proof spirits from South African brand Abstinence. The signature Tea Posy combines Water Garden tea, Abstinence Cape Floral and grenadine. Each high tea service ($63 per person) opens with a flute of sparkling tea or a tea elixir; reservations run through Tock, and monthly Soirée de Thé evenings add a twilight tea service on Fridays.

Local press embraced the concept quickly: Ladue News spotlighted the internationally inspired luxury tea experience in March 2025, Feast Magazine gave the salon a first look, and Sauce Magazine covered its opening. Early coverage also highlighted a walk-in "mocktail salon" on Thursday through Saturday evenings, though the current posted schedule centers on Thursday-to-Sunday daytime service plus the monthly Friday soirées — check before you go. Expect a refined, unhurried visit: tiered trays of sweets and savories, Parisian tea by the pot, and a calendar of etiquette lessons, language workshops and jazz — with never a wine list in sight.
venues.pressQuote: In Tower Grove South, a new tearoom offers an internationally inspired luxury tea experience.

venues.name: Flight Club
venues.description: Flight Club is a social darts venue on Walnut Street, and it carries the deepest named non-alcoholic beer list found anywhere in Philadelphia: five, all priced and named — Sam Adams Just the Haze, Athletic's Cerveza Atlética, Lagunitas IPNA, Sierra Nevada Hop Splash and Guinness 0. On the cocktail side the Midway Splash builds Seedlip Grove 42 with pineapple, lemon and tonic, and there is a Lyre's flight of three at $13 running a G&T, an Amalfi Spritz and a Classico. The format is the real draw: the evening is organised around playing darts rather than around drinking, and the venue runs to one in the morning on Friday and Saturday.

venues.longDescription:
Flight Club on Walnut Street is a social darts venue — oches with automatic scoring, table service, groups booked by the hour. It belongs in this directory for two separate reasons, and the less obvious one is the more important.

The obvious reason is the drinks list. Five non-alcoholic beers, all named and priced, is the deepest such list encountered anywhere in Philadelphia: Sam Adams Just the Haze and Sierra Nevada Hop Splash at the hoppy end, Athletic's Cerveza Atlética as the crisp lager, Lagunitas IPNA, and Guinness 0 for anyone who wants a stout. Most bars carry one non-alcoholic beer, if that; carrying five means a non-drinker can have a different beer each round, which is precisely the variety that makes an evening feel normal rather than rationed.

The cocktails back it up. The Midway Splash builds Seedlip Grove 42 — the blood orange, ginger and lemongrass expression — with pineapple, lemon and tonic. Better still is the Lyre's flight at thirteen dollars: three alcohol-free cocktails, a gin and tonic, an Amalfi Spritz and a Classico, served together. A flight is a format almost never offered without alcohol, and it does something specific for a non-drinker, turning a single order into a tasting with things to compare and talk about.

The less obvious reason is the format itself, and it is the stronger argument. Darts gives the evening a structure that has nothing to do with what anyone is drinking. There are turns to take, a score on a screen, and a reason to stand up. Every problem with a night out sober — the lulls, the visible glass, the sense of being a spectator at everyone else's evening — is a problem of unstructured time, and an activity venue simply removes it.

Open to eleven midweek and one in the morning on Friday and Saturday, with an eleven o'clock weekend opening.

venues.name: Flying Saucer Draught Emporium
venues.description: Flying Saucer Draught Emporium's downtown Houston location — one of the original outposts of the Fort Worth-founded beer-hall chain, pouring since 2000 — runs a genuinely deep non-alcoholic shelf alongside its famous 85-tap, 150-plus-bottle beer list. The venue's own listing on the NA-beer directory beerfordriving.com names 15 distinct non-alcoholic beers from at least six breweries built around low- and no-ABV brewing. That includes several Athletic Brewing styles and four Brooklyn Special Effects variants, plus Guinness 0, Clausthaler Original, Deschutes Black Butte Non-Alcoholic, Lagunitas Hoppy Refresher and Untitled Art Mango Dragonfruit — each called out by name and ABV rather than folded into a vague "N/A options available" note.
venues.address: 705 Main St Ste A, Houston, TX 77002
signatureDrinks: Athletic Brewing Free Wave (non-alcoholic hazy IPA, 0.5% ABV)
Brooklyn Special Effects Grapefruit IPA (non-alcoholic IPA, 0.5% ABV)
Deschutes Black Butte Non-Alcoholic (non-alcoholic porter, 0.5% ABV)
Lagunitas Hoppy Refresher (non-alcoholic hop water, 0% ABV)
venues.longDescription:
Flying Saucer Draught Emporium opened its Houston flagship on Main Street at Capitol in 2000, four years after Shannon Wynne and Keith Schlabs launched the first Flying Saucer in Fort Worth; the Houston location marked its 16th anniversary in August 2016 and has since passed the quarter-century mark for the chain overall. The bar occupies ground-floor space at 705 Main Street, a stretch of downtown that predates Houston's METRORail line and endured years of rail construction outside its doors before the surrounding blocks filled back in with bars and restaurants. Flying Saucer built its reputation on scale — roughly 85 taps and around 150 bottled and canned beers — plus its UFO Club, which rewards regulars who work through 200 different beers with a custom plate mounted on the wall.

That same tap-list-first approach carries over to non-alcoholic beer. Rather than stocking one or two token options, the Houston location pours a rotating slate of 15 named zero- and near-zero-ABV beers, verified on the venue's dedicated beerfordriving.com listing: several Athletic Brewing styles (Atletica, Fancy Like, Free Wave, Run Wild, Layback Lime & Salt and the radler-style Ripe Pursuit), four Brooklyn Special Effects variants (Classic Golden, Grapefruit IPA, Hoppy Amber and Pils), Guinness 0, Clausthaler Original, Deschutes Black Butte Non-Alcoholic, Lagunitas Hoppy Refresher and Untitled Art Mango Dragonfruit Fruited Sour. It's a beer-nerd's non-alcoholic list in the same spirit as the bar's full-proof one — broad enough to let a non-drinking guest actually compare styles rather than default to soda.

An early-2026 search summary had suggested the Houston Flying Saucer might have closed, but that traced back to a misread of unrelated Houston closure round-ups that do not list this venue; the beerknurd.com corporate site and Yelp both continue to show the Main Street location actively operating in July 2026, with unchanged hours, phone number and address.
venues.pressQuote: Sixteen years here is like 40 years in River Oaks or Upper Kirby.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Joshua Justice, Flying Saucer Houston manager

venues.name: FOLK Coffee & Vintage
venues.description: FOLK Coffee & Vintage is an alcohol-free cafe built into the front of a vintage and antique store on Clark Street in Andersonville. Owners Ryan Smith and Safiyah Uddin opened the shop in November 2023 and added the coffee counter in late March 2026, deliberately setting it apart from the half-dozen other cafes on the same stretch: there is no espresso machine at all. Drinks are brewed in a cezve, the Turkish-style long-handled pot, heated on a hot plate and strained to order. The short list covers Yemeni cardamom coffee steeped in milk or water, the Kurdish pistachio coffee menengic, a cinnamon-and-brown-sugar cafe de olla, iced Adeni tea, cold brew and pour-over made with Ceramic Coffee Roasters beans. Seating is a handful of barstools, by design.
signatureDrinks: Yemeni coffee (Yemeni cardamom coffee steeped in milk or water)
Menengic (Kurdish pistachio-flavored coffee sweetened with sugar)
Cafe de Olla (Mexican-style coffee with cinnamon, brown sugar and warm spices)
Iced Adeni (Yemeni-style black tea, served cold)
venues.longDescription:
Folk opened at 5668 N Clark St in November 2023, when Ryan Smith and Safiyah Uddin - then customers of the long-running Andersonville antique store Roost - went into business with its former owner after Roost closed following nearly fifteen years on the strip. Smith and Uddin are now the sole owners, and in late March 2026 they added the cafe they had been planning, renaming the business Folk Coffee & Vintage. The Clark Street corridor already had at least six coffee shops, including The Coffee Studio, The Understudy and Colectivo, so the pair built the menu around what none of them served. "We wanted to go into something that was a little more slow-brewed, a little more traditional," Smith told Block Club Chicago. "We have drinks that you can't get at other places."

The most concrete expression of that is the absence of an espresso machine. Coffee and tea are made instead in a cezve, the long-handled Turkish pot, heated on a hot plate and strained before serving. The list is short and international: Yemeni coffee at $6, made with Yemeni cardamom coffee steeped in milk or water; a menengic at $6, the Kurdish pistachio coffee sweetened with sugar; a cafe de olla at $6, Mexican-style with cinnamon, brown sugar and warm spices; iced options including cold brew, an iced London fog and an iced Adeni, the Yemeni-style black tea; and pour-over at $5 using beans from Ceramic Coffee Roasters. Seating is limited to a few barstools on purpose - Smith wanted people who came for coffee to browse the vintage furniture, artwork, decor and clothing, and vice versa. Nothing alcoholic is served, and the room closes at 6pm, so this is a daytime third place rather than a night out, but it is a genuinely distinctive alcohol-free stop in a neighborhood dominated by bars.
venues.pressQuote: Folk Coffee & Vintage sets itself apart from the half-dozen other coffee shops on Clark Street by brewing Yemeni, Kurdish and other international coffee styles.

venues.name: The Fool's Kava House
venues.description: The Fool's Kava House is a fully alcohol-free kava bar in downtown Arlington, describing itself as a sober social community and open daily until 2am — the hours of a bar, without the bar. Alongside kava it pours botanical tonics across several strains, plus drip coffee, lattes, matcha and chai. It is billed as Arlington's first and only kava bar and as the first woman- and queer-owned kava bar in Texas. Note that kava is a psychoactive botanical: the room is alcohol-free but not substance-free.
venues.longDescription:
The Fool's Kava House occupies a downtown Arlington storefront and keeps genuine bar hours — every day until 2am — which is the detail that matters most about it. The great practical problem of not drinking is not finding a beverage; it is finding somewhere that is still open and still social at eleven at night. This room answers that without serving any alcohol at all, and it describes itself plainly as a sober social community rather than a café that happens to close late.

The menu is built on kava, the Pacific Islander root traditionally prepared as a relaxing ceremonial drink, offered across several strains and in botanical tonic form. A full coffee and tea programme runs alongside it — drip coffee, lattes, matcha, chai — so a visit does not have to involve kava at all. The house is billed as Arlington's first and only kava bar, and as the first woman- and queer-owned kava bar in Texas.

One thing to be clear about, because this directory is used by people in recovery: kava is psychoactive. It is not alcohol, it is legal, and many people in sobriety drink it without issue, but it is a mood-altering botanical rather than an inert soft drink. Anyone whose sobriety means abstaining from all intoxicants should know that going in — and for anyone else, an alcohol-free room open to 2am in a college town is a rare and useful thing. Individual drink names are not published on their site, so it is worth asking what is prepared that night.

venues.name: Forget Me Not
venues.description: Forget Me Not is a cocktail lounge tucked off Clayton Street in Cherry Creek North, opened in 2019 with a bright, floral-leaning room and a small-plates menu of salmon crudo, street corn dip and wagyu steak tartare. Its drinks list carries a standing "Zero Proof" heading rather than a footnote, with three house non-alcoholic cocktails priced at $13 — the same tier as much of the low-ABV list — that rotate with the seasons. All three are built on Seedlip non-alcoholic spirits and treated as compositions rather than juice: the earthy Deep Roots, the herbal Green Machine and the floral Osaka Afternoon. Both 5280 and Visit Denver have singled the bar out for its zero-proof program.

Green Machine (Seedlip N/A spirit, cucumber, salted lemon, ginger — $13)
Osaka Afternoon (Seedlip N/A spirit, cherry blossom, elderflower, tonic, lemon — $13)

venues.longDescription:
Forget Me Not occupies a set-back space at 227 Clayton Street in Cherry Creek North, reached through a courtyard rather than off the sidewalk, and has traded as one of the neighbourhood's better-regarded cocktail rooms since its debut. The drinks list is organised into categories — sparkling and low-ABV, light and refreshing, rich and stirred — with two large-format offerings and a standing zero-proof section that rotates with the seasons. That structural decision is what separates the bar from most licensed rooms in the city: the non-alcoholic drinks are not a courtesy list kept behind the bar, they are a printed heading on the same menu at the same price point, currently $13 each against a cocktail list that sits in similar territory.

The three house zero-proof cocktails are all built on Seedlip non-alcoholic spirits and structured like the full-proof drinks around them. Deep Roots is the earthy one, combining Seedlip with tarragon, beet, ginger, citrus and Stappi red bitters, which gives it the bittersweet backbone that most alcohol-free drinks lack. Green Machine is the bright, vegetal counterpart, built from Seedlip with cucumber, salted lemon and ginger. Osaka Afternoon is the floral option, layering cherry blossom and elderflower over Seedlip with tonic and lemon. Beyond the house drinks the section carries Cali Water prickly pear cactus water at $7 and a set of large-format still and sparkling waters. Both of Denver's main food-and-drink publications have picked the bar out specifically for this program: Visit Denver's December 2025 alcohol-free cocktail guide describes it as "a bright and cheery spot to snack on small plates... while sipping a zero-proof cocktail", naming the Green Machine and Deep Roots, and 5280's mocktail round-up lists the same two drinks. The food menu runs to small plates designed for grazing rather than a full dinner — salmon crudo, street corn dip and wagyu steak tartare among them — which suits a room that fills after work and trades until 2am.
venues.pressQuote: located in the heart of Cherry Creek — is a bright and cheery spot to snack on small plates (think: salmon crudo, street corn dip and wagyu steak tartare) while sipping a zero-proof cocktail.

venues.name: Fork & Barrel
venues.description: Fork & Barrel is a Southern restaurant on lower Frankfort Avenue in Clifton, sharing its venue with sister operation Morning Fork, and the two run a shared mocktail list rather than leaving non-drinkers to the soda gun. The named builds are a sweet pepper lemonade, Molly & Lucy's Punch and the Ain't Easy Being Green, which between them cover a savoury-sweet long drink, a punch and a herbaceous option — a wider spread than most restaurant bars attempt. Louisville's official visitor bureau lists the venue in its guide to where to drink alcohol-free in the city. Service runs Tuesday to Saturday afternoons and evenings, closed Sunday and Monday.
venues.longDescription:
Lower Frankfort Avenue — the Clifton end, closer to downtown than the Crescent Hill shops — has become one of the more interesting eating stretches in Louisville, and Fork & Barrel sits in the middle of it. The cooking is Southern, the venue is shared with the daytime operation Morning Fork, and the two run as a single kitchen and bar across different parts of the day, which is why the drinks list reads as broader than a dinner-only restaurant would manage.

The mocktail list is the reason it is here, and the spread is the point. A sweet pepper lemonade is a savoury-leaning long drink — pepper against citrus and sugar, which gives it somewhere to go other than sweet. Molly & Lucy's Punch is the shareable, fruit-forward option. Ain't Easy Being Green is the herbaceous one. Three drinks that sit in genuinely different places on the palate is more thought than most restaurant bars give the category, where the usual offer is one virgin mojito and a shrug. GoToLouisville, the city's official visitor bureau, named the venue in its round-up of where to drink alcohol-free in Louisville on that basis.

Two practical points. The hours are narrower than most of this guide — Tuesday to Saturday, 3pm to 9pm, closed Sunday and Monday — so it is an early-evening proposition rather than a late one, and worth checking before travelling. And a note on finding it online: the domain forkandbarrel.com is a parked listing offered for sale and is not the restaurant; the real site is bethefork.com. Volare is six blocks east along the same avenue and Pizza Lupo two blocks west, which makes this stretch of Clifton the densest run of alcohol-free-friendly dining outside Butchertown.
venues.pressQuote: Fork & Barrel and its sister restaurant Morning Fork are shaking up a variety of refreshing mocktails in their shared venue on lower Frankfort Avenue, with options like a sweet pepper lemonade, Molly & Lucy's Punch, and the Ain't Easy Being Green.

venues.name: Forsythia
venues.description: Forsythia is a contemporary French bistro in Philadelphia's Old City, opened in 2019 by chef-proprietor Christopher Kearse. Set on Chestnut Street with an open kitchen and a bright, modern dining room, it serves elevated, often-rotating French fare alongside a wine-forward bar program and craft cocktails. The kitchen earned a spot in the MICHELIN Guide's Philadelphia recognition (Recommended, 2025). For non-drinkers, Forsythia keeps a small but real zero-proof offering at its full bar: the headliner is the "75 Year Old Virgin," a spirit-free riff on the classic French 75 built on juniper, cara cara orange, and lemon for a citrusy, botanical, gin-like character — a drink Philadelphia Magazine singled out among the city's best non-alcoholic cocktails. The bar also pours "Steep Calm," an ashwagandha-honey, coconut-water, and prickly-pear mocktail, plus Stella Artois 0.0% NA beer.
venues.longDescription:
Forsythia is a contemporary French bistro on Chestnut Street in Old City, opened in 2019 by chef-proprietor Christopher Kearse. The dining room is bright and modern with an open kitchen, the menu is elevated and rotates frequently, and the bar leans wine-forward alongside craft cocktails. The kitchen holds a place in the MICHELIN Guide's Philadelphia recognition, listed as Recommended in 2025.

The non-alcoholic offering is small and honest, and its headliner is properly built. The 75 Year Old Virgin is a spirit-free take on the French 75 — conventionally gin, lemon, sugar and champagne — reconstructed on juniper, cara cara orange and lemon. Philadelphia Magazine's Kae Lani Palmisano described it as achieving the same citrusy, spicy, botanical essence of gin through the juniper, and that is the correct way to read the drink. Juniper is the berry that legally defines gin and supplies its piney, resinous character; using it directly rather than reaching for a commercial gin substitute means the drink carries the flavour that matters without the bottle in between. Cara cara oranges are the pink-fleshed variety, lower in acid and more berry-like than a navel, which gives the drink roundness where a straight lemon build would be sharp. Steep Calm is the second named option.

The French bistro context is the reason a short list still works here. This is a restaurant where wine is the expected accompaniment and where a table settles in for a long meal, so the useful thing is not a large menu of alcohol-free drinks but one well-made aperitif to open with — which is precisely what a French 75 is for. Ordering it means starting the meal the same way as everyone else at the table.

Open for dinner only, from five in the evening until ten, and until nine on Sunday.
venues.pressQuote: A play on the French 75, Forsythia's 75-Year-Old Virgin achieves the same citrusy, spicy, botanical essence of gin with juniper, cara cara, and lemon.

venues.name: Fort Oak
venues.description: Fort Oak is a wood-fired restaurant in a converted Mission Hills car showroom, part of chef Brad Wise's Trust Restaurant Group, and its drinks list carries a standing Spirit Free section of five. Two are built in house — Adventura on the non-alcoholic spirit aplós arise with lemon, lemongrass, pandan and soda, and a NON1 sparkling served with salted raspberry and chamomile — and the rest are finished products poured straight: St. Agrestis' Phony Negroni, Athletic Brewing's Upside Dawn golden ale and an alcohol-removed cider from Golden State. That covers spirit, aperitivo, sparkling, beer and cider in five lines, which is broader than most restaurant lists manage. The kitchen is built around a hearth and a raw bar, with dry-aged steaks, whole branzino and seafood towers, and the restaurant closes on Tuesdays and runs an oyster night on Mondays.
venues.address: 1011 Fort Stockton Dr, San Diego, CA 92103
venues.hours: Mon 4pm-9pm; Tue closed; Wed-Thu 4pm-9pm; Fri-Sat 4pm-10pm; Sun 4pm-9pm
signatureDrinks: Adventura ($14) — aplós arise, lemon, lemongrass, pandan, soda
St. Agrestis Phony Negroni ($15) — the bottled non-alcoholic negroni, served straight
NON1 Sparkling ($15) — salted raspberry and chamomile
Athletic Brewing Upside Dawn ($8) — non-alcoholic golden ale
Golden State Dry + Mighty ($10) — alcohol-removed cider
venues.longDescription:
Fort Oak sits on Fort Stockton Drive in Mission Hills, in a mid-century building that used to be a car showroom, and it is the restaurant where chef Brad Wise's live-fire cooking is at its most formal — a hearth at the centre of the room, dry-aged steaks, whole fish and a serious raw bar. The group's own description calls it an ode to the fire and the sea.

The drinks list gives non-drinkers a printed Spirit Free heading with five entries, which is more than most restaurants at this price level bother with. Adventura, at fourteen dollars, is the one built from scratch: aplós arise — a hemp-free botanical non-alcoholic spirit — with lemon, lemongrass, pandan and soda, which is a genuinely aromatic drink rather than a sweetened juice. Beside it sits St. Agrestis' Phony Negroni at fifteen, the Brooklyn-made bottled aperitif that has become the default good answer for anyone who wants something properly bitter, and a NON1 sparkling at fifteen, served with salted raspberry and chamomile, from the Australian producer that makes wine alternatives for restaurant lists.

The last two cover the categories a cocktail list usually forgets. Athletic Brewing's Upside Dawn golden ale is eight dollars, and Golden State's dry and mighty is a ten-dollar alcohol-removed cider — worth knowing because cider is the hardest of the three drink categories to find without alcohol in a restaurant.

The practical notes are about timing. The restaurant is closed on Tuesdays, opens at four the rest of the week, and runs to nine on weeknights and ten on Friday and Saturday. There is a happy hour early in the evening and an oyster night on Mondays. As with the rest of the group's rooms, the spirit-free section is refreshed along with the main cocktail list, so the two house builds are the part most likely to change between visits; the bottled products tend to stay. This is a licensed restaurant with a well-chosen alcohol-free shelf rather than a destination for non-drinkers specifically, and it works best for a mixed table.

The building is worth a word, because it explains the room. Fort Oak occupies a mid-century car showroom, and the conversion kept the height and the glass, which makes it one of the brighter dining rooms in a city with a lot of dark ones. The hearth is in the middle rather than hidden in a kitchen, so the cooking is visible from most tables. If you are coming specifically for the alcohol-free list rather than dinner, the bar and the raw bar are the places to sit, and the early-evening happy hour is when the room is quiet enough to talk to the bartender about what else they can build.
venues.pressQuote: An ode to the fire and the sea, Fort Oak offers diners the bold, smoky, wood-fired flavors that have come to define Chef Brad Wise.

venues.name: Fort Point Valencia
venues.description: Fort Point Valencia is the Mission District beer hall of Fort Point Beer Company, the San Francisco brewery founded in 2014 by cousins Tyler and Justin Catalana. The 22-tap flagship reopened at 742 Valencia St in February 2022 with color-saturated plaster walls, oak woodwork, neon art, and a casual SF-style seafood menu. What earns it a spot here: Fort Point is one of the few breweries pouring its own non-alcoholic line. In January 2025, after roughly three years of R&D, it launched NA versions of its two best-known beers — NA KSA, a light, crisp Kölsch-style ale, and NA Villager, a balanced San Francisco-style IPA — both under 0.5% ABV and brewed (not dealcoholized) with a Berkeley Yeast strain that minimizes alcohol conversion. The NA beers are sold at Fort Point's San Francisco locations, including this Valencia beer hall.
venues.longDescription:
Fort Point Valencia is the Mission District beer hall of Fort Point Beer Company, the San Francisco brewery founded in 2014 by cousins Tyler and Justin Catalana in a Presidio building. The 22-tap flagship reopened at 742 Valencia Street in February 2022 after a redesign, trading the industrial look common to taprooms for colour-saturated plaster walls, oak woodwork and neon art, with a casual San Francisco seafood menu alongside the beer. It opens at noon daily and runs to 11pm on Friday and Saturday, and functions as a neighbourhood room rather than a destination brewery tour.

Fort Point belongs on this list because it is one of very few breweries pouring a non-alcoholic beer it brews itself. In January 2025, after roughly three years of research, it launched alcohol-free versions of its two best-known beers: NA KSA, a light crisp Kölsch-style ale, and NA Villager, a balanced San Francisco-style IPA. Both come in under 0.5% ABV and — importantly for flavour — are brewed rather than dealcoholized, using a Berkeley Yeast strain engineered to minimise alcohol conversion during fermentation, so the beer never has to have alcohol stripped back out of it. Mike Schnebeck, Fort Point's head of innovation, framed the goal in the brewery's own announcement: "Our NA beers are different for the same reasons our alcoholic beers are — balance, nuance, and approachability." The Valencia beer hall carries the line and prints a dedicated Zero Proof section on its menu, currently listing an NA KSA Michelada at $9, Casamara Club's Alta (juniper, allspice and clove soda) and Sera (cinnamon and orange blossom soda) at $6 each, a Pineapple Mint Tonic from Juice Shop at $6, and Mineragua sparkling water at $4. The michelada is the notable entry: a genuinely bar-shaped drink built on the house non-alcoholic Kölsch rather than a bottle handed over unopened.
venues.pressQuote: Our NA beers are different for the same reasons our alcoholic beers are — balance, nuance, and approachability.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Mike Schnebeck, Fort Point Head of Innovation

venues.name: Fount Board & Table
venues.description: Fount Board & Table is an Uptown all-day cafe and grazing-board shop that keeps a dedicated "NA Wines, Spirits & Euphorics" section stocked with 20-plus non-alcoholic bottles to drink in or take home. Alongside the espresso and charcuterie, the retail wall curates alcohol-free wines, zero-proof spirits, NA beers, and functional "euphorics," making it one of the few Dallas coffee houses that doubles as a spirit-free bottle selection. The lineup is actively maintained — the venue's zero-proof menu category was refreshed in March 2026 — and the shop is run by husband-and-wife founders Olivia and Ryan Genthe.
venues.longDescription:
Husband-and-wife catering team Olivia and Ryan Genthe opened Fount Board & Table in early 2020, transforming the former Crooked Tree Coffeehouse in Uptown's State-Thomas district into a cozy, candle-lit all-day cafe. The couple had run a grazing-board and grazing-table catering business for about a year before taking the roughly 1,300-square-foot brick-and-mortar space, which still centers on their signature charcuterie and grazing spreads alongside coffee, tea, pastries, and rarer edibles like caviar and retail cheese.

Beyond the food, Fount curates a dedicated "NA Wines, Spirits & Euphorics" retail section — a rotating selection of 20-plus non-alcoholic wines, zero-proof spirits, alcohol-free beers, and functional "euphorics" that guests can buy by the bottle or enjoy on site. Dallasites101 highlights it as a spot where a cozy coffee shop "doubles as an amazing place to shop for zero-proof sips." The zero-proof category on the venue's online store (fountdallas.com) was last refreshed in March 2026, indicating it is an actively maintained part of the business rather than a token afterthought.

Fount sits at 2414 Routh Street in Uptown Dallas and keeps daytime cafe hours (roughly 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., closing earlier on Mondays, Tuesdays, and Sundays). The kitchen leans on local and artisanal producers, and the same team books full grazing-table catering for weddings and events. Because the beverage list also includes alcoholic wine and beer, the venue is best described as a cafe with a serious alcohol-free bottle program rather than a fully sober space.
venues.pressQuote: This cozy coffee shop doubles as an amazing place to shop for zero-proof sips! Explore their eclectic variety of nonalcoholic sips, featuring 20+ wines, spirits, beers, and euphorics.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Dallasites101, "20+ Spots to Sip Mocktails in Dallas & Where to Shop Nonalcoholic Drinks"

venues.name: The Fountain Room
venues.description: The Fountain Room is a Wisconsin-style supper club in the Bottleworks District, opened in the summer of 2022 by the father-and-son restaurant team Perry and Blake Fogelsong after a pandemic-era trip north. The room is Art Deco jazz-age — velvet banquettes, chandeliers, a reel-to-reel machine — and OpenTable and People named it one of America's fifty most beautiful restaurants. The food is supper-club canon: pickled relish trays, prime rib, house desserts. Non-alcoholic drinks get their own printed "No ABV" section rather than a line at the bottom of the cocktail list, running to the Crouching Tiger, Circle City Sober, a Cherry Burlesque built on cherry, lime, honey syrup, ginger beer and mint, and an alcohol-removed Sauvignon Blanc by the glass.

venues.longDescription:
Perry and Blake Fogelsong, a father-and-son restaurant team, spent part of the pandemic driving around Wisconsin eating in supper clubs, and came back to Indianapolis wanting to build one. The Fountain Room opened in the summer of 2022 inside the Bottleworks District — the redeveloped Coca-Cola bottling plant at the top of Massachusetts Avenue — and reads as a roaring-twenties steakhouse crossed with a Midwestern supper club: velvet booths, low chandeliers, a working reel-to-reel, and a relish tray that arrives before anything else. OpenTable and People jointly named it one of America's fifty most beautiful restaurants, and Indianapolis Monthly has treated it as the district's standout since it opened.

For non-drinkers the useful detail is structural: the drinks menu carries a printed "No ABV" heading, which in a room whose entire identity is built on strong cocktails and a long wine list is a deliberate choice rather than an accommodation. The Crouching Tiger is peach purée with pear, lime and ginger beer; Circle City Sober is the house long drink; the Cherry Burlesque runs cherry and lime against honey syrup, ginger beer and mint; and there is an alcohol-removed Sauvignon Blanc poured by the glass, which is still unusual in Indianapolis outside the two Orangily shops. Prices sit around $10 to $12, in line with the cocktails rather than discounted to soft-drink level — which cuts both ways, but does mean the drinks are made to the same specification. Because this is a supper club and a destination dining room, book ahead; the bar is a reasonable walk-in option earlier in the evening, and Sundry & Vice is in the Bottleworks Hotel next door. The supper-club format turns out to suit a non-drinker better than most restaurant formats do. The meal is long, the relish tray and the prime rib do the work, and the evening is not structured around ordering a second bottle — so a table of mixed drinkers and non-drinkers ends up on roughly equal footing, which is not true in a wine-led dining room. The Bottleworks District around it is also unusually easy to spend an alcohol-free evening in: Pins Mechanical and the Living Room Theaters are in the same complex, and the whole site is a converted Coca-Cola bottling plant, which gives the neighbourhood its name and its Art Deco bones.
venues.pressQuote: A Bottleworks restaurant with supper club flair offers a selection of cocktails with no ABV and full flavor, including the Crouching Tiger, Circle City Sober, Berry Burlesque, and NA Sauvignon Blanc.

venues.name: Four Walls
venues.description: Four Walls is a cocktail bar hidden inside The Joseph hotel at 405 4th Avenue South in downtown Nashville — hard to find but not quite a speakeasy, and, as Nashville Scene put it, the sort of place where grabbing a drink is an event, with proper lighting and volume levels appropriate for easy conversation. Its menu runs in numbered volumes and is currently on Volume 5. Lead bartender Lawson Ballinger approaches each drink like a scene, layered with unexpected ingredients and tactile presentation. Its alcohol-free offering is structured unusually and rather well: rather than a fixed list, the section headed "Mocktails | Alcohol-Free Experiences" asks you to choose one of ten flavour profiles — bright and zesty, rich and indulgent, herbaceous and fresh, spiced and warm, tropical and fruity, floral and aromatic, savoury and umami, sweet and silky, playful and effervescent, or complex and robust — and then leave the rest to the bartender. It is presented identically to the bar's Elevated Highballs section, not as an afterthought. No price is printed for the mocktails. Non-alcoholic beer is listed: Untitled Art Italian-style pilsner at $8 and Athletic Run Wild IPA at $9.
signatureDrinks: Bartender's-choice mocktail from ten flavour profiles
venues.longDescription:
Four Walls sits inside The Joseph on 4th Avenue South, and finding it is part of the point — Nashville Scene's description is the accurate one: hard to find within the hotel but not a speakeasy per se, the sort of place where grabbing a drink is an event, with an ambiance that is civilised, proper lighting, and volume levels appropriate for easy conversation. In a city whose downtown is dominated by broadway bars competing on loudness, that last detail is the whole proposition. The menu runs in numbered volumes rather than seasons and is currently on Volume 5. Lead bartender Lawson Ballinger's approach, in the bar's own words, is to treat each drink like a scene — layered with unexpected ingredients, tactile presentation, and moments of interaction designed to unfold slowly across an evening.

The alcohol-free section is worth describing carefully, because it does not work like anyone else's. It is headed Mocktails | Alcohol-Free Experiences, and instead of listing finished drinks it lists ten flavour profiles and asks you to pick one: bright and zesty, rich and indulgent, herbaceous and fresh, spiced and warm, tropical and fruity, floral and aromatic, savoury and umami, sweet and silky, playful and effervescent, or complex and robust. Each carries three describing words — velvety, creamy, frothy for the rich one; earthy, vegetal, satisfying for the savoury — and then the instruction is simply to leave the rest to them. There are two reasons this is better than a fixed list. It removes the awkwardness of asking a bartender to improvise, which is what most non-drinkers have to do; and it puts the alcohol-free drinks on exactly the same footing as the bar's Elevated Highballs, which are presented in the identical format one page earlier. A non-drinker orders the same way everyone else does. Two practical notes: no price is printed against the mocktail section, which is the one gap, and if you would rather have a beer, the bar keeps Untitled Art's Italian-style pilsner at $8 and Athletic's Run Wild IPA at $9. Note also that the bar's own site links an older Volume 3 menu; the hotel's copy is the current one.
venues.pressQuote: Hard to find within the Joseph Hotel, but not a speakeasy per se, Four Walls is the sort of place where grabbing a drink is an event. The ambiance is civilized, with proper lighting and volume levels appropriate for easy conversation.

venues.name: Française
venues.description: Française is a French neighbourhood bistro on South Perry Street from Adam Hegsted, one of the Inland Northwest's most prolific restaurateurs, applying classic French technique to local produce in a room that is elegant without being formal. Its drinks list carries a named mocktail — the Lemon Sage Delight — alongside a proper loose-leaf tea selection running to earl grey, citrus chamomile, peppermint, orange spice, wild berry hibiscus, English breakfast and green. It opens at 3pm on weekdays and at 9am at weekends, which makes it one of the few rooms in this guide serving a considered non-alcoholic drink in the morning.

venues.longDescription:
The South Perry District is Spokane's most walkable food neighbourhood, a few blocks of independent businesses on the South Hill, and Française is its French bistro. It comes from Adam Hegsted, whose Eat Good Group has opened a substantial share of the Inland Northwest's better restaurants, and the cooking is classic French technique applied to locally sourced ingredients — elegant, but a neighbourhood room rather than an occasion one.

For a guide like this one, Française is a useful kind of entry rather than a spectacular one. It carries a named mocktail on the menu, the Lemon Sage Delight, which is a built drink rather than a soft-drink listing. More usefully, it keeps a real loose-leaf tea programme — earl grey, citrus chamomile, peppermint, orange spice, wild berry hibiscus, English breakfast, green — which in a French dining room means someone who is not drinking has something to order across a whole meal rather than only at the start of it. That is a specific and often-overlooked gap: the wine pairing has no equivalent for a non-drinker at most restaurants, and a serious tea list is the closest thing to one.

The grading here is three, and the reason is scale rather than doubt. One named mocktail is one named mocktail; there is no printed zero-proof section, and this directory does not inflate what it can see. The restaurant was picked out by Trending Northwest in its survey of Spokane rooms doing interesting work in the category, which is the corroboration that earns it the listing.

The hours are the practical draw. Française opens at 3pm Monday through Friday, runs to 9pm and to 10pm on Friday, and opens at 9am on Saturday and Sunday for a full weekend service — the only room in this guide serving before noon.

venues.name: Franklin Ave Cocktails & Kitchen
venues.description: Salt Lake magazine's 2025 Best Restaurant, a buzzy New American spot tucked into the historic Franklin Avenue Variety Theatre building on Edison Street downtown — the fourth Salt Lake concept from the Bourbon Group, with chef Matt Crandall's menu mixing elevated plates with sharp bar food. For non-drinkers, the kitchen runs a rotating seasonal mocktail menu alongside its whiskey- and amaro-leaning cocktail list; City Cast Salt Lake singled out a comforting hibiscus-and-cinnamon hot-toddy-style mocktail as a standout. The art-covered, leather-and-exposed-brick basement room is a frequent recommendation for the downtown Edison Street cluster (note it is 21+).
venues.address: 231 S Edison St, Salt Lake City, UT 84111
venues.longDescription:
Housed in a 100-plus-year-old building that was originally the Franklin Avenue Variety Theatre, the venue spans multiple bars across two levels and leans into a moody, artwork-on-every-surface aesthetic; The Infatuation notes you can watch bartenders mix cocktails and a seasonal selection of mocktails in the leather-trimmed basement.

Salt Lake magazine calls the room buzzy without being overbearing. Because the mocktail list rotates seasonally, specific zero-proof offerings change through the year, but the program is consistently called out by local press as one of downtown's better options for non-drinkers.
venues.pressQuote: I went to Franklin Ave over the holiday break and our server said the mocktail menu was really 'popping off.' I couldn't agree more. I got a hot toddy-esque drink with hibiscus and cinnamon that was delicious and comforting.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Terina Ria, City Cast Salt Lake
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: City Cast Salt Lake, "The Best Mocktails in Salt Lake," 2025

venues.name: Frannie & The Fox
venues.description: Wood-fired Italian restaurant inside the boutique Hotel Emeline in Ansonborough, downtown Charleston, serving shareable, locally sourced plates and thin-crust pizzas. The beverage team keeps a small lineup of named non-alcoholic cocktails alongside the full bar, including the No'Groni, built to taste like a gin negroni from Gnista wormwood, gin-flavored syrup and orange bitters, and a blueberry mocktail made on Amethyst's South Carolina blueberry-ginger-mint NA spirit. Mocktails are described by the beverage team as curated with the same approach as the alcoholic cocktail program.
signatureDrinks: No'Groni (Gnista wormwood, gin-flavored syrup, orange bitters)
venues.longDescription:
Frannie & The Fox is the wood-fired Italian eatery inside Hotel Emeline at 181 Church Street, in Charleston's Ansonborough neighborhood. The restaurant is open daily for breakfast, lunch and dinner, with weekend brunch, and remains active and well-reviewed into 2026. Its courtyard and adjacent greenhouse offer open-air dining.

The non-alcoholic offering is a curated set of named mocktails rather than a dedicated zero-proof concept. Documented options include the No'Groni, a negroni stand-in built from Gnista wormwood, gin-flavored simple syrup and orange bitters, and a blueberry mocktail made with Amethyst's blueberry-ginger-mint non-alcoholic spirit. Beverage operations specialist Amanda Phelps has said the mocktail selection is curated with the same thoughtful approach as the bar's alcoholic cocktails.
venues.pressQuote: From incorporating seasonal ingredients to showcasing local offerings, our mocktail selection is curated with the same thoughtful approach that goes into every cocktail found on our menu.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Amanda Phelps, Beverage Operations Specialist, Frannie & The Fox

venues.name: Free Spirit @ Riverdale Hub
venues.description: Free Spirit is a fully alcohol-free cocktail bar and restaurant operated by Riverdale Hub, a not-for-profit social enterprise inside a converted century-old building in Toronto's Leslieville / Gerrard India Bazaar neighbourhood. It opened April 23, 2024 and runs on a no-tipping, living-wage model, with restaurant proceeds going toward addressing barriers for equity-deserving groups in the community. The ten-drink zero-proof menu spans a Bloody Caesar, a Cosmo built on Seedlip Garden 108, and an Espresso Martini made with Seedlip Spice 94, backed by a zero-proof beer list that includes Guinness 0.0 and Heineken 0.0.
