venues.longDescription:
Hale Pele — "House of the Volcano" — is a tiki bar and Polynesian-inspired restaurant in Northeast Portland's Grant Park neighborhood, on NE Broadway. It opened in 2012 in a former tiki space named Thatch, reopened by Portland's Blair Reynolds in partnership with San Francisco tiki figure Martin Cate (of Smuggler's Cove). The room is known for its immersive design, a large sunken bar that puts seated guests at eye level with their bartenders, and signature flaming cocktails; The Oregonian once called it the best tiki bar in America.

Hale Pele runs a serious non-alcoholic program built on the same fresh-squeezed juices and house-made syrups as its full-proof menu, leaning on NA spirit brands including DHOS, Wilderton (Bittersweet Aperitivo) and All the Bitter N/A bitters. Named alcohol-free drinks include Push Pop, Jumanji (an NA twist on a Jungle Bird, with lime, pineapple, molasses and Wilderton), Saturn Return, and Raffle's Boon, and the bar also makes alcohol-free versions of tiki classics like the Lava Flow and Lapu Lapu.
venues.pressQuote: But all those fresh-squeezed juices and housemade syrups are just as fun in alcohol-free beverages at Hale Pele.

venues.name: Halfway Crooks Beer
venues.description: Halfway Crooks Beer is a Summerhill brewery founded by Andrew Bainbridge, a career engineer and longtime homebrewer, and Joran Van Ginderachter, a Belgian-trained brewer. Opened in summer 2019 at 60 Georgia Ave SE, it specializes in traditionally executed lagers, pilsners, and mixed-fermentation Belgian-influenced beers, served across a cozy bier café and bar, an open-air "Dak Bar" rooftop, and an adjacent biergarten (both dog-friendly). For non-drinkers, the draw is Brevet Pils, the brewery's own non-alcoholic German-style pilsner (under 0.5% ABV) with notes of subtle fennel, oyster crackers, lemon, and tangerine. As co-owner Shawn Cooper told Atlanta Magazine, brewing it is a technical challenge that requires halting fermentation and pasteurizing for shelf stability. Brevet Pils is poured on-site and distributed in six-packs, making this a rare Atlanta brewery offering a credible house-made NA option.
venues.longDescription:
Halfway Crooks Beer opened in summer 2019 at 60 Georgia Avenue SE in Summerhill, founded by Andrew Bainbridge, a career engineer and longtime homebrewer, and Joran Van Ginderachter, a Belgian-trained brewer. The brewing is deliberately traditional — lagers, pilsners and mixed-fermentation Belgian-influenced beers, executed patiently in a market that mostly rewards the opposite. The site runs across a cosy bier café and bar, an open-air rooftop called the Dak Bar, and the HC Biergarten a few streets away on Reed Street; the rooftop and biergarten are both dog-friendly.

For non-drinkers the draw is Brevet Pils, the brewery's own non-alcoholic German-style pilsner, brewed under 0.5% ABV with notes of subtle fennel, oyster crackers, lemon and tangerine. A pilsner is the hardest possible style to make without alcohol. There is nothing to hide behind — no hop bitterness, no roast, no fruit — so every flaw in a de-alcoholised beer shows up immediately. Attempting one is a statement of confidence, and Brevet is now distributed in six-packs well beyond Atlanta.

Co-owner Shawn Cooper described the difficulty to Atlanta Magazine in 2025: it is not really beer so much as a hybrid, and the process requires heating the product and pasteurising it for shelf stability. That is an honest account of a category most breweries market as effortless. Arresting fermentation before the alcohol develops, then stabilising the result without cooking the flavour out of it, is a technical problem, and it is why so few independent breweries make their own NA beer instead of buying it in.

The brewery pours Monday to Thursday from 4pm, and from late morning at weekends. Between this and Wild Heaven a couple of miles west, Atlanta has two independent breweries making credible house non-alcoholic beer — which is two more than most American cities of its size.
venues.pressQuote: It's not beer—it's kind of a hybrid. You basically have to heat the product up to get to a certain pasteurization unit in order to ensure that there's no living organisms in the NA product for shelf stability.

venues.name: Hamdi Coffee
venues.description: Hamdi Coffee is a Somali tea house on the first floor of Karmel Mall in Whittier, the Somali shopping centre on Pleasant Avenue that houses more than two hundred East African–owned businesses. It serves no alcohol and is open from 6:30am to around 11pm every day, which makes it one of the longest-running non-alcoholic evening rooms in south Minneapolis. The drink it is known for is a Somali tea steamed with whole milk and topped with foam, listed as the Somali Special Tea and priced under three dollars, alongside spiced shaah — black tea steeped with cardamom and cinnamon — and Somali coffee. Sambusas and other savoury pastries are sold at the counter.
venues.hours: Mon 6:30am-11pm; Tue 6:30am-10:30pm; Wed 6:30am-11pm; Thu 6:30am-10:30pm; Fri 7am-11pm; Sat-Sun 6:30am-11pm
signatureDrinks: Somali Special Tea (whole milk steamed with foam, tea)
Shaah (black tea steeped with cardamom and cinnamon)
venues.longDescription:
Karmel Mall opened on Pleasant Avenue in Whittier as the first Somali shopping centre in the United States, and it now holds more than two hundred Somali and East African businesses across several floors of narrow corridors — clothing stalls, jewellers, barbers, salons and halal food counters. Hamdi Coffee sits on the first floor and does what the mall's tea counters have always done: it stays open into the late evening and functions as a social club. Men and women sit over tea for hours; the room hums well after most of the retail has shut. Its hours are the operative fact for anyone looking for somewhere alcohol-free to spend an evening — 6:30am to 10:30 or 11pm every day of the week, including Sunday, in a city where very little that is not a bar runs that long.

The drink to order is the house preparation the shop calls Somali Special Tea: whole milk steamed to a cappuccino-like foam with tea folded through it, sold for under three dollars. Beyond Beurre Blanc, writing about Somali drinks in the Twin Cities in December 2025, noted that "they call it the Somali Special Tea and it rings in at under $3." Alongside it are shaah, the spiced black tea steeped with cardamom and cinnamon that anchors Somali hospitality and is usually taken with sweet bread, and Somali coffee. Sambusas and savoury pastries are sold from the counter. This is a tea house rather than a bar and it should be visited on those terms: the pricing is a fraction of what a comparable drink costs at a specialty coffee shop, the room belongs to its regulars, and visitors are asked not to take photographs inside the mall. There is no alcohol anywhere on the premises. The practical notes are simple: Karmel Mall stands at 2910 Pleasant Avenue South, roughly three miles south-west of Cedar-Riverside, parking is on site, and Hamdi is on the first floor rather than upstairs among the clothing stalls. The tea is hand-brewed from scratch in large batches at intervals through the day, so it is worth asking when the last one went on.
venues.pressQuote: They call it the Somali Special Tea and it rings in at under $3.

venues.name: Hamsa
venues.description: Hamsa is a modern Israeli restaurant in Houston's Rice Village from Sof Hospitality — the team behind Doris Metropolitan — serving a Mediterranean menu of Israeli and Middle Eastern dishes anchored by hummus, falafel, and shawarma. Its deep bar program pairs an extensive wine and arak list with a set of four named zero-proof mocktails.
signatureDrinks: Tea Time (yerba mate, plum, lemon, ginger beer)
Put Your Cukes Up (basil, shishito, cucumber, pink peppercorns, lime, Topo Chico)
When Mangos Tango (mango, habanero, pineapple, rosemary, lime)
Strawberries in Paradise (strawberry, lemon, grapefruit, mint, Topo Chico)
venues.longDescription:
Hamsa opened in Rice Village on May 11, 2022, the second restaurant concept from Sof Hospitality, the group behind steakhouse Doris Metropolitan. Co-founders Itai Ben Eli and Itamar Levy built the restaurant with chef Sash Kurgan, a fellow Sof partner; pastry chef Michal Michaeli runs the dessert program and general manager and sommelier Melissa Rogers oversees the wine list and floor. "Hamsa is a concept we always wanted to do, which is more of the food we bring from back home," Ben Eli told CultureMap Houston ahead of opening. The restaurant sits beside Sof Hospitality's own Badolina Bakery & Café in the heart of Rice Village.

The Mediterranean menu draws on Israeli and broader Middle Eastern influences, anchored by hummus, crispy falafel, and shawarma alongside larger plates like whole grilled branzino, lamb spare ribs, and arak mussels, built for sharing rather than a traditional appetizer-entree structure.

The beverage program runs deep, with more than 100 wine selections — including a Middle Eastern section highlighting Israeli and Lebanese producers — plus a full arak-cocktail list. Alongside it, the restaurant offers a set of named zero-proof drinks: Tea Time (yerba mate, plum, lemon, ginger beer), Put Your Cukes Up (basil, shishito, cucumber, pink peppercorns, lime, Topo Chico), When Mangos Tango (mango, habanero, pineapple, rosemary, lime), and Strawberries in Paradise (strawberry, lemon, grapefruit, mint, Topo Chico). CultureMap Houston singled the zero-proof options out in its 2026 Dry January roundup for their "inventive flavor combinations."
venues.pressQuote: Hamsa leans into inventive flavor combinations with its zero-proof options. Choose between four unique drinks, including the Yerba Mate-plum-ginger beer creation Tea Time and the Put Your Cukes Up.

venues.name: Happy Cat Cafe
venues.description: Happy Cat Cafe is Grand Rapids' first cat cafe, open since August 2017 at 447 South Division Avenue, and it serves no alcohol. The business pairs a coffee bar with a separate cat lounge stocked by Fig and Friends Animal Rescue; more than 600 cats have been adopted through the partnership since opening. The drinks are more developed than the format suggests: house-made syrups and sauces, house-made oat milk, a run of named espresso lattes, and a mocktail list built on fruit syrups and glitter. Named drinks include the Blackberry Panther, the Rosy Ragdoll, the Ginger Cat Latte, the Tabby Cat and the Tortitude. The cafe also runs cat yoga and painting classes.
venues.address: 447 S Division Ave, Grand Rapids, MI 49503
signatureDrinks: Blackberry Panther (wild blackberry syrup, Sprite, lemon, black holographic glitter)
Tabby Cat (house-made dark chocolate, almond, hazelnut, blackberry)
Tortitude (espresso, spicy chai, house-made dark chocolate sauce, chili powder)
venues.longDescription:
Happy Cat Cafe opened in August 2017 as the first cat cafe in Grand Rapids and has operated at 447 South Division Avenue since. The model is two rooms: a conventional coffee bar at the front, and a cat lounge behind it housing adoptable cats placed by Fig and Friends Animal Rescue. More than 600 cats have been adopted out through that partnership. The lounge is bookable and the cafe programs around it, running cat yoga and painting classes alongside ordinary trading. The room is wheelchair accessible, has its own parking, and is one of the few venues in this guide that is straightforwardly good for children as well as adults.

The reason it belongs in an alcohol-free guide rather than a general cafe listing is that the drinks are treated as a real menu rather than an afterthought, and there is no alcohol anywhere on the premises. Syrups and sauces are made in house, as is the oat milk. The espresso list is built around named house drinks: the Ginger Cat Latte, a twist on golden milk; the Tabby Cat, made with house-made dark chocolate, almond, hazelnut and blackberry; the Tortitude, which puts espresso together with spicy chai, house-made dark chocolate sauce and chili powder; the Meow Cha Latte, a matcha built on house-made vanilla; and Crookshanks' Caramel. The cold list runs to mocktails and what the cafe calls glitter spritzers — the Blackberry Panther combines wild blackberry syrup, Sprite, lemon and black holographic glitter, and the Rosy Ragdoll sits alongside it — plus lotus drinks and Red Bull mocktails. Opening hours are 10am to 6pm Monday through Thursday and 9am to 7pm Friday through Sunday, so like most of the city's fully alcohol-free rooms it is a daytime proposition.
venues.pressQuote: No-alcohol café serves coffees, teas and bubbly citrus refreshers.

venues.name: Haraz Coffee House (Fishtown)
venues.description: Haraz Coffee House's Fishtown room opened in October 2025 as the chain's second Philadelphia location, and it trades until midnight from Thursday through Saturday — genuinely late for a room that serves no alcohol at all. The menu is the traditional Yemeni repertoire: jubani made from coffee and the husk of the coffee cherry with cinnamon and ginger, qishr brewed from the husk alone, harazi mufawar with cardamom and cream, and sana'ani, a black coffee with cardamom. The tea side runs to adeni karak chai with the house haraz spice blend and cream, and a saffron version of the same. The Philadelphia Inquirer has covered the city's Yemeni coffeehouse boom repeatedly, describing these rooms as spaces without alcohol or reservations.
signatureDrinks: Jubani — coffee with coffee-cherry husk, cinnamon and ginger
Qishr — infusion of coffee husks with cinnamon and ginger
Harazi Mufawar — coffee, cardamom and cream
Adeni Karak Chai — black tea, haraz spice blend and cream
Saffron Adeni — black tea, haraz spice, cream and saffron
Haraz Latte — double espresso, honey, milk, haraz spice
venues.longDescription:
Haraz Coffee House opened its Fishtown room on West Girard Avenue in October 2025, the second Philadelphia site for a Yemeni coffee chain that has expanded quickly across the United States. The reason it belongs in this directory is the combination of two things that rarely occur together: a room that serves no alcohol whatsoever, and a closing time of midnight on Thursday, Friday and Saturday.

The menu is the traditional Yemeni one, and it rewards knowing what the words mean. Jubani is made from coffee together with the husk of the coffee cherry — the fruit that surrounds the bean — spiced with cinnamon and ginger. Qishr goes further and uses the husk alone, with no bean at all; it is far lower in caffeine than brewed coffee and tastes closer to a spiced fruit tea, which makes it the sensible order late in the evening. Harazi mufawar is coffee with cardamom and cream, richer and closer to a dessert. Sana'ani, named for the capital, is the plainest of them: black coffee with cardamom, and the one to order if you want to taste the bean itself.

The tea list runs in parallel. Adeni karak chai is black tea brewed with the house haraz spice blend and cream, the everyday drink of Aden, and there is a saffron version that is worth the premium. The haraz latte works the house spice into a double espresso with honey and milk.

The Philadelphia Inquirer has covered the city's Yemeni coffeehouse boom repeatedly through 2025 and 2026 — four cafes opened in 2025 alone — and its framing of what these rooms offer is exact: spaces without alcohol or reservations. That second half matters as much as the first. You do not book, you are not on a clock, and nobody is turning the table.

On alcohol, the position is evidence-based rather than a claim the venue makes in those words: the menu carries no alcoholic item, and the house is halal, Muslim-owned and keeps a prayer area on site. It serves caffeine only — no kava, no kratom, nothing else psychoactive.
venues.pressQuote: without alcohol or reservations

venues.name: Haraz Coffee House
venues.description: Haraz Coffee House is a Yemeni coffeehouse on the ground floor of the University House building at 930 Spring Street in Midtown, and the first Georgia outpost of a chain founded by Hamzah Nasser in Dearborn, Michigan in 2021. It serves no alcohol at all, and it stays open to 10pm on weeknights and midnight on Friday and Saturday, which makes it an evening room rather than a morning coffee stop. The drinks list is split into Traditional, Espresso Bar, Iced Refreshers, Frappe and Cloud Matcha sections. The Traditional column carries the Yemeni preparations the brand is built on — Harazi Mufawar, Maleki, Sana'ani, Jubani and Qishr — alongside the Adeni Chai that fuses Yemeni tea leaves with Indian masala spicing, cardamom and cinnamon. Milk cakes and Arabic pastries fill out the counter.
signatureDrinks: Adeni Chai (Yemeni tea leaves, masala spicing, cardamom, cinnamon)
venues.longDescription:
Haraz began in Dearborn, Michigan — the first Arab-majority city in the United States — where Hamzah Nasser opened the original shop in 2021 with the stated aim of putting Yemeni coffee culture on a global footing. The chain grew quickly, and the Midtown Atlanta location is the brand's first in Georgia. It took over the former Twisted Kitchen space inside University House, a student-housing tower at Spring Street and 8th, giving it roughly 2,000 square feet of room plus a 600-square-foot patio. Tomorrow's News Today first reported the lease in February 2025; the shop then ran a long soft opening from October before holding its grand opening, which The Infatuation covered in January 2026. The site matters as much as the coffee: Midtown's late-night options skew heavily towards bars, and Haraz gives the district a room that is open past 10pm and pours nothing alcoholic.

The menu is where the Yemeni specificity lives. The Traditional section lists Harazi Mufawar, Maleki, Sana'ani and Jubani — regional preparations that treat coffee as a spiced, aromatic infusion rather than an espresso extraction — plus Qishr, the coffee-husk drink brewed with ginger and cinnamon. The house Adeni Chai is the signature: Indian masala tea fused with Yemeni tea leaves, cardamom and cinnamon, served hot or iced. The Espresso Bar runs Pistachio, Mocha, Saffron and seasonal Pumpkin lattes; the Cloud Matcha section and a list of Iced Refreshers built on mango dragon fruit, hibiscus and pink coconut cover the non-coffee side. Pastries, milk cakes and bulk beans and tea bags are sold alongside. Nothing on the menu contains alcohol, and there is no bar programme of any kind — the room works as a study space by day and a social one at night, which is the pattern Yemeni coffeehouses have followed in every metro they have opened in.
venues.pressQuote: Out of more than 30 venues across multiple states, this Midtown location makes the first Haraz in Georgia.

venues.name: Haraz Coffee House
venues.description: Haraz Coffee House is a fully alcohol-free Yemeni coffeehouse on Michigan Avenue in East Dearborn, one block from the Arab American National Museum. Founder Hamzah Nasser opened the original shop in April 2021, building the menu around Yemeni staples like Mufawar (cardamom cold brew with creamy evaporated milk) and Adeni tea alongside spice-forward espresso drinks such as the Haraz Latte and Pistachio Latte. The New York Times featured Haraz in a June 2025 business story on the wave of Yemeni cafes meeting demand for late-night, alcohol-free social spaces. What started as one storefront in a converted insurance office has since scaled into a national franchise, with this East Dearborn location as the flagship.
signatureDrinks: Mufawar (cardamom cold brew, creamy evaporated milk)
Adeni (cold brew tea, Haraz spice blend, evaporated milk)
Haraz Latte (espresso, Haraz spice blend, milk)
Pistachio Latte (espresso, pistachio, Haraz spice, milk)
Saffron Latte (espresso, Haraz spice, saffron, milk)
Iced Hibiscus (organic hibiscus tea, blackberry or lavender)
venues.longDescription:
Hamzah Nasser, born in Yemen's Juban district and raised from age six in metro Detroit, opened the first Haraz Coffee House in April 2021 at 13810 Michigan Ave in East Dearborn, converting a former insurance office he'd begun renovating in 2019. Before coffee, he ran a gas station and spent seven years as a truck driver crossing 43 states — experience he's said shaped his read on what a real "third space" needed to feel like. The shop opened during Ramadan on evening hours and quickly became a neighborhood fixture a block from the Arab American National Museum.

The program is alcohol-free by design, built around Yemeni coffeehouse tradition rather than a bar substitute: Mufawar (cardamom cold brew with creamy evaporated milk), Adeni (cold brew tea with the house Haraz spice blend and evaporated milk), and Turkish- and Saudi-style cardamom coffees sit alongside an espresso bar of spiced lattes — Haraz Latte, Pistachio Latte, Saffron Latte — plus fruit refreshers like Iced Hibiscus with blackberry or lavender, matcha "Cloud" drinks, and pastries such as Bee Bites and tiramisu.

The New York Times profiled Haraz in a June 24, 2025 business piece on the broader boom in Yemeni coffeehouses, framing shops like this one as filling demand among Americans — Muslim and non-Muslim alike — for late-night gathering spaces that don't revolve around alcohol. The East Dearborn location keeps that community-first character: Edison-bulb lighting, Yemeni-heritage artwork on the walls, Arabic music, a prayer area, and kid-friendly seating.

Since 2021 the concept has expanded from that single Dearborn storefront into a national franchise with dozens of locations and more in development, but the original Michigan Avenue shop remains the flagship and the clearest expression of Nasser's founding idea for the brand.
venues.pressQuote: Coffee is a culture and it's a culture that unites people.

venues.name: Haraz Coffee House (Franklin Street)
venues.description: Haraz Coffee House is a fully alcohol-free Yemeni coffeehouse at Franklin and Bush in Cathedral Hill, the first California location of the Dearborn, Michigan chain founded by Hamzah Nasser in 2021. It trades from 7am to 11pm seven days a week, which puts it in a small group of San Francisco rooms that function as an evening gathering place without a liquor licence. The menu is built on traditional Yemeni preparations rather than on syrups: Harazi Mufawar (coffee, cardamom and cream), Adeni and Karak chai (black tea with Haraz spice and cream), Jubani, Sana'ani, Maleki, Qishr brewed from dried coffee cherry husks, and a Saudi coffee with saffron and cardamom. An espresso bar, a matcha list and a range of frappes and refreshers run alongside, with saffron cakes, honeycomb bread and Yemeni pastries from the kitchen.
signatureDrinks: Adeni Chai (black tea, Haraz spice, cream)
venues.longDescription:
Haraz Coffee House opened its first San Francisco cafe on the corner of Franklin and Bush streets in Cathedral Hill, bringing the Dearborn, Michigan chain to California for the first time. The company was started in 2021 by Hamzah Nasser, who built it around Yemeni coffee culture and heritage; by the time of this listing the group described itself as having grown to 31 locations with a further 185 in the pipeline. The San Francisco room follows the format that has made the category grow so quickly across American cities: a large, comfortable, brightly lit space designed for sitting rather than for takeaway, open until 11pm every night of the week, and serving no alcohol at all.

The drinks list is the reason the venue matters to anyone drinking without alcohol. Traditional Yemeni preparations anchor it — Harazi Mufawar, made with coffee, cardamom and cream; Adeni and Karak chai, black tea cooked with the house Haraz spice blend and cream; Jubani, Sana'ani and Maleki coffees; and Qishr, brewed from the dried husks of coffee cherries rather than from the bean itself. A Saudi coffee with saffron and cardamom and a Turkish coffee with cardamom sit alongside them, and there is a Saffron Adeni and a Red Tea for guests who want something lighter late in the evening. A conventional espresso bar covers cortados, americanos, cappuccinos and a house Haraz latte, with pistachio, saffron and salted caramel variations, plus a matcha range in strawberry, mango, lavender, dragon fruit and coconut, a set of frappes, and cold refreshers built on hibiscus, pomegranate and mango dragon fruit. Food leans on Yemeni baking: golden saffron cakes, honeycomb pastries and cream-cheese-stuffed breads served hot with honey. Because nothing on the premises is alcoholic, the venue reads as a full evening destination rather than as a daytime coffee shop with an early close.
venues.pressQuote: In 2021, Hamzah Nasser set out on a mission to bring a unique coffee experience to life by opening the first Haraz Coffee House in Dearborn, Michigan.

venues.name: Haraz Coffee House (Kearny Street)
venues.description: Haraz Coffee House's second San Francisco cafe sits on Kearny Street between Bush and Sutter, a downtown block otherwise given over to bars and old-guard restaurants. Like the Franklin Street original it is entirely alcohol-free, and it trades from 7am to 9pm seven days a week, which makes it one of very few Financial District rooms where an after-work meeting does not have to happen over a drinks list. The menu is the chain's Yemeni one: Harazi Mufawar built from coffee, cardamom and cream; Adeni and Karak chai simmered with the house spice blend; Qishr made from dried coffee cherry husks; Jubani, Sana'ani and Maleki coffees; and a saffron-and-cardamom Saudi coffee, with an espresso and matcha bar and Yemeni pastries alongside.
signatureDrinks: Adeni Chai (black tea, Haraz spice, cream)
venues.longDescription:
Haraz Coffee House announced its second San Francisco location in the summer of 2025, taking 264 Kearny Street in the Financial District, a few doors from the tiki bar Pagan Idol and the pub The Irish Bank. What Now San Francisco reported the plan in July 2025, noting that the Kearny Street cafe would carry the same late-trading format as the Franklin Street original; the shop currently lists 7am to 9pm daily. The chain was founded in Dearborn, Michigan in 2021 by Hamzah Nasser, whose stated aim was to share Yemeni coffee culture and heritage in the United States, and the Kearny Street room reproduces the group's template of a large sit-down space that serves no alcohol.

The drinks are the same Yemeni list that the Franklin Street cafe pours. Harazi Mufawar combines coffee with cardamom and cream. Adeni chai and Karak chai are black teas cooked down with the house Haraz spice blend and cream, and there is a Saffron Adeni for anyone who wants the tea richer. Qishr is brewed not from coffee beans but from the dried husks of the coffee cherry, a preparation particular to Yemen, and Jubani, Sana'ani and Maleki cover the range of traditional roasts. Turkish coffee arrives dark and cardamom-scented, and the Saudi is made with saffron and cardamom. The rest of the board is a full espresso bar — cortado, americano, cappuccino, house Haraz latte, plus pistachio, saffron and salted caramel versions — along with matcha in several fruit and floral variations, blended frappes, and iced hibiscus, pomegranate and strawberry lemonade refreshers. Yemeni baking fills the pastry case, including saffron cakes and honeycomb breads, and the kitchen serves bee bites, a cream-cheese-stuffed bread brought out hot with honey. For a downtown that empties out after the offices close, an entirely alcohol-free room trading into the evening is a genuinely distinct option, and the Kearny Street address puts it on the same block as several of the Financial District's best-known drinking rooms rather than tucked away from them.
venues.pressQuote: the Kearny Street cafe will adopt the same late-night hours as the Franklin Street location, planning to stay open until 11 pm
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Elise McCorkle, What Now San Francisco

venues.name: Haraz Coffee House
venues.description: Haraz Coffee House is a Yemeni coffeehouse at the corner of Lyndale and Lake, the first Minnesota location of a Dearborn, Michigan chain. It opened in July 2026 in the large corner room that had been the Iron Door Pub, and later Cause Spirits and Soundbar, until that bar closed in March 2025 — so a liquor-licensed room has become one that pours no alcohol at all. The menu is split into Traditional Drinks, Espresso Bar, and Coffee and Other. The traditional column carries Harazi Mufawar, Adeni and Karak chai, Maleki, Jubani, Sana'ani and Qishr; the espresso bar is anchored by the Haraz Latte, built with honey and the house haraz spice blend.
signatureDrinks: Adeni Chai (black tea, haraz spice, cream)
Saffron Adeni (black tea, haraz spice, cream, saffron)
Maleki (coffee, husks, ginger, cinnamon, light cream)
Haraz Latte (double espresso, honey, milk, haraz spice)
venues.longDescription:
The corner of Lyndale Avenue and Lake Street has been a drinking corner for decades. The Iron Door Pub held the large corner room for years, and Cause Spirits and Soundbar before it; the Iron Door closed in March 2025 and Haraz Coffee House took the space, running a soft opening through the spring and opening properly in July 2026. It is the chain's first Minnesota location. Haraz was founded in Dearborn, Michigan and has expanded across the country on the same model as its Yemeni-coffeehouse peers: long hours, room to sit, a menu that treats Yemeni preparations as the main event rather than a novelty column, and no alcohol licence. Ziad Alobaidi told Racket in July 2026 that the goal was for people "to stop by and just enjoy themselves, whether solo, with family, or with friends" — a description of a third place rather than a coffee counter, and one that Lyn-Lake had lacked after 10pm without a bar attached.

The menu runs three ways. Traditional Drinks is the Yemeni section: Harazi Mufawar, coffee with cardamom and cream, also served iced; Adeni and Karak chai, black tea with the house haraz spice blend and cream, with a saffron version; Maleki, coffee brewed with husks, ginger, cinnamon and light cream; Jubani with cinnamon and ginger; Sana'ani, black coffee with cardamom; and Qishr, the coffee-husk infusion with cinnamon and ginger. Coffee and Other covers a Turkish preparation with cardamom, a Saudi coffee with saffron and cardamom, pour-over, French press, and a green tea with ginger and cinnamon. The Espresso Bar is where the house blend does its other job: the Haraz Latte is a double shot with honey, milk and haraz spice, and the same spice turns up in the matcha latte and the shaken espresso, alongside pistachio, saffron and salted caramel builds. Sweet and savoury pastries are sold at the counter. The room is large by coffeehouse standards and stays open to midnight on Friday and Saturday. A practical note on the address: the shop occupies the large corner unit at Lyndale and Lake, and the entrance is on Lyndale rather than on Lake Street. It runs to midnight on Friday and Saturday and to 10pm on weeknights, which makes it the latest room in Lyn-Lake, by some margin, where nothing behind the counter contains alcohol.
venues.pressQuote: Our goal is for people to stop by and just enjoy themselves, whether solo, with family, or with friends.

venues.name: Haraz Coffee House
venues.description: Haraz Coffee House is a fully alcohol-free Yemeni coffeehouse on Woodland Street in East Nashville, open until midnight on Friday and Saturday. It is the Nashville franchise of the Dearborn, Michigan chain that roasts sun-dried coffee grown in Yemen's Haraz Mountains, and it opened here in 2024 under franchisees Abdelrahman Abdelwahed and Jobran Mohamed. The drinks list runs to traditional Yemeni preparations alongside the espresso menu: Harazi Mufawar, made with coffee, cardamom and cream; Adeni chai; Sana'ani black coffee with cardamom; Qishr brewed from coffee husk with cinnamon and ginger; and Jubani. The room was designed around handmade blue Turkish tiles, geometric Arabian woodwork and a Yemeni-style couch at the entrance. No alcohol is served at any hour.
signatureDrinks: Harazi Mufawar - coffee, cardamom and cream
Adeni Chai - black tea, haraz spice and cream
Saffron Adeni - black tea, haraz spice, cream and saffron
venues.longDescription:
Haraz Coffee House opened at 901 Woodland Street in June 2024, in the Wabash building next door to The Basement East, and it is the Nashville outpost of a Yemeni coffee chain founded in Dearborn, Michigan. The local franchise is run by Abdelrahman Abdelwahed with partner Jobran Mohamed. The company's whole premise is single-origin: the beans are grown in the Haraz Mountains of western Yemen, sun-dried rather than washed, and the chain markets them as organic and pesticide-free. The build-out, documented by the coffee trade title Sprudge in August 2024, was done by architect Mubarak Hauter and designer Lorraine Nassif, and the details are specific — handmade blue Turkish tiles across the counter and back wall, intricate geometric Arabian woodwork, and a Yemeni-style majlis couch set at the entrance. In the owner's own words to Sprudge, the space is beautifully illuminated with natural light.

What makes this a going-out venue rather than a morning coffee stop is the clock. Haraz runs until 10pm Sunday through Wednesday, 11pm on Thursday and midnight on Friday and Saturday, and no alcohol is served at any point. WPLN, Nashville's public radio station, reported in March 2025 on exactly this — a cluster of Muslim-owned Nashville coffeehouses keeping late hours and building what the station described as a sober nightlife culture meant to run year-round rather than only through Ramadan. The menu supports the evening: alongside lattes there is Harazi Mufawar, a coffee with cardamom and cream; Adeni chai, black tea with haraz spice and cream, and a saffron version of the same; Sana'ani, black coffee with cardamom; Qishr, brewed from coffee husk with cinnamon and ginger; and Jubani, which uses the bean with the same spices. Desserts and pastries run alongside. Two practical notes: the entrance is off the interior of the Wabash building rather than directly on Woodland Street, and the room fills late on weekend nights, when it functions much more like a bar than a cafe.
venues.pressQuote: This concept is not new in the Middle East. They've been doing this for hundreds of years.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Sam Ali, Haraz Coffee House marketing lead

venues.name: Haraz Coffee House (University City)
venues.description: Haraz Coffee House's University City room on Chestnut Street was the chain's first Philadelphia location, sitting in the middle of the Penn and Drexel campuses and keeping hours that suit them — seven in the morning to ten at night, and eleven on Friday and Saturday. The menu is the full Yemeni list: jubani and qishr built on coffee-cherry husks with cinnamon and ginger, harazi mufawar with cardamom and cream, sana'ani black coffee with cardamom, and the adeni karak chai brewed with the house haraz spice blend. A student neighbourhood is exactly where an alcohol-free room open late earns its keep, and the venue runs events — a Mahjong and Matcha night among them — rather than functioning purely as a counter service.
signatureDrinks: Jubani — coffee with coffee-cherry husk, cinnamon and ginger
Qishr — infusion of coffee husks with cinnamon and ginger
Harazi Mufawar — coffee, cardamom and cream
Adeni Karak Chai — black tea, haraz spice blend and cream
Saffron Adeni — black tea, haraz spice, cream and saffron
venues.longDescription:
Haraz Coffee House's Chestnut Street room was the chain's first Philadelphia location, and its position matters: it sits in University City, between the Penn and Drexel campuses, in a neighbourhood with tens of thousands of students, a large international population and a significant number of people who do not drink for religious reasons. That is the demand a Yemeni coffeehouse is built for, and it explains why the format arrived here first.

The menu is the full Haraz list. Jubani and qishr are the two husk-based drinks — jubani uses coffee together with the dried husk of the coffee cherry, qishr uses the husk alone — and both are spiced with cinnamon and ginger. The husk drinks are the ones worth travelling for; they are effectively unavailable outside a Yemeni house, they carry far less caffeine than a brewed coffee, and they taste like a spiced fruit infusion rather than like coffee at all. Harazi mufawar takes coffee with cardamom and cream for something richer. Sana'ani is the plain, excellent version: black coffee, cardamom, nothing else. The tea side runs adeni karak chai with the house haraz spice blend and cream, plus a saffron version.

The hours run to ten most nights and eleven on Friday and Saturday, opening at seven in the morning. That covers both ends of a student day, and the venue programmes the room rather than leaving it to fill itself — a Mahjong and Matcha evening ran in August 2026, which is precisely the sort of thing that turns a cafe into a place people arrange to meet.

The Philadelphia Inquirer has tracked the city's Yemeni coffeehouse boom closely, and described these rooms as operating without alcohol or reservations. Both halves are the point: nothing to book, nothing on the back bar.

On alcohol the evidence is the menu and the halal, Muslim-owned character of the business rather than a statement in those words from the venue. Caffeine is the only active ingredient served — no kava, no kratom, no THC. Note that this is one of two Haraz rooms in Philadelphia; the Fishtown location keeps later hours.
venues.pressQuote: without alcohol or reservations

venues.name: Hard Shake
venues.description: Hard Shake is the cocktail lounge on the 23rd floor of Waldorf Astoria Las Vegas, opened in March 2025 as part of a redesign that replaced the hotel's former SkyBar and introduced the tea lounge Peacock Alley alongside it. The bar is named for the hard shake, the stylised three-point shaking technique developed by the Japanese bartender Kazuo Uyeda, and the room is built to match that emphasis on precision: a custom mosaic tile floor, deep indigo banquettes curving along the perimeter with Art Deco detailing, a marbled dark stone bar trimmed in champagne brass, and gold-illuminated fixtures overhead, all set against floor-to-ceiling windows over the Strip. Signature drinks include The Katana, which combines Hibiki Harmony whisky with house-spiced Drambuie and pecan bitters. For guests not drinking, the Las Vegas Convention and Visitors Authority named the Reverie, made with sparkling watermelon and lime, among seven must-try spirit-free drinks in the city. A late-night menu of elevated bites runs alongside the drinks.
venues.address: 3752 S Las Vegas Blvd, Las Vegas, NV 89158
venues.longDescription:
Hard Shake opened in March 2025 on the 23rd floor of Waldorf Astoria Las Vegas, part of a full redesign of that floor which turned the hotel's former SkyBar into a pair of new rooms — this bar and the adjoining tea lounge Peacock Alley. The name is a piece of bartending history rather than a pun: the hard shake is the stylised three-point shaking technique developed by Kazuo Uyeda, the Japanese bartender whose Tokyo bar Tender made the method famous, and the whole room is designed around that idea of precision as craft. The space has a custom mosaic tile floor, deep indigo banquettes curving along the perimeter with Art Deco detailing, a marbled dark stone bar punctuated with champagne brass, and gold-illuminated fixtures casting a low, warm light — all of it set against floor-to-ceiling windows with an unobstructed view down the Strip. A late-night menu of elevated bites runs alongside the drinks, from Wagyu sliders and caviar to a signature honey shrimp served with honey citrus curry, candied walnuts and chili thread.

The cocktail list is bold and technique-forward, built around drinks like The Katana, which combines Hibiki Harmony whisky with house-spiced Drambuie and finishes with pecan bitters. The spirit-free side of the program is smaller than the list at somewhere like Alexxa's, and it is worth being clear about that: this is a bar with capable bartenders who make a good non-alcoholic drink rather than a bar running a long dedicated zero-proof menu. What is documented is the Reverie, a mixologist-designed build of sparkling watermelon and lime, which the Las Vegas Convention and Visitors Authority's own guide named among the seven must-try spirit-free drinks in the city. For a guest who wants a quiet, genuinely upscale room high above the Strip — one where the view is the point, the light is low, and nobody is going to make an issue of what is in your glass — it is one of the better options in this part of town.
venues.pressQuote: Sip this mixologist-designed combination of sparkling watermelon and lime while admiring the lights of the Strip from this elegant 23rd floor space.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Visit Las Vegas, "Seven Must-Try Mocktails in Las Vegas"

venues.name: Harley & Rose
venues.description: Harley & Rose is a wood-fired pizzeria, natural wine bar and bottle shop on Barkly Street in West Footscray, and its drinks list carries both a MOCKTAILS heading and a separate ZERO PROOF shelf. The three house mocktails are made from scratch: a Lemon Leaf Sour on house-made lemon leaf cordial and lemongrass; a Pine-Lime Splice of apricot, pineapple, lime and falernum; and a non-alcoholic mulled wine on house-made spiced syrup, which is a genuinely unusual thing to find in a suburban dining room. The zero-proof bottles cover the categories properly - Heaps Normal lager, Heaps Normal High Hopes prosecco, a zero-alcohol Squealing Pig sauvignon blanc, and Altina's Pepperberry shiraz, an Australian de-alcoholised red made in Canberra.
