venues.longDescription:
Juniper opened as Greenville's first gin-centric bar, on the roof above the Paloma restaurant at 315 South Main, and it has one of the more enviable views in the city. It is also the most interesting alcohol-free list in the metro, which is not a coincidence.

Gin is the hardest spirit to do without. Its whole character is botanical — juniper, coriander, citrus peel, root — and the non-alcoholic versions have to work much harder than a zero-proof rum or tequila to be convincing. A bar built around gin has, by necessity, a deep bench of botanical thinking, shrubs, cordials and aromatics, and that is exactly the pantry an alcohol-free drink needs.

The three Zero Proof builds show it. The Juice Bomb runs a watermelon shrub against black sesame seed syrup with lemon, grapefruit and grapefruit soda — the sesame is the unusual move, adding a savoury, nutty weight that stops the fruit dominating. Root For Me is blackberry sauce, ginger and lime cordial, sharper and more direct. The Kiwi Crush uses a kiwi cordial with pineapple, agave and club soda. All three are $10, priced with the rest of the list rather than beneath it.

Worth noting for anyone reading the local coverage: the Greenville Journal has written about Juniper rolling out low-alcohol cocktails under the headline that it should not be called a mocktail programme. That distinction is doing real work — a low-ABV list and a zero-proof list serve different people, and this bar keeps both, which is more useful than either alone.

The hours need planning around. Juniper is closed Monday and Tuesday, does not open until 5pm Wednesday through Saturday, and on Sunday trades only 11am to 3pm.
venues.pressQuote: Juniper, with one of the most enviable rooftop views downtown, offers tasty sips for all.
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: TOWN Carolina, Mocktails for Dry July

venues.name: Juniper's Gin Bar
venues.description: Juniper's is a candlelit gin-and-tapas bar in Covington's MainStrasse Village, built around a collection of 230-plus gins and a rotating, globally inspired small-plates menu. Its drinks list carries a dedicated alcohol-free section called "School Night," so zero-proof drinkers order from a named menu rather than asking for something off-list. Standouts include the Gin and Non-ic, a classic gin and tonic built on non-alcoholic gin; the Dirty Virgin, a virgin gin martini; and the Esspres-sober Martini, made with house-made NA coffee liqueur and cold brew. The vintage-styled room, with antique furnishings and candelabras, hosts live jazz on Friday and Saturday nights plus a Sunday brunch. It's a genuine option for Dry January or any night you want the craft of a well-made gin drink without the buzz.
venues.longDescription:
Juniper's occupies Suite 100 of the historic John R. Green Building at 409 West 6th Street, on the promenade of Covington's MainStrasse Village, across from the Goose Girl Fountain. The vintage-inspired room is steeped in local history, dressed with antique furnishings and candelabras for a speakeasy feel. Gin is the centerpiece: the bar keeps a collection it bills as "230+ gins and counting," paired with a rotating, monthly-changing tapas menu of globally inspired small plates. Live jazz fills the room on Friday and Saturday nights, there's a Wednesday jazz jam, and Sunday brings an elevated brunch.

For non-drinkers, Juniper's does something most gin bars don't — it prints a dedicated alcohol-free section on the drinks menu, cheekily titled "School Night." As LINK nky reported during Dry January, the list runs to creatively named alcohol-free drinks like the Gin and Non-ic, a classic gin and tonic made with NA gin, alongside the Dirty Virgin, a virgin gin martini, and the Esspres-sober Martini, built with house-made non-alcoholic coffee liqueur and cold brew. The house-made NA liqueur signals real kitchen effort rather than a token substitution, and the section gives sober and sober-curious guests a named menu to order from instead of asking the bartender to improvise.

Juniper's is generally open Wednesday and Thursday 4–11pm, Friday and Saturday 4pm–midnight, and Sunday 10am–9pm, closed Monday and Tuesday; reservations are available via Resy and by phone at (859) 291-4466. Follow @juniperscov on Instagram for menu changes and jazz lineups. One caveat worth knowing: while the School Night section is a genuine standing part of the menu, the specific NA gin brand isn't published online and the drinks list rotates, so confirm current pours when you visit. For anyone doing Dry January, driving, or simply wanting the ritual of a well-made gin drink without the alcohol, it's one of Northern Kentucky's more thoughtful zero-proof stops.
venues.pressQuote: they also offer tons of other options, including their 'School Night' menu full of creatively named alcohol free drinks like the 'Gin and Non-ic' a classic gin and tonic made with NA gin

venues.name: Kadence
venues.description: One-Michelin-star, nine-seat omakase and sake bar in Audubon Park where non-drinkers get real alcohol-free pours alongside the renowned sake list, including Copenhagen Sparkling Tea and a matcha milk tea. It's a tiny room with an outsized reputation, run by owners who are both certified sake professionals.
venues.address: 1809 E Winter Park Rd, Orlando, FL 32803
venues.hours: Mon, Tue, Wed, Fri, Sat 4:00 PM-8:00 PM; Sun 9:00 AM-12:00 PM (brunch); closed Thu
signatureDrinks: Copenhagen Sparkling Tea - Green (sencha, green tea, citrus)
Matcha Milk Tea (matcha green tea, soy milk)
venues.longDescription:
Kadence began in 2014 as Kappo, a seven-seat sushi counter tucked into Orlando's East End Market. After outgrowing that space, owners Mark and Jennifer Berdin — University of Florida alumni who trained in Michelin-starred kitchens in New York and London — reopened nearby as Kadence, a nine-seat sushi and sake bar in the Audubon Park Garden District, alongside co-owner Lordfer Lalicon. The restaurant earned its first Michelin star in Florida's inaugural 2022 guide and has retained it every year since, holding the star again in the 2026 MICHELIN Guide Florida for a fifth consecutive year. It was also named Orlando Sentinel's Restaurant of the Year in 2023.

Both Berdins are Advanced Sake Professionals, and their curated sake list anchors the beverage program, but Kadence also stocks non-alcoholic pours for guests who want a pairing without alcohol, including Copenhagen Sparkling Tea (Green), a 0% ABV sparkling blend of sencha, green tea, and citrus, and a matcha green tea milk tea made with soy milk.

Housed in an unassuming black building that one reviewer said looks more like a pop-up modern art museum than an actual restaurant, Kadence remains one of the hardest reservations in Orlando, seating just nine guests a night for a multi-course omakase built around the highest-quality seasonal fish available.
venues.pressQuote: Kadence is located inside a nondescript black building that looks more like a pop-up modern art museum than an actual restaurant.

venues.name: Kahawa Coffee House
venues.description: Kahawa Coffee House is a fully alcohol-free East African coffeehouse at 120 21st Avenue North, on the edge of the Vanderbilt campus, open until 10pm every night of the week. It opened in September 2025 under owner Zahran Almawali, serving Swahili street food alongside a specialty coffee programme. The drinks list is built around East African and Arabian preparations - Kahawa Chai spiced tea by the cup or pot, Zanzibar dirty chai, Zanzibar black tea, Dallat Qahawa Arabic coffee and Turkish coffee - plus a house line of rose and saffron lattes and a Kahawa Mojito with mango, passion fruit, strawberry and sparkling water. Food runs to sambusas, kaimati and spring rolls. The building is a low tropical hut with golden lion statues at the door. No alcohol is served.
signatureDrinks: Kahawa Chai - traditional spiced tea, by the cup or pot
Zanzibar Dirty Chai - espresso and chai
Velvet Vanilla Latte - rose and vanilla
Kahawa Mojito - mango, passion fruit, strawberry and sparkle
venues.longDescription:
Kahawa opened in September 2025 in a low, rectangular building on 21st Avenue North, hemmed in by the brick of Vanderbilt and Ascension and looking nothing like either of them: the frontage is styled as a tropical hut, a large circular sign marks the door and a pair of golden lion statues sit outside it. Owner Zahran Almawali built the room around East African hospitality, and the name is simply the Swahili word for coffee. The Vanderbilt Hustler covered the opening in January 2026 as a piece of East African culture arriving in the neighbourhood, and The Infatuation added it to its Nashville coverage in October 2025, describing rose and saffron-tinted espresso drinks served alongside Swahili street food.

The menu is worth reading in two halves. The specialty-coffee half is what you would expect - espresso, cortado, cold brew, matcha - but the flavour line is distinctly its own: Africano with coconut milk, Heaven with rose, Signature with saffron, Velvet Vanilla with rose and vanilla, Pink Lady with rose and strawberry. The East African half is the reason to make the trip: Kahawa Chai, a traditional spiced tea sold by the cup or by the pot for a table; Zanzibar Dirty Chai, which is that chai pulled with espresso; Zanzibar black tea; Dallat Qahawa, Arabic coffee; and Turkish coffee, also available by the pot. There is one drink built like a cocktail, the Kahawa Mojito, made with mango, passion fruit, strawberry and sparkling water. Food runs to sambusas, golden-fried kaimati with dips, and spring rolls stuffed with spiced chicken and vegetables. Nothing on the menu contains alcohol. The hours are what make it useful for an evening rather than a morning: 7am to 10pm on weekdays and 8am to 10pm at weekends, which is later than almost every other coffee bar in Midtown, and the pot service is designed for a table of people staying a while rather than a takeaway cup.
venues.pressQuote: serves rose and saffron-tinted espresso drinks along with Swahili street food

venues.name: Kai Po Kava Lounge
venues.description: A Polynesian-owned, family-operated kava lounge and restaurant on the State Street corridor in South Salt Lake, where the owner shares the ancestral history of kava alongside every pour. The fully alcohol-free bar serves traditional kava, an ever-rotating line of flavored kava shots (the guava version and a fall "KavaChata" kava-horchata among them), kava mocktails, and exotic teas, paired with island-style Polynesian plates and desserts. With a DJ spinning relaxed island and old-school West Coast music, it bills itself as "Good Vibes Only" and is one of the few zero-proof social bars in the metro open into the early-morning hours.
venues.address: 1465 S State St #14, Salt Lake City, UT 84115
venues.hours: Mon-Tue closed; Wed 3:30pm-3am; Thu-Fri 3:30pm-5am; Sat 4pm-5am; Sun closed
signatureDrinks: Flavored kava shots (e.g. guava, KavaChata kava-horchata)
venues.longDescription:
Kai Po describes its mission as honoring and sharing the cultural heritage of the South Pacific Islands through the authentic experience of traditional kava and other non-alcoholic beverages. The kava draws consistent praise from guests, who call the shots smooth, strong and well-mixed, and note that the owner personally walks newcomers through kava's history and his ancestral connection to the drink.

Beyond drinks, the lounge leans into a full island-restaurant experience, with mixed plates, fried fish, vilo chicken and lamb, and Polynesian desserts, plus karaoke and space for birthday parties and private gatherings.

venues.name: Kamp Kava
venues.description: Kamp Kava is an alcohol-free kava bar in the All Florida Commerce Center on State Road 7, built around a camping conceit that it commits to completely: an actual camper parked inside the room, a loft strung with hammocks, and a treehouse corner set up with retro video games. It trades from noon to midnight seven days a week. The drinks list runs traditional kava alongside kratom, coffee, kombucha, herbal teas and soft drinks, and the programming is the reason regulars come — themed nights built around anime and Dungeons & Dragons rather than around a bar tab. IMPORTANT for readers in recovery: kratom is served here as well as kava. It is a Southeast Asian leaf whose alkaloids act on opioid receptors, with real dependence and withdrawal risk; kava, a South Pacific root, does not work that way. Ask which one is in the cup.
venues.address: 5011 S State Rd 7 Ste 501, Davie, FL 33314
venues.longDescription:
Kamp Kava occupies Suite 501 in the All Florida Commerce Center on State Road 7, and it commits to its camping conceit more thoroughly than any themed room has a right to. There is an actual camper parked inside. There is a loft strung with hammocks. There is a corner fitted out as a treehouse and stocked with retro video games. It would be easy to read all of that as decoration, but it does a specific job: it gives people something to do with their hands and their evening, which is the hardest problem a room without alcohol has to solve.

The programming follows the same logic. Themed nights run around anime and Dungeons & Dragons rather than around drink promotions, which produces the thing that separates a genuine third place from a shop with chairs — people arriving because of who else will be there. The room trades from noon to midnight, seven days a week, and serves no alcohol at any point.

The drinks list is broad for the category: kava, coffee, kombucha, herbal teas, specialty beverages, soft drinks and snacks. Kava is the ground root of Piper methysticum, a South Pacific shrub, infused in cold water and drunk socially across Fiji, Vanuatu, Tonga and Samoa for around three thousand years. It contains no alcohol whatsoever. The taste is earthy and bitter and it numbs the lips and tongue on the first sip; the effect is mildly sedative and sociable rather than intoxicating in alcohol's sense. Because kava exhibits reverse tolerance, regular drinkers typically need less rather than more, so a first visit is best taken slowly.

Davie is a Broward County town of about 110,000 people with no bar district, no walkable centre and an evening economy that runs to chain restaurants and sports bars. Against that, the fact that it now supports four dedicated alcohol-free rooms — Kamp Kava alongside Kavana, 3rd Space and Davie Kava — is genuinely notable, and Kamp Kava is the one most clearly built for staying several hours rather than stopping in.

One disclosure has to be made plainly. Kratom is served here alongside the kava. The two plants are routinely sold from the same bar across Florida and are frequently spoken about in the same breath, and they are not the same class of drink. Kratom is the leaf of a Southeast Asian tree whose alkaloids act on the opioid receptors; it produces tolerance and a real withdrawal syndrome in regular users, several states prohibit it, and concentrated 7-OH kratom products are under active federal scheduling. Kava does not work that way, and a large share of the people who seek out a kava bar are doing so precisely because of that difference. Ask which one is in your cup.

venues.name: Kan-Kan Cinema & Brasserie
venues.description: Kan-Kan opened on 20 August 2021 in Windsor Park on the Near Eastside and combines a four-screen arthouse cinema with a full brasserie and bar — you can eat a proper dinner, see a restored print or a first-run independent film, and never be in a room organised around drinking. The kitchen was set up under executive chef Abbi Merriss, a five-time James Beard nominee who also oversees Bluebeard, and beverage director Dimitri Morris runs an elaborate cocktail list with a seasonal zero-proof section on it. Indianapolis Monthly singled out the mocktails as equally well crafted, naming the tropical Rupert Holmes, a frothy build of coconut, lime, orange and pineapple soda.
signatureDrinks: Rupert Holmes (coconut, lime, orange, pineapple soda)
venues.longDescription:
Kan-Kan opened on 20 August 2021 at 1258 Windsor Street, on a residential corner of the Near Eastside neighbourhood of Windsor Park, and is a genuinely unusual building: a nonprofit arthouse cinema with several screens, wrapped around a full-service brasserie and bar. The food operation was built under Abbi Merriss, a five-time James Beard Award nominee who also runs the kitchen at Bluebeard, and the beverage program is overseen by Dimitri Morris. The cocktail list is long and specific — a Hollywood Boulevardier on Backbone bourbon, a gin-based 35MM with orgeat and lime — and it is on that same list that the non-alcoholic drinks appear.

Indianapolis Monthly's review is the useful citation here, because it assessed the mocktails against the cocktails rather than mentioning them in passing, and found them equally well made. The Rupert Holmes is the one it named: coconut, lime and orange whipped frothy and lengthened with pineapple soda, which is a piña-colada reference that stops short of being sweet. The zero-proof section rotates seasonally, so the specific drinks change through the year; what stays constant is that they are built rather than poured.

The reason to send a non-drinker here specifically, though, is structural rather than liquid. Almost every good zero-proof list in Indianapolis is inside a bar, which means the evening is still shaped around a bar. Kan-Kan is shaped around a film — you can arrive at 5pm, eat in the brasserie, and be in a cinema by 7pm with a mocktail you actually chose. That makes it one of the better sober date-night options in the city, and it is a short drive from 8th Day Distillery in the Circle City Industrial Complex if you want a drink first. The bar opens at 4pm and the restaurant at 5pm daily; screenings run from thirty minutes after the cinema doors open.
venues.pressQuote: A few PG mocktails are equally well crafted and elegant, especially the tropical Rupert Holmes, a frothy concoction of coconut, lime, orange, and pineapple soda.

venues.name: Kanaka Kava
venues.description: Kanaka Kava has poured ʻawa — the Hawaiian name for kava — from the Coconut Grove Marketplace on Aliʻi Drive since 2001, and serves no alcohol. It is a Native Hawaiian family business, founded by ʻAnakala Zach and carried on by his ʻohana, and the ʻawa is grown and harvested on their own farm on Hawaiʻi Island rather than imported, served fresh in coconut-shell cups. The kitchen turns out traditional plates alongside it — kalua pork, squid lūʻau, poke, baked ʻuala and poi — in a small open-air room a few steps back from the waterfront, with open-mic and live-music nights through the week. ʻAwa contains no alcohol but is psychoactive and mildly sedating.
venues.address: 75-5803 Aliʻi Dr, Suite B6, Kailua-Kona, HI 96740
signatureDrinks: Fresh farm-grown Hawaiian ʻawa, served in a coconut shell
venues.longDescription:
Kanaka Kava has been open since 2001, which makes it older than almost every venue in this directory and older than the American kava-bar scene it is usually filed alongside. It sits in the Coconut Grove Marketplace on Aliʻi Drive in Kailua-Kona, a small open-air room set back from the town's commercial waterfront strip, with limited outdoor seating and a deliberately unpolished feel. It was founded by ʻAnakala Zach and is run now by his ʻohana.

The distinction that matters here is that this is not a bar that buys kava. It is a Native Hawaiian family farm that also runs a bar. The ʻawa is grown and harvested on their own land on Hawaiʻi Island and served fresh in coconut-shell cups, and the same farm-to-table logic runs through the food: traditional Hawaiian plates of kalua pork, squid lūʻau, poke, baked ʻuala and poi, poi bowls topped with fresh fruit and granola, fresh coconut water, kombucha and house POG. Lakea Trask, a Hawaiian farmer and land activist, is among those cultivating the ʻawa and other native crops behind it. In a state where kava's revival is bound up with Native food sovereignty — Hawaiʻi formally recognised ʻawa as a safe traditional food in 2025 — that provenance is the point rather than a marketing line.

As somewhere to spend an evening without alcohol, it works because it is not organised around abstinence. It opens at three and runs to ten or eleven, there is open-mic and live music through the week, and it draws a settled local crowd rather than a resort one. Kailua-Kona is otherwise a town of hotel bars and mai tais; this is the room that is not that, and it has been the room that is not that for twenty-five years.

What to know before a first bowl, because ʻawa is not what most visitors expect. It is drunk in one go rather than sipped, it tastes earthy and peppery, and it numbs the mouth briefly — all normal. The effect builds slowly, so newcomers routinely assume nothing is happening and order again too fast. And the standard caution applies: kava contains no alcohol but is psychoactive, a mild sedative that should not be combined with alcohol or sedating medication, and it is worth not driving straight afterwards. If you are avoiding intoxicants entirely, the food, the coconut water and the POG are all separate from the ʻawa.
venues.pressQuote: It's a small open-air, no-frills eatery set back from Ali'i Drive along the town's commercial waterfront strip.

venues.name: Kann
venues.description: Kann is a live-fire Haitian restaurant from James Beard Award-winning chef Gregory Gourdet, in Portland's Buckman and Central Eastside neighbourhood. After pandemic-delayed pop-up and "Kann Winter Village" yurt iterations beginning in 2020, the permanent restaurant opened in August 2022 and was named the James Beard Award winner for Best New Restaurant in 2023. Its name means cane — sugarcane — in Haitian Creole, a nod to Gourdet's childhood memories of sugarcane vendors in Haiti, and the menu pairs traditional Haitian flavours with Pacific Northwest ingredients while being entirely gluten- and dairy-free. It runs a dedicated zero-proof cocktail programme built on Caribbean fruits, spices and house-made cordials, complemented by its basement bar Sousòl, which gives non-alcoholic drinks the same attention as the alcoholic list. Gourdet is a longtime and vocal advocate for sobriety in hospitality, which is why the programme reads as conviction rather than trend.

venues.longDescription:
Kann is a live-fire Haitian restaurant from James Beard Award-winning chef Gregory Gourdet, in Portland's Buckman/Central Eastside neighborhood. After pandemic-delayed pop-up and "Kann Winter Village" yurt iterations beginning in 2020, the permanent restaurant opened in August 2022. Its name means "cane" (sugarcane) in Haitian Creole, a nod to Gourdet's childhood memories of sugarcane vendors in Haiti. The menu pairs traditional Haitian flavors with Pacific Northwest ingredients and is entirely gluten- and dairy-free. Kann won the 2023 James Beard Award for Best New Restaurant, was named the #1 Best New Restaurant in America by Esquire, and later placed #27 on North America's 50 Best Restaurants (2025).

Gourdet, who has been sober for over 15 years, treats the non-alcoholic program as a co-equal part of the beverage list rather than an afterthought, with the NA wines, ciders and cocktails listed on the first page of the drink menu alongside their full-proof counterparts. Verified zero-proof cocktails on Kann's own menu include AN LÒ (pineapple, yellow bell pepper, ginger, lime), ANME DOUS (hibiscus, lime, mint, clove, n/a juniper spirit, ginger), SOUF TWOPIK (papaya and passionfruit tea, lime, pineapple, soursop nectar), KOWOSÒL (soursop nectar, coconut milk, lemon, maple), and KANN KOLA (a house Haitian spice blend, coffee caramel, grapefruit spirit, lime, sparkling). The downstairs bar Sousòl extends the same philosophy with its own deep roster of non-alcoholic drinks, landing on Esquire's 2023 Best Bars in America list.
venues.pressQuote: Arguably Portland's most famous working chef, Kann owner Gregory Gourdet has been a staunch and vocal advocate for sobriety in the hospitality industry for years. So, it makes sense that the Haitian restaurant's moody, stylish basement bar, Sousòl, would put just as much thought into its NA offerings as its boozy ones.

venues.name: Karben4 Brewing
venues.description: Karben4 is a Madison brewery on Kinsman Boulevard on the far east side, and its taproom is on this list because the non-alcoholic side of the bar is stocked with intent rather than improvised. It is home to Wisco Pop soda — the Viroqua-made craft soda built from whole, organic ingredients — and to Sparkle unsweetened sparkling waters, both of which Visit Madison names in its guide to drinking alcohol-free in the city. In a taproom, having a genuinely good soda on tap rather than a gun-poured cola is most of what a non-drinker needs. Hours run afternoons and early evenings, closing at 8pm or 9pm.

venues.longDescription:
Karben4 has been one of Madison's better-known independent breweries for over a decade, operating out of a building on Kinsman Boulevard on the far east side near the airport — an industrial-park location that has become a genuine destination taproom rather than a production site with a bar attached. Its Fantasy Factory IPA is close to a Madison default order.

The reason it belongs in an alcohol-free guide is unglamorous and, for a taproom, exactly right. Visit Madison's own guide to non-alcoholic drinking in the city names Karben4 as the home of Wisco Pop soda and Sparkle unsweetened sparkling waters. Wisco Pop is made in Viroqua in the Driftless Area from whole organic ingredients — real ginger, real fruit, cane sugar rather than syrup concentrate — and it is a serious drink in its own right rather than a concession. Sparkle covers the other half of the problem, the person who wants something with bubbles and no sugar at all and is tired of being handed a soda water with a sad lime. Neither is a mocktail, and that is the point: in a room where everyone else is drinking a pint, the thing a non-drinker most often wants is a good cold drink they can hold for an hour, not a construction with six ingredients.

For planning, the hours are early: 2pm to 8pm Monday through Wednesday, 2pm to 9pm Thursday, noon to 9pm Friday and Saturday, noon to 6pm Sunday. It is a fifteen-minute drive from downtown and not walkable from anything else in this guide, so treat it as a destination — which it is, with a food menu, board games and a room that fills with families early in the evening. Be clear that this is a brewery: beer is the product, the alcohol-free offer is a well-chosen shelf rather than a programme, and the strength rating here reflects that.
venues.pressQuote: Karben4 is home to Wisco Pop Soda and Sparkle unsweetened waters, made with whole, organic ingredients.

venues.name: Karuna Kava & Tea
venues.description: Karuna Kava & Tea opened in Garden City in 2022 as Idaho's first kava bar, and it exists because of its owner's sobriety: Ben McQueen started the business on his own path out of drinking, and he and Kayleigh McQueen run it as a third space where people can gather and connect without alcohol. Nothing alcoholic is served. Kava is brewed fresh in strengths including Strong and Riptide, poured alongside an extensive organic tea list spanning herbal, white, black, green and oolong, locally roasted coffee, chicory coffee and a mushroom blend, kombucha on tap (non-alcoholic, under 0.5% ABV) and locally crafted sodas and switchels from Erth Beverage Co. The room is stocked with board games, books and playing cards, with live music on Saturday nights. Kava is a psychoactive South Pacific root drink — alcohol-free but genuinely relaxing — served to adults.
venues.address: 5220 N Sawyer Ave Unit A, Garden City, ID 83714
venues.longDescription:
Karuna Kava & Tea opened in Garden City in 2022 as the first kava bar in Idaho, and unlike most venues in this directory it has a reason for existing that is stated openly by the person who built it. Ben McQueen started the business as a result of his own path to sobriety, and he and Kayleigh McQueen run it explicitly as a third space — the sociologist's term for the place that is neither home nor work, where people encounter each other without an agenda. In a state where the default social venue is a bar, that intent does real work. The name is the giveaway: karuna is the Buddhist term for compassion, and the company's stated line is relaxation and wellness rooted in compassion. In May 2026 they opened a second room in Meridian, which is what a concept working looks like.

The drinks list is deliberately wide, because a third space fails if half the group has nothing to order. Kava is brewed fresh daily and served in named strengths including Strong and Riptide. Around it sits an extensive organic tea menu covering herbal, white, black, green and oolong; locally roasted coffee alongside chicory coffee and a mushroom blend for anyone avoiding caffeine or wanting something unusual; kombucha on tap, which the bar is careful to note is non-alcoholic at under 0.5% ABV; and locally crafted sodas and switchels from Erth Beverage Co. The room is furnished for staying — board games, books and playing cards on hand — with live music on Saturday nights. Kava itself is worth describing honestly to an audience that includes people in recovery: it is made from the ground root of a South Pacific shrub steeped in water, has been drunk socially across the Pacific for roughly three thousand years, and contains no alcohol whatsoever. It is, however, genuinely relaxing and mildly intoxicating in its own right, and it is served to adults rather than to everyone.
venues.pressQuote: Located in Garden City, Karuna Kava is zero-proof, and designed around the South Pacific Island plant kava
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: City Cast Boise, Bars With Non-Alcoholic Drinks for a Fun Dry January, January 2024

venues.name: Karuna Kava & Tea (Meridian)
venues.description: The Meridian room is Karuna Kava & Tea's second location, opened in May 2026 on East Overland Road after the Garden City original — Idaho's first kava bar — proved the idea worked. Owners Ben and Kayleigh McQueen started the company out of Ben's own path to sobriety and run both rooms as third spaces for people who want somewhere to gather that is not a bar. No alcohol is served. The menu matches the original: kava brewed fresh in named strengths, an extensive organic tea list across herbal, white, black, green and oolong, locally roasted coffee plus chicory coffee and a mushroom blend, non-alcoholic kombucha on tap at under 0.5% ABV, and sodas and switchels from Erth Beverage Co. Being fifteen minutes from Boise in the fastest-growing city in the state, it serves suburban regulars rather than a night-out crowd, running to 11pm daily.
venues.address: 2845 E Overland Rd Ste 180, Meridian, ID 83642
venues.longDescription:
Meridian is the second Karuna Kava & Tea, opened in May 2026 on East Overland Road, and it is the more interesting of the two locations strategically even though Garden City is the original. Ben and Kayleigh McQueen opened that first room in 2022 as Idaho's first kava bar, built out of Ben's own path to sobriety and framed as a third space rather than a business opportunity. Four years later they expanded into Meridian — a suburb that has been among the fastest-growing cities in the United States and which, like most American suburbs, offers people who do not drink almost nowhere to go in the evening that is not a chain restaurant. A second alcohol-free room opening there is a better signal about demand for this category than any market-size report.

The offering carries over from Garden City intact. Kava is brewed fresh daily and served in named strengths. The organic tea list is genuinely extensive, running herbal, white, black, green and oolong, and it is joined by locally roasted coffee, chicory coffee for anyone off caffeine, a mushroom blend, kombucha on tap that the company is careful to specify is non-alcoholic at under 0.5% ABV, and locally crafted sodas and switchels from Erth Beverage Co. The breadth is the point rather than a detail: a room meant for groups only works if the person who does not want kava still has six things worth ordering. Hours run to 11pm every night, which is late enough to be an actual evening out rather than an errand. On kava itself, the plain version for readers in recovery: it is the ground root of a South Pacific shrub steeped in water, drunk socially across the Pacific for around three thousand years, entirely free of alcohol but genuinely sedating and mildly intoxicating on its own terms — a real distinction if you are avoiding intoxicants rather than avoiding alcohol.
venues.pressQuote: Karuna Kava offers premium, sustainably sourced kava and wellness products crafted to promote relaxation, balance, and mental clarity

venues.name: Kasama
venues.description: Kasama is the Filipino bakery and two-Michelin-starred tasting-menu restaurant on the corner of Winchester and Augusta in Ukrainian Village, a counter-service pastry case by day and a reservation-only dining room at night. Its non-alcoholic offering is structured, not incidental: the evening tasting menu is $325, the beverage pairing $195, and a full non-alcoholic pairing is listed at $95, so a table can be split between drinkers and non-drinkers without anyone dropping out of the format. Resy's guide to Chicago's zero-proof cocktails documented the alcohol-free drinks the kitchen has served alongside the tasting menu, including a yuzu highball, the clarified-watermelon Beekeeper and a Toddy-mansi built on genmaicha tea and calamansi juice. The restaurant also holds a 2023 James Beard Award.
signatureDrinks: Beekeeper (clarified watermelon, lemon, honey - documented by Resy, 2022)
Toddy-mansi (genmaicha tea, calamansi juice - documented by Resy, 2022)
venues.longDescription:
Kasama runs two businesses out of one corner building in Ukrainian Village. From Wednesday to Sunday, 9am to 3pm, it is a counter-service Filipino bakery and cafe - longganisa breakfast sandwiches, ube crinkle cookies, pastries - with the kitchen and dining room open until 2pm or capacity. From Thursday to Sunday evening it converts into a reservation-only fine-dining room serving a Filipino-inspired tasting menu at $325. The restaurant holds two MICHELIN stars as of 2025, won a James Beard Foundation Award in 2023 and appeared on North America's 50 Best Restaurants in 2025, and it is the rare Chicago room that carries that weight while still selling coffee and pastry over a counter in the morning.

For non-drinkers the significant fact is the pairing structure. Kasama publishes three prices against the tasting menu - the menu itself at $325, a beverage pairing at $195 and a non-alcoholic pairing at $95 - which puts the alcohol-free option on the same page and in the same format as the wine. That is a materially different proposition from a restaurant that will improvise something if asked: it means the kitchen has designed a full sequence of drinks to run the length of the meal. Resy's November 2022 guide to the city's non-alcoholic cocktails documented what that has looked like in practice, describing a bright yuzu highball, a Beekeeper built as a riff on a bee's knees with clarified watermelon, lemon and honey, and a Toddy-mansi, an alcohol-free hot toddy of genmaicha tea and calamansi juice, plus an Ube Fizz using a distilled non-alcoholic spirit. Those specific drinks date from 2022 and the pairing changes with the menu, so treat them as an indication of the house style rather than a current order list; the $95 pairing itself is listed on the restaurant's own site today.
venues.pressQuote: At Kasama, pair the award-winning Filipino tasting menu with alcohol-free cocktails, including a bright and refreshing yuzu highball; the Beekeeper, a riff on a bee’s knees with clarified watermelon, lemon, and honey; and a Toddy-mansi, an alcohol-free hot toddy with genmaicha tea and calamansi juice.

venues.longDescription: Opened in 2018 on Hudson Street by Tokyo native Masahiro "Masa" Urushido (co-author of "The Japanese Art of the Cocktail") with partners Greg Boehm and James Tune, Katana Kitten channels the spirit of Tokyo's Golden Gai dive bars through a Japanese-American lens, its split-level rooms decked in Japanese film posters, Americana trinkets and dollar bills tucked into hanging lights. The bar was named America's Best New Cocktail Bar at Tales of the Cocktail in 2019 and has placed repeatedly on The World's 50 Best Bars list. The cocktail program leans on highballs, boilermakers and Japanese-inflected signatures, served alongside sake, beer, wine and Japanese whisky. Non-drinkers get a genuine option rather than an afterthought: a named no-ABV Hojicha Carajillo built on non-alcoholic agave spirit with Kyoto hojicha, milk, piloncillo, lemon and chili; non-alcoholic beer (Good Time IPA or Pilsner); and signature highballs such as the Shiso Gin & Tonic and Yokocho Paloma that can be made alcohol-free with Seedlip Garden, Seedlip Notas de Agave or Seedlip Spice.
venues.pressQuote: None do them as well as Katana Kitten, a two-floor West Village bar that should be on your short list.

venues.name: Kato
venues.description: Kato is a two-Michelin-starred Taiwanese-American tasting-menu restaurant at Row DTLA, promoted from one star to two in the 2026 guide, from chef and co-owner Jonathan Yao — who won the James Beard Award for Best Chef: California in 2025. It opened in a Sawtelle strip mall in 2016 and moved to its current 4,000-square-foot Arts District room in February 2022. The main dining room tasting menu is $325 and an abbreviated bar tasting is $185. Its non-alcoholic offering is one of the most ambitious in America: a dedicated Alcohol-Free Flight at $120, described as a progression of alcohol-free beverages created by the bar team, and priced as a genuine peer to the $145 traditional wine flight rather than a discount alternative. Bar director Austin Hennelly, who built it, believes it is the largest alcohol-free wine, beer and ready-to-drink list of any bar in the country. Documented drinks include the Garden Tonic — bitter melon and Korean cucumber, clarified and force-carbonated with white tea — and an amazake swizzle. Guests must be 21 or over to sit at the bar.
venues.address: 777 S Alameda St, Building 1, Suite 114, Los Angeles, CA 90021

naMenuItems.name: Alcohol-Free Flight
naMenuItems.description: a progression of alcohol free beverages created by our bar team.

venues.longDescription:
Kato began in a Sawtelle strip mall in 2016 and moved to Row DTLA in February 2022, into a 4,000-square-foot room. Chef and co-owner Jonathan Yao won the James Beard Award for Best Chef: California in 2025, and in June 2026 the Michelin Guide promoted the restaurant from one star to two — a correction worth noting, since most write-ups still call it one-starred. The cooking is Taiwanese-American and highly personal; the main dining room runs a tasting menu at $325, with an abbreviated bar tasting at $185, and an 18% fair-wage and operational fee applied in place of tipping. It is a strict room in some respects: no children in the dining room, no substitutions for a long list of dietary requests, and the bar is 21-and-over.

The reason Kato matters to a non-drinker is that it may run the most serious alcohol-free programme in an American restaurant. There is a dedicated Alcohol-Free Flight at $120, described on the menu as a progression of alcohol-free beverages created by the bar team — and the number to hold it against is the traditional wine flight at $145. That gap is small enough to say something: the non-alcoholic pairing is priced as a peer, not a consolation, which is almost unheard of. It is the work of bar director Austin Hennelly, who came from Majordomo, Booker and Dax, Amor y Amargo and Maison Premiere, and who believes his is the largest alcohol-free wine, beer and ready-to-drink cocktail list of any bar in the country. The drinks justify it. The Garden Tonic — a constant on the menu — takes bitter melon and Korean cucumber from a San Diego County farm, clarifies the juice, steeps it with bai mu dan white tea, sweetens it with cane syrup and force-carbonates it. The amazake swizzle builds fermented rice against masala chai, Thai coconut milk, almond and lime over crushed ice. Derek Brown, who has written a book on the subject, called it flatly the best non-alcoholic cocktail programme he had ever seen. One correction to our earlier entry: we described a "near-100-option" list; we could not source that figure anywhere and have replaced it with Hennelly's own claim, which is checkable.
venues.pressQuote: We sat at the bar and each NA cocktail came at the perfect temperature, in the perfect glassware, and with a level of detail I had only seen in the best cocktail bars and restaurants in the world. For sure, the best non-alcoholic cocktail program I've ever seen.

venues.name: Kava Chris
venues.description: Kava Chris is a small alcohol-free kava bar at 2601 West Hampden Avenue in Sheridan, in the Denver metro, open unusually late — 9am to 2am on weekdays and to 4am on Saturday, with complimentary pool tables. Its menu is short and cheap: a single shell of kava (10oz) is $8, a double (16oz) is $15, a specialty kava is $9 and an extract is $8. Boba is $2 and a lime or lemon 50 cents, with seventeen house syrups — from lavender and orgeat to passion fruit, salted caramel and Swiss chocolate — at 50 cents each. Food is minimal: ramen at $2, chips at $1. ALCOHOL-FREE BUT NOT SUBSTANCE-FREE: alongside the kava it serves kratom, listed plainly under its own "Kratom Tea" heading rather than under a euphemism — green, white or red at $8, or an extract at $10. PLEASE NOTE: unlike some other Colorado kava bars, we could find no published dosage guidance, age policy or health warning anywhere on its website, even though Colorado law requires kratom sales to be 21-and-over with photo ID. Ask at the counter before ordering.
venues.address: 2601 W Hampden Ave Ste b, Sheridan, CO 80110

venues.longDescription:
Kava Chris is a small, unpretentious kava bar on West Hampden Avenue in Sheridan, inside the Denver metro, run by an owner known to regulars simply as Chris. It keeps the kind of hours that make it genuinely useful rather than merely available: nine in the morning until two the next morning on weekdays, and until four on Saturday. There are complimentary pool tables. It is not trying to be a cocktail bar with kava in it — the menu is deliberately short and priced accordingly, which in a category prone to $14 drinks is worth saying out loud. A single shell of kava, ten ounces, is $8; a double, sixteen ounces, is $15; a specialty kava is $9 and an extract $8. Boba is $2 and a wedge of lime or lemon fifty cents. Seventeen house syrups are available at fifty cents each, running from lavender, peppermint and orgeat to passion fruit, salted caramel and Swiss chocolate, which is how the specialty drinks get built. Food is minimal and cheap: ramen at $2, chips at $1.

Two things to know, one of them a caution. The first is that this is an alcohol-free bar rather than a substance-free one, and it is refreshingly direct about that — the kratom is listed under a heading that says exactly "Kratom Tea", offered in green, white or red at $8 or as an extract at $10, with none of the euphemisms other venues use, no "Mitra tea" or "K-tea" to decode. If you are avoiding kratom you will have no difficulty identifying it here, which is more than can be said for several bars in this guide. The caution is what is missing. We could find no dosage guidance, no strength information, no stated age policy and no health warning anywhere on the bar's website — not on the menu, not on the About page, not on the Contact page. That is a notable absence given that Colorado law requires kratom to be sold only to people 21 and over with photo identification, and that 2025 legislation added further limits on potency and product form. The requirement presumably applies in the room; it simply is not published anywhere a customer could read it in advance. For a first visit, particularly if you are in recovery, ask the staff directly what is in a drink and how strong it is before ordering.

venues.name: Kava Collective
venues.description: Kava Collective is a fully alcohol-free kava lounge, tea house, and café in San Diego's University Heights, formerly known as Rooted Kava Bar. It bills itself as Southern California's premier kava destination and one of the only bars in the country still making kava in the traditional South-Pacific fashion, brewing small batches with strains sourced from Fiji and serving them in shells, quads, or the half-gallon "Otter" and gallon "Whale" sharing bowls poured from a traditional tanoa. Beyond kava, the menu spans kombucha, espresso and matcha lattes, and house non-alcoholic drinks like the Fake ID (adaptogen-infused kava mocktail), Java Kava, Afterglow, and Antidote. It's open late — to 1am weekdays and 2am weekends — with live music, art shows, yoga, and bingo nights.
venues.longDescription:
Kava Collective occupies a University Heights storefront on University Avenue and is, by its own account and by most local reckoning, Southern California's premier kava destination. It trades today under a name it took after operating as Rooted Kava Bar, and it is fully alcohol-free — a lounge, tea house and café in one room, open to 1am on weeknights and 2am at weekends, which is a genuine bar schedule rather than a café one. What sets it apart from most American kava bars is the preparation. It is one of the few rooms left in the country still making kava in the traditional South Pacific fashion, brewing small batches quart by quart rather than reconstituting instant powder, and it works across strains from Fiji, Vanuatu, the Solomon Islands, Hawaii, Samoa and Papua New Guinea rather than pouring a single house blend.

The service formats follow the tradition too. Kava comes by the shell or the quad, and for groups there are the half-gallon "Otter" and gallon "Whale" sharing bowls, poured from a traditional tanoa — the carved wooden bowl that anchors a kava circle across the Pacific. Around that sits a wider non-alcoholic list: kombucha, espresso and matcha lattes, and house builds including the Fake ID, an adaptogen-infused kava drink, plus Java Kava, Afterglow and Antidote. The room programmes heavily, with live music, art shows, book signings, yoga and bingo nights, which is what turns a kava bar from a place you try once into one you belong to. Kava deserves plain description for readers in recovery: it is the ground root of a South Pacific shrub steeped in water, containing no alcohol whatsoever and drunk socially across the Pacific for roughly three thousand years — but it is genuinely relaxing and mildly intoxicating in its own right, which matters if what you are avoiding is intoxication generally rather than alcohol specifically.
venues.pressQuote: Our expansive menu showcases kava in all its versatile glory, from traditional preparations to innovative fusion creations

venues.name: Kava Cove Lounge
venues.description: Kava Cove has been family owned and operated on West Fairbanks Avenue since 2016, which makes it one of the longest-running kava rooms in the Orlando metro, and Orlando Weekly named it Best Kava and Kratom Bar in its Best of Orlando 2024 awards. It opens at 11:30am daily and runs to midnight, stretching to 2am from Thursday through Saturday, with a daily happy hour from 4pm to 7pm at 25% off everything except canned drinks. The room is programmed with community events through the week. No alcohol is served. The drinks list spans traditional kava alongside a wide range of house builds, plus kratom drinks and kombucha on tap, and a cold case of canned options for anyone who wants something familiar.
venues.address: 2020 W Fairbanks Ave #100, Winter Park, FL 32789
venues.longDescription:
Kava Cove has been family owned and operated on West Fairbanks Avenue in Winter Park since 2016, which makes it one of the longest-running kava rooms in the Orlando metro and one of the few anywhere in Florida still run by the people who opened it. Orlando Weekly named it Best Kava and Kratom Bar in its Best of Orlando 2024 awards, calling it the paper's local favourite and noting the kratom drinks and kombucha on tap alongside the kava.

It opens at 11:30am every day and closes at midnight, stretching to 2am from Thursday through Saturday, with a daily happy hour from 4pm to 7pm at 25% off everything except canned drinks. That happy hour is worth noting for what it signals: a room pricing to fill an early evening, which is the hardest slot for an alcohol-free venue and the one that most closely substitutes for going to a bar after work.

The drinks span traditional kava alongside a range of house builds, with a cold case of canned options for anyone who wants something familiar in their hand. Kava is the ground root of Piper methysticum, a shrub native to the South Pacific, prepared as a cold water infusion and drunk socially across Fiji, Vanuatu, Tonga and Samoa for roughly three thousand years. It contains no alcohol. It tastes earthy and bitter and numbs the lips and tongue on the first mouthful; the effect is mildly sedative and sociable rather than intoxicating in the sense alcohol is. Because kava exhibits reverse tolerance, regular drinkers typically need less rather than more, so a first visit is best paced across an hour or two rather than rushed.

The room programmes community events through the week, and Winter Park — an affluent, walkable town immediately north of Orlando with a dense restaurant and bar scene along Park Avenue — is a genuinely useful place for it to sit. Anyone who has stopped drinking in Winter Park has otherwise been choosing between a coffee shop that closes at 6pm and a wine bar.

A note for readers in recovery: kratom is served here alongside the kava. Orlando Weekly's 2024 write-up lists kratom drinks on the menu, and the paper's own award category names both. Across Florida the two are usually poured from the same bar, and the difference matters — kratom is a Southeast Asian leaf whose alkaloids act on the opioid receptors, carrying tolerance and withdrawal risk that kava does not, and it is banned outright in several US states. If your reason for seeking out a kava bar is that you are avoiding substances with dependence potential rather than alcohol alone, order by name and ask at the counter which drinks contain kratom.
venues.pressQuote: Our local favorite is Kava Cove Lounge, which also offers kratom drinks and kombucha on tap, in addition to various kava drink options
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: Orlando Weekly, Best of Orlando 2024: Best Kava and Kratom Bar

venues.name: Kava Culture | Clearwater
venues.description: The Clearwater branch of Kava Culture sits on the US 19 corridor in north Pinellas and keeps the longest hours of the group's Tampa Bay rooms — 9am to 2am, every day of the week. It serves no alcohol. Pinellas County is the densest kava territory in the United States, and this is the northern anchor of it, well away from the St. Petersburg clusters where most of the county's kava bars sit. The drink is hand-brewed kava, customisable with botanical infusions. IMPORTANT for readers in recovery: those infusions are mostly kratom, sold under white, green, red and yellow vein names, plus kanna. Kratom acts on opioid receptors and carries dependence and withdrawal risk that kava does not — a distinction worth one question before you order.
venues.longDescription:
The Clearwater branch of Kava Culture sits on the US 19 corridor in north Pinellas County and keeps the longest hours of the group's Tampa Bay rooms — 9am to 2am, every day of the week. It serves no alcohol.

Pinellas County is, by a wide margin, the densest kava territory in the United States. St. Petersburg is frequently described as the unofficial kava capital of the country, with dozens of kava bars across the county, and this directory already lists Grassroots, Bula Kafe, Muddy Water, Speakeasy Central and Mad Hatters Ethnobotanical in St. Petersburg alone, plus Low Tide and The Muddy Root down in Gulfport. What Clearwater has lacked is a northern anchor: the county's kava scene is concentrated in its southern half, and the towns along the upper US 19 corridor — Clearwater, Dunedin, Palm Harbor, Safety Harbor — have been comparatively bare. This room fills that gap, and its 2am close makes it a genuine late-night option rather than an early-evening one.

Kava is the ground root of Piper methysticum, a shrub native to the South Pacific islands, prepared as a cold water infusion and drunk socially across Fiji, Vanuatu, Tonga and Samoa for roughly three thousand years. It contains no alcohol. It tastes earthy and bitter, numbs the lips and tongue on the first mouthful, and is mildly sedative rather than intoxicating in the way alcohol is. Kava exhibits reverse tolerance, which means regular drinkers typically need less rather than more to feel it, so a first visit rewards a slow pace across an hour or two.

The group's format is hand-brewed kava customised with botanical infusions, served from a bar counter with room to sit, and it is consistent across every Kava Culture site — which is genuinely useful if you have found one you like and are travelling elsewhere in Florida.

The caution is the same across the whole chain and belongs stated plainly. Those botanical infusions are mostly kratom, sold under white, green, red and yellow vein names, with kanna alongside. The vein colours are strain designations for kratom, not tea varieties, and the wellness framing on the board makes that easy to miss. Kratom is the leaf of Mitragyna speciosa, a Southeast Asian tree; its principal alkaloids act on the opioid receptors, regular use produces tolerance and a genuine withdrawal syndrome, several US states ban it outright, and its concentrated 7-hydroxymitragynine derivatives are under active federal scheduling. Kava carries no comparable dependence profile. If your reason for looking up a kava bar is that you are avoiding substances that can take hold, order the plain kava and ask before adding anything to it.

venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: Gulfshore Life, August 2020, on the Kava Culture group

venues.name: Kava Culture | Downtown Orlando
venues.description: Kava Culture's Robinson Street room sits in the middle of downtown Orlando's bar district and outlasts most of it: 7am to 2am through the week, and all the way to 3:30am on Friday and Saturday. That is the latest alcohol-free close in the city by a wide margin, and it matters on a strip where the alternative at 2am is a queue outside a nightclub. The group serves no alcohol anywhere, and its drink is hand-brewed kava customised with botanical infusions. IMPORTANT for readers in recovery: those infusions are largely kratom, sold under white, green, red and yellow vein names, alongside kanna. Kratom acts on opioid receptors and carries dependence and withdrawal risk that kava does not — the vein colours on the board are the tell.
venues.address: 33 E Robinson St Ste 100, Orlando, FL 32801
venues.longDescription:
Kava Culture's Robinson Street room sits in the middle of downtown Orlando's bar district, and it outlasts almost all of it. Doors at 7am, close at 2am from Sunday through Thursday, and 3:30am on Friday and Saturday. That is the latest alcohol-free close in the city by a wide margin, and it changes what the room is for: at 2am on a Saturday, when the bars on Orange Avenue are turning people out, this is one of the very few places downtown still serving anything at all — and it has never served alcohol.

The group behind it was born in Southwest Florida and has spread across the state, and its format is consistent: hand-brewed kava as the base, built to order with botanical infusions. Kava is the ground root of Piper methysticum, a shrub native to the South Pacific islands, prepared as a cold water infusion and drunk socially across Fiji, Vanuatu, Tonga and Samoa for roughly three thousand years. It contains no alcohol. It tastes earthy and bitter, numbs the lips and tongue on the first mouthful, and is mildly sedative rather than intoxicating in the way alcohol is. Kava also exhibits reverse tolerance, meaning regular drinkers typically need less rather than more to feel it, so a first visit rewards a slow pace across an hour or two.

Downtown Orlando has been comparatively poorly served for alcohol-free rooms given its size — the city's real depth sits south in SoDo and out toward Winter Park — so a late, central, entirely alcohol-free venue on the main nightlife strip does specific work for anyone who wants to be part of a night out without drinking through it.

The caution is the same one that applies across the whole Kava Culture group, and it is worth learning once because the shorthand recurs all over Florida. The botanical add-ons are largely kratom, marketed by vein colour — white, green, red and yellow — alongside kanna blends. Those colour names sound like tea grades and are not. Kratom is the leaf of Mitragyna speciosa, a Southeast Asian tree, and its principal alkaloids act on the opioid receptors; regular use produces tolerance and a genuine withdrawal syndrome, several US states ban it outright, and its concentrated 7-hydroxymitragynine derivatives are the subject of active federal scheduling. Kava carries no comparable dependence profile.

The practical rule at any Kava Culture counter is this: a plain hand-brewed kava is kava, and once you start adding vein colours you are ordering something else. Staff will tell you which is which if you ask, and the room is 18-plus rather than 21-plus, which quietly makes it one of the only genuine late-night options downtown for people not old enough to drink legally.
venues.pressQuote: Launched in Bonita Springs in 2017 by sisters Caroline and Jacqueline Rusher
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: Gulfshore Life, August 2020, on the Kava Culture group

venues.name: Kava Culture | Downtown Tampa
venues.description: The Franklin Street room is Kava Culture's downtown Tampa flagship and one of the few places in the central business district serving anything at 1am without a liquor licence — 7am to 1am through the week, to 2am on Friday and Saturday. The fit-out leans hard into being a destination: downtown skyline views, swinging egg chairs and the chain's signature Kava Life wall. Entry is 18 and over rather than 21, which quietly makes it one of the only genuine night-out options in the city for people too young to drink legally. IMPORTANT for readers in recovery: the menu pairs hand-brewed kava with kratom, kanna and CBD drinks. Kratom acts on opioid receptors and carries dependence risk that kava does not, so read the board before ordering.
venues.address: 514 N Franklin St STE 102, Tampa, FL 33602
venues.longDescription:
The Franklin Street room is Kava Culture's downtown Tampa flagship, and it is one of the very few places in the central business district serving anything at 1am without a liquor licence — 7am to 1am through the week, stretching to 2am on Friday and Saturday. The fit-out is built to be a destination rather than a counter: downtown skyline views, swinging egg chairs, and the chain's signature Kava Life wall, which exists to be photographed and does its job.

One detail quietly matters more than any of that. Entry is 18 and over rather than 21, because kava is not alcohol and the licensing that governs bars does not apply. In a city where every other late-night room on this strip is 21-plus, that makes this one of the only genuine night-out options available to anyone aged 18 to 20 — a group with essentially nowhere to go, and one that includes a lot of people who are not drinking by choice rather than by law.

Kava is the ground root of Piper methysticum, a shrub native to the South Pacific islands, prepared as a cold water infusion and drunk socially across Fiji, Vanuatu, Tonga and Samoa for roughly three thousand years. It contains no alcohol. It tastes earthy and bitter, numbs the lips and tongue on the first mouthful, and is mildly sedative rather than intoxicating in the way alcohol is. Kava exhibits reverse tolerance, meaning regular drinkers typically need less rather than more to feel it, so a first visit rewards a slow pace across an hour or two.

Tampa Bay is the densest kava territory in the United States, and this directory already lists Bula Kavananda in Seminole Heights, Grassroots and Bula Kafe in St. Petersburg, Mad Hatters Ethnobotanical and Low Tide in Gulfport. The Kava Culture rooms extend that into downtown, South Tampa and Clearwater.

The caution for this group is worth learning once, because the shorthand recurs across the whole state. The menu pairs hand-brewed kava with kratom, kanna and CBD drinks, and the kratom is sold by vein colour — white, green, red and yellow. Those colour names read like tea grades and are not. Kratom is the leaf of Mitragyna speciosa, a Southeast Asian tree, and its principal alkaloids act on the opioid receptors; regular use produces tolerance and a genuine withdrawal syndrome, several US states ban it outright, and its concentrated 7-hydroxymitragynine derivatives face active federal scheduling. Kava has no comparable dependence profile. Order a plain hand-brewed kava and you are drinking kava; add a vein colour and you are drinking something else entirely.
venues.pressQuote: Kava Culture serves plant-based drinks made with kava, kratom, kanna, and CBD
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: Ormond Beach Observer, November 2023, on the Kava Culture group

venues.name: Kava Culture Kava Bar — Frisco
venues.description: Kava Culture Frisco opened in January 2026 as a fully alcohol-free kava bar in Frisco Square, open daily from 8am to midnight. The menu is organised into sections including Light & Fruity, Rich & Creamy and Tonics on the Rocks, with named drinks such as the Miami Mule, Ocean Potion, Coastal Melon and Fijian Sunset, plus a Booze Free Flight running through piña colada, bellini, margarita and tiki mule builds. Its botanicals include kava, kratom, kanna and THC — alcohol-free, but not substance-free, and parts of the menu are age-restricted.
venues.longDescription:
Frisco Square is a walkable restaurant district built around the city hall plaza, and since January 2026 it has had an alcohol-free room keeping longer hours than most of its neighbours: Kava Culture opens at eight in the morning and runs to midnight, seven days a week. For a suburb where the evening options are overwhelmingly full-bar restaurants, that is a genuinely different proposition.

The menu is organised like a cocktail list rather than a health-food counter — sections titled Light & Fruity, Rich & Creamy and Tonics on the Rocks, with drinks named Miami Mule, Ocean Potion, Coastal Melon and Fijian Sunset. There is a Booze Free Flight that runs a piña colada, bellini, margarita and tiki mule in miniature, which is a smart way to spend an hour at a table without a drink in hand feeling like a compromise.

The disclosure this venue needs is the strongest in our Dallas listings, and we would rather over-state it than under-state it: alongside kava, the menu carries kratom, kanna and THC drinks, including a THC flight. Nothing served contains alcohol. But this is a psychoactive-botanical bar, not a sober bar, and for anyone in recovery from any substance — or anyone who simply wants a clear head — that distinction is the whole point.

venues.name: Kava Culture Kava Bar — North Fort Worth
venues.description: Kava Culture is a fully alcohol-free kava bar in north Fort Worth, open daily from 8am to midnight and pitched by its own team as a Texas-sized celebration of socializing differently, without booze. The menu covers kava, kratom, kanna and elixir teas, with named drinks including the Island Breeze. No beer, wine or liquor is served. Note that its botanicals are psychoactive — the room is alcohol-free but not substance-free, and parts of the menu are 21+.
venues.address: 3529 Heritage Trace Pkwy Ste 155, Fort Worth, TX 76244
venues.longDescription:
Kava Culture's north Fort Worth location sits on Heritage Trace Parkway and runs the longest hours of any alcohol-free room in this guide — 8am to midnight, every day. That span is the point: it works as a morning coffee stop, an afternoon laptop spot and a late social room, which is the pattern a bar normally serves for people who drink and almost nothing serves for people who do not.

The menu is botanical rather than mocktail-led. Kava anchors it, joined by kratom, kanna and a range of elixir and sparkling teas, with named drinks including the Island Breeze. CultureMap Fort Worth, surveying where to drink during Dry January, described the format as kava root beverages, botanical cocktails, and herbal and sparkling teas — and noted the absence of beer, wine and liquor entirely. The venue's own language is more direct, calling itself a Texas-sized celebration of socializing differently, without booze.

The caveat this directory always makes for kava rooms applies here with more force than most, because the menu reaches further: kava, kratom and kanna are all psychoactive plants, and portions of the list are restricted to 21 and over. None of it is alcohol, and for a great many people that distinction is exactly what they are looking for. But a guest whose sobriety means avoiding all mood-altering substances should treat this as a venue to know about rather than a default — and should know the coffee and tea side of the menu is substantial enough to carry a visit on its own.
venues.pressQuote: kava root beverages, botanical cocktails, herbal and sparkling teas

venues.name: Kava Culture | South Tampa
venues.description: Kava Culture's South Tampa room on Himes Avenue runs a consistent 10am to midnight, seven days a week, which puts it squarely in evening territory in a part of the city where the alternative is the bar strip on South Howard. Like the rest of the group — born in Southwest Florida and now spread across the state — it serves no alcohol and builds its menu around hand-brewed kava with botanical add-ons. IMPORTANT for readers in recovery: the add-on system is largely kratom, sold by vein colour. White, green, red and yellow vein all mean kratom, not kava, whatever the wellness framing on the board suggests. Kratom's alkaloids act on opioid receptors and carry genuine dependence and withdrawal risk; kava does not. Kanna is also on the list. Order deliberately.
venues.address: 4820 S Himes Ave Ste 2, Tampa, FL 33611
venues.longDescription:
Kava Culture's South Tampa room on Himes Avenue runs a consistent 10am to midnight, seven days a week, which puts it squarely in evening territory in a part of the city where the default alternative is the bar strip on South Howard Avenue. SoHo is one of Tampa's densest drinking districts, and a room a few minutes away that is open just as late while serving nothing alcoholic is a direct substitute rather than a consolation prize.

The group was born in Southwest Florida and has spread across the state, and the format is the same everywhere: hand-brewed kava as the base, built to order with botanical add-ons, served from a proper counter in a room designed for sitting rather than collecting. No alcohol is served at any location.

Kava is the ground root of Piper methysticum, a shrub native to the South Pacific islands, prepared as a cold water infusion and drunk socially across Fiji, Vanuatu, Tonga and Samoa for roughly three thousand years. It contains no alcohol. It tastes earthy and bitter, numbs the lips and tongue on the first mouthful, and is mildly sedative rather than intoxicating in the way alcohol is. Kava also exhibits reverse tolerance, meaning regular drinkers usually need less rather than more to feel it, so a first visit is best taken slowly across an hour or two rather than treated like a round of shots.

South Tampa is affluent, residential and heavily bar-served, and it is exactly the sort of neighbourhood where someone who has stopped drinking finds their social life quietly narrowing. A midnight close every night of the week is the specific thing that keeps this room useful — plenty of places will sell a good non-alcoholic drink at 4pm, and almost none will at 11pm.

The standing caution for this group applies here in full, and it is the most important paragraph on this page. The botanical add-on system is largely kratom, marketed by vein colour — white for energy and focus, green for mood, red for relaxation, yellow for strength and stamina — with kanna blends alongside it. That vocabulary is designed to read like a wellness menu, and it works: a customer avoiding kratom can order a green vein in good faith without ever seeing the word. Kratom is the leaf of a Southeast Asian tree, Mitragyna speciosa, whose principal alkaloids act on the opioid receptors. Regular use produces tolerance and a real withdrawal syndrome, several US states prohibit it, and concentrated 7-hydroxymitragynine products derived from it are the subject of active federal scheduling. Kava carries no comparable dependence profile, and a great many people drink it precisely because it does not. Ask what is in the cup.
venues.pressQuote: This is the 14th location for Kava Culture, which makes kava and handcrafted, all-natural botanical cocktails made by Botanical Brewing Co.
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: Ormond Beach Observer, November 2023, on the Kava Culture group

venues.name: Kava DSM
venues.description: Kava DSM closed its downtown Des Moines room on 30 August 2026 and is moving to Waukee. No opening date has been announced, so there is nowhere to visit yet — check before you go. It opened in 2021 as Des Moines' first kava bar, founded by Sarah and Ben alongside David Tracy of Northgate Marketing, and ran for five years as a three-way hybrid: coffee shop, kava bar and eatery in one room on Martin Luther King Jr Parkway. It served no alcohol. The kitchen side ran smoothie bowls, gluten-free waffles, gelato and six ice cream flavours; the bar side ran organic coffee, kava and a mocktail list, with plant-based milks and vegan whip throughout. The new home is the Natural Health Improvement Center wellness campus at 95 NE Dartmoor Drive in Waukee, where the founder also runs her clinic.
venues.address: 300 W Martin Luther King Jr Pkwy #140, Des Moines, IA 50309
venues.longDescription:
Kava DSM is between homes. It closed its downtown room at 300 W Martin Luther King Jr Parkway on 30 August 2026 — five years to the day after it opened — when the owners chose not to renew the lease, and it is moving to the Natural Health Improvement Center wellness campus at 95 NE Dartmoor Drive in Waukee, where founder Sarah Outlaw runs her clinic. She told customers the team was taking a short pause before reopening there, and no opening date had been announced as of early October 2026. Until it reopens there is nowhere to visit, so check before you go. What follows describes the downtown room and the menu it published, as a guide to what should return.

Kava DSM opened in 2021 as Des Moines' first kava bar, at 300 W Martin Luther King Jr Parkway, and it was a genuine three-way hybrid rather than a bar that also did coffee: a coffee shop, a kava bar and an eatery sharing one room. It was founded by Sarah Outlaw — a clinical herbalist and certified health coach with a nutrition background — with her husband Ben and David Tracy of Northgate Marketing, and their stated aim is to let people live their life the way they deserve to live it, to the fullest. The food side is real: paleo almond waffles from $5.50, salads from $9, gelato by the scoop, and a proper coffee programme with house coffee at $2.50 and an all-you-can-drink option at $5.50.

The alcohol-free drinks sit under a heading that says exactly what it means — Mocktails (No Alcohol) — and there are six, built on kava rather than on non-alcoholic spirits. Kavamosa, Kavajito and Kava Kolada are $9; the Kavarita, Kava on the Beach and Kava Tai are $12. The naming tells you the approach: these are kava standing in for the alcohol in a familiar drink, rather than an attempt to imitate a spirit. One limitation to note is that the venue publishes the names and prices but no ingredient lists at all for this section, so you will have to ask what is in them. Alongside them sit smoothies at $9.50 including a Kava Bula Blue of kava, coconut cream, blueberry, banana and blue spirulina, and a set of smoothie bowls at $13.50 that do carry full ingredients. On the botanical question: we checked the menu, the About page and every secondary source we could reach and found no kratom, kanna, blue lotus, THC or CBD anywhere — which is cleaner than most American kava bars. One customer account describes a mushroom cacao coffee with a choice of species, which does not appear on the published menu and may be a specials-board item. No dosage guidance, age policy or health warning is published anywhere; kava is psychoactive, so ask.

venues.name: Kava Garden South of Fifth
venues.description: Kava Garden occupies a ground-floor unit at the very bottom of Collins Avenue, in the South of Fifth blocks below the South Beach party strip, and describes itself simply as a plant-based bar. It serves no alcohol. Hours run to midnight Monday through Thursday and to 1am from Friday through Sunday, which puts it in the same trading window as the cocktail bars a few streets north. The room is built around a garden setting rather than a counter, and the drinks are kava, poured traditionally, plus coffee and teas. IMPORTANT for readers in recovery: kratom is also served here, and the venue gives it a full explanatory section of its own. Kratom's alkaloids act on opioid receptors and carry dependence and withdrawal risk; kava, the South Pacific root, does not work that way. Ask which one you are being handed.
venues.address: 100 Collins Ave # Cu-4, Miami Beach, FL 33139
signatureDrinks: Double House (NA: crushed leaf kratom brew with lemon & agave, 5 oz.)

naMenuItems.name: Double House
naMenuItems.description: crushed leaf kratom brew with lemon & agave, 5 oz.

venues.longDescription:
Kava Garden sits in unit CU-4 at 100 Collins Avenue, the southern tip of Miami Beach, in the South of Fifth neighbourhood — a few blocks and an entire register away from the Ocean Drive strip. The distinction matters for anyone using this directory: South of Fifth is residential, quieter and largely free of the sidewalk hawking that makes the rest of South Beach hard work for someone not drinking. The venue calls itself a plant-based bar, which is an accurate description of the whole proposition rather than a wellness flourish. There is no alcohol on the premises at any point.

The hours are what qualify it as a genuine alternative rather than a daytime cafe. It opens at 10am Monday through Saturday and 11am on Sunday, and closes at midnight at the start of the week, pushing to 1am from Friday through Sunday. That is a bar's schedule in a neighbourhood where the alternative is a bar. The room is arranged as a garden rather than around a service counter, with planting through the seating, and it functions as somewhere to sit for the hour or two that kava actually asks of you rather than somewhere to collect a drink and leave.

The drinks divide into three: traditional kava preparations, coffee, and teas, with the full list published as a PDF menu rather than on the page itself. Kava Garden operates two further Miami Beach sites, including one at 1201 20th Street and a Sunset Harbor location, so the group is a small local chain rather than a single room.

One thing has to be stated plainly, because this directory is read by people in recovery and because Florida kava bars almost universally pour both. Kava Garden serves kratom as well as kava, and gives it a dedicated explanatory section on its own site describing the leaf and its traditional uses. The two are not equivalent and should not be treated as interchangeable. Kava is the ground root of a South Pacific shrub, infused in water, alcohol-free, mildly sedative, drunk socially for around three thousand years and not associated with physical dependence. Kratom is a Southeast Asian leaf whose alkaloids bind to opioid receptors; it carries a real dependence and withdrawal risk, it is banned outright in several US states, and concentrated 7-hydroxymitragynine products derived from it are the subject of active federal scheduling. A large share of the people who seek out a kava bar are doing so precisely because it is not that. Read the menu headers, and ask.

venues.name: Kava House
venues.description: Kava House is Savannah's first kava and nootropic tea café, a locally and veteran-owned room on Bull Street in Thomas Square that serves no alcohol at all. The bar pours traditional kava, kratom and a range of botanical and functional teas, with a short kitchen list of ramen, baked goods, mochi donuts and house chocolate alongside. It is 18-and-over and open 9am to 8pm seven days a week, closing at 6:30pm on Sundays — hours that matter, because they cover the early evening when almost every other alcohol-free option in Savannah has already shut. Kava is mildly psychoactive and kratom is served here too, so this is a night out without alcohol rather than a substance-free room.
venues.address: 1915 Bull St Unit A, Savannah, GA 31401
venues.longDescription:
Savannah has one fully alcohol-free venue and this is it. Kava House opened on Bull Street in the Thomas Square district as the city's first kava and nootropic tea café — locally and veteran-owned, 18-and-over, and built around the idea that a room can be social in the evening without a liquor licence. In a city whose entire visitor economy is organised around to-go cups and bar crawls, that is a structurally different proposition rather than a variation on one.

The menu is kava first: traditional preparations served in the usual way, alongside kratom, botanical teas and functional blends the owners describe as chosen for their effect on mood and focus rather than as flavours alone. A small food list runs to ramen, baked goods, mochi donuts and house chocolate bars. Ordering is available in the room, by phone for pickup, or through the usual delivery platforms, which is unusual for a venue of this type and tells you something about how it is actually used — as much a daily habit for regulars as a destination.

The practical detail that earns it a place at the top of this city's list is the hours. Kava House runs 9am to 8pm six days a week and 9:30am to 6:30pm on Sunday. Savannah's licensed bars with good zero-proof lists mostly do not open until 4 or 5pm, and its cafés close mid-afternoon; this is the one room that bridges the two. If you want somewhere to sit and talk in the early evening without alcohol on the table, this is the only address in the city that answers.

One thing to know before going: kava is mildly psychoactive and kratom is on the menu. For readers in recovery that distinction matters, and the venue is straightforward about what it serves.

venues.name: Kava Kasa
venues.description: Kava Kasa is a kava and tea bar on Cherry Street SE in East Hills, founded by Riccardo Schinina and billed on its own site as Michigan's only kava bar. It serves no alcohol.
