Kava is a root from the South Pacific — Kava Kasa sources its own from Vanuatu — and it is psychoactive: it is drunk for a sedating, mildly euphoric effect, which is worth stating plainly for anyone in recovery who is weighing whether the room is right for them. Drinks are ordered in two steps, a kava grade followed by a mixer, and served in a shell with a spoon. The bar also pours teas and coffee and runs a pizza menu, and it keeps genuinely late hours for a venue with nothing alcoholic behind the bar.
venues.address: 962 Cherry St SE, Grand Rapids, MI 49506
venues.longDescription:
Kava Kasa occupies a storefront at 962 Cherry Street SE in the East Hills neighbourhood, and is the longest-running kava bar in Grand Rapids — earlier local coverage described it as the first in Michigan, and the bar now describes itself as the only one in the state. Founder Riccardo Schinina came to kava after tearing a tendon in his right arm, and built the business around introducing it to a city that had no reference point for it. The kava is sourced from Vanuatu. The ordering system is explained on the menu for newcomers: choose a kava first — everyday, premium, rare, or extract — then choose a "mana", which is the house term for the sweetener, flavour, milk, soda or add-on that goes with it. The result arrives in a shell with a spoon, and the house instruction is to lift the shell, say "Bula!", and drink it quickly. Sediment at the bottom is ground kava root, which is where the kavalactones are, so sippers are told to stir as they go.

The honest framing matters here more than at most venues in this guide. Kava contains no alcohol and Kava Kasa serves none, which is why it registers as a fully alcohol-free room. But kava is a psychoactive plant, taken for a relaxing and mildly euphoric effect, and it is not a neutral substitute in the way a zero-proof spritz is — some people in recovery avoid it deliberately, and it is stocked here as the main event rather than as a curiosity. Beyond kava the bar functions as a tea house and coffee house, and there is a pizza menu, so it is possible to spend an evening there without drinking kava at all. The hours are the other distinguishing feature: 10am to midnight Sunday through Thursday and 10am to 2am on Friday and Saturday, which makes it one of the very few places in Grand Rapids where somebody who does not drink can still be out at closing time. A kava happy hour runs Sunday mornings from 10am to noon with 20 percent off selected items.

venues.name: Kava Kavern
venues.description: Kava Kavern is a kava tea bar on Biscayne Boulevard in Miami's Upper Eastside, in the stretch of MiMo-era buildings north of the Design District, and it runs long days — 10am to 1am, every day of the week, with no alcohol served. Its stated focus is the blending rather than the pour: the bar builds kava tea blends from fresh and organic ingredients, with the flavour combinations composed by its own team rather than bought in. Fifteen hours of daily service in a single room is unusual in this category and makes it one of the more flexible options in a city with a deep kava scene — it works as a mid-morning stop, an afternoon working session and a late-night sit equally well. Kava is a psychoactive South Pacific root drink: alcohol-free, but genuinely relaxing and mildly intoxicating on its own terms.
signatureDrinks: House kava tea blends (fresh and organic ingredients)

naMenuItems.name: Virgin Like a Virgin
naMenuItems.description: create your own mocktail

venues.longDescription:
Kava Kavern sits on Biscayne Boulevard in Miami's Upper Eastside, along the MiMo strip where the mid-century motels north of the Design District have gradually turned into restaurants and bars. It opens at 10am and closes at 1am, seven days a week, and serves no alcohol at any point in those fifteen hours. That span is the most practical thing about it. Most kava bars are evening rooms, which is fine until you want somewhere to sit at eleven in the morning or somewhere to end a night that is not a bar; a venue covering both ends of the day in one place is genuinely useful, particularly in a city where the default social setting involves a drinks list.

What the bar chooses to be known for is blending. Rather than presenting kava as a single traditional pour to be endured for its effects, Kava Kavern builds kava tea blends from what it describes as the freshest and organic ingredients, with the flavour combinations crafted by its own team. That approach addresses the single biggest barrier to kava for newcomers, which is the taste — the root is genuinely earthy and peppery, and the number of people who bounce off it after one shell is not small. Miami has one of the densest kava scenes in the United States, with rooms scattered from South Beach up through North Miami and out to Doral, so a bar here has to be distinct to survive, and a blending-led menu is a reasonable answer. Kava itself deserves the plain description this directory owes its readers: it is made from the ground root of a South Pacific shrub steeped in water, drunk socially across the Pacific for around three thousand years, and it contains no alcohol whatsoever. It is nonetheless a real relaxant with an intoxicating quality of its own, which is a meaningful distinction for anyone whose recovery rules out intoxicants generally rather than alcohol specifically.

venues.name: Kava Kulture LA
venues.description: Kava Kulture LA on Glendale Boulevard in Atwater Village bills itself as Los Angeles's first kava bar, and it is run as a counter-service room where regulars settle into worn couches for conversations that run for hours. No alcohol is served. The menu is deliberately narrow — traditional kava, the house K-Tea, coffee drinks and herbal teas, with no food at all — which keeps it a drinking room rather than a cafe. Happy hour runs 3pm to 6:30pm, and the space doubles as a neighbourhood social hub with open mics for comedy, music and poetry, chess tournaments and tabletop card-gaming meetups. Everyone is welcome in the room and the coffee and tea are served to all ages, but kava itself goes only to guests 18 and over: it is a psychoactive South Pacific root drink, alcohol-free but genuinely sedating. Open to midnight on Friday and Saturday.
venues.longDescription:
Kava Kulture LA sits on Glendale Boulevard in Atwater Village and claims to be the first kava bar in Los Angeles, a city that took a surprisingly long time to get one given how much of its social life already runs on wellness and abstinence. It is counter service, and the defining detail in every account of the place is the furniture: worn couches that people sink into for hours-long conversations. That is a deliberate design choice rather than neglect. The menu is narrow on purpose — traditional kava, the house K-Tea, coffee drinks and herbal teas, and no food whatsoever — which stops it drifting into being a cafe where people work on laptops and keeps it functioning as a room where the point is talking to whoever is next to you. Happy hour runs from 3pm to 6:30pm, and it stays open to midnight on Friday and Saturday nights.

What the room actually trades in is programming. It operates as a neighbourhood social hub, with open-mic sessions covering comedy, music and poetry, chess tournaments, and tabletop card-gaming meetups filling the calendar. For a person who has stopped drinking, that combination — a fixed reason to be somewhere, on a schedule, in a room where nobody is drinking — solves the problem that alcohol-free bars often do not, which is that turning up alone to sit quietly is harder than it sounds. No alcohol is served at any hour. The house policy on age is worth noting because it reflects an honest understanding of the product: everyone is welcome in the space and the coffee and tea menu is open to all ages, but kava is served only to guests 18 and over. That is the right line to draw. Kava is made from the ground root of a South Pacific shrub steeped in water, contains no alcohol at all, and has been drunk socially across the Pacific for around three thousand years — but it is psychoactive and genuinely sedating, which is a distinction worth understanding before your first shell rather than after it.

venues.name: Kava Mama
venues.description: Kava Mama bills itself as Atlanta's first sober kava bar, opened in 2017 by Angie Lizarraga, who discovered kava while supporting her son through alcohol addiction and built the bar around that recovery story. Tucked into the Railyard complex in Mechanicsville, it is strictly alcohol-free, with co-owner Shaun Capuy ("Kava Papa") running it alongside Lizarraga. The draw is traditional, hand-squeezed kava served from a coconut shell and sourced directly from Pacific Island farmers — Fijian, Vanuatu, and Tongan varieties — plus flavored kavas, "Kavaritas," and therapeutic and kratom teas. The space leans cozy and community-first, with a mural of island ceremonies, dog-friendly seating, and a regular calendar of game nights, live music, and talent shows. It was profiled by the Atlanta Journal-Constitution and Fresh Take Georgia as a hub for the city's sober-curious community.
venues.address: 448 Ralph David Abernathy Blvd SW, Suite 6, Atlanta, GA 30312
venues.longDescription:
Kava Mama has been open since 2017 in the Railyard complex at 448 Ralph David Abernathy Boulevard in Mechanicsville, and bills itself as Atlanta's first sober kava bar. Angie Lizarraga founded it after encountering kava while supporting her son through alcohol addiction, and the bar is built around that history rather than around a trend. Co-owner Shaun Capuy, known to regulars as Kava Papa, runs it alongside her. It is strictly alcohol-free.

The kava is the reason to go and the reason it has lasted. It is prepared traditionally — hand-squeezed and served from a coconut shell — and sourced directly from farmers in the Pacific Islands, with Fijian, Vanuatu, Tongan and Papua New Guinean varieties rotating through. Every batch is lab-tested for authenticity, which is not a marketing line in this category: kava quality varies enormously by cultivar and processing, and noble-versus-tudei sourcing is a genuine safety question rather than a connoisseur's distinction. Beyond the traditional preparation there are flavoured kavas, blended Kavaritas, and therapeutic and kratom teas.

The room is small, muralled with island ceremony scenes, dog-friendly and deliberately unslick, with game nights, live music and talent shows on a regular calendar. It is open daily from noon to 11pm. As one regular put it to Fresh Take Georgia, the appeal is having somewhere to simply be at nine in the evening without the evening being about drinking — which is the whole thesis of the place, and the reason the Atlanta Journal-Constitution and Fresh Take Georgia have both profiled it as a hub for the city's sober community.

The standard caution applies and matters here more than most, given who this bar was built for. Kava is psychoactive — a mild sedative and anxiolytic — and should not be combined with alcohol or with sedating prescriptions; it has also been associated with liver concerns in heavy or prolonged use, so speak to a clinician if you take regular medication. Kratom, sold here as tea, is a different substance again, with a more contested risk profile that includes physical dependence. For anyone in recovery, those are distinctions worth making before ordering rather than after.

A practical note for a first visit, since traditional kava is not what most people expect. It is served in a coconut shell, it is drunk in one go rather than sipped, it tastes earthy and faintly medicinal, and it numbs the mouth briefly — all of which is normal and none of which is a sign anything is wrong. The effect builds slowly, so people new to it commonly assume nothing is happening and order again too quickly. Staff here are used to walking newcomers through it; the bar has been doing this since 2017, which is longer than most.
venues.pressQuote: There's not many places you can go to just hang out at like 9 p.m. if you don't want to be around alcohol. We've kind of built a community around that.

venues.name: Kava Republic
venues.description: Kava Republic is a fully alcohol-free kava bar and café on Keawe Street in downtown Hilo, pouring fresh, locally grown ʻawa alongside blended "kavatails", coffee and a shave-ice menu. It opens at nine in the morning and runs to nine or ten at night, which is an unusually long span for an alcohol-free room — it works as a café with wifi during the day and as a bar in the evening. Open mic runs on Thursdays and live music at weekends. Kava contains no alcohol but is psychoactive and mildly sedating, so this is a night out without alcohol rather than a guaranteed sober space.
venues.longDescription:
Kava Republic sits at 301 Keawe Street in downtown Hilo and is the town's fully alcohol-free room. The kava is fresh and locally grown — on an island where ʻawa is a native crop with a long cultural history, and which the state formally recognised as a safe traditional food in 2025, that is a shorter supply chain than almost any mainland kava bar can claim. Around the traditional preparation sit blended drinks the bar calls kavatails, plus coffee and a shave-ice menu, and there is wifi and enough space to actually sit and work.

The opening hours are the quietly remarkable part. Nine in the morning to nine at night Sunday through Wednesday, and to ten Thursday through Saturday. Almost every alcohol-free venue in this directory is one thing or the other — a café that shuts at five, or a bar that opens at five — and the gap between them is exactly the stretch of the day that is hardest to fill if you are not drinking and not working. Kava Republic covers the whole span from the same counter, which means it functions as a morning coffee stop, an afternoon desk, and an evening out without you having to change venues or explain yourself.

The programming leans social rather than wellness. Open mic runs on Thursday evenings, live music at weekends, and there are weekly events besides; the room's own description of itself is chill and social, with plenty of space to hang, and the reviews bear that out. For Hilo — a working town rather than a resort one, where the visitor-facing nightlife is thin and the local nightlife is mostly restaurants and brewpubs — it is the obvious answer to the question of where to go in the evening if the answer cannot be a bar.

The honest caveat, as everywhere kava is served. It contains no alcohol but it is psychoactive: mildly sedating, slow to come on, not to be combined with alcohol or with sedating medication, and worth planning your drive home around. The coffee and the shave ice are separate from the ʻawa if you are avoiding intoxicants entirely, and staff are used to being asked which is which.
venues.pressQuote: The father-daughter duo Laurent and Yaelle Olivier recently opened Kava Republic at 301 Keawe Street.

venues.name: Kava Saia
venues.description: Kava Saia is a fully alcohol-free kava bar on E Burnside in Buckman, open 11am to 1am every day of the year. It pours traditional kava alongside kava sodas, kava shots and kava mocktails, plus herbal teas and kratom, and the space doubles as an art gallery and book nook with a free pool table. The programming is what makes it a bar rather than a tea house — open mics, poetry nights, potlucks and holiday events — and reviewers repeatedly single it out as a community for people who are sober or newly not drinking. It also serves kratom, which is a separate substance from kava with a more contested risk profile.
venues.longDescription:
Kava Saia sits at 616 E Burnside Street, on the Buckman edge of the Central Eastside, and its headline fact is the opening hours: 11am to 1am, seven days a week, every day of the year. That matters more than it sounds. Portland has excellent zero-proof cocktail programmes inside ordinary bars, but those rooms still sell alcohol, and the alcohol-free alternatives mostly keep café hours. A fully alcohol-free room that is still open at midnight on a Tuesday, and open on the holidays when everything else shuts, fills a gap that is real for anyone whose hardest evenings are the late and unstructured ones.

The menu runs deeper than a single preparation. Alongside traditional kava there are kava sodas, kava shots, kava mocktails and clariteas, plus a range of herbal teas and kratom. The room itself is a mix of things — part tea house, part bar, with an art gallery hung on the walls, books to borrow and a pool table that is free to play — which gives an evening here somewhere to put your hands, rather than a table and a drink and nothing else to do.

Programming is the other half of it. Open mic nights, poetry readings, potlucks and holiday gatherings run through the calendar, and the reviews are unusually consistent about who turns up: people looking for somewhere to be sociable without alcohol, including a visible contingent who are sober or recently stopped drinking, in a space regulars describe as clean, welcoming and LGBTQ+-friendly. It is the sort of reputation a venue earns slowly and cannot advertise its way into.

Two things to know before going. Kava contains no alcohol but is psychoactive — a mild sedative that should not be combined with alcohol or with sedating medication, and that is worth planning your journey home around. Kratom, also served here, is a different substance again, with a more contested profile that includes physical dependence with regular use; it is a menu section rather than a technicality, and an alcohol-free room is not automatically a substance-free one. If you are avoiding intoxicants of every kind, the herbal teas are separate from both, and staff are used to being asked which is which.

venues.name: Kava Villa
venues.description: Kava Villa is a fully alcohol-free social lounge in the heart of Wynwood, operating since roughly 2023. Inspired by South Pacific kava tradition and shaped by Miami's nightlife energy, it offers a hangover-free way to unwind, work, or meet friends — open until 1–2am most nights. The menu is built entirely around botanicals rather than alcohol: traditionally prepared kava served by the shell, kratom teas, extracts and shots, in-house-brewed blue lotus tea, botanical wellness elixirs blended for energy, focus or mood, handcrafted mocktails, and espresso drinks. An on-site deli, "The Market," serves sandwiches, bowls, and snacks, alongside retail kava powder and capsules. The lounge hosts weekly community nights and events and holds a Tripadvisor Travelers' Choice award. It serves the Wynwood and Upper Buena Vista neighborhoods.
venues.longDescription:
Kava Villa has operated in the heart of Wynwood since roughly 2023, drawing on South Pacific kava tradition but shaped by Miami nightlife rather than by wellness culture — open until 1 or 2am most nights, and pitched as a hangover-free way to unwind, work or meet people.

The menu is built entirely around botanicals: traditionally prepared kava served by the shell, kratom teas, extracts and shots, blue lotus tea brewed in house, botanical wellness elixirs blended for energy, focus or mood, handcrafted mocktails and espresso drinks. An on-site deli called The Market serves sandwiches, bowls and snacks, and kava powder and capsules are sold to take away.

The food operation is worth noting because it addresses the practical failure of most alcohol-free venues: people leave when they get hungry, and an evening that has to relocate for dinner usually ends at a bar. A room that can feed you keeps the night intact. Weekly community nights and events fill the calendar, and the lounge holds a Tripadvisor Travellers' Choice award, serving both Wynwood and Upper Buena Vista.

The caveat that belongs on every kava listing applies here and should not be softened: kava is psychoactive and sedating, with documented case reports of liver injury, and kratom acts on opioid receptors and carries real dependence and withdrawal risk. Everything served is free of alcohol. That is a narrower claim than nothing served having an effect, and for anyone whose reason for avoiding alcohol is recovery from a substance-use disorder, the difference is the whole question. Wynwood at night is a difficult place to be the person not drinking — the strip is dense, loud and organised entirely around bars — and a room that stays open to 1 or 2am, feeds you and asks nothing of you is a genuinely useful thing to have on it. The Market is the underrated part: an evening that has to move for food usually ends somewhere with a bar.

The same caveat applies as at any kava bar. Kava is psychoactive — a mild sedative — and should not be combined with alcohol or with sedating medication, and kratom, where it is served, is a separate substance with a meaningfully different risk profile including dependence with regular use. For the recovery audience this is not a technicality: an alcohol-free room is not automatically a substance-free one, and it is worth knowing which you have walked into. Ask what is in a drink, and expect a straight answer; the long-running South Florida bars are used to the question.

venues.name: KavaDen
venues.description: KavaDen runs from 9am to 3am every day of the week in a Lakewood strip unit on West Hampden, which makes it the latest-closing alcohol-free room in the Denver metro. The fit-out is a curved bar under neon, with an open layout, comfortable seating and no loud music — built for conversation rather than for volume — and games and puzzles are left out for people to use. It serves no food, so eat first. Happy hour runs 8pm to 10pm daily at half price. IMPORTANT for readers in recovery: alongside kava the menu carries kratom teas and CBD options. Kratom acts on opioid receptors and carries dependence and withdrawal risk that kava does not, so it is worth asking what is in a given cup.
venues.address: 7625 W Hampden Ave Unit 10-11, Lakewood, CO 80227
venues.longDescription:
KavaDen sits in units 10-11 at 7625 West Hampden Avenue in Lakewood, and the single most useful fact about it is the closing time: 3am, every night of the week, from a 9am open. Nothing else in the Denver metro's alcohol-free category stays open that late, and very little in Lakewood of any kind does. For anyone who works nights, keeps unusual hours, or simply wants somewhere to be at 1am that is not a bar, this is the answer on the western side of the metro.

The room has been designed with some care for what it is for. The bar itself is built as a curve rather than a straight run, lit with neon, and the layout is deliberately open with comfortable seating throughout. Music is kept low — the venue's own emphasis is on easy conversation rather than atmosphere-by-volume — and games and puzzles are left out on the tables for people to pick up. The effect that regulars describe is a room where strangers end up talking to each other, which is the specific thing a good kava bar is supposed to produce and the specific thing that is hardest to find without alcohol involved. Happy hour runs from 8pm to 10pm daily at half price, with additional slam specials at 12:34 both am and pm, which tells you something about the humour of the place.

One practical limitation: KavaDen serves no food at all. Plan around that, particularly given the late hours.

The drinks are kava first — the ground root of a South Pacific shrub, infused in water, alcohol-free, earthy, mildly sedative and numbing on the lips, drunk socially across Fiji, Vanuatu, Tonga and Samoa for around three thousand years. Around it sits a range of herbal preparations.

That range needs one honest flag, because this directory is read by people in recovery and the products are not interchangeable. KavaDen's menu includes kratom teas and CBD options alongside the kava. Kratom is the leaf of Mitragyna speciosa, a Southeast Asian tree; its principal alkaloids act on the opioid receptors, regular use produces tolerance and a genuine withdrawal syndrome, several US states ban it outright, and concentrated 7-hydroxymitragynine derivatives are the subject of live federal scheduling action. Kava carries no comparable dependence profile, which is precisely why a lot of people choose it. Both are poured from the same bar here. Ask which one is in the cup before you drink it — the staff will tell you.

venues.name: Kavahana
venues.description: Kavahana is a dedicated kava bar at 306 Pico Boulevard in Santa Monica's Ocean Park, three blocks from the beach, opened in February 2024 by Neil Bhatia — whose family has roots in Fiji, where kava is the national drink — and Hannah Wilen, whose own search for natural remedies for anxiety led her to it. A second room opened in Hollywood in 2026. It pours its own house-made kava nectar rather than third-party products: The O.G. is kava nectar and alkaline water at $9 for a single up to $19 for a quad, and the specialty nectars are $14 — Paradise (mango, pineapple, lime), Ube Coconut, Mexican Chocolate, Mango Lassi, Golden (turmeric, ginger, lemon), Cherry Drop, and Zenergy with Kona coffee and matcha, served until 6pm. Kava lattes run $12–$14 and there is a food menu of ramen, steamed buns and shave ice. IMPORTANT: it serves kava only — we found no kratom, kanna, THC or CBD anywhere, which is unsurprising since California made kratom illegal to sell at any age in October 2025. But note it publishes no dosage figures and no age policy. Open to 1am Friday and Saturday; free parking, dog-friendly patio.
signatureDrinks: The O.G. kava nectar ($9 single, $13 double, $16 triple)
venues.longDescription:
Kavahana opened in February 2024, three blocks from the beach in Santa Monica's Ocean Park, and describes itself as the first kava nectar bar in the country. It comes from Neil Bhatia, whose family has roots in Fiji where kava is the national drink, and Hannah Wilen, who has lived with anxiety for most of her life and began exploring natural remedies about fifteen years ago — a search that led her here. The second half of the name is hers. Wilen is clear about what the room is meant to be, and it is not a bar: they do not want to be a bar and do not want to be a coffee shop either, but a kava nectar bar — somewhere you can sit on the couches and play board games, or sit at the bar, or work and study. An open third space. Her line about the drinks themselves is the sharpest defence of the category anyone has offered: they joke that mocktails are just juice, and kava nectar is something you can actually feel. It opens at eleven most days, ten at weekends, and runs to 1am on Friday and Saturday, with free parking behind and a dog-friendly patio. A second Kavahana opened in Hollywood in 2026.

What it pours is its own house-made kava nectar rather than anyone else's product. The traditional serve, The O.G., is nectar and alkaline water — $9 for a single shell, $13 double, $16 triple, $19 quad, and it is honest about the taste, describing it as the 3,000-year-old way, zero calories, very earthy. The specialty nectars at $14 are where most people start: Paradise with Indian mango, fresh pineapple and lime; Ube Coconut with house coconut foam; Mexican Chocolate with cocoa, oat milk, cinnamon and cayenne; Golden with turmeric, ginger and lemon; and Zenergy, which blends Kona coffee and matcha with the nectar and is served only until 6pm. The Kavahana at $16 arrives as a whole young coconut with a side shot. Lattes run $12 to $14, and there is real food — island ramen, steamed buns, Basque cheesecake, shave ice. On the botanical question: we checked every page and the full online shop and found no kratom under any name, no kanna, no blue lotus, no THC and no CBD. That is partly principle and partly law — California declared kratom illegal to sell for consumption at any age in October 2025. What Kavahana does not publish is any dosage figure, any age policy, or any habit-forming warning; its own guidance is simply to start small and adjust, and its safety article states kava is not considered addictive. Kava is still psychoactive, so treat it accordingly.
venues.pressQuote: We like to joke here that mocktails are just juice and kava nectar is something that you can actually feel.

venues.name: Kavana Kava Bar
venues.description: Kavana Kava Bar is a kava lounge on SW 64th Avenue in Davie, open from 8am daily and running late into the night. Its menu has three parts: brewed and flavoured cold teas, kava drinks sold under "Root Specialties" with names like the Stunner, the T.K.O and the Knock-Out, and a kratom line called "Kraymyx" that includes concentrated extract shots. No alcoholic drink appears on any published menu — but the venue has never described itself as alcohol-free either, and there is no non-alcoholic beer, wine, spirit or mocktail program here. Both kava and kratom are psychoactive, and kratom sales are restricted to adults 21 and over under Florida law, so this is a night out without alcohol rather than a guaranteed sober space.
venues.longDescription:
Kavana Kava Bar occupies Suite 102 at 3890 SW 64th Ave in Davie, in Broward County. It traded as Bula Lounge Kava Bar at the same address before adopting the Kavana name, and a stale listing for the old name — marked closed — still exists elsewhere online for the same street address; the business itself is open, and was confirmed trading through its own live ordering system on 31 July 2026. It is one of several Kavana sites across South Florida, alongside a separate Dania Beach location; each is its own room and they should not be read as interchangeable.

The drink program is built around kava, kratom and tea, with nothing else on it. Kava drinks sit under "Root Specialties" and step up in strength through the Stunner, the T.K.O and the Knock-Out; the house Bulazos, a holdover name from the Bula Lounge era, is promoted on the venue's own Instagram. The "Kraymyx" section is kratom, sold as concentrated extract shots and a bottled extract to take away rather than as brewed leaf tea. Two caveats belong on this listing. The venue has never stated in its own materials that it is alcohol-free — no alcoholic item appears on any published menu, which is a narrower and better-evidenced claim, and the question is worth asking directly if it matters to you. And the psychoactives are not incidental: kava is sedating and has documented liver-injury case reports, kratom acts on opioid receptors and carries real dependence and withdrawal risk, and Florida restricts kratom sales to over-21s. For anyone in recovery, that makes this a different proposition from an alcohol-free cafe.
venues.pressQuote: Kavana Kava Bar specializes in kava, brewed teas, and specialty root drinks like Kraymyx

venues.name: Kavasutra Kava Bar
venues.description: Kavasutra Denver is a fully alcohol-free kava and kratom social lounge on the Capitol Hill / East Colfax stretch, part of the Florida-founded Kavasutra chain and among the first true kava bars within Denver city limits. The house specialty is kava imported directly from Vanuatu and served in traditional "shells," alongside kratom teas, loose-leaf and herbal teas, cold brew coffee, and fizzy kombucha-style drinks. Open daily from 10am to 2am, it functions as a late-night, no-alcohol gathering spot — the kind of place Westword has noted draws people who don't drink or are getting sober. One important caveat: it is alcohol-free but not substance-free — it serves kratom, an active and controversial botanical that some reviewers describe as habit-forming.
venues.longDescription:
Kavasutra Denver is a fully alcohol-free kava and kratom lounge at 1232 East Colfax Avenue, on the Capitol Hill stretch of Colfax, and was among the first true kava bars to open inside Denver city limits. It is one of more than thirty Kavasutra locations across Florida, Colorado and Arizona, a chain that started in South Florida and describes its own offer as fresh, house-made kava alongside kratom and a full lineup of alcohol-free drinks. Kava is imported directly from Vanuatu, where the company points out the ceremonial use of the root goes back thousands of years, and it is served in the traditional way, by the shell, prepared behind the bar rather than poured from a bottle. Around it sits a broader alcohol-free list: loose-leaf organic green, black, oolong and herbal teas, twenty-four-hour cold-brewed coffee, and fizzy kombucha-style drinks.

The reason the bar matters to non-drinkers in Denver is structural rather than culinary. It is open from 10am to 2am every day of the week, which makes it one of very few places in the city where the late-evening social hours are available without alcohol at all; Westword has noted that the room draws people who do not drink or who are getting sober, and the format, low seating, conversation, no table service rush, supports staying for hours. One caveat is important and the bar does not hide it: alcohol-free is not the same as substance-free here. Kava is a psychoactive root with sedative and anxiolytic effects, and the bar also serves kratom, an active botanical that is legally contested in several US jurisdictions and that some regular customers and reviewers describe as habit-forming. Anyone in recovery, or anyone avoiding psychoactive substances rather than alcohol specifically, should treat this as a venue to approach with that information in hand rather than as a straightforwardly neutral alcohol-free room. Practically, the room works best as a late third place rather than as a cocktail substitute: there is no attempt at mixology here, the seating is communal and unhurried, and the appeal is the hours and the absence of alcohol rather than the drinks list.

venues.name: Kavasutra Kava Bar | Lee Road
venues.description: The Lee Road branch of Kavasutra covers the northern side of Orlando, running 8am to 2am every day of the week with no alcohol on the premises. It is the second of the chain's two metro rooms, and like the Semoran site it operates as a bar rather than a cafe: counter service, shells poured to order, long hours, and a regular crowd. IMPORTANT for readers in recovery: Kavasutra describes itself as America's premier kava and kratom bar, and the kratom half of that is a genuine half. Kratom's alkaloids act on opioid receptors, regular use produces tolerance and a withdrawal syndrome, several US states prohibit it, and concentrated 7-OH products face federal scheduling action. Kava does not work that way. Ask which one you are ordering.
venues.longDescription:
The Lee Road branch of Kavasutra covers the northern side of Orlando, between College Park and Winter Park, and runs 8am to 2am every day of the week with no alcohol on the premises. It is the second of the chain's two metro rooms, alongside the Semoran Boulevard site on the east side.

Like the rest of the group it operates as a bar rather than as a cafe. Counter service, shells poured to order, an eighteen-hour trading day, and a crowd of regulars rather than passing trade. Kavasutra's scale — more than thirty locations across the country — means the format is unusually predictable, which is genuinely useful for anyone who travels and does not drink: the room, the menu structure and the way you order are the same wherever you find one.

Kava is the ground root of Piper methysticum, a shrub native to the South Pacific islands, prepared as a cold water infusion and drunk socially across Fiji, Vanuatu, Tonga and Samoa for roughly three thousand years. It contains no alcohol. The taste is earthy and bitter and it numbs the lips and tongue on the first mouthful; the effect is mildly sedative and sociable rather than intoxicating in the way alcohol is. Kava also shows reverse tolerance, so regular drinkers generally need less rather than more to feel it, and a first visit rewards a slow pace across an hour or two.

The Lee Road corridor is a practical location for this: it sits close to I-4 and within a short drive of College Park, Winter Park and Maitland, where Elevate's social lounge covers the same northern suburbs. Between them the north side of Orlando is well covered for late alcohol-free options, which was not true a few years ago.

The disclosure that applies to every Kavasutra applies here in full, and the chain is entirely open about it. Kavasutra describes itself as America's premier kava and kratom bar, and the kratom half of that is a genuine half. Kratom is the leaf of a Southeast Asian tree, Mitragyna speciosa, whose principal alkaloids act on the opioid receptors. Regular use produces tolerance and a real withdrawal syndrome, several US states ban it outright, and its concentrated 7-hydroxymitragynine derivatives are under active federal scheduling action. Kava does not work that way and carries no comparable dependence profile.

That difference is the whole reason many readers of this directory are looking for a kava bar in the first place. In a room where both are poured from the same counter at similar prices, the only reliable approach is to order by name and ask what is in the cup before drinking it.

venues.name: Kavasutra Kava Bar | Semoran
venues.description: Kavasutra is the largest kava chain in the country, with more than thirty locations, and the Semoran Boulevard room is its east Orlando site — open 8am to 2am, seven days a week, with no alcohol served. The format across the group is consistent: a proper bar counter, shells poured to order, and a room built for regulars rather than for passing trade. IMPORTANT for readers in recovery, and this is not a detail the chain hides: Kavasutra markets itself as America's premier kava AND kratom bar. Kratom is a co-equal half of the business here, not a side listing. Its alkaloids act on opioid receptors, it produces tolerance and withdrawal in regular users, and several states ban it outright. Kava carries no comparable profile. Order specifically.
venues.longDescription:
Kavasutra is the largest kava chain in the United States, running more than thirty locations, and the Semoran Boulevard room covers east Orlando. It opens at 8am and closes at 2am, seven days a week, and serves no alcohol at any point.

The format across the group is consistent and genuinely bar-shaped: a proper counter, shells poured to order, long hours, and a regular crowd rather than passing trade. That consistency is part of the appeal — a Kavasutra in Orlando works the same way as one in Denver or on the Treasure Coast, which for someone travelling and not drinking is a real convenience. This is a bar you can walk into in an unfamiliar city and know what you are getting.

Kava is the ground root of Piper methysticum, a shrub native to the South Pacific islands, prepared as a cold water infusion and drunk socially across Fiji, Vanuatu, Tonga and Samoa for roughly three thousand years. It contains no alcohol. It tastes earthy and bitter, numbs the lips and tongue on the first mouthful, and is mildly sedative rather than intoxicating in the way alcohol is. Kava exhibits reverse tolerance, meaning regular drinkers typically need less rather than more to feel it, so a first visit is best taken slowly across an hour or two rather than treated like a round of shots.

Orlando now supports a substantial spread of these rooms — SODO Kava, House of Mana, Pacific Rootz, Z Co-Space, Z Tiki, Kava Cove, Elevate, Kava Culture downtown and both Kavasutra branches — which makes it one of the better-served metros in the country for anyone who wants a late night out without alcohol.

The caution for this chain is not something it hides, and it deserves to be stated as plainly as the chain states it. Kavasutra markets itself as America's premier kava AND kratom bar. Kratom is a co-equal half of the business here, not a side listing tucked at the bottom of a menu. It is the leaf of Mitragyna speciosa, a Southeast Asian tree, and its principal alkaloids act on the opioid receptors; regular use produces tolerance and a real withdrawal syndrome, several US states prohibit it outright, and concentrated 7-hydroxymitragynine products derived from it are the subject of active federal scheduling action. Kava carries no comparable dependence profile.

For a great many people, the entire reason for walking into a kava bar rather than a pub is to avoid substances that can get a grip. In a room where kratom is half the trade, that means ordering specifically, by name, and asking what is in the shell — which the staff will answer directly.

venues.name: Kavasutra Kava Bar
venues.description: A Phoenix outpost of the Kavasutra chain — the original of two Phoenix locations, on Thunderbird Road in the north of the city. Kavasutra has been running for roughly fifteen years across more than twenty-five US sites, which makes it one of the longest-established kava operators in the country and means the format here is a known quantity rather than an experiment: traditional kava preparations, kratom teas and botanical drinks poured in a laid-back lounge built for staying a while without alcohol. Both kava and kratom are alcohol-free and both are psychoactive; kratom in particular acts on opioid receptors and carries documented dependence risk. Alcohol-free is not substance-free.
venues.address: 777 E Thunderbird Rd Ste 105, Phoenix, AZ 85022
venues.longDescription:
Kavasutra on East Thunderbird Road was the first of the chain's two Phoenix rooms, sitting in the north of the city well away from the downtown and Arcadia clusters where most of the metro's alcohol-free options are concentrated. The chain itself has been operating for around fifteen years across more than twenty-five locations nationally, which makes it one of the longest-running kava operators in the United States and, for a customer, means the offering is consistent and understood rather than improvised.

The format is traditional rather than cocktail-led. Kava is served in the South Pacific manner — prepared from the root, poured in shells, drunk socially — alongside kratom teas and other botanical drinks. This is worth setting against the other kind of alcohol-free venue in this city: rooms like Zero Proof Lounge or The Nixer build drinks that imitate cocktails, aiming at the shape of a familiar night out. Kavasutra does not. It offers a different ritual rather than a substitute for the usual one, and for some people that is precisely the appeal — nothing on the menu is pretending to be a drink you have given up.

The practical value is straightforward: a genuinely alcohol-free room in a part of Phoenix that has very few, open late, built for sitting and talking rather than for drinking quickly and leaving.

The caveat here is the most important one on this list, and it belongs in plain language. Kavasutra serves kratom as a core part of its offering, not as a curiosity. Kratom acts on opioid receptors and carries documented dependence and withdrawal risk; kava is separately psychoactive, sedating, and has case reports of liver injury attached to it. Everything poured here is free of alcohol. None of it is inert, and for anyone whose reason for avoiding alcohol is recovery from a substance-use disorder, that distinction deserves real weight before walking in.

venues.name: Kawana Kava Bar
venues.description: A fully alcohol-free kava bar on East Thomas Road in the Arcadia area, Kawana specialises in handcrafted kava shells and plant-based mocktails alongside other botanical drinks, and describes its own aim as building drinks with the complexity of a good cocktail bar and none of the hangover. The hours are the practical draw: open from 9am on weekdays and to 2am on Friday and Saturday, it covers both ends of the day rather than only the evening, which makes it usable as a morning workspace and as a late-night alternative to a bar. A calm, community-minded room. Kava is alcohol-free but psychoactive — alcohol-free is not substance-free.
venues.address: 4041 E Thomas Rd Suite 104, Phoenix, AZ 85018
venues.longDescription:
Kawana Kava & Herbal Bar occupies a suite on East Thomas Road in Arcadia, a central Phoenix neighbourhood better known for its cocktail bars than for the alternatives to them. It is fully alcohol-free, and its own framing is worth taking seriously: handcrafted kava shells and plant-based mocktails built to rival the complexity of the city's better cocktail bars, without the hangover. That is a claim about craft rather than about abstinence, which is the right register — the venues that actually work for non-drinkers are the ones competing on quality rather than asking for allowance.

The hours do more work here than the drinks list suggests. Kawana opens at 9am on weekdays and 10am at weekends, running to midnight most nights and 2am on Friday and Saturday. That span covers the two moments a non-drinker is least well served in almost any city: the daytime, when the only third places are coffee shops that shut mid-afternoon, and after midnight, when everything still open is a bar. One room that does both, without alcohol at either end, is genuinely uncommon in metro Phoenix.

Kava itself deserves a plain description rather than a euphemism. It is a root preparation from the South Pacific, served traditionally in shells, mildly sedating and social in its effect — and the reason kava bars function as bar substitutes at all is precisely that the drink does something, which fruit juice does not. It is also not nothing. Kava is psychoactive and carries documented case reports of liver injury, and Arizona kava bars commonly pour kratom alongside it, which brings dependence and withdrawal risks of its own. Everything served at Kawana is alcohol-free. Alcohol-free and substance-free are not the same thing, and anyone in recovery should make that choice deliberately rather than discover it at the bar.

venues.name: Kaya
venues.description: Michelin-recommended modern Filipino restaurant and bar in Mills 50 helmed by chef Lordfer Lalicon and Jamilyn Bailey, and the recipient of Florida's first Michelin Green Star for sustainable gastronomy. Its zero-proof cocktail list stands on its own, with five named drinks built from Filipino ingredients like pandan, kalamansi, and shio goji.
venues.hours: Mon closed; Tue-Thu 5pm-10pm; Fri 5pm-10:30pm; Sat 9:30am-12pm & 5pm-10:30pm; Sun 5pm-9pm
signatureDrinks: Hiraya (white peony and marigold tea, szechuan peppercorn, pineapple, lime)
Pandan Cream Soda (pandan, coconut water, rice milk, shio goji)
Salabat (fresh ginger tea, kalamansi honey, citrus, served hot)
venues.longDescription:
Kaya brings modern Filipino cooking to Orlando's Mills 50 district, led by chef Lordfer Lalicon, who trained under two-Michelin-star, Green Star chef Dan Barber at Blue Hill at Stone Barns, alongside co-founder Jamilyn Bailey. In April 2024, Kaya became the first restaurant in Florida to receive a Michelin Green Star, recognizing its sustainable sourcing (roughly 90% of produce comes from Central Florida farms) alongside its MICHELIN Guide recognition; it has also been a James Beard Award finalist for Best New Restaurant.

Kaya's bar program treats zero-proof drinkers as first-class guests rather than an afterthought, with five named non-alcoholic cocktails on the regular menu: Hiraya, Honey Ko, Risoma, Pandan Cream Soda, and Salabat, a hot ginger tea. The flavors mirror the kitchen's approach, built from Filipino pantry staples like pandan, kalamansi, and shio goji rather than treated as simplified versions of the alcoholic list.

'A lot of what we do is trying to show what's possible in the restaurant industry,' co-founder Jamilyn Bailey has said of Kaya's minimal-waste, ingredient-forward philosophy, one that extends from the kitchen's cooking scraps to a bar program built to stand fully on its own, alcohol or not.
venues.pressQuote: A lot of what we do is trying to show what's possible in the restaurant industry.

venues.name: Kaya
venues.description: Kaya is a big Burrito Restaurant Group Caribbean and South American restaurant on Smallman Street in the Strip District, open since the mid-1990s; Marla Beamon became the first woman promoted to executive chef in a big Burrito kitchen when she took it over in 1997. It runs a dedicated zero-proof programme built on Seedlip and fresh citrus, printed under its own heading, "Zero-Proof Cocktails", with everything at $12 — the same price as most of the room's alcoholic cocktails. The list holds the Blood Orange Hibiscus Cosmo-Not (Seedlip Grove, blood orange purée, hibiscus syrup, lime), the No-Jito (Seedlip Garden, mint, lime), an N/A Margarita on Ritual's tequila alternative, and a Honey Hibiscus Spritz on Azzenta sparkling chardonnay. The margarita and the No-Jito can both be flavoured with blood orange, guava, mango, pineapple or strawberry. A separate "Non-Alcoholic Refreshers" section adds a Fruit Cocktail Mocktail ($10) and house Kaya Juice ($8 a glass, $22 a carafe). A Piña No-Lada appears in older coverage but is no longer on the menu.
venues.longDescription:
Kaya has been on Smallman Street in the Strip District since the mid-1990s, which makes it one of the longest-running restaurants in big Burrito Restaurant Group and one of the few places in Pittsburgh cooking Caribbean and South American food with any seriousness. Marla Beamon became the first woman promoted to executive chef in a big Burrito kitchen when she took it over in 1997. The food is bright and generous — tropical guacamole and queso chorizo fundito at $12, conch fritters at $16, jerk wings at $16, corn and lentil beignets at $14, a tropical paella at $27, jerked half chicken at $27, adobo-marinated flank steak at $32. It opens for lunch and runs late, to 10pm most nights and 11pm on Friday and Saturday, with brunch at weekends.

The zero-proof drinks have their own printed section, headed Zero-Proof Cocktails, and they are all $12 — the same price as most of the room's alcoholic cocktails, which is the tell that they are made rather than mixed. NEXTpittsburgh's summary is accurate: with warm flavours from the Caribbean islands, South America and beyond, Kaya also gives diners zero-proof cocktails to accompany their dishes, and they are built on Seedlip. The Blood Orange Hibiscus Cosmo-Not uses Seedlip Grove with blood orange purée, hibiscus syrup and lime; the No-Jito uses Seedlip Garden with fresh mint, lime and simple syrup. An N/A Margarita on Ritual's tequila alternative and a Honey Hibiscus Spritz on Azzenta sparkling chardonnay round it out, and the margarita and the No-Jito can both be flavoured — blood orange, guava, mango, pineapple or strawberry — which is the closest thing to a build-your-own zero-proof drink on any list in the city. Below that sits a Non-Alcoholic Refreshers section with a Fruit Cocktail Mocktail at $10 and house Kaya Juice at $8 a glass or $22 for a carafe, a carafe being the useful option at a table where you are the only one not drinking. One correction worth noting: a Piña No-Lada appears in older coverage but is not on the current menu.
venues.pressQuote: The fresh ingredients and dishes of the Caribbean, South America, the Pacific and beyond are folded into everything that Kaya serves. Their tropical mocktails incorporate Seedlip zero-proof spirits, sparked up with all your favorite citrus flavors.

venues.name: KC Bier Co.
venues.description: KC Bier Co. is Kansas City's largest locally owned brewery, founded in 2014 by Steve Holle alongside Bavarian native Jürgen Hager and German-trained brewer Karlton Graham. Its original home is this Waldo Bierhalle and Biergarten on West 79th Street, where German-style lagers and wheat biers are brewed on site using imported IREKS malt, Hallertau hops, and yeast strains from the Andechs monastery brewery in Bavaria. The food is classic Bierhalle fare: pretzels, sausages, and sandwiches in a relaxed, family-friendly setting. For non-drinkers, the brewery makes its own Hop Spritz, a zero-ABV, zero-calorie hop-infused sparkling water with real hop aroma — sparkling water, dried hops, hop extract, and natural flavors — poured at the Bierhalle and sold in cans. It is a genuine house-made non-alcoholic option rather than a bought-in brand.
signatureDrinks: Hop Spritz (hop-infused sparkling water — 0% ABV, zero calories, zero carbs) $3.50–$8
venues.longDescription:
KC Bier Co. is Kansas City's largest locally owned brewery, founded in 2014 by Steve Holle, the great-grandson of German immigrants who studied German at Northwest Missouri State, attended the Doemens Brewing Academy in Munich in 1997, and earned a Diploma Brewer designation from the Institute of Brewing and Distilling in London in 2003. He retired from directing real-estate investment for Northwestern Mutual in Dallas in 2013 and came home to open the brewery the following year. He runs it with Bavarian native Jürgen Hager and head brewer Karlton Graham, trained at both the Siebel Institute and Doemens. The original home is the Waldo bierhalle at 310 W 79th Street, which serves communally in the German style with an adjoining biergarten explicitly described as a public place for people of all ages, including a designated dog-friendly area. Food is the appropriate accompaniment — Bavarian pretzels, bratwurst, currywurst, a döner kebab on Tuesdays only, and Betty Rae's ice cream. Brewery tours run Saturdays at 1pm and Sundays at 12.30pm.

The non-alcoholic offering is more considered than most breweries manage, and it takes two forms. The house option is Hop Spritz, KC Bier's own hop-infused sparkling water, which the brewery lists at zero alcohol, zero calories, zero gluten and zero carbs — the ingredients are simply sparkling water, dried hops, hop extract and natural flavours, and the tap list confirms it at 0% ABV and 0 IBU. It is poured from $3.50 for a 0.35L glass up to $8 for a litre, and sold in six-packs to take home at $9.99. What lifts this above a brewery that merely stocks something is the second option: the bierhalle also carries Border Brewing's Baseline Pale and Baseline Amber in 12oz cans at $5.25 — a rival Kansas City brewery's non-alcoholic beers, listed on the menu alongside their own. For a non-drinker that means a genuine choice between a hop water and two beers, all three of them made in this city rather than shipped in.

venues.name: KERB
venues.description: KERB is a neighbourhood natural wine store and bar in the heart of Ancoats, pouring more than 150 low-intervention bottles by the glass or the bottle to drink in or take away, plus five rotating wines on tap. Its ever-changing list is organised into sections that include a dedicated 'LOW & NO', so a non-drinker gets a genuinely curated choice rather than a token soft drink. The alcohol-free shelf runs from Track Brewing's Sonoma alcohol-free pale and Hip Pop kombucha to non-alcoholic grape juice and low-intervention low-ABV bottles, alongside sparkling reds, oranges and ciders that all sit within the same natural ethos.
venues.hours: Mon closed; Tue-Thu 3pm-10:30pm; Fri-Sat 1pm-10:30pm; Sun closed
signatureDrinks: Nibiru Traubensaft non-alcoholic white grape juice
venues.longDescription:
KERB opened on Henry Street in Ancoats in August 2021, founded by Philip Hannaway and David McCall as a neighbourhood natural wine store and bar. The compact, thoughtfully designed room has curved walls washed in subtle peach and pink, shelves brimming with bottles from independent wineries, and blush-pink tables by the window for watching the world go by. Its branding — including the illustrated wine-loving gremlins by artist James Carbutt — leans into the founders' promise of 'no pretentiousness and no exclusivity, just really good wine', and the venue doubles as an art space with a rotating programme of genuinely innovative exhibitions.

The wine is the draw: more than 150 low-intervention bottles that champion smaller producers farming with minimal intervention, with five wines on tap that rotate monthly and different bottles opened daily. As Creative Tourist put it, 'the wine list is ever-changing and never, ever boring. Oranges, sparkling reds, non-alcoholic, cider specials, every inch of the wine terroir is covered.' You can drink in by the glass or bottle, take away from the off-licence shelves, and the events calendar runs to free-entry tastings, weekly winemaker-focused flights and monthly 'Sip + Shop' sessions with neighbouring Ancoats businesses. A 5-star Tripadvisor review from August 2025 praised the 'immaculate vibes, great wine' and the thought put into the whole experience, confirming it as a going concern.

For non-drinkers, KERB carries a dedicated 'LOW & NO' section on its list rather than leaving the sober guest to a lone soft drink. The alcohol-free and low-alcohol picks span Manchester brewery Track's Sonoma alcohol-free pale ale, Hip Pop's ginger and yuzu kombucha, Punchy's lime sparkling and Nibiru's non-alcoholic white grape juice (Traubensaft), alongside low-intervention low-ABV bottles from natural producers such as Romain des Grottes. It sits next door to award-winning craft-beer bottle shop The Epicurean, so this stretch of Henry Street offers a non-drinker unusually deep low-and-no choice — and at KERB that choice is treated with the same curatorial care as the natural wine that lines the walls.
venues.pressQuote: The wine list is ever-changing and never, ever boring. Oranges, sparkling reds, non-alcoholic, cider specials, every inch of the wine terroir is covered.

venues.name: Khâluna
venues.description: Khâluna is chef-restaurateur Ann Ahmed's upscale Laotian flagship, opened in 2021 at 40th and Lyndale in SW Minneapolis's Kingfield neighborhood. The dining room channels a Southeast Asian resort, and the space also houses a shop and a demonstration kitchen for cooking classes; Eater named it one of the 15 best new restaurants in the U.S. for 2022. For non-drinkers, it's a standout: Khâluna carries one of the largest dedicated non-alcoholic drink menus in the Twin Cities, with the Star Tribune noting the NA list runs "longer than the regular cocktail list." Zero-proof builds lean on alternative spirits (Dhos, Aplos, The Pathfinder) plus house syrups, ginger, citrus, cucumber, and calamansi. Named spirit-free cocktails include the Last Love and The Elixir, alongside a trio of medicinal iced teas; many drinks are sweetened with erythritol rather than sugar.

naMenuItems.name: Spritz 75

venues.longDescription:
Khâluna is chef-restaurateur Ann Ahmed's upscale Laotian flagship, opened in 2021 at 40th and Lyndale in the Kingfield neighbourhood of southwest Minneapolis. The dining room is styled after a Southeast Asian resort, and the building also houses a shop and a demonstration kitchen used for cooking classes. Eater named it one of the fifteen best new restaurants in the United States for 2022, which for a Laotian restaurant in Minneapolis is the kind of recognition that changes a city's sense of its own food scene.

For a non-drinker it is a genuine destination rather than a safe choice, because Khâluna carries one of the largest dedicated non-alcoholic drink menus in the Twin Cities. The Star Tribune's Sharyn Jackson made the point that most clearly identifies what is unusual here: "The nonalcoholic drink menu at Khâluna is longer than the regular cocktail list. The inventive drinks make use of spices, yogurt, sugar cane, roots and more." A zero-proof list longer than the spirited one is rare anywhere, and it inverts the usual experience of scanning a menu hoping to find one thing you can order.

The builds lean on alternative spirits — Dhos, Aplos and The Pathfinder — combined with house syrups, ginger, citrus, cucumber and calamansi, the sharp Filipino citrus that gives several of the drinks their acidity. Named spirit-free cocktails include the Last Love and The Elixir, alongside a No Dhos Margarita and a Spritz 75, plus a trio of medicinal iced teas. Many of the drinks are sweetened with erythritol rather than sugar, which is a deliberate choice worth flagging: it keeps them lighter across a long meal, though anyone sensitive to sugar alcohols will want to ask. Lunch service runs at weekends and dinner nightly, and the room is busy enough that booking is sensible.
venues.pressQuote: The nonalcoholic drink menu at Khâluna is longer than the regular cocktail list. The inventive drinks make use of spices, yogurt, sugar cane, roots and more.

venues.name: Kickin' it with Kava
venues.description: Kickin' it with Kava has run on South Fifth Street in St. Charles since 2018 and describes itself flatly as a non-alcoholic lounge — the only dedicated one in St. Charles County. It opens at 2pm and closes at 11pm early in the week, midnight from Thursday through Saturday, with monthly events on the calendar. IMPORTANT for readers in recovery, because this menu is broader than most: alongside kava, the lounge sells CBD and a category it labels other options, covering delta-8 and delta-9 THC, blue lotus, botanical blends and mushroom elixirs. None of that is alcohol, but several of those are psychoactive in their own right. If you are avoiding intoxicants generally rather than alcohol specifically, this room needs ordering carefully.
venues.longDescription:
Kickin' it with Kava has operated at 512 South Fifth Street in St. Charles since 2018, which makes it one of the longer-established alcohol-free rooms in the St. Louis metro and the only dedicated one in St. Charles County. Its own signage is unambiguous — non-alcoholic lounge — and the hours support the claim: doors at 2pm, closing at 11pm Sunday through Wednesday and at midnight from Thursday through Saturday, with a monthly events programme documented through the venue's photo gallery.

St. Charles sits about twenty-five miles north-west of downtown St. Louis on the Missouri River, and its historic Main Street district is heavily given over to bars, wineries and brewery taprooms. A room a couple of blocks off that strip that trades to midnight and serves nothing alcoholic fills an obvious gap for anyone living in St. Charles, St. Peters or O'Fallon who does not want to drive into the city to avoid a drink.

Kava anchors the menu. It is the ground root of Piper methysticum, a South Pacific shrub, infused in water and drunk socially across Fiji, Vanuatu, Tonga and Samoa for roughly three thousand years. It contains no alcohol, tastes earthy and bitter, numbs the lips and tongue, and is mildly sedative rather than intoxicating in the way alcohol is. It is the reason the venue is categorised as a kava bar here.

The rest of the menu requires an honest description, because it is unusually wide and because the people most likely to consult this directory are the people for whom the distinction matters. The lounge publishes three menu categories: kava, CBD, and a section it calls other options — and that third section covers delta-8 and delta-9 THC products, blue lotus, botanical blends and mushroom elixirs. None of these is alcohol, which is the venue's claim and it is true. But several of them are actively psychoactive, and delta-8 and delta-9 in particular are cannabinoid products rather than herbal teas. This directory has declined to list outright THC dispensaries that also sell kava, on the grounds that they are the wrong fit for a recovery-adjacent audience. Kickin' it with Kava is not that — it is a kava lounge whose primary identity is the kava, with a hemp counter attached — but the difference is one of degree, and the honest thing is to say so plainly rather than to let the words non-alcoholic do work they were not meant to do. If your recovery rules out intoxicants generally, read the menu headers here and ask what is in the cup.

venues.name: Killjoy Berry Hill
venues.description: Killjoy Berry Hill is the second location of Killjoy, the alcohol-free bottle shop founded by Stephanie Styll, who stopped drinking in 2020 and launched the business in 2023. After starting as a Wedgewood-Houston pop-up and opening a retail store in East Nashville, Styll expanded to Berry Hill — the neighborhood where the idea began — opening this roughly 1,000-square-foot shop in October 2025. Like the East Nashville store, it sells exclusively non-alcoholic beer, wine, spirits, and functional beverages (including adaptogenic, THC/CBD, and herbal drinks), and offers on-site sampling so customers can taste before buying. Killjoy bills itself as Nashville's first booze-free beverage shop and, per Styll, the only alcohol-free retail business of its kind in the city. The shop's stated mission is to help change the culture around drinking in Nashville.

Aplos Dragon Fruit Martini single can

venues.longDescription:
Killjoy Berry Hill is the second location of Killjoy, the alcohol-free bottle shop founded by Stephanie Styll, who stopped drinking in 2020 and launched the business in 2023. The path is worth tracing because it is the standard arc for this category done well: a pop-up in Wedgewood-Houston first, then a permanent retail store in East Nashville, and in October 2025 this roughly thousand-square-foot shop in Berry Hill — the neighbourhood where the original idea took shape. Killjoy bills itself as Nashville's first booze-free beverage shop and, by Styll's account, the only alcohol-free retail business of its kind in the city.

The shop sells exclusively non-alcoholic products: beer, wine, spirits and functional beverages, the last category covering adaptogenic drinks, THC and CBD options and herbal preparations. Best Day Brewing is among the brands stocked. The critical feature is on-site sampling — customers can taste before they buy — which addresses the single biggest barrier in non-alcoholic retail. These products are expensive and wildly inconsistent between brands, and one bad $30 bottle is enough to persuade somebody the whole category is a scam. A shop that lets you taste first is doing something a website fundamentally cannot.

The stated mission goes beyond retail. Styll frames it as cultural work: "We just want to serve the Nashville community and help to build community and help to change the culture around drinking in Nashville." That ambition is pointed in a city whose national image is bachelorette parties and Broadway honky-tonks, and where the pressure to drink is more sustained than in most places. Two shops open and a third format tested is evidence the demand underneath is real. Open Tuesday through Sunday, closed Mondays. Berry Hill is a small pocket of converted houses and studios just south of downtown, well away from the Broadway crowds, which makes it a considerably easier place to shop than the tourist core — and the neighbourhood where the whole idea began.
venues.pressQuote: We just want to serve the Nashville community and help to build community and help to change the culture around drinking in Nashville.

venues.name: Killjoy
venues.description: Killjoy is Nashville's first booze-free beverage shop, founded by Stephanie Styll, who stopped drinking at the end of 2020. It launched in 2023 as a hidden 200-square-foot space in Wedgewood-Houston before relocating in November 2024 to a storefront in The Shoppes on Fatherland in East Nashville. The shelves are entirely alcohol-free: NA beer, still and sparkling wine, zero-proof spirits, ready-to-drink cocktails, plus kava, adaptogens, and THC/CBD drinks, with a knowledgeable team to guide customers through the selection. Confirmed brands on its own store include Athletic Brewing, Best Day Brewing, Go Brewing, Untitled Art, Dromme, and Prima Pavé. Killjoy was named among the country's top nonalcoholic bottle shops by Wine Enthusiast, and Styll won a NEXT Award from the Nashville Entrepreneur Center in 2024. It runs frequent Dry January tastings and sober-social events.
signatureDrinks: Go Brewing (Gluten-free) Freedom West Coast Pale $4
Rhinegeist Ghost Haze Non-Alcoholic Hazy IPA $3

naMenuItems.name: Best Day Brewing Hazy IPA Single
Aplos Dragon Fruit Martini Single Can

venues.longDescription:
Killjoy was Nashville's first booze-free beverage shop, and its founder tells the origin story plainly: on 1 April 2023, Stephanie Styll opened it with her brother-in-law John Caldwell, in a hidden 200-square-foot room at 2020 Lindell Avenue in Wedgewood-Houston — tucked inside a gallery, entered through the Crumbly Corner Cafe. Styll grew up in Nashville, studied psychology at MTSU, then lived overseas for thirteen years, travelled to fifty-three countries and took a master's in human relations before coming home. She stopped drinking in 2020, and by her own account spent about a year drinking only sparkling water before she discovered zero-proof drinks; the shop exists because the place she wanted did not exist in Nashville, so she built it. The business has since outgrown that first room twice over: it now runs two storefronts, at 1100 Fatherland Street in East Nashville and 2813 Columbine Place, open Tuesday to Saturday 11am to 7pm and Sunday noon to 5pm, closed Mondays.

The shelves are entirely alcohol-free, and the range is far wider than non-alcoholic beer and wine. The shop organises its catalogue — several hundred products deep — into adaptogens, beer, kava, kanna, mixers, ready-to-drink cocktails, spirits and wines, so it functions as much as a guide to an unfamiliar category as a shop. That guidance is the point: a bar cart sits in the corner with open bottles, and anything on it can be tasted before you commit to a bottle, which matters in a category where a $20 mistake is easy to make. Edible Nashville described a cheerful space of shiny balloons and twinkle lights brimming with non-alcoholic wine, spirits and beers. Two things are worth knowing before you go. First, this is retail with tasting rather than a bar with table service, so it suits browsing more than an evening out. Second, alongside the straightforwardly non-alcoholic stock the shop also carries kava, kanna, functional mushroom and CBD products — actively useful to some customers, and worth avoiding for anyone steering clear of psychoactives entirely.
venues.pressQuote: We want to normalize sobriety and going out with your friends.

venues.name: Killjoy
venues.description: Killjoy is a Glenwood South cocktail bar on North West Street with a standing "Spirit-Free Cocktails" section on its menu, every drink at a flat $10. The three builds use alcohol-free aperitivo, gin and limoncello alongside Athletic Brewing's NA IPA rather than juice-and-soda shortcuts — Pine State of Mind lengthens alcohol-free gin, lime, honey and celery bitters with the IPA for bitterness — and the bar states that all drinks are treated with the same exquisite respect. Two honest caveats from the menu itself: the same section lists a build with a 5mg THC spirit, and the bar warns that everything is made where alcohol is in use. The kitchen is led by chef Jake Wood, and the room is a late one — 1am on Fridays and Saturdays, from a 3pm Saturday open.

Pine State of Mind ($10) — alcohol-free gin, lime, honey, celery bitters, Athletic NA IPA
