venues.longDescription:
Killjoy sits on North West Street in Glenwood South, Raleigh's densest strip of late-night bars, and it is one of the few on that strip where ordering without alcohol does not mean ordering off-menu. The drinks list carries a printed section headed "Spirit-Free Cocktails", flat-priced at ten dollars, and the bar's own framing is that all drinks are treated with the same exquisite respect — a claim the list mostly earns.

The Sunset Sparkler is the house spritz, built on alcohol-free aperitivo and alcohol-free prosecco, and the Lemonheloooo Spritz runs the same structure with alcohol-free limoncello. The most interesting of the three is Pine State of Mind, which combines alcohol-free gin with lime, honey and celery bitters and then lengthens it with Athletic Brewing's non-alcoholic IPA — using the hops for the bitterness and aroma that a zero-proof build usually lacks. It is a properly constructed drink rather than a soft alternative.

Two things are worth flagging before you go. The first is that the bar's spirit-free section also lists a build containing a 5mg THC spirit; it is not included among the drinks above, because THC is not alcohol-free in the sense most people avoiding alcohol mean, and anyone in recovery should know it is on the same part of the menu. Ask if you want to avoid it. The second is the bar's own disclaimer, which is more honest than most: not every beverage on the list is alcohol free, and all of them are made in an environment where alcohol is in use, so cross-contact is possible.

The kitchen is run by chef Jake Wood, the room is listed as LGBTQ+ friendly and accessible, and the hours run late — until 1am on Friday and Saturday, with a 3pm Saturday open that makes it one of the earlier starts in the neighbourhood.
venues.pressQuote: Guests who don't want to imbibe have the option to buy a delicious drink that's completely spirit-free
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: Raleigh Magazine, "A Bar for All", February 2020

venues.name: Kiln
venues.description: Kiln is a two-Michelin-star tasting-menu restaurant in San Francisco's Hayes Valley, opened in May 2023 by chef John Wesley and general manager Julianna Yang, both alumni of the Michelin-starred Sons & Daughters. Set in a converted Fell Street garage with 30-foot ceilings and a Sonoma olive tree at its center, the roughly 20-course menu leans Nordic, built on curing, drying, and fermentation. For non-drinkers, beverage director Vincent Balao — formerly of three-Michelin-star Atelier Crenn — created a dedicated spirit-free pairing ($135), offered alongside the wine and reserve pairings rather than as a substitute. It draws on housemade kombucha, seasonal shrubs, and amazake, plus Seedlip, Lyre's, and Proxies non-alcoholic wine. Named pours include the Why Yuzu Sour (yuzu, genmaicha, Seedlip Garden 108, Oro Blanco, kombu syrup, amazake foam), Verde Side, and Smoke & Mirrors.
venues.hours: Mon closed; Tue-Thu 6pm-8pm; Fri-Sat 5pm-8:30pm; Sun closed
venues.longDescription:
Kiln opened in May 2023 at 149 Fell Street in Hayes Valley, in a converted garage whose thirty-foot ceilings frame a Sonoma olive tree planted at the centre of the dining room. It is co-owned by chef John Wesley and general manager Julianna Yang, who met while working at the Michelin-starred Sons & Daughters; Wesley also cooked at Commis in Oakland and at Aska and Eleven Madison Park in New York. The tasting menu runs roughly eighteen to twenty courses and leans Nordic, organised around preservation technique — curing, drying and fermentation — rather than luxury product, in dishes such as puffed beef tendon and grilled wild mackerel with dried shellfish sauce. The Michelin Guide California awarded Kiln a star in August 2024 and named Wesley its Young Chef Award winner the same year; a second star followed in 2025, placing Kiln among a very small group of two-starred restaurants in the state.

What earns Kiln a place here is structural. The spirit-free pairing is one of three pairings sold at the table, priced at $135 and listed alongside the wine and reserve pairings rather than offered as a consolation to guests who decline wine. Beverage director Vincent Balao, formerly of the three-Michelin-starred Atelier Crenn, builds it from house-made kombucha, seasonal shrubs and amazake alongside Seedlip, Lyre's and Proxies dealcoholized wine, so most of what reaches the glass is made in the building rather than poured from a bottle. Named pours include the Why Yuzu Sour — yuzu, genmaicha green tea, Seedlip Garden 108, Oro Blanco grapefruit, kombu syrup and an amazake foam — plus Verde Side and Smoke & Mirrors. Balao told The San Francisco Standard in May 2023 that the point was hospitality rather than novelty: "Just because you're not drinking doesn't mean you should have only water, soda or ginger ale." Reviewing the restaurant for 7x7 in January 2025, Shoshi Parks described Kiln's non-alcoholic cocktails as "well-balanced mixological beauties," noting they are made with the same preservation techniques that drive the kitchen and pairing them to Scandinavian-leaning courses. Reservations open well in advance and the room seats few enough that the spirit-free pairing should be requested when booking.
venues.pressQuote: It's about being hospitable. Just because you're not drinking doesn't mean you should have only water, soda or ginger ale.

venues.name: Kimball House
venues.description: Kimball House is a bar and oyster restaurant in a converted 1890s rail depot beside the tracks in downtown Decatur, open since 2013. It is recommended in the Michelin Guide, holds the Guide's 2024 Exceptional Cocktails award for Georgia, and runs what is widely regarded as the deepest oyster programme in the metro. The zero-proof list is treated with the same seriousness as the absinthe and cocktail lists it is famous for. Tokyo Zero is the standout — ginger, yuzu, lime, pineapple and white shoyu, drawing on the same Japanese flavour vocabulary as the alcoholic menu — alongside a St. Agrestis Phony Negroni and a non-alcoholic Grapefruit Royale topped with Oddbird sparkling. Dinner is served Tuesday through Sunday from five.
signatureDrinks: Tokyo Zero (ginger, yuzu, lime, pineapple, white shoyu)
N/A Grapefruit Royale (topped with Oddbird sparkling)
venues.longDescription:
Kimball House opened in 2013 in the old Decatur rail depot at 303 East Howard Avenue, a red-brick building right against the tracks, and it has spent the decade since setting the standard for bar work in metro Atlanta. The Michelin Guide recommends it and gave it the Exceptional Cocktails award in 2024. The room is known for three things: an absinthe programme served from proper fountains, a raw bar carrying oysters from both coasts that is generally considered the best in the region, and a seasonal kitchen that changes with what is available. Service runs Tuesday through Sunday from five, to ten most nights and eleven on Friday and Saturday, with the kitchen closing an hour before the bar.

A bar with that kind of reputation could get away with a token non-alcoholic offering, and the interesting thing is that it does not. DiningOut's 2026 zero-proof survey noted that its zero-proof list does not phone it in. The house drink is Tokyo Zero, built on ginger, yuzu, lime and pineapple with white shoyu for salinity and depth — it draws from exactly the same Japanese-leaning flavour vocabulary as the alcoholic cocktail menu, which is what stops it reading as a soft drink beside a dozen oysters. The bar also pours the St. Agrestis Phony Negroni, the bottled non-alcoholic negroni that has become a shorthand for a bar taking the category seriously, and a non-alcoholic Grapefruit Royale topped with Oddbird de-alcoholised sparkling wine, which gives a table something to raise. The practical value is specific: you can sit at the bar, order a dozen oysters, and drink something built to go with them. Kimball House is fully licensed and its identity is built on spirits, so it sits at four on our scale, but the zero-proof drinks are named, constructed and permanent rather than improvised.
venues.pressQuote: This converted rail depot in Decatur has one of the most serious bar programs in the metro, and its zero-proof list doesn't phone it in.

venues.name: Kinda Tropical
venues.description: Kinda Tropical is an East Austin all-day spot housed in a renovated gas station at 3501 E 7th St, part cafe and part bar with a large dog-friendly patio set under a red oak tree. The kitchen runs a full menu of pulled barbecue jackfruit sandwiches, yucca fries, big salads, and chicken sandwiches alongside espresso and oat milk lattes on tap and Figure 8 coffee. The bar offers a wide cocktail program, and Visit Austin's official tourism blog calls out Kinda Tropical for having one of the deepest non-alcoholic drink lists in town, naming a jalapeño pineapple margarita and the Rosemary Lane as standouts. The vibe is eclectic and relaxed — vegetarian, vegan, and gluten-free options run throughout the menu, and the patio is set back from the street with vines and plants creating a quiet, plant-shaded environment that doesn't feel like a bar in the conventional sense.
venues.longDescription:
Kinda Tropical is an all-day cafe and bar in a renovated gas station at 3501 East 7th Street, with a large dog-friendly patio set under a red oak and screened from the road by vines and planting. The kitchen runs pulled barbecue jackfruit sandwiches, yucca fries, big salads and chicken sandwiches, with espresso and oat milk lattes on tap and Figure 8 coffee; vegetarian, vegan and gluten-free options run right through the menu rather than sitting in a corner of it.

Visit Austin's assessment is that Kinda Tropical keeps one of the deepest non-alcoholic drink lists in the city, singling out a jalapeño pineapple margarita and the Rosemary Lane. Depth is the operative word: plenty of Austin bars have two or three zero-proof options, and a list long enough to choose from by mood rather than by availability is rare.

The jalapeño pineapple margarita is a good illustration of why the drinks work. Capsaicin heat and pineapple acidity between them occupy the space a spirit would — the heat gives the drink a finish and a slight burn, the acid keeps it from reading as juice. That is a structural solution rather than a sweetener, and it is why the drink holds up against the food instead of competing with it.

The format is the other half of the appeal. Open daily from 11am to midnight, part cafe and part bar, it changes character across the day without ever becoming a room organised around drinking. You can work there in the afternoon and stay into the evening, and the patio is quiet enough to talk on — which, on a stretch of East 7th that gets loud after dark, is a genuinely useful thing to know.

It does not feel like a bar in the conventional sense, and for a lot of people not drinking that is precisely the recommendation.
venues.pressQuote: This eastside gem offers one of the deepest lists in town, including a jalapeño pineapple margarita or their Rosemary Lane.

venues.name: Kindrid Kava
venues.description: Kindrid Kava is a botanical cafe on West Schaaf Road in Old Brooklyn, opened in June 2026 by owner Amber Atkinson and built explicitly around community, connection and non-alcoholic gathering. It pairs kava with a coffee programme and runs long days for the neighbourhood — 8am to 9pm early in the week, to 11pm on Friday and Saturday, with a short Sunday and a Tuesday closure. The room also hosts wellness programming, including breathwork and sound sessions. As the newest addition to a Northeast Ohio kava scene that had been entirely suburban — Sacred Waters in Lakewood, and Kava Sol in Willoughby until it closed its room in 2026 — it is the first to sit inside Cleveland's own city limits.
venues.hours: Mon 8am-9pm; Tue closed; Wed-Thu 8am-9pm; Fri-Sat 8am-11pm; Sun 11am-3pm
venues.longDescription:
Kindrid Kava opened on 8 June 2026 at 2024 West Schaaf Road, and it is a genuinely new arrival rather than an established venue this directory had overlooked. Its owner, Amber Atkinson, has described it as a botanical cafe focused on community, connection and non-alcoholic gathering, and the early reception in Old Brooklyn has been that of a neighbourhood gaining a room it did not previously have.

Its location is the most significant thing about it for anyone using this directory. Northeast Ohio's kava scene, which local public radio has covered as a genuine regional trend, has until now been suburban — Sacred Waters Kava Bar on Detroit Avenue in Lakewood, and, until it closed its Willoughby room in 2026, Kava Sol out east. Kindrid is the first to sit inside Cleveland's own city boundary, on the south-west side, which makes the difference between a car journey and a walk for a large number of people.

The format is a cafe rather than a nightlife venue, and the hours reflect that: 8am to 9pm on Monday, Wednesday and Thursday, extending to 11pm on Friday and Saturday, an 11am to 3pm Sunday, and closed on Tuesday. Check before travelling on a Tuesday. Kava and coffee run side by side, which is the pattern that works best in rooms serving a residential neighbourhood — the same counter answers a morning coffee and an evening alternative to the pub.

Kava is worth explaining for a Cleveland audience, where the drink is still new to most people. It is made from the ground root of Piper methysticum, a shrub native to the South Pacific, infused in cold water and drunk socially across Fiji, Vanuatu, Tonga and Samoa for roughly three thousand years. It contains no alcohol whatsoever. It tastes earthy and bitter, numbs the lips and tongue on the first mouthful, and is mildly sedative — relaxing and sociable rather than intoxicating in the way alcohol is. It also displays reverse tolerance, meaning regular drinkers usually need less rather than more, so a first visit rewards taking it slowly across an hour or two rather than treating a shell like a shot.

Beyond the drinks, the room programmes wellness sessions — breathwork and sound events have run here since opening — which places it closer to the community-space end of the kava spectrum than to the late-night bar-substitute end. For Old Brooklyn, Brooklyn Centre and the near south-west side, it is now the local answer to wanting somewhere to sit in the evening that does not revolve around alcohol.

venues.name: Kingfisher
venues.description: Kingfisher is a basement cocktail bar on East Chapel Hill Street in downtown Durham, opened in 2019 and built around North Carolina flavours and house-made syrups, and Discover Durham lists it on the city's official non-alcoholic page for cocktails with layers of flavour, house syrups and proper presentation. From April to September the bar also runs Roadrunner, a retro camper bar parked in its patio garden on Thursday to Saturday evenings, whose published menu carries two named mocktails at $9 — the Meteor Smash on mango and orange, the Milky Way on dark chocolate milk with nutmeg and caramel — plus Heineken 0.0. The zero-proof drinks change with the seasonal list and the bartenders build off-menu from the same syrups, so what is published understates what the bar can make. Roadrunner is a concept within Kingfisher, not a separate address.
venues.address: 321 E Chapel Hill St, Durham, NC 27701
signatureDrinks: Meteor Smash ($9) — mango, orange juice (Roadrunner seasonal menu)
Milky Way ($9) — dark chocolate milk, nutmeg, caramel (Roadrunner seasonal menu)
venues.longDescription:
Kingfisher opened in 2019 in a basement space on East Chapel Hill Street and quickly became one of the most talked-about bars in Durham — a ground-to-glass programme built on North Carolina and Southern flavours, house-made syrups and a heavily designed room. Discover Durham lists it on the city's official non-alcoholic page for cocktails with layers of flavour, house syrups, fresh ingredients and proper presentation, which reflects how the bar approaches zero-proof drinks generally rather than any one fixed list.

From April through September the bar also operates Roadrunner, a retro camper parked in the patio garden behind the building, open Thursday to Saturday evenings. Roadrunner runs its own shorter menu, and while it is trading it is the list the bar publishes: two named mocktails — the Meteor Smash on mango and orange, and the Milky Way on dark chocolate milk with nutmeg and caramel, each nine dollars — plus Heineken 0.0. Both mocktails are the zero-proof versions of full-strength drinks on the same list.

This is a bar where asking is worth more than reading. The seasonal cocktail list changes regularly and the bartenders build off-menu non-alcoholic drinks from the same syrups and infusions that go into everything else, which is exactly the capability Discover Durham is pointing at. What is published at any moment understates what the bar can make.

Two things worth knowing. Roadrunner is a concept within Kingfisher rather than a separate venue, so a search for it will lead you here — same address, same building. And the only other named non-alcoholic drink you will find in older writing about this bar, "Hot Thyme in the Summertime", dates from the 2019 opening menu and has not been on the list for years.
venues.pressQuote: non-alcoholic cocktails with layers of flavor, house-made syrups, fresh ingredients and presentations

venues.name: Kingfisher
venues.description: Kingfisher is a Vietnamese-French cocktail bar and eatery in San Diego's historic Golden Hill, opened in January 2022 by sisters Ky and Kim Phan and Kim's husband Quan Le. The kitchen serves modern Vietnamese cuisine with French and East Asian influences alongside an ambitious craft-cocktail program, and the bar runs a genuine zero-proof option: general manager David Tye uses Lyre's non-alcoholic spirits to rebuild several cocktails alcohol-free while keeping the original recipe intact, including a Papaya Margarita made with NA tequila, papaya, lime, agave, and black lava sea salt. Kingfisher is listed in the Michelin Guide and on national and statewide best-of lists, making it one of Golden Hill's most acclaimed dining-and-drinking destinations.
venues.longDescription:
Kingfisher is a Vietnamese-French cocktail bar and eatery in historic Golden Hill, opened in January 2022 by sisters Ky and Kim Phan together with Kim's husband Quan Le. The kitchen serves modern Vietnamese cooking with French and East Asian influences, the cocktail programme is ambitious, and the room has collected a Michelin Guide listing along with national and statewide best-of placements — which makes it one of Golden Hill's most acclaimed places to eat and drink.

The approach to non-alcoholic drinks here is worth describing precisely, because it differs from most bars in this directory. Rather than composing separate zero-proof builds from scratch, general manager David Tye uses Lyre's non-alcoholic spirits to rebuild existing cocktails from the menu alcohol-free while keeping the original recipe structure intact. The Papaya Margarita is the clearest example — non-alcoholic tequila with papaya, lime, agave and black lava sea salt, which is the same drink the person next to you ordered rather than a different one wearing its name. Tye has explained the reasoning directly: "Lyre's makes quality stuff, and it allowed us to be able to do a quick change but keep the original idea of the cocktail intact." That is a legitimate and under-used strategy. It means the zero-proof options scale with the cocktail list instead of being frozen at whatever two drinks were written a year ago, and it means a non-drinker orders from the same menu as everyone else rather than being handed a separate card. The trade-off is that the spirit-free options are conversions rather than original compositions, so ask the bar what is possible rather than expecting a printed list. Open evenings, closed Tuesdays. Golden Hill is a small, largely residential neighbourhood, and Kingfisher is the reason most people cross the city to eat there — which makes the flexibility of its zero-proof approach more valuable than a longer fixed list at somewhere less worth travelling to.
venues.pressQuote: Lyre's makes quality stuff, and it allowed us to be able to do a quick change but keep the original idea of the cocktail intact.

venues.name: Kismet Modern Indian
venues.description: Kismet Modern Indian on West Broad Street builds its non-alcoholic drinks with the same spice-forward logic as its cooking, and keeps two named mocktails on the printed list: Tiger's Tail and Familiar Faces. Indian food is a natural fit for alcohol-free drinking — the cuisine's own drinking tradition runs to lassi, nimbu pani and spiced coolers rather than wine, and chilli heat is generally better served by something cold and acidic than by alcohol. That makes ordering a zero-proof drink here feel like a considered pairing rather than a substitution, which is a rarer experience than it should be. It sits on the Scott's Addition edge of West Broad Street, so it slots easily into an evening built around the brewery district without requiring anyone at the table to drink.
venues.longDescription:
Kismet Modern Indian sits on West Broad Street near the Scott's Addition boundary, working a contemporary register of Indian cooking rather than a traditional one. Its bar carries two named non-alcoholic drinks — Tiger's Tail and Familiar Faces — which Richmond's food coverage picks out.

The deeper reason this restaurant suits a non-drinker has to do with the cuisine itself. India's own drinking culture at the table has never been built around alcohol: lassi, nimbu pani, jaljeera, spiced buttermilk and an enormous range of cooling and digestive drinks exist because they are what the food wants. Chilli heat, ghee and heavy spice are cut better by acidity, salt, dairy and sugar than by ethanol, which is why wine pairing with Indian food remains a famously awkward exercise. Order something alcohol-free here and you are not compensating for anything — you are drinking what the cooking was designed alongside.

That is the difference between a mocktail that exists to fill a gap on the menu and one that belongs on the table. The two named drinks are the restaurant's own compositions rather than traditional preparations, but the same principle applies: they are built to sit with spice rather than to imitate a cocktail.

A practical note on timing: the restaurant is closed Mondays and runs dinner-only on Tuesdays, with lunch service starting midweek — a common pattern along this stretch of Richmond, and worth knowing if you are planning a daytime visit early in the week. The location puts it within easy reach of Three Notch'd and the rest of the Scott's Addition cluster, so it fits naturally into an evening built around that district. Pair it with Three Notch'd a few doors west and the evening covers both dinner and a taproom without anyone compromising.
venues.pressQuote: Hailing from Old Town Alexandria with a Michelin Bib Gourmand-winning sister restaurant in the capital, Kismet Modern Indian will make its debut in the former Perch space this fall
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: Richmond Magazine, Richmond Food News, August 2022

venues.name: Kitty Dare
venues.description: Kitty Dare is a Mediterranean-inspired restaurant in Atlanta's Inman Park, in the storied 1029 Edgewood Ave space. It opened in 2021, founded by owner and wine director Jamshad "Jaamy" Zarnegar, who was born in Iran and previously co-owned Athens' Last Resort Grill; the kitchen is led by chef Giuseppe Esposito, from Italy's Emilia region. The restaurant is named for Zarnegar's late friend, Kitty Dare Etheridge. The menu spans pan-Mediterranean plates such as berbere chicken with saffron rice cakes and bucatini with shrimp. Alongside its wine-forward bar, Kitty Dare runs a small named zero-proof cocktail list built on Amethyst 0.0% spirits. Named alcohol-free drinks include the Kian (Amethyst Blueberry Ginger Mint, lime, simple syrup, ginger beer) and the Farhad (Amethyst Lemon Cucumber Serrano, lemon, simple syrup, mint). The bar opens daily at 4pm.
venues.longDescription:
Kitty Dare occupies 1029 Edgewood Avenue in Inman Park, a storied Atlanta address, and has been there since 2021. It was founded by owner and wine director Jamshad Zarnegar, known as Jaamy, who was born in Iran and previously co-owned the Last Resort Grill in Athens; the kitchen is led by chef Giuseppe Esposito, from Italy's Emilia region. The restaurant carries the name of Zarnegar's late friend Kitty Dare Etheridge. The food is pan-Mediterranean and ranges wider than that label usually promises — berbere chicken with saffron rice cakes alongside bucatini with shrimp.

It is a wine-forward bar, and the zero-proof list is correspondingly short: two named cocktails, both built on Amethyst, the non-alcoholic distillery from South Carolina. The Kian uses Amethyst Blueberry Ginger Mint with lime, simple syrup and ginger beer. The Farhad is built on Amethyst Lemon Cucumber Serrano with lemon, simple syrup and mint.

Amethyst is worth noting because it turns up repeatedly in this city — the same Lemon Cucumber Serrano bottling appears in the Celery Gimlet at one-Michelin-starred Lazy Betty. A regional non-alcoholic producer being adopted by serious kitchens across a metro is a reasonable signal of quality, and it means the drinks in the Farhad and the Gimlet share a recognisable backbone: the serrano gives a slow capsaicin heat that fills the space a spirit's burn would otherwise occupy. Heat is one of the few tools that genuinely replaces alcohol's bite rather than working around it.

Two drinks is a short list, and this is a wine bar with a restaurant attached rather than a zero-proof destination — go for the food and the room, and expect a properly made drink rather than a menu of them. The bar opens daily at 4pm, with dinner from 5pm and brunch on Sundays.

venues.name: Knight Moves Cafe
venues.description: Knight Moves is a board game cafe on Beacon Street near Coolidge Corner, and one of the few places in the metro that keeps bar hours without a bar. It opens at 5pm on weeknights and runs to 11pm, and on Friday and Saturday it stays open until 2am. Guests pay a fee to take a table and play from a large game library, and the espresso counter runs the whole time. The menu carries no alcohol: espresso drinks, chai, matcha and London Fog tea lattes, hot chocolate, sodas, soda floats and milkshakes in vanilla, chocolate, Nutella, strawberry, espresso and banana, plus a rotating seasonal list of turmeric lattes, peaflower lemonade, blackberry mocha and strawberry matcha. Sandwiches and snacks fill out the food. Guests may bring their own alcohol for a per-person fee.
venues.longDescription:
Knight Moves occupies a white brick building on Beacon Street a short walk from Coolidge Corner, its front bay window filled with houseplants and a wooden chess table in the corner behind them. It was among the first board game cafes in Greater Boston and it operates on a model borrowed from bars rather than coffee shops: a cover charge buys a table and the run of the game library for the night, staff will teach a game to a table that has stalled over the rulebook, and the room fills with families, medical students, first dates and reunions until closing. Brookline.News profiled it in November 2025 under the headline 'At Knight Moves Cafe, a different kind of nightlife where play is the point,' which is an accurate description of what it does for the neighborhood.

The hours are what make it useful to someone who is not drinking. Weeknights run 5pm to 11pm and Friday and Saturday run to 2am, which is later than almost every cafe in the metro and as late as most Brookline bars. Nothing on the menu contains alcohol. The counter pulls espresso, americanos, cappuccinos and lattes with decaf available on any of them, makes chai, matcha and London Fog tea lattes, and runs a rotating seasonal list that has included a turmeric latte with ginger and peppercorn, a peaflower lemonade, a blackberry mocha and a strawberry matcha. Sodas come with the option of a vanilla ice cream float, and the milkshake list runs vanilla, chocolate, Nutella, strawberry, espresso and banana. Food is sandwiches on bread from When Pigs Fly, salads and snacks. One caveat worth stating plainly: the cafe does not serve alcohol but does allow guests to bring their own for a per-person food and beverage fee, so alcohol can be present at neighboring tables.
venues.pressQuote: Knight Moves, located on Beacon Street near Coolidge Corner, is one of the first local board game cafes, with at least 4 now in the Boston area, part of a widespread rise in the popularity of board game cafes among millennials and Gen Z.

venues.name: Kol
venues.description: Kol is chef Santiago Lastra's one-Michelin-star modern-Mexican restaurant in Marylebone, with a destination basement mezcaleria whose bar is led by former American Bar head bartender Maxim Schulte. The non-alcoholic drinks are given the same intent as the cocktail and mezcal lists: the bar folds trimmings from the food menu into a beetroot-and-hibiscus agua fresca, served alongside an in-house horchata and a hibiscus agua fresca. It is a small but genuine zero-proof offering inside one of the UK's most acclaimed Mexican kitchens.
signatureDrinks: Beetroot and hibiscus agua fresca — non-alcoholic, built from trimmings off the food menu
venues.longDescription:
Kol is the first restaurant from Mexican chef Santiago Lastra, set in the former Marylebone police station on Seymour Street. It won a Michelin star in 2022, has retained it since, and entered the World's 50 Best Restaurants list, working under the banner 'Mexican soul, British ingredients' — overlaying Mexican technique and heritage onto hyper-seasonal British produce. It is the only Mexican restaurant in the UK to hold a Michelin star.

Below the dining room sits the Mezcaleria, an atmospheric stone-walled basement bar built as Lastra's homage to Mexico's mezcal bars and run by head bartender Maxim Schulte, previously head bartender at the American Bar. The bar works in synergy with the kitchen, incorporating trimmings from the food menu into its drinks. For anyone not drinking, that means a beetroot-and-hibiscus agua fresca made from those trimmings, plus classic Mexican non-alcoholic options — an in-house horchata and an agua fresca — crafted with the same attention as the alcoholic list rather than treated as an afterthought.

The pairing of a Michelin kitchen and a serious cocktail team makes the zero-proof drinks here more considered than most restaurant soft-drink menus, even if the alcohol-free selection remains a handful of builds rather than a full printed list. The room itself is a compelling, low-lit space of stone walls and succulents, with an antojitos small-plates menu alongside the drinks.
venues.pressQuote: The bar works in synergy with the restaurant, incorporating trimmings from the food menu into creations like the beetroot and hibiscus agua fresca, a non-alcoholic drink.

venues.name: Komyuniti
venues.description: Komyuniti is the in-house bar and restaurant at YOTEL Singapore on Orchard Road, and it prints one of the few genuinely named zero-proof menu sections in the city. The drinks list is divided into seven series — DRY, WOOD, SOBER, KLASSIC, ACID, FRUIT and SPUMY — and SOBER is a standing part of that structure with its own menu page, not an afterthought tacked onto the back. Four builds run at S$16++ against S$23++ for the spirited drinks, each specified as precisely as the alcoholic list: Calm And Go with Giffard elderflower, chamomile tea, fresh herbs and soda; She's A Ginger; Kinky Pinky; and Hula Who Lah. The programme is run by mixologist As'ad Isnin.
signatureDrinks: Calm And Go (S$16++) - Giffard elderflower, chamomile tea, fresh herbs, soda
She's A Ginger (S$16++) - Giffard ginger, lemon, cranberry, fake egg white
Kinky Pinky (S$16++) - Giffard grapefruit, bitter concentrate, orange, rosemary, tonic
Hula Who Lah (S$16++) - orgeat, pineapple, orange, lemon, spice bitters, cocoa mist
venues.longDescription:
Komyuniti is the bar and restaurant inside YOTEL Singapore, on the Orchard Road hotel strip, and it is easy to overlook precisely because it is a hotel bar. That would be a mistake for anyone who is not drinking, because its menu is organised in a way that very few bars in Singapore manage: the zero-proof drinks are a named, permanent part of the structure rather than an appendix.

The list is split into seven series — DRY, WOOD, SOBER, KLASSIC, ACID, FRUIT and SPUMY. SOBER sits in that sequence as an equal, with its own page on the bar's menu site, which means a non-drinking guest is choosing from a labelled section of the main list rather than asking what can be made without alcohol. There are four drinks in it, priced at S$16++ against S$23++ for the cocktails, and each is specified with the same precision as the spirited builds. Calm And Go combines Giffard elderflower with chamomile tea, fresh herbs and soda. She's A Ginger uses Giffard ginger with lemon, cranberry and a vegan foamer in place of egg white. Kinky Pinky pairs Giffard grapefruit with bitter concentrate, orange, rosemary and tonic. Hula Who Lah is the tiki-leaning one, built on orgeat with pineapple, orange, lemon, spice bitters and a cocoa mist.

The use of Giffard across three of the four is worth noting, since it means the flavour base is a proper bar syrup and liqueur range rather than commercial cordial. The programme sits under award-winning mixologist As'ad Isnin, and the bar has run non-alcoholic craft cocktails as a stated focus for several years rather than adopting them recently. As a hotel bar it serves food throughout the day and is an easy, unfussy option in a part of Orchard Road that is otherwise dominated by malls.

venues.name: Kona's Street Market
venues.description: Around-the-world-themed cocktail bar in SoMa from the Pacific Cocktail Haven team, with a small zero-proof cocktail section built on Lyre's spirits.
venues.hours: Mon closed; Tue-Thu 4pm-10pm; Fri 4pm-11pm; Sat-Sun closed

naMenuItems.name: Zero Here
naMenuItems.description: lyre's agave, rhubarb, pineapple, citrus

naMenuItems.name: Sober Dragon
naMenuItems.description: lyre's dry london spirit, lyre's apertif, dragon fruit, lychee, coconut cream, citrus

venues.longDescription: Kona's Street Market is an around-the-world-themed cocktail bar in San Francisco's SoMa neighborhood, opened by award-winning bartender Kevin Diedrich of Pacific Cocktail Haven and named after his pitbull, Kona. The street market-inspired room is filled with film posters and vibrant neon signage, and the international cocktail list draws on ingredients from Southeast Asia to the Caribbean. The menu also carries a dedicated "Zero Proof Cocktails" section, with the Lyre's-based Zero Here (Lyre's Agave, rhubarb, pineapple, citrus) and Sober Dragon (Lyre's Dry London Spirit, Lyre's Aperitif, dragon fruit, lychee, coconut cream, citrus), plus Athletic Brewing non-alcoholic beer.
venues.pressQuote: Kona's Street Market is more than a cocktail bar: It's a passport to global flavors, tucked under neon lights in SoMa.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Virginia Miller, Time Out San Francisco

venues.name: Kosmic Community Anti Bar
venues.description: Kosmic Community Anti Bar & Coffee Shop is a fully alcohol-free "anti bar" and cafe that opened in May 2024 in the former Mug & Cup space at 115 Avenue C in the East Village. It was founded by owner and East Village resident James Lockwood along with partners Tyler Garrett and Apostolos Filippas, who built it as a judgment-free social space for people with any relationship to sobriety. The owners are, in their words, "not big on mocktails," instead pouring a full coffee bar plus house-made sodas, herbal teas, fruit presses, and kava. The drink list also carries craft NA beer from Mash Gang, Athletic Brewing, and Go Brewing. The space keeps late hours — open until 2am Fridays and Saturdays — and features a retro lounge with a vintage phone booth and a back garden, hosting community events and live programming.
venues.longDescription:
Kosmic Community Anti Bar & Coffee Shop opened in May 2024 at 115 Avenue C, in the former Mug & Cup space in the East Village, and the name is a genuine statement of method rather than a pun. It was founded by East Village resident James Lockwood with partners Tyler Garrett and Apostolos Filippas, and built explicitly as a judgment-free social space for people with any relationship to sobriety — which is a wider and more useful brief than "a bar for sober people".

The most interesting decision here is what they refused to do. The owners have said plainly that they are not big on mocktails. That runs against the entire grain of the category, where the default assumption is that a room without alcohol must offer elaborate imitations of cocktails to be taken seriously. Instead the bar pours a full coffee programme alongside house-made sodas, herbal teas, fruit presses and kava, with craft non-alcoholic beer from Mash Gang, Athletic Brewing and Go Brewing.

That choice is worth defending, because the mocktail-first model has a real weakness: an imitation invites comparison, and comparison is exactly what a lot of people trying not to drink would rather avoid. A well-made house soda or a properly brewed tea is not pretending to be anything. It is simply a good drink, ordered without subtext. Kava — the South Pacific root drink poured for its mild sedative effect — sits in the same tradition of drinks that are interesting in their own right; anyone unfamiliar with it should know it is psychoactive in a mild way rather than inert, and pace a first visit accordingly.

The room is fitted as a retro lounge, complete with a vintage phone booth, and opens onto a back garden. It programmes community events and live sessions, and it keeps hours that matter: open until 2am on Friday and Saturday. That is the specific window in which not drinking is hardest and the East Village's alternatives thinnest, and a room that is open, awake and free of alcohol at 1am on a Saturday is doing something few venues in Manhattan do at all.

venues.name: Krave
venues.description: The Carrboro branch of Krave is a fully alcohol-free kava bar and lounge on West Main Street in downtown Carrboro, minutes from the UNC campus and the Chapel Hill line, open to midnight most nights and one in the morning on Friday and Saturday. It is the original: Krave opened here in 2015, founded by UNC Chapel Hill alumna Elizabeth Gardner, and later expanded to Greensboro and Raleigh, and every room runs the same model — kava root drinks served in a shell, a long tea list covering traditional roots and a broader range of brewed teas, ambient world-lounge music, and no alcohol at all. The large seating area at the back is built for sitting rather than standing, and the crowd mixes students, graduate researchers and Carrboro locals. For a college town whose social life otherwise runs through Franklin Street's bars, it is the only alcohol-free room on this side of the Triangle that keeps bar hours.
signatureDrinks: Traditional Kava — ground aged kava root from the South Pacific, served with no additives
Yerba Mate — thirteen varieties from four countries, the largest collection in North Carolina
venues.longDescription:
Krave's Carrboro room is the alcohol-free anchor for the western end of the Triangle. It sits on West Main Street in downtown Carrboro, minutes from the UNC campus and the Chapel Hill line, and it is the original: Krave opened here in 2015, won Indy Week's Best of the Triangle award in 2016, expanded to Greensboro that year and to Raleigh in August 2022, and every room runs the same model — kava, tea, late hours, no alcohol at all. The company describes its kava as ground aged root from the South Pacific with no additives, and its yerba mate collection, thirteen varieties from four countries, as the largest in North Carolina.

Kava deserves a plain description rather than a euphemism. It is a root drink from the South Pacific — ground, steeped in water, served in a shell — and it produces a mild, calming, sociable effect without containing any alcohol. It is still psychoactive in its own way, so it is not the right choice for everyone; anyone pregnant, on medication, or watching their liver health should ask a doctor first. What it offers people avoiding alcohol is the thing that is otherwise hardest to replace: something to hold, something that does something, in a room full of other people doing the same.

The Carrboro branch leans into the lounge format, with a large seating area at the back and the same ambient, world-lounge soundtrack as the Raleigh room. The tea list runs long, covering both the traditional roots and a broader range of brewed teas, and the crowd is a mix of students, graduate researchers and Carrboro locals. For a college town whose social life otherwise runs through Franklin Street's bars, it is a meaningful alternative — and with a midnight close, it is open when the alternative matters most. Oasis Botanical Lounge, a few blocks away in Carr Mill Mall, is Carrboro's other alcohol-free room, but it closes at seven; Krave is the one open when the bars are.
venues.pressQuote: Krave provides an alcohol-free atmosphere for customers seeking to unwind and socialize in a bar environment.

venues.name: Krave
venues.description: Krave is Raleigh's fully alcohol-free kava bar and tea lounge on North Person Street, a short walk from Seaboard Station, and it keeps proper bar hours: midnight Sunday through Thursday, one in the morning on Friday and Saturday. It serves kava — the South Pacific root drink, ground, steeped and served in a shell, calming and sociable but with no alcohol in it — alongside an extensive list of teas and roots, in a low-lit lounge with ambient music and a deep seating area at the back built for staying put. Opened in August 2022 as the third room of a company founded in Carrboro in 2015 by UNC Chapel Hill alumna Elizabeth Gardner, it is an explicit alternative to the traditional bar scene rather than a cafe that happens to close late, and since Umbrella Dry Bar closed for good it is the only dedicated alcohol-free room left in Raleigh proper. Its Carrboro sibling is listed separately.
signatureDrinks: Traditional Kava — ground aged kava root from the South Pacific, served with no additives
Yerba Mate — thirteen varieties from four countries, the largest collection in North Carolina
venues.longDescription:
Krave is Raleigh's dedicated alcohol-free bar, and since Umbrella Dry Bar closed it is the only one in the city. It trades on North Person Street a short walk from Seaboard Station, and it keeps proper bar hours — midnight Sunday through Thursday, one in the morning on Friday and Saturday — which is what separates a real alcohol-free venue from a coffee shop that shuts at six.

The bar serves kava, and it is worth saying clearly what that means. Kava is a root traditionally prepared in the South Pacific, ground and steeped and served in a shell, and it produces a mild, calming, sociable effect. It contains no alcohol whatsoever. It is nonetheless psychoactive in its own right, and anyone on medication, pregnant, or managing liver health should check with a doctor before drinking it. For people avoiding alcohol it is a genuine substitute for the ritual of a drink in hand; for people avoiding everything, the Triangle's zero-proof cocktail lists are the better route.

Alongside the kava, Krave pours an extensive tea programme — ancient and exotic roots and teas, as the bar puts it — and the room is built for lingering: dim light, ambient and world-lounge music, a deep seating area at the back. It is the sort of place where a group can sit for three hours without anyone ordering a second round of anything, which is precisely the experience the Triangle otherwise lacks. Krave's sister room in Carrboro is a separate venue with its own listing, and the company — founded in 2015 by UNC Chapel Hill alumna Elizabeth Gardner, and describing itself as an exotic tea oasis serving premium kava products across North Carolina — also runs a Greensboro room outside this metro; this Raleigh room opened in August 2022 as the third. The site does not publish a full drinks list, but it describes the kava as ground aged root from the South Pacific served with no additives, and the yerba mate collection as thirteen varieties from four countries — North Carolina's largest.
venues.pressQuote: Serves exotic root and tea beverages as an alternative to the alcohol bar scene.

venues.name: Kumiko
venues.description: Kumiko is a Japanese dining bar in Chicago's West Loop, opened in 2018 by bartender and restaurateur Julia Momosé, who also leads it as creative director and beverage visionary. Named for the Japanese kumiko woodworking technique reflected in its design, the venue treats food and drink with equal reverence. Its alcohol-free program is a genuine cornerstone: Momosé created a line of zero-proof drinks she calls "Spiritfrees," built from ingredients like shiso-pickled umé, sanshō, yarrow flower, sweet osmanthus, and Japanese seven spice rather than NA spirit brands. Spiritfree is offered both à la carte and as one of four formal tasting-menu pairings, alongside light cocktails, stirred cocktails, and sake. Kumiko won the 2025 James Beard Award for Outstanding Bar and was named World's Best Bar at the 2025 Spirited Awards, and it ranked among North America's 50 Best Bars. Reservations recommended; guests 18 and older.
signatureDrinks: Bright One (yuzu juice, clover honey, Seedlip Spice 94, Fever-Tree ginger beer) $15
Uméboshi Swizzle (shiso-pickled umé, brown rice vinegar, lemon, sesame, Japanese seven spice, over crushed ice) $15
Pepperberry Tonic (Tasmanian pepperberry, sanshō, angelica root, fennel seed, Fever-Tree elderflower tonic) $15
Saved by the Bell (sanshō, yarrow flower, cubeb pepper, yellow mustard seed, kinmokusei, sparkling Fuji apple juice, Fever-Tree ginger beer) $16
Bianco (mint, fennel seed, chamomile, white peppercorn, lavender honey, verjus blanc, club soda) $16
Hōji-Hi (hōjicha, concord grape, pomegranate molasses, Maison Perrier) $16
Maple Blues (mugicha roasted barley tisane, Japanese seven spice lemon cordial, amber maple syrup) $16
Protea (adzuki, purple sweet potato vinegar, Seedlip Spice 94, verjus rouge, Fever-Tree club soda, tonic) $16
venues.longDescription:
Kumiko is a Japanese dining bar at 630 W Lake Street in the West Loop, opened on New Year's Eve 2018 and led by Julia Momosé, who was born and raised in Japan, studied at Cornell, and has become the single most influential figure in American non-alcoholic bartending. It is named for the Japanese woodworking technique of assembling wood without nails, and the drinks are built on the same principle of precision without obvious fixings. In July 2025 Kumiko was named World's Best Bar at the Spirited Awards, having already taken the James Beard Foundation's Outstanding Bar award that year, held a Michelin star since 2019, and been named Best Bar in the Midwest by North America's 50 Best every year from 2022. Momosé became executive chef in December 2024. Andrew Mainor, raised on the South Side and cooking since he was fifteen, runs the kitchen; Mai Pham, who was born in Hanoi and trained at Kendall College, manages the room.

The reason Kumiko matters here more than any other bar in Chicago is that Momosé coined the term "spiritfree" and built the category's template: drinks constructed from tisanes, vinegars, cordials and spices to have the length and bitterness of a cocktail, rather than a cocktail with the alcohol removed. The spiritfrees sit on the same menu as everything else at $15 to $16, within a couple of dollars of the alcoholic list. Uméboshi Swizzle ($15) works shiso-pickled umé with brown rice vinegar, lemon, sesame and Japanese seven spice over crushed ice. Bianco ($16) layers mint, fennel seed, chamomile and white peppercorn with lavender honey and verjus blanc. Saved by the Bell ($16) is the most elaborate, combining sanshō, yarrow flower, cubeb pepper, yellow mustard seed and kinmokusei with sparkling Fuji apple juice and ginger beer. Hōji-Hi ($16) pairs roasted hōjicha tea with concord grape and pomegranate molasses; Maple Blues ($16) uses a roasted barley mugicha tisane with a seven-spice lemon cordial and amber maple syrup. Bright One ($15) and Protea ($16) both use Seedlip Spice 94, and Pepperberry Tonic ($15) builds Tasmanian pepperberry and angelica root into an elderflower tonic. Spiritfree pairings are offered alongside the seasonal tasting menu. The bar runs Wednesday to Sunday from 5.30pm, with Café Kumiko open Friday to Sunday mornings.
venues.pressQuote: Momosé's range of alcohol-free drinks are dubbed "Spiritfrees" and are just as profound as their alcoholic counterparts.

venues.name: Kupros Craft House
venues.description: Kupros Craft House in Midtown stocks Lyre's non-alcoholic spirits and uses them properly — an Old Fashioned built on Lyre's American whiskey alternative and a mojito on the Lyre's range, alongside an espresso martini mocktail and a White Linen variation with elderflower. The Old Fashioned is the significant one: it is the hardest classic to fake, being essentially spirit, sugar and bitters with nowhere to hide, so a bar willing to put its name on a zero-proof version has bought a real product and tested it. Hop waters and sodas cover the simpler orders. It keeps the longest hours of any bar in this guide, opening at noon most days and running to 1:30am on Friday and Saturday.
signatureDrinks: Old Fashioned - Lyre's American whiskey alternative
venues.longDescription:
Kupros Craft House occupies a converted house on 21st Street in Midtown Sacramento, and its non-alcoholic offering is deeper than almost anything else in the city because it is built on stocked product rather than improvisation.

The bar carries Lyre's, one of the more established non-alcoholic spirit ranges, and uses it across several drinks. The Old Fashioned is the one that demonstrates commitment. Strip an Old Fashioned to its parts and you have spirit, sugar, bitters and ice — no citrus, no mixer, nothing to hide behind. Whatever replaces the whiskey is completely exposed, which is why most bars will not attempt one and why offering it is a genuine claim. The mojito is the easier build, since mint, lime and sugar carry most of its character anyway.

The espresso martini mocktail is smart menu design for a different reason: the alcoholic original is already dominated by coffee, so the vodka contributes texture more than flavour, and a well-made zero-proof version loses very little. The White Linen variation with elderflower covers the floral, lighter end.

Hop waters deserve a mention too. They are sparkling water dry-hopped with the same aromatic hops used in IPAs — bitter, citrusy, and completely alcohol-free — and they solve the specific problem of wanting something that tastes like a beer garden without the beer.

The hours are the best in this guide: open from noon most days, 10am at weekends, and running to 1:30am on Friday and Saturday. In a city where much of the alcohol-free provision closes by ten, a Midtown bar with Lyre's behind the counter serving past one is genuinely useful.

A note on what Lyre's actually is, since the category confuses people. It is a range of distilled non-alcoholic spirits built to match the flavour profiles of gin, whisky, amaretto and the rest — botanicals and extracts assembled to hit the same notes, with no ethanol. It is not a perfect substitute; nothing replaces the warmth and weight alcohol gives a drink. What it does deliver is the aromatic structure, so a cocktail built on it tastes like a version of the original rather than like fruit juice. For a bar, stocking it is a real cost with a single purpose, and that purchasing decision is the most reliable signal there is of a genuine programme.

venues.name: Kurasu Singapore
venues.description: Kurasu is a Kyoto specialty coffee and tea company that chose Singapore for its first overseas shop, opening here in July 2017 before later settling into a flagship on Waterloo Street. It is entirely alcohol-free, and the operation is unusually focused: there is essentially no food, and the counter concentrates on brewing rather than on the cafe trappings that surround most Singapore coffee shops. Espresso and hand-poured filter sit alongside Japanese tea, and the matcha latte has been the signature since the beginning. The room is minimal and quiet in the Kyoto manner, and it functions as a daytime working and reading space rather than an evening destination.
signatureDrinks: Matcha latte — ceremonial-grade matcha sourced from Kyoto
Usucha — a traditional bowl of matcha whisked with water, served without milk
venues.longDescription:
Kurasu began in Kyoto as a specialty coffee company with a strong design sensibility, and when it looked to expand beyond Japan it came to Singapore first, opening in July 2017 in partnership with a co-working operator at Odeon Towers. That original address is still widely cited online, but the business has since moved, and the flagship now sits on Waterloo Street in the Bras Basah arts and heritage district. Anyone working from older reviews — and most of the coverage online dates from 2017 to 2020 — will be sent to the wrong place.

The shop is narrow in scope by design. There is effectively no food menu; the counter exists to brew. Espresso-based drinks and hand-poured filter coffee run alongside Japanese tea, and the matcha latte has been the signature item since the first day of trading, prepared with the care you would expect from a company whose home market is Kyoto. Beans rotate, with the roasting programme drawing on Japanese roasters as well as the house's own work, and staff are comfortable talking through origin and method.

The room follows the same logic: minimal, pale, quiet, with limited seating and none of the clutter that fills most Singapore cafes. It is a place to sit with a notebook or a laptop rather than to hold a conversation over several hours. For a non-drinker the honest framing is that this is a daytime venue — it is a coffee shop, not an evening alternative to a bar, and it keeps weekday business hours. Within that, it is among the most rigorous cups in the city, and its position near the Bras Basah museums and the Waterloo Street temples makes it a natural stop on an afternoon spent in that part of town.
venues.pressQuote: As a matcha girlie, I thoroughly enjoyed Kurasu’s matcha latte, made with ceremonial-grade matcha sourced from Kyoto.

venues.name: Kwant
venues.description: Kwãnt is the Mayfair cocktail bar of Erik Lorincz, the Slovakia-born bartender who spent more than seven years as head bartender of the American Bar at The Savoy — helping take it to No.1 on The World's 50 Best Bars in 2017 — and who won the Diageo World Class competition in 2010. He opened the first Kwãnt in 2019 in the basement of Momo on Heddon Street, where within a year it was named Best New Opening at the World's 50 Best Bars 2020. CORRECTION TO OUR EARLIER LISTING: after Momo closed during the pandemic, Lorincz spent around eighteen months designing and relaunching Kwãnt at its current corner site at 52 Stratton Street, two minutes from Green Park, reopening in 2023 — it is no longer beneath Momo. The name is a play on "quaint", and the reborn bar drew CLASS magazine's first-ever 10/10 review. Its menu lists five dedicated non-alcoholic cocktails alongside the two dozen alcoholic ones, many built on herbs grown in-house and treated with the same craft as the full-strength drinks.
venues.longDescription:
Kwãnt is the Mayfair cocktail bar of Erik Lorincz, the Slovakia-born bartender who spent over seven years as head bartender of the American Bar at The Savoy — helping take it to No. 1 on The World's 50 Best Bars in 2017 — and who won the Diageo World Class competition in 2010. He opened the first Kwãnt in 2019 in the basement of Momo on Heddon Street, where within a year it was named Best New Opening at The World's 50 Best Bars 2020. After Momo closed during the pandemic, Lorincz spent around 18 months designing and relaunching Kwãnt at its current corner site at 52 Stratton Street, a two-minute walk from Green Park, reopening in 2023. The name is a play on the word "quaint." The reborn bar drew CLASS magazine's first-ever 10/10 review and now sits within Europe's 50 Best Bars.

The room trades the original basement for a large, high-ceilinged corner space with floor-to-ceiling windows, styled as a tropical-colonial retreat: a hand-painted Polynesian tapa-style wall mural, a Vietnamese cane-webbing ceiling, slow-turning ceiling fans, tall palms in the windows and retro furniture with mustard-coloured sofas and chessboard tables. A mixing desk shifts the space through a series of lighting moods as day turns to night. Rather than working behind a back bar, the bartenders serve from three stations around a huge central island, with a dedicated seat set aside for solo guests. Micro-herbs and garnishes are grown in-house on an Evogro hydroponic cabinet and cut to order, and drinks arrive in bespoke Rona glassware Lorincz designed for individual cocktails.

The menu is divided into signature and vintage cocktails, and alongside 24 alcoholic drinks it carries a dedicated line-up of five non-alcoholic drinks built with exactly the same techniques as the rest of the list — fermentation, clarification, carbonation and in-house distillation. The bar makes its own ferments (fermented cucumber, beetroot and lapsang-souchong vinegar) and unusual distillates, and the zero-proof drinks lean on these house-made components and the hydroponic herbs rather than simply substituting a non-alcoholic spirit; expect lighter, fruitier spritz-style builds as well as more savoury, spice-driven ones. Europe's 50 Best Bars sums up the range as running from "spirit-forward stirred concoctions, to lighter and fruitier spritzes, and a line-up of non-alcoholic drinks utilising just as much innovation and creativity." The specific zero-proof drinks rotate and aren't published online, so it is worth telling the bartenders what you like and letting them build one to taste. Kwãnt is walk-ins only, with no reservations.
venues.pressQuote: The in-house hydroponically grown garnishes and bespoke Rona glassware are minimalist, allowing the flavour of the varied drinks to shine – expect everything from spirit-forward stirred concoctions, to lighter and fruitier spritzes, and a line-up of non-alcoholic drinks utilising just as much innovation and creativity.

venues.name: LÝRA
venues.description: LÝRA is a modern Greek restaurant in Chicago's Fulton Market from DineAmic Hospitality, offering wood-hearth-fired Mediterranean fare alongside a documented non-alcoholic drinks menu that includes two named zero-proof mocktails and an alcohol-removed wine list.

venues.longDescription:
Sitting at the corner of Peoria and Fulton in Chicago's Fulton Market district, LÝRA is one of the neighborhood's more thoughtful destinations for non-drinkers. The restaurant's NA program goes beyond an afterthought soda list: the menu includes two named zero-proof cocktails and, as noted by Do312, an alcohol-removed wine list — an unusual touch for a full-service Greek concept. The 8,000-square-foot space, with its covered outdoor patio and warm earth-toned interior, means there's no penalty for ordering non-alcoholic; you're seated comfortably in the full dining room, not shuffled to a corner.

The two signature zero-proof drinks anchor the NA menu. The Halara pairs Amass Zero Proof spirit with pomegranate, lemon, mint, and tonic for a bright, herbal pour that reads like a more complex Tom Collins riff. The Cypress takes a more tropical angle — Amass Zero Proof with pineapple, lime, and ginger — clean and refreshing alongside the kitchen's grilled proteins. Both drinks were developed to reflect what the restaurant describes as the natural Greek lifestyle ethos. Note: while Block Club Chicago's earlier coverage of LÝRA referenced Seedlip in the zero-proof cocktails, the current menu (as published by the restaurant) uses Amass Zero Proof spirits in both drinks. LÝRA's culinary program is led by Chef Athinagoras Kostakos, an internationally recognized Greek chef whose menu centers on a custom wood and charcoal burning hearth.

LÝRA skews lively rather than intimate: expect a DJ and a club-like energy after 10pm on Fridays and Saturdays, dimmed lights, and sparklers during the late-night 'Weekend Ritual' service. Earlier weeknight seatings are noticeably calmer and better suited for conversation. Reservations are strongly recommended and are accepted exclusively through OpenTable, released 60 days in advance. It's a solid pick for sober or sober-curious diners who want the full Fulton Market experience — a scene-y room, serious food, and a drinks list that doesn't treat non-alcoholic as a lesser category.
venues.pressQuote: LÝRA's menu features two zero-proof mocktails: the 'Halara' with Seedlip, pomegranate, lemon, mint and tonic, and the 'Cypress' with Seedlip, pineapple, lime and ginger.

venues.name: Lady Jane
venues.description: Lady Jane is a neighborhood cocktail bar on West 32nd Avenue in Denver's LoHi (Lower Highlands), established in 2018 and known for a menu that rotates frequently and a collaborative bar team led by general manager Stuart Weaver. Westword has described the non-alcoholic program as having "a permanent place" on the menu rather than being a Dry January promotion, and the current list keeps four built zero-proof drinks at a flat $12 alongside the spirited cocktails: the Grapehojicha Swizzle (Three Spirit Livener, Concord grape, Giffard pineapple shrub, pineapple, hojicha tea, lime), the Pineapple Nogroni (AMASS Riverine, Giffard bitter aperitif, pineapple, Leopold Bros non-alcoholic aperitivo), the Cucumber Spritz (UNDONE Little French Aperitif, cucumber, matcha honey, soda) and Morning Bun & Coffee (The Pathfinder Hemp & Root, Three Spirit Nightcap, cold brew, morning bun syrup, cardamom). The bar was named Reader's Choice Best Bar in 5280's Top of the Town 2023 awards, and operates mainly first-come first-served.
signatureDrinks: Grapehojicha Swizzle (NA: Three Spirit Livener, Concord grape, Giffard pineapple shrub, pineapple, hojicha tea, lime)
Pineapple Nogroni (NA: AMASS Riverine, Giffard bitter aperitif, pineapple, Leopold Bros NA aperitivo)
Cucumber Spritz (NA: UNDONE Little French Aperitif, cucumber, matcha honey, soda)
Morning Bun & Coffee (NA: The Pathfinder Hemp & Root, Three Spirit Nightcap, cold brew, morning bun syrup, cardamom)
venues.longDescription:
Lady Jane opened in 2018 at 2021 West 32nd Avenue in Lower Highlands and states its purpose plainly on its own site: a neighbourhood cocktail bar serving drinks in a welcoming and safe space, with a list meant to be bold, seasonal and approachable while leaning on local ingredients. The room is airy and plant-filled, the team is collaborative rather than built around a single name, and general manager Stuart Weaver runs it. The full-proof menu is technically ambitious in a way that is easy to miss from the casual room: clarifications through sheep yogurt, coconut milk and whey, force-carbonated builds, and a house six-amaro blend among them. The bar took Reader's Choice Best Bar in 5280's Top of the Town 2023 awards, and its cocktail programme has been covered by Thrillist, Eater Denver, Imbibe, 303 Magazine and Denver Life. It runs mostly first-come first-served with limited reservations, and is closed Sundays.

The zero-proof drinks sit in the same column as the cocktails at a flat $12 and turn over with the rest of the menu, which is the reason the list looks different from one season to the next. The current four are the Grapehojicha Swizzle, built on Three Spirit Livener with Concord grape, Giffard pineapple shrub, pineapple, hojicha tea and lime; the Pineapple Nogroni, which layers AMASS Riverine, Giffard bitter aperitif and Leopold Bros non-alcoholic aperitivo over pineapple; the Cucumber Spritz, using UNDONE Little French Aperitif with cucumber, matcha honey and soda; and Morning Bun & Coffee, a dessert-leaning build of The Pathfinder Hemp & Root, Three Spirit Nightcap, cold brew, morning bun syrup and cardamom. Westword's January 2026 round-up wrote that non-alcoholic spirits have a permanent place at the bar, describing an earlier pair, the Bay Leaf Cream Soda and an earlier Pineapple No-groni; those specific builds have since rotated off, but the section itself has not. Happy hour runs until 6pm Tuesday through Friday and all day Monday, and the food is a short list of meze and nibbles: an olive and sweet-and-spicy pepper mix, peppadews with marinated feta, stuffed vine leaves with tzatziki feta dip, hummus with chilli crunch, whipped lemon ricotta, and burrata with fig spread.
venues.pressQuote: Non-alcoholic spirits have a permanent place at this chic hangout in LoHi. Grove 42, a citrusy infusion from Seedlip, pairs with quince, lemon and vanilla in its Bay Leaf Cream Soda mocktail. Meanwhile, its Pineapple No-groni combines bitter botanical-rich blends from Giffard, Martini and Amass — all great brands for any booze-free bar cart.

venues.name: Ladylove Lounge & Sound
venues.description: Ladylove Lounge & Sound is a '70s-inspired vinyl listening lounge in Bishop Arts with records spun live every night and a dedicated mocktail programme built alongside the cocktail list from day one. The three zero-proof elixirs are wellness-leaning rather than syrupy cocktail clones: the Orange Moon blends ginger, turmeric, honey and cardamom into coconut water and pineapple; the Sade layers rosehips, hibiscus and liquid collagen; and the Frequency mixes aloe, coconut and Blue Majik into a mojito-style fresco. All three are $10. The room runs 5pm to 2am daily, seats first-come with no reservations, and is typically at capacity by 8pm, so arrive early.

venues.longDescription:
Tucked into a back corner of Bishop Arts — the kind of spot you hear before you see — Ladylove Lounge & Sound is one of the few Dallas bars where non-drinkers are genuinely catered to rather than accommodated as an afterthought. Co-owners David Grover and Kate Siamro of Spinster Records built a dedicated zero-proof elixir program alongside the full cocktail menu from day one, a deliberate choice that runs through the venue's inclusive identity. The three mocktails are wellness-leaning and ingredient-driven, not syrupy cocktail clones, which makes Ladylove a rare find in a city where 'mocktail' too often means a soda with garnish.

Award-winning bartender Heather Poile developed the original cocktail and mocktail list, and the non-alcoholic side reflects the same level of intention as the spirited drinks. The Orange Moon blends ginger, turmeric, honey, and cardamom into coconut water and pineapple; the Sade layers rosehips, liquid collagen, and hibiscus into something both earthy and floral; and the newest of the three, the Frequency, mixes aloe, coconut, and Blue Majik into a mojito-style fresco — it replaced the earlier Healer's Green on the list. These aren't drinks designed to make sober guests feel like they're settling — they're designed to stand on their own. The cocktail side, for those who drink, runs to tequila-forward and brandy-based builds with similarly offbeat ingredient combinations.

Ladylove fills fast — typically at capacity by 8pm — and operates first-come, first-seated with no reservations (email or Instagram DM for large groups or private events). The room is dimly lit, velvet-furnished, and built around a professional DJ booth that sees a different genre every night: hip-hop, house, Afro beats, neo soul. Dress code is loose (the site explicitly welcomes mesh, PJs, and glitter), which keeps the crowd refreshingly unstuffy. It's a strong pick for date nights, small groups who want real music with their drinks, and anyone who wants a polished mocktail in a room where the vinyl matters as much as the pour.
venues.pressQuote: Ladylove Lounge & Sound takes mocktails to the next level with their nonalcoholic elixir menu — focused on wellness rather than sugary cocktail replacements, their elixirs feature ingredients like liquid collagen and turmeric.

venues.name: Laka Lono Rum Club
venues.description: Laka Lono Rum Club is Omaha's tiki bar, on Howard Street in the Old Market, open from 3pm daily and running to midnight midweek and 2am at weekends. It is listed in the city's curated drinks guide among the venues with spirit-free offerings, and the format works in a non-drinker's favour: tiki drinks are built from fresh juice, house syrups such as orgeat and falernum, spice and heavy garnish, with rum as one component rather than the whole structure — so an alcohol-free build here arrives looking and tasting like everyone else's rather than like a compromise.
venues.longDescription:
Laka Lono Rum Club is the Old Market's tiki room, on Howard Street a few doors from Clio, with the full carved-and-thatched treatment and a rum list to match. It opens at 3pm every day, which is earlier than almost anything else in this guide, and runs to midnight or 2am depending on the night.

This directory has now recommended tiki bars in four separate cities, and the reason is worth stating once properly. A tiki drink is an assembly: fresh lime and pineapple, house-made orgeat and falernum, allspice and cinnamon, several syrups, a great deal of ice and an elaborate garnish. The rum is one line in a recipe of eight. Take the spirit out of a martini and there is nothing left; take it out of a mai tai and you still have a complicated, aromatic, properly built drink. The format is structurally the most forgiving in cocktail bartending for anyone not drinking.

The presentation does the rest of the work. In a room where every drink arrives in carved wood or ceramic under a canopy of mint and fruit, nobody can tell what is in your glass, and nobody asks. That invisibility is not a small thing.

One caution that applies here specifically, and that a good tiki bar will answer immediately: falernum and some house syrups are traditionally made with rum as a preservative. Anyone abstaining completely should ask which components in a given build are alcohol-based rather than assuming a drink described as alcohol-free contains none at all.

Graded three: the spirit-free offer is attested by Omaha's curated local drinks guide but no named build could be verified for this listing, so none is recorded.

venues.name: Lake Effect
venues.description: A downtown Salt Lake City craft cocktail bar, Latin-inspired kitchen, and live-music venue that opened in 2017 inside a historic 1910 building. Spread across three spaces — the main floor, the Rabbit Hole jazz speakeasy downstairs, and the Church bar and club upstairs — it pairs an extensive cocktail program with a dedicated Non-Alcoholic Beverages menu that gets the same craft treatment as the full bar. The zero-proof list leans on premium NA spirits, with Seedlip-based mocktails like Like A Virgin and Mountain Flower, Monday Zero whiskey builds such as the New Fashioned and an NY Whiskey Sour, and Dhōs-based highballs. Axios Salt Lake City has highlighted Lake Effect's list of non-alcoholic libations as a reliable stop for a Dry January or sober night out.

venues.longDescription:
Housed in a vintage 1910 structure, Lake Effect blends old-building character with a modern, multi-room layout: nightly live music ranges from jazz in the basement Rabbit Hole to acoustic sets on the main floor and DJs upstairs in Church on weekends. The kitchen's Latin-inspired menu — including its well-known Tin Can Nachos — is built to complement what's in the glass, whether that's a mezcal old fashioned or a zero-proof pour.

The non-alcoholic section is a genuine menu category rather than an afterthought, spanning Seedlip- and Monday Zero-based mocktails, Dhōs spirit-free highballs, and an NA whiskey sour finished with a clean (de-alcoholized) cabernet float. The bar is open daily from 11am to 1am in the heart of downtown.

venues.name: Lakefront Brewery
venues.description: Lakefront Brewery is a Milwaukee institution founded in 1987 by brothers Russ and Jim Klisch, set on the Milwaukee River at the edge of Riverwest. Best known for its flagship Riverwest Stein amber lager, the brewery now makes a full lineup of sub-0.5% ABV non-alcoholic beers — Riverwest Stein NA, Eastside Dark NA, and Extended Play NA — available year-round in the taproom. Riverwest Stein NA was named 2024 Grand Champion for Non-Alcoholic Beer at the U.S. Beer Tasting Championship. It remains a working brewery and beer hall, so the NA cans sit alongside a full alcoholic menu.
venues.longDescription:
Lakefront Brewery has been one of Milwaukee's defining craft breweries since Russ and Jim Klisch founded it in 1987, and its riverside taproom and beer hall at 1872 N. Commerce St. is a longtime Brew City fixture. Its flagship, the Riverwest Stein amber lager, has been a Wisconsin best-seller for more than three decades — and it is that same beer that anchors Lakefront's non-alcoholic push.

Riverwest Stein NA is a sub-0.5% ABV amber lager built to echo the original, and it earned the 2024 Grand Champion title for Non-Alcoholic Beer at the U.S. Beer Tasting Championship along with a 93 rating from The Beer Connoisseur. It is joined by two more house NA beers — Eastside Dark NA, a Bavarian-inspired dark lager, and Extended Play NA, a citrus-forward non-alcoholic IPA — giving the taproom a genuine standing alcohol-free lineup rather than a single token option. All three are brewed to under 0.5% ABV and are available year-round.

Lakefront remains a full working brewery and beer hall, so its non-alcoholic cans share the menu with a broad range of alcoholic beers; this is a hybrid rather than a dedicated sober venue. Even so, for anyone seeking a well-regarded, locally made NA beer in Milwaukee, the taproom is among the most credible options in the city — offering award-winning zero-proof beer in the same beer hall where the alcoholic original was born.
venues.pressQuote: This is a well-brewed NA beer, the balance between the bready, grainy and caramel malt flavor and the herbal and citrus hop character makes for a very pintable beer.

venues.name: Lapis
venues.description: Lapis is a modern Afghan bistro at 1847 Columbia Road NW in the heart of Adams Morgan, run by husband-and-wife owners Zubair and Shamim Popal, who fled Afghanistan after the Soviet invasion of the 1980s and went on to build a DC restaurant group that also includes Lutece and Pascual. Chef Shamim Popal - who arrived in 1987 not knowing how to cook rice - anchors the kitchen with family recipes passed down through generations, and Lapis has earned a Michelin Bib Gourmand in every DC guide. Below the restaurant sits Lapop, a subterranean speakeasy-style cocktail bar and vinyl lounge with a marbled bar and curated bookshelves. The non-alcoholic pour to order is the Anar, made with pomegranate juice, rose water, soda and lemon zest. All meat served is halal.

venues.longDescription:
Lapis is a family restaurant in the literal sense. Zubair and Shamim Popal fled Afghanistan after the Soviet invasion of the 1980s and built a life and eventually a restaurant group in Washington - the same group that now runs Lutece in Georgetown and Pascual on Capitol Hill. Shamim Popal, who arrived in 1987 not knowing how to cook rice, anchors the kitchen with recipes passed down through generations, and the cooking has held a Michelin Bib Gourmand in every DC edition of the guide. The room sits at 1847 Columbia Road NW in the middle of Adams Morgan, and the food is what you would hope: dumplings, lamb stew, rice cooked properly.

Below the restaurant is Lapop, a subterranean speakeasy-style cocktail bar and vinyl lounge with a marbled bar and curated bookshelves, where you can drink before dinner over small plates sent down from upstairs. That two-level arrangement is useful for a group where not everyone is drinking, because it separates the bar hour from the meal without separating the party. The non-alcoholic drink to order is the Anar - pomegranate juice with rose water, soda and lemon zest, named for the Persian and Dari word for pomegranate. Washingtonian highlighted it in its Dry January roundup of great non-alcoholic cocktails, describing it as a refreshing spirit-free option, and noted that Lapop added further spirit-free choices during that month. It is designed to sit against the dumplings and the lamb stew rather than to stand alone, and the rose water is what keeps it from being simply juice.

Two things are worth knowing before you go. First, all the meat served is halal, which matters for a good number of guests and is not always easy to establish from a menu. Second, the restaurant keeps a split service - lunch from 11am and dinner from 5pm, with the gap in between - and runs seven days, opening at 10am for weekend brunch, closing at 9pm Sunday through Thursday and 10pm on Friday and Saturday. Adams Morgan gets loud late; Lapis and Lapop sit at the quieter end of that, and The Green Zone and Namak are both within a couple of minutes' walk.
venues.pressQuote: This Afghan restaurant in Adams Morgan offers refreshing NA drinks—like the “Anar” with pomegranate juice, rose water, soda, and lemon zest
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: Washingtonian, Where to Drink Great Nonalcoholic Cocktails, December 2024

venues.name: Laser Wolf
venues.description: Laser Wolf is Michael Solomonov and Steve Cook's Israeli grill in Kensington, built around salatim — a spread of small salads — followed by charcoal-grilled skewers. Its menu carries a printed "Zero Proof" section, and the reason it is thought through rather than perfunctory is that Solomonov has been sober for more than a decade; Visit Philadelphia notes that all of his restaurants carry considered non-alcoholic options. The Laser Lemonade combines lemon with cardamom, orange blossom and butterfly pea flower; the Passion Fruit Cooler runs passion fruit, lime, orange and cilantro, which is built to cut through charcoal-grilled meat. There is also a hibiscus, rose and mint iced tea and Unified Ferments kombucha.
