venues.longDescription:
Laser Wolf is the Israeli grill from Michael Solomonov and Steve Cook — the team behind Zahav — on North Howard Street in Kensington. The format is fixed and communal: a spread of salatim, the small salads that open an Israeli meal, followed by a charcoal-grilled skewer of your choosing, followed by soft-serve. It is one of the hardest reservations in the city.

The non-alcoholic list is better than it needs to be, and there is a straightforward reason. Solomonov has been sober for more than a decade, a fact he has spoken about publicly for years, and Visit Philadelphia's zero-proof guide notes that all of his restaurants carry thoughtful non-alcoholic options as a result. That is the difference between a kitchen where the zero-proof list was assigned to someone junior and one where the owner is the person most likely to order from it.

The Laser Lemonade is the drink the guide leads with: lemon with cardamom, orange blossom and butterfly pea flower. Cardamom and orange blossom are the two most characteristic aromatics of the Levantine pantry, so the drink sits inside the food's own flavour world rather than alongside it, and the butterfly pea flower gives it the deep blue-violet colour that makes it obvious across a room. The Passion Fruit Cooler — passion fruit, lime, orange and cilantro — is the one to order with the meat, because charcoal-grilled lamb needs acid and herbs against it, and cilantro does a job here that no soft drink would.

Beyond those there is a hibiscus, rose and mint iced tea, tart and floral, and Unified Ferments kombucha, which is a serious producer rather than a supermarket brand — their ferments are tea-led and dry, closer to a sparkling wine than to a sweet kombucha.

The wider point for a non-drinker is the shape of the meal. Laser Wolf serves a set format at a fixed price with the food arriving in waves; there is no bar to stand at, no rounds to buy, and the evening's rhythm is set by the kitchen. That structure does more to make an alcohol-free evening comfortable than any single drink can, and it is why this is one of the easier hard-to-book restaurants in Philadelphia to enjoy without drinking.
venues.pressQuote: Owner Michael Solomonov has been sober for more than a decade, and all of his restaurants have thoughtful non-alcoholic options.

venues.name: Last Rites
venues.description: Last Rites is a "Polynesian Noir" tiki bar that opened in San Francisco's Duboce Triangle in 2018 from Justin Lew and Ian Scalzo (the team also behind nearby Horsefeather). The room is built as a crashed-plane-in-the-jungle: a real airplane fuselage forms the bar, surrounded by banyan roots, stone booths, fire-breathing skull idols, fog, and storm effects. The cocktail program leans grown-up and rum-deep (150+ rums), skipping the blue-curaçao tiki clichés. Notably for a serious cocktail bar, it prints five named zero-proof drinks on the main menu at about $14 each — built on house-made "LR N/A Cask Spirit" and "N/A Cane Spirit" plus Pathfinder no-ABV spirit — so the alcohol-free cocktails get the same theatrical treatment as the full-proof ones. Named NA pours include the Golden Idol, Glass Ruby, Mocking Bird, Wrong Island, and El Peligosto. Wednesday bingo nights are a local draw.

venues.longDescription:
Last Rites is a "Polynesian Noir" tiki bar that opened in 2018 at 718 14th Street in Duboce Triangle. The room is built as a narrative set piece: a crashed aeroplane in the jungle, with a real fuselage forming the bar, banyan roots overhead, stone booths, fire-breathing skull idols, and periodic fog and storm effects. The drinks programme is deliberately grown-up for the genre — a rum list running past 150 bottles, and builds that avoid the blue-curaçao shorthand tiki often falls back on. It opens at 5pm most nights and runs to 2am on Fridays and Saturdays, and Wednesday bingo is a long-standing local fixture.

What makes it useful to a non-drinker is that the theatre is not reserved for the alcoholic menu. Last Rites prints five named zero-proof cocktails on its main menu at $14 each, on the same page and in the same presentation as everything else, and three of them are built on non-alcoholic base spirits rather than juice alone. The current list runs: Golden Idol (turmeric milk, coconut, orange, pineapple, lemon and nutmeg); Glass Ruby (grapefruit, lime, blueberry grenadine, cinnamon and ginger); Mocking Bird (Pathfinder non-alcoholic spirit and the bar's own no-ABV cask spirit, salted molasses, lime, pineapple, cane syrup and Last Rites salt); Wrong Island (LR N/A Cask Spirit, house cola syrup, lime and soda); and El Peligosto (LR N/A Cane Spirit, lime, cane sugar, saline and shishito pepper). The house "LR N/A Cask Spirit" and "N/A Cane Spirit" are made in-house specifically to give the alcohol-free builds the weight and length that tiki drinks normally take from aged rum, which is why these read as cocktails rather than as punch. The Golden Idol and the Glass Ruby are also listed with an optional spirit added for $3, so a table can order the same drink in both directions without anyone having to read from a different menu — a small piece of menu design that does more for a mixed group than most dedicated mocktail lists.
venues.pressQuote: This Duboce Triangle bar showcases the dark side of tiki with sky high skulls and plane-crash-in-the-tropical-jungle decor.

venues.name: Laszlo
venues.description: Laszlo is the cocktail-bar sibling of Foreign Cinema, the Mission District restaurant chef-partners Gayle Pirie and John Clark have run since 1999. It sits next door at 2526 Mission Street and works as a multi-level DJ and vinyl lounge — mezzanine booths, a large record collection and live local musicians or vinyl DJs most nights — serving craft cocktails alongside oysters and bar bites from the Foreign Cinema kitchen, with never a cover charge. Its printed menu carries a dedicated zero-proof section that rotates. Current pours include the Aplos Mandora Negroni Spritz, a sparkling non-alcoholic negroni; the Manipuri Sumac Soda (heimang sumac concentrate, lemon, soda); Coco Libre! (coconut, lime, pineapple, rhubarb shrub, Monetto non-alcoholic aperitivo); a salted raspberry and chamomile cooler; NON1 dealcoholized sparkling wine; and Fieldwork Blonde non-alcoholic pilsner.
venues.longDescription:
Laszlo is the bar half of Foreign Cinema, the Mission District restaurant that chef-partners Gayle Pirie and John Clark have run at 2526 Mission Street since 1999. It occupies the space next door and works as a multi-level lounge rather than an overflow room: open seating and private banquettes downstairs, a newly appointed upstairs lounge, an advanced sound system and a large vinyl collection, with live local musicians or vinyl DJs most nights and never a cover charge. The full Foreign Cinema menu is available from the bar, along with oysters on the half shell and bar bites. Happy hour runs 5–7pm Monday to Thursday and 5–6pm Friday to Sunday, with $12 cocktails and $3 oysters all night. The second-floor Budapest Lounge is given over to the Budapest Society, a programme donating the space to poetry readings, literary groups, fundraisers and artistic pop-ups.

The printed menu carries a zero-proof section alongside the cocktails, beer and natural wine, and it rotates with the rest of the list. The current pours are the Aplos Mandora Negroni Spritz at $9, a sparkling non-alcoholic negroni; the Manipuri Sumac Soda at $10, built on heimang sumac concentrate with lemon and soda; Coco Libre! at $12 (coconut, lime, pineapple, rhubarb shrub and Monetto non-alcoholic aperitivo); a salted raspberry and chamomile cooler at $12; and NON1 dealcoholized sparkling wine at $12 a glass or $43 a bottle. Fieldwork's Blonde non-alcoholic pilsner is stocked in 16oz cans at $9. Earlier menus carried drinks named for films and songs — Closer to the Sun, Dog with Sharper Teeth, Rebel Rouser, Piece of My Heart — which have since rotated off; the section persists even as its contents change. The sumac soda and the rhubarb shrub in the Coco Libre are the tells that these are built rather than poured.

venues.name: Late August
venues.description: Late August is a Michelin Guide-recommended restaurant in Houston's Ion District, opened March 2024 by chef Chris Williams (Lucille's Hospitality Group) with Sergio Hidalgo as executive chef, serving an Afro-Mexican fusion menu built around produce from Lucille's 1913 farm in Kendleton, Texas. It was named one of Esquire's Best New Restaurants of 2024. Alongside its cocktail program, Late August has offered named non-alcoholic drinks including the Savannah (herbed peach syrup, candied ginger beer) and the Nopalito (prickly pear, orange juice, habanero tincture, Tajín rim). (Late August closed for daily service at the Ion in August 2026. The space now hosts private events only, and the restaurant says it is relocating to The Branch at Forme, 5501 LaBranch St, with a grand opening still to be announced as of September 2026 — check before you go.)
signatureDrinks: Savannah (herbed peach syrup, candied ginger beer)
Nopalito (prickly pear, orange juice, habanero tincture, Tajín rim)
venues.longDescription:
Late August opened in March 2024 in the Ion mixed-use development in Midtown Houston, in a building that was once a Sears department store -- the restaurant's name nods to the nostalgia of the annual Sears holiday catalog arriving in late summer. It's a concept from chef Chris Williams, a James Beard-recognized chef behind Lucille's Hospitality Group, working alongside executive chef Sergio Hidalgo. The Afro-Mexican menu draws on both chefs' childhood and professional culinary experiences and leans on produce grown at Lucille's own 1913 farm in Kendleton, Texas.

The restaurant carries a Michelin Guide 'Recommended' designation -- per CultureMap Houston, it is Houston's only Black-owned restaurant to earn a spot in the Michelin Guide -- and was named one of Esquire's Best New Restaurants in America for 2024, with critic Joshua David Stein praising the kitchen's 'bravura acts of culinary invention.'

In fall 2025, Late August revamped its format around a tasting menu ($95); Houstonia Magazine reported the restaurant reworked its concept with a tasting menu and bold new dishes.

Alongside its cocktail list, Late August has featured named non-alcoholic drinks -- per CultureMap Houston's Dry January coverage, the Savannah (herbed peach syrup, candied ginger beer, $8) and the Nopalito (prickly pear, orange juice, habanero tincture, Tajín rim, $7). As these were highlighted in seasonal Dry January coverage rather than a standing printed mocktail section, continued availability of these two drinks should be reconfirmed at the next verification pass.

Late August closed for daily service at the Ion in August 2026. CultureMap Houston reported that the space was moving to an event-focused model, and the restaurant's own site now says it is relocating to a new home at The Branch at Forme Houston, 5501 LaBranch St, with the grand opening still to be announced as of September 2026. Everything above describes the restaurant as it traded at the Ion; check its own channels before making the trip.
venues.pressQuote: bravura acts of culinary invention
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: CultureMap Houston (citing Esquire's Best New Restaurants 2024)

venues.name: Latuli
venues.description: Latuli is chef Bryan Caswell's Memorial-area restaurant, and its drinks list carries a printed section headed simply "Mocktails" — set out on the same page as the cocktails rather than tucked away as an afterthought. Both builds are made with Ritual zero-proof tequila rather than fruit juice: the Ginger Spur combines it with ginger simple syrup, fresh orange juice and ginger beer, and the Spring Saddle runs it into strawberry chamomile with lemon, lime and soda. Two drinks is a short list, but the construction is the point — using an alcohol-free spirit as the base means the drink is built the way a cocktail is, with the same bitterness and length. The kitchen runs to eleven on Thursday, Friday and Saturday.
signatureDrinks: Ginger Spur — Ritual zero-proof tequila, ginger simple, fresh orange juice, ginger beer
Spring Saddle — Ritual zero-proof tequila, strawberry chamomile, lemon and lime, soda
venues.longDescription:
Latuli sits on Gaylord Drive in Memorial, and it is chef Bryan Caswell's room — a name that carries weight in Houston, where he has been one of the more visible chefs for well over a decade. The reason it earns a place in this directory is small but structural: the drinks menu has a heading that reads "Mocktails", printed on the same page as the cocktail list, and the two drinks beneath it are built on a zero-proof spirit rather than assembled from juice.

That distinction is worth spelling out because it is the difference between a real non-alcoholic drink and a soft one. The Ginger Spur takes Ritual zero-proof tequila as its base and lengthens it with ginger simple syrup, fresh orange juice and ginger beer — a build with two separate sources of ginger heat, one syrupy and one carbonated, which is what keeps it from reading as sweet. The Spring Saddle uses the same Ritual base against a strawberry chamomile preparation with lemon, lime and soda; chamomile brings a faintly bitter, hay-like note that does some of the work alcohol would otherwise do in stopping the strawberry from dominating.

Ritual is the default alcohol-free spirit in Houston bars by a wide margin, and its tequila expression is the one that translates best, because the smoky, vegetal character of agave survives the removal of ethanol better than a gin botanical does. A bar that reaches for it rather than for a bottled mixer is signalling that it expects someone to order these drinks and enjoy them.

The honest caveat is length: two drinks is a short section, and a group of non-drinkers will exhaust it in a single round. What compensates is the setting. This is a full restaurant with a serious kitchen and a dining-room service rhythm, open until eleven on Thursday, Friday and Saturday and until nine or ten the rest of the week, which makes it a place to have dinner rather than a place to drink. For an evening built around the table rather than around the bar, two well-made zero-proof options and a chef's menu is a more useful proposition than a long mocktail list attached to a mediocre kitchen.

venues.name: Laurel Brasserie & Bar
venues.description: Inside The Grand America Hotel, Laurel Brasserie & Bar pairs classic European cuisine with a modern American approach and runs a standing zero-proof, alcohol-free cocktail list the kitchen treats as the equal of its cocktail program rather than an afterthought. The lineup is anchored by the Eastside — built on Seedlip Spice with muddled cucumber, kaffir lime syrup and lime, per Utah Stories — alongside a seasonal shrub, the coconut-forward Dreamcicle, and a Tamarind Lemon Spritz, each priced like a happy-hour bite at $7. Developed under beverage director Mark Moulton and opened in late 2021, it is one of the clearest documented NA programs in a fine-dining setting downtown.

venues.longDescription:
The bar's most popular NA pour is the Eastside, which Utah Stories described as featuring Seedlip Spice non-alcoholic spirit with muddled cucumber and kaffir lime syrup and lime juice, garnished with a cucumber ribbon. Alongside it sit a rotating shrub, the coconut-forward Dreamcicle, and a Tamarind Lemon Spritz — each priced the same as a happy-hour bite at $7.

Laurel occupies the remodeled main dining room of The Grand America, with a relaxed, accessible menu — a deliberate move away from the hotel's former white-tablecloth formality — and a separate 21+ bar.
venues.pressQuote: The libations menu also addresses the nondrinkers by offering four delicious mocktails that use more than two ingredients.

venues.name: Lava Kava
venues.description: Lava Kava is Maine's first kava tea bar and the only fully alcohol-free evening venue in Portland — open 5pm to 10pm every day of the week, which is precisely the window a non-drinker usually finds closed. The menu runs to kava served in the traditional way, kratom, herbal teas and house blends, in a lounge built for sitting and talking rather than for a quick drink. In a city whose reputation rests almost entirely on its bars and its beer, having somewhere that keeps bar hours without serving alcohol changes what an evening out can look like. Note that kava is mildly psychoactive and kratom is also served, so this is a night out without alcohol rather than a substance-free room.
venues.address: 550 Washington Ave, Suite A, Portland, ME 04103
venues.longDescription:
Lava Kava sits on Washington Avenue in East Deering, a little outside Portland's tourist centre, and it is the first kava tea bar Maine has had. Every drink it serves is alcohol-free: kava prepared traditionally, kratom, herbal teas and the house's own blends, in a room set up as a lounge rather than a counter.

What makes it the most important venue in this guide is the clock. It opens at 5pm and runs to 10pm seven days a week. Portland's alcohol-free options are otherwise almost entirely daytime — Tandem's two cafes close at 1pm, Vena's shop shuts at 5pm, RSVP is a bottle shop. Everything that stays open into the evening is a bar. That leaves a sober resident or visitor with a genuine gap between dinner and bed, and Lava Kava is the only thing in the city that fills it with somewhere to actually sit.

A word on what kava is, because it matters and the marketing rarely says it plainly. Kava is a root from the Pacific Islands, prepared as a cold water infusion, and it is mildly psychoactive — relaxing and slightly numbing on the tongue. It contains no alcohol, but it is not inert, and this venue also serves kratom, which is a stronger and more contested substance. That distinction is worth understanding before you go: this is a night out without alcohol rather than a guaranteed substance-free space, and for someone whose sobriety excludes all intoxicants it may not be the right room.

For everyone else — designated drivers, the sober-curious, people taking a month off, anyone who wants to be out at nine on a Tuesday without a drink in their hand — it is the answer Portland otherwise lacks. The Washington Avenue stretch has become one of the city's more interesting corridors, so it pairs with dinner nearby rather than requiring a trip of its own. For a visitor without a car it is a manageable walk or a very short ride from the Old Port, and it is the one address in this guide worth planning an evening around rather than fitting in around something else.
venues.pressQuote: Welcome to Lava Kava, Portland's sanctuary of calm and the first kava tea bar in Maine

venues.description: LaVerne's is a retro Woodlawn neighborhood bar and restaurant that opened in September 2025 from the team behind Dig A Pony and Hey Love. Its non-alcoholic lineup — listed alongside the cocktails — includes named mocktails, NA beer (including N.A. Guinness) and rotating NA wine, priced roughly $3 to $11.

venues.longDescription:
LaVerne's is a retro neighborhood bar, restaurant, and event space that opened in September 2025 in Portland's Woodlawn neighborhood, occupying a 1909 building at 700 NE Dekum Street that still includes the historic Village Ballroom. It comes from the team behind Dig A Pony and Hey Love, led by Sophie Thomson and Aaron Hall with co-owner Lauren Kawa Funk. The owners built the venue around a playful fictional backstory of a bar "frozen in place somewhere around 1986" — wood paneling, vinyl and fringed booths, soda-fountain barstools, and a rotisserie centerpiece — with a soundtrack of postwar-through-early-'80s soul, jazz and country.

The food leans into Yucatán-style comfort fare anchored by achiote- and ancho-rubbed rotisserie chicken, street tacos, nachos and red pozole, with a notably deep roster of vegetarian and vegan options. The drink program is intentionally unpretentious, and its non-alcoholic menu is listed alongside the cocktails rather than as an afterthought: verified zero-proof options include the NA Spicy Passionfruit Margarita, the Verdita (pineapple, lime, mint, cilantro, jalapeño), and an Oregon Blackberry Soda, plus non-alcoholic beer including N.A. PBR and N.A. Guinness and rotating NA wine. Dry-January coverage has also highlighted a "Parch NA Margarita" built with the Parch non-alcoholic agave spirit.
venues.pressQuote: They offer a selection of mocktails, NA beer, NA wine, and more, priced between $3 and $11.

venues.name: Law Bird
venues.description: Law Bird is the Brewery District cocktail bar opened in November 2019 by married owners Annie Williams Pierce and Luke Pierce, both career bartenders; in 2017 Williams Pierce became the first woman to win the United States Bartenders Guild's Most Imaginative Bartender competition in London. The bar was a 2025 James Beard Foundation semifinalist for Outstanding Bar and has been named among the best bars in the United States by Food & Wine. Columbus Underground readers voted it the city's best non-alcoholic drink menu in the 2025 Best of Columbus poll. Roughly three new cocktail menus are released a year, each carrying named N/A cocktails alongside the full-proof list, and most specialty cocktails can be built without alcohol at a reduced price. Non-alcoholic beer comes from Athletic Brewing and Best Day.
venues.longDescription:
Law Bird opened on 7 November 2019 in a converted pet supply shop at 740 South High Street, at the southern end of the Brewery District. It is owned and run by Annie Williams Pierce and Luke Pierce, a married pair the owners describe as "two restaurant industry lifers," with résumés that run through Curio, Veritas, The Sycamore, Land-Grant Brewing, Brothers Drake and Watershed. Williams Pierce won the United States Bartenders Guild's Most Imaginative Bartender title in London in 2017 — the first woman to do so. The bar took the long way through its early years, opening months before the pandemic, and the recognition arrived afterwards: a 2025 James Beard Foundation semifinalist nod for Outstanding Bar, and a place on Food & Wine's list of the best bars in the country.

The non-alcoholic programme is not a separate concession but a structural feature of how the menus are written. Law Bird releases roughly three cocktail menus a year, plus recurring seasonal pop-ups including a Holiday Tiki residency and a Japanese sakura-blossom run, and each menu carries its own named N/A cocktails — the N/A Klamdag and N/A Solvregn among them — built with the same technique as the full-proof drinks rather than borrowed from a soda gun. Beyond the named list, most specialty cocktails on any given menu can be built without alcohol, and are priced lower than their spirituous counterparts, which removes the common irritation of paying cocktail money for juice. Non-alcoholic beer is stocked properly too, with Athletic Brewing's Golden Ale and Best Day's N/A IPA on the list. Columbus Underground readers voted the bar first for non-alcoholic drink menus in the 2025 Best of Columbus poll, ahead of every dedicated programme in the city. The room is small, table service is the norm, and it closes Mondays. Two practical points for anyone planning around it. First, because the N/A drinks change with each menu release rather than sitting fixed, the specific names listed here will rotate — the constant is that every menu carries them, and that the bar will build most of the full-proof list without alcohol on request. Second, the room is genuinely small, table service is the norm rather than ordering at the bar, and it fills at weekends; a weeknight visit is the better bet for anyone who wants to talk to the bartenders about what is on the zero-proof side. The bar is closed Mondays, opens at 4:30pm the rest of the week, and runs to 1am on Fridays and Saturdays.
venues.pressQuote: The cocktail menus rotate seasonally with fresh new concoctions, and many of the specialty cocktails can be made without alcohol with reduced pricing compared to alcoholic versions.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Columbus Underground, Best of Columbus 2025 reader poll

venues.name: Lawrence Hall
venues.description: Lawrence Hall is a food hall at 4609 Butler Street in Lawrenceville, in an 1890s building that has been a theatre and a car dealership, opened in April 2024 by Brett Minarik, Phoebe Fraser and Adam Harvey after five years of renovation. It holds four independent restaurants, a Leona's ice cream shop, seating for 225 and a mezzanine, anchored by its bar Dear James — named for Captain James Lawrence, whose dying order gave the neighbourhood its name. The bar did something almost no venue does: it hired a dedicated non-alcoholic beverage consultant, Katrina Tomacchio, who advised Boston-area bars on zero-proof drinks before moving here, gave up alcohol herself, and co-owns two of the hall's own tenant restaurants. The programme uses hyper-local sourcing, house-made syrups and original recipes rather than bought-in mixers. One documented example is the Capture of The Chesapeake, a campfire espresso martini of cold brew, Lyre's coffee and white cane spirits, graham cracker syrup and non-alcoholic aromatic bitters with a torched marshmallow. The list rotates by season and is published only through the bar's ordering system.
venues.longDescription:
Lawrence Hall is a food hall at 4609 Butler Street in Lawrenceville, in an 1890s building that has been a theatre and a car dealership in its previous lives, and it took Brett Minarik, Phoebe Fraser and Adam Harvey five years of renovation and red tape to open it in April 2024. Fraser's account of getting there is worth repeating: along the way they had many opportunities to stop, to give up the ship, but there was something in all of them that said keep going. It holds four independent restaurants, a Leona's ice cream shop, seating for 225 and a mezzanine over the whole operation, with a full bar called Dear James — named for Captain James Lawrence, whose dying order at sea gave the neighbourhood its name.

Dear James is the reason this belongs on any serious alcohol-free list, because the bar did something almost no venue does: it hired a non-alcoholic beverage consultant to build the programme. That consultant is Katrina Tomacchio, who spent years advising Boston-area bars and restaurants on zero-proof drinks before moving here, who gave up alcohol herself five years ago, who bills herself as Pittsburgh's Mocktail Queen, and who — with her husband Anthony — owns two of the hall's own tenant restaurants. Her design principle is the clearest statement of the case anyone in this city has made: you have to think about the guest experience first, so the guest walks away feeling as much thought, care and effort went into their mocktail as would go into a cocktail. The rest of it is the argument in full — when a bar programme excels in the non-alcoholic arena, it shows people they do not have to feel like they are missing out just because they are not drinking; you can still go out, still meet your friends for drinks, and order something that is not glorified soda or a Shirley Temple. The drinks use hyper-local sourcing, house-made syrups and original recipes. One documented example gives the flavour: the Capture of The Chesapeake, a campfire espresso martini of cold brew, Lyre's coffee and white cane spirits, graham cracker syrup and non-alcoholic aromatic bitters, served with a torched marshmallow. The menu rotates by season and is published only through the bar's ordering system, so treat that as an illustration rather than a promise.
venues.pressQuote: inclusivity is key; we want the guest to walk away feeling like as much thought, care and effort went into their mocktail as would an alcoholic cocktail

venues.name: Lazy Betty
venues.description: Lazy Betty is a one-Michelin-star tasting-menu restaurant from chef-partners Ron Hsu and Aaron Phillips, originally opened in 2019 in Candler Park and relocated in March 2024 to a larger Midtown space at 999 Peachtree Street. The kitchen serves a multi-course modern tasting menu, and the beverage program runs a full zero-proof track alongside its wine and spirits list. The menu carries a dedicated "Zero Proof" section with named N/A cocktails, non-alcoholic wines (Oddbird, Loosen Bros. "Dr. Lo"), and non-alcoholic beer from Athletic Brewing. Guests can have zero-proof cocktails coursed out and paired with each dish, the same way the wine pairing works. Named alcohol-free cocktails include the Celery Gimlet, Blueberry Mule, Strawberry Spritz, and "Spring Dreams Are Made Of These." Forbes called it one of Atlanta's best zero-proof cocktail menus.
venues.hours: Mon closed; Tue-Thu 5pm-8:30pm; Fri-Sat 5pm-9pm; Sun closed
signatureDrinks: Spring Dreams Are Made Of These
venues.longDescription:
Lazy Betty holds one MICHELIN star and is the work of chef-partners Ron Hsu and Aaron Phillips, who opened it in Candler Park in 2019 and moved it in March 2024 to a larger room at 999 Peachtree Street in Midtown. The format is a multi-course modern tasting menu. What makes it relevant here is that the beverage programme runs a genuine second track: zero-proof cocktails can be coursed out and paired dish by dish, exactly the way the wine pairing works.

That is a meaningfully different offer from a list of mocktails. A tasting menu is a two- or three-hour sequence built around progression, and a non-drinker given a single sweet drink at the start of it spends the rest of the meal excluded from the structure of the thing they are paying for. Pairing zero-proof drinks course by course puts them back inside it, and very few restaurants at this level bother.

The drinks are savoury and dry rather than fruit-led. The Celery Gimlet is the one that gets written about — the Atlanta Journal-Constitution described it in January 2026 as packed with herbal, vegetal notes from a house-made celery cordial, saline and Amethyst Lemon Cucumber Serrano, and Forbes had praised an earlier build of it with chive oil the previous June. Saline and chive oil are the giveaway: these are seasoning techniques borrowed from the kitchen, used to give a drink savour and length where alcohol would normally provide it. Alongside are the Blueberry Mule, the Strawberry Spritz and Spring Dreams Are Made Of These, plus a Something Clever built on beet shrub, lemon and club soda.

The list extends past cocktails to non-alcoholic wine — Oddbird and the Loosen Bros Dr. Lo Riesling — and Athletic Brewing beer, so a table can go the whole meal without anyone reaching for a soft drink. Reservations are effectively required.
venues.pressQuote: At Lazy Betty (another Michelin-starred standout), the Celery Gimlet—a bracing blend of Amethyst Lemon, celery-lemon cordial, and chive oil—is both savory and refreshing.

venues.name: Lazy Bones Kava
venues.description: Lazy Bones Kava is a fully alcohol-free kava and botanical tea bar on the South Lamar corridor, a few minutes south of Zilker. It describes itself as "Austin's home for kava and botanical teas" and runs on the line "where strangers become regulars" — and, tellingly, as "cafe by day, lounge by night." Alongside kava it pours exotic and botanical teas, kratom and coffee. The evening half is a genuine social room rather than a cafe with the lights down: there is a free pool table and games, and it hosts live music and a recurring KOOP 91.7 FM DJ residency, which the community station bills as taking place "in a sober-forward setting." (Kava is non-alcoholic but psychoactive — alcohol-free, not substance-free.)
venues.address: 2110 S Lamar Blvd, Ste A, Austin, TX 78704
venues.longDescription:
Lazy Bones sits on the South Lamar strip in 78704, and the useful thing to know about it is the shape of its day rather than its drinks list. The bar's own framing is "cafe by day, lounge by night": the same room works as somewhere to take a laptop in the morning and as somewhere to spend an evening, without a bar materialising in it at six o'clock. That is the specific thing an alcohol-free venue can offer and a normal bar cannot, and it is why the room reads as a social space rather than a coffee shop that closes late.

The drinks are kava first — served in the traditional way — alongside botanical and exotic teas, kratom and coffee. The room is built for staying: a free pool table, board games, and a programme of live music that includes a recurring DJ residency from KOOP 91.7 FM, Austin's volunteer-run community radio station, which advertises the night to its listeners as "a sober-forward setting." A community station choosing to put its residency in a kava bar is a fair signal of what the crowd is like.

The standard kava caution applies here as everywhere. Kava is not alcohol, but it is psychoactive: a mild sedative that should not be combined with alcohol or sedating medication, can slow reflexes enough to affect driving, and has been associated with liver concerns in heavy or prolonged use.

venues.name: LBM
venues.description: LBM is a small, deliberately eccentric cocktail bar at 12301 Madison Avenue in Lakewood's Birdtown, and Cleveland Scene's description has held up for years: best described as weird but good, not for everyone, but earning a deep well of respect for having a personality, a point of view, and the nerve to carve out an eccentric niche. Co-owner and bartender Eric Ho co-founded the Cleveland chapter of the US Bartenders Guild and works with real technique — measuring out acids to the hundredth of a gram, milk-washing tea infusions to cut the astringency. The menu runs in themed volumes, and its non-alcoholic cocktails get their own printed heading rather than a footnote: three at $10 each. Sacred Ashes builds tamarind, cardamom and chipotle against wildflower honey and rosewater; Amethyst runs chicha morada — Peruvian purple corn — with pineapple, clove, cinnamon, apple and lime; and Sigil is the autumnal one, with cider, maple, chicory, chocolate, hazelnut and orange peel. Non-alcoholic beer runs $6–$7. Open from 4pm, to 2.30am on Friday and Saturday.
venues.longDescription:
LBM sits on Madison Avenue in Birdtown, the small Lakewood district a few streets from Amazonia, and it has spent years being the bar Cleveland drinkers send people to when they want to explain what the city can do. Cleveland Scene's line remains the best summary: weird but good, definitely not for everyone, but earning a deep well of respect for having a personality, a point of view, and the nerve to carve out an eccentric niche. Co-owner Eric Ho, who co-founded the Cleveland chapter of the US Bartenders Guild, works with the kind of technique that would be at home in a much larger city — measuring out acids to the hundredth of a gram, milk-washing tea infusions to cut their astringency. The menus run in themed volumes rather than seasons, which is why the drink names change wholesale rather than one at a time. It opens at 4pm and runs to half past two in the morning on Friday and Saturday.

The non-alcoholic cocktails get their own printed heading, and there are three, each $10 — against full cocktails that cost considerably more, which is the ratio you want to see. Sacred Ashes is the most cocktail-like: tamarind and cardamom against chipotle, wildflower honey and rosewater, so it lands somewhere sour, smoky and floral all at once. Amethyst is built on chicha morada, the Peruvian purple corn drink, with pineapple, clove, cinnamon, apple and lime — a genuinely old, genuinely non-alcoholic tradition rather than a cocktail with the gin taken out, and the sort of choice that shows a bar has thought about what zero-proof drinking can be rather than what it lacks. Sigil is the autumn one, running cider and maple against chicory, chocolate, hazelnut and orange peel; chicory is the clever part, because its roasted bitterness does the job coffee or amaro would do in an alcoholic drink. On the beer list, Best Day's Electro Lime is $7 and a Lagunitas Hoppy Refresher $6. Because the menu turns over by volume rather than by season, treat these three names as current rather than permanent.
venues.pressQuote: LBM is best described as "weird but good." This Birdtown bar with the cryptic moniker definitely is not for everyone, but it earns a deep well of respect for having a personality, a point of view.

venues.name: Le Colonial (River Oaks District)
venues.neighborhood: River Oaks (River Oaks District dining complex)
venues.description: This upscale French-Vietnamese restaurant in the River Oaks District runs a dedicated Mocktails section on its beverage menu alongside its full cocktail program, built from fresh, kitchen-grade ingredients rather than syrupy defaults. The Saigon Mint Colada (coconut milk, fresh pineapple, fresh lime, fresh mint, turmeric, fresh nutmeg) got specific press coverage as the drink for "the non-imbibing" when Le Colonial unveiled its new patio and cocktail menu in 2024. Two more named non-alcoholic builds round out the list: the pomegranate-ginger Le Diable and a trio of shaken black teas (white peach, hibiscus herb honey, lychee).
venues.address: 4444 Westheimer Rd, Suite G-140, Houston, TX 77027

Le Diable (fresh pomegranate, ginger root, cilantro, fresh lime, pomegranate molasses, Q ginger beer)
Shaken Black Tea - Hibiscus Herb Honey

venues.longDescription:
Le Colonial opened in the River Oaks District in August 2016, an outpost of a French-Vietnamese restaurant group. The two-storey space channels 1920s French Indochina, with a wraparound terrace and an upstairs lounge bar. Executive Chef Fredy Cutz runs the Houston kitchen alongside Culinary Director Hassan Obaye.

In 2024 the restaurant unveiled a renovated patio and a new cocktail programme, and PaperCity Magazine's coverage of the launch singled out the Saigon Mint Colada as the pour for guests who were not drinking — naming it alongside the new cocktails rather than as a footnote.

That drink rewards a close look at its ingredient list. Coconut milk, fresh pineapple, lime and mint are the expected colada components, but turmeric and freshly grated nutmeg are not. Both are warm, earthy, faintly bitter spices, and they do the work that rum would otherwise do in stopping a coconut-and-pineapple drink from reading as dessert. Turmeric in particular brings a dry, almost medicinal edge that cuts the fat in the coconut milk.

Le Diable runs the opposite register: fresh pomegranate and ginger root with cilantro, lime, pomegranate molasses and Q ginger beer. Pomegranate molasses is the key — reduced pomegranate juice, intensely sour and slightly savoury, a staple of Levantine and Persian cooking rather than of bartending. It supplies a depth of acidity that no fresh juice can, and with cilantro's green, soapy bite and the ginger's heat the result is a properly savoury long drink. There are also three shaken black teas, in white peach, hibiscus herb honey and lychee, where the tea's tannin gives the drinks the dry astringency a sweet fruit build usually lacks.

There is a broader logic to ordering alcohol-free here. Vietnamese food is built around herbs, chilli, fish sauce and acid, and its own table drinks run to limeade, sugarcane juice, iced tea and coconut — a deep non-alcoholic tradition that has nothing to compensate for. This is a full-bar restaurant rather than an alcohol-free venue, but the mocktail section is named, distinct from the cocktail list and has drawn its own press. Open daily from half past eleven, to eleven at night Thursday through Saturday.
venues.pressQuote: Among the adult libations were lychee martinis, green makrut lime gimlets, Hanoi coffee and French kiss and for the non-imbibing the Saigon mint colada mocktail.

venues.name: Le'DRIP Coffee and Tea
venues.neighborhood: Asiatown / Chinatown (Dun Huang Plaza, Bellaire Blvd)
venues.description: Le'DRIP Coffee and Tea is a fully alcohol-free Vietnamese coffee and tea shop tucked into Dun Huang Plaza in Houston's Chinatown, pouring traditional phin-drip coffee alongside inventive foam-topped and fruit-tea specialty drinks. Every build on the menu, from the classic bac siu to pandan-foam Vietnamese coffee and coconut coffee finished with ube cream cheese foam, is coffee- or tea-based, with no alcohol served anywhere on site. It was founded by sisters Emmy Le and Amy Le, who source Vietnamese Robusta beans and import tea leaves directly from Vietnam rather than using the Arabica beans common at most U.S. coffee shops.
venues.address: 9889 Bellaire Blvd Ste E-205, Houston, TX 77036
signatureDrinks: Pandan Bac Siu (airy, fluffy pandan foam atop bac siu, the lighter, milkier sister of Le'DRIP's Vietnamese coffee)
Black Sugar Matcha Latte (culinary-grade matcha, black sugar)
Coconut Coffee with Ube Cream Cheese Foam (coconut coffee topped with ube cream cheese foam)
Watermelon Black Tea (fresh watermelon iced black tea, fresh-fruit infusion)
venues.longDescription:
Le'DRIP Coffee and Tea opened in Houston's Chinatown in October 2023, founded by sisters Emmy Le and Amy Le, who immigrated to the U.S. from Vietnam in their early twenties. In an interview with Voyage Houston Magazine, the sisters explained that despite Houston's already-diverse coffee scene, the specific Vietnamese flavors they grew up with were mostly confined to full-service Vietnamese restaurants rather than available at a quick, casual cafe -- so they built Le'DRIP to close that gap, tucked into Dun Huang Plaza on Bellaire Boulevard in the heart of the neighborhood known as Asiatown or Chinatown.

The shop's defining choice is its brewing method: rather than the Arabica-based drip and espresso common at most American coffee shops, Le'DRIP exclusively uses Vietnamese Robusta beans brewed the traditional way through a metal phin filter. The company sources its beans and tea leaves directly from Vietnam, and builds its menu of condensed-milk coffee classics reworked with contemporary foams and fruit teas.

There is no alcohol anywhere on the menu -- every drink is coffee, tea, or fruit-refresher based. Standouts include the pandan bac siu (bac siu, the shop's lighter, milkier take on Vietnamese coffee, topped with airy pandan foam), a black sugar matcha latte, coconut coffee finished with ube cream cheese foam, and a fresh watermelon black tea. The cafe has grown enough since its 2023 opening to add a second, drive-thru location in Richmond, TX, west of Houston.

venues.name: Le Jardinier Houston
venues.neighborhood: Museum District (inside the Museum of Fine Arts Houston, Kinder Building)
venues.description: Le Jardinier Houston, the Michelin-starred French restaurant inside the Museum of Fine Arts Houston's Kinder Building, keeps a standing three-drink "Zero Proof Cocktails" section on its printed menu, each drink named, priced, and built from fresh juices, house syrups, and a non-alcoholic aperitif base rather than an afterthought soda. Weekend brunch adds a separate $30-per-guest mocktail pairing of several more non-alcoholic drinks, matched course-by-course the same way the wine pairing is offered. Houston's Dry January media coverage, including CultureMap Houston and Houston Press, has repeatedly singled out the restaurant's mocktails as a highlight of the city's fine-dining alcohol-free options.

Citrus Lumiere ($15) - Veridoshe Ginesis (non-alcoholic aperitif), blood orange, lime juice, honey syrup, soda
Blush Garden ($14) - Veridoshe Ginesis (non-alcoholic aperitif), peach nectar, mint syrup, lime, soda
Fraise et Ananas (brunch mocktail pairing) - strawberry syrup, pineapple, simple syrup, non-alcoholic tequila

venues.longDescription:
Le Jardinier Houston opened in 2021 inside the Nancy and Rich Kinder Building at the Museum of Fine Arts Houston (MFAH), the museum's newest wing at the corner of Main Street and Bissonnet in the Museum District. It is the Houston outpost of The Bastion Collection's Le Jardinier group, which also operates locations in New York, Miami, and Geneva. The concept was created by culinary director Alain Verzeroli, a longtime protege of Joel Robuchon, and is run day to day by Executive Chef Felipe Botero and Pastry Chef Tiffani Ann Gkaris. The restaurant won a Michelin star at Texas's inaugural Michelin Guide ceremony in 2024 and retained the star in the 2025 guide.

The printed menu carries a standing "Zero Proof Cocktails" section of three named, priced drinks: the Le Jardin ($14 - cucumber juice, fine herb syrup, lime juice, soda, cucumber, mint), the Citrus Lumiere ($15 - Veridoshe Ginesis non-alcoholic aperitif, blood orange, lime juice, honey syrup, soda), and the Blush Garden ($14 - Veridoshe Ginesis non-alcoholic aperitif, peach nectar, mint syrup, lime, soda). On weekends, the restaurant's "Le Rose Jardin" brunch adds a separate $30-per-guest mocktail pairing built around non-alcoholic spirits, including drinks such as Fraise et Ananas (strawberry syrup, pineapple, simple syrup, non-alcoholic tequila), Pink Fizz (lime, simple syrup, cranberry, non-alcoholic gin), and a Strawberry Rose Spritz (strawberry, lemon, rose water, non-alcoholic rose wine), matched course by course alongside the alcoholic wine pairing option.

Houston's Dry January coverage has flagged the program: CultureMap Houston's January 2025 roundup highlighted the Le Jardin and a seasonal "Yellow Boots" mocktail (spiced pineapple tisane and coconut cordial). The zero-proof list and brunch pairing appear to rotate seasonally along with the rest of the kitchen's ingredient-driven menu.
venues.pressQuote: Fresh off earning a Michelin star, Le Jardinier in the Museum District is delivering indulgent mocktails such as the le jardin, a crisp cucumber and lime concoction, and the "yellow boots," a tropical mix of spiced pineapple tisane and coconut cordial.

venues.name: Le Lounge
venues.description: Le Lounge is the intimate cocktail bar inside No Vacancy, an eight-room boutique guesthouse on the corner of 18th and Wyandotte in Kansas City's Crossroads Arts District. Conceived as "a love letter to the lobby bar," it leans into traditional hotel-bar elegance: a marble-topped island, café tables, lounge seating, and cinematic lighting. The bar opened in 2024 and was later moved to a more accessible ground-floor space within the same red-brick building. It is open to walk-ins and reservations, not just hotel guests. Alongside an ambitious craft-cocktail program — lead bartenders have used liquid nitrogen to keep martini glasses cold — Le Lounge maintains a small but genuine non-alcoholic offering, including the Sober Lush (a grapefruit, citrus, and jalapeño mocktail) and a non-alcoholic golden ale from Athletic Brewing. It opens Thursday through Saturday evenings, with no cover charge.
venues.hours: Mon-Tue closed; Wed-Thu 6pm-1am; Fri-Sat 4pm-1am; Sun closed
venues.longDescription:
Le Lounge is the bar inside No Vacancy, an eight-room boutique guesthouse on the corner of 17th and Wyandotte in the Crossroads Arts District. It is genuinely hard to find on purpose: from the looks of the red brick building tucked off of 17th and Wyandotte Street, KCUR wrote, you would have no idea that there was a guesthouse with a chic hotel bar inside it. The room leans into that discovery. At first, the same piece noted, you might feel like you have wandered into a very chic house party in the 1990s — but that is the charm of it. Rather than a conventional bar with a rail and stools, service happens around a marble-covered island with the bartenders working in the middle of it, which KCUR likened to a beehive, bottles and glasses spread around them. It is a small, warm, deliberately residential space rather than a hotel lobby bar, and it is open to the public even though most people walking past do not realise it exists.

The non-alcoholic offering is short but properly made, and KCUR singled it out when surveying where to drink well without alcohol in Kansas City. The Sober Lush is the house zero-proof cocktail, built on grapefruit and citrus with jalapeño for heat — sharp and savoury rather than sweet, which suits a room where most of the list runs spirit-forward. Alongside it the bar keeps Athletic Brewing's golden ale, so there is a non-alcoholic beer option for anyone who would rather hold something familiar. Two practical notes worth having in advance. Service runs Wednesday and Thursday from 6pm and Friday and Saturday from 4pm, closing at 1am, so it is an evening venue with no daytime trade. And the venue does not maintain a working page of its own — the direct link that used to serve Le Lounge now returns an error — so hours and drinks are best confirmed through the guesthouse's main site or by asking on arrival.
venues.pressQuote: Two stand-out drinks here are the Sober Lush, a grapefruit, citrus and jalapeno concoction and a golden ale from Athletic Brewing Company.

venues.name: Le Loup
venues.description: Le Loup is a vintage-inspired craft cocktail bar from restaurateur Ford Fry's Rocket Farm Restaurants group, opened in early 2022 in Nashville's Germantown neighbourhood above its sister restaurant The Optimist. The cocktail programme was built by Kenneth Vanhooser, a Nashville native who spent a decade working in New York. The room is deep green marble and rich colour under a custom underwater mural by Rebecca Green — The Infatuation summed up the effect as the distinct feeling you're submerged in a submarine — and the food is seafood-leaning: bluefin tuna belly, West Coast uni, smoked fish dip with trout roe. The bar keeps a short section headed "Zero Proof", currently two made-to-order drinks at $8 each: Lift to the Scaffold (lemon, mint, cucumber, alfalfa, tonic) and Four (grapefruit, calpico, pineapple, ginger, chili). Athletic's Atletica zero-alcohol beer is $6.
signatureDrinks: Lift to the Scaffold (lemon, mint, cucumber, alfalfa, tonic) $8
venues.longDescription:
Le Loup occupies the floor above The Optimist at 1400 Adams Street in Germantown, part of Ford Fry's Rocket Farm Restaurants group, and it opened in early 2022 as a deliberately vintage-feeling counterpoint to the seafood restaurant beneath it. The cocktail programme belongs to Kenneth Vanhooser, a Nashville native who spent a decade in New York before coming back for this job — they always had me in mind for Le Loup, he told Nashville Lifestyles, so we bought a house almost sight-unseen and moved down. The room is the reason many people come: deep green marble runs through it, the colours are saturated and low-lit, and a custom underwater mural by the artist Rebecca Green wraps the space, producing what The Infatuation described as the distinct feeling that you are submerged in a submarine. Food is designed for grazing alongside drinks rather than for a full sit-down dinner — bluefin tuna big belly with olive oil and crunchy salt, West Coast uni on a brioche soldier, smoked fish dip with trout roe and Ritz crackers, a butter-based smash burger, and bananas Foster over house vanilla bean ice cream.

The non-alcoholic offering is printed under its own heading, "Zero Proof", and it is honest to say up front that it is short: two made-to-order drinks, each $8, roughly half the price of the bar's full cocktails. Lift to the Scaffold is served on the rocks and built from lemon, mint, cucumber, alfalfa and tonic — herbal and dry rather than sweet. Four arrives in a coupe and works grapefruit with calpico, pineapple, ginger and chili, which gives it the lactic tang and heat that a fruit mocktail usually lacks. Athletic's Atletica zero-alcohol beer is $6 on the beer list. Two drinks is a genuinely small list for a bar of this ambition, and the roster rotates, so anything named in an older article should be checked rather than ordered from memory. What the section does get right is placement and price: it sits inside the cocktail menu, made to order by the same bartenders, rather than being relegated to the soft drinks. Open from 5pm Thursday through Sunday, to 1am on Friday and Saturday.
venues.pressQuote: It makes the mere act of sitting at the bar and sipping a cocktail feel like a special occasion. From the care taken in crafting each cocktail to the attentiveness and pride of the team behind the bar, each detail is intentional.

venues.name: Le Suprême
venues.description: Le Suprême, the Parisian-inspired brasserie inside Detroit's restored Book Tower, prints non-alcoholic drinks as their own menu section, Sans Alcool, not an afterthought. Current options include Temptation (Granny Smith apple, lemon, honey), Citron Crush (Ghia aperitif, lemon, raspberry, orange), and Ze Spritz (Lyre's Rosso, tonic, raspberry). The section has held steady in some form since Hour Detroit's opening-year review, and it's bookable on Resy alongside the restaurant's 300-bottle wine list.

Ze Spritz (Lyre's Rosso, tonic, raspberry, sparkling)

venues.longDescription:
Le Suprême opened in late August 2023 as the first restaurant to occupy Detroit's Book Tower, the 1926 Italian Renaissance-style skyscraper that Dan Gilbert's Bedrock spent roughly seven years and nearly $400 million restoring. The Parisian-inspired brasserie sits at street level on Washington Boulevard downtown, its 1920s-style dining room built around faded gold walls, handmade green tile, dark wood paneling, mosaic marble floors, and oxblood leather booths.

The beverage program centers on a 300-plus-bottle wine list curated by Book Tower beverage director Patrick Jobst, one of a small number of advanced sommeliers in Michigan — but the printed menu gives alcohol-free drinks their own heading, Sans Alcool, rather than burying them as an afterthought. The current lineup is Temptation (Granny Smith apple, lemon, honey), Citron Crush (Ghia aperitif, lemon, raspberry, orange), and Ze Spritz (Lyre's Rosso, tonic, raspberry, sparkling). Hour Detroit's restaurant report from the opening year singled out an earlier version of the section built around La Vierge, an alcohol-free-absinthe-and-sparkling-wine mocktail — evidence the no-alcohol list is a maintained section that gets refreshed, not a static one-off.

Le Suprême serves brunch on weekends and dinner nightly in downtown Detroit, a few blocks from Campus Martius Park, and takes reservations through Resy alongside walk-in bar seating and a patio. No separate request is needed to order off the Sans Alcool section — it's printed right on the regular drinks menu.
venues.pressQuote: if you're avoiding booze, you may want to try La Vierge, a refreshing mocktail made with absinthe and sparkling wine (both 0 percent alcohol)
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Ric Bohy and Jack Thomas, Hour Detroit

venues.name: Leahi Health
venues.description: Leahi Health is a plant-based café and juice bar on Waialae Avenue in Kaimukī, one of several Oʻahu locations, and it serves no alcohol at all. The kitchen prepares produce fresh each day, uses real fruit rather than concentrate in every smoothie, makes its dressings in house and brews its own kombucha. Most of what it uses is organic and hand-picked from farms in Hawaiʻi. The drinks side runs to pressed juices, smoothies including the Green Monster, and the house kombucha; the food side to the Surfer Bowl, kale avocado tacos and a rotating set of sauces including ginger tahini and spicy Thai. It is a daytime room, open 8am to 6pm.
signatureDrinks: Cold-pressed juices, made with produce prepped daily
venues.longDescription:
Leahi Health occupies a storefront at 3441 Waialae Avenue on the main Kaimukī strip, one of a small group of Oʻahu locations that also includes Hawaiʻi Kai. It is a plant-based café and juice bar rather than a bar in any conventional sense, and it is included here for the simplest reason: nothing on the premises contains alcohol, and its drinks are made rather than poured from a carton. Produce is prepped fresh daily, every smoothie uses real fruit instead of concentrate or purée base, dressings are made in house, and the kombucha is brewed on site. Most ingredients are organic and hand-picked from farms in the islands, which in Hawaiʻi is a shorter supply chain than the phrase usually implies.

It is worth being straightforward about what this venue is and is not. Honolulu does not have a dedicated zero-proof cocktail bar, and it has no non-alcoholic bottle shop; its fully alcohol-free scene is built out of kava rooms and plant-based cafés rather than out of rooms that replicate a bar. Leahi Health belongs firmly in the second group. Nobody is going to mistake a Green Monster smoothie for a negroni, and the venue makes no attempt at that — there is no zero-proof spirit behind the counter and no cocktail idiom in the menu. What it does offer is a room where a person who does not drink is not making a substitution or a request, where the drinks list is the actual point of the business, and where the house kombucha gives the acid and tannin that make a glass feel like something more than juice. Kaimukī puts it within a few minutes' walk of Vintage Books, which has the neighbourhood's serious spirit-free cocktail list, so the two together cover most of a day. Opening hours are 8am to 6pm daily.

venues.name: Left Field Brewery – Liberty Village
venues.description: Left Field Brewery's taproom, kitchen and Cold Beer Store on Hanna Ave in Liberty Village run a dedicated NON-ALC section on the printed drinks menu, led by the brewery's own 0.5% ABV Everyday Player Non-Alc Lager. Guest zero-proof pours round it out, including Harmon's Jack Pine Non-Alc Pale Ale, Collective Arts' Perpetual Paloma and a Godspeed Brewery iced tea, alongside in-house sparkling water and an Italian soda built on the brewery's own Say Hey syrup. blogTO has singled out the taproom's in-house sparkling water, non-alcoholic beers, iced teas and soft drinks alongside its Pilot Coffee Roasters coffee.
signatureDrinks: Iced Tea Sencha Green Tea & Yuzu
venues.longDescription:
Left Field Brewery runs a taproom, kitchen and Cold Beer Store at 40 Hanna Ave in Liberty Village, open daily — the Tap Room & Kitchen from 11am to midnight and the Cold Beer Store from 11am to 11pm. The brewery also operates a second Leslieville location at 36 Wagstaff Drive, though its non-alcoholic lineup there hasn't been separately verified.

The Liberty Village printed drinks menu carries a dedicated NON-ALC section anchored by Left Field's own Everyday Player Non-Alc Lager, a 0.5% ABV, 12oz can described on the menu as delivering "a truly crushable lager" with "flavours of toasted white bread and subtle floral hops with an ultra-mild bitterness and a refreshing, crisp finish." A companion Everyday Player Non-Alc Kölsch, also 0.5% ABV, is sold as a 355mL can through Left Field's fanshop, with flavors of "subtle fruit, breadiness and spice, and a refreshingly dry finish," though it wasn't confirmed on the specific Liberty Village printed menu.

Guest non-alcoholic beer includes Harmon's Jack Pine Non-Alc Pale Ale (Toronto, ON, 0.5% ABV) and Collective Arts' Perpetual Paloma (Hamilton, ON), alongside a Sencha Green Tea & Yuzu iced tea from fellow Toronto brewery Godspeed. Left Field also pours its own Say Hey Sparkling Water in Raspberry Lemon and a Red Sangria Non-Alc Italian Soda made with that same Say Hey syrup, served over ice.

blogTO covered the Liberty Village spot in December 2023, describing its non-drinking options as in-house sparkling water and non-alcoholic beers, iced teas, soft drinks and Pilot Coffee Roasters coffee.
venues.pressQuote: in-house sparkling water and non-alcoholic beers, iced teas, soft drinks and Pilot Coffee Roasters coffee

venues.name: Lemon Grove at The Aster
venues.description: Lemon Grove is a rooftop restaurant, bar, lounge and garden at the top of The Aster at Hollywood and Vine, with unobstructed views of the Hollywood Sign, the Capitol Records building and the hills. IMPORTANT CLARIFICATION: The Aster below it is a private membership club, but Lemon Grove itself is open to locals, hotel guests and members alike — only the weekday members-and-guests lunch is restricted, so brunch, dinner, the bar and the lounge are all public. It opened in October 2022; Daniel Pfeifer-Kotz is now executive chef, and cocktails are credited to Ash Ramos. Its drinks list carries a printed "Zero Proof" section holding three named mocktails — The Afters (espresso, cherry syrup, cola, cocoa), Meet Me In Venice (grapefruit, ginger beer, lime, mint, smoked salt) and Leading Lady (seasonal berries, lemon, cranberry, sparkling brut) — alongside genuine non-alcoholic wine, with Lyre's Classico Grande sparkling brut and Giesen's dealcoholised Sauvignon Blanc and rosé from Marlborough, plus Athletic Brewing's non-alcoholic golden ale. The section appears to be priced at a flat $16, though we could not confirm that beyond doubt. Closed Mondays.

venues.longDescription:
Lemon Grove sits on the roof of The Aster at the corner of Hollywood and Vine, a 7,200-square-foot indoor-outdoor room with space for a hundred or so, looking straight out at the Hollywood Sign, the Capitol Records building and the hills behind them. It opened in October 2022 and has turned over its leadership since: the kitchen is now run by executive chef Daniel Pfeifer-Kotz, whose career runs through Beauty & Essex and Laurel Hardware in Los Angeles and Cacao in Miami, and the cocktails are credited to Ash Ramos. It serves dinner from five Tuesday through Sunday, brunch at weekends from ten, and closes on Mondays.

One point of access needs clearing up, because it is the thing that stops people going. The Aster is a private membership club — annual dues run into the thousands — and that puts people off assuming the restaurant is closed to them. It is not. Lemon Grove is explicitly open to locals, hotel guests and members, in its own words; the only part reserved for members and their guests is the weekday lunch. Brunch, dinner, the bar and the lounge are all public, and you can book like anywhere else. What you get for the trip, if you are not drinking, is a printed Zero Proof section rather than an off-menu favour. Three named mocktails sit on it: The Afters, which runs espresso with cherry syrup, cola and cocoa and is effectively a dessert; Meet Me In Venice, a long grapefruit and ginger beer drink finished with mint and smoked salt; and Leading Lady, seasonal berries with lemon, cranberry and sparkling brut. Alongside them the bar pours real non-alcoholic wine rather than juice — Lyre's Classico Grande sparkling brut, and Giesen's dealcoholised Sauvignon Blanc and rosé, both from Marlborough in New Zealand, which is the region that does this better than anywhere — plus Athletic Brewing's non-alcoholic golden ale. Forbes summed up the value of that fairly: bonus points for a thoughtful zero-proof menu, because everyone deserves something fun to sip under the stars. One caveat: the menu's layout suggests a flat $16 across the zero-proof list, but we could not confirm it with certainty, so check when you order.
venues.pressQuote: Bonus points for a thoughtful zero-proof menu, complete with booze-free cocktails, lemonades and non-alcoholic wine, because everyone deserves something fun to sip under the stars.

venues.name: LeNell's Beverage Boutique
venues.description: LeNell's Beverage Boutique is Birmingham's serious independent bottle shop, and it is the one place in the metro where the non-alcoholic shelf has been curated rather than stocked. The range runs to Figlia aperitivo, Ritual Zero Proof spirits and Eins Zwei Zero dealcoholised wines among others, and the shop hands out spirit-free cocktail recipes to go with them and holds occasional tastings. For a city where most alcohol-free drinking still happens inside licensed bars, having somewhere that will talk you through building the drinks at home is a different and durable kind of provision. Open noon to 7pm Monday through Saturday, closed Sunday.
venues.longDescription:
Most bottle shops that claim a non-alcoholic section have a shelf of one dealcoholised wine and a four-pack of something hoppy. LeNell's, in Birmingham, is a different proposition: an independent shop with a genuine buying point of view, whose alcohol-free range has been chosen with the same attention as the rest of the store.

What that looks like on the shelf is brands that are actually good rather than merely available. Figlia is a bitter aperitivo built for the negroni-and-spritz slot, and it is the single most useful bottle for anyone trying to replicate the pre-dinner ritual without alcohol. Ritual Zero Proof covers the spirit categories — gin, whiskey, tequila alternatives — for people who want to build familiar cocktails at home. Eins Zwei Zero is a German dealcoholised wine range that behaves like wine at the table rather than like grape juice, which is the hard part of that category. The selection extends past those.

The shop goes further than stocking them. It hands out spirit-free cocktail recipes with the bottles and holds occasional tastings, which addresses the real barrier for anyone starting out: knowing what to do with a bottle of non-alcoholic gin once you have carried it home. Advice is the thing this category is short of, and it is not something an online retailer supplies.

This entry is graded three and is a bottle shop rather than a bar, so it has no signature drinks and no on-premise service — it appears here because a city guide that only lists places to sit is only half the answer. Someone building a home bar, or hosting, needs this address more than any of the others.

Open noon to 7pm Monday through Saturday and closed on Sunday, which is worth noting before making the trip.

One thing to be clear about, since this directory takes provenance seriously: LeNell's is a full-line beverage retailer, not an alcohol-free bottle shop. Most of the store is spirits, and someone avoiding alcohol entirely should know that before walking in — the non-alcoholic range is a well-curated section within a larger shop rather than the whole premise. For readers who find that environment difficult, the range is also largely orderable, and Noble Pursuits in Lakeview is the address for a room with nothing alcoholic in it at all.

venues.name: Leopold's Books Bar Caffe
venues.description: Leopold's is a bookshop, café and bar on Regent Street in Greenbush, a format that in practice makes it one of the easiest rooms in Madison to spend an evening in without drinking — there are books, the coffee programme is real, and nobody is waiting for you to order another round. It opens at 10am six days a week and stays open until midnight every night, which is an almost unheard-of span. The non-alcoholic drinks are named and built: the Leopold's Scarlet Mule runs hibiscus and sage against ginger beer and orange bitters, and a pomegranate sage spritz sits alongside it. Both turn up in Madison's zero-proof coverage.
signatureDrinks: Leopold's Scarlet Mule (hibiscus, sage, ginger beer, orange bitters)
venues.longDescription:
Leopold's Books Bar Caffe is exactly what its unwieldy name says: a bookshop with a café counter and a bar licence, on Regent Street in Greenbush, near the western edge of the University of Wisconsin campus. The combination is not a gimmick — the books are for sale and worth browsing, the coffee is made properly, and the room is arranged so that reading alone at a table for two hours is normal behaviour rather than something that needs explaining.

That is the whole argument for it as a non-alcoholic destination, and it is a strong one. The hardest part of not drinking is not usually the drink; it is that the social venues available are all organised around drinking, so a non-drinker either performs at a bar or stays home. A bookshop that is open until midnight every single night, and from 10am six days a week, solves that without needing to be alcohol-free. The named drinks hold up too: the Leopold's Scarlet Mule sets hibiscus and sage against ginger beer and orange bitters — bitters being the detail that separates a built drink from a soft one — and a pomegranate sage spritz runs alongside it. Madison Eats Food Tours singles out the spritz; City Cast Madison names the mule.

Practically: it is on the Regent Street side of campus, walkable from the UW stadium area and an easy bus ride from downtown, and the midnight close every night is genuinely unusual for anywhere in this guide that is not a bar. It does serve alcohol, so this is not a sober space — but the centre of gravity is the books and the coffee, and the proportion of the room drinking on any given weeknight is low. For a solo visit, or for a first sober outing where a bar feels like too much, this is probably the best recommendation in Madison.
venues.pressQuote: Leopold's Scarlet Mule: hibiscus, sage, ginger beer, orange bitters.

venues.name: Life on Mars
venues.description: Life on Mars is a plant-based cocktail bar at Pike and Harvard on Capitol Hill, opened in June 2019 by KEXP DJ John Richards, Amy Lindsey Richards, Leigh Sims and Neumos co-owner Steven Severin. It has a 6,000-record vinyl wall, a covered patio, an all-vegan kitchen and one of the most developed non-alcoholic menus in Seattle — a programme that dates to January 2022, when the bar reopened with nine zero-proof cocktails for Dry January. The section is headed "N/A and Low ABV Cocktails", and the naming matters: these are not all 0%. Pathfinder Spritz (0.03%, $14) has been on the list since 2019; High Violet (0.03%, $15) uses Pathfinder with Almave Ambar and blueberry coffee syrup; Mesmerize (0.1%, $13) is black-pepper-infused Pathfinder with lemon lapsang oleo; the canned Pathfinder Negroni is 0.5% at $14; and Two of Hearts is printed at 0.12–2.98% ABV, so it is genuinely low-alcohol rather than alcohol-free. The menu's own disclaimer notes all N/A spirits may contain trace alcohol. Every drink credits its creator and year. 21+ inside and out.

venues.longDescription:
Life on Mars opened in June 2019 at Pike and Harvard on Capitol Hill, from a group with deep roots in Seattle music: KEXP's John Richards, Amy Lindsey Richards, Leigh Sims, and Steven Severin, a co-owner of Neumos. The room is built around a 6,000-record vinyl wall, with a covered patio outside and an entirely plant-based kitchen doing burgers and cauliflower wings. Brunch runs from 11am at weekends, dinner from 4pm daily, and it is 21-and-over inside and out. One small detail says a lot about how the bar thinks: every cocktail on the menu is credited to the bartender who created it and the year they did, so you can see that Kraig Rovensky has been writing drinks here since 2019 and that Anna Eisch and Mike Albert added new ones in 2026.

The non-alcoholic programme dates precisely to January 2022, when the bar reopened on the 15th with nine zero-proof cocktails for Dry January, and it has stayed. The section is headed N/A and Low ABV Cocktails, and that second half is not decoration — this is the rare bar that tells you exactly how much alcohol is in a drink that most places would simply call a mocktail. Pathfinder Spritz is 0.03% at $14 and is the oldest drink on the entire cocktail list, a 2019 original that has outlasted everything around it. High Violet at $15 layers Pathfinder Hemp & Root with Almave Ambar, non-alcoholic bitters and a blueberry coffee syrup. Mesmerize at $13 infuses Pathfinder with black pepper against a lemon lapsang oleo. Pay Day at $15 is a jungle bird that will not knock you down. Two things to know. The canned Pathfinder Negroni is 0.5%, and Two of Hearts is printed at 0.12 to 2.98% ABV, which is genuinely low-alcohol rather than alcohol-free — the menu says so plainly and so do we. And Pathfinder itself, despite the "Hemp & Root" name, is distilled from hempseed and the maker states it contains no CBD or THC.

venues.name: Lighthouse Kava Bar
venues.description: A fully alcohol-free kava bar on Apache Boulevard in Tempe, a few minutes from the ASU campus, serving kava, kratom teas, mocktails and coffee. Regulars describe a room built for staying rather than passing through: cosy lighting, themed seating areas and a layout that encourages conversation, with a noise level low enough to actually hold one, which is an unusual quality anywhere and a rare one in a student district where the alternatives are uniformly loud. Open from noon most days and to 2am on Friday and Saturday, with drinks in the $10-20 range. Kava and kratom are alcohol-free but psychoactive; alcohol-free is not substance-free.

venues.longDescription:
Lighthouse sits on Apache Boulevard in Tempe, a few minutes from the ASU campus and squarely inside a district whose nightlife is otherwise organised around student drinking. That context is most of what makes it useful. A university town is a difficult place to not drink — the social default is aggressive, the venues are loud, and the alternatives usually close early — so an alcohol-free room that stays open until 2am on Friday and Saturday is filling a real gap rather than a theoretical one.

What regulars consistently describe is the room rather than the menu: cosy lighting, themed seating areas, and a layout built to encourage people to settle and talk, with a noise level low enough that conversation is actually possible. That is a deliberate design decision and a meaningful one. Much of what people miss when they stop drinking is not the alcohol but the long, unhurried evening a good bar makes possible, and a venue engineered for lingering delivers more of that than one engineered for turnover.

The menu runs kava — served strong, by most accounts — alongside kratom teas, mocktails and coffee, with drinks generally in the $10 to $20 range. The hours are wide: from noon Tuesday through Sunday, 4pm on Monday, and late at weekends, which covers the afternoon study crowd and the late-night one with the same room.

The standard caution applies and should not be softened by the friendly description. Kava is psychoactive and sedating, with documented case reports of liver injury; kratom acts on opioid receptors and carries dependence and withdrawal risk. Nothing here contains alcohol, and that is not the same as nothing here having an effect. For a designated driver or someone taking a night off, this is an easy recommendation. For someone in recovery from a substance-use disorder, it is a decision worth making with the full picture rather than on the strength of the phrase alcohol-free.

venues.name: Liliana
venues.description: Liliana is a contemporary Italian restaurant from chef Marvin Palomo on Queen Street West in Toronto's Beaconsfield Village, open since late September 2025. Named for the chef who mentored Palomo in Italy early in his career, it pairs housemade pasta and refined antipasti with a genuine, printed non-alcoholic cocktail menu — four named, priced drinks rather than a single token mocktail. Signature options include the Willow, a non-alcoholic Italian aperitif with grapefruit and bubbles, and the Daisy, built on gentian, non-alcoholic orange liqueur, pineapple, lime and cucumber.
