venues.longDescription:
The Perry Lane Hotel sits a block off Forsyth Park on East Perry Street, and Peregrin is what happens on its roof: an all-weather lounge with a pool that runs year-round, heavy tropical planting, colour-blocked walls and loungers arranged for the long view across the Historic District. It has taken Best Hotel Bar honours in Savannah more than once, and it is one of the very few rooms in the city where a good alcohol-free drink is available at two in the afternoon.

The mocktail list is short, deliberate and priced as a set — four drinks, all $12, printed under their own MOCKTAILS heading. The Lilypad is the clearest expression of the house style: Seedlip Garden, a cucumber-and-mint simple syrup, lemon and club soda, which is a genuinely herbaceous drink rather than a sweet one. The Sav Spirit pairs Giffard's non-alcoholic elderflower with Lyre's alcohol-free brut and soda. The Azalea Spritz is an all-Lyre's build, aperitivo and brut together, and reads as a straight substitution for the Aperol spritz the rest of the roof is drinking. The Mangrove takes Seedlip Grove — the citrus expression — with lemon and blood orange ginger beer. Alongside them the beer list runs Athletic Brewing golden ale and IPA at $8, with rotating draft offerings the staff will talk through.

One detail worth flagging for anyone arriving with a printed guide: the three Peregrin mocktails named in Visit Savannah's own zero-proof article — the French 108, Pick Up Lime and Palo N/A — have all rotated off. The current four are different drinks on the same premise, which is what a live programme looks like. The kitchen sends up charcuterie, cheese boards, tacos and the hotel's burger.

venues.name: Permit Room Portobello
venues.description: Dishoom's first standalone London Permit Room, an all-day cafe-bar on Portobello Road that treats not drinking as a first-class order rather than an afterthought. The name comes from Bombay's prohibition-era drinking permits, and the menu keeps the joke going with a dedicated teetotal section: a Sober Summer Negroni built on no-alcohol gin and bitter syrups, house chai, Bombay sodas and rotating alcohol-free specials alongside the full cocktail list. It opens for breakfast and runs past midnight at weekends, holds tables for walk-ins, and serves the group's Bombay comfort cooking throughout, so an alcohol-free evening here works as a real night out rather than a compromise.

naMenuItems.name: Sober Summer Negroni
naMenuItems.description: green apple, apricot, no-alcohol gin, vermouth and bitter syrups

venues.longDescription:
Dishoom's first standalone Permit Room in London took over 186 Portobello Road at the start of 2025, spinning out a concept the group had run as in-restaurant bars since its early Bombay-cafe days. The name is a wink at Bombay's drinking laws: in prohibition-era Bombay, drinking legally required a government-issued permit, and the city's permit rooms were where that drinking happened. The Portobello outpost turns the history on its head. This is an all-day cafe-bar where the drinking-optional side of the menu gets the same attention as the boozy side, and nobody checks any papers. The room runs from morning chai through to a late bar shift, with the group's Irani-cafe styling dialled into a corner site on one of west London's most walked streets, and the kitchen sends out Dishoom's comfort cooking from open to close.

The zero-proof list is the reason it earns a place in this directory. Alongside house chai and a run of Bombay sodas, the teetotal section carries real builds rather than juice: the Sober Summer Negroni layers green apple and apricot over no-alcohol gin, vermouth and bitter syrups, and the bar rotates seasonal alcohol-free specials and collaborations through the list. Prices sit closer to the group's cafes than to Notting Hill cocktail rates, which matters when a round of zero-proof drinks so often costs the same as the alcoholic version elsewhere. Reservations are taken with a share of tables held back for walk-ins, and the room stays open past midnight on Fridays and Saturdays. That combination is rarer than it should be in west London: most of the area's late rooms are wine-led or club-adjacent, and most of its alcohol-free options close with the coffee machines. A standalone bar from a group this practised at hospitality, holding real hours and writing its teetotal list with actual intent, fills a genuine gap on the western side of the city.

venues.name: Persephone
venues.description: Persephone is an Italian amaro-and-wine bar and specialty grocer at 4857 Rainier Ave S in Columbia City, opened in January 2022 by Meredith Molli, who also owns the long-running trattoria La Medusa next door. It is part bar, part shop: you can buy local vegetables and fruit, olive oil and fresh pasta, or order lunch, dinner, drinks and snacks from noon through the evening. The Infatuation describes the room as effortlessly cosy, decorated with string lights, a lot of happy green plants, and wacky labels from shelves of natural wine bottles. The food leans fried and Sicilian — crispy fish meatballs, saffron arancini, and a chickpea panelle sandwich with mayo and lemon on a toasted sesame roll. The bar is built around a large chalkboard selection of amari, the bitter Italian herbal liqueurs, and it keeps non-alcoholic stock so non-drinkers can get a similarly nuanced, bittersweet drink rather than something sweet. NOTE: Persephone has no website of its own, and we could not confirm which non-alcoholic amari or aperitifs it pours — worth asking at the bar. Open Wednesday to Saturday.
venues.longDescription:
Persephone opened in January 2022 next door to La Medusa, the gently Sicilian trattoria that has anchored Columbia City for decades, and it belongs to the same owner, Meredith Molli. Calling it a bar undersells the shape of the thing: it is a bar, a specialty grocer and a café at once, and sometimes it cosplays as a mini farmers market. You can buy local vegetables and fruit, olive oil and fresh pasta, or sit down and order lunch, dinner, drinks and snacks straight through from noon. The Infatuation's description is the one that gets the feel right — effortlessly cosy, decorated with string lights, a lot of happy green plants, and wacky labels from shelves of natural wine bottles. The food is fried and excellent: an all-star lineup of crispy fish meatballs, saffron arancini, and a chickpea panelle sandwich with mayo and lemon on a toasted sesame roll. It opens Wednesday to Saturday from noon.

What makes it interesting for a non-drinker is the bar's whole orientation. Persephone is built around amaro — the bitter Italian herbal liqueurs — with a huge chalkboard selection of them, and the house move is a bitter red spritz. Bitterness is the hardest thing to replace when you stop drinking, because most non-alcoholic substitutes reach for sugar and fruit instead, and a room that already thinks in amari has both the palate and the glassware to build you something with a proper bitter spine. The bar keeps non-alcoholic stock specifically so that non-drinkers can get a similarly nuanced experience. Two honest limitations. Persephone has no website at all, which is why some listings wrongly report it closed — it is not; La Medusa's own site publishes its current hours, and we confirmed those there. And because there is no site, we could not establish which non-alcoholic amari, aperitifs or wines it actually pours, which is exactly the detail that would matter most here. Ask at the bar, and ask specifically for something bitter — that is what this place is for.
venues.pressQuote: You can have a similarly nuanced experience with non-alcoholic stock.

venues.name: Persimmon
venues.description: Persimmon is a fine-dining restaurant on Hope Street on Providence's East Side, and its bar runs one of the most useful non-alcoholic policies in the state: the rotating cocktail menu can be ordered in a neutral counterpart, with the bartenders swapping ingredient for ingredient rather than simply omitting the spirit. Jalapeño stands in for mezcal, prune juice for sherry. That turns the whole list, not a corner of it, into something a non-drinker can order from.
venues.longDescription:
Persimmon is one of Rhode Island's serious kitchens, on Hope Street near the Fox Point end of the East Side, and its drinks programme is run with the same attention as the food. What makes it matter to a non-drinker is a single policy, applied across the whole menu rather than to a handful of drinks: any cocktail on the rotating list can be ordered in what the bar calls its neutral counterpart.

The distinction between that and a mocktail is the entire point. Most bars, asked for a drink without alcohol, remove the spirit and add more juice, which produces something sweeter and flatter than the original. Persimmon substitutes instead — matching the role the missing ingredient played rather than the volume it occupied. Fresh jalapeño replaces mezcal, because what mezcal contributes to that particular drink is heat and a vegetal edge, not just alcohol. Prune juice replaces sherry, because sherry brings dried-fruit depth and a faint oxidised note. This is how a good bartender thinks about a drink, and it is rare to see it offered as a standing policy rather than as a favour.

Because the cocktail list rotates regularly with the seasons and the kitchen, there is no fixed alcohol-free menu to publish, and we have deliberately not listed drink names here — anything we printed would be wrong within a season. What holds is the policy. Ask for the neutral version of whatever appeals on the list, and expect it to be built rather than diluted.

The room itself is small and quiet, suited to a long dinner rather than a quick round, and the East Side location puts it a short distance from Wayland Square and the Hope Street shops.
venues.pressQuote: regularly rotating drink menu can be ordered in original form or their neutral counterpart

venues.name: Pharm Table
venues.description: Pharm Table is a Southtown restaurant built on anti-inflammatory, Ayurvedic-influenced cooking, and its drinks list follows the same philosophy — which makes it one of the few places where the alcohol-free option is the point rather than the exception. The N/A-groni is the standout, a spirit-free Negroni that keeps the bitterness the original depends on; there is a zero-proof margarita cut with aloe, and the Golden Hour. In a room where a large share of the guests are already ordering for how they want to feel afterwards, nobody registers an alcohol-free order at all. The weekend brunch service from 10am is the rarest thing it offers, since almost nothing else in San Antonio pours a considered zero-proof drink in the morning.
venues.address: 611 S Presa St #106, San Antonio, TX 78210
venues.hours: Mon-Tue closed; Wed-Thu 5pm-9pm; Fri 12pm-9pm; Sat 10am-9pm; Sun 10am-8pm
venues.longDescription:
Pharm Table sits on South Presa Street in Southtown and works from an unusual premise: chef Elizabeth Johnson built the menu around anti-inflammatory cooking drawn from Ayurvedic principles, treating food primarily as something that acts on the body. That framing changes what the bar is for.

In most restaurants the alcohol-free drink is a concession — something offered to the guest who cannot participate. Here it is continuous with the whole proposition. Somebody eating a menu designed around how they will feel tomorrow is not making a different kind of choice by skipping the wine, and the room reflects that. For anyone tired of the small performance that ordering a mocktail in a bar involves, the absence of that dynamic is worth more than the drink itself.

The drinks are properly built. The N/A-groni is the one to order, because a Negroni is defined entirely by bitterness and is therefore the hardest classic to render without alcohol — most attempts substitute something red and sweet and miss the point completely. Pharm Table also pours a zero-proof margarita lengthened with aloe, which adds body and a slightly vegetal cool that suits the food, and the Golden Hour.

The schedule takes planning: closed Monday and Tuesday, dinner only Wednesday and Thursday from 5pm, opening at noon on Friday and at 10am on Saturday and Sunday for weekend brunch. That weekend daytime service is genuinely useful — Southtown is one of San Antonio's better walking neighbourhoods and there is very little else in the city offering a considered alcohol-free drink at eleven in the morning. Mixtli is a couple of doors along the same block. Southtown as a whole is the most rewarding neighbourhood in the city to walk without drinking, with Pharm Table and Mixtli anchoring one end of it.
venues.pressQuote: Pharm Table: N/A-groni, zero-proof margarita with aloe, Golden Hour.

venues.name: Phoenix Hill Tea Merchant
venues.description: Phoenix Hill Tea Merchant is a family-run Teochew (Chao Shan) tea house on Joo Chiat Place, a purely non-alcoholic space built around Feng Huang Dan Cong oolong grown on the owners' own plantation in the Phoenix Mountains (Fenghuang) of Shantou, Guangdong. Run by Singaporean couple Julie and Stephen, the shop pours tea tastings throughout opening hours and Julie leads hands-on tea-appreciation courses over gongfu brews of charcoal-roasted Dan Cong. Alongside the signature Dan Cong the racks hold Pu-er, Da Hong Pao, Tie Guan Yin, green and flower teas, every cup alcohol-free by definition.
signatureDrinks: Feng Huang Dan Cong oolong - charcoal-roasted single-bush oolong direct from the owners' plantation in the Phoenix Mountains (Fenghuang), Shantou, Guangdong, brewed gongfu-style in-shop
Da Hong Pao - roasted Wuyi rock oolong
Tie Guan Yin - Anxi 'Iron Goddess' oolong
venues.longDescription:
Registered in 2013 and run by Singaporean couple Julie and Stephen, Phoenix Hill Tea Merchant is that rare thing in Singapore: a tea house sourcing direct from a plantation the owners actually own. Their estate spans more than 100 acres in Shantou, Guangdong, in the Fenghuang (Phoenix Mountain) belt long regarded as the home of oolong. The business is primarily a wholesaler, but the Joo Chiat Place shop keeps a steady stream of local tea lovers coming for retail leaf and tasting.

The anchor is Feng Huang Dan Cong (Phoenix single-bush) oolong, brought straight from the Guangdong estate. The leaves are always charcoal-roasted in the traditional way, which the shop credits for the tea's distinctive aroma and taste, and poured gongfu-style at the counter. Around the Dan Cong sits a deep range of Chinese leaf: aged Pu-er, Da Hong Pao and other Wuyi rock oolongs, Anxi Tie Guan Yin, plus green, flower and red (hong cha) teas.

Tea tasting is available throughout opening hours, and Julie runs structured tea-appreciation courses in-shop for those who want to learn to read a Dan Cong the way a sommelier reads a wine. It is a wholly non-alcoholic room, and a corporate and team-building venue partner for food-tour operator Singabites since 2016. There is no cocktail list here and no Michelin or 50 Best plaque, just single-origin leaf, a charcoal roast, and the patience of a proper gongfu pour, which is exactly the point for a zero-proof afternoon in Katong.
venues.pressQuote: The leaves themselves are always charcoal roasted. This is the traditional method and gives the tea its unique smell and taste.

venues.name: The Pig & The Lady
venues.description: The Pig & The Lady is a modern Vietnamese restaurant run by the Le family, which began as a stall at Honolulu's farmers markets and grew into one of the most decorated kitchens in the state. It now trades in Kaimukī on Waialae Avenue, having left the North King Street room in Chinatown that made its name — worth knowing, because a great many listings still send people downtown. The bar keeps a house mocktail built on pineapple, kaffir lime and black pepper: savoury, aromatic and peppery rather than sweet, and drawn from the same aromatics the kitchen cooks with. No published source names it, so it is listed here by its components rather than under an invented name.
signatureDrinks: House mocktail (pineapple, kaffir lime, black pepper)

naMenuItems.name: Heine(can) 0.0
naMenuItems.description: non-alcoholic

venues.longDescription:
The Pig & The Lady started as a stall at Honolulu's farmers markets, run by the Le family from their own Vietnamese recipes, and grew into one of the most decorated restaurants in Hawaiʻi. It spent years at 83 North King Street in Chinatown, and that address is the one most guides and listings still carry — but the Chinatown room is closed, and the restaurant now operates from Suite 120 at 3650 Waialae Avenue in Kaimukī. Anyone working from an older listing will find the wrong door. The move puts it a few steps from Vintage Books at 3660 Waialae, which means the two most interesting non-alcoholic offerings in Kaimukī are now next to each other, with Leahi Health a short walk away on the same avenue.

Its non-alcoholic drink is a single house build combining pineapple, kaffir lime and black pepper, and the composition says something about how the kitchen thinks. Pineapple is the obvious local sweetener and the base of half the zero-proof drinks in this guide; what is done with it here is not obvious. Kaffir lime leaf is intensely aromatic and faintly bitter, quite unlike lime juice, and it is one of the defining smells of South-East Asian cooking. Black pepper adds a dry, prickling heat at the back of the palate. The result is savoury and aromatic rather than sweet, built from the aromatics already on the stove rather than from a bar syrup — the same instinct that produces Lucky Belly's galangal-and-lemongrass swizzle. Two honest limitations. The drink is not named in any published source, so it is recorded here by its ingredients; inventing a name would make the listing look tidier and be false. And it is one drink rather than a programme, which is why the entry sits at a three. What the restaurant offers a non-drinker is a considered option at a table worth sitting at, rather than a list to work through.
venues.pressQuote: Everyone knows that The Pig & The Lady serves amazing pho (and banh mi. Oh, and don't forget the frozen custard), but did you know there's also a mocktail on the menu?

venues.name: Pig and Tiger
venues.description: Pig and Tiger is a Taiwanese night-market restaurant in Denver's Five Points, opened in August 2025 by co-chefs and co-owners Darren Chang, a Top Chef alum, and Travis Masar, who launched the concept in 2020 as a stall at Avanti in Boulder; the name comes from their Chinese zodiac signs. Cocktails and non-alcoholic drinks share one menu rather than being split, and drinks that can be built zero-proof are marked with a heart and priced at $12. The current list marks two: the May Mei, a Taiwanese salted plum spritz inspired by Chang's mother's favourite flavour, and Curious Mr. Brown, a riff on the iconic Taiwanese canned coffee built with coffee and monkey bread tea. Both are made with the same house syrups and scrap-derived sugars as the full-proof list. Large-format drinks arrive in teapots, and the menu changes with the season.
signatureDrinks: May Mei (available zero proof: Taiwanese salted plum spritz)
Curious Mr. Brown (available zero proof: coffee and monkey bread tea, after the Taiwanese canned coffee)
venues.longDescription:
Pig and Tiger opened in August 2025 at 2200 California Street in Five Points, the first bricks-and-mortar home for a concept that co-chefs and co-owners Darren Chang and Travis Masar started in 2020 as a stall inside Avanti in Boulder. The name is literal: Chang was born in the year of the Pig and Masar in the year of the Tiger. Chang is a Top Chef alum, and the cooking is Taiwanese night-market food read through European technique, with a menu built around chilli wontons of shrimp and pork with zha cai, jellyfish salad, Sichuan green beans with fermented garlic and aged vinegar, Taiwanese fried chicken with chicken-fat rice and orange hot honey, and a lu rou fan of braised pork with shiitakes, mustard greens and a soft-cooked egg. Desserts run to shaved ice with almond panna cotta and a blackberry sorbet dusted with green Sichuan and salted plum powder.

The bar's structural decision is the one that matters here: there is one drinks list, and the drinks that can be made without alcohol are marked on it with a heart and a $12 price, so a non-drinker orders from the same page as everyone else. Reviewing the restaurant, 5280 wrote that cocktails and mocktails share the same menu, which more restaurants should do so that no one feels singled out. As the menu stands, two drinks carry the mark. The May Mei is a Taiwanese salted plum spritz, described on the menu as an ode to chef Darren's mother, and it is the house signature in either format. Curious Mr. Brown is built on coffee and monkey bread tea, a nod to the ubiquitous Mr. Brown canned coffee of Taiwan, and reads as an espresso-martini analogue without the spirit. Both are constructed with the same house syrups and scrap-derived sugars as the full-proof cocktails, and large-format drinks arrive in teapots. The menu turns with the seasons, so the marked set changes; Westword's January 2026 round-up covered a broader winter list that included a shaved-ice Baobing Sour. The restaurant is closed Mondays and Tuesdays and runs 5pm to 9pm midweek and to 10pm on Friday and Saturday.
venues.pressQuote: Cocktails and mocktails share the same menu, which more restaurants should do so that no one feels singled out.

venues.name: Pig Latin
venues.description: Pig Latin is a riverside restaurant in Eagle, the affluent suburb north-west of Boise, and it covers all three registers a non-drinker might want across a day: mocktails, proper coffee and matcha. That breadth is more useful than it sounds — most venues offer one of the three, so a place serving a decent matcha in the morning and a built mocktail in the evening covers a whole day's worth of alcohol-free drinking in a part of the metro that has very little else. Open from 10am at weekends and to 11pm on Friday. Eagle sits about fifteen minutes north-west of downtown Boise and has very little else documented, which makes a single all-day venue disproportionately useful there.
venues.hours: Mon 4pm-9pm; Tue-Wed 11am-9pm; Thu 11am-10pm; Fri 11am-11pm; Sat 10am-11pm; Sun 10am-9pm
venues.longDescription:
Pig Latin sits on South Rivershore Lane in Eagle, the well-heeled suburb about fifteen minutes north-west of downtown Boise, on the Boise River. It is a restaurant rather than a bar, and its drinks list covers mocktails, coffee and matcha.

That three-way spread is the reason it earns a listing. Most venues serve one kind of alcohol-free drink well: a coffee shop does coffee, a cocktail bar does mocktails, a tea room does tea. Someone not drinking across an entire day has to move between venues to cover the range. A restaurant doing all three means the same room works for a morning coffee, an afternoon matcha and an evening mocktail — and the hours support exactly that, opening at 10am at weekends and 11am midweek, running to 11pm on Friday and Saturday.

Geography is the other argument. Everything else in this guide is downtown Boise, on the Bench, or out in Nampa. Eagle is a substantial and growing part of the metro with very little alcohol-free provision documented at all, so a single venue covering the whole day there is worth more to a local than a fourth cocktail bar on 8th Street would be.

The grade is an honest 3: the individual drinks are not documented in detail, and mocktails-coffee-matcha describes a range rather than a designed programme. But range is exactly what a suburb needs, and the riverside setting makes it a pleasant place to spend an afternoon without a drink in hand. Worth asking what the current mocktails are, since restaurant lists of this kind rotate more often than a dedicated bar's. The river setting also makes it a genuinely pleasant place to sit for an afternoon, which is rarer than it should be for a suburban restaurant.
venues.pressQuote: The innovative Latin American restaurant has covered a large portion of the former patio of Bella Aquila with glass to create an atrium that allows for year-round indoor/outdoor dining

venues.name: Pillion Tea
venues.description: Pillion Tea is a fully alcohol-free tea house on West Biddle Street in Mid-Town Belvedere, open since March 2019 and built around loose leaf sold by the ounce — Keemun Hao Ya, Iron Goddess of Mercy, Yunnan Gold, and compressed sheng pu-er cakes from Ai Lao Shan and Yi Wu. The drinks program runs well past steeped tea: the shop makes its own syrups and even a housemade non-alcoholic rum, which anchors a seasonal mocktail of sticky rice pu-er shaken with coconut milk and salted banana simple syrup. House sodas pair fresh seltzer with tea and fruit syrups — Rooibos Cream Soda, Blueberry Matcha, Hibiscus & Rose Spritzer, and the Lucky Piña built on Karigane green tea and yuzu-pineapple syrup. The caffeine-free Desert Rose Latte (honeybush, spice syrup, vanilla bean, rosewater) is an homage to the family farms in South Africa, Syria, Lebanon, Palestine, Sri Lanka, and Afghanistan whose ingredients are featured in the cup. It is a daytime room rather than a night spot: closed Sunday and Monday, with a late Friday close at 7pm.
venues.hours: Mon closed; Tue-Thu 10am-4pm; Fri 1:30pm-7pm; Sat 10am-4pm; Sun closed
venues.longDescription:
Pillion Tea is a fully alcohol-free tea house at 42 W Biddle Street in Mid-Town Belvedere, and its name is the first clue to what makes it unusual: a pillion is the seat behind the rider on a motorcycle. Co-owners Zena Lichter and Eric Mitchell built the room themselves, pulling up the floors and hand-cutting the tin tiles, and what they landed on is a punk motorcycle aesthetic married to a clean and tranquil tea shop — a combination that sounds contradictory and works. They occasionally organise motorcycle rides for the overlap between local tea drinkers and local riders, which is a smaller Venn diagram than you would think and a real community either way. Lichter's description of what she is running is the useful one: I personally know ninety per cent of the people who come in here by name. Her framing of the drink itself is broader — around the world, she told The Baltimore Banner, tea is how you welcome people into your home.

The tea programme is genuinely deep rather than decorative. Pillion works directly with dozens of producing families around the world and carries close to a hundred teas, of which twenty to thirty are rare — a yellow tea from Dongting Lake in China, purple teas from Kenya, fermented pu-erh — sold loose by weight as well as brewed in the room. Alongside the straight tea it builds a rotating set of named drinks: a seasonal mocktail, a Desert Rose latte, a rooibos cream soda, a hibiscus and rose spritzer, a ginger mint spritz, a blueberry matcha and the Lucky Piña. Nothing here contains alcohol and nothing is infused with anything else. One practical caveat: the shop's website does not render its menu in a readable form, so the current list and the hours are best confirmed by phone or in person rather than online — and given how much of the stock is rare and rotating, asking what has just come in is the right approach anyway.
venues.pressQuote: Pillion Tea opened its doors earlier this month, offering local Wight Tea Co. varieties, craft sodas, and sweet pastries like cherry scones and lemon-strawberry pound cake.

venues.name: Pilot Project Brewing
venues.description: Pilot Project Brewing, opened in August 2019 by co-founders Dan Abel and Jordan Radke, bills itself as the country's first dedicated brewery incubator — a Logan Square tasting room, café, and kitchen that gives startup and minority-owned breweries a launch pad for production and distribution. Its non-alcoholic credentials are unusually deep for a brewery: Pilot Project is the U.S. brewing and distribution partner for Mash Gang, the London NA-beer brand founded by Jordan Childs and James Loveday in 2020. Pilot Project brews Mash Gang's lineup stateside and pours it on tap here, including Journey Juice (a Tajín-spiked mango IPA at 0.5% ABV) and Stoop Lite (a light, chili-and-Szechuan-tinged lager). The rotating Mash Gang range also features Chug (hazy IPA), Glug (cerveza), and the seasonal Lesser Evil (chocolate-cherry stout). Local coffee and tea round out the zero-proof options.
venues.longDescription:
Pilot Project Brewing opened in August 2019 at 2140 N Milwaukee Avenue in Logan Square, founded by Dan Abel and Jordan Radke on a model borrowed from the record industry: it bills itself as the country's first dedicated brewery incubator, giving startup and under-represented brewing brands production capacity, a taproom to sell through, and a route to market they could not afford alone. Brands sign on as residents and, if things go well, graduate out — Dutchbag Brew Co, Brother Chimp Brewing, Luna Bay Booch and Histrionic Brew Lab have all moved on, while Brewer's Kitchen, Standard Goods, Funkytown Brewery, Cervecería Paracaidista, Azadi and others are currently in residence. The taproom itself opens at 9am seven days a week and runs a full coffee counter alongside the beer, with drip coffee from $4.25, cold brew at $5.25, Rishi teas, a London Fog at $4.50, matcha and chai lattes at $6, a honey matcha lavender lemonade at $6 and Italian sodas at $5 — which makes it usable as a morning café long before the taps matter.

The reason it belongs in a non-alcoholic guide is one of those residents. Mash Gang, the British brewery that began as a lockdown homebrewing project in London in 2020 and built its name entirely on low- and no-alcohol beer, partnered with Pilot Project for United States production, and is listed as a current resident rather than a graduated one. Its beers are brewed on site: Journey Juice, described at launch as equal parts sweet, spicy, sour and fruity; Stoop Lite, crushable and lightly hopped with a hint of chili and Szechuan pepper; and Chug, a 0.5% hazy IPA the brewery describes as crisp, juicy and bold, with tropical fruit and citrus zest. That makes this one of very few Chicago taprooms where the non-alcoholic beer is made in the building rather than bought in. One honest caveat about the incubator model: the tap list rotates constantly by design, and the venue does not publish a live list in a readable form, so which Mash Gang beers are pouring on a given day is worth checking before a special trip.

venues.name: The Pine Room
venues.description: The Pine Room is a neighbourhood restaurant in historic Harrods Creek, on River Road north-east of Louisville, and it keeps one of the better-stocked non-alcoholic back bars in the metro. Rather than a single token bottle it carries both of the Louisville-made Spiritless expressions — Kentucky 74, the non-alcoholic bourbon, and Jalisco 55, the non-alcoholic tequila — which means the two drinks most people actually want, an old fashioned and a paloma, can both be built properly here without alcohol. The paloma is the one the city's zero-proof coverage names. Dinner runs Tuesday to Sunday with weekend brunch from 9am, and the room sits close enough to the Ohio River to make the drive worthwhile.
venues.longDescription:
Harrods Creek is an old river settlement on the north-eastern edge of Jefferson County, the sort of place that had a general store and a boat dock before Louisville reached it, and The Pine Room is its restaurant. The building has a history of its own — the room was revived after a fire, and local coverage has framed the reopening as the Pine Room rising from the ashes — and what it is now is a proper neighbourhood restaurant with a serious bar, out where the city thins into the river road.

It earns its place here on inventory, which is the honest measure of whether a bar can actually make you a drink. Most restaurants that claim non-alcoholic cocktails own one bottle of something and improvise around it. The Pine Room stocks both Spiritless expressions made in Louisville: Kentucky 74, the reverse-distilled non-alcoholic bourbon that took Best Non-Alcoholic Spirit at the L.A. Spirits Awards, and Jalisco 55, its agave counterpart. With those two on the shelf, an old fashioned and a paloma — the two drinks a Kentucky bar is most often asked for — can both be built to spec rather than substituted with juice. The paloma is the build the city's zero-proof coverage names specifically.

Practically, this is a destination rather than a walk-in: about twenty minutes north-east of downtown Louisville along River Road, past Harrods Creek's marina strip. Dinner runs Tuesday through Sunday from 5pm, and there is weekend brunch from 9am, which is the easier slot for anyone who would rather not spend an evening in a room where the table is ordering wine. Watch Hill Proper in Norton Commons, which also pours Kentucky 74, is roughly ten minutes further on, which makes the north-east a more workable alcohol-free afternoon than its bourbon-heavy reputation suggests.
venues.pressQuote: The Pine Room stocks Jalisco 55 and Kentucky 74, and offers a Paloma and other cocktails featuring non-alcoholic spirits.
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: The Zero Proof, Louisville city guide

venues.name: Pink Flamingo
venues.description: Pink Flamingo is a rum-focused tropical tavern that Dutch Courage co-owners Brendan Dorr and Eric Fooy opened in April 2025 in the Remington building that ran as Dizzy Issie's from 1937, became The Dizz in 1997, and sat shuttered after closing in fall 2019. Its Spirit Free list is a standing section of the menu rather than an on-request favor: the Road Less Traveled builds Pathfinder N/A amaro into a mule with blood orange-Calabrian chile honey, lime and ginger beer, while The Shallows pours Lyre's N.A. cane spirit with fassionola and All The Bitter aromatic bitters. If The Shoe Fitz mixes Mionetto N/A prosecco with aperitif and soda water, and a Yuzu-Thai Basil-Limeade rounds out the zero-proof cocktails alongside NA cans from Athletic, Best Day and Lagunitas. Bar manager Nick Pikounis told PUNCH the Road Less Traveled is the bar's single most-ordered N/A drink. The bar was named a 2026 James Beard Award semifinalist for Best New Bar.
venues.longDescription:
Pink Flamingo opened in April 2025 at 300 W 30th Street in Remington, in the building that had been The Dizz — a beloved neighbourhood institution, which is a complicated inheritance. Co-owners Brendan Dorr and Eric Fooy, who also run the gin bar Dutch Courage, were direct about it: people were vocal about how much they loved The Dizz, Dorr told The Baltimore Banner, and they were not looking to open somebody else's business. What they opened instead is a rum-focused tropical tavern that keeps the neighbourhood-bar function intact — you can come in here and have pitchers of beer, as Dorr put it. Baltimore Magazine's review put the drinks programme plainly: rum is the star here. In January 2026 the bar was named a James Beard Award semifinalist for Best New Bar, and bar manager Nick Pikounis's reaction was the honest kind — shocked and honoured, and glad the struggle and stress had been worth it. The kitchen runs Spam chips and dip, crab dumplings, tempura green beans, pomegranate walnut wings, a half chicken and a short-rib burger.

The non-alcoholic side follows the tropical logic of the rest of the bar rather than importing a generic mocktail list: the house zero-proof drinks have included the Road Less Traveled, The Shallows, If The Shoe Fitz and a yuzu, Thai basil and limeade build. Tiki and tropical formats suit zero-proof drinking better than almost any other style, because the acid, spice and fruit are doing most of the work in the original anyway — a rum bar is a more promising place to order a non-alcoholic drink than a whiskey one. One practical caveat: Pink Flamingo publishes its menus as image-based PDFs that cannot be read by search engines or screen readers, so the current zero-proof list and its prices cannot be checked in advance. Dinner runs 4pm to 10pm daily with weekend brunch from 11am and happy hour weekdays from 4pm.
venues.pressQuote: Rum is the star here.

venues.name: Pink Gorilla Kava
venues.description: Pink Gorilla Kava is a fully alcohol-free coffee-and-kava hybrid that opened in April 2026 at 340 W Flagler St in Downtown Miami, a short walk from the Miami River and Brickell. It comes from the team behind the Miami fashion label Pink Gorilla — founders Daniel Karan and Christian Ramos — with restaurateur Giancarlo Rodriguez involved in the venue. The concept runs as a specialty coffee bar by day and a kava lounge by night, pitched as a low-key, sober alternative to the neighborhood's club-heavy scene. Mornings bring organic coffee, lattes, and ceremonial matcha with scratch-made syrups and pastries from local bakeries; evenings shift to traditional kava and botanical "k-tea." The roughly 66-seat space includes a large outdoor terrace and doubles as a retail storefront for the Pink Gorilla brand. Early reviews praise the matcha and coffee.
venues.address: 340 W Flagler St, CU #102, Miami, FL 33130
venues.longDescription:
Pink Gorilla Kava opened in April 2026 at 340 West Flagler Street in Downtown Miami, a short walk from the Miami River and Brickell. It comes from the team behind the Miami fashion label Pink Gorilla — founders Daniel Karan and Christian Ramos — with restaurateur Giancarlo Rodriguez involved in the venue, and it doubles as a retail storefront for the brand.

The concept splits the day cleanly. Mornings are a specialty coffee bar: organic coffee, lattes and ceremonial matcha made with scratch-made syrups, with pastries from local bakeries. Evenings become a kava lounge serving traditional kava and botanical k-tea. It is pitched explicitly as a low-key, sober alternative to a neighbourhood otherwise dominated by clubs, which in downtown Miami is a genuine gap rather than a marketing line.

The roughly 66-seat room includes a large outdoor terrace. Early coverage and reviews have singled out the matcha and coffee rather than the kava, which is worth knowing: for anyone curious about the format but not about the botanicals, the daytime operation stands on its own.

That a fashion label opened it is not incidental. A brand extending into a physical room is betting that sober social space is culturally desirable rather than merely therapeutic — which is a different, and probably more durable, proposition than wellness.

The caveat that belongs on every kava listing applies here and should not be softened: kava is psychoactive and sedating, with documented case reports of liver injury, and kratom acts on opioid receptors and carries real dependence and withdrawal risk. Everything served is free of alcohol. That is a narrower claim than nothing served having an effect, and for anyone whose reason for avoiding alcohol is recovery from a substance-use disorder, the difference is the whole question.
venues.pressQuote: We're social creatures. Everyone wants to socialize, but we don't have to drink alcohol. That's why kava bars are great.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Giancarlo Rodriguez, on Pink Gorilla Kava

venues.name: Pink Lantern
venues.description: Pink Lantern is downtown Birmingham's most talked-about recent opening and, for a non-drinker, its most useful: it runs from 7am to midnight on weekdays and to 2am on Friday and Saturday, which means coffee, lunch, an early drink and a late one all happen in the same room. The mocktails are built rather than poured — a Disco Paradise of club soda, lime, mint, dragon fruit and elderflower, and a Fool Me Twice where spicy ginger beer meets cantaloupe, pineapple and bright lemon. Birmingham's own Bham Now singled the bar out for them in its January 2026 guide to drinking without alcohol in the city.
signatureDrinks: Disco Paradise — club soda, lime, mint, dragon fruit, elderflower
Fool Me Twice — spicy ginger beer, cantaloupe, pineapple, lemon
venues.longDescription:
Seventeen hours a day is an unusual thing for a bar to attempt. Pink Lantern, on 1st Avenue North in downtown Birmingham, opens at 7am and runs to midnight, or 2am on Friday and Saturday — which makes it a coffee shop, a lunch spot, an early-evening bar and a late one, in the same room, without changing hands.

That single fact is why it leads the licensed half of this guide. The hardest structural problem for someone who does not drink is that the good rooms only exist between 5pm and midnight; a venue that is already open at seven in the morning has no such gap, and a non-drinker can use it the way everyone else uses a bar — as the default place to suggest.

The drinks earn it as well. The Disco Paradise is club soda, lime, mint, dragon fruit and elderflower, which is a genuinely aromatic build rather than a fruit juice — the elderflower does the floral lifting that a gin would otherwise handle. The Fool Me Twice is the better of the two for anyone who finds most mocktails too sweet: spicy ginger beer against cantaloupe, pineapple and bright lemon, with the ginger heat standing in for alcohol's bite. Both are on the menu rather than made on request.

Bham Now, the city's daily, picked the bar out specifically for these in its January 2026 round-up of where to drink without alcohol in Birmingham, describing it as the city's hottest new bar — the sort of framing that matters, because it puts the mocktails at a room people want to be in rather than at one they will settle for.

Downtown location, a short walk from Paper Doll, Neon Moon and Wooden City, which makes 1st and 2nd Avenue North the practical starting point for an evening in this city without drinking.
venues.pressQuote: Enjoy vibrant mocktails at Birmingham's hottest new bar, featuring creations like Disco Paradise—a refreshing blend of club soda, lime, mint, dragon fruit and elderflower or Fool Me Twice, where spicy ginger beer meets juicy cantaloupe, pineapple and bright lemon

venues.name: Pinky's
venues.description: Pinky's is a Scott's Addition bar and restaurant that does something quietly unusual with its non-alcoholic drinks: it prices them below the cocktails. That sounds minor and is not — plenty of bars charge full cocktail money for a drink with the expensive ingredient removed, and the resentment that causes is one of the most common complaints among people who do not drink. The list is named rather than improvised, with the Cyprus Cooler and The Afternoon in Monaco — strawberry, basil, lime and soda water — singled out by local guides, and non-alcoholic Heineken behind the bar for anyone who just wants a beer in hand.
signatureDrinks: The Afternoon in Monaco - strawberry, basil, lime, soda water
venues.longDescription:
Pinky's sits on Norfolk Street in Scott's Addition, in the middle of Richmond's densest concentration of breweries and bars, and it has built a reputation for being a good deal more thoughtful about non-drinkers than its neighbours.

The detail worth dwelling on is price. Pinky's prices its mocktails below its cocktails. It is a small operational decision with an outsized effect on how a non-drinker feels: the most frequently voiced grievance in the whole category is paying twelve or fourteen dollars for a drink whose most expensive component was deliberately left out. Charging less is an acknowledgement that the customer noticed, and it is rarer than it should be.

The drinks themselves are named menu items rather than dealer's choice. Local coverage picks out the Cyprus Cooler and The Afternoon in Monaco, the latter built from strawberry, basil, lime and soda water — a bright, herbaceous long drink rather than a sugary one, and the sort of thing that holds up across a whole evening rather than cloying after one glass. Non-alcoholic Heineken is stocked as well, which covers the other common case: someone who does not want a project, just a cold beer that happens to have no alcohol in it.

The practical shape of the place is worth knowing. It is closed Mondays and Tuesdays and runs 11am to 10pm the rest of the week, so it works for lunch and afternoons as much as evenings — useful in a district that is otherwise oriented entirely around taproom hours. For a group splitting between drinkers and non-drinkers in Scott's Addition, it is one of the easiest rooms in Richmond to suggest. The kitchen runs all afternoon rather than opening only for dinner, which matters in a district where most doors stay shut until four.
venues.pressQuote: Pinky's channels the spirit of the Mediterranean region, the menu relying heavily on the grill

venues.name: Pins Mechanical Co.
venues.description: Pins Mechanical Co. is a large South Congress games bar — duckpin bowling, pinball, patio — and its zero-proof list is specified with real ingredients rather than left as an afterthought, which is rare in the activity-bar category. Extra Credit is built on Lyre's Aperitif Rosso with Italian spritz, honey mango and rose water; Gym Class Zero pairs a non-alcoholic gin with desert pear and tonic. The venue matters for a specific reason: the whole proposition is the games rather than the drinking, so a group can spend a long evening here with no one's order standing out. Open late Friday and Saturday to 2am.
signatureDrinks: Extra Credit - Lyre's Aperitif Rosso, Italian spritz, honey mango, rose water
Gym Class Zero - non-alcoholic gin, desert pear, tonic
venues.longDescription:
Pins Mechanical Co. is a games bar on South Congress built around duckpin bowling, a wall of pinball machines, patio space and a long bar. The format is deliberately activity-first: people come to play, and the drinking happens around it. That structure is worth more to a non-drinker than most dedicated mocktail menus, because it removes the thing that makes bars hard when you are not drinking — the evening's entire purpose being the glass in your hand.

What lifts it from convenient to genuinely recommendable is that the zero-proof drinks are specified properly. Extra Credit is built on Lyre's Aperitif Rosso, a non-alcoholic aperitif designed to behave like a red bitter, then extended with Italian spritz, honey mango and rose water — a real spritz structure, bitter and aromatic rather than sweet. Gym Class Zero uses a non-alcoholic gin with desert pear and tonic, which is the closest thing on the list to a straightforward long drink and the easier order if you want something clean and dry. Both are named on Visit Austin's official zero-proof guide, and the use of a recognised NA brand rather than generic syrups is the tell that someone thought about the category.

The hours help. It runs to midnight most nights, and to 2am on Friday and Saturday, which puts it in the small group of Austin venues where an alcohol-free guest can stay out genuinely late without defaulting to a diner. Weekend evenings get busy and the bowling lanes are first-come in practice, so arriving early is sensible for a group.

One honest caveat: this is a full bar with a substantial alcohol trade, not an alcohol-free space. It suits someone who wants a good drink and a low-pressure room, rather than someone who needs a venue with no alcohol present at all.
venues.pressQuote: Pins Mechanical Co.: Extra Credit (Lyre's Aperitif Rosso, Italian Spritz, honey mango, rose water); Gym Class Zero (NA gin, desert pear, tonic).

venues.name: Pins Mechanical Co.
venues.description: Pins Mechanical Co. is a South End entertainment bar anchoring duckpin bowling, 40+ pinball machines, and classic arcade games in a lively, all-ages-friendly setting. The drinks menu includes two dedicated zero-proof cocktails — the Carmen Sandiego and Johnny Tsunami — both crafted with Lyre's non-alcoholic spirits, plus three NA beers (Athletic Run Wild IPA, BrewDog Elvis Juice AF, Sam Adams Just the Haze NA). A separate kids' mocktail section (Juice Box Hero, Lisa Simpson, Optimus Prime, Shorty Baller) rounds out the NA lineup, making it a genuinely sober-friendly destination for entertainment-seekers who want more than soda.
signatureDrinks: Carmen Sandiego (Lyre's Aperitif Rosso, Lyre's Italian Spritz, honey mango, rose water — 0.0% ABV) $11
Johnny Tsunami (Lyre's Dry London, lavender, blue razz — 0.0% ABV) $11
venues.longDescription:
Pins Mechanical Co. sits at 307 W Tremont Avenue in South End, part of a chain founded by Columbus-based Rise Brands, and it is built around things to do rather than things to drink: twelve duckpin bowling lanes, more than forty pinball machines at a dollar a play, and a free arcade whose quarter slots feed a donation to Ronald McDonald House Charities rather than the till. That framing matters for a non-drinker, because the reason to be here is not the bar. It welcomes guests of all ages until 8pm, becomes 21 and over after that Monday through Saturday with no exceptions, and has no age curfew at all on Sundays — so a family or an under-21 friend can genuinely use the place. Leashed dogs are welcome inside and on the patios outside peak hours. It opens at 4pm midweek and from late morning at weekends, running to 2.30am on Friday and Saturday, and takes no reservations except for duckpin lanes.

The zero-proof cocktails are a named section of the menu rather than an afterthought, and both are built on Lyre's rather than juice. Carmen Sandiego ($11) combines Lyre's Aperitif Rosso and Lyre's Italian Spritz with honey mango and rose water, printed on the menu at 0.0% ABV. Johnny Tsunami ($11) is Lyre's Dry London with lavender and blue razz, also marked 0.0%. Below them sits a broader Alcohol-Free Beverages section carrying non-alcoholic cans between $5 and $7, mocktails aimed at kids, and non-alcoholic slush puppies — which, in a room full of bowling lanes and pinball, is a more useful offering than another aperitivo. Worth knowing that this cocktail programme is standardised across Pins locations rather than developed in Charlotte, so the same two drinks appear in Columbus, Cincinnati and Nashville. That consistency is not a criticism here: it means the drinks are properly specified and reliably made, which is more than many one-off bar programmes manage.

venues.name: Pizza Lupo
venues.description: Pizza Lupo is a wood-fired Neapolitan pizzeria on Frankfort Avenue, opened in 2017 by the musicians Adam Turla and Sarah Balliet of Murder By Death with chef Max Balliet of Holy Molé. The drinks programme is natural wine, Italian amari and a full bar, and — unusually for a room that specific about its wine list — it prints a non-alcoholic menu described plainly as being for designated drivers. The Chinotto Dream is the build regulars name, running on chinotto, the bitter Italian citrus soda that is the closest thing in the soft-drink world to an aperitivo. Service is nightly from 5pm.
signatureDrinks: Chinotto Dream (chinotto bitter citrus soda build)
venues.longDescription:
Pizza Lupo opened in 2017 in Butchertown, at the point where Frankfort Avenue begins, and its ownership tells you most of what the room is like: Adam Turla and Sarah Balliet, who play in the band Murder By Death, with Sarah's brother Max Balliet — of the well-liked Holy Molé — running the kitchen. The pizza is wood-fired Neapolitan, the wine list is natural and low-intervention, and the back bar leans hard into Italian amari.

A restaurant that serious about bitter Italian liqueur could be a difficult evening for someone not drinking, and Pizza Lupo has handled it with unusual plainness: there is a printed non-alcoholic menu, and it is described as being for designated drivers rather than dressed up as a wellness offering. That framing is worth something. It signals that not drinking is treated as an ordinary thing a customer might be doing on an ordinary Tuesday, which is closer to how most non-drinkers actually experience it than the language of mindfulness usually gets. The Chinotto Dream is the drink to order: chinotto is the bitter myrtle-leaved orange soda that Italians have drunk for a century, and it is the one mainstream soft drink with genuine bitterness, which makes it the natural spine for an alcohol-free aperitivo in a room built on amari.

Practically, the kitchen runs nightly from 5pm to 10pm, and the restaurant takes reservations through Resy — worth having at weekends, as the room is small and popular. Butchertown puts Copper & Kings' rooftop and its named alcohol-free list a few minutes away, and Volare and Fork & Barrel are further out the same avenue in Clifton, so this end of town is the easiest part of Louisville in which to assemble an evening without alcohol in it.
venues.pressQuote: The restaurant has a non-alcoholic menu for designated drivers, with the Chinotto Dream being a recommended option.

venues.name: PKL Social
venues.description: Pickleball-and-golf-sim sports bar and beer garden on Shepherd Drive in Houston's Washington Avenue/Heights corridor, merged with sister concept FM Kitchen & Bar in July 2025, pouring a modest but real non-alcoholic lineup that includes Athletic Brewing NA beer and a house cherry limeade.
venues.longDescription:
PKL Social is a pickleball-driven sports bar, restaurant, and beer garden at 1112 Shepherd Drive, in the Washington Avenue Corridor on the edge of Houston's Heights neighborhood. It opened Thursday, March 21, 2024, next door to sister restaurant FM Kitchen & Bar (operating since 2017), under operating partner Jason Mok, with four pickleball courts, a covered dog-friendly patio, and 20-plus TVs.

On July 26, 2025, PKL Social officially absorbed FM Kitchen & Bar, retiring the FM Kitchen name and folding both spaces into a single brand, menu, and staff. The expansion added two Full Swing golf simulators next to the pickleball courts, two 140-inch LED video walls, and brought the property to 25-plus screens spread across an ice-house-style bar area, the court-side bar, and a large outdoor patio.

The bar's non-alcoholic options are real but modest for a venue this size: Athletic Brewing non-alcoholic craft beer is on the drink list alongside conventional beer, wine, and cocktails (including LALO tequila), and the non-alcoholic side of the menu also runs to a frozen strawberry lemonade, the house PKL Cherry Limeade, oat-milk lattes, craft mocktails, and prebiotic sodas. It is not a dedicated zero-proof cocktail program with a printed mocktail menu -- it's a standard sports-bar list with a handful of legitimate non-drinker options alongside frozen margaritas and bucket beers.

The restaurant and beer garden are open to all ages; the pickleball courts and golf-simulator bays are restricted to guests 21 and over.
venues.pressQuote: Pickleball has seen an incredible surge in popularity over the past few years, and we're thrilled to bring this dynamic and accessible sport to Houstonians in our own vibrant and social way.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Jason Mok, PKL Social operating partner

venues.name: Planet of the Tapes
venues.description: Planet of the Tapes is a comedy club, bar and video-store-themed hangout on Barret Avenue in Phoenix Hill, and it has the most non-drinker-friendly pricing policy in Louisville: any of its movie-inspired cocktails can be made as a mocktail for $5, a flat price well under the alcoholic version rather than the usual practice of charging cocktail money for juice. It also makes its own sodas in house — mango pineapple, raspberry pomegranate and lavender lemon — and names drinks with the same cheerful nonsense as the rest of the room, including the Shirley Temple of Doom and The Mangolorian. Shows and open mics run most nights until midnight, or 2am at weekends.
venues.longDescription:
Planet of the Tapes takes its name and its whole aesthetic from the video rental store, and operates as a comedy club, live venue and bar on Barret Avenue in Phoenix Hill, on the edge of the Highlands. The cocktails are named after films, the walls are stacked with tapes, and the calendar runs stand-up, open mics, showcases and touring comics most nights of the week.

It belongs in this guide for two reasons that have nothing to do with mixology fashion. The first is the policy: any cocktail on the menu can be made as a mocktail for a flat $5. That is unusual and it is worth being explicit about why it matters. The standard practice at bars with good zero-proof programmes — including several elsewhere in this guide — is to price alcohol-free drinks in line with the cocktails, on the argument that the labour and the components cost the same. That is defensible, but it also means a non-drinker pays $14 for a drink with no alcohol in it, every round, all night. Planet of the Tapes goes the other way, and over an evening the difference is real money. The second reason is the house sodas — mango pineapple, raspberry pomegranate, lavender lemon — made in-house rather than poured from a gun, which is what stops the $5 drink from being a compromise. Named builds include the Shirley Temple of Doom and The Mangolorian.

The comedy programming is the third thing, and structurally the most useful: an evening built around a stage is an evening not built around a bar, which is most of what makes a night out workable for someone who is not drinking. Hours run to midnight Monday through Thursday and 2am Friday through Sunday, opening at 4pm daily. Check the calendar when booking, since ticketed shows change the room's rhythm. Epiphany is a few minutes away in the Original Highlands.
venues.pressQuote: In addition to offering any of its movie-inspired cocktails as mocktails for $5, this comedy club and bar also house-makes a variety of sodas, including mango pineapple, raspberry pomegranate, and lavender lemon flavors.

venues.name: Plant Bar
venues.description: Plant Bar is a specialty coffee, tea and zero-proof bar on Manufacturers Road on the North Shore, the Chattanooga half of a two-city operation that also runs in Asheville. It serves artisanal coffee, traditional Chinese and herbal teas, boba, cacao and a zero-proof cocktail list, with locally made pastries alongside, and it describes itself plainly as a non-alcoholic venue rather than a café that happens to lack a licence. Oat, almond, coconut, soy and whole milk are all included at no extra charge, and decaf espresso is offered on every drink. It is open from 8am to 10pm most days and to 11pm Thursday through Saturday.
venues.address: 202 Manufacturers Rd Ste B, Chattanooga, TN 37405
signatureDrinks: Hydration Mertini (NA: aloe, lime, juniper, rosemary, may chang, chlorophyll, sea salt, clean and restorative.)
Relaxation Mergarita (NA: acv, honey, oat straw, nettles, lemon balm, lemongrass, lime, settle in.)
Circulation Mermosa (NA: acv, honey, orange peel, turmeric, ginger, mimosa, cinnamon, wake the body up.)
Dreamy Blue Lotus Cacao (NA: a hot cacao nightcap with blue lotus and rose, made for slowing down.)

venues.longDescription:
The problem this directory keeps running into in small metros is that alcohol-free venues open at seven in the morning and close at three in the afternoon, which is exactly the wrong shape. Plant Bar solves it: 8am to 10pm most days, 11pm from Thursday to Saturday, seven days a week. Fifteen hours a day, with no alcohol on the premises.

The Chattanooga room is on Manufacturers Road on the North Shore, and it is one half of a two-city operation that also runs in Asheville. The offer is deliberately broad — artisanal coffee, traditional Chinese teas and herbal blends, boba, drinking cacao, and a zero-proof cocktail list — so it works as a morning coffee stop, an afternoon work spot and an evening drink in the same room, which is precisely the flexibility a non-drinker's week actually requires.

The detail that separates it from a good café is the zero-proof cocktails, which are built rather than poured, and the seriousness of the tea programme underneath them. On the milk side the policy is unusually generous: oat, almond, coconut, soy and whole milk are all included at no upcharge, and decaf espresso is available on any drink — small things that add up if you are the person in the group with dietary constraints as well as no glass of wine.

Two practical notes worth carrying. The Chattanooga location shares its building with Asheville Dispensary, and as of 1 July 2026 the entire space operates as 21-and-over, so this is no longer a venue you can bring children to — a change worth knowing if you are planning around a family. And while nothing on the menu contains alcohol, the shared building means cannabis products are sold on site; readers avoiding those should factor that in.

The food is a short list of locally made pastries and bagels, with vegan options throughout.

venues.name: Planter's House
venues.description: A 2019 James Beard Award semifinalist for Outstanding Bar Program, Planter's House has anchored Lafayette Square's cocktail scene since 2013 under proprietor and beverage director Ted Kilgore. The menu carries a dedicated Spirit Free Cocktails section — six $10 drinks built with the same rigor as the house classics, using Feragaia free spirit, Dhos zero-proof gin and tequila, Giffard NA Spritz and Nozeco alcohol-free sparkling rosé. Standouts include Not a Pickle, Bell Tolls, Mace of Spades and Under The Grapefruit Moon. St. Louis Magazine calls it a St. Louis institution that 'makes mocktails with equal skill and finesse.'
