venues.longDescription:
East Johnson Street runs through Tenney-Lapham, a residential near-east neighbourhood that has quietly become one of Madison's better places to eat and drink, and Public Parking opened there in October 2024. Within a year it had a Bon Appétit Best New Bars listing for 2025 and a James Beard Best New Bar semifinalist nod for 2026, which for a bar in a city of a quarter of a million people is a substantial thing. The style is playful and precise at once: cocktail names that run to a full sentence, garnishes built rather than dropped in, glassware chosen for the joke, and drinks served in glasses chilled with nitrogen so they arrive genuinely cold.

For a non-drinker, a bar with that much critical attention is often the worst kind of room — the whole point is the spirits, and the alcohol-free option is a bought-in soda. Public Parking does not do that. Its standing zero-proof drink carries a name as long as anything on the main list — "I'm Just a Baby . . . I Can Pay You In Blocks" — and is built from smoked tea, lemon, ginger and bubbles, which is a genuinely bar-shaped construction: the smoke does the work an aged spirit would, the lemon and ginger supply acid and heat, and the carbonation gives it length. Naming it in the same register as the cocktails is not a small signal; it means the drink came out of the same development process rather than being added under protest.

Practicalities: it is open every day of the week from 4pm to 2am, which is the most generous schedule of any bar in this guide and useful when most of Madison's better zero-proof lists sit in restaurants that stop serving at nine or ten. It is small, and busy at weekends given the press attention, so early evening is the easier visit. Teasider's tea shop is a few doors along East Johnson, and Mint Mark is about a mile north-east on East Washington. There is a broader point here about how Madison's alcohol-free depth is distributed, and Public Parking illustrates it. The city has no dedicated sober bar, but it has an unusual concentration of ambitious bartenders working in small rooms — a Bon Appétit-listed cocktail bar on a residential street, a coffee-and-cocktail lounge using lapsang souchong for smoke, a golf simulator venue carrying eighteen zero-proof cocktails. What that produces is a scene where the quality of the alcohol-free drink is high but you are always drinking it in a bar. For a lot of people that is the ideal arrangement, and for some it is unworkable, and the honest version of a Madison guide has to say both.
venues.pressQuote: Bon Appétit magazine included the cocktail spot on its 2025 list of Best New Bars in the U.S.

venues.name: Public Records
venues.description: Public Records is a plant-based restaurant, cocktail bar, and hi-fi music venue in Gowanus, Brooklyn, opened in April 2019 by musician Francis Harris, designer Shane Davis, and hospitality director Erik VanderWal. It occupies a 1910s building that served as the ASPCA's Brooklyn headquarters for decades, and the all-vegan kitchen nods to that history. The campus spans several spaces, including The Atrium restaurant-lounge, where the bar program runs alongside an extensive cocktail list. The Atrium menu carries a dedicated "Zero-Proof" section of fully built spirit-free cocktails rather than an afterthought mocktail or two. Current named options include the Palomar (NA mezcal, elderflower cordial, spiced grapefruit shrub, lemon balm, soda), Not For Rita (NA agave spirit, spiced grapefruit shrub, lime, agave, damiana), and Press For Time (coffee, cinnamon-lapsang-sorghum syrup, vanilla-coconut cream whip, reishi, orange), plus housemade sodas.
venues.hours: Mon-Tue closed; Wed-Thu 6pm-10pm; Fri 6pm-4am; Sat 10am-4am; Sun 10am-9pm
venues.longDescription:
Public Records is a plant-based restaurant, cocktail bar and hi-fi music venue in Gowanus, Brooklyn, opened in April 2019 by musician Francis Harris, designer Shane Davis and hospitality director Erik VanderWal. It occupies a 1910s building that served for decades as the ASPCA's Brooklyn headquarters — a history the all-vegan kitchen nods to directly. The campus spans several distinct spaces, including The Atrium, a restaurant and lounge where the bar programme runs, and a sound room built around an audiophile system that has made it one of the more serious listening venues in New York.

The Atrium menu carries a dedicated Zero-Proof section of fully constructed spirit-free cocktails rather than the token pair most music venues manage, and the builds are genuinely complex. The Palomar combines a non-alcoholic mezcal with elderflower cordial, a spiced grapefruit shrub, lemon balm and soda — the shrub supplying the acidity and length that a paloma needs and that fruit juice alone cannot give it. Not For Rita works a non-alcoholic agave spirit against the same spiced grapefruit shrub with lime, agave and damiana, the Mexican herb traditionally used as a relaxant. Press For Time is the outlier and the most ambitious: coffee with a cinnamon-lapsang-sorghum syrup, a vanilla-coconut cream whip, reishi mushroom and orange, which is closer to a dessert course than a drink. House-made sodas fill out the list.

The combination is unusually complete for a non-drinker: an entirely vegan kitchen, a proper zero-proof cocktail list, and a hi-fi room where the point of the evening is listening rather than drinking. It runs late — to 4am on Friday and Saturday — with weekend daytime service too, and is closed Mondays and Tuesdays. The listening room is the reason to plan an evening here rather than drop in: when the point of the night is the sound system, nobody is counting what is in anyone else's glass, which is exactly what makes it comfortable.

venues.name: Pufferfish
venues.description: Pufferfish is a rooftop tiki bar perched on the sixth floor of Hotel Metro in downtown Milwaukee's East Town, pairing skyline views with a playful, island-inspired cocktail program. Its menu carries a dedicated "Spiritless Cocktails" section — a standing, named list of zero-proof tiki drinks built on Lyre's non-alcoholic spirits and served in full tiki style. Alongside an alcohol-free take on the signature PufferFish, the list includes spiritless versions of the Mai-Tai, Rum Collins, Snaquiri and Old Fashioned. The bar was named a Top 10 regional nominee for Best U.S. Hotel Bar in the 2026 Spirited Awards.
venues.longDescription:
Pufferfish is Milwaukee's only rooftop tiki bar, occupying the sixth-floor terrace atop Hotel Metro at 411 E. Mason St. in downtown's East Town. The concept began as a pandemic-era pop-up tied to the cocktail bar Lost Whale, moved through a series of pop-ups around the city, and settled permanently on the Hotel Metro rooftop in 2023. The result is a laid-back, tropical counterpoint to the hotel's art-moderne building — craft tiki drinks, a compact food menu developed with the hotel kitchen, and open-air views over the city.

The reason it belongs in a non-alcoholic guide is a genuine, standing "Spiritless Cocktails" section rather than a one-off mocktail. The zero-proof list is built primarily on Lyre's non-alcoholic spirits and given the same tiki treatment as the full-strength menu: an alcohol-free version of the house PufferFish (Lyre's London Dry, lemon, BG Reynolds falernum, passionfruit, Giffard orgeat, house Pufferfish bitters and Liquid Death sparkling), plus spiritless builds of the Mai-Tai, Rum Collins, Snaquiri and Old Fashioned using Lyre's Cane, Spiced, White, Orange Sec and American Malt. Because Pufferfish is a full bar that also serves alcohol, it is a hybrid rather than an all-NA venue, but the spiritless drinks are treated as first-class cocktails, matched glass-for-glass with the leaded menu.

The bar's craft credentials are well established: in 2026 Pufferfish was named a Top 10 regional nominee in the U.S. Central category for Best U.S. Hotel Bar in the Tales of the Cocktail Foundation's Spirited Awards, with winners set to be announced at the ceremony on July 23, 2026 — only the second time a Milwaukee bar has earned that recognition. It is a seasonal rooftop, generally open Wednesday through Saturday evenings, with holiday "Sippin' Santa" programming extending the calendar into winter.

venues.name: Punch Room at The London EDITION
venues.description: Punch Room is the celebrated cocktail parlour hidden behind the lobby of The London EDITION, a landmark Ian Schrager hotel on Berners Street in Fitzrovia, and one of the city's cosiest cocktail dens. Its 2025 'Recipe Book' menu — published as a genuine take-home recipe book — sets three no-booze punches alongside fifteen spirited ones, and the bar has highlighted its alcohol-free serves as strong sellers. All three zero-proof drinks are built on Everleaf, the British non-alcoholic aperitif, and are made sustainably from the same ingredients as the spirited cocktails earlier in the menu.
signatureDrinks: Back to My Roots (non-alcoholic) — Everleaf Forest, cardamom syrup, caramel syrup, lemon juice and carrot syrup, finished with caramel air and grated cinnamon
Southern Light (non-alcoholic) — Everleaf Marine, red shiso tea, grapefruit-and-kumquat sherbet and lime juice, topped with Crodino and a shiso leaf
Impostor (non-alcoholic) — Everleaf Mountain, ginger syrup, demerara syrup and lime juice, topped with Franklin & Sons rhubarb and hibiscus tonic
venues.longDescription:
The Punch Room sits at the rear of The London EDITION, the landmark Ian Schrager and Marriott hotel at 10 Berners Street in Fitzrovia. Guests reach it through the hotel's vaulted marble lobby, past a neon sculpture and a wood-panelled door, into an intimate room clad head-to-toe in fumed-oak panelling with teal velvet banquettes, mismatched brown and green leather armchairs and a soundtrack of throwback jazz, reggae and motown. Modelled on the members' rooms of nineteenth-century London private clubs, the concept is devoted to punch, the classic sharing serve, and the bar is listed on The World's 50 Best Bars' Discovery guide as one of the cosiest cocktail dens in the city.

The bar is run by Bars Manager Anthony Callegari, with Gates Otsuji as EDITION's Director of Bars steering the wider Punch Room concept now spread across cities including Tokyo, Barcelona and Madrid. Its signature Milk Punch blends Hennessy fine de cognac, Havana Club 3yo rum, Somerset cider, brandy, green tea, lemon juice, pineapple, spice syrup and milk. In April 2025 the venue turned its menu into a physical take-home recipe book, sold for around £30, which lays out each drink's exact measurements, method, ice, garnish and glassware — fifteen alcoholic punches and three with no booze.

The alcohol-free program is genuine rather than an afterthought: all three no-booze punches are built on Everleaf, the British non-alcoholic aperitif (probably the biggest independent NA brand a guest could source at home), and were designed to be as sustainable as possible, drawing their ingredients from the spirited cocktails printed earlier in the book. Back to My Roots pairs Everleaf Forest with cardamom and caramel syrups, lemon juice and house carrot syrup, finished with caramel air and grated cinnamon; Southern Light mixes Everleaf Marine with red shiso tea, a grapefruit-and-kumquat sherbet and lime, topped with Crodino; and Impostor stirs Everleaf Mountain with ginger and demerara syrups and lime, lengthened with Franklin & Sons rhubarb and hibiscus tonic. Each is priced at £14, the same care and glassware as the alcoholic list, and the team has pointed to the alcohol-free serves as some of the room's strongest sellers.
venues.pressQuote: Sat within The London Edition hotel in the heart of Fitzrovia, this smart joint is one of the cosiest cocktail dens in London.

venues.name: Pure Project
venues.description: Pure Project is a sustainability-focused San Diego craft brewery founded in 2015, best known for its ingredient-driven, hazy IPAs. Its North Park taproom on El Cajon Boulevard pours 20 taps in a tucked-away courtyard with URBN Pizza handling food. In April 2026 the brewery expanded into non-alcoholic beer, brewing two house NA options now poured year-round at all five of its taprooms: Grounded, an NA IPA built on Citra and Mosaic hops with lemongrass, citrus, and resin notes; and Sunsip, an NA blonde ale with flavors of fresh-baked bread, jasmine, and lemon peel — both below 0.5% ABV. The NA beers are made in-house under the same ingredient-focused ethos as the brewery's alcoholic lineup, giving sober and sober-curious drinkers a genuine craft option.

venues.longDescription:
Pure Project is a sustainability-focused San Diego craft brewery founded in 2015, best known for ingredient-driven hazy IPAs and for taking its environmental commitments considerably further than the industry norm. The North Park taproom on El Cajon Boulevard pours twenty taps in a tucked-away courtyard, with URBN Pizza handling the food, and it is one of five Pure Project taprooms around the county.

The reason it appears here is recent: in April 2026 the brewery moved into non-alcoholic beer, and now pours two house-brewed NA options year-round at all five taprooms. Grounded is an NA IPA built on Citra and Mosaic hops with lemongrass, citrus and resin notes; Sunsip is an NA blonde ale running to fresh-baked bread, jasmine and lemon peel. Both sit below 0.5% ABV and both are made in-house under the same ingredient-focused ethos as the alcoholic range, rather than being contract-brewed or bought in — which is the distinction that separates a brewery that has thought about this from one that has stocked a fridge. Co-founder Winslow Sawyer framed the move as wanting to "share our brewing ethos with the world of NA beer, while embracing the quality and standards at the core of our craft." A blonde ale is a notably sensible second choice alongside the IPA: it covers the drinker who wants something light and sessionable rather than aggressively hopped, and that person is badly served by a non-alcoholic beer market that has bet almost everything on IPAs. Between the two, a non-drinker at a table of craft beer enthusiasts has a real choice rather than a single default. Open daily, from late morning at weekends. Because both non-alcoholic beers pour year-round across all five Pure Project taprooms rather than only here, the same options are available at its other locations — useful if North Park is not the convenient one for your group.
venues.pressQuote: We've been eager to share our brewing ethos with the world of NA beer, while embracing the quality and standards at the core of our craft.

venues.name: Pusadee's Garden
venues.description: Pusadee's Garden is a family-owned Thai restaurant on Butler Street in Upper Lawrenceville, named for Pusadee Tongdee and run by her daughters Watcharee and Bootsaba Tongdee with Michael Johnson. It closed in 2017 and reopened in January 2021 after a four-year ground-up rebuild by mossArchitects that won a Design Pittsburgh Honor Award — two renovated buildings joined by an entry arcade, a glass-box bar and an open kitchen with traditional Thai tao charcoal stoves, around a courtyard garden visible from most of the dining rooms. Chef Bootsaba "Gik" Tongdee was named a James Beard semifinalist for Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic in 2024. Its bar menu has a section headed "Spirit-Free/Non-Alcoholic" holding Give it a Chai ($8, chai, ginger, lemon), the house seltzer ($6, Thai basil, pink peppercorn, strawberry) and AL's Classic Lager, a non-alcoholic lager under 0.5% ABV ($7). The Pathfinder non-alcoholic amaro ($10) is also poured but is filed with the amari rather than in the spirit-free block, so ask for it by name. Reservations are Resy-only, tables cap at six, and there are no highchairs or boosters.

venues.longDescription:
Pusadee's Garden is a family restaurant on Butler Street in Upper Lawrenceville, named for Pusadee Tongdee, who still works in the kitchen, and run by her daughters Watcharee and Bootsaba Tongdee with Michael Johnson. It closed in 2017 and reopened in January 2021 after a four-year ground-up rebuild by mossArchitects, and the result is one of the few restaurants in the city that is genuinely worth visiting as architecture. The Design Pittsburgh jury that gave it an Honor Award in 2021 wrote that each space builds on the other as a cinematic experience — that this is architecture, and also an urban intervention, creating a highly inviting in-between zone. Two renovated buildings are joined by an entry arcade, a glass-box bar and an open kitchen with tao stoves, the traditional Thai charcoal burners, and a modernist courtyard garden is visible from most of the dining rooms. Chef Bootsaba "Gik" Tongdee, who learned to cook by osmosis as a child around her mother's market stall in the province of Tak, was named a James Beard semifinalist for Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic in 2024 — semifinalist, not finalist. Khao soi with wagyu beef cheek is $48, massaman lamb shank $48, pork belly hung lay $29.

The drinks list has a section headed Spirit-Free/Non-Alcoholic and it is short, cheap and well matched to the food. Give it a Chai is $8 — chai, ginger and lemon — and it is the one the press keeps recommending, rightly: spiced tea with ginger heat is one of the few non-alcoholic things that can stand up to a red curry without being flattened by it. The house seltzer at $6 runs Thai basil, pink peppercorn and strawberry, and Thai basil is the correct herb here in a way mint would not be — it is anise-scented and it echoes what is already on the plate. AL's Classic Lager is the non-alcoholic beer at $7, under 0.5% ABV. One thing the section heading hides: The Pathfinder non-alcoholic amaro is also poured, at $10, but it is filed with the amari and aperitifs rather than in the spirit-free block, so ask for it by name. Practical notes worth knowing before booking — reservations are Resy only, opening thirty days ahead at 7am, tables cap at six, there are no highchairs or boosters, and pets are not allowed on the patio.
venues.pressQuote: Enjoy beautiful outdoor garden seating with one of this Thai restaurant's spirit-free cocktails. We recommend starting your meal with Give it a Chai, an alcoholic-free beverage containing chai, ginger, and lemon.

venues.name: Pushing Daisies
venues.description: Pushing Daisies is a subterranean agave bar beneath Fifth + Broadway in downtown Nashville, opened in November 2022 by restaurateur Sam Fox as his first bar concept. It is a licensed cocktail bar built around margaritas, tequila and mezcal, and it carries a standing zero-proof section on its printed menu headed Nada Guey: the Paloma Refresco with ruby grapefruit, lava salt, fresh lime and fizzy water; La Playa with fluffy pineapple, toasted cinnamon, pomegranate and chia seeds; and the Fresa Loca with fresh strawberry, mandarin orange and citrus tonic, each $9. The room is a low-lit lounge with a hidden entrance across from Bridgestone Arena, floral wall murals and a daisy-tiled floor, and it stays open to 2am on Thursday, Friday and Saturday.
venues.hours: Mon-Tue closed; Wed 5pm-12am; Thu 5pm-2am; Fri-Sat 12pm-2am; Sun 12pm-12am
signatureDrinks: Paloma Refresco - ruby grapefruit, lava salt, fresh lime, fizzy water $9
La Playa - fluffy pineapple, toasted cinnamon, pomegranate, drunken chia seeds $9
Fresa Loca - fresh strawberry, mandarin orange, citrus tonic $9
venues.longDescription:
Pushing Daisies opened on 17 November 2022 in the basement level of the Fifth + Broadway development, and it was the first bar concept from Sam Fox, the Arizona restaurateur behind Fox Restaurant Concepts and more than a hundred restaurants before it. The Nashville Scene's Chris Chamberlain covered the opening and described it as a luxury lounge with a slightly hidden entrance across the street from Bridgestone Arena, a speakeasy check-in at the door, sleek wall coverings and murals inside, and industrial conduit overhead that the fire marshal made the staff paint red. The floor is daisy-patterned penny tile. It matters for this directory that the room reads as a proper bar rather than a restaurant with a bar attached, because that is what people are usually looking for when they want a night out without drinking.

The main list is agave: more than forty margarita variations plus tequila and mezcal cocktails, and drinks that arrive garnished with tweezers and occasionally with fire. Alcohol is very much served here. What earns it a place is the standing zero-proof section, printed on the same menu under the heading Nada Guey. There are three, all $9: the Paloma Refresco, built with ruby grapefruit, lava salt, fresh lime and fizzy water; La Playa, with fluffy pineapple, toasted cinnamon, pomegranate and what the menu calls drunken chia seeds; and the Fresa Loca, with fresh strawberry, mandarin orange and citrus tonic. They are made by the same bar team as everything else and priced in line with the rest of the room rather than as an afterthought.

Practical notes. The bar is closed Monday and Tuesday, opens at 5pm midweek and noon at weekends, and runs to 2am Thursday through Saturday - which makes it one of the few downtown rooms with a named alcohol-free option available late. It is directly under the Broadway honky-tonk strip and across from Bridgestone, so expect it to be busy on event nights, and the entrance is genuinely easy to walk past.
venues.pressQuote: a luxury lounge with a slightly hidden entrance across the street from Bridgestone Arena

venues.name: Qahwah House
venues.description: Qahwah House is a fully alcohol-free Yemeni coffeehouse — there's no bar and never has been. The East Dearborn flagship at 6655 Schaefer Rd pours traditional preparations like Mofawar (cardamom-and-cream coffee), Rada'ey (ginger-cardamom light roast), Qishr (cascara with ginger and cinnamon), and Adeni Chai (black tea, cardamom, nutmeg, milk), made from beans sourced directly from founder Ibrahim Alhasbani's family farms in Yemen. It's the original location behind what's now a 30-plus-store chain, and the reason East Dearborn is a genuine destination for Yemeni coffee culture rather than just another espresso stop.
signatureDrinks: Adeni Chai (Yemeni black tea, cardamom, nutmeg, milk)
venues.longDescription:
Ibrahim Alhasbani grew up around coffee — his family has farmed it in the mountains outside Sana'a, Yemen, for eight generations. He immigrated to the U.S. in 2011, first to New York, then relocated to Michigan after marrying a woman from the Dearborn area. Missing the coffee he grew up on, he opened a small shop on Schaefer Road in East Dearborn with a soft opening in late 2017 and a formal grand opening in January 2018. "I did something different and unique in that I use only Yemeni coffee beans," he later said of the decision to build the entire menu around his home country's coffee tradition rather than standard espresso-bar drinks.

The East Dearborn location's menu is still built entirely around that idea. Instead of a standard coffee/espresso split, the board runs through named Yemeni preparations: Sana'ani (medium roast with cardamom), Jubani (coffee and coffee husks with cardamom, ginger, and cinnamon), Mofawar (medium roast with cardamom and cream), Rada'ey (light roast with ginger and cardamom), and Qishr, made from cascara — the dried coffee-cherry husk, not the bean — steeped with ginger and cinnamon. Tea drinkers get Adeni Chai (Yemeni black tea, cardamom, nutmeg, and milk) and a spiced Yemeni Tea (black tea, cardamom, cinnamon, and cloves), alongside a house Yemeni Latte, Turkish-style dark roast, and standard espresso drinks. The beans themselves are imported directly from Alhasbani's family farms and roasted in-house — no alcohol is served or has ever been on the menu.

What started as one shop on Schaefer Road has since grown into a chain of more than 30 locations across the U.S., but Dearborn remains home base, and the East Dearborn store is the original. The location sits in the heart of the country's largest Arab American community, on the same Schaefer Road corridor as the neighborhood's Yemeni and Lebanese restaurants and bakeries — a fitting home for a coffeehouse built specifically to bring Yemeni qahwa culture to an American audience.
venues.pressQuote: I did something different and unique in that I use only Yemeni coffee beans.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Ibrahim Alhasbani, founder of Qahwah House

venues.name: Qahwah House
venues.description: Qahwah House is a Yemeni coffeehouse on Central Avenue NE in Windom Park, the Minnesota outpost of a chain founded in Dearborn, Michigan in 2017. It serves no alcohol at all and stays open until midnight seven nights a week, which makes it an evening room rather than a morning coffee stop. Coffee is imported directly from Yemen and roasted on the premises. The menu keeps a full Yemeni Style Coffee and Tea section alongside the espresso bar: Sana'ani, Jubani, Mofawar, Rada'ey and Qishr are all listed by their regional names, and the Adeni Chai is built on Yemeni black tea with cardamom, nutmeg and milk. Sabayah and other Yemeni pastries are sold at the counter.
signatureDrinks: Jubani (medium and light roast coffee with coffee husks, cardamom, ginger and cinnamon)
Mofawar (medium roast coffee with cardamom and cream)
Qishr (coffee husks with ginger and cinnamon)
Rada'ey (light roast coffee with ginger and cardamom)
Adeni Chai (Yemeni black tea, cardamom, nutmeg, milk)
venues.longDescription:
Qahwah House began in Dearborn, Michigan in 2017, in the first Arab-majority city in the United States, and has since grown into a national chain built around a single idea: that Yemeni coffee, grown on terraces above Sana'a and traded through the port of Mokha for centuries, deserves to be served on its own terms rather than folded into an American espresso menu. The Minneapolis shop opened the week of April 28, 2025 at 1851 Central Avenue NE, taking a Central Avenue storefront in Windom Park in a stretch of Northeast where the after-dark options had been almost entirely bars. Beans arrive from Yemen and are roasted in the shop; the walls carry photographs of the Yemeni countryside, brass coffee pots and material on Sana'a's role in the coffee trade. Staff member Sue Wazwaz told the Northeaster in May 2025 that the coffee "comes straight from Yemen" and is roasted on site, and that the shop is "known for Yemeni coffee and tea. A lot of cardamom, ginger and nutmeg."

The drink list is where the specificity sits. The Yemeni Style Coffee and Tea section runs Sana'ani, a medium roast with cardamom; Jubani, a blend of medium and light roast with coffee husks, cardamom, ginger and cinnamon; Mofawar, a medium roast served with cardamom and cream; Rada'ey, a light roast with ginger and cardamom; and Qishr, the cascara drink brewed from coffee husks with ginger and cinnamon. Adeni Chai pairs Yemeni black tea with cardamom, nutmeg and milk, and a separate Yemeni Tea is spiced with cardamom, cinnamon and cloves. A ginger milk and a Turkish dark roast with cardamom fill out the traditional column, and a conventional espresso bar of lattes, americanos and cold brews sits alongside for anyone who wants it. Nothing on the menu contains alcohol and there is no bar programme of any kind. The midnight close every night of the week is the point: this is a room built for sitting for hours, and it gives Northeast Minneapolis a late option that is not a taproom. For a visitor who has not been to a Yemeni coffeehouse before, the useful orientation is that these are not espresso bars with a novelty column: the traditional drinks are the reason the room exists, they are brewed rather than pulled, and they are meant to be sat with rather than carried out. Beans are also sold by the bag at the counter.
venues.pressQuote: (The coffee) comes straight from Yemen.

venues.name: Qahwah House
venues.description: Qahwah House is a Yemeni coffeehouse on Brookpark Road in North Olmsted, the Cleveland-area cafe of a family business founded in 2017 by Ibrahim Alhasbani, whose family has grown coffee in the highlands of Yemen for eight generations. It serves no alcohol and stays open until 11pm every night, which makes it an evening room as much as a morning coffee stop. The menu keeps a full Yemeni Style Coffee and Tea section beside the espresso bar: Sana'ani, Jubani, Mofawar, Rada'ey and Qishr are all listed by their regional names, and the Adeni Chai is built on Yemeni black tea with cardamom, nutmeg and milk. Pastries, light bites and bags of the company's own roast are sold at the counter.
signatureDrinks: Jubani (medium and light roast coffee with coffee husks, cardamom, ginger and cinnamon)
Mofawar (medium roast coffee with cardamom and cream)
Qishr (coffee husks with ginger and cinnamon)
Rada'ey (light roast coffee with ginger and cardamom)
Adeni Chai (Yemeni black tea, cardamom, nutmeg, milk)
venues.longDescription:
Qahwah House describes itself as a family business founded in 2017 with the aim of sharing Yemeni coffee culture, and its founder, Ibrahim Alhasbani, comes from a family that has farmed coffee in the Yemeni highlands for eight generations. The company is run from Dearborn, Michigan and says it now has more than thirty cafes across the United States. The Cleveland-area one is in a shopping centre at 25102 Brookpark Road in North Olmsted, about twelve miles south-west of Public Square. In the company's own words, each cafe is designed to recreate the warmth and hospitality of a traditional Yemeni coffee house, with beans sourced directly from Yemen's highland farms.

The section of the menu headed Yemeni Style Coffee and Tea is the reason to come. Sana'ani is a medium roast with cardamom. Jubani mixes medium and light roast coffee with coffee husks, cardamom, ginger and cinnamon. Mofawar is medium roast served with cardamom and cream, and Rada'ey is a light roast with ginger and cardamom. Qishr is made from the husks of the coffee cherry rather than the bean, brewed with ginger and cinnamon, and drinks more like a spiced tea than a coffee. Adeni Chai is Yemeni black tea with cardamom, nutmeg and milk, and a plain Yemeni Tea comes with cardamom, cinnamon and cloves. A conventional espresso bar, iced drinks, refreshers and organic teas sit alongside, and the counter sells pastries, light bites and retail bags of the house roast.

No alcohol is served. The company's page for this cafe gives hours of 8am to 11pm, and other listings show it opening an hour earlier on weekdays and running to midnight on Friday and Saturday, so check before a very early or very late visit. Ordering is at the counter for dine-in or takeout. It is one of three Yemeni coffeehouses within about a mile and a quarter of each other in North Olmsted — Baladi Coffee House is on Lorain Road and Shibam Coffee on Brookpark Extension — which gives the west side of the metro a late-evening option with no bar attached, alongside the kava bars of Lakewood and Ohio City.
venues.pressQuote: Each cafe is designed to recreate the warmth and hospitality of a traditional Yemeni coffee house
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: Qahwah House, North Olmsted location page

venues.name: Qamaria Yemeni Coffee Co.
venues.description: The Blaine branch of Qamaria Yemeni Coffee Co. opened on Central Avenue NE with a grand opening on 15 December 2024, the chain's second Minnesota location after Little Canada. It serves no alcohol and runs to 1am on Friday, Saturday and Sunday, which makes it one of the few late rooms in the northern suburbs that is not a bar. Qamaria's coffees are organised around how different Yemeni villages prepare them, so the menu lists Mufawaar, Juban and qishr — the spiced drink brewed from coffee husks — by name rather than by roast level, alongside Aden tea, a cardamom-and-cinnamon house latte, pistachio lattes, refreshers and smoothies.
signatureDrinks: Qishr (spiced coffee husks with ginger and cinnamon)
venues.longDescription:
Blaine sits at the top of the metro, a long way from the cultural-cafe cluster that has formed along Central Avenue in Northeast Minneapolis, and until recently its evening options were the usual suburban split between chain restaurants and bars. Qamaria Yemeni Coffee Co. opened here on Central Avenue NE with a grand opening on 15 December 2024, following the chain's Little Canada debut earlier that year and preceding its Eden Prairie shop by two months. The chain was started by two Yemeni entrepreneurs and its coffee programme is organised around Yemeni village traditions rather than around roast profiles, which is why the menu board reads as a list of place-linked preparations rather than a list of drink sizes. The room follows the same pattern as its siblings: large tables, long hours, and no alcohol licence anywhere in the building.

The drinks are the Qamaria standards. Qishr is brewed from coffee husks with ginger and cinnamon — a drink that predates the bean's export and is still what many Yemeni households make at home. Mufawaar is coffee with cardamom and cream; Juban is a lighter regional preparation; Aden tea is the black-tea-and-spice drink most of these shops treat as their signature. The house Qamaria latte is spiced with cardamom and cinnamon, and a pistachio latte, an espresso bar, iced refreshers and smoothies fill out the rest. Pastries lean sweet: pistachio milk cake, honeycomb bread and Dubai chocolate. What makes the Blaine shop worth the drive for anyone not drinking is the closing time. It runs to 11pm Monday through Thursday and to 1am on Friday, Saturday and Sunday, later than every coffee shop and most restaurants in Anoka County, and it is one of only a handful of rooms in the north metro where a group can sit for three hours after a film with nothing alcoholic on the table. Seating is built for groups rather than for solo work, and the pastry counter does as much trade as the coffee bar late in the evening.

venues.name: Qamaria Yemeni Coffee Co.
venues.description: Qamaria Yemeni Coffee Co. opened on Prairie Center Drive in Eden Prairie on 15 February 2025, the chain's third Minnesota shop and the only Yemeni coffeehouse in the southwest metro. It is fully alcohol-free and open until 1am on Friday, Saturday and Sunday. The menu is the Qamaria standard: qishr brewed from coffee husks with ginger and cinnamon, Mufawaar with cardamom and cream, Juban, Aden tea, and a house latte spiced with cardamom and cinnamon, alongside pistachio lattes, an espresso list, refreshers and smoothies. Pistachio milk cake, honeycomb bread and Dubai chocolate anchor the pastry counter. The room is set up for long sittings rather than quick pickups, with large tables and no closing-time pressure until well after most Eden Prairie restaurants have shut for the night.
venues.address: 582 Prairie Center Dr, Eden Prairie, MN 55344
signatureDrinks: Qishr (spiced coffee husks with ginger and cinnamon)
venues.longDescription:
Eden Prairie's Prairie Center Drive is a suburban retail corridor of the kind that rarely produces a late-night social room, which is part of why Qamaria's arrival there on 15 February 2025 mattered locally. It was the chain's third Minnesota shop, after Little Canada in mid-2024 and Blaine that December, and it remains the only Yemeni coffeehouse in the southwest metro — the nearest comparable rooms are twenty miles north-east on Central Avenue. Qamaria was founded by Yemeni entrepreneurs and builds its coffee list around the preparations of particular Yemeni villages, so what reaches the counter is a set of named traditional drinks rather than a roast-and-size grid. There is no alcohol licence and no bar.

Qishr is the drink that most surprises first-time visitors: it is brewed from the dried husk of the coffee cherry rather than the bean, spiced with ginger and cinnamon, and drinks closer to a spiced tea than to coffee. Mufawaar is coffee prepared with cardamom and cream, Juban is a lighter regional preparation, and Aden tea is the spiced black tea that Yemeni coffeehouses across the United States have made their calling card. The house Qamaria latte carries cardamom and cinnamon; a pistachio latte, a full espresso bar, iced refreshers and blended smoothies cover the rest of the board, and the pastry case runs to pistachio milk cake, honeycomb bread and Dubai chocolate. The value of the shop for anyone not drinking is structural rather than novel: it opens at 8am and does not close until 11pm on weeknights or 1am from Friday through Sunday, which is later than any bar-free option in Eden Prairie, and it is set up for groups to sit for hours rather than to order and leave. Qamaria's three Minnesota shops share a single Instagram account and keep near-identical menus, so what is described here holds at Blaine and Little Canada as well; what differs is the drive. For the south-west metro this is the only room of its type, and the nearest alternative of any kind is more than twenty miles away.

venues.name: Qamaria Yemeni Coffee Co.
venues.description: Qamaria Yemeni Coffee Co. in Little Canada was the first Yemeni coffeehouse to open in Minnesota, soft-opening in May 2024 and holding its grand opening that June under franchisee Mohamed Hagi and his cousin and business partner Ibrahim Haji Said. It is fully alcohol-free and open to midnight on Friday, Saturday and Sunday. The menu is built on Yemeni preparations — Mufawaar, Juban, Aden tea, and qishr, the spiced drink brewed from coffee husks with ginger and cinnamon — alongside a Qamaria latte spiced with cardamom and cinnamon, pistachio lattes, refreshers and smoothies. Honeycomb bread, pistachio milk cake and Dubai chocolate fill the pastry case.
venues.address: 3 Little Canada Rd E, Little Canada, MN 55117
signatureDrinks: Qishr (spiced coffee husks with ginger and cinnamon)
venues.longDescription:
Qamaria Yemeni Coffee Co. opened at 3 Little Canada Road East in the inner northern suburbs, soft-opening on 4 May 2024 and holding its official opening on 21 June. It was Minnesota's first Yemeni coffee cafe, and it arrived ahead of the wave: Qahwah House and Haraz both reached the metro afterwards, and Qamaria itself went on to add Blaine and Eden Prairie locations. The Little Canada shop is run by Mohamed Hagi with his cousin and business partner Ibrahim Haji Said. Hagi told Sahan Journal in June 2024 that the pair "always wanted to incorporate a space here where it was an untapped market," and described the draw as being about more than the coffee — "It's more so an experience," he said, adding that the room "really reminds me of home." Sahan Journal reported that the opening drew a crowd large enough to strain the counter.

The drinks list follows the Yemeni coffeehouse template. Qishr is the traditional hot drink brewed not from the bean but from the husk, with ginger and often cinnamon; Mufawaar is coffee prepared with cardamom and cream; Juban is a lighter regional preparation; and Aden tea is the black-tea-and-spice drink that most of these shops treat as their signature. The house Qamaria latte is spiced with cardamom and cinnamon, and a pistachio latte, refreshers, smoothies and a conventional espresso list sit alongside. Food is pastry-led rather than a full kitchen: honeycomb bread, pistachio milk cake and Dubai chocolate are the counter's best-known items. No alcohol is served anywhere in the building. The hours are the reason this reads as a going-out room rather than a cafe — midnight on Friday, Saturday and Sunday, 10pm the rest of the week, in a suburb where almost nothing else non-alcoholic is open past nine. Seating is arranged for groups rather than for solo laptop work, and the room fills twice over on a weekend evening — once after dinner and again after ten. For anyone in the north-eastern suburbs looking for a place to sit with friends for two hours that is not a bar, this was the first of its kind in Minnesota and it is still the nearest one to downtown Saint Paul.
venues.pressQuote: We always wanted to incorporate a space here where it was an untapped market.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Mohamed Hagi, Qamaria Yemeni Coffee Co. owner

venues.name: Qamaria Yemeni Coffee
venues.description: Qamaria Yemeni Coffee is a large, fully alcohol-free Yemeni coffeehouse on the stretch of North Kedzie Avenue in Albany Park that has become Chicago's densest cluster of Middle Eastern cafes. It is the Chicago outpost of Qamaria Yemeni Coffee Co., founded by Yemeni entrepreneurs Hatem and Munif with the stated mission of sharing Yemeni-sourced coffee with the world, and it keeps the late hours that define the category: open until midnight most nights and until 1am on Friday and Saturday. The room is built for sitting rather than grabbing and going, with a deep floor of tables a block north of the CTA Brown Line's Kedzie stop. The menu runs on light-roast Yemeni coffee, spiced milk drinks, signature lattes and a case of Middle Eastern pastries and cakes. No alcohol is served at any hour.
signatureDrinks: Qamaria Latte (signature espresso latte with cardamom)
Qishr (sun-dried Yemeni coffee husks brewed into a tangy, fruit-flavored, low-caffeine infusion)
venues.longDescription:
Qamaria Yemeni Coffee Co. was founded by Hatem and Munif, two Yemeni entrepreneurs whose stated aim is "to share Yemeni sourced coffee products with the world" while supporting the farmers who grow the beans; the company's own account of itself quotes co-founder Hatem saying "I'm in love with Yemeni coffee and on a mission to share it with the world." The company's coffee is traditionally offered as a light roast carrying the spice-and-herb profile characteristic of Yemeni varieties, and its qishr - made from naturally sun-dried coffee husks rather than the bean - produces a tangy, fruit-flavored drink with only mild caffeine that has historically been served at evening gatherings. That evening-gathering function is exactly what the Chicago location does in Albany Park.

The Chicago cafe sits in a strip mall at 4728 N Kedzie Ave, one block north of the CTA Brown Line's Kedzie station, on the mile of Kedzie Avenue that has drawn several Middle Eastern coffeehouses within a short span. It is an unusually large room by Chicago cafe standards, with enough tables to absorb study groups, families and after-dinner crowds at once. Drinks split between the traditional Yemeni side of the menu - coffee, qishr and spiced milk teas - and the modern signature lattes the chain is known for, led by the cardamom-forward Qamaria Latte and a pistachio latte, alongside espresso classics, iced cocoa and a pastry and cake case. Nothing on the list contains alcohol, and the hours are the point: doors stay open until midnight Sunday through Thursday and until 1am on Friday and Saturday, which makes this one of the few rooms on the North Side where a late, sober night out is the default rather than an accommodation. The Kedzie corridor around the cafe has become the densest concentration of Middle Eastern coffeehouses in Chicago, with several opening within roughly a mile of one another inside a year, and Qamaria keeps some of the latest hours among them. The company sells its beans and its qishr directly as well, so what is served in the room can be taken home, and it lists wholesale and franchising alongside its cafes.

venues.name: Qamaria Yemeni Coffee Co.
venues.description: Qamaria Yemeni Coffee Co. is a fully alcohol-free Yemeni coffeehouse on East Hampden Avenue in Aurora, the first Colorado outpost of a chain founded by Yemeni entrepreneurs Hatem Al-Eidaroos and Munif, who source single-origin beans from the Haraz region of Yemen. It opened in April 2026 near the Colorado Muslim Community Center and stays open to 10pm on weeknights and 11pm on Fridays and Saturdays, which makes it a genuine late-evening alternative to a bar rather than a daytime cafe. The room is laid out for lingering, with traditional Yemeni floor seating and cushions alongside conventional tables. Alongside espresso drinks the menu runs to qishr, the tangy infusion brewed from dried coffee husks, and spiced drinks built on cardamom and cinnamon, served with baklava, milk cakes and honeycomb bread.
signatureDrinks: Qishr (dried Yemeni coffee husks brewed into a tangy, fruit-flavoured infusion; also sold as cascara)
venues.longDescription:
Qamaria Yemeni Coffee Co. opened its first Colorado location in April 2026 at 15464 East Hampden Avenue in Aurora, bringing to the Denver metro the Yemeni coffeehouse format that has become one of the fastest-growing categories of alcohol-free late-night social space in the United States. The company was founded by Yemeni entrepreneurs Hatem Al-Eidaroos and Munif, who describe the business as a mission rather than a chain: "I'm in love with Yemeni coffee and on a mission to share it with the world," Al-Eidaroos says on the company's own site. Qamaria harvests and packages beans from single farms in Haraz, Yemen, a high-altitude growing region whose elevation, soil and climate the company credits for producing some of the rarest coffee in the world. The Aurora store sits close to the Colorado Muslim Community Center and has been fitted with traditional Yemeni-style seating — low cushions on the floor as well as ordinary tables — so that groups can settle in for hours.

The draw for anyone not drinking is the combination of hours and menu. Qamaria trades until 10pm Monday through Thursday and Sunday, and until 11pm on Friday and Saturday, so it functions as a place to go out in the evening rather than a morning coffee stop. Nothing on the premises contains alcohol. The house speciality is qishr, brewed not from the bean but from the dried coffee husk, which produces a tangy, lightly fruity cup that Qamaria also sells as cascara; it sits alongside espresso-based drinks and spiced preparations built on cardamom and cinnamon that Visit Aurora singles out in its listing. Food runs to Middle Eastern sweets and bakes — baklava, milk cakes and honeycomb bread — plus savoury cheese and meat pies. Denver's non-alcoholic scene has been dominated by licensed cocktail bars with zero-proof lists; Qamaria is one of the few venues in the metro where the whole room is alcohol-free by design and stays open late enough to matter.
venues.pressQuote: brings the rich traditions of Yemeni coffee culture to Aurora, featuring single-origin beans from the Haraz region and aromatic drinks infused with spices like cardamom and cinnamon

venues.name: Qamaria Yemeni Coffee Co.
venues.description: Qamaria Yemeni Coffee Co. is a 3,600-square-foot Yemeni coffeehouse in the International Village shopping centre on North Berkeley Lake Road in Duluth, north-east of Atlanta. It is the largest cafe the chain has built, seating roughly 140 people across booths, tables and two lounge areas, and it is fully alcohol-free. Opening hours are the point of it: noon to midnight Monday through Thursday and 10am to 1am on Friday and Saturday, which puts it among the few late-night rooms in the north-eastern suburbs that pour nothing stronger than coffee. The beans are 100% Yemeni and are served in both traditional Yemeni and espresso preparations. Qishr, Adeni chai, the house Qamaria Latte and pistachio lattes anchor the drinks list, with cakes and honeycomb bread from a prep kitchen on site.
venues.address: 2645 N Berkeley Lake Rd NW Suite 221, Duluth, GA 30096
venues.hours: Mon 11am-11pm; Tue closed; Wed-Thu 11am-11pm; Fri 11am-1am; Sat 10am-1am; Sun 10am-11pm
venues.longDescription:
Qamaria Yemeni Coffee Co. was founded by Hatem Al-Eidaroos and Munif Maweri, who began as wholesalers of Yemeni green coffee before moving into bricks and mortar. The Duluth cafe is run by local business partners Wahaj Imam and Danish Dharani, who took the site at 2645 North Berkeley Lake Road NW in the International Village centre and built out what What Now Atlanta reported in April 2025 would be the largest Qamaria anywhere — about 3,600 square feet with seating for around 140 guests, split between booths, tables and two separate lounge areas, plus a prep kitchen for cakes and baked goods. It opened later that year. The location is deliberate: International Village is one of metro Atlanta's densest concentrations of immigrant-owned business, and the surrounding stretch of Gwinnett County has a large Muslim population for whom a late-night room with no alcohol is not a novelty but the default.

The coffee is 100% Yemeni and is offered in both traditional Yemeni preparation and as espresso, so the same beans appear as a spiced, cardamom-scented infusion or pulled as a shot. Qishr, brewed from coffee husks rather than the bean itself, is on the list, as is Adeni chai, the black-tea-and-spice preparation that has become the category's calling card in the United States. The house Qamaria Latte is served hot or iced, and the wider menu runs to pistachio lattes, matcha, smoothies and fruit refreshers. Food is limited but specific: cakes, pastries and the honeycomb bread — a pull-apart loaf filled with cream cheese and drizzled with honey — that What Now Atlanta singled out. What separates Qamaria from a conventional suburban coffee shop is the clock. Noon to midnight on weeknights and 10am to 1am on Friday and Saturday is bar-hours trading in a room where no alcohol is sold or permitted, and the two lounge areas are laid out for sitting for hours rather than turning tables.
venues.pressQuote: The shops serve a variety of snacks and tea and coffee beverages, including signature items like Adeni chai and the honeycomb bread, which is filled with cream cheese and drizzled with honey.

venues.name: Qamaria Yemeni Coffee Co.
venues.description: Qamaria Yemeni Coffee Co. is the Houston branch of a fast-growing Yemeni coffeehouse chain, trading on Westheimer Road in Briar Forest until eleven most nights and midnight on Friday and Saturday. The menu runs the traditional Yemeni preparations rather than a standard espresso list: iced mufawaar built on coffee with cardamom and cream, juban kettle coffee, qishr infused from cascara with cardamom, ginger and cinnamon, and Aden tea. Sweeter modern drinks sit alongside them, including an iced pistachio latte and the araysi, a mango drink finished with vanilla drizzle. No alcohol is served, and the Texas licence register holds no permit for the trade name statewide or at this address. The room is designed for long sittings, which is what separates a Yemeni coffeehouse from a coffee shop.
signatureDrinks: Iced Mufawaar — coffee with cardamom and cream
Qishr — cascara infused with cardamom, ginger and cinnamon
Araysi — mango finished with vanilla drizzle
venues.longDescription:
Qamaria Yemeni Coffee Co. trades on the stretch of Westheimer Road that runs through Briar Forest, and it is worth being precise about that location because almost every aggregator files it under Westchase. The City of Houston's own super-neighborhood boundary puts it in Briar Forest, and the distinction matters if you are navigating by district rather than by address.

The menu is the traditional Yemeni one. Mufawaar is coffee with cardamom and cream, served here iced as well as hot, and it is the house's most-ordered drink. Qishr is the older preparation and the more interesting one — an infusion of cascara, the dried fruit husk surrounding the coffee bean, spiced with cardamom, ginger and cinnamon. It contains far less caffeine than brewed coffee and tastes closer to a spiced fruit tea, which makes it the drink to order late in the evening. Juban kettle coffee and Aden tea fill out the traditional side. The modern side runs sweeter and younger: an iced pistachio latte, a Qamaria iced latte, and the araysi, a mango drink finished with a vanilla drizzle that is squarely aimed at the dessert end of the evening.

The hours are what qualify it for this directory. Eleven at night Sunday through Thursday, midnight on Friday and Saturday, every week — hours that overlap almost exactly with the bars a few miles east, which means it functions as a genuine alternative rather than a consolation. The format assumes you will sit: the rooms in this chain are built with large tables and long sightlines, because the entire cultural point of a Yemeni coffeehouse is that it is somewhere to spend three hours talking, not somewhere to collect a cup.

On alcohol, no permit exists for the trade name anywhere in Texas and none at this address, and nothing on the menu contains any. That is evidence rather than a claim the venue makes in those words, and it is worth stating that way round. Note also that this is a chain branch; its nearest sibling is in Richmond, outside Houston's city limits, so the two do not overlap within the city.

venues.name: Quarter Acre
venues.description: Quarter Acre is chef-owner Toby Archibald's New Zealand-influenced bistro on Lowest Greenville, and it keeps a genuine spirit-free section on its drinks list rather than a token soda. The zero-proof cocktails are built with real intent: the Basil Daiquiri uses Lyre's Blanco with basil and Nelson hops, and the Mirinda Spritz layers passion fruit, rosemary, and tonic. The list is rounded out with Texas-made Lady Bird craft sodas and Lagunitas IPNA non-alcoholic IPA, so a non-drinker gets a full range across cocktails, beer, and soda.
venues.hours: Mon closed; Tue-Thu 5pm-9:30pm; Fri-Sat 5pm-10:30pm; Sun closed
signatureDrinks: Basil Daiquiri (Lyre's Blanco, basil, Nelson hops)
venues.longDescription:
Quarter Acre opened December 30, 2022 in the former Rapscallion space at 2023 Greenville Avenue, on the Lowest Greenville stretch of Dallas's Lower Greenville district. It is the first solo restaurant from New Zealand-born chef Toby Archibald, who moved to Dallas in 2016 after cooking at The Greenhouse in London and Cafe Boulud in New York and Toronto, and who served as chef de cuisine at Bullion and executive chef at Georgie by Curtis Stone before striking out on his own. The name evokes the quarter-acre suburban ideal of his New Zealand upbringing, and the Coeval Studio-designed room leans into a forest-meets-island aesthetic. Quarter Acre landed on Texas Monthly's Best New Restaurants list in 2023 and was included in Texas's inaugural Michelin Guide.

For non-drinkers, the bar keeps a dedicated spirit-free section rather than defaulting to a lone Shirley Temple. The two house zero-proof cocktails are the Mirinda Spritz, made with passion fruit, rosemary, and tonic ($6), and the Basil Daiquiri, built on Lyre's Blanco non-alcoholic spirit with basil and Nelson hops ($8). Beyond the cocktails, the list carries Lady Bird craft sodas ($5), the Texas-made line named for Lady Bird Johnson, and Lagunitas IPNA, a non-alcoholic India Pale Ale ($6). The offerings mirror the kitchen's seasonal, ingredient-forward approach, and were highlighted by CultureMap Dallas in its Dry January round-up of the city's zero-proof menus.

Quarter Acre serves dinner Tuesday through Saturday and is closed Sunday and Monday; reservations run through OpenTable and are strongly recommended, since the dining room is compact and books up on weekends. It is a fit for a special-occasion dinner where one or more guests are not drinking, because the spirit-free pours are priced and presented alongside the full cocktail list rather than tucked away. The a la carte menu rotates with the seasons, and a multicourse tasting is also available.
venues.pressQuote: This Greenville Avenue restaurant has a spirit-free menu featuring Lady Bird sodas, Lagunitas IPNA India Pale Ale, and zero-proof cocktails such as the Mirinda Spritz with passion fruit, rosemary, and tonic, and the Basil Daiquiri with Lyre's Blanco, basil, and Nelson hops.

venues.name: Queen & Rook Game Cafe
venues.description: Queen & Rook is a board game cafe on South Street with a printed menu section headed "Zero Proof Cocktails & Beer", eight drinks deep and flat-priced at $8 — one of the longest non-alcoholic lists in Philadelphia. Princess Rosalina builds butterfly pea tea with lychee, lime and soda; Galadriel runs pineapple and lychee against jalapeño, tajín and cilantro; Abraxos gets Iron Teeth uses a blackberry shrub with mint and lemon; and Smaug's Scales pairs a strawberry shrub with basil and lemon. A non-alcoholic Butterbeer is $10. The bottled list carries Guinness 0, two Best Day beers and St. Agrestis Phony Negroni, and eight house loose-leaf teas are served by cup or pot. It runs to midnight on Friday and Saturday.
