venues.longDescription:
Roll Up Herbal Bar sits beside the Gateway to the Smokies arch on Main Street in downtown Waynesville, about thirty miles west of Asheville, and its owner Sam is unusually clear about why it exists: she started it for one reason, to provide culinary beverages for people who are not drinking alcohol but crave the complexity of a well-crafted cocktail. She is an experienced bartender, and also an artist and former theatre kid, which she says is why the drinks are built to look as good as they taste. The room is a small oasis — comfortable seating, magical décor, and a patio shaded by tall oaks. It is a sit-down tasting lounge rather than a pop-up, typically open Thursday to Saturday from noon to 8pm and Sundays to 4pm, though she still works events, so checking the day's hours is wise.

Despite the name, and this is worth saying because it cuts against the expectation, nothing sold here is psychoactive. There is no kava, no kratom, no THC, no CBD and no hemp anywhere on the menu — the herbal element is culinary, and the drinks are genuinely built rather than poured. All six mocktails are $7. Something Bitter layers orange, grapefruit and tangerine against juniper, rose, hibiscus and vanilla, finished with orange bitters — the closest thing here to an aperitivo. Something Spicy runs jalapeño and ginger with chili powder and pineapple over a jalapeño lime salt. Something Smutty combines passionfruit with black cardamom, clove and tart cherry under dark cacao bitters. Something Tiki uses lemongrass, ginger, pandan and pressed coconut; Something Breezy works spearmint and green cardamom with pink peppercorn and cucumber; and Something Signature is lavender, rosemary and lemon over butterfly pea flower. A matching set of specialty lattes runs at $7, and adaptogen add-ons — Wooden Spoon herbal blends and Rainbo functional mushroom tinctures — are $3, both non-psychoactive.
venues.pressQuote: provide culinary beverages for folks who aren't drinking alcohol, but crave the complexity of a well-crafted cocktail

venues.name: Roosevelt's
venues.description: Roosevelt's is a Cherry Street bar and restaurant in Tulsa, open 11am to 10pm through the week, to midnight on Friday and Saturday and from 10am at weekends — the widest hours of any venue in this city guide. Its alcohol-free drink is The Red Keep, built on blood orange, lemon, jalapeño and ginger beer: two sources of heat against citrus, which is a savoury rather than sweet approach and works alongside food. Being open from mid-morning to late seven days a week makes it the fallback when the evening-only rooms are shut. It shares Cherry Street with Nola's, which has the better zero-proof programme but keeps a narrower kitchen.
signatureDrinks: The Red Keep — blood orange, lemon, jalapeño, ginger beer
venues.longDescription:
Roosevelt's sits on Cherry Street, the East 15th Street restaurant strip, a few doors from Nola's — which makes that block the most concentrated stretch of good alcohol-free drinking in Tulsa outside downtown.

The Red Keep is the drink, and its specification is a small lesson in how to build a mocktail that adults want. Blood orange and lemon give it citrus and colour. Jalapeño and ginger beer give it two different kinds of heat — the capsaicin burn of the chilli and the volatile, aromatic heat of the ginger — layered rather than duplicated. There is no added sweetener in the description at all beyond what the ginger beer carries. The result is savoury, hot and dry, and it works alongside a plate of food, which most mocktails do not.

That matters because the failure mode of this category is sugar. A drink built to be sipped over an hour with dinner has to be low enough in sweetness not to fatigue the palate, and heat is one of the few tools available to replace the bite that alcohol supplies. Roosevelt's uses two.

Tulsa Remote ranked it among the city's must-try mocktails in January 2025.

The hours are the second argument. Eleven in the morning to ten at night Monday through Thursday, midnight on Friday and Saturday, and a 10am weekend opening for brunch — seven days, no closed evening. Across this guide the alcohol-free rooms that matter most are usually the ones with the widest opening, because a non-drinker's constraint is almost never the drink and almost always the schedule.

Graded three: one named build, no printed zero-proof section documented.
venues.pressQuote: The Red Keep: blood orange, lemon, jalapeño, and ginger beer

venues.name: Root Awakening Kava Bar
venues.description: Root Awakening opened in 2022 as New England's first kava bar and serves no alcohol at all. Owner Gregory Gately started it after losing his brother to alcohol, and built something that runs like a bar rather than a tea room: open to midnight on weeknights and 1am at weekends, with kava from Fiji, Vanuatu and elsewhere in the South Pacific, kava lattes, kava mocktails and kombucha on tap. The week is programmed the way a neighbourhood pub programmes it — movie night, ladies' night, trivia, a darts tournament, karaoke — with a games lounge and a free arcade cabinet. Kava contains no alcohol but is psychoactive and mildly sedating, and is not FDA-regulated.
venues.longDescription:
Root Awakening opened in 2022 at 300 Main Street as New England's first kava bar, and it serves no alcohol at all. Greg Gately started it after losing his brother to alcoholism not long before the pandemic, and he has been plain about what the place is for: he firmly believes his brother is looking over him and rooting him on, and that people who do not want to drink at traditional bars now have a place. He had been drinking kava himself since about 2016, and describes it with no romance whatsoever — muddy water is what they call it, because it tastes like earth. What he built runs like a bar rather than a tea room, open to midnight on weeknights and 1am at weekends, with a full week of programming: movie night on Mondays, ladies' night on Tuesdays, trivia on Wednesdays, a darts tournament on Thursdays and karaoke from 8pm on Fridays. That calendar is the point. A room that is only open until nine with nothing to do in it does not replace a bar; this does.

The drinks are built rather than poured, and they lean deliberately towards dessert and comfort rather than trying to imitate cocktails. The hand-pressed kava list runs Give Me Samoa at $13, which takes traditional kava into cocoa, salted caramel and coconut milk with a cookie on the side; the Chocolatta at $11, kava with cocoa and your choice of milk; a PB & K at $12 that adds peanut butter protein; and a cold brew kava latte at $12 made with ten-hour cold brew. The Pure Kavatails are the lighter half — a Kava Kolada at $12 in five flavours, a Kava Kreme Float at $11 built on root beer, cream soda or orange soda, the Kavarita at $12, a sweet and sour lemon-lime refresher the bar calls its signature, and The Bula at $12, locally sourced kombucha spiked with kava elixir over ice. Kombucha alone is $7 under a section headed Buzz Free. Two caveats worth having. The menu is published through a third-party listing that warns it may not be current, so prices can drift. And while kratom appears on no menu we could find, at least one customer account describes it being served here — kava is psychoactive in its own right, so ask what is in a drink if that matters to you.
venues.pressQuote: I firmly believe he's looking over me and watching every step that I'm doing and he's rooting me on. People who don't want to drink at traditional bars with alcohol, they have a place.

venues.name: Root City Kava Bar & Lounge
venues.description: Root City Kava Bar & Lounge bills itself as Maryland's first and only dedicated kava bar, a completely alcohol-free botanical lounge in a three-story historic building on Mount Vernon's Cathedral Street. Under new ownership, it serves traditional kava — your first shell is free — alongside kratom, teas, and botanical mocktails built on functional mushrooms, adaptogens, and herbal blends. The ground floor runs as a kava cafe, with a lounge for live music and events above it and a retro arcade gaming room on the top floor. It keeps genuine late-night hours, open until 2 a.m. Tuesday through Saturday, and fills the calendar with trivia, open mics, comedy, and wellness nights — all, as the bar puts it, powered by plants, not booze.
venues.longDescription:
Root City Kava Bar & Lounge occupies three floors at 917 Cathedral Street in Mount Vernon, and The Baltimore Banner describes it as the only bar and social lounge dedicated to kava beverages in Maryland. It opened in October 2024, and the building is used properly: a cafe on one level, a bar and lounge on another, and a retro arcade with gaming above. Programming runs to live music, open mics and themed nights, and the hours are built for a genuine night out rather than an early one — 2pm to 2am Tuesday through Saturday, midnight on Mondays, with Sundays from noon to 8pm. One of the founders came to kava while navigating his own sobriety, which is the origin story behind a good many kava bars and explains why they tend to be better at hospitality than the wellness framing suggests.

What is served needs stating precisely, because the category is not well understood and Maryland's drinks landscape has changed. The venue's own description of its drinks list is "kava, kratom, teas and mocktails" — so alongside traditional kava shells and genuinely inert botanical mocktails and teas, this bar serves kratom, which is a distinct substance with its own risks and its own dependence profile, and which many people avoiding alcohol will want to make a deliberate decision about rather than encounter as a menu item. Kava itself is psychoactive too. No alcohol is served. The executive director of the Kava Coalition, speaking to The Banner about the category generally, was clear that people under eighteen should not partake at all. Two further caveats: the venue does not render its menu in a readable form online, so no prices or ingredient lists can be checked in advance, and its site currently describes itself as being under new ownership without naming who — press from 2024 and 2025 names different people, so ownership here has moved more than once.
venues.pressQuote: The only bar and social lounge dedicated to kava beverages in Maryland.

venues.name: Root of Happiness Kava Bar | Davis
venues.description: The Davis branch of Root of Happiness sits on F Street in the downtown grid, minutes from the UC Davis campus, and runs 11am to 1am seven days a week — a rare late alcohol-free option in a university town where the alternative is a bar crowd. Root of Happiness has traded since 2006 and describes itself as the original California kava bar, now six rooms across Northern California; two of them, in Midtown Sacramento and Rancho Cordova, are already listed here. The group's focus from the start has been sourcing: identifying exceptional kava from across the Pacific and building reliable ways to evaluate its quality. No alcohol is served, and no kratom appears on the published menu.
venues.longDescription:
Root of Happiness opened its first kava bar in 2006, which makes it older than almost the entire American kava scene — it predates the Berkeley and New York rooms that are usually credited with starting the category, and the group describes itself, fairly, as the original California kava bar. It now runs six locations across Northern California. This directory already lists the Midtown Sacramento and Rancho Cordova rooms; the Davis and Roseville branches are new here.

The Davis room is at 211 F Street, in the compact downtown grid a few minutes' walk from the UC Davis campus, and it opens at 11am and closes at 1am every day of the week. That combination — a university town, a 1am licence-free close, and no alcohol on the premises — makes it one of the more useful rooms in the group. Davis nightlife runs heavily to student bars, and a venue on the same streets that stays open just as late without serving a drop is a genuine structural alternative rather than a token one.

What distinguishes Root of Happiness from most multi-site kava operators is that it began as a sourcing business rather than as a hospitality one. The founding objective, in the company's own account, was to identify exceptional kava from across the Pacific and to develop reliable ways of evaluating its quality — and the company still sells kava root and extracts as a retail operation alongside the bars. Tyler Blythe and Travis Lowin are named as the people behind it. The practical consequence for a customer is that the kava is treated as a varietal product with provenance, the way a serious coffee roaster treats beans, rather than as a generic ingredient.

Kava is the ground root of Piper methysticum, a shrub native to the South Pacific, infused in cold water and drunk socially across Fiji, Vanuatu, Tonga and Samoa for around three thousand years. It contains no alcohol. It tastes earthy and bitter, numbs the lips and tongue on the first mouthful, and is mildly sedative — relaxing and sociable rather than intoxicating in the way alcohol is. It exhibits reverse tolerance, so regular drinkers usually need less rather than more, and a first visit is best taken slowly across an hour or two.

One point in the group's favour is worth recording, because this directory has to flag the opposite so often across the category: Root of Happiness's published material covers kava, with no kratom listed on the menu. For readers whose recovery excludes substances with dependence potential rather than alcohol alone, that makes this a straightforward room to order in.

venues.name: Root of Happiness Kava Bar | Roseville
venues.description: The Roseville branch of Root of Happiness sits on Vernon Street in the middle of the town's revitalised downtown, and like the rest of the group it runs 11am to 1am every day of the week with no alcohol served. It covers the Placer County side of the Sacramento metro — Roseville, Rocklin and Granite Bay — where dedicated alcohol-free rooms are otherwise absent entirely. The group has traded since 2006, calls itself the original California kava bar, and built its reputation on sourcing exceptional kava from across the Pacific and evaluating it systematically. No kratom appears on the published menu, which sets it apart from most American kava operators.
venues.longDescription:
Root of Happiness's Roseville room occupies 232 Vernon Street, on the pedestrianised stretch at the centre of Roseville's downtown regeneration, and it opens at 11am and closes at 1am seven days a week. Its significance is geographic as much as anything: Placer County, covering Roseville, Rocklin, Lincoln and Granite Bay, is one of the fastest-growing parts of the Sacramento metro and has essentially no other dedicated alcohol-free social venue. Vernon Street itself is lined with bars and restaurants, so this is a direct alternative on the same walk rather than an out-of-town errand.

The group behind it is the oldest operator in California kava. Root of Happiness opened its first bar in 2006 — before the wave of kava rooms that spread across Florida and Colorado in the 2010s — and describes itself as the original California kava bar, now running six locations across Northern California. Two of the others, in Midtown Sacramento and Rancho Cordova, are already listed in this directory; the Davis branch is added alongside this one.

The company's origin is unusual for a bar group in that it started from the product rather than the room. Its founding objective, in its own account, was to identify exceptional kava from across the Pacific and to develop reliable ways to evaluate its quality, and it continues to operate as a kava retailer alongside its bars, with Tyler Blythe and Travis Lowin named as the people behind it. That matters at the counter: kava here is handled as a varietal product with origin and grading, not as an undifferentiated commodity.

For anyone new to it, kava is the ground root of Piper methysticum, a shrub native to the South Pacific islands. It is infused in cold water and drunk socially — across Fiji, Vanuatu, Tonga and Samoa the practice runs back roughly three thousand years. It contains no alcohol at any point. The taste is earthy and bitter and it numbs the lips and tongue on the first mouthful; the effect is mildly sedative and sociable rather than intoxicating in the sense alcohol is. Kava shows reverse tolerance, meaning regular drinkers typically need less rather than more to feel it, so a first visit rewards a slow pace across an hour or two rather than a single fast serving.

As with the Davis room, one thing is worth noting positively. Root of Happiness's published menu covers kava, with no kratom listed on it — unusual in a category where the two are normally poured side by side, and materially easier to navigate for anyone avoiding substances with dependence potential rather than alcohol alone.

venues.name: Root of Happiness Kava Bar | Midtown
venues.description: Root of Happiness Kava Bar's Midtown room opened in March 2023 in a warehouse space on the R Street Corridor, the newest of four Northern California locations run by Travis Lowin and Tyler Blythe, who started the company in Rancho Cordova around 2013. Nothing alcoholic is served. The bar prepares noble kava only, ground fresh and hand-prepared each day from fresh-frozen root sourced in Hawaii, Fiji and the company's own American farms, and serves it traditionally in shells alongside a house specialty coffee programme built on its Bula Blend and a list of functional botanical drinks and iced tonic pours. Kava is a psychoactive root drink from the South Pacific — alcohol-free, but sedating and intoxicating in its own right, which is why the bar serves it only to guests 18 and over with ID while keeping the coffee and botanical menu open to all ages. The room runs daily from 11am to 1am, with spray-painted street art across the walls, pink neon over the bar and regular live music.
signatureDrinks: Traditional kava shell (noble root, ground fresh and hand-prepared)
Cloud Breaker (kava with lemon honey concentrate)
venues.longDescription:
Root of Happiness is the reason Sacramento can reasonably claim to have had a kava scene before most American cities did. Travis Lowin and Tyler Blythe started the company in Rancho Cordova around 2013 — ahead of the first kava bars in Berkeley and New York, which arrived in 2015 — and have since grown it to four rooms around the region, each serving a noticeably different crowd. The Midtown location is the youngest of them, opened in March 2023 in a warehouse on the R Street Corridor, and it reads that way: a big, loud, high-ceilinged room with spray-painted street art across the walls, pink neon glowing over the bar, and live music on a regular schedule. It runs from 11am to 1am every day of the week, which makes it a genuine alternative to a bar rather than a daytime cafe that happens to sell kava.

The kava itself is treated as the point rather than as a novelty. The bar uses noble root only — the traditional cultivars, as opposed to the tudei kava that causes most of the unpleasant reports — sourced fresh-frozen from Hawaii, Fiji and the company's own American farms, then ground fresh and prepared by hand rather than reconstituted from instant powder. It is served traditionally in shells, and the surrounding menu is unusually developed for a kava bar: a specialty coffee programme built around the house Bula Blend, plus functional botanical drinks, ancient tonic herbs and iced botanical pours for anyone who wants the room without the root. Kava deserves plain description for this audience: it is psychoactive, made from the ground root of a South Pacific shrub steeped in water and drunk socially for roughly three thousand years. It contains no alcohol at all, but it is sedating and mildly intoxicating on its own terms — a distinction that matters if your recovery rules out intoxicants generally rather than alcohol specifically. The bar draws the same line itself, serving kava only to guests 18 and over with ID while keeping the coffee and botanical list open to everyone.
venues.pressQuote: Today, Root of Happiness has four locations around the region, including an industrial-chic spot in a converted warehouse in Midtown

venues.name: Root of Happiness Kava Bar | Rancho Cordova
venues.description: The Rancho Cordova room is where Root of Happiness began: Travis Lowin and Tyler Blythe opened it around 2013, which puts it ahead of the first kava bars in Berkeley and New York and makes it one of the older continuously operating kava bars in the continental United States. It is fully alcohol-free. The kava is noble root only, ground fresh and hand-prepared daily from fresh-frozen root sourced in Hawaii, Fiji and the company's own American farms, served traditionally in shells, with a specialty coffee list built on the house Bula Blend and a range of functional botanical drinks alongside. Kava is a psychoactive South Pacific root drink — no alcohol, but genuinely sedating — so the bar restricts it to guests 18 and over with ID while keeping coffee and botanicals open to all ages. Fifteen miles east of downtown Sacramento, it serves a suburban regular crowd rather than a night-out one, and runs 11am to 1am daily.
signatureDrinks: Traditional kava shell (noble root, ground fresh and hand-prepared)
venues.longDescription:
This is the original. Travis Lowin and Tyler Blythe opened Root of Happiness in Rancho Cordova around 2013, at a point when kava bars barely existed in the continental United States — Berkeley and New York did not get theirs until 2015 — which makes this unassuming suburban room roughly fifteen miles east of downtown Sacramento one of the older continuously operating kava bars in the country, and the seed of what is now a four-location Northern California company. Comstock's Magazine, surveying the region's kava scene, noted that each of the four rooms ends up serving a distinctly different set of people; this one is the neighbourhood regulars' bar rather than the night-out destination its Midtown sibling has become. It opens at 11am and runs to 1am every day.

What has stayed constant across thirteen years is the sourcing discipline, which is the thing worth knowing about this company. The bar prepares noble root only — the traditional cultivars, rather than the cheaper tudei kava behind most bad first experiences — from fresh-frozen root brought in from Hawaii, Fiji and the company's own American farms, ground fresh and prepared by hand each day instead of mixed from instant powder. It is served in the traditional way, by the shell, with a specialty coffee programme built on the house Bula Blend and a list of functional botanical drinks and tonic-herb pours for anyone in the group who does not want kava. That last detail matters more than it sounds: the most common reason a non-drinker ends up somewhere they would rather not be is that their friends had nothing to order. Kava is worth describing plainly here, because this directory's readers include people in recovery — it is a psychoactive drink made from the ground root of a South Pacific shrub steeped in water, containing no alcohol whatsoever but genuinely sedating and mildly intoxicating in its own right. Root of Happiness draws that line itself, serving kava only to guests 18 and over with ID while leaving the coffee and botanical menu open to everyone.
venues.pressQuote: Root of Happiness was founded by Travis Lowin and Tyler Blythe, two Sacramento locals with an interest in the business potential of traditional plant medicines

venues.name: Rooted In Sanity Kava Lounge
venues.description: Rooted In Sanity is Madison's first and only kava lounge, tucked at the back of the SolEscape Healing Arts Building on Williamson Street — lower level, down the ramp, following a painted teal line. Nothing served contains alcohol. It pours traditional kava by the shell alongside housemade mocktails, locally made teas and a full craft coffee menu, and furnishes the room for staying rather than drinking up: swinging chairs, couches and board games at the tables. It runs evening hours to 10pm most nights and 11pm at weekends, which makes it one of the very few genuinely alcohol-free rooms in Madison that is open when the bars are. Kava contains no alcohol but is psychoactive and mildly sedating.
signatureDrinks: Craft coffee and locally made teas
venues.longDescription:
Wisconsin drinks more than almost anywhere in America, and Madison — a capital city that is also a Big Ten college town — is not the easy end of that. Rooted In Sanity is the city's answer, and until something else opens it is the only one of its kind: Madison's first and still only kava lounge, on Williamson Street in the Marquette neighbourhood, in the back of the SolEscape Healing Arts Building. You go down to the lower level and follow a teal line painted on the floor, which tells you most of what you need to know about the register the place operates in.

The offer is traditional kava served by the shell, housemade mocktails built on it, locally made teas and a full craft coffee menu, and the room is furnished deliberately for sitting: swinging chairs, couches, board games left out on the tables. Crucially the hours are bar hours rather than café hours — open until 10pm Monday and Wednesday through Thursday, 11pm on Friday, Saturday and Sunday, closed Tuesdays. That matters more than it sounds. Madison has genuinely good zero-proof drinks in a dozen bars and restaurants, but a bar is still a bar; the number of rooms in this city where you can be out at 9pm on a Saturday with no alcohol anywhere in the building is, as of 2026, exactly one.

Two things to be straight about. Kava is alcohol-free but it is psychoactive — mildly sedating, with a numbing effect on the tongue and a slow onset that catches first-timers out — so the staff will tell you to have one shell and wait rather than order three. And for anyone whose sobriety is abstinence-based rather than alcohol-specific, that distinction is worth sitting with before going. Taken on its own terms it is a genuine third place: Williamson Street puts I/O Arcade Bar and State Line Distillery within a few blocks, and the Marquette neighbourhood is the most walkable part of Madison's east side. It is also worth naming what Madison does not have, because Rooted In Sanity's significance depends on it. There is no alcohol-free cocktail bar here, no dry nightclub, and no second kava room. Sober Social in Middleton, the state's first all-non-alcoholic bottle shop, closed its storefront in February 2026, which leaves this the only room in the metro where a person avoiding alcohol can be somewhere social in the evening with none in the building. For a city with as much genuinely good zero-proof bartending as Madison has, that is a striking gap, and it is why a basement kava lounge behind a healing-arts building carries more weight here than its size suggests.
venues.pressQuote: Madison's first kava lounge takes the bitter with the sweet.

venues.name: Roots And Leaves: Mile High Kava Bar
venues.description: Mile High Kava is the Westminster branch of the Roots & Leaves group, on the northwest edge of the Denver metro. The venue describes itself as "a unique 18+ non-alcoholic tea and kava bar experience, perfect for those who prefer to socialize without alcohol", and it is programmed like a bar rather than a tea room: a stage for open-mic nights and karaoke, two pool tables, Skee-Ball, darts, couches and a full-size bar. It also has a kid-friendly area with toys, and hookah is available. Drinks are house-brewed kava and a range of traditional and ethnobotanical teas, both psychoactive plant preparations rather than soft drinks. Happy hours run three times a day, including a late slot from 10pm to midnight.
venues.longDescription:
Mile High Kava sits at 7703 West 92nd Avenue in Westminster, at the northwestern edge of the Denver metro, and is the largest and most bar-like of the Roots & Leaves group's Colorado rooms. Its own description is unambiguous about the offer: "a unique 18+ non-alcoholic tea and kava bar experience, perfect for those who prefer to socialize without alcohol", sold under the group's "join the sober shift — kava, teas & togetherness" line. The venue trades daily and on holidays, with three happy hours a day — 10am to noon, 5pm to 7pm and 10pm to midnight — and is fitted with a full-size bar with ample seating, lounge areas with couches, a stage used for open-mic nights and karaoke, two pool tables, Skee-Ball, darts and free WiFi. There is a kid-friendly area with toys, and hookah is served, which is worth knowing in advance for anyone avoiding smoke.

The drinks are the Roots & Leaves house programme. Traditional kava is poured by the shell in five, eight and eleven ounce sizes; Grape Ape brews kava with grape juice; and Chupakava is a CO2-extracted kava served in ten or seventeen ounce measures. The house ethnobotanical tea is offered in red, white and green versions, each brewed with light citrus and cinnamon. Speciality kava drinks include Kavachata, which puts CO2-extracted kava into horchata, plus a Rocket POP and a Cherry Limeade; speciality teas include Frankenjuice, Caribbean Crush and an apple cider-based drink called The Bitch. Shots run to Chupakava, Slapshot and kanna, and seven smoothie flavours can be built on either a kava or a tea base. As with the rest of the group, the honest framing matters: kava is a sedative-acting root from the South Pacific, and the house tea blends are listed as including blue lotus, California poppy, cat's claw, chamomile, white willow and wild lettuce. These are active plant preparations. The venue serves no alcohol at any point, and the 18-plus door policy and 2am close mean it functions as a direct substitute for a late-night bar rather than as a cafe.

venues.name: Roots and Leaves: Peak Kava
venues.description: Peak Kava is the Lakewood branch of Roots & Leaves, a seven-strong kava bar group operating across Colorado and New Mexico. The venue states its position without hedging: "Peak Kava is a non-alcoholic bar dedicated to nurturing social connections without alcohol", and the group markets itself under the line "join the sober shift". It is fitted out as a bar rather than a cafe — two pool tables, giant Jenga, a multicade, a fireplace, bar seating and lounge seating — and runs happy hours from 5pm to 7pm and again from 10pm to midnight. The drinks are kava and ethnobotanical teas, both psychoactive: the house tea blends include blue lotus, California poppy, wild lettuce and white willow, and the kava is served traditionally by the shell or CO2-extracted.
venues.longDescription:
Peak Kava, at 7576 West Jewell Avenue in Lakewood, is one of five Colorado locations of Roots & Leaves, a group that also runs bars in Fort Collins, Westminster, Loveland and Greeley plus two in New Mexico. The Lakewood room is the closest of them to central Denver and is explicit about what it is for: "Peak Kava is a non-alcoholic bar dedicated to nurturing social connections without alcohol." The group's campaign line is "join the sober shift — kava, teas & togetherness", and the fit-out follows through on the bar framing rather than a cafe one. There are two pool tables, giant Jenga, a multicade cabinet, a fireplace, plenty of lounge seating and a full-length bar with bar stools, plus free WiFi. Happy hours run 5pm to 7pm and again 10pm to midnight, the second of which tells you what kind of trade the venue is built for.

The menu is short and specific. Traditional kava is served by the shell in five, eight and eleven ounce pours; Grape Ape is kava brewed with grape juice; and Chupakava is a CO2-extracted kava preparation available in ten and seventeen ounce serves. A house ethnobotanical tea comes in red, white and green versions, all brewed with light citrus and cinnamon and marketed for relaxing, energising and euphoric effects respectively. The speciality kava list includes Kavachata, which serves CO2-extracted kava in horchata, a Rocket POP, and a Cherry Limeade; the speciality tea list runs to Frankenjuice, a citrus combination, Caribbean Crush, and The Bitch, which is apple cider-based. Shots include Chupakava, Slapshot and kanna, and Blasters pair a shot with a kava or tea chaser. Seven smoothie flavours can be built on either kava or ethnobotanical tea. Readers in recovery should note that these are active plant preparations, not soft drinks: the tea blends are listed as containing blue lotus, California poppy, cat's claw, chamomile, white willow and wild lettuce, and kava itself is a sedative-acting root. What the venue does not contain, at any point, is alcohol.

venues.name: Roots and Leaves: Tanoan Kava
venues.description: Tanoan Kava is the Albuquerque room of Roots & Leaves, a six-site group across Colorado and New Mexico whose Denver-area bars — Peak Kava in Lakewood and Mile High Kava in Westminster — are already listed here. The group describes itself as a sober kava bar and a social space that does not revolve around alcohol, and this room runs 10am to midnight every day of the week on 12th Street NW in the Near North Valley. The drinks are handcrafted kava and a range of botanical teas. It joins Luna's Kava Root downtown and Gaia's Kava Root on Central as the third dedicated kava room in Albuquerque, and it is the only one belonging to a multi-state group.
venues.longDescription:
Tanoan Kava sits at 2500 12th Street NW, in Albuquerque's Near North Valley just north of Old Town, and it is the New Mexico outpost of Roots & Leaves — a group of six kava bars spread across Colorado and New Mexico. Two of its Colorado siblings already appear in this directory: Peak Kava in Lakewood and Mile High Kava Bar in Westminster, both of which trade as full late-night alcohol-free bars. The group's other rooms are NoCo Kava, Stampede Kava and Casa de Kava.

The group's self-description is the clearest statement of purpose in the category — a sober kava bar, and a social space that doesn't revolve around alcohol — sold under the line join the sober shift. That framing is deliberate and it is the reason these rooms read differently from wellness cafes: the offer is not a healthier drink, it is a different place to spend an evening. This room opens at 10am and closes at midnight, seven days a week, which puts it in genuine evening territory rather than cafe hours.

The drinks are handcrafted kava alongside a range of traditional and ethnobotanical teas. Kava is the ground root of Piper methysticum, a shrub native to the South Pacific, prepared as a cold water infusion and drunk socially across Fiji, Vanuatu, Tonga and Samoa for roughly three thousand years. It contains no alcohol. The taste is earthy and bitter, it numbs the lips and tongue on the first mouthful, and the effect is mildly sedative and sociable rather than intoxicating in the way alcohol is. Kava exhibits reverse tolerance, so regular drinkers generally need less rather than more, and a first visit is best paced across an hour or two. The group's wider tea programme uses active plant preparations rather than ordinary infusions, so it is worth asking what is in a given blend if you are sensitive to that.

For Albuquerque specifically, this is the third dedicated kava room in the city, joining Luna's Kava Root on Gold Avenue downtown and Gaia's Kava Root on Central Avenue in the university district. The three together give the city an alcohol-free spine that most metros of its size do not have. One practical note: the venue goes by two names, the full Roots & Leaves branding and simply Tanoan Kava, both at the same 12th Street address. They are the same room.

venues.name: Rorschach Brewing Co.
venues.neighborhood: Leslieville (South Riverdale, near the border of The Beaches)
venues.description: Rorschach Brewing Co. is a craft brewery and taproom on Eastern Avenue in Leslieville, near the border of The Beaches, with its own on-site kitchen. It brews its non-alcoholic beer in-house under the sub-brand Free Spirit, whose flagship Adventure IPA is sold on tap and in cans right alongside Rorschach's regular lineup rather than as an afterthought. The 0.5% ABV IPA is brewed with oats, wheat and Galaxy hops, and packaged to go in 355ml cans ($2.45) or 6-packs ($13.70) at the taproom.
venues.address: 1001 Eastern Ave, Toronto, ON M4L 1A8, Canada
signatureDrinks: Free Spirit Adventure IPA — Rorschach's in-house non-alcoholic beer, 0.5% ABV, brewed with oats, wheat, and Galaxy hops; sold at the taproom as "Adventure Non-Alcoholic IPA" (355ml can $2.45; 6-pack $13.70)
venues.longDescription:
Rorschach Brewing Co. is a craft brewery and taproom at 1001 Eastern Avenue, on the Leslieville side of the border with The Beaches in Toronto's east end. The taproom serves food from its own kitchen alongside its house beers, open seven days a week from noon — Sunday and Monday until 9pm, Tuesday through Thursday until 10pm, and Friday and Saturday until 11pm — with the kitchen closing roughly an hour before the bar each night.

Since 2020, Rorschach has brewed its non-alcoholic beer under a dedicated house sub-brand, Free Spirit — by its own description, "a Canadian brewing company dedicated to using the choicest malts and hops to brew uncompromisingly flavourful alcohol free craft beer," made for drinkers who want "the exceptional taste of premium craft beer without compromising on your healthy, active lifestyle."

The flagship is the Free Spirit Adventure IPA, brewed with oats, wheat and Galaxy hops to 0.5% ABV. It's poured at the taproom as the "Adventure Non-Alcoholic IPA" and sold to go in 355ml cans ($2.45) or 6-packs ($13.70), stocked alongside Rorschach's alcoholic beers rather than set apart as a token option. Bartender Atlas's non-alcoholic drinks guide describes it as "soft, well-rounded, with notes of stone fruit and peach candy finishing on a pleasant bitterness."
venues.pressQuote: Free Spirit Adventure IPA is the first beer from Rorschach Brewing Co.'s non-alcoholic line, Free Spirit — soft, well-rounded, with notes of stone fruit and peach candy finishing on a pleasant bitterness.

venues.name: Rosa Sky Rooftop
venues.description: Rosa Sky is a rooftop bar and lounge on the 22nd floor of the dual-brand AC & Element Hotel Miami Downtown in Brickell, opened in 2022. Known for panoramic skyline views, globally inspired tapas, DJ-driven nights, and a popular Sunday Soirée bottomless brunch, it pairs handcrafted cocktails with a compact but genuine zero-proof section. The non-alcoholic lineup is built on Ritual Zero Proof spirit alternatives and Giffard syrups: Feeling Frisky (Ritual Whiskey Alternative, Giffard ginger, lemon), Rooftop Retreat (Ritual Tequila Alternative, Giffard pineapple, basil, coconut water, citrus), and Pom Pom (Ritual Gin Alternative, pomegranate, vanilla, citrus). The Pom Pom also appears as a zero-proof pour during the bottomless brunch. It's a full-service rooftop rather than a dedicated NA venue, but the named mocktails are real and ingredient-specific.

venues.longDescription:
Rosa Sky occupies the 22nd floor of the dual-brand AC & Element Hotel Miami Downtown in Brickell, opened in 2022, and trades on what a 22nd-floor room in Brickell trades on: panoramic skyline views, globally inspired tapas, DJ-driven evenings and a Sunday Soiree bottomless brunch.

Rooftop bars are a difficult category for non-drinkers. The economics reward volume and speed, the menus lean frozen and sweet, and the alcohol-free option is usually whatever comes out of the soda gun. Rosa Sky instead runs a compact but ingredient-specific zero-proof section built on Ritual Zero Proof spirit alternatives and Giffard syrups — the same syrup house used on the full cocktail list, which is the detail that shows the two menus share a station rather than running in parallel.

Feeling Frisky is the Ritual Whiskey Alternative with Giffard ginger and lemon. Rooftop Retreat uses the Ritual Tequila Alternative with Giffard pineapple, basil, coconut water and citrus. Pom Pom takes the Ritual Gin Alternative into pomegranate, vanilla and citrus. Three drinks on three different alcohol-free base spirits is a stocked bar rather than a gesture.

The Pom Pom also appears as a zero-proof pour during the bottomless brunch, which is the practically important part: bottomless formats are where non-drinkers usually pay full price for orange juice, and having a named cocktail included changes the arithmetic of joining.

The Greater Miami Convention & Visitors Bureau picked out the Feeling Frisky as a bold, ginger-forward mocktail. It is a full-service rooftop rather than a dedicated NA venue, and it gets busy and loud after dark — but the mocktails are real and specific rather than improvised. Go early if the view is the reason — the room fills after dark and the DJ takes over the volume.
venues.pressQuote: zero-proof lineup includes the Feeling Frisky, a bold, ginger-forward mocktail with Ritual Whiskey

venues.name: Rosalie Italian Soul
venues.description: Rosalie Italian Soul is chef Chris Cosentino's Italian-American restaurant inside Downtown Houston's C. Baldwin Hotel, and its printed drink menu carries a standing Mocktails section built on Ritual Zero Proof spirit alternatives. The list runs a Ritual Margarita, a Ritual Espresso Martini, and a non-alcoholic Jungle Bird, each printed with full ingredients right alongside the restaurant's cocktail list rather than as an afterthought. A fourth mocktail, The Black Tie, appears under a repeated "Rosalie Mocktails" heading.

Ritual Espresso Martini (Ritual Rum Alternative, cold brew or espresso, simple syrup)

venues.longDescription:
Rosalie Italian Soul is chef Chris Cosentino's Italian-American restaurant, opened on 15 October 2019 inside Downtown Houston's C. Baldwin Hotel on Dallas Street. Cosentino is also known for Cockscomb in San Francisco and Jackrabbit in Portland. He closed Rosalie early in the pandemic and reopened it on 15 September 2021.

The same printed menu that carries the cocktail list has a standing zero-proof section labelled Mocktails, repeated further down as Rosalie Mocktails. Printing them on the same page as the cocktails, with full ingredients, is the detail that matters — it means ordering one requires no conversation with a server about what can be made.

All three published builds run on Ritual Zero Proof's spirit alternatives. The Ritual Margarita is the simplest, pairing the tequila alternative with fresh lime and agave. The Ritual Espresso Martini uses the rum alternative with cold brew or espresso and simple syrup — a sensible substitution, since an espresso martini's character comes far more from the coffee's bitterness and the shake's foam than from the vodka.

The Jungle Bird is the interesting one, and the most technically ambitious drink on any Houston hotel menu. The original is a 1970s tiki classic built on dark rum and Campari, and it is defined by that bitter red aperitivo cutting through pineapple — remove it and the drink collapses into fruit juice. Rosalie's version layers two different Ritual products, the Aperitif Alternative and the Rum Alternative, with pineapple juice, lime and simple syrup. Using two alcohol-free spirits in a single build is something very few bars bother with, and here it is the only way the drink works at all. A fourth mocktail, The Black Tie, appears on the menu without published ingredients.

The hours are unusual and worth reading carefully: Monday to Thursday the restaurant serves breakfast from half past six, then runs from eleven in the morning all the way to two in the morning. Friday and Saturday are dinner only, half past five to ten, and it is closed on Sunday. A downtown room serving properly built zero-proof cocktails at one in the morning midweek is a genuinely rare thing.
venues.pressQuote: This food represents immigrant cuisine in America.

venues.name: Rosemary's Wynwood
venues.description: Rosemary's Wynwood is the Miami outpost of Carlos Suarez's beloved West Village Italian restaurant (Casa Nela group), which opened in New York in 2012; the Wynwood location debuted February 7, 2025 in a converted former shoe warehouse. Executive chef Craig Giunta (previously Mother Wolf, Macchialina) leads a seasonal menu of housemade pastas, antipasti, and seafood. A defining feature is the 3,500-square-foot indoor-outdoor space — nearly a third of it a living garden grown with Little River Cooperative, supplying herbs and produce used across the kitchen and bar. The beverage program runs an Italian spritz-forward cocktail list alongside a named zero-proof section: a Ghia Sour (Ghia aperitivo, lemon, egg white), a Hugo Fizz (elderflower cordial, Athletic Brewing Upside Dawn, club soda, mint, lime), and a Non #1 Bollicine Rosato, plus an Athletic Brewing Upside Dawn NA lager. Non-drinkers get composed, named options rather than an afterthought.

venues.longDescription:
Rosemary's Wynwood opened on 7 February 2025 in a converted former shoe warehouse, the Miami outpost of Carlos Suarez's West Village Italian restaurant, which has been running in New York since 2012 under the Casa Nela group. Executive chef Craig Giunta, previously of Mother Wolf and Macchialina, leads a seasonal menu of house-made pastas, antipasti and seafood.

The defining feature is agricultural rather than culinary. The 3,500-square-foot indoor-outdoor space devotes nearly a third of itself to a living garden, grown in partnership with Little River Cooperative, which supplies herbs and produce used across both the kitchen and the bar. A bar drawing on an on-site garden has an advantage in exactly the place non-alcoholic drinks usually fail: without spirit to carry it, a zero-proof cocktail depends almost entirely on the quality and freshness of what goes into it.

The drinks list is Italian and spritz-forward, with a named zero-proof section rather than an afterthought. The Ghia Sour uses the Ghia aperitivo with lemon and egg white — a sour, which needs texture rather than sweetness to work. The Hugo Fizz combines elderflower cordial with Athletic Brewing's Upside Dawn, club soda, mint and lime, using a non-alcoholic beer as a cocktail ingredient rather than a fallback. There is a Non #1 Bollicine Rosato for anyone wanting something in a wine glass, and Upside Dawn is available on its own.

Resident Magazine described the list as leaning into balance and freshness. That is accurate, and it is what a garden gets you: non-drinkers here get composed, named options rather than a bowl of fruit juice. Ask to sit in the garden — it is the reason the drinks taste the way they do, and it is the most pleasant seat in Wynwood.
venues.pressQuote: leans into balance and freshness

venues.name: Rosette
venues.description: Rosette is a small worker-owned bar and restaurant at 9262 57th Avenue S in Rainier Beach, opened in 2025 by members of the collective behind Jude's Old Town, Seattle's first worker-owned bar and restaurant, two doors down. It focuses on non-alcoholic cocktails, natural and biodynamic wine and small bites, and the room is petite — a rectangular space just under eleven feet wide. Worker-owner Mark Paschal's reason for building it is the clearest statement of the case we have found: for too long, people who don't drink alcohol have been treated as an afterthought in bar spaces, and at Rosette thoughtfully constructed non-alcoholic cocktails are meant to shine and offer a true bar experience without alcohol. The N/A Cocktails list is flat $15: In Bloom (Figlia Fiore, Lumette Bright Light, lemon, rose blossom, Woody's non-alcoholic sparkling), Minimal Intervention (DHOS vodka, lemon, strawberry-mint), Refined Prop Comic (Lumette LumRum, Ghia, lemon, orange-carrot) and Spirited Away (Free Spirits bourbon, Pathfinder, vermouth, bitters). PLEASE NOTE: a fifth, Pine for the Days, contains KAVA — a mildly sedative plant — under the same non-alcoholic heading. Happy hour 3–6pm; open Wednesday to Saturday.
venues.longDescription:
Rosette is a small worker-owned bar and restaurant in Rainier Beach, opened in 2025 by members of the same collective that runs Jude's Old Town — Seattle's first worker-owned bar and restaurant — two doors down the same block. It signs its own about page "in solidarity, the members of Rosette", and the room is genuinely tiny: a rectangular space just under eleven feet wide, painted teal. Mark Paschal, who helped found Jude's and spearheaded this one, has explained the thinking twice and both versions are worth having. To Seattle Refined: for too long, people who don't drink alcohol have been treated as an afterthought in bar spaces, and at Rosette thoughtfully constructed non-alcoholic cocktails and spirits are meant to shine and offer a true bar experience without alcohol — drinkers can still enjoy the ritual of the cocktail without needing alcohol to do so. And to the South Seattle Emerald, more sharply: even when places do have non-alcoholic cocktails on the menu it can still feel like you're being ignored, so they wanted to put front and centre the idea that there can still be sociality in bars where the social lubricant is other people and not alcohol. Nyannah Jackson is among the other worker-owners. Food is small and good — marinated olives at $7, a cassava cake with plum cardamom sauce at $13, a cacio e pepe ice cream at $12.

The drinks list is headed N/A Cocktails and everything on it is $15. In Bloom is the aperitif, layering Figlia Fiore and Lumette Bright Light with lemon, rose blossom syrup and Woody's non-alcoholic sparkling wine. Minimal Intervention is deliberately spare — DHOS non-alcoholic vodka, lemon, strawberry-mint syrup. Refined Prop Comic runs Lumette's non-alcoholic rum with Ghia against an orange-carrot syrup. Spirited Away is the serious one, and the closest thing here to a stirred whiskey cocktail: Free Spirits bourbon with Pathfinder, vermouth, red bitter and aromatic bitters. Alongside them sit real wines and a non-alcoholic sparkling rosé from Woody's at $11, with an N/A cocktail of the day at $12 during happy hour. One thing to know before ordering: a fifth drink on that same non-alcoholic list, Pine for the Days, contains kava — a plant with genuine mild sedative effects, not alcohol and not cannabis, but not inert either. It is not flagged as such on the menu, so order around it if you are avoiding all intoxicants.
venues.pressQuote: For too long, people who don't drink alcohol have been treated as an afterthought in bar spaces. At Rosette, thoughtfully constructed non-alcoholic cocktails and spirits are meant to shine and offer a true bar experience without alcohol.

venues.name: Royal Kumete Kava Lounge
venues.description: Royal Kumete is a Polynesian-owned and operated kava lounge on South Broadway, just north of Evans, and it is the only venue in the Denver metro that frames itself first as a cultural room and second as an alcohol alternative. The house line — where tradition meets tranquility — describes a programme built on the traditional serving of kava with a modern presentation, named for the kumete, the carved wooden bowl kava is prepared and shared from across the South Pacific. It is an evening venue rather than a café, opening at 5pm and running late, in a stretch of South Broadway otherwise given over to tattoo shops, vintage stores and bars. Kava is served; the lounge does not serve alcohol.
venues.longDescription:
Royal Kumete Kava Lounge sits at 2174 South Broadway, a few blocks north of Evans Avenue, on the stretch of the Broadway corridor that runs to tattoo parlours, vintage storefronts and dive bars. It is Polynesian owned and operated, and that is the first thing the business says about itself — ahead of the drinks, ahead of the hours. In a category where most American kava bars present kava as a wellness product or an alcohol substitute, a room run by people from the culture the drink comes from, framing it as the traditional serving of kava with a modern twist, is a genuinely different proposition.

The name carries the point. A kumete is the carved wooden bowl in which kava is prepared and from which it is shared, and across Fiji, Tonga, Samoa and Vanuatu the bowl is the social unit — you sit around it, you are served in turn, you stay for as long as the bowl lasts. The venue's own material builds on the legend of Kava'onau, one of the Tongan origin stories for the plant. The room is fitted to match: softer lighting, earthy herbal aromas, and an emphasis on relaxation rather than intoxication.

Operationally it is an evening lounge, not a daytime café. It opens at 5pm and trades late into the night, which puts it in direct competition with the South Broadway bars around it rather than with the coffee shops. Kava is the drink — the ground root of a South Pacific shrub, infused in water, alcohol-free, earthy and numbing on the lips, mildly sedative, and drunk socially. No alcohol is served at any point.

A practical note before you go. Royal Kumete's published hours are inconsistent across sources — the venue's own listings describe a Monday-through-Saturday evening operation from 5pm, but other listings show far less — and its website is a single-page placeholder rather than a full site. This is a small, owner-run room rather than a chain with a marketing department, and the sensible move is to call ahead on (720) 709-0160 before making a trip across the city. What is not in doubt is the nature of the place: it is a kava lounge, it is Polynesian-run, it serves no alcohol, and it is the only one of its kind on this side of Denver.

venues.name: Royal Sushi & Izakaya
venues.description: Royal Sushi & Izakaya in Queen Village runs a front-of-house izakaya and a twelve-seat omakase counter behind it, and chef-owner Jesse Ito is himself sober — which shows in how the non-alcoholic side is handled. The Yuzu Spritz builds yuzu and lime with plum bitters and soda; the Ginger Mint Smash runs mint and a ginger syrup with lime. Beyond the house builds the fridge is unusually well chosen: Athletic's Upside Dawn at 0.5%, Leitz Eins Zwei Zero sparkling Riesling as a genuine alternative to sake or wine with the food, and Kimino sodas made with Japanese fruit. For a sushi restaurant, having a proper non-alcoholic pairing rather than green tea is the whole point.
venues.hours: Mon closed; Tue-Thu 5pm-10pm; Fri-Sat 5pm-11pm; Sun closed
signatureDrinks: Yuzu Spritz — yuzu, lime, plum bitters, soda
Ginger Mint Smash — mint, ginger syrup, lime
Athletic Brewing Upside Dawn (0.5%) — non-alcoholic golden ale
Leitz Eins Zwei Zero — de-alcoholised sparkling Riesling
Kimino sodas — made with Japanese yuzu and ume
venues.longDescription:
Royal Sushi & Izakaya sits on South 2nd Street in Queen Village and runs as two restaurants in one building: a lively izakaya at the front serving skewers, rice dishes and sake, and behind it a twelve-seat counter where chef-owner Jesse Ito serves one of the most sought-after omakase menus in the country. Ito is himself sober, and the non-alcoholic offer reflects someone who orders from it.

The house builds are restrained in a way that suits the food. The Yuzu Spritz uses yuzu — the intensely aromatic Japanese citrus, more floral and less sweet than lemon — with lime, plum bitters and soda. Plum bitters are the detail worth noting: umeboshi and ume plum carry a salty-sour depth that reads as savoury, and a few dashes give a soda-based drink the bitter complexity it would otherwise lack entirely. The Ginger Mint Smash is the more refreshing of the two, mint and ginger syrup with lime.

The bottled list is where this becomes genuinely useful for a meal. Athletic's Upside Dawn covers the beer drinker. Leitz Eins Zwei Zero is a de-alcoholised sparkling Riesling from a serious Rheingau producer, and it is the important one — sushi is conventionally paired with sake, dry sparkling wine or beer, all of which do the same job of cutting through fat and resetting the palate between pieces. A dry sparkling Riesling with the alcohol removed does that job properly, where green tea does not. Kimino's sodas, made with Japanese yuzu and ume, run alongside.

That is the argument for this entry. At a sushi counter the pairing is part of the meal rather than an accompaniment to it, and the default offer to a non-drinker — tea, or water — quietly removes them from half the experience. A restaurant that stocks a real alternative, run by a chef who does not drink, is one of the few places in Philadelphia where an omakase without alcohol is not a diminished version of the same dinner.

Closed Sunday and Monday; five in the evening until ten midweek and eleven on Friday and Saturday.
venues.pressQuote: Royal Izakaya is one of Philly's most popular restaurants, offering upscale Japanese fare
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: Visit Philadelphia, A Guide to Zero-Proof Restaurants & Bars in Philly, January 2025

venues.name: RSVP Discount Beverage
venues.description: RSVP on Forest Avenue is Portland's serious beverage store, and its non-alcoholic section has grown into the best place in the city to actually buy this category — alcohol-free beers by the shelf, mocktail-ready mixers, sparkling tonics and zero-proof bottles, alongside the beer and wine selection that made its reputation. It is not a dedicated dry shop, and that is worth saying plainly, but with Vena's now a weekday-only operation twenty minutes away in Westbrook, RSVP is the practical answer for anyone in Portland who wants to stock a fridge on a Sunday afternoon. It is a conventional beverage store with a strong alcohol-free section rather than a dedicated dry shop, which is worth knowing in advance.
venues.longDescription:
RSVP Discount Beverage on Forest Avenue in Deering Center is a Portland institution among people who care about what they drink — a large, unglamorous store with genuine depth in beer and wine and staff who know the stock. Over the last few years its non-alcoholic section has expanded from a token shelf into something worth making the trip for.

The range covers the categories that matter: alcohol-free beers in real variety rather than the two national brands most stores carry, mixers and tonics suitable for building drinks, and zero-proof bottles. For anyone drinking at home without alcohol — which is where the overwhelming majority of alcohol-free drinking actually happens — that breadth is worth more than any bar's mocktail list.

It is important to be accurate about what this is. RSVP is not a dedicated dry bottle shop like Ceremony in Norfolk or Point 5 in Richmond; it is a conventional beverage store with a good and growing alcohol-free section. Someone in early sobriety who would rather not walk past walls of spirits should know that before going, and the grade here reflects it honestly.

What makes it matter in Portland specifically is the gap it fills. Vena's Fizz House, the city's historic alcohol-free specialist, is now a weekday-hours shop in Westbrook, twenty minutes inland and closed at weekends. That leaves RSVP as the only place in Portland proper where you can buy a decent range of non-alcoholic drinks on a Sunday afternoon. It opens 9am to 8pm Monday to Saturday and 10am to 6pm on Sunday, which is exactly when people actually shop. Forest Avenue is a short drive from the peninsula rather than a walk, so plan it as an errand rather than a stop on a night out.

venues.name: Runner Up Rooftop Bar & Garden
venues.description: Runner Up is a hidden rooftop bar and garden tucked above the Collingwood Yards creative precinct, reached via a small terrace and elevator off Johnston St. Alongside its cocktails it keeps a genuine no/low line-up: Heaps Normal XPA 0% and Drivers Non-Alc Lager on tap-style pours, NON7 Stewed Cherry & Coffee, a Lyre's Italian non-alcoholic spritz, and a rotating set of house mocktails. It's a relaxed, plant-strewn perch with 270-degree views over Melbourne's inner north.

venues.longDescription:
Runner Up sits on level two above 35 Johnston St, inside the Collingwood Yards arts and enterprise hub. Getting there is part of the appeal — you dart through the Yards' corridors to a small terrace, then take an elevator up to a rooftop with a retractable awning, heaters and 270-degree views across the inner north. The room reads, as Time Out put it, "like being in a sleeker version of your creative mate's sharehouse," with vintage furniture, houseplants, board games and live vinyl DJ sets. It was opened by a crew drawn from some of Melbourne's better-known small enterprises, including A Lounge, Colour Club, Mildlife and Confetti Studio.

The drinks list runs from budget pours to a rotating cocktail menu, and the non-alcoholic options are more than an afterthought. Beer drinkers get Heaps Normal XPA 0%, the Australian-made zero-alc pale, while Drivers Non-Alc Lager turns up on the venue's weekday sundown special (a bargain A$7 alongside the mulled wine). NON7 Stewed Cherry & Coffee — a sparkling grape-based drink from Melbourne's own NON (No Nasty Naturals) — is poured by the glass, and there's a Lyre's Italian-style non-alcoholic spritz built around the Australian Lyre's range.

The house mocktails round out the zero-proof offering, with builds such as the French Raspberry, the Maple Plum Spritz and the Coconut Cold Open. Snacks stay simple — dolmades, olives, chips — so the focus stays on the view and the drinks.

Bookings are limited during peak weekend hours (generally after 5pm), but the space takes reservations outside those windows and hosts larger functions with exclusive hire when arranged out of hours.

venues.name: Søbr Market (The Well)
venues.neighborhood: King West / Fashion District (inside The Well)
venues.description: Søbr Market is a fully non-alcoholic bottle shop and tasting bar on the lower level of Wellington Market, the food hall inside The Well, in Toronto's King West/Fashion District. The Toronto location relocated here at the end of 2025 after opening on Richmond Street, and functions as a retail shop rather than a full bar - every bottle, can, and pour on the shelves is zero-proof. Shoppers can still sit at the in-store tasting bar to sample spirits and de-alcoholized wines before buying, including brands like Lyre's, Ghia, Free Spirits, and Dr. Zero Zero.
venues.address: 486 Front St W, Lower Level (inside Wellington Market), Toronto, ON M5V 0V2, Canada
venues.longDescription:
Søbr Market's Toronto shop occupies the lower level of Wellington Market, the food hall inside The Well - the mixed-use development at 486 Front St W in Toronto's King West/Fashion District. It is a dedicated non-alcoholic bottle shop: no alcohol is sold on the premises, and the shelves are stocked entirely with zero-proof spirits, wines, beers, and ready-to-drink cocktails rather than a bar pouring drinks by the glass.

The Well location relocated here on December 31, 2025, moving from its original Richmond Street storefront into the Wellington Market space. Søbr Market operates as a small Canadian retail chain with a companion online store offering country-wide shipping, and the Toronto shop carries the same curated non-alcoholic lineup - including Lyre's, Ghia, Free Spirits, and Dr. Zero Zero - alongside the wider wine, beer, and spirits categories the company sells nationally.

Despite the move, the shop kept its signature format: an in-store tasting bar where customers can sit down and sample the spirits and de-alcoholized wines before committing to a bottle. "We still have the tasting bar. You can still come and have a seat at our bar and try samples of all of our spirits," co-founder Jessie Halliburton told 6ix Retail in January 2026 - underscoring that even after the relocation, Søbr Market still functions as much as a tasting room as a retail counter.
venues.pressQuote: We still have the tasting bar. You can still come and have a seat at our bar and try samples of all of our spirits.

venues.name: Saba
venues.description: Saba is chef Alon Shaya's modern Israeli restaurant on Magazine Street in Uptown New Orleans, the flagship of his Pomegranate Hospitality group (the name means "grandfather" in Hebrew). Known for blistered wood-fired pita baked steps from the table, it opened in 2018 and earned a 2025 Michelin Bib Gourmand. IMPORTANT CORRECTION: Saba's gazoz — the sparkling Israeli soda it is best known for — is served alcoholic on the current menu. All three seasonal builds are $18 and contain spirits: strawberry lemon with bourbon, cucumber agave with tequila, and pineapple shrub with white rum. Do not order a gazoz assuming it is zero-proof. The genuinely non-alcoholic offering is narrower: Athletic Brewing's Upside Dawn ($6) is the only NA beer, and there is a carefully built coffee and tea list with Moroccan mint tea and a seasonal herbal tea ($10 each), an iced halva latte ($8), cold brew ($6) and a pot of coffee for two ($8). Dinner Wednesday to Sunday, brunch Friday to Sunday.
venues.address: 5757 Magazine St, Suite A, New Orleans, LA 70115
venues.hours: Mon-Tue closed; Wed-Thu 5pm-8pm; Fri 11am-9pm; Sat 10:30am-9pm; Sun 10:30am-2:30pm & 5pm-8pm
venues.longDescription:
Saba opened on Magazine Street in 2018 as Alon Shaya's modern Israeli restaurant and the flagship of Pomegranate Hospitality, the group he founded with his wife Emily in 2017. The name means grandfather in Hebrew. Shaya was born in Israel, raised in Philadelphia and is now a New Orleanian, and he won the James Beard Award for Best Chef: South in 2015 for his cooking at Domenica, before the restaurant that carried his own name took Best New Restaurant in 2016 — both awards predate Saba, which has its own 2025 Michelin Bib Gourmand. The signature is wood-fired pita baked steps from the table, and dinner runs Wednesday to Sunday with brunch from Friday.

One thing here needs stating plainly, because getting it wrong would matter. Saba is known for gazoz, the sparkling Israeli soda built on fruit and house syrups, and it would be reasonable to assume that is the zero-proof drink on the menu. It is not. Every gazoz on the current list is $18 and contains a spirit: strawberry lemon with bourbon, cucumber agave with tequila, pineapple shrub with white rum. Ask before ordering one. What is genuinely alcohol-free is smaller but real. Athletic Brewing's Upside Dawn is the only non-alcoholic beer at $6. The rest sits in a coffee and tea list that has clearly had thought put into it rather than being a default: Moroccan mint tea and a rotating seasonal herbal tea at $10 each, an iced halva latte at $8 that turns the restaurant's own sesame-sweet register into a drink, cold brew at $6 and a pot of coffee that serves two. For a meal built around bread, hummus and wood fire, tea at that level is a fair pairing and the halva latte is genuinely worth ordering. But this is a restaurant with an excellent kitchen and a thin zero-proof list, not a destination for the drinks — and the one drink it is famous for is not one of them.
venues.pressQuote: Saba, which means grandfather in Hebrew, gives diners a portrait of modern Israeli cuisine with an eye to the generations of immigrants and the influences who helped shape it.

venues.name: Sacred Springs Kombucha
venues.description: Sacred Springs is an urban kombucha micro-taproom at 1059 Wealthy Street SE, opened in December 2018 by Joel Andrus and Geoff Lamden after several years of brewing without a permanent home. Twelve rotating taps pour house kombucha, with bottles and howlettes to take away and a short food menu built on bagel sandwiches from Grand Rapids Bagel. Named brews include Root of Life, made with beets, ginger and turmeric; Flower of Life, with jasmine, elderberries and hibiscus; Thursday Knight, a chamomile lavender; Trop Hopics, a pineapple and hops build; and The Grapeful Harvest, made with concord grape. Note that the taproom also serves hard kombucha and mead, so it is not an alcohol-free room.
venues.address: 1059 Wealthy St SE, Grand Rapids, MI 49506
venues.longDescription:
Sacred Springs began as a kombucha brand and spent several years selling into the Grand Rapids market before Joel Andrus and Geoff Lamden opened a taproom of their own at 1059 Wealthy Street SE in early December 2018. The pair had wanted a bricks-and-mortar site from the beginning — "We have always wanted the taproom," Andrus told Grand Rapids Magazine at the opening. "We believe that we can reach the community with a brick and mortar." The room is deliberately small, a micro-taproom rather than a brewery hall, and sits on the Wealthy Street stretch in East Hills within a few minutes' walk of Chartreuse Sisters and Buffalo Traders Lounge. Twelve taps rotate through the house range, with bottles and howlettes sold to go, and the food offer is short and complementary rather than a full kitchen: bagel sandwiches supplied by Grand Rapids Bagel.

The brewing is where the interest lies, because the flavours are built as compositions rather than as fruit sodas. Root of Life is made with beets, ginger and turmeric; Flower of Life with jasmine, elderberries and hibiscus; Thursday Knight is a chamomile lavender; Trop Hopics puts pineapple with hops, borrowing the aromatic trick that makes an IPA read as fruit-forward; and The Grapeful Harvest is built on concord grape, which in Michigan is a local ingredient rather than an imported one. Kombucha is tart, tannic and lightly effervescent, which makes it one of the more convincing substitutes for a dry sparkling wine or a sour beer, and a flight across twelve taps is a genuine tasting exercise. One important qualification, and the reason this venue is rated a three rather than a five: Sacred Springs serves hard kombucha and mead alongside the standard range, so a guest who is avoiding alcohol needs to order deliberately rather than assume the whole board is safe. This is worth stating plainly because the venue reads, at a glance, like a fully alcohol-free room — it is a kombucha taproom, the branding is wellness-adjacent, and most of the twelve taps are non-alcoholic. But hard kombucha typically runs between four and seven percent ABV and is poured from the same style of tap into the same style of glass, which makes it one of the easier things in this guide to be handed by mistake. Ask which taps are the standard range before ordering, and be specific if someone else is buying.

With that caveat understood, the taproom is a genuinely useful room. Standard kombucha carries trace alcohol from fermentation, in the same range as a ripe banana or a sourdough loaf and well under the 0.5 percent threshold that defines a non-alcoholic drink in the United States, so it sits comfortably within what most people avoiding alcohol will drink. The tartness is the point: it gives a glass the acid backbone that fruit juice lacks and soda cannot fake, which is why it works where a sweet mocktail does not. The taproom opens Wednesday through Sunday, noon to 7pm, closed Monday and Tuesday, and sits within a short walk of Chartreuse Sisters, The Winchester and Buffalo Traders Lounge on the same Wealthy Street corridor.
venues.pressQuote: We have always wanted the taproom. We believe that we can reach the community with a brick and mortar.

venues.name: The Sacred Vortex Teahouse & Kombuchery
venues.description: The Sacred Vortex is an alcohol-free teahouse, kombuchery and kava bar on Lorain Avenue in Ohio City. David Kovatch and his wife Julie Moran took the building that Platform Beer Co. had used as its original Ohio City taproom — one of the addresses that defined Cleveland's craft beer boom — and reopened it in late summer 2024 as a room where nothing served contains alcohol; the symbolism was not lost on anyone locally. Kovatch already ran Sacred Waters in Lakewood, Ohio's first kava bar, and this is the larger, more ambitious expression of the same idea, with a lengthy bar, soft seating, communal high-tops and a substantial patio. It serves kava by strain, kombucha brewed on site, botanical sodas, adaptogen drinks, tea and coffee, plus named alcohol-free mixed drinks, and runs to 2am most nights. Cleveland Scene readers voted it Best Alcohol-Free Bar in 2025 and 2026. Kava and kratom-based drinks are part of the menu.
venues.longDescription:
David Kovatch and his wife Julie Moran took the Lorain Avenue building that Platform Beer Co. had used as its original Ohio City taproom — one of the addresses that defined Cleveland's craft beer boom — and reopened it in late summer 2024 as a room where nothing served contains alcohol. The symbolism was not lost on anyone locally. Kovatch already ran Sacred Waters in Lakewood, which he opened in 2022 as Ohio's first kava bar; the Sacred Vortex is the larger, more ambitious expression of the same idea, with a lengthy bar, soft seating, communal high-tops and a substantial patio. Cleveland Scene readers voted it Best Alcohol-Free Bar in both 2025 and 2026, with Sacred Waters as runner-up and Verbena Free Spirited, which closed in September 2026, third — the whole podium, in other words, went to rooms that opened in the last four years.

The menu is built around functional drinks rather than imitations of cocktails. Kava is poured by strain — Vanuatu, Tonga, Fiji, Solomon, Samoan and Purple Temu — and also mixed into longer drinks such as a piña colada of pineapple, orange juice, coconut and oat milk. The kombucha is brewed on site, including a version fermented from kratom tea, and it anchors mixed drinks like the Moscow Mule of ginger, lime and kombucha. Other named builds include the Lake Erie Breeze of pineapple, mango, passionfruit and coconut, and the Lavender Serenity of blackberry, lavender and lemonade. Botanical sodas, drinks built on adaptogens and nootropics, coffee and a broad loose-leaf tea list fill out the rest; food is limited to vegan snacks and outside food is welcome, with nearby restaurants filling the gap.

Programming is much of the draw. Live bands, open mics, karaoke, yoga, meditation and creative-writing workshops run through the week, and the bar keeps genuinely late hours — 2am Tuesday through Saturday — which is the practical argument for it. Kovatch frames the whole thing as community infrastructure rather than a beverage business: these are safe spaces for people to come and build community, he told Cleveland Scene, and that is what the business is about.
venues.pressQuote: There's this huge sober-curious movement going on. There are a lot of people who are waking up to the fact that alcohol is not good for you and are looking for an alternative.

venues.name: Sacred Waters Kava Bar
venues.description: Sacred Waters is an alcohol-free ethnobotanical bar on Detroit Avenue in Lakewood, and the room that started Northeast Ohio's kava scene. David Kovatch opened it in 2022 as Ohio's first kava bar, with Mike Young and three further partners, after encountering kava while travelling and coming home to look for a space; it traded earlier as Muddy Waters Kava Bar, which is how some older listings still refer to it. Kovatch has been sober for more than a decade. It pours kava by the shell and by origin — Vanuatu, Tonga, Solomon Isle — alongside cold-brew kava lattes, spritzers, a kava mule, responsibly sourced botanical teas and coffee, and stays open to midnight or 1am seven nights a week. NOTE: it also serves kratom, kanna and blue lotus — psychoactive botanicals rather than alcohol substitutes, and worth knowing before you go.
venues.longDescription:
Sacred Waters occupies a Detroit Avenue storefront in Lakewood and is the room that started Northeast Ohio's kava scene. David Kovatch opened it in 2022 as Ohio's first kava bar, with Mike Young and three further partners, after encountering kava while travelling and coming home to look for a space; it operated earlier under the Muddy Waters Kava Bar name, which is still how some older listings refer to it. Kovatch has been sober for more than a decade and describes the appeal in physical terms — kava melts the stress and anxiety away and leaves a clean euphoric feeling, as he put it to Cleveland Magazine. He went on to open the larger Sacred Vortex in Ohio City on the same alcohol-free premise, and Cleveland Scene readers voted Sacred Waters runner-up for Best Alcohol-Free Bar in 2026.

Kava is served traditionally, by shell and by origin, and priced accessibly: Solomon Isle at around $3.50, Vanuatu at $4, Tonga on a wider scale depending on preparation. It is also blended into longer drinks — cold-brew kava lattes, kava spritzers and a kava mule sit around $7 — and responsibly sourced botanical teas, coffee and non-alcoholic botanical cocktails round out the list. The hours are much of the point: open to midnight Sunday through Wednesday and 1am Thursday through Saturday, it is somewhere to go late without drinking, in a suburb where that otherwise means a diner. Kovatch keeps the room deliberately low-key and describes walking in as walking into his living room.

One thing to be clear about: Sacred Waters is an ethnobotanical bar, not simply a non-alcoholic one. Alongside kava it serves kratom, kanna and Egyptian blue lotus, and mixes kratom into drinks. These are psychoactive botanicals with their own effects, risks and interactions, and they are a different proposition from a zero-proof cocktail — anyone choosing an alcohol-free venue for recovery reasons should weigh that. The Lakewood room is now the only Sacred Waters; a second bar in North Olmsted is no longer listed on the company's own site.
venues.pressQuote: Alcohol can spur great conversation. With kava, the conversations are more lasting, more worthwhile.

venues.name: Sadie's
venues.description: Sadie's is a modern Mediterranean-American restaurant in Nashville's Edgehill Village, opened in September 2021 in the former Taco Mamacita space on the corner of Villa Place. It belongs to Red Pebbles Hospitality, the local group led by Howard Greenstone and Ken Levitan that also runs Adele's, The 404 Kitchen and Shep's Delicatessen, and the kitchen is mezze-driven and share-focused with vegetarian and gluten-free options throughout. For non-drinkers, Sadie's keeps a dedicated "Mocktails" section priced flat at $8 and built from fresh purées, citrus and house sodas rather than bought-in zero-proof spirits: Pathos (passionfruit, lime, hibiscus ginger beer), Pineapple Express (mint, almond orgeat, lime, pineapple soda) and Guava Ginger (guava purée, ginger, lime, guava soda). The list rotates — a Blueberry Butterfly and, more recently, a Strawberry Lemonade have both come and gone. Two non-alcoholic beers, Athletic Lite and an Untitled Art juicy IPA, round out the options, and mocktail specials are part of the weekday happy hour.
