venues.longDescription:
Soft Bar is an all-day, fully alcohol-free cafe and cocktail bar at 200 Banker Street in Greenpoint, Brooklyn, opened in September 2025 by Bravo "Summer House" personality Carl Radke. By day it serves premium coffee, espresso, matcha and teas alongside light bites; in the evening it pours what the team calls "soft cocktails" — zero-proof drinks built by beverage director Richard Millwater, previously of Eleven Madison Park and Clemente Bar. Radke's framing of the concept is deliberate: "We don't make mocktails here, we make soft cocktails. It's an elevated, sophisticated, premium non-alcoholic drink."

The nine soft cocktails are built on the serious end of the non-alcoholic spirits market, and the bar layers several of them in one glass rather than making one-for-one swaps. Bitter Beginning stacks Three Spirit Social, Pathfinder and roots divino rosso over cherry sarsaparilla — three different alcohol-free products in a single drink, which is how you build the depth a bitter aperitif needs. Foam Party runs jasmine-infused Seedlip Grove and roots divino bianco against acidified pineapple, almond orgeat and coffee under a jasmine foam. Garden Party is the savoury outlier, taking almave blanco into tomato, basil, lemon thyme and lemon verbena with aquafaba for texture — aquafaba being the liquid from cooked chickpeas, which whips like egg white and is how a shaken drink gets its head without egg or dairy.

The cafe list is a menu in its own right rather than an afterthought: Steel Magnolia pairs lavender earl grey with espresso or matcha under a salted honey cloud, Low Flame runs hazelnut and reishi cacao with maple, and Indigo Muse is a butterfly pea flower milk tea. Bar snacks run to citrus-marinated Castelvetrano and Nicoise olives, a house mix of roasted chickpeas and fava beans with urfa chili and thyme, and chili snap peas with lime and sesame.

One thing to know before ordering, because our readers include people in recovery: every soft cocktail is built around a functional botanical, and the menu prints it beside each drink — ashwagandha, reishi, lion's mane, damiana leaf, California poppy, cordyceps, ginseng and rhodiola among them. None of these is alcohol, and the bar is entirely alcohol-free. But they are active ingredients rather than flavourings, and anyone on medication, pregnant, or who would simply rather drink something inert should say so at the bar and order from the cafe side instead.

It is closed Mondays, and opens at eight in the morning the rest of the week, running to ten at night Tuesday through Saturday and seven on Sunday.
venues.pressQuote: Soft Bar serves well-crafted N/A cocktails in a chill space.

venues.name: SoHo Social
venues.description: SoHo Social is a restaurant and bar in downtown Homewood, the walkable suburb immediately south of Birmingham over Red Mountain, and it will build any of its signature seasonal cocktails as a mocktail — a policy Bham Now recorded in its January 2026 guide to the city's non-alcoholic drinking. Because those cocktails rotate with the season, the alcohol-free versions do too, so what is available in August is not what was available in January. It is also the only venue in this guide serving from 11am to 10pm seven days a week, which makes it the reliable option when the downtown rooms are shut.
venues.longDescription:
Homewood is the suburb over Red Mountain from downtown Birmingham, and its centre is one of the few genuinely walkable town cores in the metro. SoHo Social sits in the middle of it, functioning as a neighbourhood restaurant and bar rather than a destination — which is exactly the role that makes it useful here.

The alcohol-free offer is a policy rather than a list: any of the bar's signature seasonal cocktails can be built as a mocktail, which Bham Now documented in its January 2026 round-up of non-alcoholic drinking in Birmingham. This directory usually treats "we can make anything without alcohol" as a weak answer, and the grade of three reflects that. What lifts it above the usual version is the word seasonal. A bar with a rotating signature list is working from a live pantry of house syrups, shrubs and infusions, and those components are what an alcohol-free build actually needs — the spirit is the easiest part to leave out when everything else is made in-house.

The practical case is stronger than the programme. SoHo Social serves 11am to 10pm Monday through Saturday and 11am to 9pm on Sunday: seven days, all day, no closed evening. Several of Birmingham's better alcohol-free rooms shut on Sunday and Monday and none of the downtown bars open before four. If the question is where a family, or someone who does not drink, can reliably go on a Sunday lunchtime in this metro, this is close to the only answer in the guide.

No signature drinks are recorded, deliberately: the mocktails mirror a rotating cocktail list, so any specific name would be wrong within a season. Ask what the current signatures are and have one built without the spirit.
venues.pressQuote: Soho Social can make any of its signature seasonal cocktails into a delicious mocktail

venues.name: Sol & Luna
venues.description: Sol & Luna is a Latin-European rooftop bistro on level 17 of CapitaSpring, the tower in the middle of Singapore's financial district, with an outlook across the CBD towards the Marina Bay waterfront. The kitchen works across Italian, French, Portuguese and Spanish cooking on an all-day menu, and the bar keeps named zero-proof mocktails on the list rather than improvising them on request. The one documented in the local press is the Dous Et Frais, a bright, layered build of fresh passion fruit, honeycomb syrup, cinnamon and purple cabbage soda — the cabbage supplying colour and a faint earthiness that stops it reading as simply sweet. The sunset view is the main draw.
signatureDrinks: Dous Et Frais - fresh passion fruit, honeycomb syrup, cinnamon and purple cabbage soda
venues.longDescription:
CapitaSpring is one of the more distinctive towers in Singapore's financial district, a 51-storey building threaded with planted sky gardens, and Sol & Luna occupies a rooftop position on level 17. The view is the reason most people come: it takes in the surrounding CBD and reaches out towards the Marina Bay waterfront, and it is at its best in the hour before sunset, when the office towers below start to light up.

The kitchen describes itself as Latin-European and works across four cuisines — Italian, French, Portuguese and Spanish — on a menu that runs all day rather than splitting into rigid services. That makes it flexible in a way that suits a group with mixed plans, and it is one of the few rooftop venues in the district that is as workable at lunch as it is in the evening.

For a non-drinker the relevant point is that the zero-proof drinks are named items on the list rather than something assembled on request. The build documented in the local press is the Dous Et Frais, which layers fresh passion fruit with honeycomb syrup, cinnamon and a purple cabbage soda. That last ingredient is the interesting one: purple cabbage brings both a striking colour and a faint earthy, vegetal edge, and it stops the drink collapsing into the tropical sweetness that passion fruit and honey would otherwise produce on their own. It is a genuine piece of construction rather than a juice blend. The wider zero-proof selection has not been documented in as much detail, so it is worth asking what else the bar is running when you sit down — but the intent is clearly there, and in a rooftop setting of this kind that is not something to take for granted.

venues.name: Solar Intentions
venues.description: Solar Intentions is a 100% non-alcoholic bottle shop and hangout in Chicago's Edgewater neighborhood, proudly lesbian-owned and stocked with NA beers, wines, spirits, and RTD cocktails for both browsing and on-site sipping.
venues.address: 1056 W Bryn Mawr Ave, Chicago, IL 60660
venues.longDescription:
Tucked into the historic Bryn Mawr corridor of Edgewater, about a block from the Bryn Mawr Red Line stop, Solar Intentions is Chicago's dedicated zero-proof bottle shop and social hangout. Every product on the shelves and in the cold fridge is non-alcoholic — there is no split personality here between an NA section and a full bar. The 1,000-square-foot, ground-level storefront is fully accessible and designed to function as a genuine third space: you can grab something to drink on-site, browse the retail shelves for a bottle to take home, or simply settle in for an event. It draws sober locals, sober-curious visitors, and anyone who just doesn't feel like drinking that day.

The shop is the project of owner Morgan Martinez, who opened Solar Intentions in April 2025 after a $47,000 Kickstarter campaign. Martinez reached one year of intentional sobriety on January 1, 2023, and shaped the shop around her own interests in astrology and community — the aesthetic leans into tarot and cosmic imagery rather than the clinical wellness branding common to the NA category. The retail selection spans NA beer, wine, spirits, and ready-to-drink canned mocktails, with a cold case for anything you want to open right there on the couch. Pick-up and local delivery are also available through the website.

Solar Intentions stands out in Chicago's growing sober scene because it isn't a bar trying to accommodate non-drinkers — it was built from scratch for them. The vibe is relaxed and neighborhood-focused: regulars linger to talk, the space hosts community events and workshops, and the ownership is visibly present. No dress code, no reservations needed for a casual visit. It's a good fit for solo explorers new to the NA category, sober LGBTQ+ Chicagoans looking for a home base, or anyone wanting a social outing that doesn't revolve around alcohol. The Bryn Mawr Red Line stop makes it easy to reach from anywhere on the North Side.
venues.pressQuote: Solar Intentions debuted as an LGBTQ+-friendly bottle shop and lounge for the sober and sober-curious while it waits on permits to build out a bar.

venues.name: Sollip
venues.description: Sollip is a Michelin-starred, Korean-influenced modern-European tasting-menu restaurant tucked in the backstreets near London Bridge, run by husband-and-wife team Woongchul Park and Bomee Ki. Alongside its wine list it offers a dedicated non-alcoholic pairing that sommelier Vita Gargiulo says is fast becoming more popular than wine. The soft pairing is built bespoke with the kitchen rather than pulled off a shelf, running house-made pours like a coffee kombucha and a burnt-cabbage juice with lemon-thyme oil that track the tasting menu course for course.
venues.address: Unit 1, 8 Melior Street, London SE1 3QP, United Kingdom
venues.hours: Mon-Tue closed; Wed-Thu 6pm-11pm; Fri-Sat 12pm-3pm & 6pm-11:30pm; Sun closed
signatureDrinks: Coffee kombucha - paired with the Mont Blanc dessert of chestnut cream, pine nuts, crispy rice and tonka bean Chantilly
Burnt cabbage juice with lemon thyme oil - served with barbecued wagyu, Jerusalem artichoke, jangajji and baechu kimchi puree
venues.longDescription:
Sollip holds one star in the 2026 Michelin Guide and sits in a quiet new-build just off Melior Street, in the shadow of the Shard a short walk from London Bridge station. The name means 'pine needle' in Korean, and the kitchen of husband-and-wife chefs Woongchul Park and Bomee Ki plates Korean flavours through French technique and British seasonal produce across a roughly seven-course dinner tasting menu and a shorter lunch.

What makes it a genuine non-alcoholic destination is that the drink pairing is treated with the same creativity as the food. Sommelier Vita Gargiulo told Club Oenologique that the restaurant's soft pairing is 'fast becoming more popular than wine,' and that the team works directly with the kitchen so each pour is designed around a specific dish rather than assembled from bottled soft drinks.

The non-alcoholic flight leans on house-made and low-intervention builds: a coffee kombucha poured alongside the Mont Blanc dessert of chestnut cream, pine nuts, crispy rice and tonka-bean Chantilly, and a burnt-cabbage juice cut with lemon-thyme oil served with barbecued wagyu, Jerusalem artichoke, jangajji and baechu kimchi puree. A spruce-tip sorbet palate cleanser nods to the restaurant's name.

The room itself is small and understated - graceful and modest, in Time Out's words - which keeps the focus on the plates and the glass in front of you. For a non-drinker, the appeal is a serious, chef-led alcohol-free pairing at a fine-dining level rather than a token mocktail bolted onto the menu.
venues.pressQuote: There really is no limit to creativity when it comes to soft pairing.

venues.name: Sonder Social Club
venues.description: Sonder Social Club was Dunedin's first craft cocktail bar and has been voted the best in Tampa Bay more than once, known for inventive house ingredients like its Golden Grahams-infused "Sonder Milk." Non-drinkers aren't an afterthought: signature drinks such as the Sky Miles can be made as mocktails, and the bartenders will build custom zero-proof drinks on request.  Opened by Zachary and Christina Feinstein, who were specific from the outset that guests should have a mocktail option whether abstaining or simply curious — which is why the zero-proof work draws on the same house syrups, infusions and milks as the full menu.
venues.longDescription:
Sonder Social Club opened on Douglas Avenue as Dunedin's first craft cocktail bar, run by the Feinstein Group — the husband-and-wife team of Zachary and Christina Feinstein — and has been voted the best cocktail bar in Tampa Bay more than once since. It is known locally for house ingredients that sound like jokes and are not, chief among them Sonder Milk, infused with Golden Grahams, and for a deliberate no-Wi-Fi policy intended to make people talk to each other.

Its relevance here rests on a decision made at the outset rather than added later. Christina Feinstein was specific that guests should have a mocktail menu to choose from whether they were abstaining or simply wanted something different — which is why the zero-proof options are not a separate, lesser list but a property of the main one. Signature drinks including the Sky Miles can be built without alcohol, and the bartenders will construct custom spirit-free drinks on request, drawing on the same house syrups, infusions and milks that make the full-strength menu what it is.

That model has a real advantage over a fixed mocktail list: a bar this ingredient-driven can put its best work into a zero-proof glass, rather than confining a non-drinker to two builds chosen months ago. It also has a limitation worth knowing — with no printed section, ordering means a conversation, which is easy at a quiet hour and less so at midnight on a Saturday.

Practical notes: it opens at 4pm daily and runs to midnight midweek and 2am at weekends. The no-Wi-Fi rule is enforced. It is a full craft cocktail bar; the alcohol-free work is genuine and made to order rather than a section of the menu.  Ask early in the evening rather than at midnight, when the bar is at its busiest and a conversation is harder to have.
venues.pressQuote: If you can't or don't want to drink, that doesn't mean you have to feel left out. You can still have something pretty to sip on.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Christina Feinstein, co-owner, Sonder Social Club

venues.name: Songbird
venues.description: Songbird opened in July 2026 on East Whitaker Mill Road near Raleigh's Five Points as an all-day room — Willow House espresso, cold-press juices and seasonal smoothies from 8am, turning into an ingredient-driven bar with small plates in the evening. Between a third and a half of the drinks menu is non-alcoholic depending on the season, and every item is labelled with its ABV so you can see exactly what you are ordering; low-proof and THC drinks are labelled on the same system. That labelling policy is the most non-drinker-friendly design decision of any bar in the metro. The zero-proof build it has been written up for, "I'll Still Have What Meg's Having", runs Rasāsvāda's Rose Bergamot with rose cordial, lime and a rose-strawberry soda, but the list moves with the season. Founded by Meg Paradise and Charlie Blue Arm.
venues.address: 1020 E Whitaker Mill Rd, Raleigh, NC 27608
signatureDrinks: I'll Still Have What Meg's Having — Rasāsvāda Rose Bergamot, rose cordial, lime, rose-strawberry soda
venues.longDescription:
Songbird is the most significant thing to happen to non-alcoholic drinking in the Triangle in years, and it only opened in July 2026. Founded by Meg Paradise and Charlie Blue Arm on East Whitaker Mill Road near Five Points, it runs as a single continuous room from eight in the morning to late — seasonal coffee, tea, cold-press juice and smoothies in the daytime, an ingredient-driven bar and small-plates menu in the evening.

The reason it matters is structural rather than decorative. Between a third and a half of the drinks menu is non-alcoholic at any given time, varying with the season, and the bar labels every item on the list with its ABV. That second detail is the one that non-drinkers notice: it removes the need to ask, to explain, or to trust that a server understood the question. A drink that is zero is marked zero. The menu also runs low-proof and THC options, which are labelled on the same system — worth knowing if you are avoiding all intoxicants rather than alcohol specifically.

The drinks themselves are built around what is actually growing in North Carolina, which gives the seasonal rotation a real basis rather than a marketing one. The zero-proof build the bar has been written up for is "I'll Still Have What Meg's Having", made with Rasāsvāda's Rose Bergamot, a rose cordial, lime and a rose-strawberry soda — floral and tart rather than sweet. Because the list moves with the season, expect the specific drinks to change; the proportion of the menu that is alcohol-free is the part that holds.

The daytime programme is genuinely a programme rather than a coffee machine in the corner — the roaster is Willow House, and the juices and smoothies are made in house. For anyone looking for a venue that works at 9am and 9pm without the character of the room changing, this is currently the best answer in Raleigh. Note that some early press listed the address as East Franklin Street; the venue's own site gives East Whitaker Mill Road, which is what is used here.
venues.pressQuote: Cocktails range from THC and zero-proof to low- and full-proof, with between one-third and half of the menu non-alcoholic depending on the season, and everything clearly labeled with ABV.

venues.name: Sorekara
venues.description: Two-Michelin-star Japanese tasting counter in Baldwin Park where chef-owner William Shen's multi-hour omakase comes with a genuine non-alcoholic beverage pairing built from fermented teas, pickled fruit juices, and a house-made NA 'Chardonnay' crafted just for the restaurant. It's one of the most ambitious zero-proof pairings in Orlando fine dining, priced and presented with the same seriousness as the wine and sake list.
signatureDrinks: Carrot Soda (carrot juice, yuzu, tea, Japanese ginger soda)
NA Chardonnay (house-made, exclusive to the restaurant)
venues.longDescription:
Sorekara opened in March 2024 in Orlando's Baldwin Park neighborhood from chef-owner William Shen and business partners Johnny and Jimmy Tung, whose tasting menu is built around Japan's 72 micro-seasons and unfolds across several rooms over multiple hours; desserts are helmed by pastry chef Francesco Benedetto, previously of the three-Michelin-starred Quique Dacosta in Denia, Spain. In April 2025 Sorekara became just the second restaurant in Florida, after Miami's L'Atelier de Joël Robuchon, to earn two Michelin stars, cementing it as one of Central Florida's most significant fine-dining destinations; the same year, Sorekara team member Austin Joseph won the Michelin Guide's Florida Service Award.

Alongside its roughly $345 tasting menu, Sorekara offers a dedicated non-alcoholic beverage pairing (around $195) built from fermented teas, de-alcoholized sparkling wine, and pickled fruit juices, plus a house-made non-alcoholic 'Chardonnay' created specifically for the restaurant and not sold anywhere else. Diners are also welcomed with a pre-meal carrot soda, served in the waiting room before the tasting begins.

Located across the street from fellow Baldwin Park restaurant Camille, Sorekara draws visitors from across Florida willing to book far in advance for one of its limited nightly seatings, Thursday through Saturday.
venues.pressQuote: Surreal, just surreal. I'm so happy for the team because I know how hard they work and I just feel so blessed to have everyone I love here.

venues.name: Sorelle
venues.description: Sorelle is a two-story coastal-Italian restaurant in Historic Downtown Charleston, listed in the MICHELIN Guide and helmed by chef Nick Dugan. Its printed drinks list carries a titled Zero Proof section rather than a handful of substitutions, and as of August 2026 it runs to seven items. Three are house builds: the Francoise 75 (Seedlip Grove 42, citrus, bitters and non-alcoholic bubbles), a Dolce Vita of Lupo's aperitivo, pineapple and lime, and a rotating Seasonal Spritz finished with soda water. The rest are bought-in bottles - the St. Agrestis 'Phony Negroni', a Leitz Blanc de Blancs sparkling, Baladin 'Passione in Rosso' and an Untitled Art non-alcoholic Italian pilsner from Waunakee, Wisconsin. House builds are priced at $18 to $19 against $22 for most of the cocktails.

venues.longDescription:
Sorelle sits at 88 Broad Street and spans a mercato, a central bar, a wine room and a dining room across two floors, serving chef Nick Dugan's modern take on Southern Italian cooking with Lowcountry ingredients. The restaurant appears in the MICHELIN Guide, and the bar team has treated the no-and-low list as a standing part of the offer rather than an accommodation made on request. The Zero Proof section is printed on the same page as the cocktails, at prices that sit within a few dollars of the spirited list - $18 and $19 for the house builds against $22 for most of the cocktails - which is the practical signal that a restaurant is taking the category seriously rather than defaulting a non-drinker to soda water.

As of the August 2026 menu that section holds seven items. The Francoise 75 is the most cocktail-like: Seedlip Grove 42 with citrus, bitters and non-alcoholic bubbles, built as a spirit-free answer to the French 75. Dolce Vita pairs Lupo's aperitivo with pineapple and lime, and a Seasonal Spritz rotates with whatever the kitchen is working with, finished with non-alcoholic bubbles and a splash of soda water. The bottled side runs to the St. Agrestis 'Phony Negroni', served bittersweet and tall; Leitz Blanc de Blancs, a crisp de-alcoholised sparkling; Baladin 'Passione in Rosso', a berry spritz with tart sparkle; and an Untitled Art non-alcoholic Italian pilsner brewed in Waunakee, Wisconsin. In summer 2025 the restaurant ran a Tomato Summer collaboration with the local non-alcoholic brand Sipland, headlined by a Tomato Water Martini offered in both spirited and spirit-free versions alongside a Palmetto Paloma. Those drinks were seasonal and are no longer listed, as is the vanilla-cream Sorelle Italian soda and the N/A Aperol-style spritz that once sat in the same section; Dolce Vita is the survivor from that collaboration, and the Seasonal Spritz is where the rotation now happens.
venues.pressQuote: It's just another place to be creative
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Matt Rak, head bartender at Sorelle

venues.name: Soul at The Joseph
venues.description: Soul is the ground-floor bar and restaurant of Le Méridien Columbus, The Joseph, on North High Street in the Short North, open from 6am for breakfast through to late. Its cocktail programme is built around a research-led list called the Lost Cocktails of Columbus, which revives drinks tied to the city's own bar history — the Deshler, the Kahiki Coffee Grog and the Midwestern Negroni among them. A separate printed section headed ZERO-PROOF BEVERAGES carries four built drinks rather than a list of sodas: the Casablanca Fog and the Lawn Dart, both made with Garden Spirit, kiwi, kefir and agave; an Orange Blossom of Lyre's non-alcoholic gin with house orange cordial and New Orleans N/A bitters; and an Old Old Fashioned using Lyre's non-alcoholic whiskey with ginger and non-alcoholic orange bitters.

venues.longDescription:
Soul is the resident bar and restaurant on the ground floor of Le Méridien Columbus, The Joseph, at 620 North High Street — next door to The Guild House and across from Marcella's, on the stretch of the Short North that has become the densest concentration of printed zero-proof menus in the city. It opens at 6am for breakfast and runs through to 11pm on weeknights and 1am on Fridays, which makes it one of the few rooms in the district where a non-drinking guest can get a properly built drink either side of dinner.

The bar's signature work is the Lost Cocktails of Columbus, a researched list that reconstructs drinks connected to the city's own bar and hotel history: the Deshler, named for the downtown hotel; the Kahiki Coffee Grog, a nod to the vanished Kahiki Supper Club; alongside a Pink Squirrel, a Clover Leaf, a Jack Rose and a Midwestern Negroni. Set apart from that list is a printed section headed ZERO-PROOF BEVERAGES, and it is composed rather than defaulted. The Casablanca Fog and the Lawn Dart share a base of Garden Spirit with kiwi, kefir and agave — kefir being an unusual choice that gives both drinks a lactic weight most zero-proof builds lack. The Orange Blossom uses Lyre's non-alcoholic gin with a house orange cordial and New Orleans N/A bitters. The Old Old Fashioned is the one that shows the intent most clearly: Lyre's non-alcoholic whiskey stirred with ginger and non-alcoholic orange bitters, a spirit-forward drink for someone who wants the shape of a whiskey cocktail without the alcohol, rather than something fruit-led. The usual hotel roster of sodas, Fever-Tree mixers and sparkling waters sits beneath, but the four named builds are the reason to go.
venues.pressQuote: Sip on "curiously crafted" concoctions at Le Meridian, The Joseph's resident bar, Soul.

venues.name: Southern Belle
venues.description: Southern Belle is Chef Joey Ward's New American restaurant in Atlanta's Poncey-Highland neighborhood, opened in fall 2019 two doors from the historic Plaza Theatre. Ward, a James Beard-recognized chef who spent years as executive chef at Gunshow, builds shareable, seasonal plates from locally sourced ingredients, paired with craft cocktails, biodynamic wines, and a notably deep zero-proof program. The restaurant is recommended in the MICHELIN Guide. Its bar keeps a standing "Zero Proof" cocktail section — historically 10 to 12 spirit-free drinks at any time, plus an NA pairing option for the kitchen's tasting fare — making it one of the city's most serious nonalcoholic destinations. Current zero-proof cocktails include Fugazi (botanical spirits, floral aperitivo, elderflower), Purple Rain (blueberry, ginger, pea flower, lemon), Secret Siesta (aperitif, agave spirit, grapefruit, habanero), and Amoreena (amaretto, pineapple, lemon). It connects via a passageway to Ward's tasting-menu spot, Georgia Boy.
venues.address: 1043 Ponce de Leon Ave NE, Atlanta, GA 30306

naMenuItems.name: Fugazi

venues.longDescription:
Southern Belle is chef Joey Ward's New American restaurant at 1043 Ponce de Leon Avenue in Poncey-Highland, two doors from the historic Plaza Theatre, opened in autumn 2019. Ward spent years as executive chef at Gunshow before going out on his own, and has been recognised by the James Beard Foundation; the restaurant is recommended in the MICHELIN Guide. A passageway connects it to Georgia Boy, his tasting-menu counterpart, so the two operate as a single building with two very different ambitions.

Its zero-proof programme is among the most serious in the American South, and the numbers are the argument. The bar has historically kept ten to twelve spirit-free cocktails on at any one time — not a token pair, but a list long enough that a non-drinker can have a different drink every course — and offers a non-alcoholic pairing alongside the wine pairing for the kitchen's tasting fare. Resy called it perhaps the queen of nonalcoholic drinks in the city, which is a fair reading of the effort involved in maintaining a list that size.

The drinks reward the attention. Fugazi builds botanical spirits with a floral aperitivo and elderflower. Secret Siesta runs an aperitif and an agave spirit against grapefruit and habanero, using chilli where a lesser drink would use sugar. Amoreena is amaretto, pineapple and lemon. Purple Rain is the one that gets written about: the Atlanta Journal-Constitution described tannic blueberry and the zing of ginger mingling with pea flower, and the colour turning to an earthy indigo when the lemon juice hits.

That tannic note is the technical point. Tannin gives a drink grip and a dry finish, which is precisely what alcohol contributes to a cocktail and precisely what most zero-proof drinks lack. Building it back in deliberately — through tea, blueberry skins or vinegar — is the difference between a drink that stands up to a plate of food and one that does not. Southern Belle is the Atlanta restaurant that most reliably gets that right.
venues.pressQuote: Perhaps the queen of nonalcoholic drinks, Southern Belle offers an extensive menu of thoughtfully prepared and flavorful spirit-free drinks.

venues.name: Southern National
venues.description: Southern National is a chef-driven Southern restaurant in Atlanta's Summerhill neighborhood, opened July 7, 2023 by chef Duane Nutter and restaurateur Reggie Washington, the James Beard-nominated duo behind the airport restaurant One Flew South; it followed an earlier Southern National in Birmingham, Alabama. The kitchen serves globally inspired Southern cuisine, and the bar program — shaped in part by veteran Atlanta bartenders Greg Best and Paul Calvert — carries a genuine zero-proof section alongside its cocktails and wine. The non-alcoholic list is built around named house mocktails such as the Young Mr. Collins (ISH London Botanical, lemon, cane sugar, soda), the Bluegrass Fizz (blueberry-lemongrass-thyme shrub, lime, sparkling water), and the Bella Sparkler (lemon, OJ, pineapple syrup, tonic), plus a bottled St. Agrestis "Phoney Negroni" and Athletic Brewing's Run Wild N/A IPA.
venues.address: 72 Georgia Ave SE, Ste 100, Atlanta, GA 30312
venues.longDescription:
Southern National opened in Summerhill in the summer of 2023 at 72 Georgia Avenue, from chef Duane Nutter and restaurateur Reggie Washington — the James Beard-nominated pair behind One Flew South, the airport restaurant at Hartsfield-Jackson where Nutter broke the rules by putting fancy sushi, elevated Southern cooking and craft cocktails on a terminal menu. It followed an earlier Southern National in Birmingham, Alabama. Nutter was born in Louisiana and raised in Seattle, and calls the restaurant a compilation of his greatest hits; Atlanta Magazine's Christiane Lauterbach wrote in November 2023 that it announces itself from the get-go as an ambitious showcase. The cooking is globally inflected Southern — mussels with shiitake and bacon in Southern greens, berbere-spiced chicken thighs on maque choux, sheet-pan biscuits with pepper jelly.

The bar was created by Greg Best and Paul Calvert, the pair behind Ticonderoga Club and two of the most consequential bartenders in the city, and the non-alcoholic list carries that seriousness rather than sitting apart from it. The Young Mr. Collins is built on ISH London Botanical with lemon, cane sugar and soda. The Bluegrass Fizz uses a blueberry, lemongrass and thyme shrub with lime and sparkling water. The Bella Sparkler runs lemon and orange juice with pineapple syrup and tonic. A bottled St. Agrestis Phoney Negroni and Athletic Brewing's Run Wild non-alcoholic IPA round it out.

The shrub in the Bluegrass Fizz is the tell of who designed this list. A shrub is a vinegar-based fruit syrup — an old preservation method that pre-dates refrigeration — and vinegar does the one thing zero-proof drinks most often lack: it makes the drink finish dry and sharp instead of trailing off sweet. Bartenders of Best and Calvert's generation use it as a matter of course, and its presence here means the non-alcoholic drinks were built by the same hands and to the same standard as the rest.

Dinner runs Monday to Saturday, with brunch on Sundays.
venues.pressQuote: The restaurant announces itself from the get-go as an ambitious showcase.

venues.name: Southernside Brewing Co.
venues.description: Southernside Brewing sits on Delano Drive beside the Swamp Rabbit Trail, north-west of downtown Greenville, in a large indoor-outdoor space built around a beer garden. Its position on alcohol-free drinking is stated openly in the local coverage — the bar is happy to craft an alcohol-free drink on request — which for a brewery taproom is more than most manage. Open 11am to 10pm Tuesday through Thursday, to 11pm on Friday and Saturday and 9pm on Sunday, with the trail running past the door, it is the most practical daytime stop in this guide.
signatureDrinks: Mocktail (NA: enjoy a non-alcoholic cocktail! pick sweet or spicy!)

naMenuItems.name: Mocktail
naMenuItems.description: enjoy a non-alcoholic cocktail! pick sweet or spicy!

venues.longDescription:
Southernside Brewing is on Delano Drive in the neighbourhood it is named for, just north-west of downtown Greenville and directly on the Swamp Rabbit Trail — the converted rail corridor that runs through the city and is the reason a lot of people are here in the first place, on foot or on a bike.

That setting is the argument for the listing. A brewery on a trail is somewhere people arrive mid-afternoon having done something else, which is a much easier social context for a non-drinker than a bar at ten at night. The space is large, part indoor and part beer garden, and nobody is counting rounds.

The alcohol-free position is honestly modest and this entry grades it accordingly at three. TOWN Carolina's survey of Greenville's mocktail scene records that Southernside is happy to craft an alcohol-free drink — an on-request offer rather than a printed list, which is normally where this directory stops reading. It is included here for two reasons. The offer is stated publicly rather than having to be extracted at the bar, which removes the social cost of asking. And a brewery is the venue type where a non-drinker most often finds nothing at all, so a taproom that will actually build something is worth knowing about.

What is not documented, and so is not claimed here: any named build, any non-alcoholic beer stocked, or any standing zero-proof section. Ask at the bar and expect to describe what you like rather than to read a menu.

Open 11am to 10pm Tuesday through Thursday, 11am to 11pm on Friday and Saturday, and 11am to 9pm on Sunday. Closed Monday. The all-day hours and the trail access together make it the easiest venue in this guide to fold into a daytime rather than an evening.
venues.pressQuote: Southernside Brewing is happy to craft an alcohol-free drink.
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: TOWN Carolina, Mocktails for Dry July

venues.name: Sovereign Kava
venues.description: Sovereign Kava is North Carolina's first kava bar and a founding piece of Asheville's alcohol-free social scene, open since 2010 — its own slogan is doing its part to keep Asheville weird since then. Its history maps the city's kava scene: Keely Flow and Andrew Procyk left Florida in 2010 to open Vanuatu Kava Bar on South Lexington Avenue, moved to Eagle Street in 2012 as Noble Kava, spent a brief period on Haywood Road in West Asheville in 2015, and settled at 268 Biltmore Avenue in 2017, rebranding as Sovereign Kava around 2019. It sits halfway up the hill between McCormick Field and Mission Hospital, well away from the riverside Biltmore Village that flooded in Helene, and it is dog-friendly and open past midnight. It serves hand-prepared traditional South Pacific ceremonial kava, kava cocktails, kratom and Mitra teas, and local Buchi kombucha. It is alcohol-free but not substance-free — kava and kratom are the house pours — which it discloses openly.
signatureDrinks: Traditional kava, hand-prepared South Pacific style
venues.longDescription:
Sovereign Kava has been part of Asheville since 2010 — its own slogan is doing its part to keep Asheville weird since then — and its history is a small map of the city's kava scene. Keely Flow and Andrew Procyk left Florida in 2010 to open Vanuatu Kava Bar on South Lexington Avenue; it moved to Eagle Street in 2012 and became Noble Kava, spent a brief period on Haywood Road in West Asheville in 2015, and settled at 268 Biltmore Avenue in 2017, rebranding as Sovereign Kava around 2019. The bar sits halfway up the hill between McCormick Field and Mission Hospital, which is a meaningfully different stretch of Biltmore Avenue from the riverside Biltmore Village that flooded in Helene. It is dog-friendly with indoor and outdoor seating, runs live music every Friday and Saturday with no cover, and hosts an open mic that was voted Best of WNC in 2019. The Asheville Citizen-Times captured why people go: oddly enough, one regular said, this place is way more social than an alcohol bar. It opens daily from noon to midnight, later on Wednesday, Friday and Saturday.

What is served needs stating carefully. The bar's own description of its range is traditional kava made by hand the way it has been prepared ceremonially in the South Pacific for centuries, plus kava cocktails, Buchi kombucha, CBD edibles and tinctures — and "Mitra tea" in several varieties. Mitra is the venue's own name for products made from Mitragyna speciosa, which is kratom; the word kratom does not appear anywhere on its website. That distinction matters here more than almost anywhere else in this guide. Kratom is not a mild botanical: as Mountain Xpress reported when covering the region's kava and kratom culture, it carries some forty alkaloids, two of them close to those in morphine, acting as a stimulant at low doses and a sedative at higher ones, and the FDA advises consumers not to use products containing it. Sovereign Kava publishes no dosages and no warning text. Kava itself is psychoactive too. There is no alcohol here, and for some people that is exactly the point — but anyone in recovery should go in knowing precisely what is behind the bar.
venues.pressQuote: Oddly enough, this place is way more social than an alcohol bar.

venues.name: Space Bar
venues.description: Space Bar is a science-fiction-themed molecular mixology lounge at 22 Market Square in Downtown Pittsburgh, opened on 18 November 2023 by Elizabeth Menzel, a retired trauma healer who bills herself as Healer to the Stars, and Dale Thomas Vaughn, a science-fiction writer who works in AI. The room is built around screens of deep space and neon, and Vaughn's stated intent is that a spaceship is inherently optimistic — people need hope, and they want to be a centre for the dreamers. The food is entirely vegetarian, including an Olympus Mons Gyro of oyster mushrooms with house-made socca and a Binary Hummus Platter. The non-alcoholic offering has grown substantially since opening: where early coverage said any cocktail could simply be made virgin, a dated 2026 guide describes five or six standing zero-proof cocktails at any time, including alcohol-free versions of menu drinks and originals, singling out an NA Tartooine Sour. The bar's live menu is published through a system we cannot read, so confirm the current list on arrival. Open from 4pm, closed Mondays.
venues.longDescription:
Space Bar opened on 18 November 2023 at 22 Market Square, and it is exactly as committed to its theme as the name suggests: a room of screens showing the vastness of space, neon, and drinks built with molecular technique. It comes from an unlikely pair. Elizabeth Menzel is a retired trauma healer who goes by Healer to the Stars; Dale Thomas Vaughn is a science-fiction writer who has worked in artificial intelligence with Microsoft and Google. Vaughn's explanation of the point is better than most bar mission statements: a spaceship is inherently optimistic, people need hope right now, and they want to be a centre for the dreamers. Arum Krause built the drinks programme. The kitchen is entirely vegetarian, running to an Olympus Mons Gyro made with oyster mushrooms and house-made socca and a Binary Hummus Platter with edamame and roasted beet hummus. It opens at 4pm, until 11pm most nights and midnight at weekends, and closes on Mondays.

Our rating for this bar has been raised, and the reason is worth setting out. When Space Bar opened, coverage noted it had no dedicated zero-proof menu — any cocktail could be made virgin on request, which is better than nothing but is not a programme. That is no longer the description. A dated 2026 Pittsburgh guide records that the bar keeps five or six non-alcoholic cocktails available at any given time, calls it one of the most robust non-alcoholic cocktail offerings in the city year-round, and singles out an NA Tartooine Sour as a favourite; the bar has also hosted a Pittsburgh mocktail meetup. Molecular technique is genuinely useful here in a way it is not everywhere — foams, gels, clarified juices and smoke give a zero-proof drink the texture and theatre that alcohol usually supplies, which is why a bar like this can make a better alcohol-free cocktail than a conventional one. The honest limitation is that the live menu is published through an ordering system we cannot read, so we cannot list the current five or six by name. Go and ask; there will be more than one.

venues.name: Spark Social House
venues.description: Spark Social House is a daytime cafe and evening bar at 2009 14th Street NW in the U Street Corridor, one block from U Street Metro, billed as the country's first non-alcoholic LGBTQ+ bar and cafe when it opened on 8 March 2025. Co-founded by Nick Tsusaki and Shua Goodwin in the former Gibson space, it runs from 9am to as late as 1am. In December 2025 it added a full liquor licence and adopted a one-for-one menu: every cocktail, wine and beer has a non-alcoholic counterpart, so it is NA-forward rather than dry. Named drinks include Jalapeno Business, It's That Me Espresso, Side Eye, Ultra Violet and Executive Orchard. It also serves kava and functional-mushroom drinks. Voted Best Coffee Shop by LGBTQ+ readers in 2025.
venues.longDescription:
Spark Social House opened on 8 March 2025 at 2009 14th Street NW, in the room that used to be The Gibson, and the Washington Post billed it as the nation's first non-alcoholic LGBTQ+ bar and cafe. Co-founders Nick Tsusaki and Shua Goodwin built it as a room that changes character through the day: from nine in the morning it is a bright working cafe pouring locally roasted Lost Sock coffee, matcha and wellness drinks, with fast wifi, an outlet at every seat and a dog-friendly patio, and by evening it is a lounge. Its own description of what it is aiming at - DC's LGBTQ+ third place, open to everyone - is the clearest statement of the idea. Tsusaki, a former bartender, has framed it around a gap rather than an ideology: DC has more than twenty gay bars, and plenty of people were staying home because none of them was a place for them.

One thing has changed since it opened and it matters. The original programme was fully zero-proof, developed by Shakers alum Salina Flores and Mindful Drinking Fest co-founder Maria Bastasch. In December 2025 the bar took a full liquor licence and moved to a one-for-one menu: every cocktail, wine and beer on the list exists in both a full-strength and a non-alcoholic version. So this is an NA-forward bar rather than a dry one, and anyone choosing it specifically because no alcohol is present should know that alcohol service now runs from 11am to close.

The zero-proof side is properly stocked: non-alcoholic spirits from Lyre's, Ritual and Seedlip, NA beer and cider from Athletic Brewing and Best Day, and NA wines including Giesen, Oddbird and TOST. Current named drinks include Jalapeno Business, made with zero-proof tequila, orange juice, cayenne and Tajin, plus It's That Me Espresso, Side Eye, Ultra Violet, Venetian Sunset, The Spice Boy and Executive Orchard. The bar also serves kava and drinks infused with functional mushrooms, which are alcohol-free but psychoactive, and worth avoiding for anyone steering clear of psychoactives entirely. Practical notes: happy hour runs 4-7pm Monday to Friday, the room goes 21-plus after 8pm on Friday and Saturday, and it is one block from U Street Metro.
venues.pressQuote: the country's first LGBTQ+ non-alcoholic bar/café officially opened its doors on Saturday, March 8

venues.name: Speak in Code
venues.description: Speak in Code is a technique-driven, plant-based cocktail bar tucked down Jackson's Row just off Deansgate, a long-standing fixture of the UK's Top 50 Cocktail Bars where the entire drinks list — ferments, carbonations, distillates and house syrups — is made in-house. Its current menu booklet carries a dedicated 'alcohol free' section rather than mocktails on request, every serve priced at £8. Named zero-proof drinks include the Junebug AF (banana, melon and pineapple fermented into a soda), a house Shandy of Citra hops, Nashi pear, apple and dandelion, and Raspberries + C.R.E.A.M., built on ice-cream-washed Almave 0.0% agave with a carbonic raspberry soda.
signatureDrinks: Junebug AF (banana, melon and pineapple fermented into a soda)
Shandy (Citra hops, Nashi pear, apple, dandelion, CO2)
Raspberries + C.R.E.A.M. (ice-cream-washed Almave 0.0% agave, carbonic raspberry soda)
venues.longDescription:
Speak in Code — styled [SiC] — opened in 2018 on Jackson's Row, a narrow lane running off Deansgate in Manchester's Civic Quarter, close to the Town Hall and Central Library. It is the work of a small, self-consciously nerdy team built around two obsessions: flavour exploration and hip hop. The bar has become a near-permanent fixture of the UK bar-awards circuit, ranked inside the national Top 50 Cocktail Bars — it was named No. 10 in the UK at the 2022 awards and has remained on the list since — and it built that reputation on a fully plant-based, made-from-scratch approach in which fermentation, carbonation, distillation and house syrups all happen on site.

The room reads as an 'industrial New York' den: a cosy, brick-lined space with subdued lighting, dark wood, plush velvet furnishings and kintsugi-style gold repairs on chipped glassware, soundtracked by laid-back lo-fi hip hop. It is deliberately intimate — low-lit and capped at six people per booking — and pairs its forward-thinking cocktails with plant-based comfort food and small plates. The whole operation leans hard on a reuse-and-repurpose ethos, from homemade cordials to banana-skin 'bacon', so little is wasted behind the bar.

Crucially for non-drinkers, the alcohol-free drinks are a named section of the current menu booklet (version 16-3, uploaded June 2026) rather than an off-menu afterthought, and they are built with exactly the same in-house technique as the full-strength list, every one priced at £8. The line-up includes the Junebug AF, in which banana, melon and pineapple are fermented into a house soda; a Shandy carbonated from Citra hops, Nashi pear, apple and dandelion; Raspberries + C.R.E.A.M., which washes Almave 0.0% agave spirit through ice cream and lengthens it with a carbonic raspberry soda; and the [SiC] Chinotto, a bittersweet build of zero-proof Amaro Lucano over house chinotto soda, alongside an alcohol-free Tepache. Because the base spirits used here — Almave and Amaro Lucano 0% — sit outside the usual non-alcoholic-brand roster, the zero-proof drinks feel genuinely of the bar rather than assembled from off-the-shelf bottles.
venues.pressQuote: The forward-thinking, plant-based cocktail menu earns rightful acclaim, and their reuse-and-repurpose approach to creating drinks is as admirable as it is impressive.

venues.name: Speakeasy Central Kava Bar
venues.description: Speakeasy opened in St. Petersburg's Grand Central District in 2020 and trades 7am to 1am every day, with a menu poured by staff the bar calls kavatenders — a job title that tells you how seriously the kava is taken here. The walls carry rotating work by local artists, live music runs every Saturday night, and karaoke and trivia fill other nights of the week. The list extends well past kava to ethnobotanical and loose-leaf teas, coffee, kombucha, yerba mate, soft drinks and snacks. IMPORTANT for readers in recovery: the curated menu is explicitly kava and kratom. Kratom acts on opioid receptors and carries dependence and withdrawal risk that kava does not — ask your kavatender which is which.
venues.longDescription:
Speakeasy opened in St. Petersburg's Grand Central District in 2020 and trades 7am to 1am every day of the week. It pours its drinks through staff the bar calls kavatenders — a coinage that tells you how the room thinks about the job. A bartender's skill is not only mixing but reading the person in front of them and pacing what they are given, and applying that title to kava service signals a bar treating the drink as something requiring knowledge rather than a scoop and a cup.

The room is programmed as a neighbourhood venue rather than a wellness space. Rotating work by local artists hangs on the walls, live music runs every Saturday night, and karaoke and trivia fill other nights of the week. The drinks list extends well past kava — ethnobotanical and loose-leaf teas, coffee, kombucha, yerba mate, soft drinks and snacks — which keeps the room usable across a full day rather than only in the evening.

Kava is the ground root of Piper methysticum, a shrub native to the South Pacific islands, prepared as a cold water infusion and drunk socially across Fiji, Vanuatu, Tonga and Samoa for roughly three thousand years. It contains no alcohol. It tastes earthy and bitter, numbs the lips and tongue on the first mouthful, and is mildly sedative rather than intoxicating in the way alcohol is. Kava exhibits reverse tolerance, meaning regular drinkers usually need less rather than more to feel it, so a first visit is best paced across an hour or two.

The Grand Central District is one of St. Petersburg's most walkable neighbourhoods, dense with independent businesses and bars, and Speakeasy sits on Central Avenue among them rather than tucked into a strip mall. That placement is the point: it is on the same street as the drinking, at the same hours, and going there instead is an ordinary choice rather than a retreat.

One disclosure belongs in the open. The bar's own description of its menu is kava and kratom, curated by its kavatenders — so kratom is an explicit half of the offer here, not a hidden listing. Kratom is the leaf of Mitragyna speciosa, a Southeast Asian tree, and its principal alkaloids act on the opioid receptors; regular use produces tolerance and a genuine withdrawal syndrome, several US states ban it outright, and its concentrated 7-hydroxymitragynine derivatives are under active federal scheduling. Kava has no comparable dependence profile. The upside of a room that staffs a proper counter is that the person serving you can answer the question directly — so ask your kavatender which of the two is in the cup.
venues.pressQuote: Serving tasty, feel-good ethnobotanical beverages in a welcoming atmosphere–we've got something for everyone to enjoy!

venues.name: specialTEA Lounge & Café
venues.description: specialTEA Lounge & Café has traded on Coral Way in Westchester since June 2009 and bills itself as Miami's original tea lounge. The counter carries more than sixty premium loose-leaf teas, from Chinese green and Taiwanese oolong to South African rooibos and Indian spiced chai, served as hot pots, iced teas, London fogs and tea lattes. A full boba programme runs alongside it with classic tapioca pearls, popping pearls and fruit jellies in more than ten flavours, including taro boba cremes, Thai tea lattes and matcha boba. The coffee is USDA organic, fair trade certified and roasted locally, poured as French press, cold brew, lattes and mochas. Frozen drinks include a matcha freeze and a chilly vanilla chai. It stays open until 11pm six nights a week.
venues.longDescription:
specialTEA Lounge & Café sits in the Columbia Shopping Plaza at 10766 SW 24th Street — Coral Way — in the Westchester area of unincorporated Miami-Dade, a short drive from Florida International University. It has been independently run since June 2009 and describes itself as Miami's original tea lounge. The hours are unusual for a suburban cafe and are the reason it belongs on a list like this one: 8am to 11pm Monday through Friday, 11am to 11pm on Saturday, and 11am to 8pm on Sunday, which gives the neighbourhood a place to sit over a drink well after the shopping plaza has gone quiet.

The menu is organised around four drink programmes. The tea list runs past sixty premium loose-leaf varieties spanning Chinese green tea, Taiwanese oolong, South African rooibos and Indian spiced chai, prepared as hot pots, iced teas, London fogs and tea lattes. The boba programme covers classic tapioca pearls, popping pearls and fruit jellies across more than ten flavours, with taro boba cremes, Thai tea lattes and matcha boba called out by name on the shop's own site. Coffee is USDA organic, fair trade certified and locally roasted, served as French press, cold brew, lattes, mochas and a house drink the shop calls its legendary eye opener. A frozen section covers a matcha freeze, a chilly vanilla chai and coffee-free frozen cremes. Food is limited to breakfast sandwiches, lunch plates and vegan cookies in six flavours. The shop's own telephone number is published in letters — (305) 554-TEAS — and it posts as @specialtealounge. Food is a secondary concern to the drinks: breakfast sandwiches in the morning, a short lunch list, and vegan cookies in six flavours at the counter. The room reads as a study cafe as much as a lounge, and the reason it appears in this catalogue is the combination of a large, entirely non-alcoholic named drink list with hours that run three hours past when most of Westchester has closed for the night.

venues.name: Spice Finch
venues.description: Spice Finch is a Mediterranean restaurant on South 17th Street in Rittenhouse whose menu carries a printed "Non-Alcoholic Cocktails" section, priced between $6 and $7 — noticeably cheaper than most zero-proof lists in the city, and two of them drop to $4 at happy hour. Tradewinds builds mint tea with a coriander syrup and lemon, which is the most interesting of the three because coriander seed is a warm, citrusy spice rather than a sweet one. Cooler Than A Cucumber runs cucumber with juniper and lime, using the defining botanical of gin without the gin. French 37.5 is the aperitif-style option, grapefruit and lavender with lemon and tonic. The kitchen opens at four and runs to nine.
signatureDrinks: Tradewinds ($6) — mint tea, coriander syrup, lemon
Cooler Than A Cucumber ($7) — cucumber, juniper, lime

venues.longDescription:
Spice Finch sits on South 17th Street just off Rittenhouse Square, cooking a Mediterranean menu built around spice blends — the name is not decorative, and the kitchen's identity is the pantry. That matters for the drinks, because the three non-alcoholic cocktails on its printed list are built from the same shelf as the food rather than from a separate bottle of syrup.

Tradewinds is the clearest example. It combines mint tea with a coriander syrup and lemon, and coriander seed is the ingredient worth paying attention to: warm and faintly citrusy, closer to orange peel than to the fresh herb, it is one of the defining botanicals in gin. Used in a syrup against mint and lemon, it gives the drink an aromatic backbone that a mint lemonade would never have.

Cooler Than A Cucumber runs the same logic with juniper — the botanical that legally makes gin gin — alongside cucumber and lime. Anyone who misses a gin and tonic will recognise what is happening here immediately; it is the flavour architecture of the drink with the ethanol removed, rather than a substitute pretending to be something else. French 37.5 is the aperitif of the three, grapefruit and lavender lengthened with lemon and tonic, and the tonic's quinine bitterness gives it a genuinely dry finish.

The pricing deserves a mention because it is unusual. At six and seven dollars these are among the cheapest properly-constructed zero-proof drinks in Philadelphia, and two of the three fall to four dollars during happy hour. Most bars price non-alcoholic cocktails within a dollar or two of the alcoholic ones on the grounds that the labour is identical — which is defensible — but the effect is that a non-drinker often pays fourteen dollars for something with no spirit in it. Spice Finch does not, and over an evening that difference is substantial.

The restaurant opens at four in the afternoon on weekdays and adds a late-morning service at weekends, closing at nine throughout.
venues.pressQuote: The dinner menu at Spice Finch is a mix of Mediterranean and Middle Eastern flavors

venues.name: Spirited Away
venues.description: Spirited Away was America's first booze-free bottle shop and it is still the most complete one in New York, now on Eighth Avenue in Chelsea after starting life on Mott Street. Nothing on the shelves contains meaningful alcohol. The buy runs past 100 brands — Seedlip and Ritual Zero Proof alongside Ghia and The Pathfinder, Copenhagen Sparkling Tea, Unified Ferments, non-alcoholic wines from Sovi and Prima Pave, plus beers, bitters, shrubs, amari, mixers and ready-to-drink cocktails. It opens noon to 8pm every day of the week and delivers across Manhattan, free over $100. The shop is not just retail: it runs in-store tastings and events, which for a lot of people is the low-pressure way into the category.
venues.longDescription:
Spirited Away opened in November 2020 as America's first booze-free bottle shop, which makes it a genuinely historic address in this category rather than simply a good one. It has since moved from its original Mott Street home to 228 Eighth Avenue in Chelsea, and it remains the deepest non-alcoholic retail selection in New York City.

The premise is total: there is no alcohol in the shop. Everything on the shelves is at or under 0.5% ABV, which is the legal non-alcoholic threshold and the same trace level found in a ripe banana or a glass of kombucha. What that buys you is a room where you can browse the way anyone browses a wine shop — reading labels, asking questions, changing your mind — without navigating around the thing you are avoiding.

The range runs past a hundred brands and is unusually well spread across the category's real divisions. The established distilled alternatives are here — Seedlip, which effectively created the modern segment, and Ritual Zero Proof, whose spirit analogues are built to be mixed rather than sipped. So are the newer botanical drinks that make no attempt to imitate a spirit at all: Ghia, the aperitif built on fig and yuzu and gentian, and The Pathfinder, a hemp-derived amaro alternative. Beyond spirits the shop carries Copenhagen Sparkling Tea and Unified Ferments for anyone who wants complexity without imitation, non-alcoholic wines from Sovi and Prima Pave, and a full supporting cast of beers, bitters, shrubs, amari, mixers and ready-to-drink cocktails.

Hours are 12pm to 8pm, seven days a week, and delivery covers Manhattan with free shipping over $100.

The part that matters most for anyone new to drinking this way is the programming. Spirited Away runs in-store tastings and events, and tasting before buying is the single best defence against the category's real problem: these bottles are expensive, they vary enormously, and a bad first purchase convinces people the whole category is a con. Being able to try Seedlip next to Ghia next to a sparkling tea, and to ask someone which one behaves like what you actually miss, is worth more than any amount of label-reading. For a visitor, the Chelsea location also sits within a short walk of the Hotel Chelsea's Lobby Bar and a few subway stops from most of the alcohol-free rooms in this guide.

venues.name: Spoon and Stable
venues.description: Spoon and Stable is the North Loop flagship of James Beard Award-winning chef/owner Gavin Kaysen, opened in 2014 inside a 1906 former horse stable. Backing came from mentors Daniel Boulud and Thomas Keller, and the restaurant was a 2015 James Beard nominee for Best New Restaurant and Food & Wine's 2015 Restaurant of the Year. Its zero-proof offering is a genuine, on-menu program: the bar menu carries a dedicated "Spirit Free Libations" section of bar-crafted mocktails, attributed to bar manager Jessi Pollak. Current named pours include the Toasted Oak (pu'er tea, toasted oak, demerara, aromatic bitters), Solstice (blood orange aperitif, blueberry rooibos, lemon, cinnamon), and Café Negroni (Pathfinder hemp amaro, cold brew, blood orange, Floreale). The list rounds out with Oddbird sparkling rosé and non-alcoholic beers from Athletic, Bauhaus, and Heineken 0.0.

venues.longDescription:
Spoon and Stable is Gavin Kaysen's North Loop flagship, opened in 2014 inside a 1906 former horse stable, with backing from his mentors Daniel Boulud and Thomas Keller. It was a 2015 James Beard nominee for Best New Restaurant and Food & Wine's Restaurant of the Year that same year, and it is broadly credited with accelerating the North Loop's turn from warehouse district to the centre of Minneapolis dining. Kaysen himself has since won the James Beard Award for Best Chef: Midwest.

The zero-proof offering is a genuine on-menu programme rather than an accommodation, carried as a dedicated Spirit Free Libations section and attributed to bar manager Jessi Pollak — the same beverage director behind the Temperance Pairing at Kaysen's tasting-counter restaurant Demi next door, which is the strongest signal available that this is a group-wide commitment rather than one room's initiative. The current builds work across registers rather than clustering in fruit: Toasted Oak combines pu'er tea with toasted oak, demerara and aromatic bitters, which is about as close as a non-alcoholic drink gets to the weight and wood of a spirit; Solstice pairs a blood orange aperitif with blueberry rooibos, lemon and cinnamon; and the Café Negroni is built on Pathfinder hemp amaro with cold brew, blood orange and Floreale, covering the bitter end properly. Around them the list carries Oddbird sparkling rosé and non-alcoholic beers from Athletic, Bauhaus and Heineken 0.0, so a table ordering wine has a real parallel rather than a substitute. Mpls.St.Paul Magazine put it simply: "Every picture-perfect plate would pair beautifully with one of bar manager Jessi Pollak's four mocktails." Dinner nightly, with brunch on Sundays. Being able to eat at a restaurant of this stature, in a converted 1906 stable, and drink something built by the same person responsible for one of America's best non-alcoholic tasting pairings next door, is a rare combination anywhere in the country.
venues.pressQuote: Every picture-perfect plate would pair beautifully with one of bar manager Jessi Pollak's four mocktails.

venues.name: Sprecher Brewing Co.
venues.description: Sprecher Brewing Co. is Milwaukee's original craft brewery (est. 1985) and the maker of what The New York Times once crowned America's No. 1 root beer. Its Glendale taproom pours a full line of fire-brewed, all-ages craft sodas -- root beer, cream soda, ginger ale, orange dream and more -- right alongside its beers, and the brewery tour includes unlimited soda samples for every age. For a non-drinker it is one of the rare "breweries" where the zero-proof menu is the main event rather than an afterthought.
venues.longDescription:
Founded in 1985 by Randal Sprecher, Sprecher was Milwaukee's first craft brewery since Prohibition and has since become far better known for soda than suds -- it fire-brews more root beer than all of its beers combined. The house sodas are made in small batches with real Wisconsin honey (and locally grown ginger in the ginger ale) and are gluten-free, kosher-certified and fully non-alcoholic. In 2008 a New York Times panel ranked Sprecher's root beer first among 25 American root beers, calling it "a wonderfully balanced and complex brew."

The Glendale taproom at 701 W. Glendale Ave. leans into that heritage. Alongside the beer taps, guests can order the full soda lineup -- flagship fire-brewed root beer, cream soda, ginger ale, orange dream and cherry cola among them -- and the roughly 45-minute brewery tour pours four beer or hard-soda samples for guests 21+ plus unlimited soda samples for all ages, making it a genuinely welcoming stop for kids, designated drivers and anyone drinking zero-proof. An on-site kitchen serves food until an hour before close.

Sprecher's non-alcoholic bona fides extend beyond its own walls: the brewery was among the 50-plus vendors at Milwaukee Record's fifth-annual N/A Day "Dry January" beverage festival on Jan. 3, 2026, sharing the room with Athletic Brewing, Best Day Brewing, Ghia and Guinness 0.0. For the greater-Milwaukee sober or sober-curious drinker, it is a Brew City institution where the best thing in the glass never contained alcohol in the first place.
venues.pressQuote: a wonderfully balanced and complex brew
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: The New York Times root beer taste test, which ranked Sprecher the No. 1 root beer in America (2008)

venues.name: SquareRüt Kava Bar – Oak Hill
venues.description: SquareRüt Kava Bar – Oak Hill is the second Austin location of the kava bar Scott Pingel and Tracy Moreno founded in 2011, the first in Texas. It sits at 6266 West US Highway 290 near the Oak Hill “Y” and is fully alcohol-free. Kava is served by strain and by size — Low Tide, High Tide and Tsunami — across Aolani (Vanuatu; spicy, focused, cerebral), Waka (Fiji; mild, peppery, social), Lomi (Vanuatu; gentle, sedative, a muscle relaxant and sleep aid) and the Hawaiian green kava Moi. House kava drinks include Kaptain’s Kava, Name was Mud, Kava Chai and the seasonal OG Grog. There is a full kitchen doing pizza, garlic knots, salads and Easy Tiger pastries, plus locally roasted coffee, teas and non-alcoholic beer. It opens at 7am and runs to 10pm daily, and children ten and under eat free on Thursdays with any pizza. (Kava is non-alcoholic but psychoactive — alcohol-free, not substance-free.)

venues.longDescription:
SquareRüt opened its Oak Hill location as the second Austin outpost of the kava bar Scott Pingel and Tracy Moreno started in 2011 after discovering kava in 2008 — the first kava bar in Texas, and one of the earliest anywhere in the American South. The company's stated mission is to make kava as accessible and beloved as coffee, and the Oak Hill room is the clearest expression of that: it opens at 7am and closes at 10pm, which is a coffee shop's day rather than a bar's.

That span is the reason to know about it. Most alcohol-free venues open in the late afternoon and compete for the evening, which means they are only useful for the part of the day people were already going out. A room that serves from seven in the morning works as a place to have breakfast, take a meeting, spend an afternoon working, and then stay into the evening — without the composition of the room changing around you, and without a bar appearing in it at six o'clock.

Kava is served the traditional way, by strain and by size: Low Tide, High Tide and Tsunami, across Aolani from Vanuatu (spicy, focused, cerebral), Waka from Fiji (mild, peppery, social, euphoric), Lomi from Vanuatu (gentle, sedative, a muscle relaxant and sleep aid) and Moi, a Hawaiian green kava. Being able to choose a strain by intended effect rather than by flavour is unusual outside dedicated kava bars, and it is the main thing that separates one from a cafe that happens to stock kava.

The house drinks soften the taste for newcomers: Kaptain's Kava is sparkling prickly pear kava with black ginger, Name was Mud puts sparkling prickly pear against traditional kava, and there are the Kava Chai, the seasonal OG Grog and the Kavarita. A full kitchen runs pizza, garlic knots, salads and Easy Tiger pastries, with children ten and under eating free on Thursdays with any pizza — which tells you what kind of room this is.

The standard caution applies. Kava is not alcohol, but it is psychoactive: a mild sedative that should not be combined with alcohol or sedating medication, can slow reflexes enough to affect driving, and has been associated with liver concerns in heavy or prolonged use.

venues.name: SRV
venues.description: SRV is a Venetian bacaro and wine bar at 569 Columbus Avenue in Boston's South End, opened in 2016 as the third concept from Coda Restaurant Group, which also runs The Salty Pig, Gufo and Baleia. The name is short for Serenissima Repubblica di Venezia, and the kitchen follows the format: cicchetti to pick at, pasta made from locally milled flour, and risotto cooked to order. The drinks list carries a standing section headed Zero & Low Proof, which is split three ways into non-alcoholic cocktails at $11 to $12, three non-alcoholic wines by the glass at $13 to $14, and three non-alcoholic beers. The cocktails are house builds rather than bought-in mixers.

venues.longDescription:
SRV opened in 2016 on Columbus Avenue in the South End as the third restaurant from Coda Restaurant Group, which began with CODA in 2008 and added The Salty Pig in 2012 before going on to open Gufo in East Cambridge in 2023 and Baleia in the South End in 2024. The concept is a bacaro, the Venetian wine bar where people stand and eat cicchetti — small, sharp, mostly cold plates — between glasses, and the name abbreviates Serenissima Repubblica di Venezia, the Serene Republic of Venice. The kitchen mills its pasta from locally sourced flour and cooks risotto to order rather than parcooking it, and the wine list leans hard into Italian bottles. Boston Magazine has covered the bar's alcohol-free work in its running guide to the city's best mocktails, singling out the Non-Groni by name.

The Zero & Low Proof section is printed as a standing block on the drinks list and covers three categories. The house non-alcoholic cocktails are the Sirocco Spritz at $11, built on oregano, yuzu, lemon and soda; the Non-Groni at $11, a negroni substitute made from an aperitif syrup with grapefruit and juniper; and the Mule of Trieste at $12, which uses Lucano non-alcoholic amaro with vanilla, lime and ginger and is flagged at under 0.5% ABV. The bought-in St. Agrestis Phony White Negroni from Brooklyn is offered at $12 alongside them. Non-alcoholic wine runs three glasses: Wolffer "Spring in a Bottle" sparkling rose from New York and Wander + Found "Cuvee Blanc" field blend from Germany at $13 each, and Oddbird G.S.M., a Grenache-Syrah-Mourvedre blend from Germany, at $14, all under 0.5%. Non-alcoholic beer covers Athletic Brewing's Free Wave hazy IPA from Connecticut at $8, Deschutes Black Butte porter from Oregon at $8 and Delirium's Delirio Belgian blonde at $15. SRV opens at 5pm most nights and 4:30pm at weekends.
venues.pressQuote: SRV’s Non-groni features aperitif syrup, grapefruit, and orange blossom water.

venues.name: St. Cecilia
venues.description: St. Cecilia is chef-owner Ford Fry's coastal-European restaurant, open since January 2014 in Buckhead's Pinnacle Building. Named for the patron saint of music and the sirens of Greek mythology, the 160-seat dining room leans on Romanesque tiled columns and distressed mirrors, with a menu of fresh pastas, crudo, and roasted fish inspired by the Ligurian coast and broader Italian, Spanish, and French shorelines. Its bar has quietly built one of Atlanta's more respected non-alcoholic programs: Resy notes the restaurant "has been offering nonalcoholic cocktails before it was cool." The zero-proof list is opera-themed and built on fresh juice, honey, and herbs rather than packaged NA spirits, with named drinks including Madame Butterfly (grapefruit, lemon, honey), La Bohème (almond, lavender, lemon, pineapple), and Carmensita (blueberry, pomegranate, thyme, lemon).
venues.longDescription:
St. Cecilia has been open since January 2014 at 3455 Peachtree Road in Buckhead's Pinnacle Building, from chef-proprietor Ford Fry. It is named for the patron saint of music and the sirens of Greek mythology, and the 160-seat room leans on Romanesque tiled columns and distressed mirrors. The cooking is coastal European — fresh pasta, crudo and roasted fish drawn from the Ligurian coast and the wider Italian, Spanish and French shorelines.

Its non-alcoholic programme is one of the oldest serious ones in the city, and Resy's line is the accurate one: St. Cecilia was offering non-alcoholic cocktails before it was cool. The list has been running since well before the zero-proof spirits boom, which shows in how it is built.

The drinks use no packaged non-alcoholic spirits at all. They are constructed from fresh juice, honey and herbs, in the opera theme the restaurant's name invites: Madame Butterfly is grapefruit, lemon and honey; La Bohème works almond and lavender against lemon and pineapple; Carmensita is blueberry and pomegranate with thyme and lemon.

That is a genuinely different philosophy from the prevailing one, and it has aged well. Most zero-proof menus now start from a bottled substitute — an NA gin, an NA aperitivo — and build a familiar cocktail around it. St. Cecilia's approach treats the drink as its own thing rather than as an imitation of an alcoholic one, which sidesteps the problem those substitutes still have: they are expensive, they vary wildly in quality, and the good ones are trying to taste like something that is not there. Honey gives body where alcohol would, thyme and lavender give the aromatic length, and the result does not invite comparison to a drink it is not.

Lunch runs weekdays and brunch at weekends from 10am, with the bar through the afternoon and dinner nightly.
venues.pressQuote: St. Cecilia has been offering nonalcoholic cocktails before it was cool, and they continue to craft some of the best in the city.

venues.name: Stampede Cocktail Club
venues.description: Stampede Cocktail Club is a cocktail bar at 119 N 36th Street in Fremont, opened in 2018 by Paul Shanrock in the former Helm space, known for a heavily themed menu published as a lavishly illustrated zine that changes with each season. Its non-alcoholic programme is genuine and long-running — Seattle Met reported that bar manager Adam Fought estimates one person in every party of five or six goes spirit-free, that the bar was among the first in the city to plant a flag on making great temperate drinks, and that it maintains roughly six non-alcoholic cocktails on the rotating themed menu, with each taking two or three times as long to develop as a standard cocktail. IMPORTANT: because the menu is themed and rotates every season, the drink names change completely — none of the spirit-free names documented in past coverage survive on the current list, so do not travel for a specific drink. What is permanent is a standing "Non Alcoholic Spirits" list of nine pours at $9 each: Jalisco 55, Kentucky 74, Pathfinder Amaro, Seedlip Garden, Grove and Spice, and Wilderton Aperitivo, Earthen and Lustre. Non-alcoholic Athletic beer and Gruvi dry red are $8. Dumplings are $15 for ten. Happy hour 5–7pm daily.
signatureDrinks: Non-alcoholic spirits by the pour ($9): Seedlip, Wilderton, Pathfinder, Jalisco 55, Kentucky 74
venues.longDescription:
Stampede Cocktail Club took over the former Helm space in Fremont in 2018, under owner Paul Shanrock, and built its identity around a menu that is genuinely a piece of design work: a lavishly illustrated zine that changes theme entirely with each season. Past editions have run from an homage to 1940s comic books and art-deco travel posters to a vaporwave alcove to the current Gundam-inflected one. The food is deliberately singular — dumplings, ten to an order, at $15, or a full rack at $55 — and happy hour runs 5 to 7 every day with cocktails and pork dumplings at $9.99.

Its non-alcoholic programme is real and unusually well established. Seattle Met's 2024 report on the city's zero-proof bars found that bar manager Adam Fought estimates one person in every party of five or six now goes the spirit-free route, that Stampede was among the first bars in Seattle to plant a flag on making great temperate drinks, and that it keeps roughly six non-alcoholic cocktails on the rotating themed menu at any time — each of which takes two or three times as long to develop as an ordinary cocktail, because, as Fought puts it, you get so much flavour from fermentation and alcohol. An earlier bar lead, Kayleigh Blome, described falling head over heels with making something special for an underserved demographic, and framed the offer as letting people be intentional about the choice, whether they are not drinking or simply choosing to drink less. The practical consequence of a fully themed, fully rotating menu is that no drink name survives long. Not one of the spirit-free cocktails documented in coverage of this bar over the past several years — under any of its themes — appears on the current list. So come for the programme, not for a name. What does stay put is a standing list of nine non-alcoholic spirits sold by the pour at $9 each: Jalisco 55, Kentucky 74, Pathfinder Amaro, Seedlip in Garden, Grove and Spice, and Wilderton in Aperitivo, Earthen and Lustre. That shelf means the bar can build almost anything for you on request. Athletic non-alcoholic beer and Gruvi dry red are $8.
venues.pressQuote: The bar was one of the first to plant a flag at making great temperate drinks; today it maintains roughly six NA cocktails on its rotating themed menu.

venues.name: Standby
venues.description: Standby's zero-proof drinks aren't a side menu — they're built into the same rotating cocktail list that's earned the bar James Beard semifinalist nods and a 2025 Two Pin "Outstanding" rating from The Pinnacle Guide. The Buddy Boy Negroni (N/A aperitif, charred citrus, maple, green coffee) and California Sober (hemp & root spirit, ginger, lemongrass, acidified orange, CO₂) are formulated as zero-proof cocktails from the ground up, while the Farm to Highball is available zero-proof on request. Tucked into The Belt, Detroit's mural-lined art alley, Standby applies the same technical rigor to its no-alcohol drinks as to the award-winning ones next to them on the menu.
