venues.longDescription:
Standby opened in 2015 inside The Belt, the mural- and gallery-lined alley off Library Street in Downtown Detroit, and quickly became one of the city's most decorated bars: James Beard Award semifinalist for Outstanding Bar Program (2017 and 2018), Eater Detroit's Bar of the Year (2016), and repeated Tales of the Cocktail regional honors. In 2025 The Pinnacle Guide gave it Two Pin "Outstanding" status, and in summer 2024 chef Matty Matheson (of "The Bear") joined as a partner — his first U.S. bar venture.

That same acclaimed cocktail program treats zero-proof as a first-class category rather than an afterthought. Standby's current menu marks select drinks "Zero proof" right alongside the alcoholic list: the Buddy Boy Negroni, credited to M. Matheson, is built on an N/A aperitif with charred citrus, maple, and green coffee; the California Sober uses a hemp & root spirit base with ginger, lemongrass, acidified orange, and CO₂ for lift and carbonation. The Farm to Highball — usually built on vodka with seasonal produce and a botanical soda — is also made available zero-proof on request, meaning guests aren't limited to a separate, shrunken mocktail list.

The Belt itself is part of Detroit's downtown arts revitalization, a narrow alley of large-scale murals and small storefronts entered off Gratiot Avenue and Library Street. Standby sits at the center of it, open late most nights of the week, which has made it as much a hangout for the city's own bar-industry crowd as for visitors chasing its national reputation.
venues.pressQuote: Several of the drinks on the regular cocktail menu including the Sweet Potato Apple Streusel, Baklava, and Lemon Bar are all available to order sans alcohol.

venues.name: Stanley's Northeast Bar Room
venues.description: Stanley's Northeast Bar Room is a casual neighborhood bar and gastropub on University Avenue NE in Northeast Minneapolis, housed in a building more than 130 years old that has carried the Stanley's name for over 15 years. It runs 32 craft-beer taps alongside a full menu of burgers, sandwiches, nachos, and reubens, plus a year-round dog-friendly patio. For non-drinkers, Stanley's keeps a real named mocktail list on its drink menu: the NAz Rita (Seedlip Grove 42, agave, lime juice, salt rim), the Blood Orange Mock Mule (blood orange, lime, ginger beer, in a copper mug), the Blackberry Fizz, the Lavender Lemonade, and Berry Nice. The Meet Minneapolis tourism office highlights Stanley's NAz Rita and Blood Orange Mock Mule in its citywide mocktail roundup. In early 2025, community support saved the bar from a road-construction-driven closure.

venues.longDescription:
Stanley's Northeast Bar Room is a casual neighbourhood bar and gastropub on University Avenue NE, in a building more than 130 years old that has carried the Stanley's name for over fifteen years. It runs thirty-two craft beer taps alongside burgers, sandwiches, nachos and reubens, and keeps a dog-friendly patio open year-round. In early 2025 it came close to closing because of road construction outside, and community support kept it open — which tells you most of what you need to know about its place in Northeast.

The reason it earns a listing is that a bar of this type, in this category, usually offers a non-drinker nothing but soda, and Stanley's keeps a real named mocktail list on the printed drink menu. The NAz Rita is built on Seedlip Grove 42 with agave, lime juice and a salt rim — a genuine margarita structure rather than limeade. The Blood Orange Mock Mule combines blood orange, lime and ginger beer and is served in a copper mug, which sounds trivial and is not: being handed the same vessel as everyone else is a large part of not feeling conspicuous. Alongside those sit a Blackberry Fizz, a Lavender Lemonade and Berry Nice. Meet Minneapolis, the city's tourism office, highlights the NAz Rita and the Blood Orange Mock Mule in its citywide mocktail round-up.

This is not an ambitious cocktail programme and does not claim to be. What it is, is the specific thing that is hardest to find and most needed: an ordinary neighbourhood bar with thirty-two taps, a patio and a burger, where somebody who has stopped drinking can meet friends on a Tuesday and order something made for them off the actual menu. Open daily, from 9am at weekends.

venues.name: The Starlite Bar
venues.description: The Starlite Bar sits on East 11th Street — historic Route 66 — in Tulsa's Pearl District, and it keeps the same 4pm to 2am schedule six nights a week that the city's better downtown rooms do. Its alcohol-free drink is the Ginger Rogers: ginger beer, fresh lime, house ginger syrup and club soda, a double-ginger build that gets its bite from the syrup rather than from sugar. It is a simple drink, honestly described, and the reason it is here is that a long, dry, spicy highball is the single most useful thing a late bar can offer someone who is not drinking. The room itself is a Route 66 neighbourhood bar rather than a cocktail destination, and it is priced accordingly.
signatureDrinks: Ginger Rogers — ginger beer, fresh lime, ginger syrup, club soda
venues.longDescription:
East 11th Street through Tulsa is historic Route 66, and the Pearl District stretch of it has become a small bar quarter. The Starlite is one of its anchors — a neighbourhood room rather than a destination cocktail bar, open 4pm to 2am from Tuesday through Sunday.

The alcohol-free drink is the Ginger Rogers, and it is worth explaining why a simple build earns a listing. Ginger beer, fresh lime, house ginger syrup and club soda is a double-ginger highball: the commercial ginger beer provides carbonation and a baseline of spice, and the house ginger syrup layers a fresher, sharper heat on top of it. Lime supplies acid and soda extends it. The result is long, dry and genuinely spicy rather than sweet, which is exactly what someone wants to hold for two hours in a bar.

That is the practical test this directory applies to a room like this. A late neighbourhood bar does not need an elaborate zero-proof programme; it needs one drink that is properly made, low in sugar and long enough to last, so that a non-drinker can sit through an evening without either getting bored or getting sick of sweetness. The Ginger Rogers is that drink, and Tulsa Remote picked it out in its January 2025 ranking of the city's mocktails.

This entry is graded three, honestly: one named build, no printed zero-proof section, no non-alcoholic spirits programme documented. It is not Nola's or Oren. What it is, is open until two in the morning six nights a week with something decent to order — and across this whole directory, that combination turns out to be rarer than a long mocktail menu.

Closed Monday.
venues.pressQuote: Ginger Rogers: Ginger beer, fresh lime, ginger syrup, and club soda

venues.name: Starlite
venues.description: Starlite is the 21st-floor bar of the Beacon Grand hotel on Powell Street in Union Square, a room that has served cocktails since 1928 and reopened after the hotel's restoration with drinks by Scott Baird and a bites menu by chef Johnny Spero. Its non-alcoholic programme is a printed menu section titled The Free Spirited, holding four zero-proof cocktails at $16 named for the seasons: Spring, built on Navarro verjus with lemon, honey, chamomile and club soda; Summer, with passion fruit, lime, vanilla, coconut water, butterfly pea flower and saline; Autumn, with jasmine tea, pomegranate, ginger five-spice syrup, white miso and lemon; and Winter, with carrot juice, toasted almond milk, cinnamon, star anise and Meyer lemon. NON 1 zero-proof wine and Athletic Brewing's Upside Dawn complete the section.

venues.longDescription:
Starlite occupies the top floor of the Beacon Grand, the Union Square hotel formerly known as the Sir Francis Drake, and dates its bar programme to 1928. The room reopened as part of the hotel's restoration with a cocktail list designed by Scott Baird, a San Francisco bartender best known for The Bon Vivants and Trick Dog, and a small-plates menu from Michelin-awarded chef Johnny Spero. The drinks are written as short stories about the city — a Cable Car Redux, a Pisco Punch that nods to Duncan Nichol's lost recipe at the old Bank Exchange, a Baghdad by the Bay borrowed from Herb Caen — served on the 21st floor with panoramic views and an all-vinyl soundtrack.

The non-alcoholic drinks are not an afterthought bolted onto the back of the list. They occupy a named section of the printed menu, The Free Spirited, and are built with the same technique as the full-proof cocktails. The four zero-proof drinks are named for the seasons and priced at $16, against $16 to $22 for the alcoholic ones. Spring is Navarro verjus with lemon, honey, chamomile and club soda. Summer combines passion fruit, lime, vanilla, coconut water, butterfly pea flower and saline. Autumn is jasmine tea with pomegranate, a ginger five-spice syrup, sweet white miso and lemon. Winter uses carrot juice, toasted almond milk, cinnamon, star anise and Meyer lemon. Below them the section lists NON 1, the Australian zero-proof bottling made from whole raspberry, chamomile, Murray River salt, cane sugar and verjus, available by the glass at $16 or by the bottle at $64, and Athletic Brewing's Upside Dawn golden ale at $7. Because the four seasonal drinks change with the calendar rather than sitting static, a returning guest gets a different zero-proof list through the year, which is unusual for a hotel bar of this size. The bar trades Thursday to Sunday only, from 4pm, running to 2am on Friday and Saturday nights, and a 20 per cent service charge is added to every check and shared among the team.
venues.pressQuote: With close to a century of splashy cocktails and shared stories within its walls, Starlite shines as a historic and revered San Francisco establishment.

venues.name: State Line Distillery
venues.description: State Line Distillery makes craft spirits on Northern Court, just off Williamson Street on Madison's near east side, and runs a cocktail lounge attached to the still house. It is in this guide because the lounge will build non-alcoholic versions of its seasonal rotating cocktails and of the classics, rather than restricting non-drinkers to soda — a distillery choosing to serve a drink with none of its own product in it is a deliberate act of hospitality. Because the list rotates with the season, ask what is on rather than arriving expecting a fixed menu. The lounge opens at 5pm on weeknights and 3pm at weekends.
venues.longDescription:
State Line Distillery takes its name from the Illinois border a few miles south and makes gin, vodka, whiskey and seasonal spirits in a building on Northern Court, tucked behind Williamson Street on the near east side. The cocktail lounge sits alongside the production floor, which gives it the particular atmosphere of a distillery bar — you can see where the thing in your glass was made, and the menu changes as the stills produce different things.

A distillery is the least likely kind of venue to accommodate a non-drinker well, because the entire commercial logic points the other way: every drink sold without the house spirit in it is a drink that does not showcase the product. State Line does it anyway. Visit Madison, the city's official visitor bureau, records that the lounge offers non-alcoholic alternatives to its seasonal rotating cocktails and to the classics, which means the bartenders are rebuilding the same drinks without the base rather than offering a separate list of three sweet things. In practice that gives a non-drinker the best possible outcome — the drink the table is having, made to the same specification.

Because it rotates, we have not recorded named builds here; the honest advice is to describe what you like and let the bar work. Practically, the lounge keeps good hours for the neighbourhood — 5pm to 10pm Monday through Thursday, 3pm to midnight Friday and Saturday, 3pm to 9pm Sunday — and it sits within a few minutes' walk of two other entries in this guide: Rooted In Sanity, Madison's only kava lounge and one of just two fully alcohol-free rooms in the metro, and I/O Arcade Bar. The Marquette neighbourhood is the most walkable part of Madison's east side and the easiest place here to string an evening together on foot.
venues.pressQuote: State Line Distillery's eastside taproom offers NA alternatives of some of their seasonal rotating cocktails and classic cocktails.

venues.name: Steak 48
venues.description: Steak 48 is an upscale, white-tablecloth steakhouse in Charlotte's SouthPark, set in the Apex SouthPark development at Sharon Road and Morrison Boulevard. Its bar takes zero-proof seriously, building craft mocktails on Seedlip non-alcoholic spirits with fresh fruit purees and pressed citrus — the year-round Blueberry Lemon Sour (Seedlip Spice 94) and Passionfruit Margarita (Seedlip Notas de Agave) anchor the program. It is a polished pick for anyone who wants a celebratory, alcohol-free pour alongside a serious steak dinner.
signatureDrinks: Blueberry Lemon Sour (Seedlip Spice 94, blueberry purée, fresh-pressed lemon, egg white) $16
Lychee and Tonic (Seedlip Garden 108, lychee purée, lime, Fever-Tree elderflower tonic, mint) $16
Passionfruit Margarita (Ritual Zero Proof agave, passionfruit purée, fresh-pressed lime, Tajín) $16
venues.longDescription:
Steak 48 sits at the corner of Sharon Road and Morrison Boulevard in the Apex SouthPark development, at 4425 Sharon Road, from the Mastro family — brothers Jeffrey and Michael with their father Dennis, alongside business partner Scott Troilo, a family with a long history in American steakhouses. It is a white-tablecloth room and it says so: the dress code discourages athletic wear, revealing clothing and printed t-shirts, and prefers collared shirts and sports coats. The menu is priced accordingly, running prime steakhouse meatballs at $16, chef's cut hanging bacon with local honey and togarashi at $29, Pacific yellowtail hamachi with crispy shallot and yuzu ponzu at $39, a king crab and avocado stack at $43, and steaks from a 12oz New York strip at $65 up to a 46oz bone-in wagyu tomahawk at $295. Queen City Nerve readers made it runner-up for both Best SouthPark Restaurant and Best Steakhouse in 2024. Doors open at 4pm daily.

The bar prints a section headed "zero proof", and all three drinks are $16 — the same price as much of the cocktail list, which at this kind of restaurant is the signal that matters. Two are built on Seedlip. The Blueberry Lemon Sour uses Seedlip Spice 94 with blueberry purée, fresh-pressed lemon and egg white, giving it the weight and foam a sour needs. Lychee and Tonic pairs Seedlip Garden 108 with lychee purée, lime, Fever-Tree elderflower tonic and mint — the lightest of the three and the one that works best before a heavy meal. The Passionfruit Margarita is built on Ritual Zero Proof's agave alternative with passionfruit purée, fresh-pressed lime and a Tajín rim, and it is worth noting that this drink has been described elsewhere, including previously on this page, as using a Seedlip agave expression; the restaurant's own current menu says Ritual. If you are choosing on the basis of a specific brand, that distinction is real.
venues.pressQuote: This spot serves classic, zero proof mixed drinks made with fresh fruits and syrups.

venues.name: Steep LA
venues.description: Steep LA is a Chinese and Taiwanese teahouse in Mandarin Plaza in Chinatown, serving premium leaf handpicked from China and Taiwan across five of the six major Chinese tea categories - black, green, oolong, white and pu-er. Teas are sold by the pot with published fragrance and taste profiles: Yingde black at $15, Lapsang Souchong at $18, Longjing green at $18, Gailan Houkui at $24, Snow Mountain oolong at $18, Oriental Beauty at $21 and Wild Baimudan white at $21, with freshly brewed cups from $6. Food is Chinese and Taiwanese comfort cooking, and a retail section carries work by sustainability-focused local makers. Note that the room is licensed in the evening: from 4pm it runs as Steep After Dark, a tea-cocktail bar, so the alcohol-free offer here is the tea programme rather than the whole venue.

Lapsang Souchong - orchid, malt, chestnut, wood; smooth and lightly sweet $18 / $40
Longjing green tea - grain, mung bean, pine nut, biscuit $18 / $35
Gailan Houkui green tea - grassy, coconut, nutty, vegetal $24 / $50
Snow Mountain oolong - cotton candy, mung bean, jasmine, caramel $18 / $35
Oriental Beauty oolong - herbal, woodsy, honeysuckle; sweet with plum $21 / $45
Wild Baimudan white tea - mellow, grassy, floral, lotus, grape $21 / $45
venues.longDescription:
Steep occupies a unit in Mandarin Plaza in Chinatown, and The Infatuation's review describes the daytime version accurately: sleek, all-white interiors and monochrome furniture, a daytime tea shop and lunch counter with a prolific selection of teas that the staff are happy to help you make sense of. That last part is the actual service being sold. The list covers five of the six major Chinese tea categories - black, green, oolong, white and pu-er - all handpicked by the founders from growers in China and Taiwan, and each tea on the steeped menu is published with a fragrance profile and a separate taste profile, which is a level of documentation almost no cafe in Los Angeles offers.

What that looks like in practice: Yingde, a black tea, listed with fragrance notes of chocolate, walnut, caramel and fruit and taste notes of cherry, licorice and red bean, at $15 for the smaller pot and $35 for the larger. Lapsang Souchong at $18, with orchid, malt, chestnut and wood on the nose and a smooth, thick, lightly sweet finish. Longjing green at $18, reading grain, mung bean, pine nut and biscuit. Gailan Houkui at $24, the most expensive on the list, thick and grassy with coconut. Snow Mountain oolong at $18, which the menu describes as cotton candy and mung bean turning to jasmine and caramel. Oriental Beauty at $21 and Wild Baimudan white at $21. Freshly brewed cups - black, green, oolong, white, ginger pu-er and a caffeine-free herbal - are $6, and there are cold-brewed teas at the same price. The shop also keeps a retail corner for sustainability-focused local designers and craft makers.

One thing to be clear about, because it changes what the venue is depending on when you arrive. Steep is not an alcohol-free room. From 4pm it turns into Steep After Dark, a low-lit lounge with a tea-infused cocktail programme - a chrysanthemum vodka drink, a black tea whisky build with housemade Sichuan peppercorn syrup - and it stays open to 11pm Wednesday through Sunday. The teas remain available throughout, and the bar has a habit of sending guests off with a small cup of high-grade green tea on the house. If you want the teahouse rather than the bar, come before four; if you want somewhere to sit at nine at night with a genuinely serious pot of tea in front of you, the evening works too, alongside people drinking.
venues.pressQuote: a prolific selection of teas, which they are happy to help you make sense of

venues.name: Sterling Bar
venues.description: Sterling is a subterranean cocktail bar hidden in the old bank vault beneath the Stock Exchange Hotel, the third venue from the Manchester team behind Schofield's Bar and the Atomeca wine bars. Leaning into a roaring-twenties glamour of wood panelling, live music and award-winning cocktails, it keeps a named 'Temperance' section on its drinks list rather than leaving non-drinkers to a lone soft drink. The four alcohol-free serves run from the raspberry-and-rose Blush and a chilli-spiked Salsa to a from-scratch Virgin Mary and the Wild Earth, built on Seedlip Spice 0.0% with honey, lemon and tea. Corona Cero 0.0% and a Seedlip Spice aperitif serve round out the low-and-no options.
venues.hours: Mon closed; Tue-Fri 5pm-12am; Sat 2pm-12am; Sun closed

venues.longDescription:
Sterling opened in September 2022 on the lower ground floor of the Stock Exchange Hotel, tucked inside the old bank vault of the former Manchester Stock Exchange on Norfolk Street. It is the third venue from bartender brothers Joe and Daniel Schofield — the team behind the multi-award-winning Schofield's Bar in Sunlight House and the Atomeca wine bars — who opened it with wine specialist James Brandwood. The Schofields honed their craft at rooms such as the American Bar at the Savoy, Singapore's Tippling Club and Little Red Door in Paris, and Schofield's Bar took Best New Bar at the 2022 Class Bar Awards; Sterling was conceived as a larger, more glamorous companion piece, its name nodding both to the building's financial history and to a benchmark of quality.

The room is far bigger than the city's typical intimate cocktail dens, seating just over 100 across a bespoke, wood-panelled interior that plays up the history and glamour of the old exchange. A roaring-twenties theme runs through the space, with live music from 8pm on Friday and Saturday nights, an award-winning wine list and bar snacks originally developed by two-Michelin-starred chef Tom Kerridge's events company, Lush Hospitality — oysters, croquettes with aged Manchego, salt-and-pepper squid and the like. It is an adults-only, cash-free venue, open Tuesday to Saturday, with an optional 12.5% service charge added to the bill.

For non-drinkers, Sterling keeps a dedicated 'Temperance' section on its drinks list rather than treating alcohol-free as an afterthought. Four zero-proof cocktails are built to order: Blush pairs raspberry and rose with ginger, lime and soda (£9); Salsa is a bright, savoury mix of lime, red chilli and pineapple (£9); the Virgin Mary is made from scratch with tomato, Worcestershire sauce, a house spice mix, celery and lemon (£9); and the Wild Earth is the most cocktail-like of the four, building Seedlip Spice 0.0% with honey, lemon and tea (£12). Beyond the Temperance list, Corona Cero 0.0% is stocked by the bottle (£5) and Seedlip Spice 0.0% is offered as a standalone £9 aperitif serve, so the alcohol-free options carry the same considered, made-to-order approach as the rest of the bar.
venues.pressQuote: Named to reference the building's history as well as representing outstanding quality, the exciting new cocktail bar also has a fantastic wine programme and a bespoke, wood-panelled interior that fittingly reflects the history and glamour of the old Stock Exchange building.

venues.name: Stillwell's
venues.description: Stillwell's is the steakhouse inside Hôtel Swexan in the Harwood District, and its drink list carries a printed Non-Alcoholic section — the kind of room where not drinking has historically meant sparkling water for three hours. The Golden Pear is built on Lyre's Classico non-alcoholic sparkling wine with pear and lemon; the Ginger Snap uses Seedlip Garden 108 infused with rooibos, then cinnamon, lime and ginger beer. Heineken 0.0 rounds out the beer list. Both builds are priced alongside the bar's cocktails rather than beneath them. Two drinks is a short list and we would rather say so, but both are made with real non-alcoholic spirits and printed under their own heading.
signatureDrinks: The Golden Pear (Lyre's Classico NA sparkling, pear, lemon)
Ginger Snap (rooibos-infused Seedlip Garden 108, cinnamon, lime, ginger beer)

venues.longDescription:
Hôtel Swexan opened in the Harwood District as one of the most deliberately theatrical hotels in Dallas, and Stillwell's is its steakhouse — a dark, clubby room on the seventh floor where the wine list runs long and the cooking is built around dry-aged beef. It is exactly the kind of restaurant where not drinking has historically meant sparkling water for three hours while everyone else works through a bottle, which is what makes its printed Non-Alcoholic section worth recording rather than a formality.

There are two builds, and both are constructed rather than poured. The Golden Pear uses Lyre's Classico, a non-alcoholic sparkling wine, with pear and lemon — a drink designed to hold its own against a steak course and, just as importantly, to look right in the room. The Ginger Snap is the more technical of the pair: Seedlip Garden 108, the herbal expression of the British distillate, infused with rooibos and then lengthened with cinnamon, lime and ginger beer. The rooibos infusion is the detail that marks this as a bar programme rather than a concession; it is an extra preparation step taken for a drink most steakhouses would not bother to make at all. Heineken 0.0 sits on the beer list for anyone who would rather keep it simple.

Two drinks is not a deep list, and we would rather say so than inflate it. But they are made with real non-alcoholic spirits, they appear in print under their own heading, and they are priced with the cocktails rather than below them — in a hotel steakhouse, that combination is meaningfully better than the norm. Service runs from 5pm daily, to 10pm Sunday through Thursday and 11pm on Friday and Saturday, so this is a dinner booking rather than a bar you drop into. Come for the steak with a table that is drinking, and you will be handed something built with the same intent as everyone else's glass. The Harwood District setting helps too: it is a dense, walkable pocket of hotels and restaurants rather than a strip you drive between, so an evening here does not have to end when the meal does, and it does not require anyone to be the designated driver to make the logistics work.

venues.name: STIR
venues.description: STIR is a downtown Greenville restaurant and bar on East McBee Avenue with the widest hours of any venue in this city guide: 11am to midnight Monday through Thursday, to 1am on Friday and Saturday, and from 10am at weekends — seven days, no closed day, breakfast through last call. For a non-drinker that availability is the whole value. It appears in local listings for mocktails in the city, and while the specific drinks are not published in a form this directory could verify, it is the one Greenville address that is open whenever you need it.
venues.longDescription:
Across sixty-odd cities, this directory keeps arriving at the same conclusion: the venue that ends up mattering most to someone who does not drink is rarely the one with the cleverest list. It is the one that is open. STIR, on East McBee Avenue in downtown Greenville, is that venue here.

The hours are 11am to midnight Monday through Thursday, 11am to 1am on Friday, 10am to 1am on Saturday and 10am to midnight on Sunday. Seven days a week, no closed day, and a weekend service that starts before most of this city's bars have unlocked. Set that against the rest of the guide — Juniper closed Monday and Tuesday, Bar Margaret closed Sunday and Monday, Oak & Honey closed Sunday and Monday, Southernside closed Monday, Crafted closed Sunday — and STIR is the answer on every one of the days the others are not.

That matters more than it sounds. The experience of not drinking is substantially shaped by how often the answer to "where can we go" is "nowhere good", and a room that is reliably open removes that friction from a whole week rather than one night.

On the drinks, this entry is deliberately restrained. STIR appears in Greenville's mocktail listings, but no named build could be confirmed against a current menu, there is no verified printed zero-proof section, and no non-alcoholic spirit is documented on the back bar. It is graded three with no signature drinks recorded, and the honest advice is to ask what the bar can make rather than to arrive expecting a list.

It sits within a couple of minutes of Oak & Honey, Crafted and UP on the Roof, so downtown Greenville is genuinely walkable for an evening built this way.

venues.name: The Stockpot
venues.description: The Stockpot is a downtown Norfolk cafe and eatery on Plume Street, open from 7am on weekdays, and its alcohol-free drinks are a proper little menu rather than a line: fruit refreshers in pineapple mango and blood orange coconut ginger, a lavender basil lemonade and a cranberry limeade spritzer. The daytime hours are what make it useful — most of Hampton Roads' considered non-alcoholic drinks are locked behind 5pm bar openings, so a place serving something carefully built at nine in the morning or two in the afternoon covers hours the rest of the scene simply does not. The schedule shifts noticeably day to day, so check before a late-afternoon trip.
venues.longDescription:
The Stockpot sits on East Plume Street in downtown Norfolk and works as a cafe and all-day eatery rather than a bar. Its non-alcoholic list runs to four named drinks: refreshers in pineapple mango and blood orange coconut ginger, a lavender basil lemonade, and a cranberry limeade spritzer.

Four named options is a real menu, and the compositions are more considered than the format suggests — blood orange with coconut and ginger is a genuinely interesting combination, bringing warmth and body to something that could easily have been a fruit juice. Lavender with basil does the same job from the herbal side.

But the reason The Stockpot earns its place in a Hampton Roads guide is the clock. Look at the rest of the region's good alcohol-free drinking: Only You opens at 5pm and is closed three days a week, Gershwin's opens at 5pm, Press 626 shuts on Sunday and Monday, Ceremony closes at 7pm. Almost all of it is evening trade. Someone who is not drinking often wants the opposite — a morning meeting, an afternoon between things, a place to sit at eleven on a Saturday — and that entire window is thinly served across the region.

The Stockpot opens at 7am on weekdays and 8am at weekends, and stays open to 9pm on Wednesdays. It is not a night out, and the grade reflects a modest programme honestly, but it is one of the few places in downtown Norfolk where a considered non-alcoholic drink is available during the hours most people are actually awake and out. The schedule varies by day more than most, so it is worth checking before making a trip for a late afternoon. The downtown location puts it within walking distance of Freemason Abbey and the waterfront, so it slots easily into a day spent on foot.
venues.pressQuote: Stockpot: Refreshers (pineapple mango, blood orange coconut ginger); "lavender basil lemonade" or "cranberry limeade spritzer".

venues.name: Sugar Monk
venues.description: Sugar Monk is a speakeasy-inspired lounge on Frederick Douglass Boulevard in Harlem, founded by mixologist, distiller and artist Ektoras Binikos, from Ikaria in Greece, with Montreal-born photographer and designer Simon Jutras. Its drinks are built on foraged and wild botanicals supplied for years by forager Tama Matsuoka Wong, worked into bitters, tinctures, infusions and syrups, and the bar distils its own non-alcoholic amaro and vermouth under its Atheras Spirits label. READ THE MENU CAREFULLY BEFORE ORDERING: its section headed "Follow the Gleams" is subtitled "Low ABV/Non-Alcoholic", and two of its five drinks contain real alcohol at printed strengths — the Ganesha at 19% ABV and the Strawberry Spritz at 25% ABV, both $18. The genuinely alcohol-free drinks in that section are the Butterfly Field ($16, and note it contains pasteurised egg white), the Ba-Lue Bolivar ($16) and a zero-proof Negroni Sbagliato ($16). A Faux Negroni, explicitly labelled non-alcoholic, is $12 during the daily 5–7pm happy hour. Shortlisted at NYC's Best Bars for NA 2025.
venues.address: 2292 Frederick Douglass Blvd, New York, NY 10027
venues.longDescription:
Sugar Monk sits on Frederick Douglass Boulevard near the Apollo, and it is one of the few bars in New York whose drinks genuinely could not be made anywhere else. Ektoras Binikos — a mixologist, distiller and visual artist from the Greek island of Ikaria, with a thirty-year career behind him — founded it with Simon Jutras, a Montreal-born photographer and designer, to revive the spirit of the Harlem speakeasy. The botanical programme is not decorative: the forager Tama Matsuoka Wong has supplied the bar with wild plants, roots, fruits and flowers for years, and those go into aromatic bitters, tinctures, infusions and syrups used across the list, with the ethnobotanist Elizabeth Kontou of Ikaria also credited. More unusually still, the bar makes its own non-alcoholic spirits at a Brooklyn micro-distillery under the Atheras Spirits name, including a zero-proof amaro and a zero-proof sweet vermouth — so several of its alcohol-free drinks are built from components that exist nowhere else. It opens at 5pm and runs to half past one in the morning.

One thing must be read carefully here, and it is the reason this entry has been rewritten. The menu's non-alcoholic-looking section is headed Follow the Gleams and subtitled "Low ABV/Non-Alcoholic" — and that first half is doing real work. Two of its five drinks contain a substantial amount of alcohol, with the strength printed on the menu: the Ganesha at 19% ABV and the Strawberry Spritz at 25% ABV, which contains Aperol and sparkling wine, both $18. Anyone scanning for the alcohol-free part of the list could order either by mistake. The genuinely zero-proof drinks in that section are three: Butterfly Field at $16, on Lyre's London Spirit with yuzu, lime, lavender, butterfly pea, orange blossom and juniper — note it contains pasteurised egg white; Ba-Lue Bolivar at $16, clarified, on Seedlip Spice 94 with grape, green apple, Meyer lemon, cinnamon and patchouli; and a Negroni Sbagliato at $16 built on Pathfinder with the house Atheras zero-proof vermouth. There is also a Faux Negroni at $12, explicitly labelled non-alcoholic, on the daily 5–7pm happy hour menu. Order those by name and the bar is superb.
venues.pressQuote: A broader shortlist highlighted bars with strong NA options citywide, including Sugar Monk, Lobby Bar at Hotel Chelsea, Dante, Pearl's Social & Billy Club, Dynaco, Saint Eve's, Pitts and more.
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: Time Out New York, NYC's Best Bars for NA Awards 2025

venues.longDescription:
Summer House on the Lake is a Lettuce Entertain You restaurant at Disney Springs West Side in Lake Buena Vista, Florida, bringing a Southern California coastal menu to Walt Disney World Resort. It's the fourth Summer House location following sister restaurants in Chicago, North Bethesda, and Las Vegas, with lakeside patio seating spread across three bars overlooking Lake Buena Vista and its own Cookie Bar serving 15+ flavors of oversized cookies for dessert.

Its drink menu carries a distinct 'Zero Proof' section with four $9 builds: the Waitlist (sparkling rosé lemonade, elderflower, lemon), Pineapple Kick (pineapple, orange, habanero honey), Strawberry Fields (strawberry, sage, lavender), and the Lakeside Cooler (kalamansi, Fever-Tree yuzu lime, mint).

Reviewing the Strawberry Fields for Disney Food Blog, writer Lydia Storks found it 'bubbly like soda water, and had a strong strawberry flavor,' noting it 'wasn't very sweet until I got to the bottom of the glass, but it was nice and refreshing' — one of several zero-proof choices she noted alongside the restaurant's spritzes and specialty cocktails.

Beyond dinner, Summer House also runs weekend brunch Saturday and Sunday from 9am-2pm and a Monday-Friday Martini Hour from 3-6pm at the bar.
venues.pressQuote: It was bubbly like soda water, and had a strong strawberry flavor. It wasn't very sweet until I got to the bottom of the glass, but it was nice and refreshing.

venues.name: Summit Brewing Company
venues.description: Summit Brewing has brewed in Saint Paul since 1986 and is the state's best-known independent brewery; its Ratskeller taproom sits at the brewery on Montreal Circle in the West Seventh district. Summit is one of very few Minnesota breweries producing its own non-alcoholic line: Nialas, launched in September 2022 and named after the Irish for nothing, in tribute to Summit's Irish head brewer. The range includes a non-alcoholic IPA — hop-forward, with toast and English-biscuit malt notes and apricot, tangerine and mixed-berry aroma — and a non-alcoholic Irish-style dark carrying espresso, chocolate and caramel, both under 0.5% ABV. The Ratskeller runs Wednesday through Sunday with a view into the brewhouse, on the bluff above the Mississippi rather than in a commercial strip.
signatureDrinks: Nialas Non-Alcoholic IPA (under 0.5% ABV; apricot, tangerine, mixed berry aroma)
Nialas Non-Alcoholic Irish-Style Dark (under 0.5% ABV; espresso, chocolate, caramel)
venues.longDescription:
Summit Brewing Company opened in Saint Paul in 1986 and is the reason a large part of Minnesota's craft-beer culture exists; Extra Pale Ale has been a fixture of the state's bars for four decades. The brewery sits on Montreal Circle in the West Seventh - Fort Road district, on the bluff above the Mississippi, and its taproom — the Ratskeller — operates Wednesday through Sunday with a view into the brewhouse. What puts a full-strength brewery on this site is that Summit is one of a very small number of Minnesota producers who brew their own non-alcoholic beer rather than stocking someone else's cans.

The line is called Nialas, launched on 2 September 2022. Explore Minnesota's guide to non-alcoholic drinking in the state records that the name comes from the Irish for nothing and was chosen in tribute to Summit's Irish head brewer. The Nialas non-alcoholic IPA is a hop-forward beer built to read as an IPA rather than as a dealcoholised approximation, with toast and English-biscuit malt character underneath aromas of apricot, tangerine and mixed berries. The Nialas non-alcoholic Irish-style dark is the more unusual of the two: a stout-shaped beer carrying espresso, chocolate and caramel against a spicy hop finish, in a category where almost every producer defaults to a pale lager. Both come in under 0.5% ABV and are sold in six-packs of twelve-ounce cans across Summit's distribution territory, which covers most of the Upper Midwest. One caveat worth stating plainly before a trip: Summit does not publish a live tap list for the Ratskeller, so while the Nialas beers are made on this site, this entry cannot confirm which of them are pouring in the taproom on any given day — call ahead if a non-alcoholic pour is the reason you are going. For context on how unusual this is locally: the great majority of Minnesota taprooms that offer a non-alcoholic beer are pouring somebody else's can, usually from a national producer. Summit is one of the few brewing the category itself, at scale, from its own Saint Paul brewhouse — which is also why the Nialas beers are among the easiest non-alcoholic options to find on a liquor-store shelf anywhere in the Upper Midwest.
venues.pressQuote: Summit Brewing launched its Nialas non-alcoholic lineup in 2022. Inspired by Summit's Irish Head Brewer, the name (Gaelic for 'nothing') reflects the brand's creative approach to brewing without the buzz.

venues.name: Sun King Brewery
venues.description: Sun King is Indianapolis's largest independent brewery, founded in 2009, and its original downtown taproom sits on North College Avenue in the Cole-Noble district. It is on this list because it brews its own non-alcoholic beer rather than stocking someone else's: the N/A Sunlight Cream Ale is an alcohol-free version of Sunlight, the award-winning flagship, at under 0.5% ABV and available year-round. Visit Indy counts two Sun King brews reimagined without alcohol alongside guest zero-proof beers and four classic mocktails at the taproom. One caution worth knowing before you go: Sun King also cans hemp-derived THC seltzers under its Sun King Hemp line, and those are sold in the same room.
signatureDrinks: N/A Sunlight Cream Ale (alcohol-free version of the flagship cream ale, under 0.5% ABV)
venues.longDescription:
Sun King opened in 2009 in a warehouse on North College Avenue and grew into the defining Indianapolis brewery — the one whose cans are in every corner shop in the state and whose Sunlight Cream Ale functions as the local house beer. The original downtown taproom is still on College, in the Cole-Noble commercial arts district a few blocks east of Mass Ave, and it is a working brewery floor rather than a designed bar: high ceilings, tanks visible, long tables, food trucks outside.

What earns it a place in a non-alcoholic guide is that Sun King brews the alcohol-free option itself. N/A Sunlight Cream Ale is a genuinely dealcoholised version of the flagship, kept under 0.5% ABV and produced year-round rather than as a January novelty, and it holds the malt-forward, faintly sweet character that makes the original work. In a brewery taproom the difference between that and a bought-in national NA brand is considerable: you are drinking the same beer the room is built around, poured from the same bar, at the same table, which is most of what a non-drinker actually wants in a brewery. Visit Indy's guide counts two Sun King brews reimagined without alcohol, plus guest zero-proof beers and four standing mocktails.

Two honest caveats. First, this is a brewery, and the overwhelming majority of what is poured here contains alcohol — the non-alcoholic option is real and well made, but the room is not a sober space. Second, Sun King also produces the Sun King Hemp line of hemp-derived THC seltzers in flavours including wild cherry, blood orange, blueberry and lemonade, and those are sold on the same premises. They contain no alcohol but they are intoxicating, and anyone avoiding psychoactives should read the can rather than assume that everything labelled zero-proof here is inert. The taproom opens at 11am seven days and closes between 8pm and 10pm depending on the day.
venues.pressQuote: Sun King Brewery has two of their signature brews reimagined to be non-alcoholic, plus zero-proof beers and four classic mocktails.

venues.name: Sundry and Vice
venues.description: Sundry and Vice is an apothecary-themed craft cocktail bar that opened in 2015 at 18 W. 13th Street in Over-the-Rhine, its era-authentic storefront lined with antique jars, medical ephemera and framed vintage prescriptions. Alongside a nationally celebrated cocktail list, the bar keeps a dedicated N/A and zero-proof section of house-built mocktails: the Ube Driver (pineapple, ube, almond, lime and tonic water), the Almond Brothers (lime, almond and ginger beer), the Lil' Fizz (lime, pineapple, ginger, mint and seltzer) and the elderflower-and-chamomile Herbal Remedy. These are made in-house from fresh juices, housemade syrups and vintage-fountain sodas, so the alcohol-free drinks get the same craft as the cocktails. Low-proof and custom non-alcoholic drinks are also available on request.
venues.longDescription:
Sundry and Vice opened March 27, 2015, in the heart of historic Over-the-Rhine, taking its cue from the turn-of-the-century apothecary — back when druggists dispensed alcoholic tonics and elixirs for everything from the plague to indigestion. The room is dressed as an era-authentic pharmacy, with antique jars and bottles, assorted medical ephemera and framed vintage prescriptions on the walls (including one for cocaine, a former painkiller and dandruff cure). Within a few years it drew national attention, earning nods from the New York Times and Eater, and in 2018 it was named one of the world's best bars. In June 2025 longtime regional manager Mary Barnett acquired the brand from founder Stuart King, and the bar continues to operate under her ownership.

The zero-proof drinking here is treated as its own craft rather than an afterthought. A standing "N/A and zero proof" menu section anchors on house-built mocktails: the Ube Driver blends pineapple, ube, almond, lime and tonic water; the Almond Brothers pairs lime and almond with ginger beer; the Lil' Fizz mixes lime, pineapple, ginger, mint and seltzer; and the Herbal Remedy leans on elderflower and chamomile. These are made the same way as the cocktails — fresh juices, housemade syrups and sodas dispensed through a vintage fountain soda draft arm. As WCPO notes, low-proof or non-alcoholic cocktails are also available upon request, so bartenders will build something bespoke and buzz-free if nothing on the list fits.

The bar sits at 18 W. 13th Street, an easy walk from Washington Park and the Vine Street corridor. It opens in the late afternoon most days (from 2 p.m. on weekends) and runs late — to 2 a.m. on Fridays and Saturdays — with a dim, vintage-parlor atmosphere that suits a date, a small group or a solo nightcap. Reach the bar at (513) 721-8423 or on Instagram @sundryandvice. The mocktail lineup rotates with the seasons, so specific drinks may change; call ahead if you're coming for a particular pour.
venues.pressQuote: Low-proof or non-alcoholic cocktails are available upon request, but the bar also has its own mocktails.

venues.name: Sundry & Vice
venues.description: Sundry & Vice is an apothecary-themed cocktail bar inside the Bottleworks Hotel at the top of Massachusetts Avenue, opened on 23 October 2021 as the second location of the Cincinnati bar of the same name in Over-the-Rhine. The fit-out runs to pharmacy cabinetry, tincture bottles and a soda-fountain sensibility, and the program is built on house-made syrups, freshly squeezed juice and cocktails on draft. That component-driven approach is why the zero-proof drinks work: The Young and the Spiritless layers Spiritless non-alcoholic bourbon with pineapple, cinnamon, orgeat, plum bitters, mint and ginger beer, and 24 Carrot Magic builds Seedlip Grove over carrot, lemon, pineapple, black pepper and ginger.
signatureDrinks: The Young and the Spiritless (Spiritless non-alcoholic bourbon, pineapple, cinnamon, orgeat, plum bitters, mint, ginger beer)
24 Carrot Magic (Seedlip Grove, carrot, lemon, pineapple, black pepper, ginger)
venues.longDescription:
Sundry & Vice started in Cincinnati's Over-the-Rhine as an apothecary-styled cocktail bar with an unusually serious hospitality culture, and in October 2021 it crossed a state line for the first time, opening inside the Bottleworks Hotel at 850 Massachusetts Avenue. The Bottleworks District is the redeveloped Coca-Cola bottling plant that anchors the north end of Mass Ave, and the bar fits the building: pharmacy cabinets, apothecary bottles, a soda-fountain lineage and a room that reads as pre-war chemist rather than speakeasy pastiche. The house style is modern readings of classics, built on syrups made in-house and juice squeezed to order, with an unusual emphasis on cocktails poured from draft lines.

That infrastructure is exactly what makes a good non-alcoholic drink possible, and Sundry & Vice uses it. The Young and the Spiritless is the more elaborate build: Spiritless non-alcoholic bourbon carrying pineapple, cinnamon, orgeat, plum bitters and mint, lengthened with ginger beer, so the drink has the weight and bitterness a bourbon sour would have rather than reading as a soft drink. 24 Carrot Magic is the vegetal counterpart, layering Seedlip Grove — the citrus expression of the London-made non-alcoholic distillate — over carrot, lemon, pineapple, black pepper and ginger. Both appear in Visit Indy's official Buzz-Free Drinks guide, which is the closest thing the city has to a municipal endorsement of a zero-proof list.

The practical case for coming here is location as much as menu. Within roughly two hundred metres you also have The Fountain Room's printed No ABV section in the same complex, and BODHI and Ball & Biscuit a short walk down Mass Ave, which makes this the densest concentration of credible non-alcoholic drinking in Indiana. Being inside a hotel, it also runs a more consistent evening than a standalone bar and is a reasonable solo stop.
venues.pressQuote: "The Young and the Spiritless" — spiritless bourbon, pineapple, cinnamon, orgeat, plum bitters, mint, ginger beer.

venues.name: Sunken Harbor Club
venues.description: Sunken Harbor Club is an immersive tropical cocktail bar on the second floor above Gage & Tollner on Fulton Street, opened in October 2021 and led by Chief Cocktail Officer Garret Richard — one of the most respected tiki technicians working in the United States. It won its category at the inaugural NYC's Best Bars for NA Awards, recognised for tiki-style non-alcoholic drinks, which is a harder trick than it sounds: tiki depends on rum's weight and funk, so building the same lushness without it demands real work with syrups, acids and spice rather than a swap from a bottle. The bar serves alcohol as well. It trades 5pm to 11pm, and to midnight on Friday and Saturday.

venues.longDescription:
Sunken Harbor Club occupies the second floor above Gage & Tollner on Fulton Street in Downtown Brooklyn, and it is one of the most completely realised bar concepts in the city — a tropical room run by Garret Richard as Chief Cocktail Officer, with St. John Frizell as partner and Tom Wolfson as quartermaster. Richard is among the most respected tiki technicians working in America and co-wrote Tropical Standard: Cocktail Techniques and Reinvented Recipes, which is effectively the modern reference text for the category. A second location opened in Bermuda in 2022. It is walk-in only, first come first served, and 21-and-over after 7pm, open from 5pm daily.

It was one of seven winners at NYC's Best Bars for NA 2025 — the awards run one flat, unranked winners tier rather than named categories, so "winner" is the accurate word and "won its category" is not. The judges' reasoning is the useful part: they praised it for pulling off an extremely committed tiki bar concept with excellent non-alcoholic drinks that are not just juicy mocktails, calling the five On Dry Land concoctions diverse and complex — and adding that any bar which sets drinks on fire is a winner in their books. That section name, On Dry Land, is subtitled simply Nonalcoholic, and the five are entirely house-made, using no bought-in non-alcoholic spirits at all, which is rare and is why they taste unlike anyone else's. Jubilee at $18 is the bar's spin on a cherry phosphate, combining sour cherry and wild cherry bark with seltzer, lime and juniper over pebble ice. Scrimshaw at $18 is the ambitious one — clarified grapefruit and elderflower stirred with bitter herbs and spices as a genuine alternative to amaro, served on a big rock. The Elixir at $16 is a carbonated brew of gentian, sarsaparilla and wintergreen. Silk Road Swizzle at $16 is Assam tea with cardamom, spiced lime and quinine. Eye of the Storm at $16 sets golden passion fruit against the force of the house ginger beer.
venues.pressQuote: Kudos to Sunken Harbor Club for pulling off an extremely committed tiki bar concept with excellent non-alcoholic drinks that aren't just juicy mocktails. Their five "On Dry Land" concoctions are diverse and complex.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Judges, NYC's Best Bars for NA 2025

venues.name: Sunny's
venues.description: Sunny's (originally "Sunny's Steakhouse") is a Little River destination restaurant from co-owners Will Thompson and Carey Hynes, the team behind Miami's Jaguar Sun, with Aaron Brooks (ex–Four Seasons) as executive chef. It opened permanently in October 2024 after evolving from a pandemic-era outdoor pop-up, and quickly landed in the MICHELIN Guide. The 13,000-square-foot space spans chandelier-lit indoor rooms and a courtyard shaded by a banyan tree, with two bars. For non-drinkers, Sunny's runs a named "Cold Sober" mocktail menu (around $14–18) built around real zero-proof products and house ingredients. Documented pours include the Chickadee (NA Lucano, grapefruit, passion fruit, mace, lime), the Sanbitter Spritz (Sanbitter NA Campari soda, cucumber, strawberry, lemon), the Golden Spritz (Martini Floreale NA aperitivo, Mt. Olympus tea, citrus, bubbles), and the Annabel Lee (watermelon, pineapple, lime, champagne vinegar, house habanero syrup).
venues.longDescription:
Sunny's began as a pandemic-era outdoor pop-up and opened permanently in Little River in October 2024, from co-owners Will Thompson and Carey Hynes — the team behind Jaguar Sun — with Aaron Brooks, formerly of the Four Seasons, as executive chef. It landed in the MICHELIN Guide quickly. The 13,000-square-foot site runs from chandelier-lit indoor rooms to a courtyard shaded by a banyan tree, with two bars.

A steakhouse is among the hardest rooms in which to not drink. The format is built around big red wine and brown spirits, the meal is long, and the non-drinker spends two hours watching a bottle get poured. Sunny's answer is a named Cold Sober menu, priced around fourteen to eighteen dollars, built on real zero-proof products and house ingredients rather than juice.

The range is unusually wide. The Chickadee uses non-alcoholic Lucano with grapefruit, passion fruit, mace and lime. The Sanbitter Spritz is built on Sanbitter, the zero-proof Campari soda, with cucumber, strawberry and lemon. The Golden Spritz uses Martini Floreale with Mt. Olympus tea, citrus and bubbles. The Annabel Lee works watermelon and pineapple against lime, champagne vinegar and a house habanero syrup — vinegar and chilli rather than sugar, which is what lets a drink stand up to a steak.

Four drinks across four different non-alcoholic bases, several of them bitter or savoury, is a properly considered list. Bitterness is the quality most often missing from zero-proof menus and the one that makes a drink work alongside rich food.

It is a full-service restaurant with two bars and a wine programme, not an alcohol-free venue — but the Cold Sober list means the meal works either way. The courtyard under the banyan is the seat worth asking for, and the Cold Sober list runs at both bars.
venues.pressQuote: A classy party that breezes between a tree-covered courtyard and stylish dining rooms.

venues.longDescription: Superbueno is a Mexican-American cocktail bar at 13 First Avenue in Manhattan's East Village (at the corner of 1st and 1st), opened in April 2023 by acclaimed bartender Ignacio "Nacho" Jimenez with Cocktail Kingdom Hospitality Group's Greg Boehm. It was named Best New U.S. Cocktail Bar at the 2024 Tales of the Cocktail Spirited Awards and ranked No. 2 on North America's 50 Best Bars in both 2024 and 2025. Alongside its spice-driven agave cocktails, Superbueno maintains a serious, well-regarded non-alcoholic program: its zero-proof list includes an alcohol-free version of the signature Mole Negroni, the La Shammami (a hibiscus-habanero tonic with lemongrass and watermelon agua fresca), and the Michela-Na, a non-alcoholic michelada, plus non-alcoholic beer. Time Out included Superbueno among the NYC bars serving the best non-alcoholic drinks in the city.
venues.pressQuote: At this East Village industry favorite bar that happens to be on the 2025 World's 50 Best Bars list, you'll find a distinctly Mexican American twist on cocktails where the zero-proof options are far from an afterthought.

venues.name: Supernormal
venues.description: Supernormal is Andrew McConnell's modern-Asian dining room on Flinders Lane, and its cocktail card gives alcohol-free drinks a printed section of their own rather than an afterthought at the bottom. Five house builds cover the range: Plum & Petal on passionfruit husk, plum and basil soda; Matsurika on jasmine, apple and lemon verbena; a seasonal soda of tamarind, bay leaf and Vermont maple; Mockingbird with grapefruit sherbet and lime; and Tea Totaler, chamomile, jasmine and ginger, at A$12 the cheapest considered drink in the room. Behind them sit alcohol-free and low-ABV beers from Bridge Road and Hop Nation, five de-alcoholised wines including Leitz Eins-Zwei-Zero and Kolonne Null sparkling rose, and a reserve tea list poured with the same seriousness as the wine.

venues.longDescription:
Supernormal opened on Flinders Lane in 2014 as the loose, late-running counterpart to Andrew McConnell's more formal rooms, and it has stayed one of the busiest dining rooms in the Melbourne CBD: an open kitchen, a long bar you can eat at alone, a karaoke room downstairs, and a modern-Asian menu that leans Japanese. Gourmet Traveller called it "free-wheeling, fun, flavour-forward and far better than any carbon copy", which is also a fair description of how the drinks list behaves.

What earns it a place here is structural rather than incidental. The cocktail card, dated on its face and reprinted as it changes, prints ALCOHOL FREE COCKTAILS as a heading with five drinks under it, then ALCOHOL FREE & LOW ABV BEER, then ALCOHOL FREE & LOW ABV WINE. That is three separate alcohol-free categories on a card that runs to eight pages, and the drinks in them are built the way the alcoholic ones are: Plum & Petal uses passionfruit husk rather than juice, Matsurika sets jasmine against apple and lemon verbena, and the seasonal soda has run tamarind with bay leaf and Vermont maple. Tea Totaler, at A$12, is chamomile, jasmine and ginger, and is the drink to ask for if you want something long and low-sugar.

The bottled side is unusually deep for a restaurant. Bridge Road 'Free Time' pale ale and Hop Nation 'Mind Ya Head' XPA cover beer at 0.5%; the wine runs Vinada sparkling chardonnay, Kolonne Null sparkling rose at 0.0%, a Chalmers vermentino from Heathcote, a Plus + Minus rose from the Adelaide Hills and Leitz 'Eins-Zwei Zero.Five' pinot noir, all available by the glass. There is also a reserve tea selection - gyokuro, genmaicha, yuzu kukicha - which for a non-drinker at a long dinner is the most useful part of the whole list. Book ahead; the room is loud and full most nights, and the bar seats are the best place to drink from this card.
venues.pressQuote: Free-wheeling, fun, flavour-forward and far better than any carbon copy.

venues.name: Supperland
venues.description: Supperland is a southern steakhouse and cocktail bar set inside a restored church at 1212 The Plaza in Plaza Midwood — the bar occupies the original 1948 building, the dining room the 1956 sanctuary — from husband-and-wife owners Jeff Tonidandel and Jamie Brown. It is Michelin Selected. Head mixologist Colleen Hughes, fifteen years with the restaurant group, was named Esquire's Cocktail Guru of the Year in 2022 and received a 2025 Michelin Guide American South Exceptional Cocktails Award. Her "Spirit-Free Cocktails" section runs four drinks, every one marked vegan on the menu: the Spirit-Free Italian Spritz ($13, Lyre's non-alcoholic Italian spritz, Freixenet non-alcoholic sparkling wine, soda, acid phosphate, orange), Golden Hour ($15, Sentia GABA Gold botanical, passionfruit syrup, ginger kombucha, containing adaptogens), Bright and Spritzy ($15, verjus blanc, Amethyst grapefruit basil, simple syrup, soda), and the Spirit-Free Amaretti Sour ($15, two Lyre's expressions with lemon stock and a vegan egg white). Athletic Free Wave and Lenny Boy kombucha are $6, with three non-alcoholic wines by the glass.

venues.longDescription:
Supperland occupies a restored church at 1212 The Plaza in Plaza Midwood, and the building is genuinely two buildings: the cocktail bar sits in the original 1948 structure, which held about a hundred people, while the main dining room fills the larger sanctuary completed for the Church of Christ congregation in 1956. Between the congregation and the restaurant the property was a frame shop, a gallery and a bead shop. It is run by Jeff Tonidandel and Jamie Brown, a husband-and-wife team behind a handful of Charlotte restaurants — Jeff came to hospitality in 2009 after working in NASCAR. The kitchen is a Southern steakhouse: a ten-ounce prime filet at $91, a whole shelled lobster at $125, wagyu pot roast at $42, ambrosia salad at $10. It has been Michelin Selected, and it is worth booking rather than arriving, with the restaurant recommending a car service given how little street parking there is.

The reason a non-drinker should pay attention here is the person making the drinks. Head mixologist Colleen Hughes has been with the restaurant group for fifteen years, was named Cocktail Guru of the Year by Esquire in 2022, and received a 2025 Michelin Guide American South Exceptional Cocktails Award. Her spirit-free section runs four drinks, every one marked vegan on the menu — a detail almost no bar bothers to state. The Spirit-Free Italian Spritz ($13) combines Lyre's non-alcoholic Italian spritz liqueur with Freixenet non-alcoholic sparkling wine, soda, acid phosphate and orange. Golden Hour ($15) is the most unusual, built on Sentia GABA Gold, a botanical supplement, with passionfruit syrup and ginger kombucha — the menu notes plainly that it contains adaptogens. Bright and Spritzy ($15) uses verjus blanc with Amethyst grapefruit basil, and the Spirit-Free Amaretti Sour ($15) works two Lyre's expressions with lemon stock over a house-made vegan egg white. Athletic's Free Wave hazy IPA and a Lenny Boy ginger kombucha are $6, and there are three non-alcoholic wines by the glass.
venues.pressQuote: Supperland also features a Spirit-Free Italian Spritz on their menu, as well as non-alcoholic sparkling white wine as a standalone option, and a phony negroni.

venues.name: SÜRENITEA Wellness Kava Bar
venues.description: SÜRENITEA is a fully alcohol-free wellness and kava bar in Miami's Wynwood Arts District, styled as a Pacific-island-inspired "oasis of calm" with a plant-filled interior and the tagline "Meditation in a cup." Instead of alcohol, the menu is built entirely around botanical and functional beverages: ceremonial-grade kava (including Vanuatu and Tongan varieties), kratom drinks, functional-mushroom "cocktails," nootropic and biohacking elixirs, brewed teas, and a range of fruit-forward mocktails, alongside vegan food. The venue emphasizes COA-tested ingredients and staff who help guests choose drinks by desired effect — relaxation, energy, or recovery. It operates as a community-focused space where locals work, socialize, and unwind without alcohol, and stays open late on weekends. SÜRENITEA holds a 4.9-star rating from roughly 100 reviewers and is frequently cited among Wynwood's notable kava and wellness bars.
venues.longDescription:
SURENITEA occupies a plant-filled room in Wynwood and styles itself an oasis of calm, with the tagline meditation in a cup — a deliberate contrast with the arts district around it, which is among the loudest nightlife strips in Miami. The menu is botanical rather than alcoholic throughout: ceremonial-grade kava including Vanuatu and Tongan varieties, kratom drinks, functional-mushroom builds, nootropic elixirs, brewed teas and fruit-forward mocktails, with vegan food alongside.

Two things distinguish it from the other kava rooms in the neighbourhood. The first is that its ingredients are COA-tested — certificates of analysis, meaning independent lab verification of what is actually in the product. In a category that is largely unregulated in the United States, that is a meaningful and uncommon commitment. The second is how the staff are trained to sell: guests are guided by desired effect rather than by flavour, choosing between relaxation, energy or recovery. That framing treats the drinks as functional rather than decorative, which is at least honest about what people are buying.

It holds a 4.9-star rating across roughly a hundred reviewers and is consistently named among Wynwood's notable kava and wellness bars. It works as a daytime workspace as readily as a late-night room, staying open late at weekends.

The caveat that belongs on every kava listing applies here and should not be softened: kava is psychoactive and sedating, with documented case reports of liver injury, and kratom acts on opioid receptors and carries real dependence and withdrawal risk. Everything served is free of alcohol. That is a narrower claim than nothing served having an effect, and for anyone whose reason for avoiding alcohol is recovery from a substance-use disorder, the difference is the whole question. For a first visit, tell the staff what you want the evening to do rather than what you want to drink — the menu is organised around effect, and that is how it is meant to be read.

The standard kava-bar caution applies. Kava is psychoactive rather than merely herbal — a mild sedative and anxiolytic — and it should not be mixed with alcohol or with sedating prescriptions. Where kratom is on the menu it is a distinct substance carrying a distinct and more contested risk profile, dependence included. That matters most to exactly the people an alcohol-free room serves best, so ask what is in a drink rather than assuming, and speak to a clinician if you are on medication.

venues.name: Swamp Cow Kava Lounge
venues.description: Swamp Cow was Seattle's first kava bar, opened on Denny Way in Uptown by a couple of locals with roots in the Florida sober nightlife scene — the part of the country where alcohol-free lounges were normal long before the Pacific Northwest caught up. It calls itself the one and only late-night alcohol-free lounge in Seattle, and it works as a retail shop and a hangout at the same time: a wide range of prepackaged and branded adaptogenic drinks including kava, blue lotus and kanna, plus kombucha, ginger beer, non-alcoholic beer, seltzers, teas, coffee and sodas. The room has ample comfortable seating, WiFi, a full sound system and a modest stage for local artists, and the calendar is dense — weekly trivia, a Thursday open mic, highlighted artists, video games, movie nights, sporting events, dance and art groups, and EP release shows. Kava, blue lotus and kanna are all psychoactive botanicals rather than soft drinks: no alcohol, but not inert either.
venues.longDescription:
Swamp Cow holds a specific place in this city's history as Seattle's first kava bar, and its origin explains a lot about how it operates. The founders are locals who spent time in the Florida sober nightlife scene — Florida is where the American kava bar took hold first and where alcohol-free lounges have been a normal part of going out for years — and they brought that template north to a city that had somehow never had one. The result sits on Denny Way in Uptown and describes itself, fairly, as the one and only late-night alcohol-free lounge in Seattle. The model is half retail shop and half living room: you can buy something and leave, or take a seat and stay, and the room is set up for the second option with ample comfortable seating, WiFi throughout, a full sound system and a modest stage.

The drinks list is broader than kava and worth understanding before you order. Alongside prepared kava the shop carries a wide range of prepackaged and branded adaptogenic beverages, including blue lotus and kanna, plus a conventional non-alcoholic backbone of kombucha, ginger beer, non-alcoholic beer, seltzers, teas, coffee and sodas. That range matters because it means a group can walk in with genuinely different needs — one person wanting kava, one wanting an NA beer, one wanting a coffee at 9pm — and all be served properly. What fills the room, though, is the programming: weekly trivia, a Thursday open mic that has become the anchor event, highlighted local artists, video game nights, movie nights, televised sport, dance and art groups, and EP release shows. For anyone rebuilding a social life without drinking, a fixed weekly calendar is worth more than any particular drink on the menu. One honest note: kava, blue lotus and kanna are psychoactive botanicals, not soft drinks. None contains alcohol, and none is habit-forming in the way alcohol is, but all three act on mood, which is worth knowing if what you are avoiding is intoxication in general.

venues.name: Swift Soho
venues.description: Swift opened on Old Compton Street in November 2016, taking over the site of the long-running Soho drinking den Lab. It is the work of Bobby Hiddleston and Mia Johansson — a bartending couple who met while working at the celebrated, now-shuttered Milk & Honey — in partnership with Edmund Weil and Rosie Stimpson, the team behind Nightjar and Oriole. The name is a promise: an upstairs bar built for a quick, well-made drink before dinner or the theatre, with no booking required, and a dark cocktail den below for settling in. It has since grown into a small group with further bars in Shoreditch and Borough, and is a near-permanent fixture on the World's 50 Best Bars list. The walk-in upstairs room carries a dedicated non-alcoholic list alongside its aperitivo menu, and the sibling Swift Borough pours a named low/no serve, the Atopia, with spiced citrus, Botivo, strawberry and pink peppercorn.
venues.longDescription:
Swift opened on Old Compton Street in November 2016, taking over the site of the long-running Soho drinking den Lab. It is the work of Bobby Hiddleston and Mia Johansson — a bartending couple who met while working at the celebrated (now-shuttered) Milk & Honey — in partnership with Edmund Weil and Rosie Stimpson, the team behind the acclaimed Nightjar and Oriole. The name is a promise: an upstairs bar built for a quick, well-made drink before dinner or the theatre, no booking required. It has since grown into a small group, with further Swift bars in Shoreditch and Borough, and is a near-permanent fixture on the World's 50 Best Bars list.

The Soho original is really two bars in one. The ground-floor room is bright, compact and briskly run, with a menu of aperitivos, wines, low-ABV serves and non-alcoholic cocktails poured over hand-cut clear ice with minimal garnish. Downstairs is a darker, reservations-only basement lounge with leather booths, an enormous whisky collection (more than 300 bottles across a 68-page list) and live jazz on Tuesday and Sunday evenings. Cocktails on the ground floor are grouped by character — Bright, Delicate, Rich and Stiff — so you order by mood rather than by base spirit.

The alcohol-free options sit inside those same categories rather than being exiled to an afterthought, each marked "0%" and priced around £9. The 0% Working Holiday is the effervescent, juicy one: Atopia spiced-citrus distillate lengthened with hops, passion fruit, pink grapefruit sherbet and sparkling green tea. The 0% Rock Garden is the short, zesty sour — Atopia spiced citrus and Seedlip Spice 94 shaken with almond, lemon and egg white for a properly foamed texture. Both lean on Swift's house sherbets and the same clarified, clean-glass presentation as the full-strength list, so they read as considered cocktails rather than fruit juice. The upstairs menu also carries non-alcoholic beer, alcohol-free wine and a rotating aperitivo section, and the bar team will build off-menu zero-proof serves on request.
venues.pressQuote: The non-alcoholic section of this Soho spot's menu is packed full of fun and interesting drinks.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: The Infatuation, "Where To Go For A Drink When You're Not Drinking"

venues.name: Switchback Brewing Co.
venues.description: Switchback is an employee-owned Burlington brewery on Flynn Avenue, best known for its unfiltered Switchback Ale, and since January 2026 it has been the most heavily invested non-alcoholic producer in Vermont. The brewery installed a BrewVo de-alcoholisation system to bring production of Switchback N.A. fully in-house after the beer outgrew its trial run, and the same equipment makes Burlington the East Coast production site for BrewVo-made beers on behalf of other breweries and drinks brands. The tap room pours the full range and is open Wednesday to Sunday from noon to 9pm, Tuesday evenings from 5pm, closed Monday.
