Tartine Bistro occupies a small house on Old Detroit Road in Rocky River, the lakefront suburb ten miles west of downtown, and has been the west side's reference French bistro for years — croissants and quiche at the front of the day, steak frites and the rest of the canon at dinner, and a Sunday brunch that fills the room. Service runs from midday Tuesday through Saturday, which makes it one of the few kitchens on this list open across a long afternoon rather than only from 4pm.

The non-alcoholic drinks are the work of a bar that treats them seasonally, and both current builds are $13 — the same territory as the cocktails, which is the honest test of whether a kitchen means it. The Petit Autumn layers cider with vanilla, maple, ginger and cayenne, then finishes with apple butter and a bruléed apple, so it arrives warm-spiced and textured rather than sweet; the cayenne is doing the structural work, stopping the drink collapsing into dessert. Mon Petit Coeur is the more unusual of the two, built on an alcohol-removed red wine with apple cider, cinnamon and maple — effectively a zero-proof mulled wine served as a composed cocktail, and one of the very few uses of de-alcoholised wine as a base rather than simply poured by the glass anywhere in the Cleveland market.

The restaurant's general manager told Cleveland Magazine's 2026 mocktail roundup that a wellness focus has taken alcohol out of a growing share of guests' lives and that people appreciate having something made for them rather than being handed a soft-drink list. For a slightly formal dinner on the west side where part of the table is not drinking, Tartine is the strongest option outside the Lakewood cluster, and the only one with a French wine list running in parallel.
venues.pressQuote: A wellness focus has removed alcohol from their lives, and people appreciate it.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Tartine Bistro general manager, via Cleveland Magazine

venues.name: Tavern of Tales
venues.description: Tavern of Tales is a board game cafe and bar on Tremont Street in Mission Hill, with a free curated game shelf, a full library catalogued on BoardGameGeek and private soundproof rooms available to book. It is licensed and serves cocktails, but its menu also runs a printed nonalcoholic section that is longer than the cocktail list. Three house mocktails are $6.99: Red Flags, a fizzy strawberry drink with lime and ginger; Ticket to Ride, its version of an Arnold Palmer built with a house lavender syrup and honey; and Dispelled Magic, orange and cranberry juice with cinnamon. A house lavender lemonade, Barritt's ginger beer, George Howell cold brew and espresso, and a specialty latte list round it out.
signatureDrinks: Red Flags (fizzy strawberry drink with bright notes of lime and ginger)
Ticket to Ride (Arnold Palmer with house lavender syrup and honey)
Dispelled Magic (orange and cranberry juice with cinnamon)
Lavender Lemonade (lemonade with house lavender syrup)
Honeybee Latte (rooibos latte with honey, turmeric and cinnamon, caffeine free)
venues.longDescription:
Tavern of Tales sits at 1478 Tremont Street in Mission Hill, between Roxbury Crossing and the Longwood medical area, and bills itself as Boston's only board game cafe and bar. There is a shelf of free games curated by staff for anyone who walks in, a much larger library catalogued publicly on BoardGameGeek, and private soundproof rooms that can be reserved for longer sessions. Opening hours run 3pm to 10pm on weekdays and from 10am at weekends, so it works both as a Saturday afternoon and as a weeknight evening.

The drinks card is a single sheet with the cocktails on one half and a nonalcoholic block on the other, and the nonalcoholic block is the larger of the two. Three house mocktails are listed at $6.99 with the same descriptions the bar gives its cocktails: Red Flags is a fizzy strawberry drink with bright notes of lime and ginger; Ticket to Ride, punning on the MBTA, is the house version of an Arnold Palmer made with a house lavender syrup and honey; Dispelled Magic is orange and cranberry juice with cinnamon. A lavender lemonade at $5 uses the same house syrup, a Shirley Temple is $4, and Barritt's extra zesty ginger beer from Bermuda is $4. The coffee side is more serious than the format suggests, with George Howell's Dota Blend on cold brew and the Alchemy Blend for espresso, and a specialty latte list available until 5pm that includes a caffeine-free Honeybee latte of rooibos with honey, turmeric and cinnamon, plus matcha, strawberry matcha, lavender matcha and spicy chai. Alcohol is served in the room, so this is a licensed venue with a genuine but simple zero-proof list, not an alcohol-free one. Brunch runs at weekends from 10am, and the specialty latte list is cut off at 5pm, which leaves the three mocktails, the lavender lemonade, the ginger beer and the cold brew as the evening options.

venues.name: Tavolàta
venues.description: Tavolàta is the Boise outpost of Ethan Stowell's Italian restaurant group, built around long communal tables and handmade pasta, and it keeps two named alcohol-free drinks on the list: Donn's Fizz and White Sands. The communal-table format is quietly useful for a non-drinker — a long shared table with food at its centre makes the meal the event rather than the drinking, and nobody is counting rounds. It opens at 4pm seven days a week, which is more consistent than most of Boise's better options. In a city where the good alcohol-free drinks come with awkward schedules, a seven-day restaurant is the reliable default when plans change late.
venues.longDescription:
Tavolàta on West Grove Street is the Boise location of Ethan Stowell's Italian group, and the concept is built around a long communal table running down the centre of the room, handmade pasta, and a menu meant to be shared.

That format does something specific for a non-drinker. At a bar, the drink is the entire proposition, and the person not holding one is visibly outside the activity. At a communal table with plates arriving in the middle, the food is the event and the drinking is incidental to it — nobody is tracking who is on their third glass, because everyone is reaching for the same bowl of pasta. It is the same reason restaurants are generally easier than bars, amplified by the seating.

The two named alcohol-free drinks are Donn's Fizz and White Sands. The first is almost certainly a nod to Donn Beach, the founder of tiki, whose drinks were built on layered syrups, citrus and spice — a style that translates unusually well to zero-proof because the character never lived entirely in the rum.

The hours are the practical strength. Tavolàta opens at 4pm and serves until 10pm every day of the week, which sounds unremarkable until you look at the rest of this guide: Free Spirits is open two days, Art Haus four, Saltbrush six, Craft Lounge six. Boise's alcohol-free scene has good drinks and awkward schedules, and a seven-day restaurant with named zero-proof options is the reliable default when a plan changes. It sits next to Saltbrush and a short walk from the 8th Street cluster. For a group where only some people are drinking, a shared-table restaurant is usually a better call than a bar, and this is the most convenient one downtown.
venues.pressQuote: Situated in downtown Boise, Idaho, at the heart of the state's capital, Tavolàta is all about the pasta

venues.name: Tazza Kitchen Scott's Addition
venues.description: Tazza Kitchen's Scott's Addition location is a wood-fired neighbourhood restaurant whose bar keeps thoughtfully constructed non-alcoholic drinks on the standing list — the Centerfold is the one local guides name. What makes it useful in this particular district is the split-service schedule and the food-first orientation: Tazza trades lunch and dinner with a break between, so it functions as a proper meal out rather than a drinking session, which is exactly what a group needs when it is anchoring an evening in Richmond's brewery quarter around someone who is not drinking. Scott's Addition is otherwise organised almost entirely around taprooms, and a wood-fired kitchen with a real dinner service is a scarce thing in it.
venues.longDescription:
Tazza Kitchen is a small Virginia and Carolina group built around wood-fired cooking, and its Scott's Addition location on Roseneath Road serves the district that has become Richmond's brewery centre. That context shapes why it appears in an alcohol-free guide: Scott's Addition is a hard place to spend an evening without drinking, because almost everything in it is organised around a taproom.

Tazza is a restaurant first. It runs a genuine lunch and dinner service with a break in between, and the room is oriented around tables and food rather than a bar and a queue. For a group where one person is not drinking, that structure quietly solves the problem: the evening has a purpose beyond the glass, and nobody is counting rounds.

The bar keeps non-alcoholic drinks on the standing list rather than offering to improvise, and the Centerfold is the one Virginia food press names specifically. A single documented drink is a modest programme and the grade reflects that honestly — this is a restaurant that has thought about non-drinkers, not a destination for the drink itself.

The wood-fired oven is the kitchen's centre of gravity and the menu is built around it, which suits a long table and a slow evening — the format that works best when only part of the group is drinking. The schedule is worth reading before you go, because it is more complicated than most: Monday is dinner only from 4:30pm; Tuesday to Friday split into a lunch service from 11:30am and dinner from 4:30pm; Saturday runs straight through from 11am to 10pm; and Sunday splits again around a 2:30pm close and a 4:30pm reopening. Arriving at three in the afternoon on a weekday will find the doors shut. Once inside, it is among the easiest rooms in Scott's Addition for a mixed group.

venues.name: Tea & Poets
venues.description: Tea & Poets is a tea lounge and arts space in the Shops at Sunset Place in South Miami, established in 2016. Its drink list is built entirely on tea, and the largest section of the menu is headed "Tea Cocktails" with the subtitle "non-alcoholic" printed directly beneath it: ten named builds including the Blueberry Mojito (spearmint green tea, fresh lemon, mint, blueberry), the Blood Orange Basil (English breakfast, blood orange bitters, fresh basil, lemon juice, cane sugar), the Immune Intervention (ginger Ubud, lemon juice, honey, activated charcoal) and the Julley Butter Tea (Kashmir chai, whipped butter, brown cane sugar). Tea baristas will also blend a custom tea to order. The room hosts a long-running open mic on Wednesday nights at 7pm and stays open until 10pm on Wednesday, Friday and Saturday.
venues.address: 5701 Sunset Dr Unit 126, South Miami, FL 33143
venues.hours: Mon-Tue 12pm-8pm; Wed 12pm-10pm; Thu 12pm-8pm; Fri 12pm-10pm; Sat 11am-10pm; Sun 11am-8pm
signatureDrinks: Blueberry Mojito (spearmint green tea, fresh lemon, mint, blueberry)
Blood Orange Basil (English breakfast tea, blood orange bitters, fresh basil, lemon juice, white cane sugar)
Immune Intervention (ginger Ubud tea, lemon juice, honey, activated charcoal)
Julley Butter Tea (Kashmir chai, whipped butter, brown cane sugar)
Berry Beautiful (green tea, lemon juice, red berry, white cane sugar)
Green Tea Lemonade (gunpowder green tea, lemon juice, white cane sugar)
venues.longDescription:
Tea & Poets opened in 2016 in Unit 126 of 5701 Sunset Drive, inside the Shops at Sunset Place complex in South Miami, and describes itself as a community space that brings together tea, arts, crafts, poetry and music. The room functions as a cafe by day and a small performance venue by night: the open mic runs on Wednesdays at 7pm and has become the shop's best-known fixture, with visiting and local performers filling the back half of the room. Closing time is 8pm on Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Sunday, and 10pm on Wednesday, Friday and Saturday.

What separates Tea & Poets from a standard coffee shop is that the menu is written like a bar list. The dominant section is titled "Tea Cocktails" and carries the word "non-alcoholic" as a subtitle, with every build priced at $5.50 small and $6.50 large. The list includes the Blueberry Mojito (spearmint green tea, fresh lemon, mint and blueberry), the Chocolate Mountain (chocolate syrup, milk, cocoa and chocolate bitters), the Julley Butter Tea (Kashmir chai, whipped butter and brown cane sugar), the Immune Intervention (ginger Ubud, lemon juice, honey and activated charcoal), the Lion's Mane (rooibos red tea and African vanilla), the Blood Orange Basil (English breakfast tea, blood orange bitters, fresh basil, lemon juice and white cane sugar), the Green Tea Lemonade (gunpowder green tea, lemon juice and white cane sugar), the Berry Beautiful (green tea, lemon juice, red berry and white cane sugar), plus a Chai Tea Latte and a Thai Tea Latte. A separate Matcha Life section covers a matcha tea latte, a Choco Matcha, a Matcha Lemonade and a straight matcha shot, and the baristas will build a custom blend from scratch with optional "bumps" of agave, activated charcoal, bitters, citrus, herbs, elderflower or vanilla.

venues.name: Tea at Shiloh
venues.description: Tea at Shiloh is a reservation-only Arts District teahouse opened in March 2022 by founder Shiloh Enoki, built entirely around alcohol-free socializing. Enoki started it after struggling to find late-night spots in Los Angeles that didn't revolve around drinking, so she created a screen-free "third place" of floor sofas, exposed brick, candles, and lanterns. By day it runs as a quiet co-working tea lounge (a roughly five-hour day pass, around $37, with unlimited tea); by night it hosts late-night tea sessions (about 7–11pm, ~$35, unlimited refills) plus jazz nights, sound baths, tarot, and art workshops. Drinks are entirely zero-proof: premium loose-leaf teas like the caffeinated Moonlight White, the red-rooibos Leche de Tigre, and the floral Love Potion, alongside a kava pop-up station. Everything is by advance reservation; no alcohol is served.
venues.address: 2035 Bay St, Ste 102, Los Angeles, CA 90021
venues.longDescription:
Tea at Shiloh is a reservation-only teahouse in the Arts District of downtown Los Angeles, founded by Shiloh Enoki, who built it after struggling to find places to go late at night that did not revolve around serving alcohol. Her description of the intent is simple: she wanted it to feel like you are entering my home where everything is cozy and free inside. The Infatuation, reviewing it in May 2024, described a reservation-only tea house fond of floor sofas and screen-free interactions, where a day pass buys five hours of unlimited tea in a serene loft surrounded by exposed brick walls and barefoot introverts, and where after dark the space becomes a late-night lounge, candles and oat-coloured lanterns giving the room a soft glow while the couches fill with couples in deep conversation. A separate private tea lounge is described by the venue as inspired by the natural world and caves in particular — ancient yet modern, a place to make contact with mystery.

What is served here is tea, and the format is the draw as much as the drinks. Sessions are booked in advance through the venue's own calendar, with a limit of four reservations per group, and the late-night window runs to a hard 11pm close. Reservations carry a strict no-cancellation, no-refund policy because of how small the room is. The teas rotate rather than sitting on a fixed list, and have included Moonlight White, a caffeinated white tea; Leche de Tigre, built on red rooibos; and the floral Love Potion. A retail shelf sells the same leaves to take home, including pressed tea cakes. Evening programming is a significant part of what the space does — jazz nights, sound baths, tarot readings, art workshops — which makes it one of the few places in Los Angeles designed from the outset for a long, sociable, entirely sober night rather than an early dinner. All ages are welcome. Guests are asked not to bring pets or emotional support animals, and photography rules are strict: no flash, no professional cameras and no tripods.
venues.pressQuote: I wanted it to feel like you're entering my home where everything is cozy and free inside.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Shiloh Enoki, Tea at Shiloh founder

venues.name: Tea Chapter
venues.description: Tea Chapter is Singapore's best-known traditional Chinese teahouse, occupying a pair of conserved shophouses at 9 and 11 Neil Road on the edge of Chinatown and trading since 1989. It is entirely alcohol-free, and it is one of the few tea rooms in the city that stays open into the evening — until 10:30pm on Fridays and Saturdays — which makes it a workable alternative to a bar rather than only a daytime stop. Guests sit at low tables in the upstairs rooms and brew their own leaf in gongfu sets with staff guidance, and the house runs formal tea appreciation classes. Queen Elizabeth II visited in 1989, and the seat she used is still marked.
signatureDrinks: Imperial Golden Cassia — the house signature tea, a light-oxidised oolong from Fujian, served to distinguished guests since the Queen's visit
venues.longDescription:
Tea Chapter has been operating out of two conserved shophouses on Neil Road since 1989, which makes it one of the longest-running tea houses in Singapore and by some distance the most recognised. The building is part of the appeal: guests remove their shoes and sit at low tables on the upper floors, in rooms that have been kept deliberately quiet and unmodernised. Downstairs there is a retail counter selling leaf, ware and gift sets, and the shop does a substantial trade in its own blends.

The format is self-brewing under guidance. Rather than being handed a finished cup, guests are given a gongfu set — gaiwan or small clay pot, fairness pitcher, scent and drinking cups — and taken through the steps by staff, then left to run their own infusions for as long as they like. The leaf list covers the usual Chinese categories, with oolongs particularly well represented, and the house also runs structured tea appreciation classes for people who want the theory rather than just the drink. Light snacks are available, but the tea is the point.

For a non-drinker the practical value is the evening trade. Tea Chapter runs to 9pm on most nights and to 10:30pm on Fridays and Saturdays, so it functions as a genuine place to take someone for an evening rather than an afternoon stop that closes at five. It sits a short walk from the Neil Road and Bukit Pasoh cluster of cocktail bars, which makes it an easy substitute when the rest of a group is heading somewhere licensed. The house also trades on a piece of history: Queen Elizabeth II visited in 1989, and the spot where she sat is still marked in the room.

The royal visit is also the origin of the house signature. Tea Chapter's own account records that the teahouse was visited by Queen Elizabeth II not long after it opened, and that the Imperial Golden Cassia — a light-oxidised oolong from Fujian — became the tea it serves to distinguished guests from that point on. It is still the leaf to order if you want the thing the house is actually known for, rather than working through the list at random.

The business began in October 1989 as a joint venture between thirteen tea enthusiasts who had been shown a proper Chinese tea ceremony by a Taiwanese friend and were captivated by it. That founding detail explains the format better than any description of the room: the place was built by people learning the practice, which is why guests are handed the equipment and taught rather than served a finished cup, and why the tea appreciation workshops are a core part of the trade rather than a tourist add-on.

Eatbook, reviewing the teahouse, described stepping inside to a charming and cosy setup made for tea appreciation, with the Oriental Room upstairs alongside Korean- and Japanese-style seating areas. Prices for the premium leaf are not low, and that is the honest expectation to set — this is closer in cost to a round of cocktails than to a cafe order, which is rather the point when it is standing in for one.
venues.pressQuote: Step inside the spacious tea house and you’ll be welcomed with a charming and cosy setup that’s perfect for tea appreciation.

venues.name: Tea Do
venues.description: Tea Do has traded on North 10th Street in Chinatown for fifteen years — it marked the anniversary in July 2026 — and it runs to half past ten most nights and half past eleven on Friday and Saturday. The tea list is numbered like a menu in a proper tea house rather than a coffee shop: the Grasshopper Tea Special pairs green apple and pear with green tea and lychee jelly, Honey Jazz builds honey, jasmine and lemon over cold jasmine green tea, The Hulk runs kiwi, green apple and lychee, and First Love combines red guava and passion fruit. The Tiger Milk Tea is the brown sugar and tapioca build, and Fire Dragon layers red bean, milk, grass jelly and tapioca. No alcohol is served.
signatureDrinks: T2 Grasshopper Tea Special — green apple, pear, green tea, lychee jelly
T5 Honey Jazz — honey, jasmine, lemon, cold jasmine green tea
T8 The Hulk — kiwi, green apple, lychee, jasmine green tea
T9 First Love — red guava, passion fruit, jasmine green tea
T10 Fire Dragon — red bean, milk, grass jelly, tapioca
T12 Tiger Milk Tea — brown sugar, black tea, tapioca
H2 Juliet — rose, pomegranate, green tea
H4 Tasty Maze — white peach, raspberry, jasmine green tea
venues.longDescription:
Tea Do has been on North 10th Street in Chinatown for fifteen years, marking the anniversary in July 2026 — a long run in a category where most bubble tea shops turn over in three or four. It stays open until half past ten from Sunday to Thursday and half past eleven on Friday and Saturday, which puts it squarely in evening territory rather than afternoon.

The menu is numbered, which tells you something about how seriously the tea is taken: this is a list built to be worked through rather than a handful of flavours. The Grasshopper Tea Special pairs green apple and pear over green tea and finishes with lychee jelly, and the jelly is not a garnish — it changes the texture of the last third of the glass. Honey Jazz is the most restrained on the list, honey and jasmine with lemon over cold jasmine green tea, and it is the one to order if you dislike sweet drinks. The Hulk runs kiwi, green apple and lychee against jasmine green tea for something sharper. First Love uses red guava and passion fruit, both tropical and both acidic enough to hold up.

The milk teas are the other half. Tiger Milk Tea is the brown sugar and tapioca build — the streaked-glass drink that made the category famous — and Fire Dragon is the maximalist one, layering red bean, milk, grass jelly and tapioca into something closer to a dessert than a drink. The house list adds Juliet, with rose and pomegranate over green tea, and Tasty Maze, with white peach and raspberry.

The practical case for a tea house on a night out is texture and duration. A bubble tea takes twenty minutes to drink because you are chewing part of it, which solves the specific problem of holding an empty glass while everyone else orders another round. And Chinatown at ten at night is busy, well lit and full of places still serving food, which makes it one of the easier parts of Philadelphia to spend a late evening in without a bar.

On alcohol: no licence, nothing alcoholic on the menu. This is recorded as evidence rather than as a statement from the venue.

venues.name: Tea Room by Ki-setsu
venues.description: Tea Room by Ki-setsu is a private, fully alcohol-free Chinese tea room on the seventh floor of Orchard Plaza, run as a booked session rather than a walk-in cafe. Groups of two to five are seated for roughly an hour at around S$68 per person, and a host works through a curated flight of rare leaf in gongfu format, explaining each infusion as it changes across successive steepings. The teas are sourced directly rather than through wholesalers, with material from Bulang Mountain and Yiwu — both serious pu-erh origins in Yunnan. It is the most technically ambitious tea experience in Singapore, and the closest local equivalent to a tasting-menu bar programme without alcohol.
venues.hours: By appointment only; sessions run about an hour
venues.longDescription:
Tea Room by Ki-setsu is an offshoot of the Ki-setsu group, and it takes a deliberately different approach from the walk-in tea houses elsewhere in Singapore. There is no counter and no drop-in service. Sessions are reserved in advance for two to five guests, run for approximately an hour, and cost in the region of S$68 per person. The room sits on the seventh floor of Orchard Plaza, an older mall on Orchard Road, which gives the whole thing the character of something you have to know about to find.

What the money buys is guided gongfu cha with genuinely rare material. The house sources directly from origin rather than through the wholesale market, with leaf from Bulang Mountain and Yiwu — two of the most respected pu-erh producing areas in Yunnan, and names that carry real weight with anyone who follows Chinese tea. A host runs the session, brewing through successive short infusions and talking through how the character of the leaf shifts from the first steeping to the eighth. That progression is the substance of the experience, and it is closer in structure to a tasting flight than to ordering a pot.

For a non-drinking visitor, this is the Singapore equivalent of booking a seat at a chef's counter. It is not a place to spend an unplanned evening — it must be reserved, and the format is fixed — but it is a proper occasion built entirely around a non-alcoholic drink, taken seriously, with someone knowledgeable talking you through it. That combination is rare anywhere. Because the sessions are appointment-only and the room is small, booking well ahead through the group's own site is essential, and the format suits a pair or a small group rather than a large party.

venues.name: Teardrop Lounge
venues.description: Teardrop Lounge is a celebrated Pearl District cocktail bar, opened by Daniel Shoemaker in 2007 and widely credited with launching Portland's cocktail renaissance. Beyond its acclaimed spirits list it publishes a standalone "N/A Drinks" menu of named non-alcoholic cocktails built on craft NA ingredients — including Lyre's Dark Cane and Pathfinder — several of them zero-proof riffs on classics like the Negroni.
venues.longDescription:
Teardrop Lounge is a pioneering craft cocktail bar in Portland's Pearl District, at 1015 NW Everett Street. It was opened in 2007 by Daniel Shoemaker, who has owned and operated it since, and is widely credited with helping launch Portland's cocktail renaissance, building drinks from house-made and hard-to-find ingredients around a circular island bar. It has been recognized by Esquire, Food & Wine ("50 Best Bars in America"), Travel + Leisure, and North America's 50 Best Bars; Food & Wine called it "one of America's seminal bars."

Teardrop runs a dedicated, fully developed non-alcoholic menu rather than an afterthought list of mocktails. Named zero-proof drinks include Jacob's Ladder (The Pathfinder Hemp & Root, black pepper-caraway shrub, grapefruit, lemon bitters, club soda), Fisher King (Lyre's Dark Cane, house TDL Aperitif Rosso, white verjus, pineapple, lime), Pascal's Wager — a spirit-free take on the Negroni (house TDL "gin-ish," TDL Aperitif Rosso, red verjus) — and Press Club. The program leans on non-alcoholic spirits and aperitifs including The Pathfinder, Lyre's Dark Cane, and Drømme, alongside Teardrop's own house-made zero-proof bases; several N/A cocktails are noted as containing less than 0.5% ABV.
venues.pressQuote: Teardrop Lounge is one of America's seminal bars.

venues.name: Tea's Me Cafe
venues.description: Tea's Me is an alcohol-free tea café owned by Tamika Catchings, the Indiana Fever forward, four-time Olympic gold medallist and Basketball Hall of Famer, who bought the business in 2017 after retiring. The tea list is the point: loose-leaf blends sourced worldwide and served properly, among them Vanilla Rooibos, Honeybush, a Sparkling Wine herbal infusion, Earl Grey, Japanese Cherry green and Raspberry Champagne white, alongside coffee and a short breakfast and lunch menu. Catchings launched a bottled line into local grocery in 2023 and has used the cafés as a first-job pipeline for Indianapolis teenagers. Note that the company contracted sharply in 2026: the original 22nd Street shop and the Tarkington Park community café have both closed, and this campus location at IU Indianapolis is the one that remains.
venues.longDescription:
Tamika Catchings spent her whole WNBA career with the Indiana Fever, won four Olympic gold medals and entered the Basketball Hall of Fame; in 2017, a year after retiring, she bought a small Indianapolis tea shop called Tea's Me rather than leave the city. The premise she has run it on since is that a tea room can do the civic work a bar does — somewhere to sit for two hours, meet people and be a regular — without alcohol anywhere in the building. She has also used it deliberately as an employer, hiring high-schoolers into first jobs, and has rotated a new local artist onto the walls every month. In 2023 she put a bottled Tea's Me line into grocery stores across central Indiana.

The tea itself is loose-leaf and sourced widely: Vanilla Rooibos and Honeybush on the herbal side, a Sparkling Wine herbal infusion, Earl Grey among the blacks, Japanese Cherry in the greens, and Raspberry Champagne among the whites, plus espresso drinks and a short menu that covers breakfast, lunch and dessert with vegetarian options throughout. Be aware that the business has contracted hard this year. The original café at 140 East 22nd Street has closed, and on 23 July 2026 Catchings announced by video that the Tea's Me Community Cafe at Tarkington Park would shut after five years; it served its last day on 1 August 2026. She was explicit that the company is not winding up, and that it is consolidating onto the IU Indianapolis location on University Boulevard. That is a campus café with campus hours — Monday to Thursday 8am to 7pm, Friday to 5pm, Saturday 10am to 3pm, closed Sunday — so check before making a trip across town. The consolidation is worth understanding rather than glossing, because it changes what this entry is for. Tea's Me at Tarkington Park was a genuine third place, sited beside a basketball court, a splash pad and an amphitheatre, and its closure removes one of the few alcohol-free community rooms on the near north side. What survives is smaller and more specific: a well-run, fully alcohol-free tea counter inside the IU Indianapolis campus centre, open Monday to Saturday, with the same loose-leaf program and the same bottled range on the shelf. For a visitor it is a good stop if you are already downtown or on campus, and not worth a special journey; for the tea itself, the bottled line is stocked in grocery stores across central Indiana.
venues.pressQuote: We have been here for five years, which is insane to think about. I thank you for being a part of this journey. It's never easy to say goodbye.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Tamika Catchings, owner, announcing the Tarkington Park closure

venues.name: Teetotalist at Propagate
venues.description: The Teetotalist is Sacramento's first alcohol-free bar and social club, operating out of the Jungle Room at Propagate in Midtown — a plant shop and event space that hosts it rather than a licensed bar making room. Nothing it pours contains alcohol, and the framing is deliberately social rather than therapeutic: it exists so that people who do not drink, for any reason at all, have somewhere to go together. It runs as a residency and event programme rather than a nightly bar, including Dry January pop-ups, so check the current schedule before making the trip. It keeps no fixed hours, which reflects that format rather than any doubt about the venue.
venues.longDescription:
The Teetotalist is Sacramento's first alcohol-free bar and social club, and it operates inside the Jungle Room at Propagate on I Street in Midtown — a plant shop and event venue rather than a licensed bar clearing a shelf. That host arrangement is now a familiar pattern in this guide, and it exists for a hard commercial reason: a standalone dry bar has to carry a full lease on evening trade alone, which is the arithmetic that has closed alcohol-free venues in Richmond, Portland and elsewhere. Sharing premises with a daytime business removes that pressure.

What it offers is non-alcoholic drinks and small bites, and a room where the absence of alcohol is the premise rather than an accommodation. The framing matters. A great deal of alcohol-free hospitality is pitched at recovery, which is right for some people and alienating for others — the pregnant, the driving, the medicated, the merely uninterested. Calling it a social club puts the emphasis on the company rather than the abstinence, which is a more durable proposition and reaches more people.

Because it runs as a residency and an events programme rather than a nightly service, the schedule is the thing to check. There are no fixed hours: Teetotalist appears at Propagate on particular nights, and expands during Dry January with pop-up bars. Anyone planning around it should confirm the current calendar rather than turning up hopefully.

Its significance to this guide is structural. Sacramento has real depth in licensed rooms — Juju, Kupros, Revival and others all build proper zero-proof drinks — but Teetotalist is the only entry where alcohol is simply not present, and that is a different offer entirely.

Sacramento matters for this in a way that is easy to miss. It is California's capital, a city of half a million with a state workforce, two university towns in its orbit and a farm-to-fork food culture that has drawn national attention — and it is close enough to the Bay Area that trends arrive quickly. A first alcohol-free bar in a city like that is not a novelty; it is a marker that the demand has reached the middle of the country's largest state rather than staying on the coast. Whether Teetotalist eventually takes a lease of its own is the question worth watching. For now, the residency model is what keeps it alive, and that is worth more than a shopfront that closes in eighteen months.

venues.name: Teller
venues.description: Teller is an all-day bar and eatery set inside a converted 1918 bank on Lygon Street in Brunswick East, and it carries one of Melbourne's deeper no-and-low drinks lists. The zero-proof menu runs five named mocktails built on real NA spirits - 'Rumour Has It' with Brunswick Aces Sapiir Diamonds gin, yuzu and pomegranate, and 'The Spritz You Miss' built on Lyre's Italian Spritz - alongside NA beers (Heaps Normal Quiet XPA, Guinness 0.0, Blackman's Zero, Capital Pacific Ale) and alcohol-free wines from Altina, Leitz and NON. NoLo Life rates its alcohol-free range five stars. The East Brunswick beer garden runs a non-alcoholic list that keeps going — beer, cocktails and wine all available alcohol-free.
signatureDrinks: Rumour Has It (A$15) - Brunswick Aces Sapiir Diamonds gin, yuzu, pomegranate, mint, lime
The Spritz You Miss (A$17) - Lyre's Italian Spritz, soda, Plus & Minus prosecco & orange
Bloody Mojito (A$14) - Four Pillars Bloody Bandwagon, lime, mint, soda
Rustic Verve Spritz (A$13) - NON #9 blackberries & Stanley plum, beetroot & pink peppercorn syrup, lemonade
Wildwood Shrub (A$14) - house-made berry coulis, house-made lemon & ginger shrub, soda
venues.longDescription:
Teller occupies the former State Savings Bank of Victoria, a 1918 heritage building on Lygon Street in Brunswick East that has been reworked into an all-day diner and bar. The room keeps the bank's bones under modern, warm decor and opens out to a front bar, a leafy beer garden and an upstairs function room, with a serious bar stocking around 11 independently brewed beers on tap. The kitchen leans into elevated pub food with a Mediterranean tilt, spanning brunch through to atmospheric dinners.

The non-alcoholic offering is a genuine, printed part of the drinks list rather than an afterthought. Five zero-proof cocktails carry named builds and ingredients: 'Rumour Has It' (A$15) with Brunswick Aces Sapiir Diamonds gin, yuzu, pomegranate, mint and lime; 'The Spritz You Miss' (A$17) on Lyre's Italian Spritz with soda and Plus & Minus prosecco and orange; the 'Bloody Mojito' (A$14) with Four Pillars Bloody Bandwagon; the 'Rustic Verve Spritz' (A$13) using NON #9 blackberries and Stanley plum; and the 'Wildwood Shrub' (A$14) with a house-made berry coulis and lemon-and-ginger shrub.

The fridge and wine list back it up. Non-alcoholic beers include Heaps Normal Quiet XPA (A$11), Guinness 0.0 (A$13), Blackman's Zero lager and Capital Pacific Ale, plus Perla sparkling mate tea. Alcohol-free wines run to Altina 0% sparkling brut, Leitz Eins Zwei alcohol-free chardonnay and NON #9, so a non-drinker can move across sparkling, white and aromatic alternatives.

EatDrinkPlay called Teller a standout local, and NoLo Life lists it as a five-star alcohol-free favourite for its curated AF range and casual bites in a relaxed indoor/outdoor setting - the kind of neighbourhood all-day venue where the zero-proof drinker gets a real list rather than a token soda.

The beer garden is what people come for, and it happens to be the format in which not drinking is easiest. Pub With No Booze calls Teller a cracking spot to sit in the garden over good food with a non-alcoholic list that just keeps on giving, with beer, cocktails and wine all available.

All three categories is the part worth noting. Most venues that stock alcohol-free options cover one — usually beer, because it is the easiest to buy in and the fastest to pour. Covering beer, cocktails and wine means someone has made three separate purchasing decisions and found space for three sets of stock, which is a real commitment rather than a gesture. In practice it means a table of four in the garden on a Sunday can order the same rounds as each other for a whole afternoon, which is the actual test of whether a venue works for a mixed group rather than merely permits one.
venues.pressQuote: Teller situated in East Brunswick is a cracking spot to be able to sit in their beer garden eating great food and a non alcoholic list that just keeps on giving. Beer, cocktails and wine are all there for you.

venues.name: Temple Cellars
venues.description: Temple Cellars is a walk-in neighbourhood bottle shop in the leafy Binjai Park precinct of Bukit Timah, specialising in small independent natural-wine, craft-beer and spirits producers - and it keeps a genuine, browsable 'Zero Alcohol' section for mindful drinkers. The alcohol-free shelf carries Plus & Minus alcohol-removed wines (Shiraz, Pinot Noir, Rose and more, from S$30), Heaps Normal and Verdant PSYCH! AF beers (from S$6), fermented tazaTe and Acala pet-nat sparkling teas, and ready-to-pour Pentire non-alcoholic cocktails. It is a general bottle shop rather than a dedicated NA venue - alcohol sits alongside the zero-proof range - but the AF selection is real, curated and stocked to buy in person.
signatureDrinks: Plus & Minus alcohol-removed wines - Shiraz, Pinot Noir, Pinot Grigio, Sauvignon Blanc and Rose, 2025 releases (S$30 each)
Heaps Normal Third IPA - Australian alcohol-free IPA, 375ml (S$6)
tazaTe Pet-Nat Tea - fermented sparkling teas incl. Pines, Wild Flowers, Hai and Bamboo (S$25-S$48)
Acala Sparkling Tea - Spritz Style, Mimosa, Rose and Red (S$35-S$40)
Pentire non-alcoholic cocktails - Margarita and Paloma, 200ml (S$9)
venues.longDescription:
Temple Cellars describes itself as "a neighbourhood bottle shop dedicated to small, independent producers from around the world," curating natural wines, craft beers, sake, small-batch spirits and non-alcoholic alternatives. Its retail home is a walk-in shop at 31 Binjai Park, a quiet parade of shophouses in the Bukit Timah residential belt, and the business also runs one-hour islandwide delivery and trade wholesale alongside free in-store pick-up.

What earns it a place on an alcohol-free map is a real, dedicated 'Zero Alcohol' section rather than a token bottle or two. On the shelves you can browse Plus & Minus alcohol-removed Australian wines across five styles - Shiraz, Pinot Noir, Pinot Grigio, Sauvignon Blanc and Rose (2025 releases, S$30 each); alcohol-free beers from Heaps Normal (Third IPA, S$6) and Verdant (PSYCH! AF IPA, S$10); and a strong showing of fermented and sparkling teas from tazaTe (Pines, Wild Flowers, Hai and Bamboo pet-nats, S$25-S$48) and Acala (Spritz, Mimosa, Rose and Red, S$35-S$40). Ready-to-pour non-alcoholic cocktails from Pentire (Margarita and Paloma, S$9) round out the mindful-drinking range.

It is worth being clear about what Temple Cellars is: a full-range bottle shop that happens to run a serious NA corner, not a dedicated non-alcoholic venue or a bar. There is no cocktail service or seated bar programme here - the value is being able to physically pick up genuine alcohol-free wines, beers and sparkling teas in Singapore, from a shop that treats them as a proper category rather than an afterthought. Contact is via @templecellars on Instagram or the shop's online store.

venues.name: TEN 3
venues.description: TEN 3 sits at 10,300 feet on Sandia Peak, reachable only by the Sandia Peak Tramway, and it is the most spectacular place in New Mexico to order a drink of any kind — the room looks out over eleven thousand square miles of desert. Its mocktails are named for the setting: On Mountain Thyme and Elevation Elixir. Because the only way up is the tram, and the tram has a schedule, this is a planned outing rather than a stop, and it works particularly well as an alcohol-free one given that altitude amplifies alcohol considerably. Book the restaurant and the tram together, and check the weather, which closes the tramway at short notice.
venues.longDescription:
The Sandia Peak Tramway climbs from the eastern edge of Albuquerque to 10,378 feet, and TEN 3 is the restaurant at the top of it. The view runs across roughly eleven thousand square miles of New Mexico, and on a clear evening you watch the sunset from above the desert with the city lights coming on below.

There is a specific and slightly unusual reason this venue belongs in an alcohol-free guide, beyond its two named mocktails — On Mountain Thyme and Elevation Elixir, both recorded by Visit Albuquerque. At 10,300 feet, alcohol hits considerably harder than at sea level; the reduced oxygen amplifies its effects, and every mountaintop restaurant in the world knows it. Which means TEN 3 is one of the rare places where ordering a drink without alcohol is not a compromise but the obviously sensible choice, and where nobody at the table thinks anything of it. For a reader who is tired of explaining, an evening where the setting does the explaining is worth something.

The practicalities are unlike anywhere else in this guide. The only access is the tramway, which runs on a schedule and stops running; you cannot linger past the last car down, and weather closes the tram outright with little notice. Book the restaurant and the tram together, check conditions the day of, and dress for a temperature drop of twenty or thirty degrees from the valley floor.

This entry is graded three. Two named drinks are documented by the city's tourism board, but their ingredients are not published, there is no verified printed zero-proof section, and no non-alcoholic spirits programme could be confirmed.

Open 10:30am to 7:30pm Monday and Thursday through Sunday; closed Tuesday and Wednesday.
venues.pressQuote: TEN 3, at the top of the Sandia Peak aerial tramway, pours On Mountain Thyme and Elevation Elixir.
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: Visit Albuquerque, Where To Find Mocktails in Albuquerque

venues.name: That's Kava
venues.description: That's Kava is an alcohol-free kava bar on South Broadway in Englewood, on the southern end of the Denver metro's Broadway corridor. The venue states plainly on its own site that "We are an alcohol free establishment" and describes itself as a sober bar. It trades from 8am until 2:30am, which makes it one of the latest-closing alcohol-free rooms in the metro, and it programmes trivia, bingo and board-game nights most evenings of the week. Readers should know what is actually being served: alongside kava, the traditional South Pacific root drink, That's Kava pours kratom and other psychoactive ethnobotanicals, and Colorado law restricts kratom sales to over-21s. The drinks list is organised into kava, teas, on-tap, shots, mocktails and a high-potency "extreme" section.
signatureDrinks: That's Karma (kratom, orange juice, spearmint, turmeric, black pepper — on tap)
Majestic Mule (kava and kratom extract, nitro kava)
venues.longDescription:
That's Kava occupies a storefront at 3394 South Broadway in Englewood, on the stretch of the Broadway corridor that runs south out of Denver proper. It is one of a small number of Denver-area venues that are alcohol-free by policy rather than by accident, and it says so directly on its own website: "We are an alcohol free establishment." The bar frames kava in explicitly harm-reduction terms — "Kava is a traditional root drink from the South Pacific Islands. It's a popular alternative to alcohol, promoting relaxation and a sense of calm without the drawbacks of inebriation" — and builds the rest of the room around that idea, with trivia, bingo and board-game nights running most nights and an 8am-to-2:30am trading day that outlasts almost every licensed bar nearby.

The menu is unusually explicit about what is in each drink, which matters because much of it is psychoactive. The kava section runs from House Kava, a lab-tested blend, through Premium Kava sourced from Fiji, Vanuatu or Hawaii, to Stone Kava made from high-kavalactone lateral root and Green Kava, a flash-frozen Fijian preparation. A separate teas section is built on kratom — Indonesian kratom in white, red and green strains, and freeze-dried Thai kratom with high mitragynine content — alongside non-kratom botanicals such as sakae naa, hirsuta and javinica. On tap there is That's Karma, which combines kratom with orange juice, spearmint, turmeric and black pepper, plus nitro kratom, house-flavoured seltzer and rotating local kombucha. Shots include Golden Glow Elixir made from lateral root, and Mucuna Matata, which adds mucuna to a Golden Glow base. The mocktail list — Majestic Mule, Manny's Painkiller and a Spicy Passion Fruit Paloma — layers kava or kratom extract over nitro kava. Anyone in recovery should treat this as a psychoactive venue rather than a neutral soft-drink bar: there is no alcohol here, but kava and kratom are not inert, and kratom sales are restricted to 21 and over under Colorado law.

venues.name: Thaxton Speakeasy
venues.description: Hidden in the lower level of a circa-1927 building downtown, the Thaxton has been pouring Prohibition-style cocktails behind a password-protected door since 2007 — the weekly password drops on Instagram. Alongside the boozy classics, the menu carries a dedicated 'Temperance' section of zero-proof cocktails built on DHOS Gin Free, like the egg-white-frothed 20/20 Tim Vision and the Greek-yogurt-smoothed Razz But No Tazz, plus a Faux Blueberry Sage French 75 and NA beers including 4 Hands' non-alcoholic Incarnation IPA and Bud Zero. It's open Thursday through Saturday nights when not privately booked, with limited first-come seating — one of downtown St. Louis's most distinctive date-night rooms.
venues.hours: Mon-Wed closed; Thu 8pm-12am; Fri-Sat 8pm-1am; Sun closed

naMenuItems.name: Faux Blueberry Sage French 75
naMenuItems.description: topo chico, blueberry sage syrup, lemon

venues.longDescription:
The Thaxton has been hiding in plain sight since 2007. Tucked into the lower level of a circa-1927 building at 1009 Olive Street, the downtown lounge runs on a genuine speakeasy ritual: a weekly password posted to its Instagram account gets you through the door, seating is limited and first-come, first-served, and tables are capped at two hours to keep the waitlist moving. Public speakeasy nights run Thursday from 8 p.m. to midnight and Friday and Saturday from 8 p.m. to 1 a.m. — but only when the room isn't privately booked, since the space doubles as a wedding and event venue, so checking the posted calendar and grabbing the password before heading down is part of the fun.

The drink menu's dedicated 'Temperance' section treats zero-proof drinkers to real cocktails rather than afterthoughts. The 20/20 Tim Vision shakes DHOS Gin Free with lime, cranberry, simple syrup, and egg white; the Razz But No Tazz blends the same NA gin with raspberry syrup, lemon, and Greek yogurt (the menu suggests omitting its dash of bitters for a fully alcohol-free build); and the Faux Blueberry Sage French 75 tops blueberry-sage syrup and lemon with Topo Chico. The NA fridge adds local heft with 4 Hands Brewing's non-alcoholic Incarnation IPA alongside Bud Zero, and the zero-proof list rotates over time — St. Louis Magazine's guide to nonalcoholic drinks previously flagged a Fauxrita and the kombucha-based Fatale Mule here.

That same St. Louis Magazine guide urged readers to come for 'one of the most distinctive date night experiences in St. Louis' and stay for 'a varied selection of mocktails, non-alcoholic beers, and more,' while Explore St. Louis bills the Thaxton as the city's only password-protected night spot, serving vintage vibes in a 1920s Art Deco building. Expect an intimate basement room, carefully built drinks, and a crowd that's in on the secret — arrive early, since the two-hour seatings and small footprint mean the room fills fast on weekend nights.
venues.pressQuote: Come for one of the most distinctive date night experiences in St. Louis.

venues.name: The 126
venues.description: The 126 is a downtown cocktail bar on College Street whose alcohol-free drinks are printed as Temperance Cocktails — a deliberate joke, each one named after a leader of the Temperance Movement that brought in Prohibition, including a Carrie the Hatchet built in tribute to Carrie Nation. The structural decision behind the section is more interesting than the naming: the bar makes every house syrup and every batch of bitters without alcohol, so any drink on the list can be built alcohol-free without substitution or compromise. Co-owner Emily Morton insists on the Temperance label over the word mocktail. Open Tuesday to Saturday from 5pm, closed Sunday and Monday.
venues.longDescription:
The 126 sits behind an unmarked door on College Street in downtown Burlington, and it has made a single technical decision that puts it ahead of almost every cocktail bar in the state on alcohol-free drinking. House syrups and house bitters are normally built on alcohol — bitters especially, where high-proof spirit is the standard extraction medium and the reason a dash of Angostura disqualifies a drink for anyone who is genuinely abstaining. The 126 makes all of its without. Co-owner Emily Morton put it to Edible Vermont plainly: non-alcoholic beverages get exactly the same attention as the alcoholic cocktails, and because no alcohol goes into the homemade syrups or bitters, any of them can go into a non-alcoholic drink.

That means the bar is not working from a separate, smaller pantry when it builds you something alcohol-free. It is working from the same one, which is the difference between a real programme and a short list of juices.

The drinks are printed as Temperance Cocktails, a sly reference to the movement that produced Prohibition, and each is named for one of its leaders — Carrie the Hatchet, for instance, in tribute to Carrie Nation, who campaigned against saloons with an actual hatchet. Morton reportedly insists on the Temperance label rather than the word mocktail and has been outvoted more than once by the rest of the bar, which is the sort of detail that tells you how seriously the category is taken here.

The drink names rotate, so none are recorded as signature drinks in this listing beyond the one Edible Vermont documented. What does not rotate is the section itself or the no-alcohol-in-the-syrups rule underneath it.

The bar opens at 5pm Tuesday through Saturday and runs to midnight, 1am on Friday and Saturday. It is closed Sunday and Monday.
venues.pressQuote: Nonalcoholic beverages get exactly the same attention as our alcoholic cocktails. The 126 uses no alcohol in homemade syrups or bitters, so any of them can go into a nonalcoholic cocktail.

venues.name: The Archives
venues.description: The Archives is a downtown arcade bar on College Street — vintage cabinets, pinball, a long craft beer list and a cocktail programme that is a good deal more considered than the format suggests. Hotel Vermont's guide to drinking in Burlington names it as one of two bars in the city making creative N/A cocktails, alongside Devil Takes a Holiday. It is also the most useful room in this guide for anyone not drinking, for a structural reason: it opens at noon at weekends and runs to 2am every night, and there is something to do with your hands that is not a glass.

Dawn of the Dragon (NA: dragonfruit, passionfruit, blueberry, ginger beer)
Basilisk Venom (NA: passionfruit, lemon, honey, basil, soda)
Clear Eyes Lonely Heart (NA: yellow bell pepper, lime, grapefruit, strawberry, basil)

venues.longDescription:
An arcade bar is an unexpectedly good answer to a problem non-drinkers know well: what to do with the four hours everyone else spends holding a drink. The Archives, on College Street in downtown Burlington, fills a room with vintage cabinets and pinball and puts a genuine cocktail bar along one wall — original builds plus reworked classics, including a house drink called The Archive, a clarified milk punch, and seasonal work like a bourbon-and-pumpkin-foam Witching Hour.

The alcohol-free case for it rests on a peer recommendation rather than a printed menu. Hotel Vermont's guide to drinking in Burlington — written by a hotel that spends every evening sending guests to other people's bars, and therefore has no reason to flatter — names exactly two rooms in the city for creative N/A cocktails. One is Devil Takes a Holiday. The other is The Archives. Given the technique on display in the alcoholic list, that is a credible claim; the bar is clearly capable of building a drink rather than pouring one.

This entry is graded three rather than four because the non-alcoholic drinks are not printed as a named section on any menu published online, and no specific drink could be confirmed, so none are recorded here. Ask at the bar and expect to be looked after.

What is unambiguous is the access. The Archives runs from 4pm to 2am on weekdays and from noon to 2am at weekends, with happy hour 4pm to 6pm on weekdays and noon to 6pm at weekends — the longest hours of any venue in this city guide, and by some margin the easiest place in Burlington to spend a late night without drinking and without feeling like you are waiting for everyone else to finish.
venues.pressQuote: Devil Takes a Holiday and Archives for creative N/A cocktails.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Hotel Vermont, Grab a Drink guide to Burlington

venues.name: The Aviary
venues.description: The Aviary is the avant-garde cocktail bar of The Alinea Group — the Chicago restaurant empire of Michelin-starred chef Grant Achatz and partner Nick Kokonas — opened in 2011 in the Fulton Market District of the West Loop. It treats drinks with fine-dining rigor, using molecular techniques, custom glassware, and a dedicated ice chef. Critically, its non-alcoholic program is a first-class equal, not an afterthought: every experience, from multi-course cocktail progressions to the à la carte list, is available fully zero-proof, with a dedicated NA pairing menu. The kitchen's commitment runs deep enough that the Alinea Group published "ZERO: A New Approach to Non-Alcoholic Drinks," a book of nearly 100 alcohol-free recipes. Named NA pours include the 310 to Yuzu and the Fill Collins. Accolades include a James Beard Award for Outstanding Bar Program (2013) and repeated World's 50 Best Bars rankings.
venues.hours: Mon closed; Tue-Thu 5pm-11pm; Fri 5pm-1am; Sat 4:30pm-1am; Sun closed
venues.longDescription:
The Aviary is The Alinea Group's cocktail bar at 955 W Fulton Market in the West Loop, the drinks counterpart to Grant Achatz's Michelin-starred restaurants, and it does not operate like a bar in any ordinary sense. There is no standing at a rail and no ordering off a list on arrival: guests book a seated experience through Tock and are served a progression of drinks the way a tasting menu is served, from a three-course cocktail progression up to a five-course Aviary Experience and a seven-course Kitchen Table Experience. Drinks arrive with purpose-built vessels, ice engineered for a specific dilution rate, and techniques borrowed from a pastry kitchen rather than a bar. It is the sort of place where the mechanism of the drink is part of the point, and it has shaped how ambitious bars around the world present cocktails.

For a non-drinker the important fact is short and unusually generous: every experience on the menu is available in a non-alcoholic version. Not a substitute drink, not one zero-proof option tucked at the end of the list — the entire progression, at whatever length you book, can be built without alcohol. That means a non-drinker gets the same number of courses, the same theatre and the same seat as everyone else at the table, which almost nowhere at this level offers. The group's commitment to this is not incidental either: Achatz and his team published ZERO: A New Approach to Non-Alcoholic Drinks, a roughly 250-page book of nearly a hundred non-alcoholic recipes developed in these kitchens, which remains one of the most serious references in the field. Two practical caveats. The Aviary does not publish the contents of its non-alcoholic progressions in advance — the drinks change constantly and no fixed list exists to check — so you are booking the format rather than choosing specific drinks. And because everything is prepaid and seated, this is a planned evening rather than a walk-in, and worth flagging your preference at booking so the bar can build the progression accordingly.

venues.name: The Baker's Table
venues.description: The Baker's Table is chef Dave Willocks' farm-to-table tasting-menu restaurant in Newport's historic Monmouth Street district, and its non-alcoholic program is unusually serious for a fine-dining room. Alongside the six-course seasonal menu, guests can add a four-course Spirit-Free Pairing ($45) that runs parallel to the Wine Pairing ($60), matching a considered zero-proof beverage to the canapes, starter, pasta and main. The bar always keeps a rotating seasonal mocktail on hand -- past pours include The Petal (hibiscus, chamomile, egg white) and the wintry The Partridge (cider, pear, cinnamon) -- plus Athletic Brewing non-alcoholic beer. Willocks, a 2026 James Beard finalist for Best Chef: Southeast, brings the same California-farmers-market rigor to the drinks that regulars say gets as much thought as the wine.
venues.hours: Mon-Tue closed; Wed-Thu 5pm-9pm; Fri-Sat 5pm-10pm; Sun closed
venues.longDescription:
The Baker's Table opened in Newport's historic Monmouth Street district and drew national attention early, landing on Eater's Best New Restaurants in America list. Chef Dave Willocks built his cooking over a 16-year career in San Francisco and Oakland, where menus grew out of weekly farmers-market trips, and that produce-first instinct carried east: the restaurant runs a monthly-changing six-course tasting menu built on Ohio Valley ingredients, house sourdough, hand-made pasta and whole-animal butchery. In 2026 Willocks was named a James Beard Foundation finalist for Best Chef: Southeast.

The beverage program treats non-drinkers as full guests rather than an afterthought. Its centerpiece is a four-course Spirit-Free Pairing ($45), offered alongside the four-course Wine Pairing ($60); both accompany the canapes, starter, pasta and main course. Beyond the pairing, the kitchen always keeps a rotating seasonal mocktail and Athletic Brewing non-alcoholic beer available. Seasonal mocktails have included The Petal -- hibiscus, chamomile and egg white -- and The Partridge, a wintry mix of cider, pear and cinnamon. Guests who don't drink note that the alcohol-free pairings receive a great deal of thought and preparation, as much as the wine.

The dining room is open Wednesday through Saturday, with seating from 5pm (last seating 8:30pm Wednesday and Thursday, 9pm Friday and Saturday) and closed Sunday through Tuesday. Because this is a prix-fixe tasting-menu format, reservations are effectively required, and the spirit-free pairing is chosen as an add-on when you book. There's free parking in the county lot next to the restaurant or on Monmouth Street above 10th. Reach the restaurant at (859) 261-1941 or hello@bakerstablenewport.com.
venues.pressQuote: The Baker's Table also shines when it comes to drinks, and their beverage menu offers several season-inspired mocktails to choose from.

venues.name: The Bar at Saint Kate
venues.description: The Bar at Saint Kate is the art-filled lobby bar of Saint Kate - The Arts Hotel in downtown Milwaukee's Theater District, where live music plays nightly amid rotating gallery works. It anchors one of the city's more serious hotel mocktail programs, originally built with Lost Whale mixologists Daniel Beres and Trip Duval, and it remains a fixture on Visit Milwaukee's Dry January mocktail trail. The crafted zero-proof list runs alongside full cocktails, wine and beer, so it is a hybrid rather than a fully alcohol-free room. Note that the Bar has recently added intoxicating THC-infused sips, which are separate from its genuinely alcohol-free mocktails.

naMenuItems.name: Fauxloma
naMenuItems.description: seedlip spice, giffard na pamplemousse, lime, grapefruit

venues.longDescription:
The Bar at Saint Kate sits just off the lobby of Saint Kate - The Arts Hotel, Milwaukee's arts-forward boutique hotel in the Theater District, surrounded by works from three on-site galleries and backed by live music starting at 5 p.m. daily. Its non-alcoholic identity is genuine and long-standing: the house mocktail menu was developed in collaboration with Lost Whale's Daniel Beres and Trip Duval, and named zero-proof drinks have included The Hibby (blueberry-hibiscus syrup, Rishi tea, cucumber, rose and mint), Mi Casa Su Casa (pineapple, red chili, lime, ginger beer, vanilla and mint) and Silk Road (rhubarb, sparkling grape, jasmine and chamomile, built to echo a French 75).

The program is still current. In January 2026, Visit Milwaukee featured the Bar on its mocktail trail with a drink called "A Walk in the Park," framing a sophisticated night among the galleries as exactly what Dry January ordered. One honest caveat for sober guests: the Bar's own menu now leads with THC-infused sips alongside its cocktails, so it is worth asking for the alcohol-free mocktails specifically. The intoxicating THC drinks and the genuinely zero-proof mocktails are two different things here.

The property doubles down on non-alcoholic options in its sister restaurant, The Studio Kitchen & Cocktails, which opened in September 2025 in the former ARIA space and pours zero-proof drinks built on Seedlip and Lyre's non-alcoholic spirits. Between the two rooms, Saint Kate remains one of downtown Milwaukee's most dependable stops for a well-made drink with nothing in it.
venues.pressQuote: A sophisticated night in an art gallery with live music and a drink in your hand is just what Dry January ordered at the Bar inside Saint Kate – The Arts Hotel.

venues.name: The Bardo Coffee House
venues.description: The Bardo Coffee House is the South Broadway flagship of a small Denver chain that bills itself as "Denver's Late Night Coffee House", trading 6am to midnight every day of the week one block north of Alameda. No alcohol appears anywhere on its menus; the drinks list is coffee, espresso, tea and a set of house-blended speciality drinks made in-house rather than from commercial syrups. That combination — midnight closing, seven days a week, on the SoBo strip — makes it a working alternative to a bar rather than a daytime cafe, and it is a rare one on a block otherwise dominated by licensed venues. The room runs on 100 percent wind power and offers free WiFi, ample seating, free customer parking and a public colour laser printer.
signatureDrinks: #17 Turmeric Latte (house-made blend of turmeric, ginger, coconut sugar, three types of pepper, vanilla bean and other spices)
Matcha Latte (all-natural house-made blend of matcha, brown sugar and coconut milk powder)
Spumoni Mocha (chocolate, cherry and pistachio with espresso)
venues.longDescription:
The Bardo Coffee House opened its South Broadway room at 238 South Broadway, one block north of Alameda, and has since grown to four Denver-area locations — SoBo, West 38th Avenue in Wheat Ridge, South Wadsworth, and a West Colfax store that opened in July 2026. The SoBo store is the one that anchors the brand's identity as "Denver's Late Night Coffee House": it trades from 6am to midnight, seven days a week, holidays included, on a stretch of Broadway otherwise given over to bars, music venues and record shops. Denver's official neighbourhood boundaries place 238 South Broadway in the Speer statistical neighbourhood, on the east side of Broadway; Bardo itself describes the address as being in the Baker neighbourhood, which is the commercial district name commonly used for this stretch of the SoBo strip.

Nothing on Bardo's menus contains alcohol, and the venue's own framing is about drink quality rather than abstinence: "Beyond the usual drinks you'd expect at an independent coffee house, we also offer some unique ones found only here." Those house drinks are genuinely house-made. The #17 Turmeric Latte is built on a blend of turmeric, ginger, coconut sugar, three types of pepper, vanilla bean and further spices; the Matcha Latte uses an all-natural in-house blend of matcha, brown sugar and coconut milk powder; and a variant called The Grinch adds pistachio and oat milk to the same matcha base. The dessert-leaning end of the list includes the Spumoni Mocha, which combines chocolate, cherry and pistachio with espresso, and the Cordial Cherry Latte, made with cherry, almond, half and half and espresso. Seasonal drinks include the Caramel Apple Jack, built from apple cider, heavy cream and caramel, and the Lumberjack, which pairs apple cider with Bhakti Chai and heavy cream. The store describes its aim modestly — "Working to be the best coffee house in the Denver area. Friendly & comfortable with locally sourced drink and food options" — and runs entirely on wind power.

venues.name: The Barnes
venues.description: The Barnes is the restaurant and bar on Powell Street inside the Union Square hotel of the same name, open daily from 5pm to 11pm. Its beverage menu carries a named non-alcoholic section of three built cocktails priced at $16, the same as most of the alcoholic list: a Non-Alcoholic Negroni made with Ritual zero-proof gin, Lyre's Italian Spritz and orange; Your NA Poolside, combining Lyre's Italian Spritz with Ritual agave blanco, lime and almond syrup; and Never Been Kissed, built on Seedlip Spice with lime, hibiscus, ginger beer and mint. Athletic Brewing's Run Wild IPA is stocked at $8 alongside a non-alcoholic Asahi. The kitchen runs shareable plates, a superfood salad, burgers and steak frites.
signatureDrinks: Non-Alcoholic Negroni (Ritual zero-proof gin, Lyre's Italian Spritz, orange)
Your NA Poolside (Lyre's Italian Spritz, Ritual agave blanco, lime, almond syrup)
Never Been Kissed (Seedlip Spice, lime, hibiscus, ginger beer, mint)
