venues.longDescription:
The Barnes sits at 225 Powell Street, a block from the cable car turnaround, as the ground-floor restaurant and bar of the Union Square hotel that shares its name. The hotel's own description of the room is straightforward about what it wants to be — handcrafted cocktails and shareable appetizers, with a food menu running from a superfood salad through burgers and steak frites — and it is open every day from 5pm to 11pm, which makes it an option for the stretch of the evening when much of Union Square is oriented towards tourists rather than to anyone looking for a proper drink.

What makes it worth listing is that the zero-proof drinks are named, built and priced level with the rest of the bar. The beverage menu carries a distinct non-alcoholic heading holding three cocktails at $16, against $18 for the full-proof house list. The Non-Alcoholic Negroni is made with Ritual zero-proof gin and Lyre's Italian Spritz, finished with orange, and reproduces the bitterness of the original rather than substituting a sweet red soda. Your NA Poolside pairs Lyre's Italian Spritz with Ritual's agave blanco, lime and almond syrup for something closer to a sour. Never Been Kissed is built on Seedlip Spice with lime, hibiscus, ginger beer and mint, the longest and most refreshing of the three. Below the cocktails the bar stocks Athletic Brewing's Run Wild IPA at $8 and a non-alcoholic Asahi at the same price, so beer drinkers are covered as well. The hotel's dining pages describe the bar as offering zero-proof drink options as a standing part of the programme rather than as a seasonal promotion, which is unusual for a Union Square hotel bar of this size. The three cocktails are built rather than poured from a bottle, using two different non-alcoholic base spirits plus a botanical distillate, so a table can order a bitter aperitivo, a sour and a long highball without repeating an ingredient. A five per cent Healthy San Francisco mandate surcharge is added to all checks.

venues.name: The Bartender's Handshake
venues.description: The Bartender's Handshake is a vintage-styled cocktail bar on Ingersoll Avenue, open 2pm to 1am seven days a week and to 2am at weekends — the widest hours of any venue in this city guide. Its two documented alcohol-free builds are unusually savoury: the Vacation Email uses orange spice tea with grapefruit, lime, cinnamon, tonic and coconut, and the Karate Kid runs carrot and ginger syrup against lime, ginger beer, ancho chili and mint. Two sources of heat and a vegetable base is about as far from a sweet mocktail as a bar can get, and it is what makes both drinkable across a long evening.
signatureDrinks: Vacation Email — orange spice tea, grapefruit, lime, cinnamon, tonic, coconut
Karate Kid — carrot, ginger syrup, lime, ginger beer, ancho chili, mint

naMenuItems.name: Ghia Tonic
naMenuItems.description: ghia non-alcoholic aperitif, fever tree tonic, orange

venues.longDescription:
The Bartender's Handshake sits on Ingersoll Avenue west of downtown Des Moines, a cosy vintage-styled room with a patio, and it opens at 2pm every single day of the week, running to 1am and to 2am on Friday and Saturday. That is the widest availability in this city guide by a distance, and across this whole directory the reliably open room usually turns out to matter more than the clever one.

It happens to be both. The two documented alcohol-free builds are among the most savoury in this entire batch of cities. The Karate Kid is built on carrot with ginger syrup, lime, ginger beer, ancho chili and mint — a vegetable base, two forms of ginger heat and a dried chili, with no fruit sweetness carrying it at all. The Vacation Email uses orange spice tea as its backbone with grapefruit, lime, cinnamon, tonic and coconut, where the tea supplies tannin, the tonic supplies quinine bitterness and the coconut supplies fat.

Both are worth studying if you order a lot of alcohol-free drinks, because they demonstrate the principle that separates a good one from a bad one. Alcohol contributes bitterness, weight and burn; a drink that removes it and adds sugar instead is unbalanced and becomes tiring within a glass. These replace those qualities with chili heat, ginger, tannin, quinine and fat. That is why a carrot drink works at eleven at night and a fruit punch does not.

Des Moines' tourism board documented both in January 2026, describing the bar as serving fashionable and tasty mocktails alongside its handcrafted cocktails.

The Ingersoll location puts it a couple of miles west of the downtown cluster, near Eatery A and Fresko, so that stretch works as its own evening.
venues.pressQuote: Karate Kid (carrot, ginger syrup, lime, ginger beer, ancho chili, mint)

venues.name: The Bay Kava Lounge
venues.description: The Bay has been trading on Brandon Boulevard since 2014, which makes it one of the longer-running kava rooms in Hillsborough County, and it is the main alcohol-free option in Brandon itself rather than in Tampa proper. It opens at 9:30am and runs to 11pm through the week, later at weekends, with a pool table and comfortable seating for people staying a while, plus late-night community events and wellness-room sessions. The drinks are kava, herbal and botanical teas, and craft non-alcoholic builds. IMPORTANT for readers in recovery: the lounge is known for an extensive kratom selection alongside the kava. Kratom acts on opioid receptors and carries dependence and withdrawal risk that kava does not, so order with that in mind.
venues.address: 2119 W Brandon Blvd G, Brandon, FL 33511
venues.longDescription:
The Bay has been trading on Brandon Boulevard since 2014, which makes it one of the longer-running kava rooms in Hillsborough County and considerably older than most of the category. It opens at 9:30am and runs to 11pm through the week, later at weekends, and it is the main alcohol-free option in Brandon itself rather than in Tampa proper — a distinction that matters, because Brandon is a suburb of well over 100,000 people whose evening economy is almost entirely chain restaurants and sports bars.

The room is fitted for staying: a pool table, comfortable seating, and a programme of late-night community events alongside wellness-room sessions. The venue's own line is that since 2014 it has been dedicated to providing a fun and welcoming atmosphere, and eleven years of continuous trade in a format that has seen a lot of openings and closings is reasonable evidence for the claim.

The drinks are kava, herbal and botanical teas, and craft non-alcoholic builds. Kava is the ground root of Piper methysticum, a shrub native to the South Pacific islands, prepared as a cold water infusion and drunk socially across Fiji, Vanuatu, Tonga and Samoa for roughly three thousand years. It contains no alcohol. It tastes earthy and bitter, numbs the lips and tongue on the first mouthful, and is mildly sedative rather than intoxicating in the way alcohol is. Kava exhibits reverse tolerance, so regular drinkers usually need less rather than more, and a first visit rewards a slow pace across an hour or two.

A point of history worth knowing: the lounge's social accounts still carry the handle from its earlier life as a vapour bar, and the business has evolved into its current kava-led form over time rather than opening as one. That is a common trajectory in Florida, where a lot of today's kava rooms began as smoke or vape shops, and it is part of why the category's menus are broader than the name suggests.

Which leads to the caution. The Bay is known for an extensive kratom selection alongside the kava, and on a menu of this breadth the two are easy to conflate. Kratom is the leaf of Mitragyna speciosa, a Southeast Asian tree, and its principal alkaloids act on the opioid receptors; regular use produces tolerance and a genuine withdrawal syndrome, several US states ban it outright, and its concentrated 7-hydroxymitragynine derivatives are the subject of active federal scheduling. Kava carries no comparable dependence profile. If you are here because you are avoiding substances with a hold on you, order by name and ask what is in the cup.
venues.pressQuote: Meet at The Bay for kava, botanical teas, craft drinks, and late-night community in Brandon, Florida
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: The Bay Kava Lounge, company statement

venues.name: The Berry & Rye
venues.description: The Berry & Rye is the oldest craft cocktail lounge in Omaha, a dim Prohibition-styled room in the Old Market on Howard Street, and it has an explicit policy of welcoming guests who are not drinking and building custom mocktails for them on request. It is open 5pm to 2am seven days a week, from 3pm on Friday and Saturday. For a bar of this vintage and reputation the willingness to make something properly rather than pointing at the soda gun is the relevant fact, and it is stated openly rather than left to be discovered.
signatureDrinks: Night Flower (NA: house zero proof bitter elixir, hibiscus, pomegranate, malic acid)

naMenuItems.name: Night Flower
naMenuItems.description: house zero proof bitter elixir, hibiscus, pomegranate, malic acid

venues.longDescription:
The Berry & Rye opened as Omaha's first serious craft cocktail lounge and remains its oldest, in a low-lit Prohibition-styled room on Howard Street in the Old Market. It is open until 2am every night of the week.

The alcohol-free position here is a policy rather than a printed list: the bar states that it welcomes sober guests and will build custom mocktails on request. This directory usually treats "on request" as a weak answer, and the grade of three reflects that honestly — there is no standing zero-proof section, no non-alcoholic spirits programme documented, and no named build that could be verified for this guide.

What lifts it above the venues excluded on the same basis is that the offer is stated openly rather than extracted. The practical difficulty for a non-drinker in a room like this is not that a good bartender cannot make something; it is the small social cost of asking, in a dark serious cocktail bar, for something the menu does not mention. A bar that says in advance that it will do this removes that cost entirely, which is most of the problem solved.

It is also worth being clear about what you are walking into: this is a spirits-led room with an extensive whiskey list and the atmosphere to match. For some readers in recovery that environment is fine and for others it is not, and that is a personal call rather than something a directory should make for them.

Open 5pm to 2am Sunday through Thursday and 3pm to 2am on Friday and Saturday — one of the few Omaha rooms in this guide with no closed day and a genuinely late licence. It sits a minute from Clio and Laka Lono in the middle of the Old Market.

One more reason it is worth listing despite the grade. Bars with this much reputation set the local standard, and when the oldest and most respected cocktail room in a city says publicly that it looks after people who are not drinking, other bars notice. Several of the venues in this guide opened long after The Berry & Rye did, into a scene where that expectation was already established. Influence is harder to measure than a printed menu, but it is real, and Omaha's alcohol-free drinking is better for this room having taken the position early.
venues.pressQuote: The Berry & Rye is the oldest craft cocktail lounge in Omaha.
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: Hurrdat ONE, 10 Best Zero-Proof & Nonalcoholic Bars in Omaha, Nov 18, 2025

venues.name: The Bluebird Cocktail Room
venues.description: The Bluebird Cocktail Room is a literary-themed cocktail bar on the second floor of a Hickory Avenue building in Hampden, above the Belgian beer bar De Kleine Duivel. Its printed menu carries a dedicated zero-proof section built on real non-alcoholic spirits rather than juice: the current list offers zero-proof builds of Baba's Bee's Knees (whose house build pairs the bar's own bee's-knees kombucha with honey and lemon), the Sage and Maple Smash, and a Daiquiri, with additional NA spirits available on request. The NA-whiskey Mata Hari that formerly anchored the section has rotated off the menu. It is an evenings-only room, open from 5 p.m. nightly.
signatureDrinks: Baba's Bee's Knees (zero-proof build with the bar's own kombucha, honey and lemon)
venues.longDescription:
The Bluebird Cocktail Room is a literary-themed bar upstairs on Hickory Avenue in Hampden, opened in 2017 by Paul Benkert, previously bar manager at Woodberry Kitchen. His stated brief was refreshingly unpretentious for a room this considered: he was basically making a bar that he wanted to go to. The result is a small, romantic space above a Belgian beer bar, reached by a staircase, with the literary theme carried through the drinks list rather than pasted onto the walls. It has become one of the reference cocktail rooms in a neighbourhood that has several.

The non-alcoholic drinks sit under their own printed heading, "Zero-Proof Cocktails", and the bar's approach is to build zero-proof versions of its own drinks rather than keep a separate token list. Baba's Bee's Knees is the clearest example — the full-strength version is gin with the bar's own kombucha, and the zero-proof build keeps the kombucha, honey and lemon while dropping the spirit, so the drink that arrives is recognisably the same cocktail. A zero-proof Daiquiri and a Sage and Maple Smash complete the printed list, and the menu notes that additional non-alcoholic spirits are available, which in practice means the bartenders will build something off-list if you tell them what you like. That flexibility matters here because the list rotates hard: press coverage from 2024 and 2025 named a zero-proof Mata Hari, built on non-alcoholic whiskey with lemon, chai and grenadine, and a kombucha-infused Vain Desires, neither of which is on the current menu. Treat any named list, including this one, as a snapshot of the house style rather than a guarantee, and note the bar publishes ingredients for its alcoholic drinks but not its zero-proof ones. One last practical point, because it genuinely catches people out: published sources disagree about both the street number and which floor the bar is on, giving 3600 or 3602 Hickory Avenue and the second or third floor. What is consistent across all of them is the landmark — look for the Belgian beer bar at street level and take the stairs up.
venues.pressQuote: I'm basically making a bar that I want to go to.

venues.name: The Boheme
venues.description: A French Revival-inspired fine-dining restaurant inside the Grand Bohemian Hotel Orlando (Autograph Collection) in the downtown City District, known for live jazz and its Sunday Jazz Brunch. The Boheme runs a Seedlip-built zero-proof cocktail program shared with the hotel's Altira rooftop lounge.
signatureDrinks: Orange Grove Margarita (Seedlip Grove 42, lime, orange)
Grapefruit & Honey (Seedlip Spice, grapefruit, lemon, honey)
venues.longDescription:
The Boheme sits inside the art-filled Grand Bohemian Hotel Orlando, an Autograph Collection property downtown, serving European-inspired dishes described as 'a culinary revival' that applies modern technique to hand-selected, locally sourced and heirloom ingredients. The restaurant is a downtown date-night destination and hosts a Sunday Jazz Brunch with live jazz performances.

The bar program is built around Seedlip non-alcoholic spirits, including the Orange Grove Margarita (Seedlip Grove 42, lime, orange) and the Grapefruit & Honey (Seedlip Spice, grapefruit, lemon, honey). The same zero-proof cocktail program extends to the hotel's Altira rooftop pool lounge one floor up.

With live jazz most nights and a sought-after Sunday Jazz Brunch, The Boheme has long been one of downtown Orlando's special-occasion rooms -- a Fodor's Choice pick in Fodor's Travel's guide to the city -- and its Seedlip-based zero-proof list means non-drinkers get a composed cocktail rather than a default soda in a setting built for celebration.
venues.pressQuote: The Grand Bohemian, a luxury boutique hotel, is the setting for this sleek city-center restaurant.

venues.name: The Boneyard
venues.description: The Boneyard is a late bar on Station Street in Chattanooga's Southside, open to 1am most nights and 2am on Friday and Saturday, in the short pedestrian block that concentrates most of the neighbourhood's nightlife. Its recommended alcohol-free drink is a non-alcoholic paloma built on grapefruit, lime and triple syrup, and the bar will make other mocktails on request. Combined with the late hours and its position a few doors from 330 Main, the fully alcohol-free kava bar, it makes the Southside the easiest part of the city to spend a whole evening in without drinking.
venues.hours: Mon 5pm-1am; Wed-Thu 5pm-1am; Fri-Sat 5pm-2am; Sun 5pm-1am; Tue closed
signatureDrinks: Non-alcoholic paloma — grapefruit, lime, triple syrup
venues.longDescription:
Station Street is a single pedestrianised block on the Southside, between the Chattanooga Choo Choo and Main Street, and it holds a disproportionate share of the city's late-night drinking. The Boneyard is one of its anchors — a proper late bar, open to 1am most nights and 2am on Friday and Saturday.

The alcohol-free recommendation is a non-alcoholic paloma: grapefruit, lime and triple syrup, which is the right drink for the setting. A paloma is long, sour and slightly bitter from the grapefruit, so it holds up over an evening in a way that a sweeter build would not, and the bar will make other mocktails on request beyond it.

This is graded three rather than four, and the reason is the phrase "on request". This directory generally treats "we'll make you something without alcohol" as a strength-two answer and excludes it, because it puts the work on the customer and produces a different drink every time. The Boneyard clears the bar because there is a specific documented build it recommends by name — NOOGAtoday recorded it in the city's guide to non-alcoholic drinking — rather than only an offer to improvise. It is a modest programme honestly described.

What pushes it onto the list is geography. The Boneyard sits a few doors from 330 Main, the fully non-alcoholic kava bar and coffee house, and around the corner from Oddstory's taproom with its alcohol-free fridge. That cluster means the Southside is the one part of Chattanooga where a non-drinker can spend an entire evening moving between rooms rather than making do in one, which is a genuinely different experience from finding a single good venue.

Closed Tuesday. Doors at 5pm the rest of the week.
venues.pressQuote: This spot recommends trying a NA Paloma made with grapefruit, lime, and triple syrup + can make other mocktails on request.
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: NOOGAtoday, Local mocktails + non-alcoholic drinks in Chattanooga

venues.name: The Boneyard
venues.description: The Boneyard is an all-ages craft cocktail lounge in the Greenacres part of Spokane Valley, opened by a mixologist who also produces Side Hustle Syrups — the craft syrup line every drink in the room is built on, alcoholic or not. That vertical integration is the reason its mocktails hold up: a Spokane Mule, a zero-proof Old Fashioned and a White Linen are made from the same house components as their full-strength counterparts rather than from a separate bottle of cordial. Being all-ages makes it one of very few rooms in the metro where a family or an under-21 group can sit at a proper cocktail bar. Wednesday to Saturday, 3pm to 9pm.
venues.address: 17905 E Appleway Ave Suite A, Spokane Valley, WA 99016
venues.longDescription:
The Boneyard sits on East Appleway in Greenacres, out in Spokane Valley rather than downtown, and it was opened by a mixologist rather than a restaurateur — which shows in the drinks and in one structural decision that puts it in this guide.

Every mixed drink in the room, with alcohol or without, is built on Side Hustle Syrups, the craft simple-syrup line the owner produces. That is unusual and it matters. The commonest failure in a mocktail is that it is assembled from different, worse components than the cocktails: bottled mixers, canned juice, a splash of soda. When the syrups are the house product and the bar's own business, the alcohol-free drinks are made from the identical pantry — the only difference is the absence of the spirit. The mocktail list reflects that, with a non-alcoholic Spokane Mule, an Old Fashioned build and a White Linen sitting alongside cocktails like the Hello Clarice, a whiskey sour clarified with milk.

The second thing worth knowing is that The Boneyard is an all-ages lounge. Spokane Valley is a suburban, family-heavy part of the metro, and an all-ages craft cocktail bar means a group does not have to split itself by who is drinking or who is old enough. For readers with kids, or for a designated driver who would rather not be the person nursing a Coke in a 21-plus room, that changes what an evening out can look like.

The trade-off is the schedule. The bar opens Wednesday through Saturday only, 3pm to 9pm, and closes Sunday through Tuesday — early hours by cocktail-bar standards, which suits an all-ages room but rules out a late night. It is roughly a fifteen-minute drive east of downtown Spokane.

One more thing worth understanding about the syrup arrangement, because it is the whole argument for this listing. A bar that buys its mixers is limited to what a distributor stocks, and the alcohol-free versions of those products are almost always the cheapest line. A bar that manufactures its own syrups has no such constraint and no cost incentive to cut corners on the drinks with no spirit in them, because the expensive ingredient was never the spirit. That is why owner-produced house components are the single most reliable signal this directory has found for a mocktail list that is worth ordering from.
venues.pressQuote: Our atmosphere is probably a little more on the adult side, but … kids get to feel like they're part of the fancy nature of things with a more craft-oriented beverage.

venues.name: The Bower
venues.description: The Bower is a seasonal, locally-sourced American restaurant and bar on Magazine Street in the Lower Garden District, opened in 2020 by Mark Latter of Latter Hospitality (the group behind Tujague's); an adjacent cocktail-focused Bower Bar followed in 2022. The kitchen and beverage programs are ingredient-driven, with menus shaped by produce, herbs, and flowers from Sugar Roots Farm. Under beverage director Mickey Mullins, the "field-to-glass" bar program extends to a dedicated non-alcoholic section, where house-made mocktails are built from the same fresh, garden-driven ingredients as the cocktail list rather than bottled zero-proof spirits. Current non-alcoholic offerings include Moody Judy (vanilla bean lemonade, butterfly pea flower), No-Loma (grapefruit, lime, soda), and Walk the Lime (sweet lime and coconut), all available at the daily happy hour.

naMenuItems.description: vanilla bean lemonade, butterfly pea flower

naMenuItems.name: No-Loma
naMenuItems.description: grapefruit, lime, soda

naMenuItems.name: Walk the Lime
naMenuItems.description: sweet lime & coconut

venues.longDescription:
The Bower is at 1320 Magazine Street in the Lower Garden District — worth stating plainly, because at least one published guide has printed a Metairie address for it, which is wrong. It opened in March 2020 as a farm-to-table American restaurant from Mark Latter of Latter Hospitality, the group behind Tujague's, and managed three days of service before the pandemic closed everything. It came back. In January 2022 the group added the Bower Bar next door in the old Claret wine bar space, twenty seats around a central bar and twenty-four more at tables, with living green walls planted by a local landscape studio. Marcus Woodham runs the kitchen and Mickey Mullins the bar. Latter's own line about the food is the useful one: chef Marcus will make you want to eat vegetables, even if you are not vegetarian. Service runs from 4pm daily, with happy hour from 4 to 6.

The non-alcoholic drinks are printed under a plain heading, NON-ALCOHOLIC, and there are three of them, each $9. That price is the thing to notice. The full cocktails on the same card run $14 to $17, so the zero-proof drinks are roughly half — and they are made in-house rather than poured from a bottled non-alcoholic brand, which usually pushes prices the other way. Moody Judy is a vanilla bean lemonade with butterfly pea flower, the blue-violet flower that shifts colour as acid hits it, so the drink changes in the glass as the lemon works through. No-Loma is grapefruit, lime and soda — the simplest of the three and the one that lasts an evening. Walk the Lime is sweet lime and coconut, and is closer to dessert. None of them pretends to be a spirit, which is a deliberate choice and a defensible one; a kitchen this committed to local produce is going to build a drink from fruit rather than from an imported bottle. It is a short list, but it is honest, cheap and made on the premises.
venues.pressQuote: a chic, contemporary restaurant on Magazine Street in the Lower Garden District

venues.name: The Breeze Coffee Bar & Wine Shop
venues.description: The Breeze is a combined coffee bar and wine shop in Shelby Park, run by Sarah Height and Chelsea Moore next door to their natural wine bar Canary Club. It bills itself as Louisville's first and only coffee bar and wine shop, opening in the morning for espresso from Cincinnati roaster Deeper Roots and running through the day as a bottle shop for natural, low-intervention wine. For non-drinkers it is the closest thing Louisville has to a non-alcoholic bottle shop: alongside the natural wine the shop carries a range of non-alcoholic wines and spirits, including a non-alcoholic Kentucky bourbon — which in this city is the bottle people actually want. It relocated here from Logan Street Market.
signatureDrinks: Non-alcoholic Kentucky bourbon by the bottle
venues.longDescription:
Louisville does not have a dedicated non-alcoholic bottle shop. That is a real gap in a metro of well over a million people, and it is the single biggest structural difference between this city's alcohol-free scene and those of comparable metros like Grand Rapids or Indianapolis, both of which have shops selling nothing but zero-proof. The nearest Louisville comes is The Breeze: a coffee bar and wine shop in Shelby Park, run by Sarah Height and Chelsea Moore, which carries a working range of non-alcoholic wines and spirits alongside its main trade in natural, low-intervention wine — including a non-alcoholic Kentucky bourbon, which is the obvious thing to want here and surprisingly hard to buy off a shelf locally.

The shop's own framing is that it runs from am to pm: espresso in the morning from Deeper Roots, the Cincinnati roaster widely rated that city's best, and wine retail through the day, with the natural-wine selection described by the owners as the biggest in Louisville. Its focus is on environmentally sustainable, naturally fermented, additive-free bottles from small farmers and producers. The pairing with Canary Club, the owners' natural wine bar immediately next door, means you can taste something in the bar and buy it in the shop, or the reverse.

One point of confusion worth heading off, because it appears in current listings: The Breeze began in 2019 as a wine bar inside Logan Street Market at 1001 Logan Street, and that original unit is closed — Yelp still carries the Logan Street listing with a CLOSED flag, which reads as though the business has folded. It has not; it moved to Shelby Park alongside Canary Club and is trading. Go to the Shelby Street address. For a non-drinker the practical value is morning-to-evening range: this is one of the few places in Louisville where you can start with coffee, browse alcohol-free bottles, and end up somewhere with late hours next door without ever ordering a drink you did not want. Set expectations correctly, though: this is a wine shop that also stocks alcohol-free bottles, not a dedicated non-alcoholic retailer. The zero-proof range is a shelf rather than a department, the staff expertise runs deepest on natural wine, and you will not find the forty-bottle spread that a specialist shop in a comparable city would carry. Treat it as the best available option in a metro that does not yet have a proper non-alcoholic bottle shop — and, given how quickly the category is growing, as the most likely place in Louisville for one to appear.
venues.pressQuote: From am to pm, The Breeze Coffee Bar & Wine Shop is home to Louisville's biggest and best selection of natural and eclectic wines.

venues.name: The Butcher's Wife
venues.description: A gluten-free, Brazilian-inspired restaurant and natural wine bar tucked into Tiong Bahru, The Butcher's Wife gives non-drinkers a genuine fermented, sit-down option: the kitchen brews its own house kombucha with regularly rotating flavours, sold by the 450ml bottle (S$15). Beyond it, there is a short but real line of named mocktails built to order - the Roselle & Pineapple (hibiscus tea, pineapple, almond syrup), the Apple Lemon Mint (apple juice, lemon, mint, soda) and Dansel's Virgin (elderflower, lychee, cranberry, mint) - plus cold-pressed juices like the Wife's Cooler (watermelon, cucumber, coconut water). The gut-friendly, fermentation-forward kitchen means the zero-proof pours are part of the same philosophy as the food, not an afterthought.
signatureDrinks: The Homemade Kombucha - house-fermented, regularly rotating flavours (450ml, S$15)
Roselle & Pineapple - hibiscus tea, pineapple, almond syrup (S$13)
Apple Lemon Mint - apple juice, lemon, mint, soda (S$13)
Dansel's Virgin - elderflower, lychee, cranberry, mint (S$13)
Wife's Cooler - watermelon, cucumber, coconut water (S$13)
venues.longDescription:
The Butcher's Wife opened in Tiong Bahru as a Spa Esprit Group concept from founder Cynthia Chua, developed with Argentine consultant chef Diego Jacquet (of London's boCHINche). The kitchen is 100% gluten-free with a Latin-Mediterranean, Brazilian-leaning menu that leans hard on fermentation, pickling and preserving - a small, community-minded room at 19 Yong Siak Street that trades on freshness and gut-friendly cooking rather than scale.

The drinks list is best known as a natural wine bar, but the same fermentation ethos gives non-drinkers a real anchor: The Homemade Kombucha is brewed in-house with regularly rotating flavours and served by the 450ml bottle at S$15, making it a proper sit-down alternative to a glass of wine rather than a token soft drink. Around it sits a genuine mocktail section - Roselle & Pineapple (hibiscus tea, pineapple, almond syrup), Apple Lemon Mint (apple juice, lemon, mint, soda) and Dansel's Virgin (elderflower, lychee, cranberry, mint), each S$13 - plus fresh juices including the Super C (orange, carrot, ginger) and the Wife's Cooler (watermelon, cucumber, coconut water).

Because the food is fully gluten-free and fermentation-driven, the non-alcoholic pours pair naturally with the Brazilian-inspired plates: the kombucha's acidity and the herbaceous mocktails are built to sit alongside the kitchen's pickles, preserves and gut-friendly cooking. It is a restaurant NA program rather than a zero-proof cocktail den, but the house-brewed kombucha and named builds make it a credible option for anyone eating and drinking alcohol-free in Tiong Bahru.

The fermentation is not a garnish on the concept; it is the concept, and it is what makes the drinks list unusually reliable for non-drinkers. Reviewing the restaurant, MiddleClass.sg noted that the menu is packed with fermented indigenous ingredients and that a great deal of it is handcrafted entirely from scratch — which is also how the kitchen holds its fully gluten-free status, by making the components itself rather than buying them in.

A kitchen already running its own ferments for the food has the equipment, the routine and the staff knowledge to run one for the drinks. That is why the house kombucha is a rotating, genuinely made product rather than a bought-in bottle with the label turned outward, and it is the honest reason to trust an alcohol-free order here more than at a restaurant of similar size that simply lists a mocktail.

The room helps too. It is small and colourful, with natural light coming through near the back of the restaurant and alfresco seats by the entrance that are pet-friendly. It reads as a neighbourhood restaurant rather than a destination bar, which suits a table where only some people are drinking: nobody is performing, and the kombucha arrives in a bottle you pour and share like everything else.
venues.pressQuote: The menu here at The Butcher’s Wife is packed with fermented indigenous ingredients with lots of elements handcrafted entirely from scratch.

venues.name: The Butterfly Bar
venues.description: The Butterfly Bar opened in February 2011 inside The VORTEX, a long-running non-profit live theatre in East Austin's Manor Road corridor, evolving from the theatre's small beer-and-wine cafe into a full-service bar after it secured a mixed-beverage license in 2013. Every drink purchased supports the resident performing artists. The bar pours from a historic bartop reportedly over 200 years old and opens onto a patio that is a certified monarch butterfly garden, with butterflies present in summer. Alongside craft cocktails, bar manager Kellee Broadway runs a dedicated, named mocktail menu priced around $8. Confirmed zero-proof drinks include Aphrodite's Kiss (pomegranate, pineapple, lime, ginger beer) and the Queen Bey, a strawberry-limeade mocktail dusted with tajín that Broadway created. The on-site Patrizi's food truck serves housemade Italian pasta in the garden, and the adjoining black-box theatre hosts live performance most Thursday through Sunday, plus trivia, improv, and movie nights.
venues.longDescription:
The Butterfly Bar opened in February 2011 inside The VORTEX, a long-running non-profit theatre on the Manor Road corridor in East Austin. It began as the theatre's small beer-and-wine cafe and became a full bar after securing a mixed-beverage licence in 2013. The VORTEX is a 501(c)(3), and every drink bought here supports the resident performing artists — which makes it one of the few bars in the country where the drinks are the funding model for something else entirely.

That structure shapes the room. The bar pours from a bartop reported to be over two hundred years old and opens onto a patio that is a certified monarch butterfly garden, with butterflies actually present through the summer. Patrizi's serves house-made Italian pasta from a truck in the garden, and the adjoining black-box theatre runs live performance most Thursday to Sunday, plus trivia, improv and movie nights.

Bar manager Kellee Broadway runs a dedicated, named mocktail menu priced around eight dollars — roughly half what a zero-proof cocktail costs at most bars, and a deliberate decision rather than a shortcut. Aphrodite's Kiss combines pomegranate, pineapple, lime and ginger beer. The Queen Bey is a strawberry limeade dusted with tajín, created by Broadway; the chilli-lime salt is doing the same job a salt rim does on a margarita, giving the drink a savoury edge that keeps it from reading as sweet.

A theatre bar is an unusually easy place not to drink, for the same reason a listening room is. The evening has a fixed centre that is not the bar — there is a show, it starts at a time, and afterwards people talk about it. Nobody is counting rounds, and there is a reason to be there that does not require a glass in your hand.

Open 5pm to midnight Sunday to Friday and to 1am on Saturday, at 2307 Manor Road.

venues.name: The Café at Thistle Farms
venues.description: The Café at Thistle Farms is a fully alcohol-free cafe, tea room and event space on Charlotte Avenue in West Nashville, run as a nonprofit social enterprise that employs women survivors of trafficking, prostitution and addiction. It sits on the Thistle Farms campus alongside the organisation's shop and body-care workshop. The kitchen serves locally sourced breakfast and lunch, and the cafe runs a daily seated tea service - by reservation, 1pm to 3pm - with a steeped pot, a china cup donated by a supporter or programme graduate, and six chef's-choice bites on a tiered tray. The loose-leaf list includes Earl Grey Lavender, Casablanca Twist, Cha Cha, Masala Chai and a house blend called Communi-Tea. No alcohol is served. Closed Sundays.
signatureDrinks: Earl Grey Lavender - citrus, lavender, sweet and floral
Casablanca Twist - black tea with sweet peppermint
Cha Cha - green tea, jasmine and peppermint
Masala Chai - spiced, cardamom and cinnamon
venues.longDescription:
Thistle Farms was founded in Nashville by Becca Stevens as a residential and employment programme for women survivors of trafficking, prostitution and addiction, and the cafe on its Charlotte Avenue campus is one of the social enterprises that funds and staffs that work. The women who make the coffee, run the floor and serve the tea are programme participants and graduates. That is stated plainly by the organisation itself: it describes the cafe as a nonprofit social enterprise helping heal, restore and employ women survivors of trafficking, prostitution and addiction. For a directory used substantially by people in recovery, this is worth knowing before you arrive rather than after - it is not a marketing line attached to an ordinary coffee shop.

No alcohol is served. The kitchen does locally sourced breakfast and lunch, and the thing that makes the room a destination is the seated tea service, which runs Monday to Saturday from 1pm to 3pm by reservation with at least 48 hours' notice, at $30 a head. It comes as a steeped pot with a china teacup - the cups are donated, sent in by supporters and Thistle Farms graduates from around the world, and a chandelier of them hangs in the room - plus six chef's-choice savoury and sweet bites on a tiered tray. Quiche, a demi salad or a cup of soup can be added. The organisation's own framing of the ritual is that chado is about more than preparing tea; it is about serving and sharing it from a deep place of love and intention.

The loose-leaf list is genuinely worth ordering from rather than defaulting to coffee: black teas include Earl Grey Lavender and Casablanca Twist with sweet peppermint; the greens include Cha Cha, jasmine and peppermint, and a pomegranate raspberry; the caffeine-free herbals include pure moringa, Honeybush Vanilla and a house blend called Communi-Tea made with moringa, hibiscus and orange peel. There is a Masala Chai, and the espresso bar's best-known drink is a lavender honey latte. One practical note: the cafe closes at 3pm and is shut on Sundays, so this is a daytime venue - the shop next door is worth the extra half hour.
venues.pressQuote: A nonprofit social enterprise helping heal, restore, and employ women survivors of trafficking, prostitution, and addiction.

venues.name: The California Clipper
venues.description: The California Clipper is Humboldt Park's longest-standing neighborhood bar, established in 1937 in a building that has stood at California and Augusta since 1912, and it carries one of the deepest non-alcoholic lists of any old-line Chicago tavern. The drink menu keeps a standing Non-Alcoholic section rather than a token substitution: two built zero-proof cocktails - the Last Call N/A with Seedlip Notas de Agave, white peach and lemon, and the Choomjito N/A - plus bottled Lyre's Prosecco, Amalfi Spritz and gin and tonic, a St Agrestis Phony Negroni, Athletic Brewing hazy IPA, Old Mil N/A lager and yerba mate. Note that the Choomjito and the Choom soda contain THC and the Chelsea B soda contains CBD; the rest of the list is free of both.
signatureDrinks: Last Call N/A (Seedlip Notas de Agave, white peach, lemon)
Choomjito N/A (Choom, mint, lime - contains THC)

naMenuItems.name: Choomjito N/A
naMenuItems.description: choom thc, mint, lime

naMenuItems.name: Last Call N/A
naMenuItems.description: seedlip notas de agave, white peach, lemon

venues.longDescription:
The building at 1002 North California Avenue went up in 1912 as the L.L. Freeman Theater and closed during the influenza epidemic at the end of the First World War; it reopened as the California Clipper in 1937, four years after the repeal of Prohibition, and has been a bar ever since. Orbit Group revived it after a short pandemic closure, and the room still reads post-Prohibition: red leather booths, vintage red light fixtures and Tannoy speakers of the type used at Abbey Road. Live music runs nearly every night across jazz, blues, funk, country, house and DJ sets, and a back room called the Lil Clip - the former home of the C.C. Ferns coffee shop - handles late-night dancing on Friday and Saturday with programming aimed at newer and independent acts.

For a bar of this vintage the non-alcoholic list is unusually complete, and it sits as its own menu section rather than an afterthought under sodas. Two zero-proof drinks are built to order: the Last Call N/A, made with Seedlip Notas de Agave, white peach and lemon at $14, and the Choomjito N/A, which combines Choom, mint and lime at the same price and does contain THC. Alongside them the bar keeps a bottled and canned range - Lyre's Prosecco, Lyre's Amalfi Spritz and Lyre's Gin and Tonic at $7 each, a St Agrestis Phony Negroni, Athletic Brewing hazy IPA, an Old Mil N/A lager at $4, yerba mate and Liquid Death - plus a 30mg CBD soda from Chelsea B and a 3mg THC Choom soda. Anyone avoiding psychoactives as well as alcohol should order around the Choom and Chelsea B items specifically; everything else on the non-alcoholic list is free of both. The kitchen does not serve food, so plan to eat before or after.
venues.pressQuote: Hospitality group Orbit Group (Segnatore) revived The California Clipper, founded in 1937, after a brief closure during the pandemic.

venues.name: The Captain at Hotel Hartness
venues.description: The Captain is the bar at Hotel Hartness, the luxury property east of downtown Greenville, and it does something almost no hotel bar does: it dedicates an entire page of its menu to mocktails. A full page is a different order of commitment from a couple of drinks at the foot of the cocktail list — it means the drinks have been developed, costed and trained on as a category in their own right. It is open noon to 10pm most days and to midnight on Friday and Saturday, seven days a week, which for a non-drinker makes it one of the few all-day options in the metro.
venues.longDescription:
Hotel Hartness sits on a wooded estate east of downtown Greenville, and The Captain is its bar. It earns a place in this guide on a single structural fact reported by TOWN Carolina in its survey of the city's alcohol-free drinking: the bar gives mocktails an entire page of its menu.

That is worth dwelling on, because menu real estate is the most honest signal a bar gives. Two drinks tucked under the beer list is a gesture. A full page means someone has developed a range with variety in it — something bitter, something long, something with body — costed each build, stocked the components, and trained the staff to make them consistently on a Saturday night. It also means a guest can read and choose rather than describe and hope, which is most of what a bar offers anybody.

Hotel bars are also, quietly, one of the most useful categories for readers of this directory. They keep long hours, they are open every day including the Sundays and Mondays when independent cocktail rooms close, they are comfortable to sit in alone, and nobody is measuring how long you have been nursing a glass. The Captain runs noon to 10pm Sunday through Thursday and noon to midnight on Friday and Saturday — seven days, no closed day, and open through the afternoon.

This entry records no signature drinks. The mocktail page is not published in a form that could be read for this guide, and this directory does not print a drink name it has not seen on a current menu. Ask for the mocktail menu specifically; it is a page, not a footnote.

One practical note: Hartness is a genuine drive from the South Main cluster, roughly eight miles east, so this is a destination rather than part of a downtown crawl.
venues.pressQuote: The Captain at Hotel Hartness dedicates an entire menu page to mocktails.
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: TOWN Carolina, Mocktails for Dry July

venues.name: The Chapman
venues.description: A 6,700-square-foot Florida-centric steak-and-seafood restaurant on Park Avenue, named for Winter Park founders Loring Chase and Oliver Chapman, with the adjoining Chase Lounge bar. The Chapman offers named zero-proof cocktails, the Winter Park Vice and Gentle Breeze, alongside its citrus- and seafood-forward menu.
venues.address: 500 S Park Ave, Winter Park, FL 32789
signatureDrinks: Winter Park Vice (hibiscus, coconut cream, pineapple, lime, toasted coconut)
Gentle Breeze (blood orange, fassionola, lemon, vanilla, ginger beer)
venues.longDescription:
The Chapman opened on Park Avenue with a fin-de-siecle theme that, according to Artistry Restaurants chief concept officer Daniel Harf, was inspired by 'the style, architecture and romance of the Seminole Hotel, the history of the neighborhood, and how it offered a winter respite for Northerners.' The space honors Winter Park's founding fathers, Loring Augustus Chase and Oliver Everett Chapman, across both the main dining room and its attached Chase Lounge bar.

The Chapman and Chase Lounge opened with a soft launch of dinner service on January 20, 2025, with full lunch, brunch, and dinner menus following in early February 2025. The concept is part of Artistry Restaurants, founded by Barry Goff (whose son, Mitch Goff, serves as executive vice president); the project was reportedly first initiated by the Holler family roughly three years before opening.

Menu development was overseen by Clifford Pleau, a Culinary Institute of America graduate who was the opening-day chef of Disney's California Grill in 1994 and later spent 12 years creating concepts for Darden, including Seasons 52. Executive Chef Ibis Lopez sources proteins from family-run farms including Joyce Farms, Cheshire Farms, and Kvarøy Arctic, always featuring a fresh Florida catch of the day.

Beyond the Chase Lounge's classic and old-fashioned cocktail list, The Chapman's zero-proof offerings include the Winter Park Vice (hibiscus, coconut cream, pineapple, lime, toasted coconut) and the Gentle Breeze (blood orange, fassionola, lemon, vanilla, ginger beer).
venues.pressQuote: We were intrigued by the style, architecture and romance of the Seminole Hotel, the history of the neighborhood, and how it offered a winter respite for Northerners.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Daniel Harf, Chief Concept Officer, Artistry Restaurants

venues.name: The Charles
venues.description: The Charles is one of the Design District's most booked dining rooms — a dim, loud, Italian-leaning room that has traded on being hard to get into since 2018 — and its Summer 2026 menu carries a printed Mocktails section. The Blossom Spritz builds cherry blossom and grapefruit over Fre sparkling, the Nada Colada covers the creamy tropical end, and the Blueberry di Capri the fruit-forward one. None is built on a non-alcoholic distillate, which places the list a step below the Ritual and Lyre's programmes elsewhere in this guide. The quietly more useful entry is a separate N/A Sparkling listing: Fre Brut by the glass or the bottle, so a non-drinker can share a bottle at the table rather than order around the wine list. Closed Sundays.
signatureDrinks: Blossom Spritz (cherry blossom, grapefruit, Fre sparkling)
venues.longDescription:
The Charles opened in the Design District in 2018 and has stayed one of the harder Dallas reservations to get — a dim, loud, Italian-leaning room that treats dinner as an event rather than a meal. Its non-alcoholic drinks appear under a printed Mocktails heading on the Summer 2026 menu, refreshed in late July, which already puts it ahead of the many Dallas rooms whose zero-proof lists appear each January and quietly vanish by March.

Three builds carry the section. The Blossom Spritz is the most complete drink of the set, combining cherry blossom and grapefruit with Fre sparkling to give it length and lift — the one to order if you want something that reads as a cocktail across a candlelit table. The Nada Colada handles the creamy tropical end and the Blueberry di Capri the fruit-forward one. We would rather be straight about the ceiling here: none of the three uses a non-alcoholic distillate, so there is no botanical bitterness or spirit-like backbone to them, and the list sits a step below the Ritual, Lyre's and Almave programmes elsewhere in this guide. What they are is properly built, printed under their own heading, in a restaurant where the wine list is the main event.

The more quietly useful entry is the separate N/A Sparkling listing: Fre Brut, offered by the glass and by the bottle. At a table ordering wine, a bottle a non-drinker can actually share changes the evening more than a single cocktail does — it removes the moment where one person is handed something different while everyone else is poured from the same bottle. Service runs Monday to Thursday to 10pm and Friday and Saturday to 11pm, with the room closed on Sundays, so this is a dinner reservation rather than a drop-in. Worth knowing before you arrive from older coverage: the Lavender Limonata, Peary Freshe and Honey Please that appear in press write-ups have since come off the menu, and asking for them will get you a blank look. The distinction that matters is between a printed heading and a bartender willing to improvise: the first survives a change of staff and a busy Friday, the second does not. The Charles has the first, which is why it holds a place here despite the modest depth of the list itself.

venues.name: The Charlotte
venues.description: The Charlotte on Henderson Avenue prints a boxed Zero Proof section, and unusually every drink in it is a martini variant — the format zero-proof lists almost always skip, because a drink served up with nothing to hide behind is the hardest kind to build without alcohol. The Dirty Martini runs Ritual's gin alternative with olive juice and blue cheese-stuffed olives; alongside it sit a Pornstar Martini made with vanilla, pineapple, passion fruit and non-alcoholic sparkling, an espresso martini and a pomegranate martini. The restaurant publishes no telephone number and no closing times, and its own Instagram says only that it opens daily at 11am, so check before a late visit.
signatureDrinks: Dirty Martini (Ritual gin alternative, olive juice, blue cheese olives)
Pornstar Martini (vanilla, pineapple, passion fruit, NA sparkling)
venues.longDescription:
Zero-proof menus have a predictable shape: something with cucumber, something with ginger beer, something fruit-forward and long. The Charlotte's boxed Zero Proof section on Henderson Avenue is worth recording because it does the opposite — all four drinks are martini-format, served up, which is the hardest style to pull off without alcohol and the one non-drinkers most often miss. A long drink can hide a thin base behind ice and soda; a martini cannot, because there is nothing in the glass but the thing itself.

The Dirty Martini is the proof of intent. Built on Ritual's gin alternative with olive juice and blue cheese-stuffed olives, it is savoury, cold and bracing in the way the original is, and it gives a non-drinker something to hold that reads as an adult drink at a glance — which, in a room where everyone else is holding stemware, is a substantial part of what people are actually after. The Pornstar Martini uses vanilla, pineapple and passion fruit topped with non-alcoholic sparkling; an espresso martini and a pomegranate martini complete the set, covering the after-dinner and the fruit-forward ends respectively.

Two practical notes, because this is a venue where the published information is thinner than the menu deserves. The restaurant publishes no telephone number and no closing times — its own Instagram says it opens daily at 11am, which is all we can confirm, so treat a late visit as a gamble unless you have checked that day. And for anyone arriving from a listicle: there is no non-alcoholic French 75 on the current menu, despite it being widely reported, including by outlets that also get the Pornstar Martini right. The four martinis above are what is actually served, and they are enough of a reason to go.
venues.pressQuote: Pornstar Martini with vanilla, pineapple, passion fruit, and NA sparkling

venues.name: The Chill Room
venues.description: A fully alcohol-free bar and lounge on Broadway Road in Tempe, built around spirit-free cocktails, kava, Fijian extract, botanical root teas, herbal teas and coffee. What sets it apart from the metro's other kava rooms is the calendar: open mic nights, live music, DJs, movie nights, trivia and poker, run weekly rather than occasionally, which is what turns a bar into somewhere people come back to. Open daily from 2pm and to 2am on Friday and Saturday, it functions as a genuine third place for the sober and sober-curious in the East Valley. Kava and kratom are alcohol-free but psychoactive — alcohol-free is not substance-free.
venues.address: 1320 E Broadway Rd Suite 108, Tempe, AZ 85282
venues.longDescription:
The Chill Room sits in a suite on East Broadway Road in Tempe, and its claim on this directory rests less on any single drink than on how much it programmes. The drinks list is what you would expect of a serious kava room — spirit-free cocktails, traditional kava, Fijian extract, botanical root teas, herbal teas and coffee, served from early afternoon until late. The calendar is the part that is unusual: open mic nights, live music, DJs, movie nights, trivia and poker, running weekly rather than as occasional specials.

That distinction is the whole argument. The hardest thing about not drinking is rarely the drink itself; it is that the social infrastructure of an evening — the reason to leave the house, the thing that happens between 8pm and midnight — is almost entirely built around bars. A venue that serves excellent alcohol-free drinks but offers nothing to do is competing with someone's sofa, and usually loses. A venue with a Tuesday trivia night and a Thursday open mic is competing with a pub, and can win. The Chill Room is built on the second model, and in the East Valley — where the alternative is largely ASU-adjacent drinking — that fills a real gap.

Hours suit the purpose: daily from 2pm, to midnight Sunday through Thursday and to 2am on Friday and Saturday, which means it is genuinely available at the hours when the temptation to go to a bar is highest rather than closing at nine like a cafe.

One caveat to carry in. Kava is mildly psychoactive and sedating, and kratom — served here as at most Arizona kava bars — acts on opioid receptors with documented dependence and withdrawal risk. Everything poured is alcohol-free, and none of it is inert. For someone in recovery that distinction is worth making deliberately rather than discovering at the bar.
venues.pressQuote: The Chill Room, a family business operated by the brothers Vincent and Anthony Cartagine, caters to the growing trend of alcohol alternatives in social settings

venues.name: The Chloe
venues.description: The Chloe is a boutique hotel, restaurant, bar and lounge from New Orleans hospitality group LeBlanc + Smith, opened in 2020 inside a restored 19th-century St Charles Avenue mansion designed by architect Thomas Sully, with a front porch and a tiki-style pool bar. READ THIS BEFORE ORDERING: the bar's "Spirit Free" section mixes alcohol-free drinks with two hemp-derived THC drinks under the same heading — Louie Louie Blackberry Lemon and Reba Water Sparkling Water, each labelled "(THC 5mg)" and priced at $11. The genuinely alcohol-free options in that section are the Typhoon Lagoon ($13) with Ritual non-alcoholic rum, passionfruit, guava, pomegranate, papaya, pineapple and lemon; the N/Aperitif Spritz ($16) with Lyre's Classico sparkling and orange; a bottled St. Agrestis Phony Negroni ($13); and Lyre's Classico sparkling wine by the glass ($14). These are built on bottled non-alcoholic brands rather than made from scratch. Dining runs 11am to 10pm Monday to Thursday, later Friday and Saturday, with weekend brunch and free on-street parking.
venues.address: 4125 St Charles Ave, New Orleans, LA 70115
venues.longDescription:
The Chloe occupies a restored 19th-century mansion on St Charles Avenue designed by Thomas Sully, and works as a hotel, an all-day restaurant, a bar, a front porch and a tiki-style pool bar all at once. It opened in 2020 from LeBlanc + Smith, and Where Y'at recommends the backyard as a mini staycation, with the pool bar open 11am to 8pm and happy hour from 3 to 5. Dining runs 11am to 10pm Monday to Thursday, to 11pm Friday and Saturday and to 9pm Sunday, with brunch at weekends. Reservations are encouraged rather than required, and street parking outside is free for guests — a small thing that is not small on that stretch of St Charles.

The zero-proof list needs reading carefully, because of how it is arranged. The menu has a section headed Spirit Free, and two of the drinks filed under it contain hemp-derived THC: Louie Louie Blackberry Lemon and Reba Water Sparkling Water, each printed with "(THC 5mg)" on the item line at $11. The dose is disclosed, which is more than many venues manage, but no warning text sits near them and the heading itself would lead most people to assume everything beneath it is inert. Spirit free is being used here to mean free of distilled spirits, not free of intoxicants. Order by name. What is genuinely alcohol-free and worth ordering: the Typhoon Lagoon at $13, a properly built tropical drink on Ritual's non-alcoholic rum with passionfruit, guava, pomegranate, papaya, pineapple and lemon; the N/Aperitif Spritz at $16 with Lyre's Classico sparkling and orange; a bottled St. Agrestis Phony Negroni at $13; and Lyre's Classico by the glass at $14 if you want something wine-shaped with dinner. These lean on bottled brands rather than house syrups and shrubs, which makes them consistent and a little less interesting than the room deserves. The Typhoon Lagoon is the one to have by the pool.
venues.pressQuote: Only St. Charles Avenue could make a mansion like the one known now as The Chloe seem to subtly blend in.

venues.name: The Church of Root Kava Bar
venues.description: The Church of Root is a small alcohol-free kava bar on NE 15th Avenue in Portland's Sabin neighbourhood, open 4pm to 10pm every day of the week. It prepares traditional kava beverages from high-quality roots using time-honoured methods rather than instant powder, and rounds the list out with a varied menu of other non-alcoholic drinks. The stated purpose is narrower and more specific than most bars manage: a welcoming environment designed for socialising, conversation and genuine connection, built around authentic kava, a relaxing room and engaging conversation. It joins Bula Kava House, Kava Saia and Nalu in giving Portland one of the deeper kava scenes on the West Coast. Kava is a psychoactive root drink from the South Pacific — no alcohol in it at all, but genuinely relaxing and mildly intoxicating on its own terms, which is worth knowing before a first shell.
signatureDrinks: Traditional kava beverage (hand-prepared from whole root)
venues.longDescription:
The Church of Root occupies a small storefront on NE 15th Avenue in the Sabin neighbourhood of inner Northeast Portland, and it keeps deliberately compact hours — 4pm to 10pm, seven days a week. That evening-only schedule tells you what it is for. This is not a cafe that sells kava as a sideline to laptops and lunch; it opens at the hour when people finish work and want somewhere to go, and it closes before the small hours. The whole proposition is stated plainly by the bar itself: authentic kava, a relaxing environment, and engaging conversation, in a welcoming space designed for socialising and genuine connection. Nothing alcoholic is served.

The kava is prepared traditionally, from high-quality roots following time-honoured methods, which in practice means the root is ground and strained by hand rather than reconstituted from an instant powder — the difference between the two is roughly the difference between brewed coffee and a sachet, and it is the single biggest variable in whether somebody's first kava experience is a good one. Around it sits a varied menu of other non-alcoholic drinks, so a group is not obliged to order kava to have a reason to sit down. Portland has quietly built one of the deeper kava scenes on the West Coast — Bula Kava House on SE Division, Kava Saia on East Burnside and Nalu in North Portland were already here — and the Church of Root adds a specifically neighbourhood-scaled room to that list rather than another destination. Kava deserves a plain description for readers in recovery: it is made from the ground root of a South Pacific shrub steeped in water, contains no alcohol whatsoever, and has been drunk socially across the Pacific for roughly three thousand years. It is, however, genuinely relaxing and mildly intoxicating in its own right, which matters if what you are avoiding is intoxication generally rather than alcohol specifically.

venues.name: The Commoner
venues.description: The Commoner is the American-tavern restaurant and bar inside the Kimpton Hotel Monaco at 620 William Penn Place in Downtown Pittsburgh, and the hotel's own site confirms it as the operating restaurant there. Its zero-proof programme is led by Kyle Turner, a sober bartender, who designs a rotating line-up of non-alcoholic cocktails built on the serious bottles — Seedlip, Pathfinder, Lyre's and Trejo's. Drinks including a Pandan Express, The Wandering Path, a Machete and an N/Aperol Spritz have appeared on the list. IMPORTANT PRACTICAL NOTE: The Commoner publishes its food menus online but not its cocktail list, so the current zero-proof line-up cannot be checked in advance and we could not confirm which of those drinks is pouring today — the programme is real and well regarded, but the specific drink is a question for the bar. The bar runs later than the kitchen, to 11pm most nights and midnight on Friday and Saturday, with a seasonal biergarten. Do not confuse it with The Commoner Corner, a small separate to-go concept at the same building that has closed. Parties of eight or more carry an automatic 20% gratuity.
venues.longDescription:
The Commoner is the American tavern inside the Kimpton Hotel Monaco at 620 William Penn Place Downtown, and the hotel's own site still lists it as the operating restaurant, which is worth confirming because hotel restaurants change name and management more often than freestanding ones. Its dining room does not behave like a hotel restaurant: focaccia with herb butter at $9, crispy potato with taleggio fondue at $17, spicy crab with chili crunch and cheese bread at $19, casareccia with aged parmesan cream and arugula pesto at $30, a tandoori-marinated half chicken at $35, a vegan soy daikon steak at $27, and an Allen Brothers prime steak at $68. The bar runs later than the kitchen — to 11pm most nights and midnight on Friday and Saturday — and there is a seasonal biergarten. One thing to avoid confusing: a small separate to-go concept called The Commoner Corner has closed; the restaurant itself has not.

What sets the zero-proof programme apart here is who runs it. It is led by Kyle Turner, and Table Magazine's line is the one that matters — with a sober bartender at the helm, you can trust that this non-alcoholic menu is truly outstanding, a rotating line-up of clever non-alcoholic cocktails designed with real thought. A bartender who does not drink is rare and it shows in the results, because the person building the drink is also the person who has to live on it. The list is built on the good bottles — Seedlip, Pathfinder, Lyre's and Trejo's — and drinks including a Pandan Express, The Wandering Path, a Machete and an N/Aperol Spritz have appeared on it. Be aware of one practical limitation before you plan around a specific drink: The Commoner publishes its food menus online but not its cocktail list, so the current zero-proof line-up cannot be checked in advance and we could not confirm which of those names is pouring today. The programme is real and well regarded; the specific drink is a question for the bar. Reservations are strongly recommended, and parties of eight or more carry an automatic 20% gratuity.
venues.pressQuote: With a sober bartender at the helm, you can trust that this non-alcoholic menu is truly outstanding.

venues.name: The Crunkleton
venues.description: The Crunkleton is a lodge-style craft cocktail bar and restaurant at 1957 E 7th Street in Charlotte's historic Elizabeth neighbourhood, opened in December 2018 as the second location from Gary Crunkleton, who began bartending in Chapel Hill more than twenty years ago. It runs a full kitchen — a prime New York strip at $74, crab cakes at $26, a house pecan pie — with dinner from 5pm nightly and weekend brunch from 11am. Its menu carries a printed "Non-Alcoholic Cocktails" section, of which three are genuinely free of both alcohol and anything else, all $13: the N/A Sour (A Cut Above non-alcoholic gin, elderflower syrup, lime, fresh ginger, cucumber), the Painlesskiller (fresh pineapple, coconut cream, lime, orange, demerara), and a Phony Negroni built on the Spiritless negroni alternative. NOTE: two further drinks under that same heading — Desert Bloom and Spiced Mule, $15 each — are made with Calmezzi THC spirits and contain 4mg of THC apiece. They are alcohol-free but not mocktails.
signatureDrinks: N/A Sour (A Cut Above NA gin, elderflower syrup, lime, fresh ginger, cucumber) $13
Painlesskiller (fresh pineapple, coconut cream, lime, orange, demerara syrup) $13
venues.longDescription:
The Crunkleton opened its Charlotte location in December 2018 at 1957 E 7th Street in historic Elizabeth, the second room from Gary Crunkleton, whose first bartending job was more than twenty years ago at an undergraduate bar in Chapel Hill while he was a student at the university there. The Charlotte bar is lodge-style and unhurried, built around a long bar and a floor-to-ceiling backbar, and it runs a full kitchen rather than bar snacks — a prime New York strip at $74, crab cakes at $26, a burger the menu calls simply a really good one at $19, and a house-made pecan pie. Dinner runs from 5pm nightly with weekend brunch from 11am. The bar operates a Top Shelf loyalty programme at $19.57 a year, a nod to the year that recurs through the room's design.

The zero-proof drinks have their own printed heading, "Non-Alcoholic Cocktails", and three of the five are genuinely alcohol-free and free of anything else. The N/A Sour ($13) is built on A Cut Above, the bar's own non-alcoholic gin, with elderflower syrup, lime, fresh ginger and cucumber. Painlesskiller ($13) is the tropical one — fresh pineapple, coconut cream, lime, orange and demerara syrup, a Painkiller with the rum taken out rather than replaced. A Phony Negroni ($13) uses the Spiritless negroni alternative. The other two items under that same heading need flagging clearly, because the heading does not distinguish them: Desert Bloom and Spiced Mule ($15 each) are built on Calmezzi THC spirits and each contain 4mg of THC. They are alcohol-free, which is why they sit in that section, but they are not mocktails, and anyone avoiding intoxicants of any kind should order from the first three. This pattern is worth knowing about across Charlotte generally, since Calmezzi's THC spirits are turning up under non-alcoholic headings at more than one bar in the city.

venues.name: The Dabney
venues.description: The Dabney is a Michelin-starred Mid-Atlantic restaurant at 122 Blagden Alley NW, a tucked-away corner of Shaw, opened in October 2015 by chef-owner Jeremiah Langhorne. The 55-seat dining room is built around a ten-foot wood-burning stone hearth, and almost everything passes through it. Langhorne's hyper-regional cooking won a Michelin star in 2017, the first year the guide reviewed Washington, and the 2018 James Beard Award for Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic, on top of a place on Bon Appetit's Best New Restaurants of 2016. The bar, run by bar director Daniel Todd, keeps a dedicated spirit-free list available a la carte at the bar or paired alongside the tasting menu: a Fennel Sour built with toasted fennel, egg white, lime and lemon, and a Manhattan riff on a house sorghum-based faux whiskey with spicebush amaro and black walnut bitters.

venues.longDescription:
The Dabney opened in October 2015 in Blagden Alley, a cobbled service alley behind Shaw that has since become one of the more interesting corners of the city, and it remains hard to find on purpose. Chef-owner Jeremiah Langhorne built the 55-seat room around a ten-foot wood-burning stone hearth, and the hearth is not decorative: it is the primary cooking method, and the menu is hyper-regional Mid-Atlantic, driven by what is available close by rather than by a fixed carte. The accolades came quickly and have held - a Michelin star in 2017, the first year the guide covered Washington, the 2018 James Beard Award for Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic, and a place on Bon Appetit's Best New Restaurants of 2016.

The bar programme, overseen by bar director Daniel Todd, maintains a dedicated spirit-free list, and Washingtonian's Dry January guide made the useful practical point about it: the list is available a la carte at the bar as well as alongside the tasting menu, so you do not have to commit to a full dinner to drink from it. The two named builds show what a kitchen-led bar can do that a spirits-led one cannot. The Fennel Sour uses toasted fennel with egg white, lime and lemon - the toasting is what gives it the depth a sour normally gets from the base spirit, and the egg white gives it the texture. The Manhattan riff is the more ambitious: it swaps in a house-made sorghum-based faux whiskey, adds a spicebush amaro built in-house, and finishes with black walnut bitters. Both drinks are made from things the kitchen already works with, which is the coherent way to run a spirit-free list in a restaurant of this kind.

Practical notes. The Dabney serves dinner Tuesday through Saturday only, from 5.30pm, closed Sunday and Monday, with last seatings at 9.30pm midweek and 10pm on Friday and Saturday. Sitting at the bar is the flexible option and the better one for the drinks. Blagden Alley itself is worth arriving early for - it is a short walk from the Mount Vernon Square and Shaw Metro stations, and the alley holds several other bars if the evening continues.

venues.name: The Daily Kitchen & Bar
venues.description: The Daily Kitchen & Bar is a Richmond Restaurant Group restaurant in the Greengate Shopping Center in Short Pump, in Henrico County, and since September 2026 it is the only Daily: the original restaurant on West Cary Street in Carytown closed after 13 years. Its drinks menu has a six-drink mocktail section — the Cucumber Cooler (basil, cucumber, lemongrass, coconut water, soda), a Passionfruit Lime Soda, a Strawberry Limeade, the Coco-Mo, a rotating daily shrub with club soda, and Blue Ridge Bucha ginger kombucha from Virginia — plus Athletic Brewing and Stella Liberte 0.0% in bottles and cans. Lunch starts at 11am on weekdays and brunch at 10:30am at weekends, and it serves until 9pm every day.
