Hello, Nurse! (pick-your-proof) — orange blossom, blue matcha, citrus; gin at half or full proof
Dreams of Oaxaca (pick-your-proof) — pineapple, jalapeño; mezcal at half or full proof
The Rabbit of Caerbannog (pick-your-proof) — carrot, black pepper, honey; gin at half or full proof
The Kilt Lifter (pick-your-proof) — hibiscus, ginger, árbol chilli; scotch at half or full proof
venues.longDescription:
The Haymaker has anchored Fayetteville Street, downtown Raleigh's main spine, since 2017; it closed for a short hiatus and reopened in early 2026 under new owner Glenn Shriver, a mixology veteran, and it presents itself as a craft cocktail bar with speakeasy leanings — a specialty list of rye, amaro and Chartreuse drinks, a run of classics from a Sazerac to a Vieux Carré, wines by the glass and a rotating draught selection. It is not an alcohol-free room and does not claim to be.

What makes it worth a non-drinker's evening is the section the bar calls Pick-Your-Proof. Six house cocktails are listed once and can be ordered three ways — zero proof, half proof or full proof — and the bar's own site describes it as the first ever menu of its kind. Raleigh Magazine, covering the launch in March 2026, reported the pricing as fourteen dollars at full proof, eleven at half and eight at zero, and quoted Shriver on the reasoning: people who are drinking less still want going out for drinks to be part of being social. The point is not the novelty. It is that the zero-proof version of a drink is a printed option with the same name and the same base as the full-strength one, so a non-drinker at a table orders exactly what everyone else does and specifies the proof, rather than asking a bartender to improvise.

The six are built to survive the removal of their spirit. Mama Said Knock You Out is beets, herbes de Provence and citrus under tequila or mezcal; Hello, Nurse! is orange blossom, blue matcha and citrus under gin; Dreams of Oaxaca is pineapple and jalapeño under mezcal; The Rabbit of Caerbannog is carrot, black pepper and honey under gin; Barbie's Second Marriage is strawberry, lavender, citrus and brut under vodka; The Kilt Lifter is hibiscus, ginger and árbol chilli under scotch. Vegetable juices, tea, chilli and floral cordials carry the flavour, which is exactly what a zero-proof build needs and what a spirit-and-mixer drink lacks once the spirit is gone. How the bar handles the sparkling wine in Barbie's Second Marriage at zero proof is worth asking about at the bar.

Hours run late for downtown: four until midnight on Tuesday and Wednesday, four until two in the morning on Thursday and Friday, five until two on Saturday, with a short Sunday afternoon session from three to eight and a Monday close at ten. The bar takes private events and the menu changes, so check that the Pick-Your-Proof heading is still on the list; it was read from the bar's own site in September 2026.
venues.pressQuote: letting imbibers sip the same flavors with a Goldilocks-style buzz factor: full-proof, half-proof or zero-proof in most every bev
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: Raleigh Magazine, "Sober-Curious? Half-Proof Cocktails Are Here", March 2026

venues.name: The Hills Market Downtown
venues.description: The Hills Market Downtown is an independent grocer on North Grant Avenue in the Discovery District, and it is the closest thing Columbus has to a bricks-and-mortar zero-proof bottle shop. Rather than scattering non-alcoholic products through the beer and wine aisles, the store runs a dedicated end cap of nearly forty different alcohol-free wines, beers and spirits — non-alcoholic gin, whiskey, tequila and rum, ready-to-drink cocktails and gin and tonics, dry sodas and alcohol-free sparkling wine. That breadth matters in a city with no dedicated non-alcoholic retailer: it is the only place in central Columbus where a shopper can compare a range of zero-proof spirits side by side before buying. The market also serves prepared food and coffee and has run occasional happy hours.
venues.longDescription:
The Hills Market Downtown occupies a corner site at 95 North Grant Avenue in the Discovery District, the quarter east of the central business district around Columbus State and the Columbus Museum of Art. It is the downtown sibling of the original Hills Market on Olentangy River Road, and functions as a full independent grocer — produce, butcher counter, prepared food, coffee — rather than a specialist drinks retailer. It is included here for one specific reason: the zero-proof section.

Columbus does not have a dedicated non-alcoholic bottle shop with a shopfront. Better Beverage, the city's specialist, trades through pop-ups and delivery; the wine merchants that carry alcohol-free bottles carry a handful each. The Hills Market Downtown instead runs a standing end cap of close to forty different non-alcoholic wines, beers and spirits gathered in one place — alcohol-free gin, whiskey, tequila and rum, ready-to-drink cocktails and pre-mixed gin and tonics, dry sodas, fruit juices and alcohol-free sparkling wine. The practical value of that is comparison. Buying a zero-proof spirit unseen is an expensive gamble, because the category varies enormously in quality and the bottles cost near enough what the alcoholic equivalents do; a shelf where four or five can be read side by side, with a member of staff nearby, is a materially different proposition from ordering online. The store has also run occasional happy hours around the section. Opening is daily from 8am on weekdays and Saturdays and 9am on Sundays, closing at 7pm throughout — early by bar standards, so it is a stop to make before an evening rather than during one. The store is the downtown counterpart to the original Hills Market on Olentangy River Road, and functions day to day as a neighbourhood grocer for the Discovery District — produce, butcher counter, prepared food and coffee alongside the packaged aisles — which means the zero-proof section can be folded into an ordinary shop rather than requiring a separate trip. Non-alcoholic beer is also stocked more broadly here than in most central Columbus retail, and the range extends to dry sodas and fruit juices for anyone building a drinks table rather than buying a single bottle.
venues.pressQuote: Shop their inventory for a variety of zero-proof beverages (and stay tuned to their website and Facebook page for info on the happy hours).

venues.name: The Horn Midtown
venues.description: The Horn Midtown is the second site of the family-run Somali cafe that began in 2015 on Murfreesboro Pike, and like the original it serves no alcohol. It sits on Scarritt Place, on the Scarritt Bennett campus between Vanderbilt and Belmont, which makes it a student and staff room as much as a neighbourhood one. The counter runs on chai rather than espresso: Somali chai, brown sugar chai and a dirty chai pulled with a shot, plus a short coffee list including a cinnamon white mocha, with hand-folded sambusas alongside. Nashville Public Radio featured The Horn in 2025 in a report on Muslim-owned coffeehouses that reopen at night through Ramadan and want that alcohol-free evening culture to last all year. Outside Ramadan the hours are daytime.
signatureDrinks: Dirty Chai - chai pulled with espresso
venues.longDescription:
This is the Midtown branch of The Horn, the Somali cafe a Nashville family opened in 2015 after their father arrived from Somalia and sold sambusas out of his car. The address puts it on Scarritt Place, inside the Scarritt Bennett Center campus between Vanderbilt and Belmont - a quiet pocket of Gothic stone buildings a short walk from both universities and from the Music Row end of Midtown. That location shapes the room: students, faculty and conference guests during the week, and a neighbourhood counter at weekends. No alcohol is served.

The menu is the same as the Murfreesboro Pike original and it is chai-led, which is worth stating plainly because most Nashville coffee bars are not. Somali chai is the house pour; there is a brown sugar version, and a dirty chai that adds a shot of espresso to it. All are made iced as well as hot, and priced around $4. The coffee menu behind it is deliberately short - americano, latte, white mocha, cinnamon white mocha - and the food is the sambusas the family has been folding by hand since the beginning, plus sweets.

WPLN, Nashville's public radio station, reported in March 2025 on The Horn alongside Deir Cafe and Haraz Coffee House, in a story about Muslim-owned coffeehouses in the city that shut for the daylight fast during Ramadan and reopen at night to long lines - and about the owners' ambition to make that alcohol-free evening culture a year-round fixture rather than a seasonal one. Outside Ramadan, though, this branch keeps daytime hours: 7am to 5:30pm on weekdays, with a split on Friday around midday prayer, 9am to 5:30pm on Saturday and 9am to 3pm on Sunday. Come for chai and a sambusa in the afternoon rather than for a night out, and note that the campus setting means parking is on the street rather than in a lot.
venues.pressQuote: Muslim-owned shops that want to make this sober nightlife culture a year-round thing.

venues.name: The Horn
venues.description: The Horn is a family-run Somali cafe on Murfreesboro Pike in South Nashville, serving no alcohol at any hour. It began in 2015, after the founder's father arrived from Somalia and sold sambusas out of his car, and it has grown into a two-site business hand-folding sambusas and brewing Somali chai daily. The drinks list is built around chai rather than espresso: Somali chai, brown sugar chai and a dirty chai pulled with espresso, alongside a short coffee menu that includes a cinnamon white mocha. Food runs to sambusas and East African plates. Nashville Public Radio featured The Horn in 2025 as part of a group of Muslim-owned coffeehouses that reopen at night through Ramadan and want that alcohol-free late culture to run year-round. This is a daytime cafe outside Ramadan hours.
signatureDrinks: Dirty Chai - chai pulled with espresso
venues.longDescription:
The Horn started the way a lot of good food businesses start, which is without a building. The founder's father left Somalia, came to Nashville and sold sambusas out of his car; the family opened the first proper shop in 2015 and has been hand-folding sambusas and brewing Somali chai ever since. The business now runs two Nashville sites - this one, the headquarters on Murfreesboro Pike in South Nashville, and a second in Midtown - and describes what it does in five words on its own site: crispy sambusas, spiced chai, and hospitality. No alcohol is served at either.

The reason to know about it beyond lunch is what happens in Ramadan. WPLN, Nashville's public radio station, reported in March 2025 on a cluster of Muslim-owned Nashville coffeehouses that close for the daylight fast and reopen at night to long queues of customers breaking it - and on the fact that the owners want that alcohol-free evening culture to be a year-round habit rather than a seasonal one. The Horn is one of the shops in that story. Outside Ramadan the normal hours are daytime: 7am to 5:30pm Monday to Thursday, a split day on Friday around midday prayer, and shorter weekend hours.

The drinks are the thing to order. Chai is the anchor, and the shop makes several versions - Somali chai, a brown sugar chai, and a dirty chai pulled with a shot of espresso - all available iced, all around $4. The coffee side is short and unfussy: americano, latte, white mocha, cinnamon white mocha. Alongside them are the sambusas the business was built on, filled and folded by hand. Two practical notes. First, the Friday split means the shop shuts around midday for prayer, so check before making a lunchtime trip. Second, this is a cafe and a counter rather than a bar with a zero-proof list: what you are buying is a good cup of chai and a room where nobody is drinking, which for many people is the whole point.
venues.pressQuote: Muslim-owned shops that want to make this sober nightlife culture a year-round thing.

venues.name: The Intan
venues.description: The Intan is an award-winning Peranakan home museum in Joo Chiat whose by-appointment, 60-minute Tea Experience is a fully non-alcoholic affair: owner-curator Alvin Yapp guides guests through his collection before serving The Intan Signature Tea alongside a spread of traditional nyonya kueh. There is no bar and no alcohol here at all, only heritage tea service in a lived-in Straits Chinese home. Sittings run Friday to Sunday and cost S$64.20 for adults (S$32.10 for children under 12). Founder Alvin Yapp has spent more than four decades collecting Peranakan antiques and hosts the tea sessions in his own home himself, which is why the visit reads as a social gathering rather than a museum tour.
signatureDrinks: The Intan Signature Tea — the house heritage tea served with an assortment of traditional nyonya kueh
venues.longDescription:
The Intan, whose name means rose-cut diamond, is Singapore's first home museum, opened by antique collector and curator Alvin Yapp in the Joo Chiat/Katong heritage district. The two-storey shophouse-turned-museum is packed with Peranakan artefacts, kebaya, beadwork and embroidery made by Nyonya women, and antique furniture, all shown in the setting of a genuine lived-in Straits Chinese home rather than a conventional gallery.

The venue is best known to the wider public through its 60-minute Tea Experience, a by-appointment session in which Yapp personally walks guests through the collection and explains Peranakan wedding customs and daily rituals before the visit closes with The Intan Signature Tea and an assortment of traditional nyonya kueh. The entire experience is alcohol-free, making it a rare heritage-led tea option for non-drinkers in a city dominated by cocktail culture. Sittings are held Friday at 4:00pm, Saturday at 10:00am and 4:00pm, and Sunday at 4:00pm, with private visits arranged by email.

The Intan was voted Best Overall Experience at the Museum Roundtable Awards and has been featured internationally on CNN Travel, the Discovery Channel and National Geographic. It is a small, intimate space, so tea sittings are capped and booking ahead is essential.

What separates The Intan from a conventional museum is that it is genuinely a home, and Yapp is genuinely the host. In his own words on the museum's site, a deep love for all things Peranakan led him to devote his home to the culture's treasures, and to share a glimpse of the yesteryear with visitors as guests in that home. The collection grew from small objects that caught his eye into something larger and more diverse, and it is arranged as a lived-in Straits Chinese house rather than as a gallery with labels.

For a non-drinker deciding how to spend an evening or a weekend afternoon, this is a genuinely different proposition from a bar or a cafe. It is a booked, hosted, sit-down experience with a beginning and an end, built around tea and kueh and conversation — the social architecture of going out, without alcohol anywhere near it. Visitors consistently describe the sessions as closer to a gathering than a presentation, and the host's enthusiasm for the material as the thing that carries the hour.

The practical constraints follow from that. Sittings are small and capped, held on Friday, Saturday and Sunday afternoons with an additional Saturday morning slot, and private visits are arranged by email. Book well ahead. The Intan has been voted Best Overall Experience at the Museum Roundtable Awards and covered by CNN Travel, the Discovery Channel and National Geographic, so weekend slots go early.

venues.name: The Interval at Long Now
venues.description: The Interval is the cafe, bar and salon of The Long Now Foundation at Fort Mason Center, a space built around long-term thinking, with a floor-to-ceiling library, an eight-foot mechanical orrery and artwork by Brian Eno. Its bar program was created by Jennifer Colliau, founder of Small Hand Foods, and later shaped by Todd Myles Carnam; both have since moved on, and a "Time Capsule" section of the current menu preserves their signature drinks. The no- and low-ABV list is treated as core rather than supplementary, built on house-made seasonal shrubs, non-alcoholic bitters and dealcoholized aperitifs. Current spirit-free pours include Asimov's Crater, the Bitter Orange Old Fashioned and The Maiden, alongside non-alcoholic beer and sparkling cider.

venues.longDescription:
The Interval is the cafe, bar and salon of The Long Now Foundation at Fort Mason Center, and it is unlike any other bar in San Francisco because it was built as an argument. The Long Now Foundation exists to encourage thinking on a ten-thousand-year timescale, and the room is furnished accordingly: a floor-to-ceiling library intended to hold the books required to rebuild civilisation, an eight-foot mechanical orrery, prototype components of the Clock of the Long Now, and generative artwork by Brian Eno. It opens for coffee in the daytime and runs as a bar into the evening, which makes it usable across a whole day rather than only at night.

The drinks programme was created by Jennifer Colliau, founder of the syrup and cordial maker Small Hand Foods, and later shaped by Todd Myles Carnam. Both have since moved on from The Interval, and a section of the current menu titled "Time Capsule" keeps their most requested drinks in circulation — the menu notes that a few "became iconic, so inseparable" from the bar that removing them would be unthinkable. What Colliau established and the bar has kept is a treatment of no- and low-ABV drinks as core rather than supplementary, made from the same house-made ingredients as everything else. The house shrub changes with the equinoxes; in autumn and winter the bar makes a cranberry syrup infused with its own blend of clove, anise, allspice and cinnamon, served tall with seltzer. Current alcohol-free pours include Asimov's Crater ($16), built on Wilfred's aperitif with pineapple, almond and lime; the Bitter Orange Old Fashioned ($12), made with Chinotto, dashes of non-alcoholic bitters and a lemon peel over ice, which the menu describes as "a paragon of our ongoing commitment to providing alternatives for sober social drinking"; and The Maiden ($12), pomegranate, almond, ginger, lemon and seltzer, written up as the bar's answer to the question "Do you have a Shirley Temple?" Untitled Art non-alcoholic beer and Dupont sparkling apple cider round out the list. Punch profiled the venue as "A San Francisco Bar Meant to Last 10,000 Years."
venues.pressQuote: A San Francisco Bar Meant to Last 10,000 Years

venues.name: The Kanna Collective Lounge & Coffee Bar
venues.description: Appears to be closed for now, as of late October 2026: the lounge's own page has been taken off the company's website, its Locations menu no longer lists it, and its dated events stop in mid-October. No reason or reopening date has been published, so call (980) 237-6651 before you go. The Kanna Collective Lounge & Coffee Bar is a woman-owned, 21+ Amsterdam-style cannabis lounge on W Worthington Ave in South End, from a dispensary business founded in 2019, with the group's separate South End THCA dispensary in the unit next door. READ THIS BEFORE VISITING: the venue advertises "specialty zero-proof mocktails", but zero-proof here means zero ALCOHOL, not non-psychoactive. Every named beverage it sells is cannabis-infused — its Kanna Mocktail Seltzers carry 10mg Delta-9 hemp-derived THC and 10mg CBD per can and warn that use "may result in a failed drug test", and Queen City Nerve describes its signature drink plainly as "the cannabis-infused Pretty High for a Dry Guy mocktail". No fully non-psychoactive named drink is published anywhere on its menu. The consumption lounge is members-only ($5 day passes sold in person); the cafe and patio are open to the public. Despite the name, no kanna plant or kratom is sold.

venues.longDescription:
As of late October 2026 the lounge appears to be closed for now. The Kanna Collective has taken the lounge's page off its website, its Locations menu no longer lists it, and its dated event listings stop in mid-October 2026, though a KANNAWEEN party is still listed for 31 October. No closing notice, reason or reopening date has been published; the company's website points to its Instagram, @thekannacollective, for updates. Call (980) 237-6651 before making a trip. The lounge is at 207 W Worthington Ave; the Kanna dispensary next door at 209 is a separate shop.

The Kanna Collective began in 2019 as a woman-owned operation hand-packing made-to-order pre-rolls through the pandemic, and has grown into two Charlotte retail locations, a mobile van, a national online store, and this lounge and coffee bar on W Worthington Avenue in South End — a block and a half from the East/West Boulevard stop on the Lynx Blue Line. It describes itself as Charlotte's Amsterdam-style lounge: a relaxed, 21-and-over space to sip, socialise and consume safely, with four 65-inch televisions, card games, a rotating pastry case, and a window onto its own grow room. The consumption lounge itself is members-only, with $5 day passes and tiered memberships sold in person, while the cafe and patio stay open to the public. One practical note from the venue: do not park in the gravel lot beside the building.

This listing needs a plain warning rather than a description, because the language used here is genuinely misleading if you are not reading closely. The lounge advertises infused coffee and specialty zero-proof mocktails, and in this context zero-proof means only that there is no alcohol in the glass. It does not mean the drink is inert. Every named beverage the business sells is cannabis-infused: the Kanna Mocktail Seltzers — sold under names like Pretty High for a Dry Guy and Resting Peach Face — carry 10mg of Delta-9 hemp-derived THC and 10mg of CBD per can, and the label itself warns that consuming them may result in a failed drug test. Queen City Nerve describes the house drink simply as the cannabis-infused Pretty High for a Dry Guy mocktail. There is no published, named drink here confirmed to be free of both alcohol and cannabis. If you are avoiding alcohol only, and cannabis is something you actively want, this is a well-run and welcoming room. If you are in recovery, subject to drug testing, or simply want a coffee that does nothing, this is not the venue the words on its menu might suggest — ask precisely what is in anything before you order it. Despite the name, no kanna plant or kratom is sold.
venues.pressQuote: The shop offers beverages like the cannabis-infused Pretty High for a Dry Guy mocktail.

venues.name: The Karma Casa
venues.description: The Karma Casa is an alcohol-free kava bar on Youngfield Street in the Applewood area of Golden, open daily from 10am to 2am. It states its purpose directly: a safe, alcohol-free space for work, arts, games and community building — so the room is set up for people to occupy for hours rather than to pass through, and it works as a daytime workspace and a late-night alternative from the same fit-out. Happy hour runs twice daily, 2pm to 4pm and again 7pm to 9pm. The menu covers kava, kratom and herbal teas. IMPORTANT for readers in recovery: kratom acts on opioid receptors and carries real dependence and withdrawal risk, which kava does not — the two are poured side by side here, so order deliberately.
venues.longDescription:
The Karma Casa occupies 1821 Youngfield Street in the Applewood area of Golden, on the western edge of the Denver metro where the suburbs run up against the foothills, and it is open from 10am to 2am every single day. It states what it is for without hedging: a safe, alcohol-free space for work, arts, games and community building. That sentence describes a fairly specific kind of room — one that has to function as a laptop-friendly daytime space and as a genuine late-night social venue out of the same fit-out, and that is programmed around things to do rather than things to consume.

The west side of the metro has quietly become the centre of gravity for Colorado's kava scene. Within a few miles of here are Golden Kava Lounge on South Golden Road, KavaDen and Roots & Leaves' Peak Kava in Lakewood, and Roots & Leaves' Mile High Kava Bar up in Westminster — all alcohol-free, all trading late. The Karma Casa's particular contribution is the emphasis on arts and work: it is the one that reads most like a community centre that happens to serve kava, and its two daily happy hours, from 2pm to 4pm and again from 7pm to 9pm, are timed around the rhythms of people who are there for the afternoon rather than dropping in for one drink.

The drinks are kava, kratom and herbal teas. Kava, the venue's namesake, is the ground root of Piper methysticum, a South Pacific shrub; it is infused in water, contains no alcohol, tastes earthy and bitter, numbs the lips, and is mildly sedative rather than intoxicating in alcohol's sense. It has been drunk socially across Fiji, Vanuatu, Tonga and Samoa for roughly three thousand years, and it exhibits reverse tolerance — regular drinkers usually need less rather than more — so a first visit rewards taking it slowly across an hour or two.

The kratom on that list needs stating clearly rather than in passing, because the people most likely to use this directory are the people for whom the difference matters most. Kratom is served here alongside kava. It is the leaf of a Southeast Asian tree, Mitragyna speciosa, and its principal alkaloids act on the opioid receptors. Regular use produces tolerance and a real withdrawal syndrome; several US states prohibit it outright; and its concentrated 7-hydroxymitragynine derivatives are the subject of active federal scheduling action. Kava has no equivalent dependence profile. A great many people come to kava bars specifically because they are looking for the social ritual without a substance that can get a grip on them. In this room, that means reading the menu headers and asking what is in the cup.

venues.name: The Karma House
venues.description: The Karma House is an alcohol-free kava bar at 608 Garrison Street in Lakewood, just west of Denver — a registered 501(c)(3) nonprofit run by co-owners Nick Gnieski, Mollie Paige and Deonna Lupola, open 8am to 3am daily including holidays. Its drinks run from freshly brewed kava to a long retail shelf: Leilo kava at $8, Kin Euphorics at $6, Hiyo at $5, Sir Inkwell's yerba maté at $6, Odyssey mushroom elixirs at $5, Rowdy Mermaid kombucha at $4 and Karma Water at $4. ALCOHOL-FREE BUT NOT SUBSTANCE-FREE, and unusually explicit about it: alongside kava it sells kratom in several forms — Mitra 9 seltzers at $8 (20mg kratom extract per can), White Rabbit at $8, Kiody by vein colour at $40, Krabot capsules at $35 — plus CBD soda at $5 (20mg), CBD chocolate at $10, and chewables combining kratom extract, kava and blue lotus. It publishes a dated Legal & Safety Policy: kratom is 21-and-over with photo ID required and kept behind the counter, and it warns against combining botanical drinks with alcohol. No per-gram dosage table is published. The freshly brewed kava itself carries no published price.
venues.address: 608 Garrison St Suite E, Lakewood, CO 80215
signatureDrinks: Freshly brewed kava tea (price not published)
venues.longDescription:
The Karma House sits on Garrison Street in Lakewood, immediately west of Denver, and it is structured unusually for a bar: it is a registered 501(c)(3) nonprofit, with Nick Gnieski as founder and board president, Mollie Paige as treasurer and bar manager, and Deonna Lupola — a registered nurse — as secretary and director of events. It keeps genuinely long hours, 8am to 3am every day including holidays, which makes it one of the few places in the metro open when nothing else alcohol-free is. Freshly brewed kava is what it specialises in, and around that sits a long shelf of ready-to-drink alternatives: Leilo kava at $8, Kin Euphorics at $6, Hiyo at $5, Sir Inkwell's yerba maté at $6, Odyssey mushroom elixirs at $5, Rowdy Mermaid kombucha at $4 and its own Karma Water at $4.

This is an alcohol-free venue that is emphatically not substance-free, and it deserves credit for being clearer about that than most. Alongside kava it sells kratom in several forms — Mitra 9 seltzers at $8, each can carrying 20mg of kratom extract; White Rabbit at $8; Kiody sold by vein colour at $40; Krabot capsules at $35 — plus CBD soda at $5 with 20mg a can, CBD chocolate at $10, and chewables combining kratom extract, kava and blue lotus. What separates it from most venues in this category is that it publishes a dated Legal and Safety Policy rather than leaving customers to guess: kratom may only be sold to people 21 or over, valid government photo ID is required for every kratom purchase, the products are stored behind the counter, customers are told to avoid combining botanical beverages with alcohol or other intoxicating substances, and anyone pregnant, nursing or on medication is told to consult a healthcare professional. That is a real policy, and more than almost any comparable bar offers. What it stops short of is a quantified dosage table — there is no per-drink or per-day limit in grams, only the per-can potency printed on individual retail products. Colorado regulates rather than bans kratom: a 2022 act imposed labelling and a 21-plus rule from July 2024, and a further bill signed in May 2025 capped 7-hydroxymitragynine content and banned candy-like and vapeable kratom products.
venues.pressQuote: If you over-consume it, which takes a bit to do, then eventually your liver can be damaged, which honestly can be said for almost anything.

venues.name: The Kava Bar — Fort Worth
venues.description: The Fort Worth outpost of The Kava Bar, which trades as The Sagebrush Social, is fully alcohol-free — its own description is that alcohol is replaced by a menu of kava, coffee and botanical drinks. The house pours classic and blended kava, botanical elixirs, teas, and a coffee and matcha programme built on Lemma Coffee Roasters. Its location-exclusive drink is The Cowtown Calm, kava blended with local wildflower honey, coconut milk and a pinch of smoked salt. Kava is a psychoactive botanical, so the room is alcohol-free but not substance-free.
signatureDrinks: The Cowtown Calm (kava, wildflower honey, coconut milk, smoked salt)
venues.longDescription:
The Kava Bar runs three rooms across the metroplex, each given its own name and one exclusive drink, and the Fort Worth location trades as The Sagebrush Social on Locke Avenue near Camp Bowie. Like its siblings in Oak Cliff and North Dallas, it is fully alcohol-free, and it says so directly: alcohol is replaced by a menu of kava, coffee and specialty botanical drinks.

The list divides into kava served classic or blended, botanical elixirs, a tea selection, and a genuine coffee programme — beans from Lemma Coffee Roasters, espresso drinks, matcha. That last part matters more than it sounds, because it means a visit does not have to involve kava at all; this works as a straightforward coffee house for anyone who wants the room without the root. The Fort Worth exclusive is The Cowtown Calm, which blends kava with local wildflower honey, coconut milk and a pinch of smoked salt.

Two honest notes. First, kava is psychoactive — legal, non-alcoholic, and widely used by people who have stopped drinking, but mood-altering, which anyone whose sobriety excludes all intoxicants should weigh. Second, this venue's published hours conflict between its own site and third-party listings, so we have not recorded any; call ahead rather than trust a listing.

venues.name: The Kava Bar – North Dallas
venues.description: The Kava Bar – North Dallas is a fully alcohol-free social lounge in the Pepper Square center on Preston Road, next to Trader Joe's, pouring kava, kratom, botanical elixirs, coffee, matcha, and tea — no alcohol served. It opened at this address in 2023 as one of North Dallas's first kava bars and bills itself as "a social bar experience: minus the alcohol, plus the good vibes," open daily 8am to midnight. Flavored kava builds like the Churro Cha Cha (chocolate or vanilla, cinnamon agave, coconut cream) are made the traditional way — the root squeezed and served from a coconut shell — and the space runs open-mic and sober-social events for a late-night crowd that wants somewhere to hang without booze.
signatureDrinks: Churro Cha Cha (kava with chocolate or vanilla, cinnamon agave, and coconut cream)
venues.longDescription:
The Kava Bar – North Dallas occupies Suite 212 of the Pepper Square retail center at Preston Road and Belt Line, next door to Trader Joe's. The location opened in the spring of 2023 as one of the area's first dedicated kava bars, launched by David Darrigan, an emergency-room physician who wanted to offer a healthier alternative to alcohol; it now trades under The Kava Bar banner, which runs sister locations in Oak Cliff, Denton, and Fort Worth.

The entire menu is alcohol-free. The core pour is kava — an ancient South Pacific root prepared the traditional way, squeezed and served from a coconut shell — alongside kratom and botanical "elixir" teas, plus Lemma-roasted coffee, matcha, and herbal teas. Signature flavored-kava builds include the Churro Cha Cha (chocolate or vanilla with cinnamon agave and coconut cream), Peanut Butter Cup, Mango Bango, and Choco-Cherry, and staff will guide first-timers through the options.

The lounge is styled as a cozy, community-driven alternative to nightlife — neon lighting, local art, couches, games, and books — and is family- and pet-friendly. It stays open daily from 8am to midnight and hosts a regular calendar of open-mic nights, sober social mixers, and wellness pop-ups, giving North Dallas a late-night gathering spot with no alcohol on the premises.
venues.pressQuote: I see the negative effects of alcohol and addiction all the time, and I have a passion for trying to provide healthy alternatives.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: David Darrigan, who opened the Pepper Square kava bar

venues.name: The Kava Bar — Oak Cliff
venues.description: The Kava Bar — Oak Cliff is a fully alcohol-free botanical lounge at 337 W Jefferson Boulevard, just off the Bishop Arts District, opened on 15 February 2025 as part of a small Texas group with sibling locations in Denton, North Dallas and Fort Worth. Instead of liquor it pours kava — the earthy South Pacific root prized for its calming effect — alongside house kratom brews, botanical elixirs, matcha, herbal teas and single-origin coffee. ALCOHOL-FREE BUT NOT SUBSTANCE-FREE: kava and kratom are both psychoactive, and kratom in particular is one we would normally warn hard about. This venue is the exception worth naming. It publishes a printed dosage table — roughly 1.3g of kratom per 8oz drink, a recommended maximum of 4g per drink and 16g in 24 hours — plus explicit warnings that it is not for pregnant or nursing women, not to be followed by driving, and that "anything that makes you feel good can become habit-forming... Consider avoiding any potentially habit-forming substances if you have a history of substance abuse." Kratom is 18-and-over. Guests under 18 are welcome with a guardian until 8pm, with a kid-friendly menu that is 100% kava-free. Named drinks include The Classic Shell ($8), The Bula ($9) and The Teal Latte ($7).

The Bula ($9, kava, coconut milk, vanilla)
The Teal Latte ($7, ceremonial matcha, oat milk, raw honey)
House kratom brews, red/green/white vein ($9, 18+ only)
venues.longDescription:
The Kava Bar opened its Oak Cliff room on 15 February 2025 at 337 West Jefferson Boulevard, a short walk from Bishop Arts, and it is part of a small Texas group with siblings in Denton, North Dallas and Fort Worth. Its own line for the place is "no alcohol, no judgment, just a genuinely good night", and the room is built for that — booth seating, a softly lit bar, a covered patio and a private event space for up to forty. The menu is organised by category rather than by cocktail: kava, kratom, elixirs, coffee, tea and a short list of bites (house bliss balls at $4, a single-origin dark chocolate square at $3, a rotating pastry from a local bakery at $5). The Classic Shell is $8, ceremonial-grade kava served traditionally in a coconut bilo. The Bula at $9 softens it with coconut milk and vanilla. The Teal Latte at $7 is ceremonial matcha with oat milk and raw honey, and there is a genuine coffee programme underneath all of it.

This is an alcohol-free venue that is not substance-free, and normally that is the point at which we warn readers that a bar is selling psychoactive botanicals without telling anyone what is in them. The Kava Bar is the opposite, and it deserves credit for it. Its menu carries a printed dosage table — about 1.3g of kratom in an 8oz drink, a recommended maximum of 4g per drink and 16g in twenty-four hours — alongside explicit warnings not to use it while pregnant or nursing, not to drive or operate machinery afterwards, and, most unusually, a plain statement that anything which makes you feel good can become habit-forming, including caffeine, alcohol, sugar and kratom, and that anyone with a history of substance abuse should consider avoiding habit-forming substances altogether. That is more candour than almost any venue in this category offers, and it is exactly what someone in recovery needs in order to make their own decision. Kratom is 18-and-over here; under-18s are welcome with a guardian until 8pm and there is a kava-free menu for them. Two caveats: the elixirs include blue lotus and reishi and lion's mane mushrooms, which carry no equivalent warnings, and the venue's own website contains unfinished template content — placeholder phone numbers, a location page giving a different street address, and an origin story we could not corroborate anywhere. Trust the menu; verify the practical details by phone.
venues.pressQuote: A new bar serving alcohol alternatives like kava opens in Dallas' Oak Cliff.

venues.name: The Kava Konnection
venues.description: The Kava Konnection is the only fully alcohol-free bar in Greenville, on Wade Hampton Boulevard north-east of downtown, serving traditionally prepared kava and botanical teas with no alcohol on the premises. Its hours are the reason it leads this guide rather than a footnote to it: noon to midnight Sunday through Thursday and noon to 2am on Friday and Saturday, seven days a week. That is a genuine bar schedule — later than every licensed room in this city guide except one — and it means a non-drinker in Greenville has somewhere to be at one in the morning rather than somewhere to leave early from.
venues.address: 1540 Wade Hampton Blvd Ste H, Greenville, SC 29609
venues.longDescription:
Every city in this directory is judged partly on whether a person who does not drink can be out at midnight. Greenville can, and this is where. The Kava Konnection sits in a strip on Wade Hampton Boulevard, a few miles north-east of the downtown bar blocks, and it runs noon to midnight from Sunday to Thursday and noon to 2am on Friday and Saturday — every day of the week, with no closed day and no early shutter.

Set that against the rest of this guide. Bar Margaret closes Sunday and Monday. Juniper does not open until 5pm and is dark Monday and Tuesday. Oak & Honey and South Main Social both close two days a week. The Kava Konnection is open all of those nights, and open later than any of them.

What it serves is kava, prepared traditionally, alongside botanical teas and house preparations. There is no alcohol in the building — not a licensed room with a good mocktail list, but a bar whose entire premise is the alternative. For a group deciding where to go, that changes who gets to make the suggestion, which is the social mechanic this whole category turns on.

The honest caution, as everywhere in this guide that lists a kava room: kava is mildly psychoactive, and this is a night out without alcohol rather than a substance-free evening. Readers in recovery weigh that differently and it is theirs to weigh, so it is stated plainly rather than buried.

One practical note on geography. Wade Hampton is not walkable from South Main, so this is a drive or a short rideshare from the downtown cluster rather than a stop on the way. Treat it as the destination — which, given it is the only room in the metro with no alcohol in it at all, it deserves to be.

One further note on what Greenville is missing, because a guide should say so. Herban Spirits has been announced as the city's first non-alcoholic taproom and bottle shop and is not open yet; it will be a significant addition when it is, and it is deliberately excluded here rather than listed early. Urban Wren, which still appears in current mocktail round-ups of the city, is permanently closed. Until Herban opens, The Kava Konnection is the entire alcohol-free category in this metro, which is why its seven-day, late-night schedule carries so much weight in this guide.

venues.name: The Kingstide
venues.description: A coastal, ingredient-driven seafood and steak restaurant on Daniel Island's Wando River waterfront from the Indigo Road Hospitality Group, open since 2021 with a fine-dining downstairs room and a relaxed upstairs rooftop bar. The cocktail menu includes a dedicated "Spirit Free" section of zero-proof drinks, alongside canned non-alcoholic beers from Athletic Brewing.
venues.address: 32 River Landing Drive, Daniel Island, SC 29492
signatureDrinks: Passion Fruit Punch (passion fruit, toasted coconut cream)
Hibiscus Citrus (hibiscus, agave, lime, ginger beer)

venues.longDescription:
The Kingstide is Daniel Island's riverfront dining destination, a two-story coastal restaurant from the Charleston-based Indigo Road Hospitality Group overlooking the Wando River marshlands. The downstairs is a dinner-only fine-dining room serving raw and wood-fired seafood and steaks, while the upstairs rooftop bar offers a more casual menu and weekend brunch.

The bar program carries a printed "Spirit Free" section of zero-proof cocktails, including a Passion Fruit Punch (passion fruit, toasted coconut cream) and a Hibiscus Citrus (hibiscus, agave, lime, ginger beer), each $10. Non-alcoholic beer drinkers can order Athletic Brewing's Upside Dawn golden ale or Run Wild IPA, both $6.
venues.pressQuote: reserve a seat downstairs in its dining room or grab a first come, first served spot upstairs, where patrons will find a large indoor-outdoor bar and patio

venues.name: The Laundry
venues.description: The Laundry is an all-day bistro, wine bar and wine shop on Coldharbour Lane in Brixton, run by chef-sommelier Melanie Brown. Alongside its wine-led list it keeps a small but genuine alcohol-free selection, with non-alcoholic mocktails including a Seedlip Spritz built on the zero-proof distilled spirit and a house Watermelonade. It gives south London a low-and-no option to sit with beyond the central cocktail rooms, whether at brunch, on the terrace, or over an evening plate.
venues.address: 374 Coldharbour Lane, London SW9 8PL, United Kingdom
signatureDrinks: Seedlip Spritz - non-alcoholic Seedlip distilled spirit, lengthened over ice
venues.longDescription:
The Laundry occupies Walton Lodge, an Edwardian building on Coldharbour Lane that operated as a traditional steam-press laundry until 2014 - the source of both the room's name and its exposed-brick, tiled-floor, vintage-furnished character. It is the first solo venture of chef-sommelier Melanie Brown, previously a chef at The Providores and the wine buyer behind The New Zealand Cellar at Pop Brixton, and it trades all day as a neighbourhood bistro, cafe, bar and wine shop.

Wine is the anchor: a curated, roughly 50-strong list of old- and new-world bottles, a weekday L'Apero, brunch bellinis and Bloody Marys, and cold-weather Sunday roasts served across two semi-private dining rooms and a covered, heated terrace that runs food and drinks until late.

The non-alcoholic side is modest but real. The bar lists mocktails including a Seedlip Spritz, built on the pioneering British zero-proof distilled spirit, and a house Watermelonade, so guests who aren't drinking have proper made-to-order options rather than just a soft drink. For a wine-forward Brixton bistro, that alcohol-free thread makes it a workable low-and-no destination in a part of south London otherwise thin on dedicated NA programs.

venues.description: The Libertine is a Lower Greenville neighbourhood pub whose printed Mocktails section has proven genuinely durable — all four drinks covered by press in January 2025 are still on the menu today, which is rare in a category built on seasonal promotions. The Aper-not Spritz uses Ritual's aperitif alternative with orange juice and grapefruit soda; alongside it sit a Lavender Bee's Knees, a Cucumber Mint Gimlet and a Shirley De-Luxe, all at one price. Athletic Brewing's Run Wild and Upside Dawn and Sam Adams Just the Haze cover non-alcoholic beer.

venues.longDescription:
The Libertine is the kind of bar Lower Greenville is short of these days — a proper neighbourhood pub with a long bar, a decent kitchen and no particular interest in being a destination. Its non-alcoholic list arrives under a printed Mocktails heading, and its most useful quality is that it has stayed put.

When CultureMap surveyed Dallas mocktail programmes in January 2025, it recorded four alcohol-free drinks here, led by the Aper-not Spritz built on Ritual's aperitif alternative with orange juice and sparkling grapefruit. Checking the current menu against that coverage, all four are still being poured: the spritz, a Lavender Bee's Knees, a Cucumber Mint Gimlet and a Shirley De-Luxe, all at a single price. In a category where January lists routinely vanish by spring — this directory found several Dallas venues whose widely-cited mocktails no longer exist — an eighteen-month-old press description that still matches the menu is the strongest evidence of a real programme that we can gather without visiting.

The beer list backs it up with Athletic Brewing's Run Wild IPA and Upside Dawn golden ale plus Sam Adams Just the Haze. With a kitchen running late and doors open to 2am on Friday and Saturday, it works as an ordinary night out rather than an early dinner, which is the harder thing to find without alcohol.

venues.name: The Lincoln
venues.description: The Lincoln is a corner pub on Cardigan Street in Carlton, a Critic's Pick in The Age Good Food Guide, and its drinks list prints a ZERO ALC. section beside the wine and cocktails rather than burying soft drinks at the back. The four house builds are made, not poured: elderflower soda with lime and mint; a fizzy spiced pineapple with chamomile, honey and lemon; a Wild Mother raspberry shrub cut with cider vinegar and soda; and yuzu and peach tea with soda and lemon, all at A$10. A Gruppetto L'aperitivo non-alcoholic Veneziano spritz covers the aperitivo hour. Six alcohol-free tinnies under 0.5% round it out - Heaps Normal XPA, Guinness 0.0, Carlton Zero, Hiatus, Drivers lager and Willie Smith's non-alcoholic apple cider.

venues.longDescription:
The Lincoln has stood on the corner of Cardigan and Faraday Streets in Carlton since the nineteenth century, and it is the kind of pub that keeps winning things quietly - Pub of the Year at the Time Out Melbourne Pub Awards, Hotel of the Year from Australian Bartender, a Critic's Pick in The Age Good Food Guide. Iain and Stella Ling took it over in late 2014 and left the bones alone: tiled floors, a fireplace, a dining room hung with prints, and a bar that treats a drinks list as something to write rather than stock.

That habit is why it belongs in this guide. The single-page drinks list carries a heading marked ZERO ALC., and the drinks under it are built from the same pantry as the cocktails above. Elderflower soda comes with lime and mint; the fizzy spiced pineapple is finished with chamomile, honey and lemon; the Wild Mother raspberry shrub is cut with cider vinegar and soda, which gives it the acid a good non-alcoholic drink needs; and there is a yuzu and peach tea lengthened with soda and lemon. All four are A$10, which is roughly half what a cocktail costs here. Above them sits a Gruppetto L'aperitivo non-alcoholic Veneziano spritz at A$15 and T.I.N.A 2.0, raspberry fruit and leaf with jasmine pearl green tea.

The packaged side is properly stocked rather than token: a NON-ALC TINNIES <0.5% ABV block listing Drivers non-alc lager, Carlton Zero, Hiatus premium pacific pale ale or lager, Heaps Normal XPA, Willie Smith's non-alcoholic apple cider and Guinness Draught 0.0, plus three non-alcoholic sodas - Mateo sparkling yerba mate, Notto Blotto hopped soda by Moo Brew, and Strangelove very mandarin. Practically, it is a pub rather than a bar: kitchen hours, a Sunday roast, and enough room that a group where half are drinking and half are not can sit comfortably. Cardigan Street is a five-minute walk from Melbourne University and the Lygon Street strip.
venues.pressQuote: The wine list is divided into useful headings that actually tell you something about the drops below them - that they're lean, deep or aromatic, for example.

venues.name: The Little Blackbird
venues.description: The Little Blackbird is an artisan wine bar at 3309 Connecticut Avenue NW in Cleveland Park, opened in September 2023 by veteran restaurateur Ashok Bajaj of Knightsbridge Restaurant Group. Designer Martin Vahtra gave the intimate, Paris-inspired room moody interiors brightened by floral wallpaper, blush-pink and pale-green seating, herringbone floors and a white marble bar under a blackbird light fixture. The wine list leans on family-owned, sustainable and organic producers, while executive chef Ryan Moore runs a Mediterranean small-plates menu anchored by a stone oven. For non-drinkers there is a dedicated Dry Spell programme: the bar makes its own zero-proof wines - a full-bodied red with juniper-berry and black-pepper notes and a stone-fruit white with almond syrup and apricot - plus a non-alcoholic gin fizz with egg white, lemon and a non-alcoholic gin syrup.
venues.longDescription:
The Little Blackbird opened in September 2023 at 3309 Connecticut Avenue NW in Cleveland Park, in the space that had previously held Ashok Bajaj's Bindaas and, before that, Bardeo. Bajaj is one of Washington's longest-established restaurateurs, and this is a small, deliberately charming room rather than a flagship: designer Martin Vahtra built moody interiors brightened by floral wallpaper, blush-pink and pale-green seating and herringbone floors, with a white marble bar topped by a blackbird light fixture. The boutique wine list favours family-owned, sustainable and organic producers from South America, France, Italy, the United States and the Mediterranean, and executive chef Ryan Moore, who also runs neighbouring Sababa, cooks Mediterranean small plates anchored by a stone oven. The bar is also known for its whimsical playful pairings, matching brand-name snacks and sweets with wines by the glass.

The non-alcoholic offer is unusual for a wine bar, because it is a made thing rather than a bought one. Under a dedicated Dry Spell heading the bar produces its own zero-proof wines: a full-bodied red carrying juicy juniper-berry and black-pepper notes, and a stone-fruit white built with almond syrup and apricot. That is a meaningfully different proposition from stocking a dealcoholised bottle - the flavours are constructed to sit alongside the food rather than to imitate a specific grape - and it is the reason Resy's January 2025 roundup singled the bar out for making its own zero-proof wines and cocktails for anyone who might be sober-curious. Alongside them the bar pours a popular non-alcoholic gin fizz built with egg white, lemon and a non-alcoholic gin syrup, which is the drink to order if you want texture rather than fruit.

Practical notes. The bar opens at 5pm Monday through Saturday, closing at 9.30pm on Monday, 10pm Tuesday through Thursday and 11pm on Friday and Saturday, and Sunday runs a brunch from 11am to 3pm before an evening service. It is small enough that a weekend walk-in is a gamble, and it sits directly on the Cleveland Park Metro stretch of Connecticut Avenue, which makes it one of the easier upper-Northwest options to reach without driving.
venues.pressQuote: Cleveland Park's most popular wine bar also makes their own zero-proof wines and cocktails for anyone who might be sober-curious

venues.name: The Local by Dunloe Brewing
venues.description: The Local, Dunloe Brewing's taproom in Davis, makes its own dry-hopped lemonades — Centennial hops combined with a hibiscus-lime concentrate — which is a genuinely house-made alcohol-free drink rather than a bought-in can. It also pours the Barbless Hook, a 2.5% ABV light lager, which is low-alcohol rather than alcohol-free and worth knowing about clearly: it is not a zero-proof option and should not be treated as one by anyone avoiding alcohol entirely. Davis sits about fifteen miles west of Sacramento. The taproom opens at 2pm daily and runs to 10pm Tuesday through Saturday, serving a college town with a heavy drinking culture.
signatureDrinks: Dry-hopped lemonade - Centennial hops, hibiscus-lime concentrate
venues.longDescription:
The Local is Dunloe Brewing's taproom on 3rd Street in Davis, the university town about fifteen miles west of Sacramento and part of the wider metro. Its alcohol-free contribution is a house-made dry-hopped lemonade: Centennial hops combined with a hibiscus-lime concentrate.

That is a more considered drink than it sounds. Centennial is a classic American hop, floral and citrusy with a firm bitterness, and dry-hopping a lemonade with it produces something with genuine aromatic lift and a dry finish rather than a sweet one. The hibiscus adds tartness and colour. Crucially the brewery makes it rather than buying it, which means the alcohol-free option is a product of the same craft as everything else on the bar.

One point requires care. The taproom also pours the Barbless Hook, a 2.5% ABV light lager, and low-alcohol is not alcohol-free. For someone cutting down it may be exactly right; for someone who does not drink at all — in recovery, pregnant, on medication, or abstaining for faith — it is not an option, and the distinction gets blurred constantly in coverage of this category. This listing separates them deliberately: the dry-hopped lemonade and the seltzers are the zero-proof choices here.

Davis is a college town with a large student population and correspondingly heavy drinking culture, so a taproom making a proper non-alcoholic drink in-house has real local value. Hours run 2pm to 10pm Tuesday through Saturday and to 8pm on Sunday and Monday.

Davis also justifies its own entry rather than being folded into Sacramento generally. It is fifteen miles west, a separate town with its own downtown, and the University of California campus gives it a population of tens of thousands of students — a group both heavily targeted by drinking culture and increasingly likely to opt out of it, since American under-25s now drink markedly less than the generation before them. A taproom in that town making its own alcohol-free drink is meeting a demand that is growing rather than performing a courtesy.
venues.pressQuote: The Local by Dunloe Brewing: dry-hopped lemonades (Centennial hops with hibiscus-lime concentrate), Barbless Hook (2.5% ABV light lager), seltzer waters and sodas.

venues.name: The Local Taphouse
venues.description: A long-running St Kilda East craft-beer institution that carries its obsession with good beer over to the zero-alcohol side. Alongside its rotating tap wall, The Local keeps genuine craft NA beers on hand, including Australia's Heaps Normal and Melbourne brewer Hop Nation, plus the occasional European alcohol-free import. It's a rare spot where a non-drinker can order a considered craft brew rather than a token soft drink.
venues.address: 184 Carlisle Street, St Kilda East VIC 3183
venues.longDescription:
Heavily influenced by the European taverns of the 1930s, The Local Taphouse has been a beer-lover's landmark on Carlisle Street in St Kilda East for years, a two-time winner of Time Out's People's Choice Best Pub in Melbourne. The two-storey room pairs a ground-floor bar of dark wooden floors, leather couches and low green lamps with an upstairs dining area and a rooftop courtyard, giving it the feel of an old English reading room reimagined as a taphouse. It's overseen by manager Justin Joiner, with a food menu from head chef Richard Smith.

The draw has always been craft beer, and that ethos extends to drinkers skipping alcohol. As Broadsheet's guide to Melbourne's best non-alcoholic bars puts it, this is a boozer that is "all about craft beer - even the non-alc variety," so you can still cool off with a few suds, including pours from Heaps Normal and Melbourne's own Hop Nation, plus the occasional European alcohol-free import.

The NA offering is a genuine craft selection rather than a printed zero-proof cocktail menu - it sits within the same beer-forward program the venue is known for, making it a comfortable landing spot for a non-drinker who still wants something interesting in the glass, especially on the weekly curry nights. The kitchen and generous opening hours (from noon daily) round out a neighbourhood tavern that treats alcohol-free beer with the same seriousness as the rest of its list.
venues.pressQuote: This boozer is all about craft beer - even the non-alc variety. Which means you can still cool off with a few suds on the weekly curry night, with the likes of Heaps Normal, Hop Nation and the occasional European import.

The bar backs these up with a "For All Ages" lineup of house-made sodas and lemonades, including a house lemongrass ginger-beer and hibiscus lemonade.

The Longboard is a tropics-leaning seafood and raw-bar restaurant at 2213-B Middle Street on Sullivan's Island, the second location of a concept that originated on St. John in the U.S. Virgin Islands. Beyond the oysters, poke and ceviche, the cocktail list reserves a printed "Non-Alcoholic Bevs" section for zero-proof drinks built with the same care as the bar's rum-forward cocktails.

Three named $10 mocktails anchor the section: "I'm Driving" (cucumber-basil lemonade and strawberry soda), "Anonymous Unanimous" (hibiscus tea, lime and ginger beer), and "You Have No Proof" (blueberry, lime, mint and soda). A separate "For All Ages" list adds house-made options such as lemongrass ginger-beer, seasonal soda, lemonade, hibiscus lemonade and coconut water.

venues.name: The Lounge at Liberty Exhibition Hall
venues.description: The Lounge occupies the ground floor of Liberty Exhibition Hall, a 1970s-styled cocktail lounge and live-jazz room in Northside. Alongside a full cocktail, wine and beer list, the bar keeps a dedicated "teatails" section of tea-based zero-proof drinks: one built on pu'erh tea with cherry bark, honey and citric acid, and another blending lemongrass-and-chamomile tea with lavender syrup, lemon oleo and soda. These are house-made from steeped teas and syrups rather than canned NA brands, so the buzz-free options drink like intentional craft cocktails. The room evokes a basement-era hangout with vintage seating vignettes and subdued lighting, and it is best known for Monday-night jazz jam sessions that draw the region's top players with no cover charge or drink minimum.

venues.longDescription:
The Lounge sits on the first floor of Liberty Exhibition Hall, a Northside arts space at 3938 Spring Grove Ave that also connects to the Clifton Performance Theatre organization. Conceived as a 1970s-styled cocktail lounge and music venue, it soft-opened in December 2021 and quickly built a reputation as a throwback hangout — the venue's own site notes it was voted Best Throwback Bar by CityBeat. As CityBeat music writer Anne Arenstein described it, "The Lounge crew created comfortable vignettes with varied seating options, tables and subdued lighting that evokes a past era of basement venues," and house-band member Josh Strange put it more plainly: "It feels like you're in someone's living room."

The bar pours a full slate of cocktails, wine and beer, but it also carries a genuine dedicated zero-proof section. CityBeat's January 2022 roundup of Greater Cincinnati mocktails singled out The Lounge for its house-made "teatails": one built on pu'erh tea with cherry bark, honey and citric acid, and a second layering lemongrass-and-chamomile tea with lavender syrup, lemon oleo and soda. Because these are steeped and built in-house rather than poured from canned NA brands, the buzz-free options read as deliberate craft drinks rather than an afterthought — a good fit for a designated driver or anyone spending a long night listening to music without alcohol.

The Lounge is first and foremost a live-music room, and its signature draw is the Monday-night jazz jam: the house band plus an open session that pulls in many of the area's top players and rising young talent, running roughly 8–11 p.m. with no cover charge or drink minimum. "We have a great wine and cocktail menu," bar manager Emma Roberts told CityBeat, noting patrons settle in with drinks once the session starts. Hours outside of Monday nights vary by ticketed show, so it is worth checking their Instagram (@thelounge_northside) or Facebook before heading over. Reach the venue at (513) 813-7469.

venues.name: The Loyalist
venues.description: The Loyalist is a chef-driven restaurant and bar at 177 N Ada Street in Chicago's West Loop, occupying the garden level beneath Smyth, its three-Michelin-starred sibling, both run by husband-and-wife chefs John Shields and Karen Urie Shields. It opened in summer 2016 and is best known for a dry-aged burger that has appeared on national best-of lists, now served as The French Smash with herb butter, cornichon, mornay and frites. Its non-alcoholic list is a full section headed "Spirit Free Cocktails", six drinks at a flat $12, each built on a real zero-proof base rather than juice: Bright & Refreshing (AMASS Riverine, chamomile, lemon, lovage, NA prosecco), Herbal & Citrus (Seedlip Garden, basil, yuzu, ginger), Juicy (Seedlip Grove, pineapple, smoked morita pepper, lime), All Barq's No Bite (St. Agrestis Amaro Falso, vanilla bean foam), Italian Spritz (Lyre's orange, NA prosecco, bubbles) and Velvety & Smooth (Lyre's Amaretti, almond orgeat, lemon, lime, egg white — note the egg white is not vegan). Dinner runs Monday to Saturday, 5–10pm, with reservations through Tock.

venues.longDescription:
The Loyalist sits at garden level beneath Smyth at 177 N Ada Street in the West Loop, the more casual half of a two-restaurant building run by husband-and-wife chefs John Shields and Karen Urie Shields — upstairs holds three Michelin stars, downstairs does not try to. It opened in summer 2016 and built its reputation on a dry-aged burger that has turned up on national best-of lists for the better part of a decade, now on the menu as The French Smash with herb butter, cornichon, mornay and frites at $28. Around it the kitchen cooks with the same seriousness as its sibling but far less ceremony: half chicken with sourdough, smoked dates and foie gras mousse at $39, and trout à la grenobloise with Meyer lemon, brown butter and gooseberry at $34. The New York Times has placed it among the twenty-five best restaurants in Chicago, and Chicago Magazine included it in its fifty best.

The zero-proof list is one of the strongest in the city, and it is worth explaining how it is organised because it is easy to misread. The section is headed "Spirit Free Cocktails" and holds six drinks, all $12 — and the names are the drinks, not flavour categories. Bright & Refreshing is built on AMASS Riverine with chamomile, lemon, lovage and non-alcoholic prosecco. Herbal & Citrus uses Seedlip Garden with basil, yuzu and ginger; Juicy uses Seedlip Grove with pineapple, smoked morita pepper and lime, which gives it heat and smoke rather than sweetness. All Barq's, No Bite is the cleverest of them, working St. Agrestis Amaro Falso under a vanilla bean foam into something closer to a root beer float than a cocktail. Italian Spritz is Lyre's orange with non-alcoholic prosecco and bubbles, and Velvety & Smooth is Lyre's Amaretti with almond orgeat, lemon, lime and egg white — worth knowing if you avoid egg, since it is the one drink here that is not vegan. Every one is priced the same as the others and made behind the same bar as the full-proof list. Dinner is Monday to Saturday, 5–10pm, booked through Tock.

venues.name: The Lucky Saint
venues.description: The Lucky Saint is the alcohol-free beer brand's first permanent pub, on Devonshire Street in Marylebone — a restored Victorian pub built around the alcohol-free pint rather than treating it as an afterthought. It serves a full bar of spirits, wine and cask beer as well, so this is a mixed room rather than a dry one, but the depth of the no-and-low list is the reason to come: around fifteen per cent of drinks sold here are alcohol-free. It pours the brand's own unfiltered 0.5% lager and a newer IPA alongside a rotating range of low- and no-alcohol beers, ciders and cans, Italian aperitivo bitters such as Crodino, and a short list of alcohol-free cocktails, with a full food menu. It is one of the clearest signs of London's shift: a busy, all-day pub where ordering a zero-proof pint is the unremarkable choice.

venues.longDescription:
The Lucky Saint is the first pub in the country owned and run by an alcohol-free beer brand. It opened in March 2023 under founder Luke Boase, who started Lucky Saint in 2018 and developed its 0.5% unfiltered lager with a family brewery in Bavaria. The site — on the corner of Devonshire Street and Hallam Street on the Marylebone–Fitzrovia border, a short walk from the BBC's Broadcasting House — is the former Masons Arms, a pub that had stood empty for around three years before Lucky Saint restored it over roughly five months with Orla Read Interior Design and Hipgrave Construction. The upper floors double as the company's headquarters, and in a nod to the building's long history as a local for broadcasters, there is a bookable podcast studio on site.

Crucially, it reads as a proper London boozer rather than a themed "sober bar". The four-storey red-brick Regency terrace curves around the corner, and the ground-floor room keeps its traditional character: dark wood panelling, a grand central bar, etched mirrors and a mix of benches and stools. The food is deliberately pub-classic and kept short — small plates such as Pecorino and truffle mixed nuts, pork crackling, St John sourdough, a chicken, leek and truffle terrine, pork pies with Montgomery cheddar and pickled eggs — built to sit alongside a pint rather than compete with it.

The real point of difference is what's poured. Lucky Saint's own 0.5% unfiltered pale lager leads the taps, backed by a genuinely deep low-and-no range: Guinness 0.0 and Asahi Super Dry 0.0 in the fridge, alcohol-free beers from brewers such as Big Drop, Lervig, Erdinger and Tiny Rebel, plus non-alcoholic wines and zero-proof aperitifs and spirits including Botivo, Pentire and Everleaf. The cocktail list mixes low-ABV serves with fully alcohol-free builds — the Pentire Radler stretches 100ml of Lucky Saint with 35ml of Pentire Adrift (a Cornish-foraged non-alcoholic spirit), fresh lemon juice and agave over ice, while the Michelada builds Lucky Saint with chilli, lime and hot sauce. The brand reports that around 15% of the drinks sold here are alcohol-free, against a UK pub average nearer 1%, so ordering a zero-proof pint never feels like the odd choice.
venues.pressQuote: Alcohol-free beer brand Lucky Saint's first official pub, in the middle of Marylebone.

venues.name: The Mockery
venues.description: CHECK BEFORE YOU TRAVEL — we cannot confirm this venue is still trading. The Mockery is a fully alcohol-free bar and non-alcoholic bottle shop that operated inside the Nashville Farmers' Market in Germantown, pairing a working bar with retail so guests could drink on site or take bottles home. Its own channel describes the range as non-alcoholic wines, beer, sparkling-wine cocktails and classic cocktails, made by hand to order, on Farmers' Market trading days rather than bar hours — Friday to Sunday, closing in the afternoon. Three things now point the other way. Its website domain no longer resolves at all. It does not appear anywhere in the Nashville Farmers' Market's own current merchant directory, which does list the market house's other restaurants and shops by name. And we can find no dated activity — no post, review or listing — newer than early 2025. Its Instagram account does still exist. No closure has been announced anywhere, so we have kept the listing rather than remove a business that may simply be dormant or have moved, but message the bar before making a trip.
venues.address: 900 Rosa L. Parks Blvd, Nashville, TN 37208
venues.longDescription:
The Mockery was a genuinely unusual thing: a fully alcohol-free bar and bottle shop operating from inside a public food market. It sat in the Nashville Farmers' Market in Germantown, and the pairing of a working bar with retail shelves is a format that suits non-drinkers particularly well — you can have something made for you by hand, decide you like it, and take a bottle of the same thing home, which is how most people actually build a repertoire of drinks they enjoy. Its own description of the range is non-alcoholic wines, beer, sparkling-wine cocktails and classic cocktails, made to order. Because it traded on market days rather than bar hours, it kept a schedule almost no bar keeps: Friday through Sunday, opening at ten in the morning and closing in the early afternoon. For anyone whose sobriety is easier in daylight, or who has children, or who simply does not want to be in a bar at eleven at night, a Saturday-morning alcohol-free bar is close to ideal.

We have to be straight about its current status, because the evidence has moved. The domain it used to publish no longer resolves — not a lapsed page, but no DNS record at all. More significantly, it does not appear anywhere in the Nashville Farmers' Market's own merchant directory, which does name the market house's other restaurants and shops; we checked that directory directly rather than relying on a search result, and confirmed its other tenants are listed there while The Mockery is not. A market controls who trades in it, so absence from its own tenant list carries real weight. And we can find no dated activity of any kind — no post, review or listing — newer than early 2025. Set against that, the Instagram account still exists and still carries its opening hours, and no closure has ever been announced by the owners or reported anywhere. That is not enough for us to delete a business, because a venue that has gone dormant, moved, or simply stopped posting looks identical from the outside. So the listing stays, honestly labelled. Message them before you go.

venues.name: The Monarch Club
venues.description: The Monarch Club prints a named "Zero Proof Libations" section on its cocktail menu, not an afterthought tacked to the wine list. The Golden Court (guava purée, pineapple juice, lavender syrup, honey, ginger ale, Tajín) and Pea Tea SD (butterfly pea tea, lemon, honey) are built with the same layered technique as the bar's signature cocktails, plus Root Chakra (lemon, ginger, lavender, tonic) and Athletic Brewing NA IPA on draft. It's a real menu section, priced and composed to match the rest of the program, on the 13th-floor rooftop of the restored Metropolitan Building.
signatureDrinks: Golden Court (guava purée, pineapple juice, lavender syrup, honey, ginger ale, Tajín)
Pea Tea SD (butterfly pea tea, lemon juice, honey)
Root Chakra (lemon, ginger, lavender, tonic water)
