venues.longDescription:
The Semi-Tropic has been an Echo Park fixture since 2015, and its name comes from local history rather than marketing: the Semi-Tropic Spiritualists Association was an early-1900s utopian collective that kept a rustic base in the wooded hills at the northern edge of the neighbourhood. The Infatuation described the room as a mellow wine and bar with a large, couch-filled space that feels more like a co-op community room than an actual bar - which is the useful detail for anyone choosing where to spend an evening without drinking. Couches, chaises, an outdoor area with fire pits, a good sound system and a room that does not push you to keep ordering are more decisive than the drinks list on that question.

The drinks list is good too. The bar is licensed, with beer, wine, spirits and cocktails, and the menu carries a Non-Alcoholic section with three shaken drinks made to order rather than poured from bottles. Plantasia, $13, is built on Amass Riverine - a Los Angeles-made non-alcoholic botanical distillate - with cucumber, cilantro, lime and yuzu soda, and the cilantro is what stops it reading as a cucumber cooler. Pineapples in Stereo, also $13, uses Martini and Rossi's Floreale, the alcohol-free version of their aperitivo, with pineapple, sugar snap pea and lime; the snap pea is the unusual ingredient and it works as a green, vegetal counterweight to the fruit. Garden Lemonade at $8 is the simplest and the one to order over ice on a hot afternoon: fresh lemonade with lavender, chamomile, soda and butterfly pea extract, which turns it violet. Beyond the cocktails the non-alcoholic list carries Stumptown nitro cold brew at $8, Tehuacan sparkling mineral water, Mexican Coke and a house wellness shot of ginger, honey, lemon, turmeric and black pepper at $7.

Practical notes. The bar opens at 2pm on weekdays and 11am at weekends, closes at midnight most nights and 2am on Friday and Saturday, and serves a full food menu from a kitchen that runs later than most neighbourhood bars. Happy hour is until 6pm daily but covers beer, wine, well drinks and three classic cocktails rather than the non-alcoholic list. It is 21-plus at all times, which is worth knowing if you are planning around a group.
venues.pressQuote: This mellow wine and bar in Echo Park has a large, couch-filled space

venues.name: The Ship's Hold
venues.description: The Ship's Hold is a hidden craft cocktail bar tucked behind The Galley in downtown St. Petersburg, holding one of Central Florida's largest rum and amaro collections — and a dedicated "Spirit Free" menu to match. The bartenders' house-made shrubs, syrups, and infusions turn up in zero-proof builds like Apple-A-Day and Show Pony (both on Seedlip Spice 94) and the Flightless Bird (Lyre's Rosso, lemon-vanilla oleo, pineapple), with Athletic and Guinness 0.0 on hand for NA beer drinkers. Unusually, the bar distils its own alcohol-free spirits in house rather than only buying them in, which is what I Love The Burg singled it out for. It is a late room, open to 3am seven nights, reached through The Galley.

venues.longDescription:
The Ship's Hold is reached through The Galley on 4th Street North in downtown St. Petersburg — a bar behind a bar, which is a format that usually promises more than it delivers. This one earns it. The room holds one of Central Florida's largest rum and amaro collections, keeps hours that run to 3am seven nights a week, and is regarded locally as one of the best craft cocktail bars in the Tampa Bay area rather than a novelty attached to a better-known restaurant.

What makes it exceptional for a non-drinker is not the size of the zero-proof list but how it is made. The bar distils its own non-alcoholic spirits in house — a step almost no cocktail bar takes, because buying a bottle of Seedlip is far easier — and works them alongside house-made shrubs, syrups and infusions produced for the full-strength menu. The dedicated Spirit Free section runs builds like the Apple-A-Day (Seedlip Spice 94, acidulated apple butter, lemon, sparkling apple cider), the Show Pony (Seedlip Spice 94 against a blueberry-horseradish shrub, lemon and orange flower water) and the Flightless Bird (Lyre's Rosso, lemon-vanilla oleo, pineapple, bubbles). Athletic Brewing and Guinness 0.0 cover anyone who would rather have a beer.

I Love The Burg put the distinction plainly in January 2024: not only do they make some of the best drinks in St. Pete, they even make their own NA spirits. That is the tell. A bar that produces its own alcohol-free base has decided the category is worth engineering for, rather than stocking to avoid turning customers away.

Practical notes: it is a late bar, opening at 6pm most nights and 7pm on Thursday, and the hidden-entrance format means arriving early is wise at weekends — the room is small and fills from the restaurant it sits behind. Ask at The Galley if the door is not obvious; it is deliberately unsignposted from the street. It is a full cocktail bar with a serious spirits collection — the Spirit Free menu is a genuine parallel programme, not the character of the room.
venues.pressQuote: Not only do they make some of the best drinks in St. Pete, they even make their own NA spirits.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Bob Carskadon, I Love The Burg

venues.name: The Slow House (Maison Garden)
venues.description: The Slow House is the daytime cafe inside Maison Garden, a florist-cafe-and-event-space hybrid at Dempsey Hill, and its core drinks list is almost entirely non-alcoholic: a botanical matcha flight of three cups for S$12.90 alongside garden sodas, floral-infused brews, smoothies and specialty coffee. Set within a glasshouse flower market, it only leans into champagne and cocktails after hours, so the whole daytime offering is zero-proof by design. Opened in mid-2025 as an extension of homegrown floral studio The Florte, it has quickly become one of Dempsey Hill's most talked-about new destinations.
venues.hours: Mon closed; Tue 9:30am-6:30pm; Wed closed; Thu-Sun 9:30am-6:30pm
signatureDrinks: Botanical Matcha Flight - three cups of botanical matcha for S$12.90
venues.longDescription:
Maison Garden opened in mid-2025 as one of Singapore's first floral lifestyle sanctuaries, tucked into the perennially busy Dempsey Hill enclave as an extension of homegrown floral studio The Florte, itself inspired by the flower markets of Covent Garden in London. The space brings together three distinct experiences under one roof: The Slow House, an all-day cafe; The Conservatory, a climate-controlled glass-house flower market where visitors hand-pick from more than twenty seasonal blooms displayed market-style; and The Canvas, a private event room for intimate dinners, brand activations and workshops.

The Slow House is the drinking-and-brunch heart of the venue, and by day its beverage program is built for zero-proof sipping. The anchor is a botanical matcha flight - three cups for S$12.90 - served alongside garden sodas, floral-infused brews, house smoothies, specialty coffee and teas. Because the room only turns to champagne and cocktails in the evening, the daytime menu that most guests come for is effectively alcohol-free, poured in a light-filled setting surrounded by fresh flowers with both indoor and alfresco seating.

The atmosphere leans toward relaxed luxury - warm lighting, soft natural textures and abundant greenery - and the venue is pet-friendly with free parking across the Dempsey estate. A signature quirk is the flower bar buffet, where for S$25++ guests can fill a vase with as many fresh stems as they like, blurring the line between cafe visit and florist run.

The Slow House does not hold a Michelin or Asia's 50 Best accolade; its draw is the novel florist-market-meets-cafe format and a genuinely botanical, largely non-alcoholic daytime menu rather than a formal named zero-proof cocktail list.

venues.name: The Snug
venues.description: The Snug is the Irish Hospitality Group's Midtown bar and carries the same alcohol-free stock as its siblings — the St. Agrestis Phony Negroni and Guinness 0 — with the significant advantage of being open until 2am every night of the week. That combination is rarer than it sounds: most bars still serving at one in the morning have nothing for a non-drinker beyond soda, and most places with decent zero-proof options have closed hours earlier. Here you get both. The Snug is on 15th Street in Midtown, within walking distance of Kupros and Ro Sham Beaux, and it has no closed days at all.
venues.longDescription:
The Snug is on 15th Street in Midtown Sacramento, part of the Irish Hospitality Group along with Ro Sham Beaux and The Butterscotch Den, and it stocks the same alcohol-free products as both: the St. Agrestis Phony Negroni and Guinness 0.

What distinguishes this location is the clock. It opens at 4pm and serves until 2am, seven nights a week, with no closed days. That is worth dwelling on, because late-night is the hardest gap in sober hospitality anywhere. The pattern in almost every city is the same: the thoughtful zero-proof drinks are served in restaurants and cocktail bars that close by ten or eleven, and the venues still open at one in the morning have nothing but soda and cranberry juice. A non-drinker who wants to stay out late is usually choosing between going home early and holding a glass of Coke for three hours.

A bottled Phony Negroni solves that particular problem well. At 1am a busy bartender has neither the time nor the inclination to build a considered mocktail, and asking for one produces either a long wait or something disappointing. A bottle from the fridge takes ten seconds, arrives correct every time, and tastes properly bitter. It is not craft, but at that hour craft is not what is available to anyone.

Being in Midtown puts it within walking distance of Kupros and Ro Sham Beaux, so it works as a late stop after somewhere with a fuller menu earlier in the evening.

The Irish pub format helps in a way that is easy to overlook. Pubs are built around sitting and talking rather than around a drinks list — there are booths, the music is usually low enough for conversation, and nobody is working through a cocktail menu. That structure suits a non-drinker better than a cocktail bar does, because the evening was never organised around what is in the glass. Add a bottle of something properly bitter from the fridge and the gap between your night and everyone else's effectively closes.
venues.pressQuote: Irish Hospitality Group (The Snug, Ro Sham Beaux, The Butterscotch Den): Phony Negroni by St. Agrestis, Guinness 0, and various NA cocktails.

venues.name: The Sylvester
venues.description: The Sylvester is a Midtown Miami cocktail bar opened in April 2019 by Florida natives Ben Potts and Brian Nasajon, the duo behind Beaker & Gray. Set in the former Bardot space at 3456 N Miami Ave, it pairs vintage Miami décor — colorful retro wallpaper and repurposed antique furniture — with a craft cocktail program built on locally sourced ingredients, reopening in 2021 with a refreshed Florida-themed menu. Its alcohol-free offerings live in a dedicated menu section headed "No Hangovers," featuring built-to-order zero-proof cocktails alongside Heineken 0.0. Current named NA drinks include the Dama Verde (Aplos Ease, Ritual Zero Proof Gin, honeydew, matcha, clarified), the Venetian Pathway (Pathfinder Hemp & Root, raspberry cordial, soda), and the Sex Panther V.26 (Seedlip Grove, vanilla, passion fruit, mint). DJs play Thursday through Saturday.
venues.hours: Mon closed; Tue-Thu 5pm-2am; Fri-Sat 5pm-3am; Sun closed

venues.longDescription:
The Sylvester opened in April 2019 in Midtown Miami from Ben Potts and Brian Nasajon, the Florida natives behind Beaker & Gray, taking over the former Bardot space on North Miami Avenue. The room leans into vintage Miami — retro wallpaper, repurposed antique furniture — and reopened in 2021 with a refreshed Florida-themed menu built on locally sourced ingredients. DJs play Thursday through Saturday, which places it firmly in nightlife rather than in restaurant dining.

Its alcohol-free drinks sit in a named menu section headed No Hangovers, and the naming is doing something. A section called Mocktails signals a compromise; No Hangovers reframes the choice as an advantage, which is a small piece of copywriting that changes how it feels to order from it in a bar at midnight.

The builds are made to order and use real products rather than juice. The Dama Verde combines Aplos Ease and Ritual Zero Proof Gin with honeydew and matcha, clarified. The Venetian Pathway is Pathfinder Hemp & Root with raspberry cordial and soda. The Sex Panther V.26 works Seedlip Grove with vanilla, passion fruit and mint. Heineken 0.0 covers anyone who would rather have a beer.

Three named zero-proof cocktails using three different alcohol-free spirits is a deliberate range rather than a default bottle — Aplos, Ritual and Pathfinder each behave differently, and stocking all three means the bar has tasted the category rather than ordered from it.

It is a full cocktail bar with DJs and a late crowd. The No Hangovers section is a genuine part of the menu rather than the character of the venue, which for a Midtown night out is exactly the point. Midtown is walkable to Wynwood and the Design District, which makes this an easy first or last stop on an evening rather than a destination in itself.
venues.pressQuote: The Sylvester gets it: Sometimes you just want a good drink without the aftermath. Their "No Hangovers" section makes it clear that mocktails are welcome here.

venues.name: The Tatarian
venues.description: The Tatarian is a contemporary neighbourhood cocktail bar on Tennyson Street in Berkeley, opened in 2018 and named for the Tatarian maples that shade the sidewalks outside. Its drinks are themed around trees of the world, and the theme extends into the non-alcoholic list: the house zero-proof cocktail, Luna, is named in honour of the activist Julia Butterfly Hill, who occupied a thousand-year-old California redwood to stop it being logged. Unusually for a Denver bar, the back bar carries non-alcoholic spirits as stocked bottles rather than as a single house pour — CleanCo Tequila Blanco, Lyre's London Spirit and Seedlip Garden 108 are all listed by the glass — alongside Partake's non-alcoholic IPA. 303 Magazine picked the bar out in its 2025 sober-summer guide.
signatureDrinks: Luna (non-alcoholic: skullcap tea, lemon, basil, green pepper, blueberry, balsamic vinegar, egg white — $14)
CleanCo Tequila Blanco, non-alcoholic, by the glass ($12)
Seedlip Garden 108, non-alcoholic, by the glass ($12)
venues.longDescription:
The Tatarian opened at 4024 Tennyson Street in 2018 as, in 303 Magazine's phrase at the time, Berkeley's newest bar, and took its name and its whole design language from the Tatarian maples planted along the street outside. The tree theme runs through the cocktail list, where drinks are named for trees and, in some cases, for the people who defended them. That is how the bar's flagship non-alcoholic drink got its name: Luna is named after the thousand-year-old California redwood that the activist Julia Butterfly Hill occupied for more than two years to prevent it being logged.

Luna is listed on the menu under a plain "NON-ALCOHOLIC" heading at $14 — the same price band as the bar's full-proof cocktails — and it is a properly constructed drink rather than a sweetened juice: skullcap tea, lemon, basil, green pepper, blueberry, balsamic vinegar and egg white, which gives it acidity, a savoury edge and texture. The more distinctive part of the offer is the back bar. Rather than keeping one non-alcoholic spirit for emergencies, The Tatarian stocks several and sells them by the glass, so a guest can order a non-alcoholic pour the way anyone else orders a spirit: CleanCo Tequila Blanco at $12, Lyre's London Spirit at $11 and Seedlip Garden 108 at $12 are all on the list, which also allows the bartenders to build alcohol-free variations of the standing cocktails on request. That is what 303 Magazine's Dorothy Lopez described in the magazine's August 2025 sober-summer guide, recommending "a refreshing variation of the Oyamel with NA tequila or the Luna, a light, citrusy and summer forward mocktail option", and calling the bar "a neighborhood haunt that is sure to become your next favorite go-to". Non-alcoholic beer is covered by Partake IPA at $8, and there is Mineragua sparkling water and bottled Coca-Cola for anyone who wants neither. The bar opens at 4pm on weekdays and 2pm at weekends.
venues.pressQuote: Enjoy a refreshing variation of the Oyamel with NA tequila or the Luna, a light, citrusy and summer forward mocktail option.

venues.name: The Tavern
venues.description: The Tavern is a downtown Tulsa restaurant in the Brady Arts District that has curated a mocktail menu of its own and stocks zero-proof beer alongside it — a combination that puts it ahead of most restaurants in the metro, since carrying both means a non-drinker gets to choose rather than take what is offered. Local news coverage of Tulsa's growing sober-friendly scene has used it as the example of what that shift looks like in practice. Open from 11am seven days a week, to 11pm most nights and 1am on Friday and Saturday.
venues.longDescription:
The Tavern occupies a corner of North Main Street in the Brady Arts District, Tulsa's downtown arts quarter, and it does the two things a restaurant needs to do to be genuinely useful to a non-drinker: it has written a mocktail menu of its own, and it keeps zero-proof beer in the fridge.

Those are different needs and it is unusual for a restaurant to meet both. A mocktail menu serves the person who wants an occasion drink, something constructed and interesting, and it is what makes a birthday dinner feel like a birthday dinner. Alcohol-free beer serves the person who just wants what everyone else is having without any fuss, and it is what makes a Tuesday feel normal. Restaurants that carry only one of the two are answering half the question.

The Tavern has been picked out in local news coverage of Tulsa's growing sober-friendly scene as an example of the shift, alongside Nothing's Left's non-alcoholic brewing — the argument being that it is becoming easier to go out and feel included as more businesses add mocktail menus and zero-proof beer and wine.

This entry records no signature drinks. The mocktail menu is not published in a form that could be read for this guide, and this directory does not print a drink name it has not seen, so what is recorded is the standing structure rather than the current list. Ask for the mocktail menu by name; it exists.

The hours are broad and consistent: 11am to 11pm Sunday through Thursday, 11am to 1am on Friday and Saturday, seven days a week with no closed day. It is a two-minute walk from Saturn Room and Shuffles, which makes the Brady district the most practical base for an evening out in Tulsa without drinking.

venues.name: The Times Bar & Coffee Shop
venues.description: The Times Bar & Coffee Shop occupies part of the S&W Building at 56 Patton Avenue downtown, a 1929 Art Deco landmark built as the S&W Cafeteria and one of the finest buildings in the city — the interior still keeps Prohibition-era details including dumbwaiters and hidden tunnels. It is really two businesses running from one address, and that is the reason it belongs in this guide: a coffee shop through the day and a cocktail bar at night, in the same room, with the same staff, so a non-drinker arriving at 11am and one arriving at 9pm order from the same counter. The spirit-free list is seasonal, unusual and savoury-leaning rather than sugary, rotating with the same kitchen-driven creativity as the cocktails. A standout has been the Kimchi Refresher — kimchi, mandarin, almond orgeat and lime — the kind of drink that makes ordering the non-alcoholic option feel like the interesting choice.
venues.hours: Mon closed; Tue 5pm-11pm; Wed-Thu 10am-11pm; Fri-Sat 10am-1am; Sun 10am-11pm
signatureDrinks: Kimchi Refresher (kimchi, mandarin, almond orgeat, lime)
venues.longDescription:
The Times Bar & Coffee Shop occupies part of the S&W Building at 56 Patton Avenue in downtown Asheville, a 1929 Art Deco landmark built as the S&W Cafeteria and one of the finest buildings in the city — the interior keeps prohibition-era details including dumbwaiters and hidden tunnels. The venue is two businesses running from one address, which is the reason it belongs in this guide: a coffee shop through the day and a cocktail bar at night, in the same room, with the same staff. That format matters more than it sounds. A non-drinker who arrives at 11am and one who arrives at 9pm are in the same place ordering from the same counter, rather than choosing between a café that closes at four and a bar that only pours alcohol.

The coffee side runs Wednesday through Sunday from 10am to 4pm, and the bar runs later — to 11pm most nights and 1am on Friday and Saturday, closed Mondays. It becomes 21 and over after 4pm, takes no reservations at all with seating strictly first come first served, and does not permit commercial photography or photoshoots of any kind, which is a rare and rather welcome policy in a building this photogenic. Two honest caveats about the drinks. The venue publishes its menus as images rather than text, so nothing can be read online in advance, and the list changes with the season — the current one is themed around the 1990s. And a Kimchi Refresher and a Buckthorn Shrub that have been attributed to this bar could not be found on any menu we could access, so treat them as unconfirmed rather than as things to order by name. What is dependable is the format: espresso and cocktails from one bar, all day, in one of the best rooms downtown.

venues.name: The Underground Speakeasy & Distillery at The Mob Museum
venues.description: The Underground is a Prohibition-era speakeasy and working distillery tucked into the basement of The Mob Museum (the National Museum of Organized Crime and Law Enforcement) in Downtown Las Vegas, complete with a secret side door whose daily password is posted to Instagram. Alongside its award-winning house moonshine and period craft cocktails, the bar keeps a standing zero-proof lineup so non-drinkers aren't left out: the official menu lists the Raspberry Lavender Fizz, The Test Pilot, Pineapple Smash and Sober Spritz (each $10), plus Heineken 0.0 non-alcoholic lager and a California non-alcoholic sparkling wine. Visit Las Vegas named The Test Pilot among its must-try Las Vegas mocktails, noting that while "the story here is all about spirits in secret, the cocktail menu acknowledges the sober, too." The venue also offers shareable bites and a full coffee/espresso menu, making it a comfortable stop for alcohol-free guests. It's open daily during museum hours and is a notable Downtown tourist landmark.

venues.longDescription:
The Underground opened in April 2018 in the basement of The Mob Museum — formally the National Museum of Organized Crime and Law Enforcement — at 300 Stewart Avenue in downtown Las Vegas, and it is simultaneously an immersive Prohibition history exhibition, a working distillery and a speakeasy bar. Getting in is part of the exhibit: you look for the barrel, find the staircase behind it, and reach a door with a sliding peephole that requires a password, which the museum posts daily to its Instagram account. With the password, the bar can be entered free of the museum admission. Inside, surrounded by genuine 1920s artefacts, the bar pours period-accurate craft cocktails and the distillery's own award-winning moonshine, made on site.

What makes it unusually good ground for a non-drinker is that a room built entirely around the mythology of illegal alcohol has nonetheless committed to a real zero-proof list rather than a token gesture. Four named drinks sit on the official menu at $10 each: the Raspberry Lavender Fizz, The Test Pilot, the Pineapple Smash and the Sober Spritz. Beyond those, the bar stocks Heineken 0.0 non-alcoholic lager and a California non-alcoholic sparkling wine, and it runs a full coffee and espresso menu alongside shareable bites, which quietly makes it one of the easier places downtown to sit for an hour without ordering alcohol at any point. Visit Las Vegas named The Test Pilot among its seven must-try mocktails in the city, observing that while the story here is all about spirits in secret, the cocktail menu acknowledges the sober too. Since the museum is one of downtown's principal attractions, the practical upshot is that a visitor in recovery can do the single most-recommended Prohibition experience in Las Vegas without being handed a drink they do not want. It is open daily during museum hours.
venues.pressQuote: Sure, the story here is all about spirits in secret, but the cocktail menu acknowledges the sober, too.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Visit Las Vegas, "Seven Must-Try Mocktails in Las Vegas"

venues.name: The Urban Oyster
venues.description: The Urban Oyster is chef Jasmine Norton's oyster bar at 914 W 36th Street on the Avenue in Hampden. Norton was introduced to oysters by her father at seven and taught to shuck shortly after; she sold dressed and grilled oysters at Baltimore-area farmers' markets from around 2017 before opening a bricks-and-mortar location and moving to Hampden in summer 2022. The Baltimore Sun described it as the only Black, woman-owned oyster bar in the country, though the restaurant's own site words the claim two different ways on two different pages — once as the first in Maryland, once as the first in the United States. The kitchen runs deviled eggs topped with a fried oyster fritter, charred prawns in Calabrian chilli-lemon butter, and chargrilled oysters in four styles. Its "Zero Proof Cocktails" section lists four drinks — UO Lemonade, Kiwi-Me, Spa Day and Pink Ginger — though ingredients and prices are not published for them, so ask at the bar. The list rotates.
venues.longDescription:
The Urban Oyster is chef Jasmine Norton's oyster bar at 914 W 36th Street on the Avenue in Hampden. Norton grew up in Baltimore and traces the whole business to being seven years old, when her father introduced her to oysters and taught her to shuck them shortly after. She built the business the hard way, selling dressed and grilled oysters at Baltimore-area farmers' markets from around 2017 before opening a bricks-and-mortar location and moving to the Hampden site in summer 2022. The Baltimore Sun reported that her fans had travelled from as far as Kentucky, describing the venue as the only Black, woman-owned oyster bar in the country — a claim worth stating carefully, since the restaurant's own website words it two different ways on two different pages, once as the first in Maryland and once as the first in the United States. The menu runs deviled eggs topped with a fried oyster fritter, charred prawns in Calabrian chilli-lemon butter, and chargrilled oysters in four styles including a Cheese Louise and a bacon-barbecue-cheddar.

The drinks list carries a section headed "Zero Proof Cocktails" holding four named drinks: UO Lemonade, Kiwi-Me, Spa Day and Pink Ginger. Two honest caveats about that list. The restaurant publishes the ingredients for its alcoholic cocktails but not for its zero-proof ones, and no prices are shown for either, so what is actually in a Spa Day or a Kiwi-Me has to be asked at the bar — an odd asymmetry, and the one thing a non-drinker most needs from a menu. And the list rotates: a Tamarind Tradewinds that appeared on earlier menus is no longer served. What is dependable is the format — four built drinks with their own heading rather than an on-request afterthought, in a room where the food is the reason to come. Service runs Wednesday to Saturday from 4pm and Sundays from 1pm, with reservations through Resy.
venues.pressQuote: Norton's many fans have come from as far as Kentucky to try oysters at the only Black, woman-owned oyster bar in the country.

venues.name: The Usual
venues.description: The Usual is Fort Worth's benchmark craft cocktail bar on Magnolia Avenue, and its menu carries a printed section headed "Practical Choices (NA)" — four zero-proof drinks built with the same technique as the spirituous list rather than tacked on as an afterthought. The lineup leans on Lyre's non-alcoholic spirits: the namesake Practical Choices pairs Lyre's London Spirit with lemon, molasses and sage, while Great Obsession stacks Lyre's NA gin with an NA verbena aperitif, Earl Grey and non-alcoholic IPA. It is a full bar, not an alcohol-free room, but the NA builds are priced and made like the rest of the menu.
venues.address: 1408 W Magnolia Ave, Fort Worth, TX 76104
signatureDrinks: Practical Choices (Lyre's London Spirit, lemon, molasses, sage)
Great Obsession (Lyre's NA gin, NA verbena aperitif, lemon, Earl Grey, NA IPA)
Fire Adjacent (Black Ginger NA spirit, lemon, honey-ginger, chicory pecan bitters)
La Curandera (Lyre's Spiced Cane, lemon, Earl Grey, orgeat, smoked sea salt)
venues.longDescription:
The Usual has anchored the cocktail end of Fort Worth's Near Southside since well before zero-proof drinking became a category, and the way its non-alcoholic list is presented tells you how the bar thinks about it. Rather than a courtesy line at the bottom of the menu, the NA drinks occupy their own printed section titled "Practical Choices (NA)," named for the drink at its head, and they are built and priced alongside the spirituous list rather than beneath it.

Four builds carry the section. Practical Choices combines Lyre's London Spirit with lemon, molasses and sage. Great Obsession is the most ambitious of the four, layering Lyre's non-alcoholic gin with a non-alcoholic verbena aperitif, lemon, Earl Grey and a non-alcoholic IPA — a stacked, bitter-leaning drink of the kind that usually only exists in alcohol. Fire Adjacent works Black Ginger non-alcoholic spirit against lemon, honey-ginger syrup and chicory pecan bitters, and La Curandera finishes with Lyre's Spiced Cane, Earl Grey, orgeat and smoked sea salt.

This is a working cocktail bar with a full spirits program, not an alcohol-free room, and the NA drinks sit at the upper end of the price list rather than the bottom. What it offers a non-drinking guest is parity: an order that arrives looking and tasting like everyone else's, in a room where the bartending is the reason people come. The bar keeps late hours by Fort Worth standards, running to 2am Thursday through Saturday.
venues.pressQuote: La Curandera, crafted with Lyre's Spiced Cane, Earl Grey tea, lemon, orgeat syrup, smoked sea salt, and rosemary, and the Great Obsession, featuring Lyre's London Dry, lemon, Earl Grey, and non-alcoholic IPA.

venues.name: The Vandy
venues.description: The Vandy, the Grove cocktail bar from the STL Barkeep team, opened in early 2023 and treats zero-proof drinking as a first-class program. Co-owner and beverage director Patrick Gioia maintains a dedicated Zero Proof Beverages menu: four $10 NA cocktails — Crimson Gimlet, Pack Mule In Recovery, Nojito and Alternative Expression — built on BARE Zero Proof, Lyre's and Ritual alternatives, plus Leitz dealcoholized Pinot Noir and Blanc de Blanc and Gruvi NA beers. Feast Magazine observed the menu 'has just as many NA drinks as it does tequila-based cocktails,' and Gioia's staff even teaches classes on making NA and low-proof cocktails.
venues.address: 1301 S. Vandeventer Ave., St. Louis, MO 63110
venues.hours: Mon closed; Tue-Thu 4pm-10pm; Fri-Sat 4pm-12am; Sun closed
venues.longDescription:
The Vandy opened in early 2023 at 1301 S. Vandeventer Avenue in the Grove, giving a permanent home to STL Barkeep, the pop-up cocktail operation that had been mixing drinks at events around St. Louis since 2017. Co-owner and beverage director Patrick Gioia runs the bar with a deliberately understated, hidden-gem aesthetic — exterior signage is minimal, and the building still wears its old John B. Gutmann Construction Co. lettering — while the back bar holds more than 290 whiskeys and bourbons. St. Louis Magazine wrote that The Vandy 'quickly became a must-visit stop for cocktail aficionados' after opening.

Zero-proof drinkers get a dedicated menu here, not a footnote. The Zero Proof Beverages list runs four $10 NA cocktails: the Crimson Gimlet (BARE Zero Proof gin, burnt-off red wine reduction, guar gum and lime), Pack Mule In Recovery (BARE Zero Proof reposado tequila, Lyre's Agave Blanco, red wine syrup, lime and ginger beer), a Nojito built on Ritual's NA rum alternative, and the Alternative Expression, which shakes orange-infused Ritual NA whiskey alternative with lemon and simple syrup. Leitz dealcoholized Pinot Noir and Blanc de Blanc pour at $10, and the beer list adds Gruvi's Juicy IPA and Golden Lager. Sauce Magazine notes the bar 'keeps things fresh with a rotating alcohol-free craft cocktail,' and per St. Louis Magazine, Gioia and his staff 'will even teach a class on making N/A or Low/A cocktails.'

The program has drawn steady press. Feast Magazine built an October 2024 Sober October guide around Gioia, observing that the menu 'has just as many NA drinks as it does tequila-based cocktails' and quoting the beverage director — who doesn't drink 'except to taste my work' — on how far the category has come: 'People are much less judgmental. Alcohol doesn't have to be part of the experience. We've moved beyond that.' Sauce Magazine, meanwhile, points NA-curious drinkers straight here for deep-cut classic cocktails with a zero-proof twist. Expect an understated, whiskey-forward room with happy hour Tuesday through Friday until 6pm, open from 4pm Tuesday through Saturday.
venues.pressQuote: The Vandy is your place to go if you want to dive down the rabbit hole of classic cocktails with an NA twist, as the zero-proof spirits collection runs deep at this establishment.

venues.name: The Venetian Soda Lounge
venues.description: The Venetian Soda Lounge is a 1920s-styled hideaway in Burlington's South End Arts District, built around a family soda recipe: Venetian Ginger Ale, a Burlington brand lost during the Second World War and revived in 2017. The lounge opened on Pine Street in 2022 and prints a full Zero Proof mocktails section — six drinks at $9 to $12, three of them built on CleanCo's alcohol-free gin and whiskey — alongside seven house-made craft sodas at $5, soda floats, creemees and milkshakes. It serves alcohol too, but it is the rare licensed room where the non-alcoholic side is the founding idea rather than an accommodation. Live jazz, low light, closed Monday and Tuesday.
signatureDrinks: The Clean Getaway — CleanCo alcohol-free gin, lemon juice, simple syrup, chilled coupe
Yes-groni — Amaro Lucano non-alcoholic, CleanCo alcohol-free gin, white grape juice, orange
Perp on Maple — CleanCo alcohol-free whiskey, maple cream syrup, bitters, seltzer
Green Light Mule — lemon juice, mint, Venetian Ginger Ale, bitters
Mr. White in the Kitchen — smoked rosemary grapefruit syrup, lime, tonic

naMenuItems.name: Nightcap Confidential
naMenuItems.description: brio flash chill espresso, vanilla syrup, heavy cream, orange bitters

venues.longDescription:
Most zero-proof programmes are retrofitted onto a bar that already existed. The Venetian Soda Lounge worked the other way round: the soda came first. Venetian Ginger Ale was a Burlington brand that disappeared during the Second World War, and the family behind it brought the recipe back in 2017 before opening this room on Pine Street in 2022, in the middle of the South End Arts District. The result is a bar whose identity is a soft drink, which turns out to be an excellent foundation for taking alcohol-free drinking seriously.

The menu prints Zero Proof mocktails as its own section. The Clean Getaway is a straight alcohol-free gin sour — CleanCo gin, lemon, simple syrup, served up in a chilled coupe. The Yes-groni is the negroni answer, with a non-alcoholic Amaro Lucano, CleanCo gin and white grape juice over a large rock. Perp on Maple uses CleanCo's alcohol-free whiskey with a maple cream syrup, bitters and seltzer, which is about as Vermont as a highball gets. Two more work without any spirit substitute at all: the Green Light Mule, built on the house ginger ale with lemon and mint, and Mr. White in the Kitchen, a smoked rosemary grapefruit syrup with lime and tonic. Nightcap Confidential closes the list with flash-chilled espresso, vanilla and cream.

Underneath them sit the seven house craft sodas at $5 — ginger ale, maple cream, strawberry hibiscus, raspberry lime, spiced pineapple, cranberry lemon and cherry lime — which also turn into floats, creemees and milkshakes. The kitchen runs to hot franks and sausages.

The room is licensed, so this is not an alcohol-free venue: wine, beer and amaro are on the list too. What makes it unusual is that a non-drinker ordering here is choosing from the bar's signature category rather than its consolation one. Live jazz most weeks; closed Monday and Tuesday, and it does not open before 4:30pm.
venues.pressQuote: It's going to be a workshop of flavor.
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: Seven Days, Venetian Soda Lounge to Open in Burlington's Soda Plant

venues.name: The Watch Rooftop Kitchen & Spirits
venues.description: A seventh-floor rooftop kitchen and bar atop The Restoration hotel in downtown Charleston, serving modern American Lowcountry food alongside 360-degree views of the historic district. The bar carries a standing set of zero-proof cocktails built with the same approach as its spirited drinks, including options adapted from classics like the Negroni and the French 75. Mocktails on the menu have included the Apple Patch, Beet-i-ful, The Fake ID, and Green Queen.

venues.longDescription:
The Watch Rooftop Kitchen & Spirits sits on the 7th floor of The Restoration hotel at 75 Wentworth Street, with an industrial-chic indoor dining room and two outdoor terraces overlooking Charleston's skyline and harbor. The kitchen serves modern American fare with Lowcountry and global influences across lunch, dinner, and Sunday brunch.

The bar pours a dedicated lineup of zero-proof cocktails, several adapted from classic recipes, and states that its mocktails get the same attention to detail as their alcoholic counterparts. Named non-alcoholic drinks documented on the menu and in local mocktail coverage include the Sechey 75 (a French 75 riff with NA gin alternative, lemon, and rosemary), the Apple Patch, Beet-i-ful, The Fake ID, and Green Queen.
venues.pressQuote: 5 different mocktails all adapted from a classic cocktail like Negroni, margaritas, etc.
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: Leisurely Linds, Best Mocktail Bars in Charleston

venues.name: The Waterman Fish Bar
venues.description: The Waterman Fish Bar is a casual neighborhood seafood restaurant and oyster bar in Charlotte's South End, operating since 2018 with a focus on sustainably sourced, American-caught seafood. Its seasonal second-floor rooftop bar, Topside, seats 80 and offers panoramic views of the South End skyline. The venue offers craft mocktails available at Topside, though no dedicated NA menu or named zero-proof drinks are documented publicly.
venues.address: 2729 South Blvd Ste D, Charlotte, NC 28209
signatureDrinks: Passionstar Martini (Undone No. 2 Not Gin, passionfruit, vanilla, lime) $8
Midnight Swim (lavender and butterfly pea flower simple, lemon, club soda, edible glitter) $6.50
venues.longDescription:
The Waterman Fish Bar opened in October 2018 at 2729 South Boulevard, Suite D, in the South End shopping centre anchored by Harris Teeter, from Paul Manley and Andrew Chapman — the pair behind Sea Level in Uptown, with investors including Dennis Thompson of Firebirds and Viva Chicken and Frank Scibelli of Mama Ricotta's and Yafo. The shared ownership shows on the plate: the Sea Level Salt oyster, farmed at Sea Level on North Carolina's Down East coast, is served here at $2.50 with a house cocktail sauce, shredded horseradish and two mignonettes. Walk in on the ground floor and you see the oyster shucking happening in front of you, under a mural of a salty old seaman. A rooftop terrace called Topside opened in March 2019, seating eighty with a clear view back towards Uptown. The kitchen runs a lobster mac and cheese at $17, citrus salmon at $23.50, a lobster roll served Maine or Connecticut style at $28, and a fried platter of North Carolina mountain trout, oysters and East Coast shrimp at $36.

The non-alcoholic drinks are a recent addition and are printed under their own "Mocktails" heading, which is worth knowing because older coverage of this restaurant predates them entirely. There are two, and they are pitched at opposite ends. The Passionstar Martini ($8) is the serious one, built on Undone No. 2 Not Gin with passionfruit, vanilla and lime — the same drink logic as its sibling restaurant's version, and the vanilla is what gives it the body a martini format needs. Midnight Swim ($6.50) is the cheaper and more theatrical: a lavender and butterfly pea flower simple syrup with lemon and club soda, finished with edible glitter, and butterfly pea flower is the ingredient that shifts colour as the acid hits it. Athletic's Free Wave hazy IPA is $5.50 for anyone who would rather drink beer with oysters. There is no non-alcoholic wine on the list. Service runs from 11am daily, to 11pm on Friday and Saturday.
venues.pressQuote: Known for their fresh seafood and oyster happy hour, The Waterman also offers craft mocktails that are perfect for sipping on their rooftop Topside Bar.

venues.name: The Well Social Club and Kava Bar
venues.description: The Well is an alcohol-free social club and kava bar on West Charleston Boulevard, and it states its position in four words: no alcohol, no pressure. The house line — gather with purpose, drink with intention — describes a room built around weekly events and connection rather than around a counter. The list runs ceremonial-grade kava alongside root tonics, botanical teas and wellness-led drinks, with no kratom listed on its published menu, which is unusual enough in this category to be worth noting. Hours are moderate rather than late: noon to 10pm midweek, to 11pm on Friday and Saturday, and 2pm to 9pm on Sunday. It is a community room rather than a nightlife substitute.
venues.address: 5191 W Charleston Blvd Ste 185, Las Vegas, NV 89146
venues.longDescription:
The Well Social Club sits in a suite on West Charleston Boulevard, several miles west of the Strip, and its distance from the casinos is close to the whole point. Las Vegas is a city organised around drinking to an extent few others are, and the alcohol-free options that exist here have tended to be either casino-adjacent mocktail programmes or specialist kava rooms tucked into strip malls. The Well belongs to the second group but reads differently from most of it: less a bar substitute, more a club in the older sense of the word.

Its framing is explicit and repeated — no alcohol, no pressure; gather with purpose, drink with intention. What that means practically is a room programmed around weekly events that bring people together rather than around maximising covers, and hours that reflect a community space rather than a nightlife venue. It opens at noon Monday through Saturday, closing at 10pm early in the week and 11pm on Friday and Saturday, with a shorter Sunday from 2pm to 9pm. Anyone looking for a 2am alternative should know that this is not that; anyone looking for somewhere to spend a Tuesday evening in company will find it well suited.

The drinks are led by ceremonial-grade kava, sitting alongside root tonics, botanical teas and a wider wellness-inspired list. Kava is the ground root of a South Pacific shrub, prepared as a water infusion; it contains no alcohol, tastes earthy and bitter, numbs the lips on the first mouthful, and is mildly sedative — which is why it functions as a social drink rather than merely as a soft one. It has been drunk communally across Fiji, Vanuatu, Tonga and Samoa for around three thousand years.

One detail is worth flagging in the venue's favour, because this directory flags the opposite so often. Most American kava bars pour kratom alongside kava — a Southeast Asian leaf whose alkaloids act on opioid receptors, which carries real dependence and withdrawal risk, is banned outright in several states, and whose concentrated 7-OH derivatives face federal scheduling action. The Well's published menu lists kava, root tonics and botanical teas, with no kratom on it. For readers whose recovery rules out intoxicants with dependence potential rather than alcohol specifically, that makes this a materially easier room to order in than most in the category. As always, confirming at the counter costs nothing.

venues.name: The Whale: A Craft Beer Collective
venues.description: The Whale is a beloved West Asheville craft-beer bar that, in Beer City, runs one of the deepest non-alcoholic beer programs around: regularly eight or more NA beers — IPAs, stouts, pilsners, and sours — rotating on tap and by the can, plus NA cider from Normandy, kombucha, and sparkling water. It treats 0.5%-and-under beer as a real, curated part of the board rather than a token option, which is exactly the point in a town this obsessed with beer.
venues.longDescription:
The Whale: A Craft Beer Collective opened in October 2017 at 507 Haywood Road in West Asheville, behind Haywood Common, from owners Jesse Van Note and Andrew Ross — two friends who met working together at an Asheville brewery years earlier. Their framing of the project explains the odd name: a craft beer collective was something they spent a long time thinking about, and they wanted to approach it by gathering ideas about what the community was lacking and building a space they all wanted to hang out in. The aim, in their words, was something approachable and friendly that was also an elevated drinking experience. The room has a Scandinavian aesthetic and a large patio, well-behaved dogs are welcome inside and out, and food comes from the Haywood Common kitchen next door rather than a kitchen of its own. It opens at noon most days and 2pm early in the week, running to 11pm on Friday and Saturday.

What makes it relevant to a non-drinker is the collective model itself. The Whale is a bottle shop as much as a bar, built around curation rather than around its own production — which means the non-alcoholic range is chosen the same way the beer is, by people whose job is finding good things rather than selling their own. Its beer listings carry non-alcoholic categories across styles rather than a single token option: non-alcoholic IPA, porter and stout, sour, lager and other beer all appear as distinct categories, which is a broader spread than most dedicated bars manage and reflects how much genuinely good non-alcoholic beer now exists. The caveat is that neither the shop's own site nor its live listings publish the specific products, brands or prices in a readable form, so what is in the fridge on a given day has to be asked about or browsed in person. Given the format, browsing is the point.
venues.pressQuote: regularly eight or more non-alcoholic IPAs, stouts, pilsners and sours; bonus points for the NA cider from Normandy

venues.name: The Winchester
venues.description: The Winchester is a long-running gastropub on the Wealthy Street corridor at 648 Wealthy Street SE, and one of the anchors of that strip. It carries a standing spirit-free cocktail list rather than seasonal improvisation: One For The Honey is built on Ghia aperitif with honey, lemon, strawberry puree and soda, and Kelly Kapowski combines strawberry, vanilla simple syrup and mandarin Jarritos under a marshmallow cold foam. Rotating non-alcoholic beer from Athletic Brewing and rotating High Noon seltzers fill out the range. One practical warning worth carrying: the domain thewinchester.net is not theirs and now serves unrelated casino content. The venue's actual site is winchestergr.com, and reservations run through Toast.
venues.address: 648 Wealthy St SE, Grand Rapids, MI 49503
signatureDrinks: One For The Honey (Ghia aperitif, honey, lemon, strawberry puree, soda)
Kelly Kapowski (strawberry, vanilla simple syrup, mandarin Jarritos, marshmallow cold foam)

naMenuItems.name: Kelly Kapowski
naMenuItems.description: strawberry, vanilla simple, mandarin jarritos, marshmallow cold foam

naMenuItems.name: Athletic Brewing Co.

venues.longDescription:
The Winchester has held its corner of Wealthy Street SE for well over a decade and is one of the fixtures that made that stretch a destination, alongside the independent shops and restaurants filling the blocks either side of it. The format is a gastropub — a full kitchen, a serious bar, and a room that works equally for a weeknight dinner, a weekend brunch or a late drink. It sits a few doors from Chartreuse Sisters and within an easy walk of Sacred Springs and Buffalo Traders Lounge, which together make the Wealthy Street corridor the densest concentration of alcohol-free-friendly venues in Grand Rapids outside the downtown core. Service runs 11am to 11pm Sunday through Wednesday and 11am to midnight Thursday through Saturday, with brunch on Saturday and Sunday from 11am to 3pm.

The spirit-free list is printed alongside the cocktails and built to the same specification. One For The Honey is the more considered of the two standing drinks: it uses Ghia, the bitter Mediterranean aperitif made from gentian root, elderflower, ginger and yuzu, and layers honey, lemon, strawberry puree and soda over it — a build that keeps genuine bitterness rather than falling back on sweetness, which is the failure mode of most zero-proof menus. Kelly Kapowski runs in the opposite direction and is unapologetic about it, putting strawberry and vanilla simple syrup with mandarin Jarritos under a marshmallow cold foam. Beyond the mixed drinks the bar keeps rotating non-alcoholic beer from Athletic Brewing and rotating High Noon seltzers, so there is a straightforward can option as well as a made drink. Earlier menus carried seasonal builds including Ugg Season, a pumpkin, cinnamon, lemon and soda combination, and The Afterlife, made with basil-infused simple syrup, grapefruit, lime and soda; those rotated out, which is a useful signal that the list is actively maintained rather than printed once and forgotten. Two practical notes. First, thewinchester.net has nothing to do with this business and now hosts unrelated casino content — the real site is winchestergr.com. Second, Wealthy Street is scheduled for full reconstruction from 2026 into 2028, so access and parking along the corridor will be disrupted; the restaurants stay open through it, but check before making a special trip.
venues.pressQuote: Ugg Season (pumpkin puree, cinnamon simple, lemon, soda); The Afterlife (basil-infused simple, grapefruit, lime, soda).

venues.name: The Wine Loft
venues.description: The Wine Loft is an upscale wine bar in Charlotte's South End neighborhood offering over 50 wines by the glass and a full tapas menu alongside live music Thursday through Saturday. Their drink menu includes a dedicated zero-proof section described as "sips crafted with the same care, balance, and vibe as our cocktails," featuring named mocktails like the Orange Maple Old Fashioned, Paloma Squeeze, Italian Spritz, and Blood Orange Mule. Staff can also prepare off-menu zero-proof classics including a daiquiri, gimlet, and "No" Fashioned on request.
venues.hours: Mon closed; Tue-Thu 4pm-11pm; Fri 3pm-11pm; Sat 2pm-11pm; Sun closed
venues.longDescription:
The Wine Loft is an upscale wine bar at 2201 South Boulevard, Suite 120, in South End, open since around 2009 and bought in late 2019 by the Menagerie Hospitality Group from longtime owner Sam Kalioby on his retirement. It pours more than fifty wines by the glass alongside a tapas menu — meatballs and burrata, bang bang shrimp, charcuterie slates, and flatbreads including a prosciutto and fig — and it programmes live music from local and national artists every Thursday, Friday and Saturday evening at 7pm, which is what distinguishes it from the other wine rooms in the neighbourhood. It trades Tuesday through Saturday, opening at 4pm midweek and as early as 2pm on Saturdays, with Mondays and Sundays reserved for private events.

The bar keeps a section headed "Mocktails", introduced on its own menu as zero-proof sips crafted with the same care, balance and vibe as the cocktails. There are four: an Orange Maple Old Fashioned, a Paloma Squeeze, an Italian Spritz and a Blood Orange Mule. Two things are worth setting out honestly. First, the venue publishes no ingredients and no prices for any drink on its site — alcoholic or otherwise — so the four names above are all that is documented, and what goes into them has to be asked at the bar. Second, and more surprising for a room built on wine: there is no non-alcoholic wine on the list at all. A wine bar with fifty wines by the glass and no zero-proof bottle is a real gap, and it means a non-drinker here is choosing from four mixed drinks rather than from the thing the venue actually specialises in. Older listings for this bar, including earlier versions of this page, have named several other zero-proof drinks that do not appear on the current menu; treat those as historical.

venues.name: The Zero Co.
venues.description: The Zero Co. is Atlanta's first dedicated non-alcoholic bottle shop, opened in December 2022 in the Poncey-Highland neighborhood by Cory and Malory Atkinson, the husband-and-wife team behind nearby Elemental Spirits Co. The shop grew out of the rapidly growing zero-proof section at Elemental and stocks more than 500 non-alcoholic products — spirit alternatives, de-alcoholized wines, NA beers, and ready-to-drink cans — alongside locally made shrubs, vinegars, bitters, and elixirs. A bar-cart sample station lets customers taste before buying, and the space hosts tastings and events. Carried brands include Ghia, Seedlip, Lyre's, Wilderton, Ritual Zero Proof, De Soi, Three Spirit, Free Spirits, Athletic Brewing, and more. As co-owner Malory Atkinson put it, the goal was a "warm and welcoming" space for all kinds of drinkers and non-drinkers.
venues.address: 626 N Highland Ave NE, Atlanta, GA 30306
venues.longDescription:
The Zero Co. was Atlanta's first dedicated non-alcoholic bottle shop when it opened in December 2022 at 626 North Highland Avenue in Poncey-Highland. It came from Cory and Malory Atkinson, the husband-and-wife team behind Elemental Spirits Co. a short walk away, and it exists because of what happened at that other shop: the zero-proof shelf kept outgrowing the space allotted to it until the obvious move was to give it a building of its own.

The range runs past 500 products and is organised the way a good liquor store is — by what you would actually do with the bottle. Spirit alternatives, de-alcoholized wines, non-alcoholic beer, ready-to-drink cans, aperitifs, adaptogens, and mixers, alongside locally made shrubs, vinegars and bitters for anyone building drinks at home. Ghia, Seedlip, Lyre's, Wilderton, Ritual Zero Proof, De Soi, Three Spirit, Free Spirits and Athletic Brewing are all stocked. A bar-cart sample station is the detail that matters most: non-alcoholic spirits are expensive and wildly variable, and being able to taste before committing to a bottle solves the single biggest problem in the category.

Malory Atkinson described the intent to Atlanta Magazine as a small space meant to feel warm and welcoming for all kinds of drinkers — which is the useful framing, because the shop is not aimed only at people who have quit. It sells to hosts buying for a mixed table as readily as to anyone else.

The shop also carries hemp-derived THC and CBD products and runs a subscription for them called the Cann Club. Worth knowing before you walk in: those are intoxicating and sit on the same shelves as the non-alcoholic drinks. If you are avoiding all intoxicants, the distinction is not obvious from the storefront, and it is worth asking.

Open Tuesday to Saturday from 11am to 8pm and Sunday from noon to 6pm, with local delivery and private events.
venues.pressQuote: It's a lovely, small space that we want to feel warm and welcoming for all kinds of drinkers and non-drinkers.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Malory Atkinson, The Zero Co. co-owner

venues.name: Thevar
venues.description: Thevar is chef Mano Thevar's two-Michelin-star modern South Indian restaurant, now relocated from Keong Saik Road to Mohamed Sultan Road in River Valley. Alongside a wine list of more than 400 labels, its tasting menu offers a fully composed non-alcoholic pairing (S$138) built course by course for teetotallers, sitting beside the S$248 alcoholic pairing. It is a genuine kitchen-driven zero-proof pairing rather than a token mocktail add-on, which is why teetotal diners can follow the full tasting experience. Time Out Singapore sums the kitchen up as modern South Indian cooking with spot-on seasoning, complex spice blends and stellar presentation.
signatureDrinks: Non-alcoholic beverage pairing — a full course-by-course zero-proof flight, S$138 (the alcoholic pairing is S$248)
venues.longDescription:
Thevar is the modern South Indian restaurant of chef Manogren "Mano" Thevar, who trained classically in French kitchens before opening the restaurant in 2019 on Keong Saik Road. It has since relocated to 16 Mohamed Sultan Road in the River Valley area. The kitchen holds two Michelin stars in the Michelin Guide Singapore 2025 and features on the Asia's 50 Best Restaurants list, making it one of the city's most decorated Indian-rooted dining rooms.

The experience centers on a seasonal tasting menu (around S$298) that reworks Chettinad and broader South Indian flavors through refined technique. For drinks, the restaurant runs a deep cellar of more than 400 wine labels with an alcoholic pairing at S$248, and crucially offers a thoughtfully composed non-alcoholic pairing at S$138 for guests who do not drink. Five cocktails are also available at S$28 each. The non-alcoholic pairing is designed to track the courses rather than default to a single juice, giving alcohol-free diners a course-by-course progression alongside the wine drinkers at the table.

The room seats 28 in the main dining hall and adds a chef's table and a private dining room, dressed in terracotta walls and Chettinad-inspired motifs that echo the food. Reservations are essential, and the menu changes seasonally, so the specific non-alcoholic pours rotate with the kitchen's produce.

The non-alcoholic pairing is the reason this room earns a place here rather than the two stars. At S$138 it is priced as a real product — a little over half the S$248 wine flight — and it is poured across the same courses, which is the practical test of whether a kitchen means it. A restaurant that charges three figures for an alcohol-free flight has to defend that price at every course, and cannot fall back on a single juice served twice.

The cooking it accompanies is heavily spiced in ways that reward the format. Chef Mano Thevar trained in French kitchens before opening in 2018, and the menu runs Chettinad and wider South Indian flavours through that discipline: complex masalas, charred meats, and the Mysore-spiced lamb rack that reviewers keep returning to. Spice-forward food is difficult territory for wine and comfortable territory for tea, tamarind, buttermilk and fermented drinks, so the zero-proof flight is arguably the better match rather than the lesser one.

A practical note for non-drinkers: the five cocktails on the list are alcoholic, including a jasmine gin fizz and a coconut negroni, so the pairing rather than the cocktail list is the route through the evening. Book ahead — the main dining hall seats 28, plus a chef's table and a private room, and the menu changes seasonally, so the specific pours rotate with the produce.
venues.pressQuote: Modern South Indian cuisine with spot-on seasoning, complex spice blends and stellar presentation.

venues.name: Thick as Thieves
venues.description: Thick as Thieves is a second-floor cocktail bar on Idaho Street with three named alcohol-free drinks — Queen Pine, the Thieves Root Beer Float and the Northside. The root beer float is the interesting inclusion: it is unapologetically a dessert drink rather than a cocktail imitation, and giving a non-drinker something that is straightforwardly good on its own terms is a different and often better move than approximating a Negroni. Its sibling bar, Bar Please!, occupies the suite above and keeps identical hours, so the building offers two rooms in one trip. Both run to midnight midweek and 1am at weekends, and both open Sundays, which is unusual downtown.
venues.address: 620 W Idaho St Ste 200, Boise, ID 83702
venues.longDescription:
Thick as Thieves occupies the second floor at 620 West Idaho Street in downtown Boise, part of a building that also houses Bar Please! a level above — two distinct bars, same address, same hours, which makes the block unusually efficient for an evening out.

Its alcohol-free list runs to three named drinks: Queen Pine, the Thieves Root Beer Float and the Northside. The Northside is a recognisable cocktail name, a mint-and-citrus build in the Southside family, so the zero-proof version sits in the same tradition as the alcoholic list.

The root beer float deserves attention because it declines to play the substitution game. Most alcohol-free menus are built on imitation — a Negroni without the Campari, a margarita without the tequila — and the drink is measured against something absent. A root beer float is not pretending to be anything. It is simply a good thing to drink, served in a bar, at night, with no apology attached. For a lot of non-drinkers that framing is more comfortable than a drink whose whole identity is what it lacks, and there is a small but real pleasure in ordering something the table might envy rather than tolerate.

The hours are strong: 4pm to midnight through the week, to 1am on Friday and Saturday, and open Sundays until 10pm. Combined with Red Feather a couple of blocks away and Bar Please! directly upstairs, this corner of downtown gives a non-drinker three properly stocked options within a few minutes on foot — which for a city of Boise's size is a genuinely good showing, and largely the product of three years of Temperance Trail groundwork. It is worth naming that causation directly: Boise punches above its size here because one shop decided to organise a scene rather than simply supply it.
venues.pressQuote: Thick as Thieves crafts zero-proof creations that feel indulgent and unique
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: This Is Boise, The Boise Area's Best Non-Alcoholic Drinks and Mocktail Spots, January 2025

venues.name: Third Place Lounge
venues.description: Third Place Lounge opened in January 2024 on Broadway Boulevard, in the former Coda music venue, as a socializing-first hangout where drinking is optional. Owner Amanda Blancarte, a Kansas City West Side native who worked at Crossroads bars Grinders, Nara, and The Cashew, built the room around inclusive, low-pressure gathering: midcentury chairs, upcycled couches, and rope swings hung from the ceiling. The bar runs a full cocktail program alongside a dedicated zero-ABV menu given equal billing, plus seven rotating non-alcoholic beers and coffee. The Pitch's "Drink This Now" column spotlighted its zero-proof cocktails, including the "No'groni, No Problems," the espresso-martini-style "Death Before Decaf," and the "First-time Crush" (non-alcoholic PBR and grapefruit syrup). Named for the sociological "third place" concept, it caters to a mix of sober, sober-curious, and drinking guests.
venues.hours: Mon closed; Tue-Thu 3pm-10pm; Fri 3pm-12am; Sat 2pm-12am; Sun closed
venues.longDescription:
Third Place Lounge opened in January 2024 at 1744 Broadway Boulevard in the Crossroads, in the room that had been the Coda music venue, and its name states its purpose: a third place, the sociologist's term for somewhere that is neither home nor work, where the point is being among people rather than what is in your glass. Owner Amanda Blancarte built it as a socialising-first hangout where drinking is optional rather than assumed, and the room reads that way — The Pitch described it as cute and comfy, like a boho-chic den at your cool cousin's bungalow, fitted with rope swings and soft furnishings rather than a long hard bar. It opens in the afternoon rather than at night, from 3pm Tuesday through Friday and 2pm on Saturday, running to midnight at weekends, which makes it usable for an early evening that does not have to turn into a late one.

The zero-proof drinks are the reason to know about it, and The Pitch devoted a whole column to them in January 2025 under the headline "Drink This Now" — concluding that the thoughtful menu establishes Third Place Lounge as an inclusive spot. Three stand out. No'groni, No Problems ($12) delivers, in the reviewer's words, the herbal and bitter taste without the intensity, which is the hard part of a zero-proof Negroni and the part most bars skip. Death Before Decaf ($12) is a non-alcoholic espresso martini built on a brown sugar simple syrup rather than plain sugar, giving it the body that usually goes missing when the vodka does. First-time Crush ($7) is the cheapest and the most inventive use of an unlikely ingredient — non-alcoholic PBR lengthened with grapefruit syrup for a light effervescence and gentle sweetness. One practical note: the lounge publishes its menus as images dated June 2024, so the printed list online is well behind what the bar is actually pouring. Treat the drinks above as the house style rather than a guaranteed current list, and ask what is on.
venues.pressQuote: The thoughtful menu establishes Third Place Lounge as an inclusive spot.

venues.name: Third Rail
venues.description: Third Rail is a cocktail bar on 20th Street in Dogpatch, known for craft drinks served alongside house-made jerky. Its approach to alcohol-free drinking is unusually practical: rather than confining zero-proof options to a short list, the bar marks individual cocktails on the main menu as available as non-alcoholic, so the same builds are offered either way. Four of the shaken drinks carry that note, including the Yuzu Cute with elderflower, yuzu, pineapple, lemon and mint, the grapefruit-and-elderflower Pawloma, the house Third Rail with lemon, honey and orange bitters, and the smoky Evil Twin. The menu also lists one purpose-built zero-proof cocktail, Dragonfly, made with Ritual Zero Proof tequila, butterfly pea flower, agave, lime and clove.
signatureDrinks: Dragonfly (Ritual Zero Proof tequila, butterfly pea flower, agave, lime, clove)

venues.longDescription:
Third Rail occupies a corner on 20th Street in Dogpatch, a neighbourhood the city's drinking guides tend to skip in favour of the Mission. The Infatuation lists it among the twenty best cocktail bars in San Francisco and notes the bar's other speciality: house-made jerky, cured on site and sold by the bag alongside the drinks. The room is small and dark, with house-made bitters and cordials behind the bar, and it trades late on Friday and Saturday, opening at 2pm and running to 2am.

What distinguishes the alcohol-free offering here is the structure rather than the length of the list. Instead of a separate mocktail section, Third Rail annotates the main cocktail menu, marking individual drinks as available as non-alcoholic so the same build, the same house cordials and the same house bitters go into the glass either way. Four of the shaken drinks carry the note. The house Third Rail is lemon, honey and orange bitters. Evil Twin is grapefruit and lemon with the bar's house-made spicy bitters. Pawloma pairs grapefruit, lime, agave and elderflower with sparkling grapefruit soda, and proceeds from it go to Muttville Senior Dog Rescue. Yuzu Cute combines elderflower, yuzu, pineapple, lemon and mint. Alongside those, the bar keeps one purpose-built zero-proof cocktail on the list year-round: Dragonfly, made with Ritual Zero Proof tequila, butterfly pea flower, agave, lime and clove, which is priced as a standard cocktail with a small supplement if a guest wants a well tequila or mezcal added. The result is that a table can order together from the same menu, which is a materially better experience than being handed a separate card of three sweet drinks. The bar is closed on Mondays, opens at 4pm Tuesday through Thursday and on Sunday, and from 2pm on Friday and Saturday, and takes bookings for parties by email. For Dogpatch, which has very little in the way of a cocktail scene compared with the Mission or North Beach, it is the neighbourhood's most serious drinks room and the only one in the district running a standing zero-proof build.
venues.pressQuote: At this Dogpatch spot, they're serving cocktails alongside homemade jerky.
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: The Infatuation, The 20 Best Cocktail Bars In SF

venues.name: Third Space Brewing
venues.description: Third Space Brewing is a Menomonee Valley craft brewery that makes one of Milwaukee's few genuine house non-alcoholic pours. Its Happy Water, a zero-proof sparkling hop water brewed with the same hop blend as its Happy Place Midwest Pale Ale, pours on tap in the taproom, and a canned Mosaic Lime Hop Water 6-pack is sold through the brewery's shop. It's a beer-first room, but a rare one where non-drinkers get a real, hop-forward option rather than an afterthought.
venues.address: 1505 W St Paul Ave, Milwaukee, WI 53233
venues.longDescription:
Third Space Brewing anchors Milwaukee's Menomonee Valley with a production brewery and a bright, family- and dog-friendly taproom, and, unusually for a beer-first operation, it brews a genuine non-alcoholic pour of its own. Happy Water is a zero-proof sparkling hop water built on the same hop blend as the brewery's Happy Place Midwest Pale Ale, carrying that beer's tropical-fruit, blueberry, and apricot character with none of the alcohol. It has poured on tap in the taproom since 2019 at just a dollar or two a glass, giving designated drivers, pregnant guests, and the sober-curious a hop-forward option in a room built for beer.

The brewery has since packaged the idea for takeaway: a canned Mosaic Lime Hop Water 6-pack, sold through its online shop, is described as a crisp sparkling water with a burst of Mosaic hops and natural lime. Both are true non-alcoholic hop waters rather than low-ABV beers, so a non-drinker can order confidently at the bar or stock the fridge at home. Alongside the beer program, the taproom runs regular trivia, live music, and a seasonal beer garden.

Third Space remains firmly in business in 2026. Its Milwaukee taproom keeps daily hours, its review listings are freshly updated, and the company has been expanding, opening the Innovation Brewhouse restaurant and taproom in Menomonee Falls and launching a new West Allis beer garden at Liberty Heights Park in June 2026. For a visitor mapping out alcohol-free options in Milwaukee, it's a rare stop: a working craft brewery where the house non-alcoholic choice is made with the same care as the beer.

venues.name: 3rd Street Beverage
venues.description: 3rd Street Beverage is a liquor store with a non-alcoholic section far better than the category usually manages — alcohol-removed spirits, non-alcoholic wines and a deep NA beer range, enough to build a home bar from rather than just grab a six-pack. Open from 9am daily, to 9pm Thursday through Saturday.
venues.longDescription:
3rd Street Beverage is, on the face of it, an ordinary liquor store on Bend's 3rd Street commercial strip. Visit Bend's own zero-proof guide calls it a hidden gem, and the reason is the size and seriousness of its non-alcoholic section — a range covering alcohol-removed spirits, non-alcoholic wines and a wide NA beer selection, in a shop where you would expect a single shelf of alcohol-free lager next to the mixers.

That combination is genuinely useful in a way a supermarket aisle is not. Alcohol-removed spirits are the hardest category to buy locally: they are expensive, the quality varies enormously between producers, and most people never get to try one before committing to a bottle. Having a range of them in one room, alongside non-alcoholic wines and enough NA beer to compare styles, makes this the place in Bend to experiment — to work out whether you actually like a hemp-derived botanical spirit or prefer a dealcoholised gin, before building a home bar around the answer.

For visitors, it doubles as the practical stop for a trip. Bend runs on the cooler-in-the-back model — river floats, trailheads, camp evenings — and this is where you fill it if you are not drinking. It opens at nine every morning and runs to nine on Thursday, Friday and Saturday, which covers both the early start and the late restock.

Worth knowing that this is a liquor store, so the non-alcoholic range sits inside a shop full of alcohol; if that is something you would rather avoid, Bend's grocers also carry NA sections, though narrower ones.
venues.pressQuote: even though it's a liquor store, their lineup of alcohol-removed spirits, wines, and n/a beers is seriously impressive

venues.name: Three Dots and a Dash
venues.description: A World's 50 Best Bars honoree tucked in a River North basement, Three Dots and a Dash brings the same obsessive tiki craft to its dedicated mocktail menu that it applies to its rum-forward cocktail program.
