venues.longDescription:
Wallace Dry Goods opened on Lancaster Avenue in Ardmore in early 2024 as the Main Line's first fully non-alcoholic bottle shop, owned by Robin Cummiskey. Note the location before planning a trip: Ardmore sits on the Main Line, west of the city proper, reachable on the Paoli/Thorndale regional rail line rather than by walking from Center City.

The design decision that makes it work is that it looks exactly like a normal bottle shop. Shelves of whiskey, wine, gin and mixers, arranged the way any liquor store arranges them — except that not a single bottle contains alcohol. That staging is doing something specific. Buying alcohol-free drinks usually means a single shelf at the back of a supermarket, next to the soft drinks, and the experience quietly communicates that this is a lesser category. A room laid out like a proper bottle shop, where browsing takes time and the staff can talk about what you are looking for, restores the ritual that people who stop drinking most often say they miss.

The range covers non-alcoholic spirits, beer, wine, cider, mixers, bitters, syrups and ready-to-drink cans, plus barware — so a customer leaves with the same tools to build a cocktail at home that a drinker would. Brands carried include Ghia, Ritual Zero Proof, Cut Above, Seedlip, Lyre's, Athletic Brewing, Abstinence and Mingle Mocktails, which spans the market from bitter aperitifs through spirit substitutes to beer.

Philadelphia Magazine's Best of Philly coverage argued that Cummiskey has created more than a bottle shop — a community hub redefining how people socialise. For a category still largely sold online and shipped in unmarked boxes, a physical shop where non-drinkers can browse, ask questions and taste before committing is a genuinely different proposition.

Open from eleven most days, closing at six and at four on Sunday, and closed Tuesdays.
venues.pressQuote: Robin Cummiskey has created more than just a bottle shop — it's a community hub redefining how we socialize.

venues.name: Walrus Rodeo
venues.description: Walrus Rodeo is a wood-fired restaurant on NE 2nd Avenue in Little Haiti, which describes its own cooking as contemporary wood-fired and is emphatic that it is not just a pizzeria. Dinner is the only service, 5:30pm to 10:30pm seven nights a week. Its documented alcohol-free build is the Rodeo Limonada, which blends strawberry, orgeat and lime — a short, straightforward drink that leans on the almond weight of the orgeat rather than on syrup. RESIDENT covered it in December 2025 and described the approach as easygoing and well made. It is one of the few documented alcohol-free drinks north of the Design District.
venues.longDescription:
Walrus Rodeo occupies a storefront at 5143 NE 2nd Avenue, on the strip of NE 2nd that runs north out of the Design District into Little Haiti — the City of Miami assigns this address to its Little Haiti district. The restaurant is built around a wood-fired oven and describes its own cooking on its site as unique contemporary wood-fired cuisine, with the explicit note that it is not just a pizzeria. Service is dinner only, 5:30pm to 10:30pm, seven nights a week.

The alcohol-free build documented at the restaurant is the Rodeo Limonada: strawberry, orgeat and lime. It is deliberately simple, and the orgeat is what makes it work — almond syrup gives a non-alcoholic drink body and a slightly savoury edge that a straight fruit-and-citrus build does not have, which is why the same ingredient turns up in serious zero-proof lists across the city. RESIDENT documented the drink in its December 2025 survey of twenty Miami venues, writing that Walrus Rodeo keeps things straightforward and calling the result a refreshing, approachable drink and an easygoing way to take part in Dry January while still having something well made. The venue's own site does not publish a beverage list online beyond linked PDFs, and no telephone number is recorded here. Only one named alcohol-free drink is documented, so the programme is graded as real but modest — but it is one of very few verified options in the blocks north of the Design District, where the registry is otherwise thin. The neighbourhood label is worth explaining, because published coverage is inconsistent about it: the venue is variously described as Little River, Little Haiti and Design District in press write-ups. The City of Miami's own neighbourhood assignment for the point at 5143 NE 2nd Avenue is Little Haiti, which is what this entry records, rather than the street-level guess. Practically, the restaurant is a short drive north of the Design District and sits on the same corridor as Boia De and Sunny's, both already carried here.
venues.pressQuote: Walrus Rodeo’s Rodeo Limonada keeps things straightforward, blending strawberry, orgeat, and lime into a refreshing, approachable mocktail.

venues.name: Warka Coffee
venues.description: Warka Coffee is a fully alcohol-free Ethiopian specialty coffee house that opened in August 2025 at 500 New Jersey Avenue NW, in the National Association of Realtors building at E Street, a few blocks from Union Station and the Capitol. It is named after the warka tree, a symbol of shelter and gathering in Ethiopia, and the business runs the whole chain itself: long-term relationships with smallholder growers in Yirgacheffe and Sidama, direct importing, roasting at its own Rockville, Maryland roastery, and serving here. The cafe pours single-origin Ethiopian coffee sorted by taste rather than region - floral and clean, fruit-forward, chocolate and full, espresso - alongside signature drinks, breakfast and lunch. A second service point operates inside Georgetown Law. No alcohol is served.
venues.address: 500 New Jersey Ave NW, Washington, DC 20001
signatureDrinks: Fruit-forward naturals - berry, stone fruit, syrupy body
Chocolate & Full - rounder, sweeter cups built for milk and batch brew
Espresso roast - stable extraction and sweetness under milk
Single-origin Ethiopian filter, roasted to order in Rockville
venues.longDescription:
Warka opened in August 2025 in the National Association of Realtors building at New Jersey Avenue and E Street NW, a few blocks from Union Station and within sight of the Capitol, and PoPville covered the arrival. The name is the point of the place: the warka is a broad fig tree that Ethiopian villages traditionally gather under, a symbol of shelter and connection, and the cafe is built around the idea that coffee is what brings people together rather than what they buy on the way somewhere else. Its own summary of the room is the useful one - specialty coffee, signature drinks, breakfast and lunch, and a space built for actually sitting down.

What makes it unusual among DC cafes is that Warka runs the entire chain rather than buying roasted beans from a wholesaler. The business maintains long-term relationships with smallholder farmers in Ethiopia's Yirgacheffe and Sidama regions, imports directly, roasts in small batches at its own roastery in Rockville, Maryland, and serves the results here. That vertical structure shows up in how the coffee is presented. Rather than organising the menu by region and expecting customers to know what that means, it sorts by taste: floral and clean for washed coffees with jasmine lift and a tea-like finish; fruit-forward for naturals and extended ferments carrying berry and stone fruit; chocolate and full for rounder, sweeter cups built for milk and batch brew; and espresso, roasted for pressure and clarity under milk. The washed Yirgacheffe on the roster carries published notes of jasmine, bergamot and honeycomb. Every bag shows its region, process, roast direction and roast date before you commit, and the same coffees are sold to take home.

No alcohol is served. There are two practical points. First, the hours are early and short - 6.30am opening on weekdays but a 3pm or 4pm close, and only 8am to 1pm on Sunday - so this is a morning and lunchtime cafe, not somewhere to spend an evening. Second, there is a second Warka service point inside Georgetown Law's Capitol Hill campus at 111 Massachusetts Avenue NW, open weekdays only, which is a different and smaller proposition than the main room.
venues.pressQuote: Named after the iconic Warka tree, a symbol of shelter and connection in Ethiopia

venues.name: Watch Hill Proper
venues.description: Watch Hill Proper is a bourbon bar and restaurant in Norton Commons, the walkable development in Prospect north-east of Louisville, and it claims the largest bourbon collection in the country alongside the most extensive American whiskey menu it can assemble. That is exactly the sort of room a non-drinker usually writes off — which is why it matters that it also keeps Spiritless Kentucky 74, the non-alcoholic bourbon made in Louisville, on the menu. The bar runs later than the kitchen, to 11pm midweek and midnight at weekends, and a Tuesday night live music series gives the room a reason to be in it that is not the whiskey list.
venues.longDescription:
There is a particular kind of difficulty for a non-drinker in Kentucky, and Watch Hill Proper is the sharpest version of it. The restaurant sits in Norton Commons, the new-urbanist town centre in Prospect, and its entire proposition is American whiskey: it advertises the most extensive American whiskey menu and the largest bourbon collection in the country, alongside a curated wine list and an elevated dining room. If you are not drinking, this is the room your friends will choose and you will dread.

What makes it workable is that the bar carries Spiritless Kentucky 74 — the non-alcoholic bourbon distilled in Louisville by a company founded by three mothers who wanted their evenings without losing their mornings. Kentucky 74 is made by reverse distillation, taking the alcohol out of a finished distillate while keeping the caramel, vanilla and oak, and it is the single most useful bottle a Kentucky bar can stock for a non-drinking guest. Ordering from it in a room built around the largest bourbon collection in America is a different experience from ordering a soda, and the staff here are used to the request rather than surprised by it.

Two practical notes. First, the bar and the kitchen keep different hours — the bar runs an hour past the kitchen, to 11pm Tuesday through Thursday and midnight on Friday and Saturday, with last kitchen seatings at 9:30pm and 10:30pm respectively — so a late arrival can still sit at the bar. Second, the Tuesday Night Music Series is the best entry point if you want the room without the tasting-flight atmosphere: live sets give the evening a shape that is not the whiskey list. Norton Commons is about twenty-five minutes from downtown.
venues.pressQuote: Watch Hill Proper has Kentucky 74 on the menu.
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: The Zero Proof, Louisville city guide

venues.name: Water Witch Tiki
venues.description: Water Witch Tiki is a 21-and-over tiki bar in the Starland District, a dark, densely decorated room on Bull Street that takes its rum programme seriously and applies the same thinking to the drinks without any. Its menu carries a standing Non-Alcoholic section of four builds at $8 to $9, made with the same house syrups, shrubs and proprietary bitters as everything else — chamomile and green cardamom, tamarind-mango-mint purée, blueberry shrub, a Sichuan-hibiscus bitters the bar makes itself. Three Athletic Brewing alcohol-free beers sit in the cans list at $7. It opens at 5pm midweek and 11am on Friday and Saturday, and closes on Sundays.
signatureDrinks: Fountain of Youth — chamomile tea, green cardamom, sage, lemon, plant-based foam, grapefruit bitters
Tarmarindo — tamarind-mango-mint purée, coconut, toasted rice syrup, pineapple, lime, Thai bitters
Don the Honeycomber — house Sichuan-hibiscus bitters, white grape, peach, honey, orange, ginger, chamomile tea, turmeric, soda
venues.longDescription:
Tiki bars are usually the worst place in a city to ask for something alcohol-free — the whole format is built on rum and volume. Water Witch, on Bull Street in the Starland District, is the exception, and the reason is that its non-alcoholic drinks are made from the same pantry as the rest of the menu rather than from a bottle of juice kept under the bar.

The Non-Alcoholic section runs four drinks and prices them at $8 and $9, a dollar or two under the rum builds. The Fountain of Youth is chamomile tea with green cardamom, sage and lemon, given body with a plant-based foam and finished with grapefruit bitters — the technique a good bar uses on an egg-white sour, applied without the egg or the spirit. The Tarmarindo is the tropical one: a tamarind-mango-mint purée with coconut, toasted rice syrup, pineapple, lime and Thai bitters. The Farkleberry is the simplest and the most refreshing, a house blueberry shrub with grapefruit and soda. The Don the Honeycomber is the show-off — white grape, peach, honey, orange, ginger, chamomile tea and turmeric, built around a Sichuan-hibiscus bitters the bar makes in-house.

Alongside them the cans list carries three Athletic Brewing beers at $7: the Lite lager, Athletic Copper cerveza and the IPA, all listed with their origin in Milford, Connecticut in the same format as the alcoholic cans. Nothing about the presentation treats them as a concession.

Practical notes: the bar is 21-and-over, which rules it out for a family stop; it does not open until 5pm from Monday to Thursday; it opens at 11am on Friday and Saturday and runs to 1am; and it is closed all day Sunday. Starland is a walkable stretch, so it pairs naturally with Kava House ten blocks north on the same street.
venues.pressQuote: Set your sights on Starland's tropical oasis, Water Witch Tiki.
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: Visit Savannah, Where to Find Incredible Mocktails in Savannah

venues.name: Watershed Pub & Kitchen
venues.description: Watershed Pub & Kitchen is a family-owned neighbourhood pub at 10104 3rd Ave NE in Northgate, opened in 2014 by Ben Curran, who wanted a pub for a district that had none and deliberately skipped the dark-bar-and-fried-food model for something family-friendly, fresh and local. Its non-alcoholic section is one of the more developed in Seattle: two zero-proof cocktails — The Honey Pot ($14, Empress 1908 0.0 indigo, lemon, honey) and the Kava Kalada ($8) — plus Best Day kölsch and west coast IPA at $7 each (both under 0.5% ABV) and house specialty drinks including a quinine cold brew ($9) and a peach-rosemary-thyme lemonade ($8). IMPORTANT: the Kava Kalada contains real kava, and the menu separately sells a Goldfinch ginger kava cocktail neat ($10) and an Ablis CBD drink ($9). All three are marked 21+ but carry no printed dosage. It is one of the most accessible venues we list: an ADA-accessible facility with limited-mobility drop-off from 3rd Ave NE, highchairs and boosters, a dog-friendly patio, free parking, and plant-based, gluten-free and alcohol-free options stated as standard.

venues.longDescription:
Watershed opened in 2014 because Ben Curran noticed that Northgate was turning residential and had no neighbourhood pub. His decision then still shapes the place: he ditched the idea of a dark bar with greasy fried food and went for family-friendly, fresh and local instead. "When we opened," he has said, "we were pretty committed to having a greater sense of purpose." It shows in the details more than the slogans. The room has more than twenty taps, an outdoor pavilion with hanging lights and heaters, and dark-wood dividers between tables. The kitchen's best-known thing is an award-winning grilled cheese at $19 — Beecher's Flagship and Appel Farms gouda with caramelised onions — alongside a BLT pie fold at $18, a spicy reuben at $21, burrata at $24, and pão de queijo at $10.

What makes it genuinely valuable is the combination of a real non-alcoholic list and the best accessibility statement of any venue in this city guide. On the drinks: The Honey Pot at $14 is built on Empress 1908's 0.0 indigo with lemon and honey — the colour-changing one — and Best Day's kölsch and west coast IPA are $7 each at under 0.5% ABV. There are house soft drinks made with some thought too, including a quinine cold brew at $9 and a peach, rosemary and thyme lemonade at $8. Two things to order around if you are avoiding all intoxicants. The Kava Kalada at $8 contains real kava — Goldfinch's ginger kava — and the same kava drink is sold neat at $10, while an Ablis CBD drink is $9. All three are age-gated at 21 and sit under the non-alcoholic heading, and none carries a printed dose. On accessibility, the pub publishes what most do not: it is an ADA-accessible facility with limited-mobility drop-off directly from 3rd Ave NE, highchairs and booster seats, guide and service animals always welcome and a dog-friendly patio, free time-limited street parking plus garage and transit-centre parking, and plant-based, gluten-free and alcohol-free options named as standard rather than as an afterthought. For anyone bringing family, that list is the reason to come here.
venues.pressQuote: They list their entire selection of "spirits" on the menu, so you can get creative with your order.

venues.name: Watr at the 1 Rooftop
venues.description: Watr at the 1 Rooftop is the eighteenth-floor bar and restaurant on top of 1 Hotel South Beach, looking straight out over the Atlantic from Collins Avenue. It stays open to midnight on weeknights and 2am on Friday and Saturday, which makes it usable as a late destination rather than a sunset stop. The documented alcohol-free build is the Sunburnt on South Beach, mixing coconut water with mango, lime, mint and Fever-Tree ginger beer — long, hydrating and built for the heat rather than for imitation of a cocktail. The Greater Miami Convention & Visitors Bureau calls it one of Miami Beach's most refreshing ginger beer drinks and highlights the hotel's sustainability-led design.

venues.longDescription:
Watr at the 1 Rooftop sits on the eighteenth floor of 1 Hotel South Beach at 2341 Collins Avenue, and is the hotel's rooftop bar and restaurant, facing the Atlantic. The city's tourism bureau describes the property as a sustainability-inspired spot and treats it as the place to go in South Beach for a spirit-free drink. Opening hours are the practical detail worth knowing: 11am to midnight Sunday through Wednesday, to 1am on Thursday, and to 2am on Friday and Saturday, so the room stays usable long after the beach empties.

The alcohol-free drink documented here is the Sunburnt on South Beach, which mixes coconut water with mango, lime and mint and lengthens it with Fever-Tree ginger beer. It is a long drink rather than a stirred one, and the ginger beer gives it enough bite to hold up against the food. The Greater Miami Convention & Visitors Bureau, the city's official tourism body, lists the drink in its rooftop section and describes it as a light, tropical option that pairs with ocean breezes and sunset views, adding that the bureau considers the hotel the place to go in South Beach for a spirit-free drink. Only one named alcohol-free build is published, which is why this entry is graded as a real but modest programme rather than a serious one. AVIV, the Israeli restaurant from Michael Solomonov and Steve Cook, operates in the same building at street level and is listed separately. One practical note for a first visit: the bar is on the eighteenth floor of the hotel, so access is through the building rather than directly from Collins Avenue, and the hours below are the rooftop's own rather than the hotel's. The hotel switchboard is (305) 604-1000 and the venue posts as @watr.southbeach.
venues.pressQuote: Perched 18 stories above the ocean, Watr delivers one of Miami Beach's most refreshing ginger beer mocktails.

venues.name: Watts & Ward
venues.description: Watts & Ward is a below-ground prohibition-themed cocktail lounge off Moore Square on South Blount Street, and its menu carries a "Zero Proof Cocktails" section headed "all the craftsmanship, none of the spirits". Four builds at $10 run across Mock One's non-alcoholic rum, tequila, gin and whiskey — a Faux Tai with lime and orgeat, My Little Secret on strawberry and lemon, Après Tout against a blueberry shrub and tonic, Village of the Deer with grapefruit and honey — and, more useful than the list itself, the bar will substitute Mock One for the spirit in any house cocktail for $5. That turns a four-drink section into most of the full menu. Open Tuesday to Saturday from four until two in the morning, Sunday from two until midnight. Older directories still credit it with Seedlip; the current menu runs on Mock One.

My Little Secret ($10) — Mock One NA tequila, strawberry, lemon, soda
Après Tout ($10) — Mock One NA gin, blueberry shrub, lime, tonic

venues.longDescription:
Watts & Ward is a prohibition-styled lounge in a basement space off Moore Square in downtown Raleigh — low ceilings, exposed brick, a long list of barrel-aged and classic cocktails. Its zero-proof section is one of the better-built ones in the city, and it is introduced on the menu with a line that sets the tone: all the craftsmanship, none of the spirits.

The four listed builds are structured to cover the spirit categories rather than to offer four variations on a spritz. The Faux Tai is a mai tai built on Mock One's non-alcoholic rum with lime and orgeat. My Little Secret uses the NA tequila with strawberry, lemon and soda. Après Tout runs the NA gin against a blueberry shrub, lime and tonic — the shrub doing the acid work. Village of the Deer is the darkest of them, pairing NA whiskey with grapefruit and honey. All four are ten dollars, several dollars below the bar's full-strength list.

The more valuable part of the programme is the standing substitution policy: any house cocktail can be made with Mock One in place of its spirit for an extra five dollars. That matters because it means a non-drinker at this bar is not choosing from four drinks but from the whole menu, including the classics the bar is known for. Very few venues in the Triangle offer that, and none advertise it as plainly.

One correction worth carrying, if you have read about this bar elsewhere: several non-alcoholic directories still describe Watts & Ward as pouring Seedlip and substituting Seedlip on request, and credit it with an "Espresso MartiNO". The current menu runs on Mock One throughout and that drink is gone. The substitution policy survives — only the brand has changed.
venues.pressQuote: Watts & Ward is slick and stylish, with plush brown leather couches and dark wood galore
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: Indy Week, The Triangle's Ten Best Cocktail Bars, November 2018

venues.name: Waypoint by Bend Brewing Co.
venues.description: Waypoint is Bend Brewing Co.'s cocktail-forward room on the west side, and its spirit-free drinks are built to the same structure as the rest of the list rather than offered as a workaround. Two Pathfinder-based builds anchor the zero-proof section — an E & T and a Negroni — with seasonal zero-proof cocktails rotating in through the year. Open daily to 10pm.
venues.address: 921 NW Mount Washington Dr, Bend, OR 97703
signatureDrinks: Pathfinder E & T — built on Pathfinder non-alcoholic spirit
Pathfinder Negroni — spirit-free negroni on Pathfinder
venues.longDescription:
Waypoint is the newer, cocktail-led room from Bend Brewing Co., out on Mount Washington Drive on the west side of town near NorthWest Crossing. Where the original brewery is a beer hall, Waypoint is a bar — and its treatment of zero-proof drinks is the clearest example in Bend of the difference between accommodating non-drinkers and actually serving them.

The spirit-free options are built with the same structure and balance as the alcoholic list. Both anchors use Pathfinder, a hemp-derived non-alcoholic spirit made in Oregon that is bitter, herbal and aggressively aromatic — closer in character to an amaro than to a soft drink, and one of the few NA spirits with enough backbone to carry a stirred drink. The Pathfinder Negroni is the test case: a negroni is nothing but bitterness, sweetness and botanical weight, so there is nowhere for a weak substitute to hide. The E & T is the longer, more sessionable of the two.

What lifts this above a two-drink token list is that the zero-proof cocktails rotate seasonally alongside the rest of the menu. That means the bar is doing development work on them through the year rather than printing two and forgetting about them, and it means what is pouring in October will not be what was pouring in June.

The room is comfortable and modern with mountain views, and the location makes it a natural stop coming back into town from Tumalo Falls or the Phil's Trail network. Hours run to ten every night, with an earlier Saturday open.
venues.pressQuote: a cocktail-forward bar where ordering zero-proof doesn't feel like a workaround

venues.name: Wendigo Tea Co.
venues.description: Wendigo Tea Co. is a fully alcohol-free (and substance-free) tea bar tucked beside Findlay Market inside Findlay Launch, the market's storefront accelerator. It's the second location for the Cincinnati company founded in 2013 by Sky White, keyboardist of the rock band Foxy Shazam, who fell for rare loose-leaf tea while touring the world. The Elm Street tea bar pours hot and iced service plus what the shop calls "absurd crafted teas," alongside retail tins of Wendigo's curated, organic, hard-to-source blends — signatures like Bigfoot Black Tea, FireBird Chai, Nessy Jasmine Tea and Siren Throat Health Herbal Tea. Tastings are free, the room is casual, and there is zero alcohol on the menu. A separate appointment-only tasting room operates on Warsaw Avenue in East Price Hill.
venues.longDescription:
Wendigo Tea Co. began in 2013 as the passion project of Sky White, keyboardist for the Cincinnati rock band Foxy Shazam, who developed a taste for high-grade tea after more than 2,000 shows touring the world. Named for the mythological monster, the company built its reputation on a deliberately small, curated selection of rare and hard-to-source loose-leaf teas — steering clear of cheap products and flavored blends, and carrying leaf that meets or beats strict organic and EU pesticide standards. "I wanted an entire company of the higher price point stuff and wanted to steer clear of the flavored teas and the cheaper things," White told Cincinnati Magazine. He opened his first brick-and-mortar tasting room in East Price Hill's Warsaw Avenue Creative Campus, then in July 2025 marked the company's 10-year milestone by opening this second storefront at Findlay Launch, Findlay Market's storefront accelerator.

The Findlay Market tea bar is entirely alcohol-free and substance-free — no beer, wine, spirits, kava or kratom, just tea. The counter pours hot and iced service and a rotating list of what the shop bills as "absurd crafted teas," backed by retail tins of Wendigo's signature blends: bold Bigfoot Black Tea, FireBird Chai, Nessy Jasmine Tea, and the throat-soothing Siren Throat Health Herbal Tea (long sold as Siren Vocal Health); the ceremonial-grade Kappa Matcha was listed as sold out as of August 2026. Tastings are complimentary, and the staff — "entirely comprised of artists and musicians," per the shop — will brew samples to help you find a leaf worth taking home. White frames the whole enterprise around shared discovery: "I want it to revolve around how do we all get better at tasting cool teas together and create a culture around that."

Practically, the tea bar sits at 1811 Elm Street, right beside Findlay Market in Over-the-Rhine, open Wednesday–Thursday 10am–3pm, Friday–Saturday 10am–6pm and Sunday 10am–4pm (closed Monday–Tuesday). It's a relaxed, caffeine-forward stop rather than a nightlife alternative — ideal for a sober daytime market visit. Reach them at (513) 827-5555 or @wendigotea; the separate East Price Hill tasting room on Warsaw Avenue runs long-form tastings by appointment.
venues.pressQuote: I want it to revolve around how do we all get better at tasting cool teas together and create a culture around that.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Sky White, founder, quoted in Cincinnati Magazine

venues.name: The Westside Local
venues.description: The Westside Local is a farm-to-table New American restaurant that has anchored Kansas City's Westside neighborhood since 2009, set in a historic exposed-brick, wood-beam space with a grapevine-covered beer garden. Known for seasonal, locally sourced cooking, it also keeps a small but thoughtful named non-alcoholic drink list that runs alongside its beer and wine program. The zero-proof menu, highlighted in a 2023 KCUR guide to KC's mocktail scene, includes house-built drinks like the Aesop (red bell pepper and mango shrub, chamoy, Hellfire Bitters, Perrier, lime) and the Mother Goose (passion fruit, carrot juice, coconut water, lime, salted toasted coconut), plus a dealcoholized sparkling option, the Secco, made with Germany's Fritz Müller alcohol-removed semi-sparkling white. Guests are encouraged to ask their server about the mocktail menu.
venues.longDescription:
The Westside Local has anchored 1663 Summit Street in Kansas City's Westside neighbourhood since 2009, a farm-to-table New American restaurant in an exposed-brick, wood-beamed room with a grapevine-shaded patio that is the reason many people come in warm weather. Its early years were rocky — The Pitch reviewed it in 2009 and could not recommend it, then returned in 2014 to say it had finally become as good as its fans always insisted — and it changed hands along the way, with founding partner McEvers selling his interest to the other partners in 2010 under current owner Brandon Strick. It has since settled into being one of the neighbourhood's fixtures: The Pitch's Tiffany Watts wrote in 2025 that few places hold her heart quite like Westside Local, calling it a go-to for meetings, lunch dates and catching up with friends. The kitchen leans vegetable-friendly without being restrictive — its Portabella Sammy is a beer-and-tempura-battered mushroom with mashed avocado, jicama, Thai-chilli slaw, fresh jalapeño and a vegan sriracha aioli.

The bar keeps four non-alcoholic drinks, and they are built rather than poured. Mother Goose is the most interesting: passion fruit and carrot juice with coconut water and lime, finished with salted toasted coconut — savoury-sweet in a way most zero-proof menus never attempt. Secco is a bottled option, a fruity, fizzy non-alcoholic sparkling from Fritz Müller, the German producer founded in 2009. Aesop is a Perrier-based drink with lime, red bell pepper, mango shrub and chamoy — and it carries one caveat worth knowing before you order, which KCUR flagged when it covered the list: the Bitterman's Hellfire Bitters that give it its heat are made with alcohol. Trace amounts in bitters are below most thresholds, but anyone avoiding alcohol completely should ask for it without, or choose Mother Goose or the Secco instead. Note also that the restaurant's website sits behind a bot-protection challenge that often blocks access, so hours and the current list are easier to confirm by phone.
venues.pressQuote: Westside Local also offers four N/A drinks.

venues.name: Where The Light Gets In
venues.description: Where The Light Gets In is Sam Buckley's Michelin Green Star restaurant on the upper floors of a former Victorian coffee warehouse in Stockport Old Town, serving a single no-choice tasting menu built from hyper-seasonal British produce, much of it grown at the restaurant's own rooftop garden, The Landing. There is no a la carte and no printed menu — the dishes shift day to day with the weather, the tides and the harvest. Crucially for non-drinkers, the wine flight has a genuine equal: a fully non-alcoholic juice flight built in-house from pressed and fermented juices, kombucha and botanical infusions, matched course by course. It is one of the UK's benchmark alcohol-free pairings, treated with the same seriousness as the cellar.
venues.hours: Mon-Tue closed; Wed-Fri 6pm-11pm; Sat 12pm-2pm & 6pm-11pm; Sun closed
venues.longDescription:
Where The Light Gets In opened in October 2017, founded by chef Sam Buckley, and quickly became one of the most talked-about restaurants in the North of England — an acclaimed early Guardian review reportedly brought a thousand bookings in two days. It occupies the upper floors of a converted 19th-century coffee warehouse on Rostron Brow, a steep cobbled lane in Stockport Old Town, and the dining room is a light-filled, loft-like space of exposed brick and timber where the open kitchen sits directly within the room rather than behind a pass. Around 40 guests eat at once, and the team — who also run the nearby Yellowhammer bakery and pottery studio, which supplies both the sourdough and the tableware — treat the whole service as a single shared performance.

The restaurant holds a Michelin Green Star for its sustainability, and its entire philosophy is built around food sovereignty and near-zero waste. There is no choice: guests are served an ever-evolving set menu of contemporary British cooking that bends day to day with the seasons, sourced directly from named farmers and fishermen and from The Landing, a community kitchen garden the team created five minutes away on top of a Stockport car park with Manchester Urban Diggers. Preserving is central to how the kitchen works — pickling, drying, salting and, above all, fermenting extend the seasons and turn offcuts into ingredients, from a soy sauce made with sourdough trimmings to a deep bank of house ferments.

That same fermenting culture is what makes the drinks pairing so unusual. Alongside the tasting menu the restaurant offers three routes — water, a low-intervention wine flight, or a fully non-alcoholic juice flight — and the juice flight is no afterthought: it is composed in-house from seasonal pressed juices, house-fermented kombuchas, non-alcoholic infusions and botanical steepings, each matched to a specific course exactly as the wine is. Because the kitchen already presses, ferments and preserves at this level for the food, the alcohol-free flight carries real acidity and savoury depth rather than reading as sweet fruit juice, and it is repeatedly singled out as the equal of the wine pairing. For anyone eating alcohol-free it turns a full Michelin-level tasting menu into a complete experience with no compromise — one of the strongest non-alcoholic pairings anywhere in Greater Manchester.

venues.name: Whisler's
venues.description: Whisler's is an award-winning craft cocktail bar on the historic East Sixth Street in Austin, opened in a hundred-year-old building that was originally a 1916 grain mill. The interior is candlelit and rustic-chic — described variously as "Gothic" and "castle-like" — with a large back patio, mist system for hot Texas summers, and palo santo greeting guests at the door. The cocktail program emphasizes handcrafted drinks made with fresh, high-quality ingredients. Mezcaleria Tobala, a weekend-only Oaxacan mezcal bar, sits upstairs. Award-winning Thai food from the Thai-Kun food truck is available on the patio (Thai-Kun was named to Bon Appétit's Hot 10 Best New Restaurants list in 2014). Non-alcoholic options are mentioned positively in recent reviews, though specific NA drinks are not publicly named.
venues.longDescription:
Whisler's occupies a hundred-year-old building on East Sixth Street that started life as a 1916 grain mill, and it is one of the most decorated cocktail bars in the city — an eleven-time nominee and five-time winner of Austin's Best Cocktail Bar. The Infatuation's Nicolai McCrary described it as built into an old warehouse that feels more like it belongs in Brooklyn than across from a hotel in East Austin, and called it home to some of the best cocktails east of I-35.

The interior is candlelit and rustic, variously described as Gothic and castle-like, with palo santo burning at the door. The back patio is large and misted for the Texas summer, Thai-Kun serves from a truck on it — the food truck named to Bon Appétit's Hot 10 in 2014 — and Mezcalería Tobalá, a weekend-only Oaxacan mezcal bar, sits upstairs.

For a non-drinker the position is honest but limited. Whisler's produces four seasonal cocktail menus a year and the bartending is genuinely accomplished, so a well-made zero-proof drink is within easy reach of anyone who asks. But there is no published, named non-alcoholic list, and the rotation means anything you are told today may not exist next season.

What makes it work anyway is the shape of the place. Two full bars, a large open patio with a food truck on it, and a rooftop mezcaleria mean the evening does not have to happen at a bar counter — you can eat, move between spaces, and sit outside, which is most of what makes a long night out manageable without drinking. It is also open from 4pm on weekdays and from 2pm at weekends, so it works as an afternoon patio rather than only as a late-night room.

Go for the patio, the food and the room. Ask the bar for something bitter and dry rather than for a mocktail, and expect it to be made properly.
venues.pressQuote: It's built into an old warehouse that feels more like it belongs in Brooklyn than across from a hotel in East Austin.

venues.name: Wicked Rabbit
venues.description: Wicked Rabbit is a downtown Omaha cocktail bar open 5pm to 2am every single day of the week, and it runs the most locally rooted alcohol-free list in the city. Its zero-proof drinks are built on Sandhills Elixir — a small-batch range of non-alcoholic spirits made in Valentine, Nebraska from native prairie botanicals and water drawn from the Ogallala Aquifer — in drinks including the Sandhills Spiced Sour, alongside a Sunset in Wonderland and a Blushing Cow. Using a Nebraska-made zero-proof spirit rather than an imported one is a genuine point of difference, and it means the non-alcoholic order is as regional as the whiskey list. Harney Street puts it inside the walkable downtown cluster.

venues.longDescription:
Wicked Rabbit sits on Harney Street at the edge of Omaha's Old Market, and it is open 5pm to 2am seven days a week — no closed night, no short Sunday. For a reader who does not drink, that consistency is worth as much as any drink list, because the recurring complaint in every city in this directory is that the good alcohol-free rooms are shut when you want them.

What makes the bar genuinely distinctive is what its zero-proof drinks are built on. Sandhills Elixir is a range of non-alcoholic spirits made in small batches in Valentine, Nebraska — up in the Sandhills, the grass-stabilised dune region that covers a quarter of the state — using native prairie botanicals and water from the Ogallala Aquifer beneath it. It is a genuinely local product rather than a bottle shipped in from London or Cape Town, and Wicked Rabbit builds with it: the Sandhills Spiced Sour takes its name from it directly.

That matters more than it might sound. Most alcohol-free drinking anywhere in America runs on the same four or five imported brands, which makes the category feel generic wherever you order it. A bar pouring a zero-proof spirit distilled three hundred miles up the road is offering a non-drinker the same thing a whiskey drinker gets from a local rye — a sense that the drink belongs to the place. The rest of the list, the Sunset in Wonderland and the Blushing Cow, carries the bar's own naming rather than being labelled generically as mocktails.

Omaha's local drinks writing has documented all three by name, which is the sourcing behind this entry.

Practically: Harney Street puts it within a few minutes' walk of Wilson & Washburn, Mercury, Anna's Place and Châm Pang Lanes, so downtown Omaha is genuinely walkable for an evening built around alcohol-free drinking rather than a single stop.
venues.pressQuote: Known for its moody lighting and exclusive ambiance, they craft incredible zero-proof drinks like Sunset in Wonderland, Sandhills Spiced Sour, and Blushing Cow with the same passion as their signature cocktails.
venues.pressQuoteSourceLabel: Hurrdat ONE, 10 Best Zero-Proof & Nonalcoholic Bars in Omaha, Nov 18, 2025

venues.name: Wicked Sisters
venues.description: Wicked Sisters is a neighbourhood tavern at 3845 Falls Road on the edge of Hampden and Woodberry, in the building that was McCabe's until a fire closed it. Charlie Gjerde took the space over in June 2015 and reopened it in late October 2016, naming it for his wife Lori Gjerde and Carrie Podles, who are real-life sisters. The white-brick, 150-seat room serves comfort food without pretension — Baltimore Magazine noted there is no concerted attempt to pass for healthy. Its drinks list carries two non-alcoholic headings. "Non-Alcoholic Spirit-Free Cocktails" holds Peachy Keen ($12, Lyre's NA tequila, Crodino, peach purée, lime, pineapple), Sunset Fizz ($13, Mionetto NA prosecco, Crodino, Mionetto spirit-free aperitivo, blood orange) and Gingerberry Snap ($11, Lyre's NA tequila, blueberry syrup, ginger, lime, soda). A second heading, "Non-Alcoholic Spikeable Options", lists a seasonal Wicked Lemonade at $8 and a Caramel Apple Mule at $9, either of which can take a spirit for $5 — useful for a mixed table. The list rotates.

venues.longDescription:
Wicked Sisters occupies 3845 Falls Road at the edge of Hampden and Woodberry, in the building that was the old Hampden bar McCabe's until a fire closed it. Restaurateur Charlie Gjerde took the space over in June 2015 and reopened it in late October 2016, naming it for his business partners — his wife Lori Gjerde and Carrie Podles, who are real-life sisters. The room seats about 150 in a stark, fresh white-brick minimalism with bare wood tables, exposed ductwork and photographs of local landmarks. Baltimore Magazine's verdict on the food captured the appeal exactly: there is zero pretension here, no concerted attempt to pass for healthy — just say yes to the crab mac and cheese — and no talk of local sourcing. It opens at 11am on weekdays and 10am at weekends, running to 10pm later in the week.

The non-alcoholic drinks are split across two headings, and the second one is the interesting idea. "Non-Alcoholic Spirit-Free Cocktails" holds three built drinks: Peachy Keen ($12) combining Lyre's non-alcoholic tequila and Crodino with peach purée, lime and pineapple; Sunset Fizz ($13), the most elaborate, layering Mionetto's non-alcoholic prosecco and spirit-free aperitivo with Crodino and blood orange; and Gingerberry Snap ($11), Lyre's tequila with blueberry syrup, ginger, lime and soda. Separately, a heading called "Non-Alcoholic Spikeable Options" lists a seasonal Wicked Lemonade at $8 and a Caramel Apple Mule at $9, each of which can have vodka, rum or tequila added for $5. That is a genuinely good piece of menu design for a mixed table: everyone orders the same drink and only some of them take the spirit, so nobody has to explain themselves. Note the list rotates — several drinks that appeared on earlier menus, including a Hampden Punch, are no longer served.
venues.pressQuote: There's zero pretension here, no concerted attempt to pass for healthy, and no talk of local sourcing.

venues.name: Wild Child
venues.description: Wild Child (Wild Child Libations) opened in July 2023 in downtown Shawnee, Kansas, the brighter, more casual sister bar to James Beard-nominated Drastic Measures next door. Owner Jay Sanders was named a James Beard semifinalist for Outstanding Professional in Cocktail Service in 2025 — the first Beard recognition for a Shawnee bar — and Bon Appétit named Wild Child one of the best new bars in America in 2024. Its zero-proof programme is the deepest in the Kansas City metro and unusually self-sufficient: Sanders distils his own non-alcoholic spirits in house, having worked out it was cheaper than buying them in. Nine drinks run $10 to $12, including an N/A Negroni built at full strength and then stripped of alcohol by atmospheric distillation, Up & At Em (Aplos Arise, clarified green apple, malic acid, pandan leaf), Bearing Fruit (de-alcoholised alpine liqueur, kiwi, Seedlip Garden, lime), Best Medicine (smoked-tea-infused NA ginger liqueur, local pear, maple foam) and an N/A Espresso Martini on espresso-infused non-alcoholic amaro. Food is a small-plates menu built by Jeff Workman.

venues.longDescription:
Wild Child opened on 15 July 2023 at 11022 Johnson Drive in downtown Shawnee, next door to Drastic Measures, the James Beard-nominated bar it is the vibrant sister to. Owner Jay Sanders called it a drinkery for everyone, and the room backs that up — Bon Appétit named it one of the best new bars in America in 2024, with Emily Farris describing consistently kind staff, warm wood panelling and more than fifty pretty plants that make anyone feel welcome in this world of pure imagination. Food comes from Jeff Workman, who built the small-plates menu of savoury popcorn, salads and charcuterie. In January 2025 Sanders was named a James Beard semifinalist for Outstanding Professional in Cocktail Service, the first Beard recognition for a Shawnee bar.

The zero-proof list here is the most technically serious in the Kansas City metro, and the reason is that Sanders makes his own non-alcoholic spirits in house — he worked out it was cheaper to buy distilling equipment and produce them himself than to keep buying them in. Nine drinks run $10 to $12. The N/A Negroni ($12) is the clearest demonstration: a full classic negroni built with alcohol and then stripped of it by atmospheric distillation, which is a genuinely different process from assembling a substitute. Up & At Em ($12) uses Aplos Arise with clarified green apple, malic acid and pandan leaf. Bearing Fruit ($10) combines a de-alcoholised alpine liqueur with kiwi, Seedlip Garden, lime and a vegan foamer. Best Medicine ($11) infuses a non-alcoholic ginger liqueur with smoked tea and finishes it with maple foam, and the N/A Espresso Martini ($12) uses an espresso-infused non-alcoholic amaro rather than coffee liqueur. Palomania and Sound & Fury ($10 each) go the acid-and-vinegar route with chipotle and habanero respectively. Sanders's own summary of the project is the best line written about the category locally: non-alcoholic, he said, doesn't mean it has to suck. Open Tuesday to Sunday; reservations run 90 minutes and cap at six people.
venues.pressQuote: Consistently kind staff, warm wood paneling, and more than 50 pretty plants will make anyone feel welcome in this world of pure imagination.

venues.name: Wild Heaven Beer
venues.description: Wild Heaven Beer was founded in 2010 by Georgia natives Nick Purdy and Eric Johnson, making it one of the state's earliest craft breweries. After opening its flagship in Avondale Estates in 2014, the company launched this West End location in late 2019 inside the Lee+White development, directly on the Atlanta BeltLine's Southwest Trail. The 21,000-square-foot brewery and restaurant pours its own craft beer, housemade cocktails, and Georgia farm wines, with food and coffee on site. For non-drinkers, Wild Heaven brews its own zero-proof option: Near Wild Heaven Non-Alcoholic IPA (0.5% ABV), poured on draft alongside the full-strength lineup. Made with Trident, Centennial, and El Dorado hops for grapefruit, pine, and citrus notes, it is also 99.9% gluten-free. Copresident and brewmaster Eric Johnson and head brewer Josh Franks developed the beer, which Atlanta Magazine highlighted in 2025.

venues.longDescription:
Wild Heaven Beer was founded in 2010 by Georgia natives Nick Purdy and Eric Johnson, making it one of the state's earliest craft breweries. The West End location opened in late 2019 inside the Lee+White development at 1010 White Street SW, directly on the BeltLine's Southwest Trail — a 21,000-square-foot brewery and restaurant with food and coffee on site, joining the Avondale flagship and a Toco Hills location.

The reason it earns a listing is that Wild Heaven brews its own non-alcoholic beer rather than stocking someone else's. Near Wild Heaven is a non-alcoholic IPA under 0.5% ABV, built with Trident, Centennial and El Dorado hops for grapefruit, pine and citrus, and it is poured on draft beside the full-strength lineup as well as sold in six-packs.

The production detail is genuinely unusual. Rather than brewing a normal beer and stripping the alcohol out — the standard industrial method, which tends to strip flavour with it — Wild Heaven ferments with a maltose-negative yeast strain that simply cannot consume most of the sugar, so very little alcohol is ever created. The beer is then treated with a gluten-reducing enzyme to 99.9 percent gluten-free and pasteurised to remove live yeast. That last step matters for shelf stability, and it is the reason a low-alcohol beer can sit safely on a shelf at all.

Drinking a house-brewed NA beer on draft in the taproom that made it is a different experience from being handed a bottle from the back of the fridge, and there are only a handful of breweries in the country where it is possible. Copresident and brewmaster Eric Johnson developed the beer with head brewer Josh Franks, and Johnson told Atlanta Magazine in 2025 that it was a project the two of them put a lot of energy into — which, for a beer that by design contains almost no alcohol, is the point.
venues.pressQuote: It is a project that me and my head brewer, Josh Franks, put a lot of energy into.
venues.pressQuoteAttribution: Eric Johnson, Wild Heaven copresident & brewmaster

venues.name: Wild
venues.description: Wild — stylized "W!ld" — is a Bali- and Southeast Asia-inspired coffee bar, cocktail lounge and legal hemp dispensary on North Shepherd Drive in the Heights, opened in February 2022 by cousins Adyson and Andrew Alvis. The plant-filled room works as a specialty coffee bar by day, pouring beans roasted with Heights roaster Tenfold Coffee, and becomes a full bar at night alongside an in-house "Bud Bar" stocked with hemp-derived CBD products. Its drink program was created by Laurie Harvey and Kris Sowell of Ladies of Libation and centers on hemp-infused elixirs: the Pink Loco with raspberry, coconut, citrus and mint; the coffee-based Skywalker OG; and Marfa Days with hibiscus, Topo Chico, citrus and tropical fruit. Readers avoiding all intoxicants should note these carry 20mg of full-spectrum CBD, and the venue will not mix CBD with alcohol. The Montrose second location has closed.

venues.longDescription:
Wild — stylized "W!ld" — is a Bali- and Southeast Asia-inspired coffee bar, cocktail lounge, and legal hemp dispensary at 2121 N. Shepherd Drive in Houston's Heights, opened in February 2022 by cousins Adyson and Andrew Alvis. The plant-filled space runs as a specialty coffee bar by day, pouring beans roasted in collaboration with Heights-based Tenfold Coffee, and turns at night into a full bar plus a "Bud Bar" in-house dispensary stocked with legal, hemp-derived CBD products — tinctures, gummies, flower, and pre-rolls — carrying THC at 0.3% or under.

Alongside standard beer, wine, and cocktails, Wild built its drink program around hemp-infused elixirs created by Laurie Harvey and Kris Sowell of Ladies of Libation, with Kevin Dikdan serving as food and beverage director for Wild Concepts. The alcohol-free cocktails can, if you wish, be combined with either alcohol or CBD — but not both, as the venue does not mix CBD with alcohol. Named non-alcoholic options include the Pink Loco (raspberry, coconut, citrus, mint, 20mg full-spectrum CBD), the coffee-based Skywalker OG (in-house vanilla syrup infused with 20mg full-spectrum CBD), the Marfa Days (hibiscus, Topo Chico, citrus, a house blend of mixed tropical fruits, "electric dust," sea salt, and 20mg full-spectrum CBD), and the Orange Crush.

A second Wild location in Montrose has since closed — the company's own Locations page now lists that address as closed. As of mid-2026 the original Heights flagship remains open daily from 8am to midnight.
venues.pressQuote: Wild brings a one-of-a-kind experience, whether you're looking to grab a coffee or cocktails with friends or looking for a product to help with muscle pain or relaxation.

venues.name: Wild Sage Bistro
venues.description: Wild Sage Bistro is a long-running fine-dining room on West 2nd Avenue in downtown Spokane, serving contemporary American food seven nights a week from 4pm to 9pm. Its bar prints three named mocktails as a fixed part of the drinks list: a Spicy Sage Lemonade of freshly squeezed lemon with jalapeño and organic sage leaves, a caramelised Pineapple Mojito with fresh orange, organic mint and soda, and a Blackberry Limeade built on muddled blackberries with fresh lime and simple syrup. All three are constructed from produce rather than mixers, which is what distinguishes a restaurant that has thought about the category from one that keeps a bottle of grenadine.

venues.longDescription:
Wild Sage has been one of Spokane's better dining rooms for years — contemporary American cooking on West 2nd Avenue downtown, white tablecloths without stiffness, and a bar that does more than pour wine for the tables. It earns its place here on the strength of three drinks that are printed on the menu, named, and made from ingredients rather than from bottles.

The Spicy Sage Lemonade is the house signature and the one that gives the restaurant its name back: freshly squeezed lemon, jalapeño and organic sage leaves, which lands somewhere between a shrub and a sour and carries real heat. The Pineapple Mojito is built on caramelised pineapple — an actual technique, not a syrup — with fresh orange, organic mint and soda. The Blackberry Limeade muddles whole blackberries with fresh lime and simple syrup and lengthens it with soda.

What those three have in common is that a cook has to make them. Caramelising fruit, muddling berries and slicing jalapeño are kitchen jobs, and a restaurant that sends them out on a Tuesday has committed real labour to the non-alcoholic list. That is the practical test this directory applies to a fine-dining room, and it is a harder one to pass than printing the word "mocktails" at the foot of a page.

The restaurant was picked out by Trending Northwest among a small set of Spokane rooms doing genuinely inventive work in the category, alongside The Boneyard — good company for a dining room rather than a bar.

One of the easiest venues in this guide to actually visit: Wild Sage serves 4pm to 9pm every day of the week, including Sunday and Monday, when several of Spokane's better alcohol-free lists are dark.

venues.name: Wilder
venues.description: Wilder is a three-story, 150-seat restaurant, bar, and private-event space that opened in March 2022 in Rittenhouse, inside the former Philadelphia Academy of Social Dance building at 2009 Sansom Street. It was founded by husband-and-wife team Brett Naylor and Nicole Barrick, who designed the eclectic interior and brought on executive chef Bob Truitt (formerly of Corton, Buddakan, and Morimoto). Because Barrick and Naylor are both sober, Wilder maintains one of the most developed non-alcoholic drink programs in Philadelphia, with zero-proof cocktails on both the regular and happy-hour menus, each around $10. Named alcohol-free options include Doctor's Orders (lapsang souchong, ginger, honey), One Last Question (sarsaparilla, vanilla, lime), and Top Shelf Bubbles (a spritz of orange, lime, and TÖST NA Sparkling). Visit Philadelphia and Philadelphia Magazine have both spotlighted the venue's zero-proof offerings.

venues.longDescription:
Wilder occupies the former Philadelphia Academy of Social Dance building at 2009 Sansom Street in Rittenhouse — three storeys, a hundred and fifty seats, a restaurant, bar and private event space that opened in March 2022. It was founded by the husband-and-wife team Brett Naylor and Nicole Barrick, who designed the eclectic interior themselves and brought in executive chef Bob Truitt, formerly of Corton, Buddakan and Morimoto.

The reason its non-alcoholic programme is one of the most developed in Philadelphia is straightforward: both owners are sober. Philadelphia Magazine made the same connection, noting that because Barrick and Naylor do not drink, they have put considerable effort into the N/A list. That fact changes the economics of the decision. For most restaurants a zero-proof menu is a market bet with an uncertain return; for owners who will be drinking from it every night they work, it is simply the house list.

What that produces in practice is the detail worth knowing: zero-proof cocktails appear on both the regular menu and the happy-hour menu, at around ten dollars. Happy hour is where non-drinkers are usually quietly excluded — the discounted list is almost always beer, wine and well drinks, so the person not drinking pays full price while everyone around them pays less. Extending the discount to the alcohol-free drinks is a small, unglamorous decision that almost nobody makes.

The named options include Doctor's Orders, One Last Question and Top Shelf Bubbles, the last of which points at the other thing non-drinkers routinely lose: something to raise at a toast. A three-storey venue that hosts private events and keeps a proper alcohol-free sparkling option is solving for weddings and birthdays, which is where the absence is felt most.

Open from half past eleven in the morning until ten at night, seven days.
venues.pressQuote: Wilder's owners Nicole Barrick and Brett Naylor are both sober, so they've made a considerable effort in crafting an N/A drinks list. Honestly, there's no bad order here.

venues.name: Wildflower
venues.description: Wildflower is the restaurant of the Gravity Haus Denver hotel on Navajo Street in Highland, serving locally-sourced, carefully curated dishes and listed in the Michelin Guide. Its non-alcoholic list is short but built with the same technique as the cocktails: Westword describes the El Corazón as melding coconut, lemon, orgeat and hoja santa, the Mexican herb whose flavour runs close to root beer, and the Padre Pio as combining chamomile honey, lavender and lemon. A sparkling green tea rounds out the list. The pairing of a hotel restaurant with an outdoor-focused hospitality group means the room draws a mixed crowd, and the drinks are priced and presented alongside the full-proof list rather than tucked away. Wildflower serves dinner Monday to Saturday and closes on Sundays.

venues.longDescription:
Wildflower sits at 3638 Navajo Street in Denver's Highland neighbourhood, inside the Gravity Haus Denver hotel — the newest property from a hospitality group built around outdoor recreation and long-stay membership rather than conventional hotel guests. The restaurant describes its own cooking as locally-sourced and carefully curated, and has been listed in the Michelin Guide for Colorado. It is a dinner-only room, opening at 4:30pm Monday through Saturday and closing entirely on Sundays, which makes it a destination booking rather than a drop-in.

The non-alcoholic list is deliberately short, and Westword's January 2026 survey of Denver's non-alcoholic options described it as "a short but stellar list". What distinguishes it is that the drinks are composed rather than assembled. The El Corazón is built on coconut, lemon and orgeat with hoja santa, the large-leafed Mexican herb whose aromatics sit somewhere between sassafras and anise — Westword characterises it as having "flavors akin to root beer" — which gives the drink a savoury, rooty length that fruit-forward alcohol-free drinks generally lack. The Padre Pio takes the opposite direction, combining chamomile honey with lavender and lemon into something floral and gentle, and there is a sparkling green tea for anyone who wants tannin rather than sweetness. All three sit on the same drinks list as the cocktails and wine, which is the practical test of whether a program is real: a guest can order from it without asking the server to check with the bar. For a mixed table in the Highlands where one or two people are not drinking, Wildflower is one of the few Michelin-listed rooms in Denver where the non-drinkers get something made for them rather than a soda gun. The restaurant's connection to Gravity Haus also means the bar is used to serving people coming off a day in the mountains who would rather not start drinking at 5pm.
venues.pressQuote: El Corazón melds coconut, lemon, orgeat and hoja santa, a Mexican herb with flavors akin to root beer; while the Padre Pio features chamomile honey, lavender and lemon.

venues.name: Wildseed
venues.description: Wildseed is a 100% plant-based restaurant on the corner of Union and Buchanan in Cow Hollow, serving a Mediterranean-leaning menu of shareable plates, mezze, and pizzas. Its bar treats non-alcoholic drinks as a real category rather than an afterthought: a dedicated mocktail list and a "0% ABV" refreshments section appear right on the cocktail menu. Zero-proof builds lean on NA spirits and house ingredients — fresh juices, shrubs, kombuchas, and homemade extracts — including a Negroni AF (NA Ritual gin, melati amaro, house aperitivo, orange), a Love & Lavender (NA Ritual gin, lavender, butterfly pea tea, Wilderton citrus, fee foam), an NA Spicy Pineapple Margarita (jalapeño-infused NA tequila, pineapple, lime, Tajín), and a Serenity Spritz. Lower-effort options include Charcoal Lemonade, Koast Kombucha, house sodas, and cold-pressed juices, making it a dependable spot for an alcohol-free dinner out.

venues.longDescription:
Wildseed is a fully plant-based restaurant and bar on the corner of Union and Buchanan Streets in Cow Hollow, opened on 20 September 2019 by restaurateur Adriano Paganini's Back of the House group in the former Belga space, a four-year-old Belgian sausage-and-beer restaurant that Paganini closed in order to make the switch. Blair Warsham, previously with the group at the fried chicken sandwich shop The Bird, opened the kitchen. The menu is Mediterranean-leaning and entirely vegan — shareable plates, mezze, grain bowls and pizzas — and the room is bright and glassy rather than earnest, which is part of why it reads as a night out rather than a health errand. Paganini told SFist at the opening: "I wanted to create this restaurant because I work across the street and this is a concept that I felt was missing in this neighborhood."

The bar was built on the same logic as the kitchen, and non-alcoholic drinks are a named category on the cocktail menu rather than an afterthought. The mocktail list runs $14 and currently comprises the Negroni AF (non-alcoholic Ritual gin, melati amaro, house aperitivo and orange), Love & Lavender (non-alcoholic Ritual gin, lavender, butterfly pea tea, Wilderton citrus and fee foam), the NA Spicy Pineapple Margarita (jalapeño-infused non-alcoholic tequila, pineapple, lime and Tajín), the Serenity Spritz (non-alcoholic Lucano amaro, strawberry, lemon and ginger kombucha) and the Blueberry Brightside (ginger, blueberry compote, lemon, kombucha and mint). A separate "0% ABV Refreshments" section covers lower-effort ordering: a blueberry matcha latte with oat milk at $11, charcoal lemonade with agave and activated coconut charcoal at $8, a rotating seasonal soda at $8 and Koast Kombucha in mango yuzu or lemon ginger at $10, plus cold-pressed juices at $10. The practical upshot is a full dinner-and-drinks evening with no alcohol anywhere on the table and no negotiation with the server.
venues.pressQuote: I wanted to create this restaurant because I work across the street and this is a concept that I felt was missing in this neighborhood.

venues.name: Wildwood Kitchen & Bar
venues.description: Wildwood Kitchen & Bar at Pavilions builds its blood orange margarita on CleanCo alcohol-free tequila rather than leaving the spirit out, which is the difference between a margarita and a limeade. There is also a lychee Moscow mule mocktail and Heineken 0.0 for anyone who wants a beer in hand. Stocking a named non-alcoholic tequila is a purchasing decision with only one purpose — serving people who are not drinking — and it means the drink keeps the agave note that makes a margarita taste like one. It is out at Pavilions in Arden-Arcade rather than downtown, and opens from 10am at weekends for brunch.
signatureDrinks: Blood orange margarita - CleanCo alcohol-free tequila
venues.longDescription:
Wildwood Kitchen & Bar sits at Pavilions, the upmarket shopping centre in the Arden-Arcade area east of downtown Sacramento. It is a neighbourhood restaurant rather than a destination bar, and its non-alcoholic drinks are better than that description suggests.

The blood orange margarita is built on CleanCo alcohol-free tequila. That single choice separates it from most restaurant mocktails. A margarita without tequila is citrus and sugar — pleasant, but not the drink, because the agave is what gives it its slightly vegetal, earthy backbone. A non-alcoholic tequila substitute keeps that note, and blood orange adds a bitterness that ordinary orange liqueur would not. The result is recognisably the same drink rather than an approximation of one.

The lychee Moscow mule takes the easier route, and sensibly so: a mule is ginger beer and lime with vodka contributing almost no flavour, making it one of the few classics that survives the substitution almost intact. Adding lychee gives it a floral sweetness that suits the format. Heineken 0.0 covers the third case — the guest who does not want a project, just a cold beer.

Between those three, Wildwood covers the range of what a non-drinker actually orders: something crafted, something familiar, something simple. Few restaurants manage all three.

The food side matters here too, more than at the bars in this guide. Wildwood is a full restaurant, which means the evening has an anchor other than drinking — courses arrive, the table talks about the meal, and the pace is set by the kitchen rather than by rounds. For anyone finding the early weeks of not drinking difficult in bars, restaurants with a real zero-proof list are the easiest reintroduction to going out, and a place stocking CleanCo tequila is doing more than the token Shirley Temple most restaurants consider sufficient.

The hours are broad and family-friendly — 11:30am to 9pm early in the week, to 11pm midweek and Saturday, from 10am at weekends for brunch. Being out at Pavilions rather than downtown, it serves a residential part of the metro that the K Street and Midtown venues do not reach.
venues.pressQuote: This art-filled bistro in the Pavilions shopping center has one of the most welcoming patios in town

venues.name: Williams & Graham
venues.description: Williams & Graham is a Prohibition-style speakeasy in Denver's LoHi neighborhood, entered through a hidden door disguised as a bookcase in a faux bookstore. Bartender Sean Kenyon opened it in 2011 with partner Todd Colehour, and it has become one of the country's most decorated bars — a James Beard nominee for Outstanding Beverage Program, a World's 50 Best Bars listee and a Tales of the Cocktail Spirited Awards winner. Alongside its classics it keeps a standing "Temperance" section of seven zero-proof options priced $8 to $12 and built on serious non-alcoholic spirits: Staycation (The Pathfinder, chocolate and roasted corn, Coco Lopez), My Bitter Clementine (Earl Grey, clementine shrub, Giffard aperitif, lemon), Heat Seeker (Three Spirit Nightcap, Amass Riverine, lime, gochujang and tea, Coco Lopez, cucumber), Imposter Syndrome (Giffard aperitif, The Pathfinder, Giesen zero-proof sauvignon blanc, strawberry rose living vinegar), Windowshopper, Passionate Earl and three house-made sodas. A second outpost operates at Denver International Airport.

venues.longDescription:
Williams & Graham opened in 2011 at 3160 Tejon Street in Highland, behind a working bookstore front whose bookcase swings open into the bar. Sean Kenyon opened it with partner Todd Colehour, and it went on to become one of the most decorated cocktail bars in the United States: a James Beard nominee for Outstanding Beverage Program, a World's 50 Best Bars listee, and a Tales of the Cocktail Spirited Awards winner, with a shelf of awards running from 2012 onward. A second outpost operates inside Denver International Airport on Pena Boulevard. The bar is open every night from 5pm to 1am and does not take the speakeasy conceit much further than the door: inside it is a working, high-volume classic cocktail bar with a kitchen, not a performance. The bar sits behind a working bookstore front on Tejon Street, and the door is the only piece of theatre; a kitchen runs alongside the bar and the room takes reservations as well as walk-ins.

The non-alcoholic drinks are listed on the same menu under the heading Temperance, one of five sections alongside Seasonal, Classic, Beers and Wine, and the section is unusually deep for a bar of this vintage. Seven options are current. Staycation ($12) builds The Pathfinder against chocolate and roasted corn with Coco Lopez. My Bitter Clementine ($12) is the one the press names most often, a spare blend of Earl Grey, clementine shrub, Giffard aperitif and lemon. Heat Seeker ($12) is the most aggressive, Three Spirit Nightcap and Amass Riverine with lime, gochujang and tea, Coco Lopez and cucumber. Imposter Syndrome ($12) layers Giffard aperitif, The Pathfinder and Giesen zero-proof sauvignon blanc over a strawberry rose living vinegar. Windowshopper ($12) uses Amass Riverine with lime, berry tea, Okinawa brown sugar and mint. Passionate Earl ($10) runs Earl Grey with green apple, passion fruit, lime and mint. House-made sodas in blackberry sage, ginger beer and orange cream are $8. Westword's January 1, 2026 round-up highlighted My Bitter Clementine and Staycation by name. At $8 to $12 the section is also priced below the full-proof list rather than at parity, which is unusual for a bar of this stature and makes it a realistic place to spend an evening not drinking.
venues.pressQuote: Behind a bookcase, this iconic LoHi speakeasy (which also has an outpost at DIA) serves timeless cocktails and “temperance drinks” without the booze.

venues.name: WLVS Den Kava Lounge
venues.description: WLVS Den Kava Lounge is a fully alcohol-free, Star Trek-themed kava bar in the Spring Valley/Southwest area of Las Vegas at 5447 S Rainbow Blvd E7. Billing itself as "Nevada's only licensed kava bar" and the "unofficial Las Vegas Star Trek headquarters," it serves traditional Pacific Island kava in shells, quads, jugs and Tanoa bowls alongside botanical specialty teas and functional, non-alcoholic mocktails (no alcohol is served). The venue is the current branding of the lounge that originally launched in 2019 as 9th Island Kava Lounge at this same address; it now operates as WLVS Den Kava. It positions itself as a safe, relaxing space for socializing and celebrating sobriety, hosting monthly Star Trek watch parties, live music, board games and karaoke. Open daily from noon (until midnight Sun-Thu and 2 AM Fri-Sat), with a daily 3-6 PM happy hour offering half-off shells and teas.
